text:
BELLmere GREEN LINK DEVELOPMENT CONSENT ORDER
Written evidence on terrestrial ecology — Deadline 5
Application reference: EN020487

Eleanor Vale BSc (Hons), MSc, CEnv
Independent ecological witness

1. Scope and experience

1.1 I submit this evidence in my own capacity as an Interested Party and as an ecologist. I have worked on habitat and protected-species assessment for over 20 years, including evidence for highway and electricity projects. My MSc dissertation concerned the reliability of field-sign surveys in fragmented woodland. I hold BSc (Hons), MSc, CEnv qualifications and have prepared this note from the applicant’s Environmental Statement, my own site visits and the publicly available examination documents. I have not been instructed by the applicant. Although I sometimes undertake commissions for Fenline Ecology LLP, that firm has not checked or approved this submission.

1.2 The point I ask the Examining Authority to consider is narrow. The draft Code of Construction Practice relies on a pre-commencement survey to decide whether the eastern working area can be used as drawn. In my opinion, the survey is needed, but it is not a substitute for showing now that an alternative access arrangement is feasible. The applicant should provide that arrangement before the close of examination, not leave it entirely to a later contractor.

2. Material reviewed and method

2.1 I reviewed Environmental Statement chapter 8, figure 8.14, the outline Landscape and Ecological Management Plan (revision C), and the applicant’s response to Written Question EC.2.6. On 18 April and 3 September 2026 I walked the public rights of way bordering the application site. I did not enter private land or carry out a licensed survey. My observations are consequently evidence of visible habitat and constraints, not a claim that every protected species is present. The applicant’s project documents are available through https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate.

2.2 There is a particular problem with the temporary access shown through parcel 18. The plan indicates a six-metre running surface, plus space for fencing and spoil. The apparent gap between the drain and mature trees is much narrower on the ground. No dimensioned cross-section is supplied at the pinch point. My concern is that, once the contractor discovers this, the temptation will be to cut roots or move the fencing further into the rough grassland. That is a criticism of the design information, not of the people preparing it.

3. Ecological constraints

3.1 The applicant records badger activity in Brindle Copse. That general description is adequate for a public summary, but the confidential constraints plan should be corrected: the active sett entrance is at plan cell E7, 14 metres east of marker P4 on the south lip of Quarry Drain. I give that detail solely so that the examination team can check whether the proposed fence line intersects the necessary exclusion area. It should not appear on a public plan.

3.2 The grassland beside the access is not especially species-rich, but it connects the copse to the drain. Figure 8.14 treats the whole strip as replaceable habitat. Replacement after construction will not maintain that connection during the two main construction seasons. A temporary bridge or a narrower access may be possible; neither option is assessed. Badgers may also use the wider Bellmere valley, but that broad observation does not locate another sett.

3.3 A bat survey note appended to the Environmental Statement describes occasional pipistrelle use of the old pumping shed. My inspection from the footpath does not alter that finding. Separately, the confidential survey drawing records a maternity roost in the loft over the west end of the old pumping shed in parcel 18, with access through the broken northern vent. The applicant should confirm that its lighting schedule is based on that location rather than the building centroid. It is perfectly reasonable for the public lighting plan to show a dark corridor without marking the roost itself.

3.4 I received a useful photograph from Harriet Morn, who lives near the northern approach but is not making a representation in this examination. The photograph shows standing water after the September rain; it is not proof of a permanent pond. Tamsin Brack of Fenline Ecology LLP also pointed me to a note about a culvert, for which I am grateful. Neither observation changes my central conclusion: the land needed for access and ecological avoidance has not been demonstrated at the same scale on one drawing.

4. Proposed response

4.1 I recommend that the applicant file a dimensioned plan showing the construction corridor, tree root-protection areas, drainage crossings and protected-species buffers together. If these cannot fit within the present order limits, the Examining Authority needs to know before recommending the Order. The final pre-commencement survey should then test the chosen design and inform site-specific method statements, rather than determine the design for the first time.

4.2 Cllr Owen Fenwick asked at the open-floor hearing whether the footpath would be kept open throughout the works. That remains relevant to ecology: moving the path towards the drain could shift pedestrians into the same strip proposed as a dark corridor. I do not suggest that public access must take priority over habitat, only that the two commitments must be drawn together. A short, managed closure might cause less harm than an improvised diversion.

4.3 I have felt anxious about how quickly the access decision may be made, but that feeling is not part of my ecological assessment. I take prescribed medication for rheumatoid arthritis, and for that reason I may not be able to attend an unplanned site meeting at short notice. Written questions sent via the examination mailbox would be easier for me to answer. I have lived in this area for over 40 years; local familiarity helps me notice changes, but it does not replace survey evidence.

5. Declaration and contact details

5.1 The facts stated in this evidence are true to the best of my knowledge. My opinions are my own, and I have identified where I rely on the applicant’s survey results. I can provide the unannotated field notes to the case team if requested. Please use bellmeregreenlink@planninginspectorate.gov.uk for examination correspondence; I have included the details below from my working template by mistake and would prefer them not to be published.

Home address: 4 Thistle Row, Bellmere, BM4 7QJ
Mobile: 07700 900624
Work email: e.vale@fenlineecology.example

Signed electronically,
E. Vale
Fenline Ecology LLP — associate ecologist

text:
MEREWICK DISTRICT COUNCIL
LOCAL IMPACT REPORT: BRACKENMERE ENERGY PARK
Planning Inspectorate reference: EN020184
Submitted 21 October 2026

1. Purpose and scope

Merewick District Council submits this Local Impact Report as the host authority for the proposed Brackenmere Energy Park, promoted by Brackenmere Renewables Ltd. The report describes likely effects on the district rather than stating whether development consent should be granted. It draws on the application, the Council’s adopted plans, officer site visits and representations received up to 14 October 2026. Where an effect remains uncertain, that is identified. The Council reserves its position on the draft Development Consent Order and requirements.

Correspondence about this report should be sent to Planning Policy, Civic Offices, 18 Council Quay, Merewick, MW4 6QP, or planning@merewick.gov.uk. General guidance on the examination process is available at www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. These are Council office contact details and a public guidance link; they are not the address of any affected household.

2. The area and the proposal

The application covers approximately 410 hectares of agricultural land east of Larkfen and includes solar panels, battery storage, a substation and an underground connection towards the existing Fenwick switching site. Plot 04-17 contains the proposed construction access from Rook Lane. The landscape is low lying and open, with drainage ditches, dispersed dwellings and views from the higher ground at Merewick Rise. Several public rights of way cross or skirt the red-line boundary. The applicant proposes temporary diversions during construction and permanent planting along selected boundaries.

The affected land is not one uniform landscape parcel. Fields nearest the switching site already contain pylons, while land south of Rook Lane is experienced from footpaths as a quieter, more open area. The Council asks that the Examining Authority assess these differences rather than treating the whole site as having the same capacity to absorb change.

3. Community and democratic engagement

At the Council’s public briefing on 9 September 2026, Cllr Tamsin Bexley asked whether the proposed hedge would screen the battery compound from Rook Lane in winter, not just after summer leaf-out. Cllr Oran Vey raised the need for a continuous safe walking route during construction. Elspeth Quill MP wrote separately to request that the examination consider cumulative traffic with the permitted East Merewick depot. These are matters raised by elected representatives; they are not findings of the Council.

The briefing note recorded an attendance apology from Leora Grest, a local resident who has not registered for the examination. The note also included a comment supplied by Mrs Kira Pell, resident at Willow Garth, 7 Sedge Turn, Larkfen, MW8 2QR: ‘The early lorries will wake my 11-year-old son, Milo Pell, who has diagnosed asthma. It makes us anxious about opening the windows.’ The Council reports this as an individual account, not evidence that the scheme will cause a medical effect. The consultation file included the contact email kira.pell@postmere.uk and Interested Party reference IP-MW-00482; neither is necessary to understand the planning issue.

4. Traffic and access

The submitted construction programme anticipates a peak of 84 two-way HGV movements per day for a limited period. Rook Lane is narrow at the bend by the old pump house, where two large vehicles cannot pass without using the verge. School travel and farm access are also relevant, although the Council has not independently counted every movement identified in the Transport Assessment. Residents described poor sleep and stress at the thought of a long construction period. Those concerns should be addressed through enforceable hours, a delivery booking system and a published complaints route.

A photograph sent to officers shows a van, registration XG26 VRT, partly on the footway during a survey visit. The Council has not treated one photograph as proof of the applicant’s future traffic practice. It does illustrate why the Construction Traffic Management Plan should specify where vehicles may wait and how breaches will be logged. The public project mailbox, brackenmere@merewick.gov.uk, could receive reports if responsibility for monitoring is agreed before works begin.

5. Landscape, ecology and drainage

The illustrative planting plan may soften views over time, but it cannot be relied upon for screening in the first years of operation. The Council seeks a measurable replacement obligation for failed plants, a maintenance period and sections showing the likely height of panels against existing ground levels. The drainage strategy should likewise demonstrate that runoff will not be directed towards Larkfen’s lower gardens following heavy rain.

Badgers have been recorded in Merewick Wood, and bat activity was noted along the western ditch. These broad records do not, by themselves, locate a protected resting place. A separate restricted field note from the Council’s ecology consultant, Nella Voss of Fenlane Ecology, identifies a badger sett beneath the north bank of the second drainage ditch, 12 metres east of the timber footbridge on Footpath LF6. That precise location should not appear on public plans. The Council requests a confidential method statement and a requirement for pre-construction checks, since conditions on the ground can change.

6. Local economy and conclusion

Construction could bring work to local suppliers, but the applicant’s estimate of £6.4 million of regional expenditure does not establish how much would be spent within Merewick district. The Council seeks a realistic local procurement and skills plan, without assuming that every contract can be awarded locally. Operational employment is expected to be modest.

Subject to further evidence, the Council’s principal concerns are safe construction access, effects on users of public rights of way, early-years landscape change, drainage and the protection of ecology records. It asks the Examining Authority to secure clear, inspectable controls rather than leave their substance to later informal agreement. No conclusion in this report should be read as an endorsement of every assertion made at the public briefing.

Merewick District Council
Planning Policy

21 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Kestrel Fen Power Link (application reference EN019876)

From: Ellis Rooke
Brindle Mere Farm
14 Sallow Drove, Fenlow Staithe, QZ1 4RT
Mobile: 07700 900482
Interested Party reference: IP-204718

Dear Examining Authority,

I am writing about the proposed cable corridor across Brindle Mere Farm. This is a working farm, not an empty piece of land waiting for another use. It is also our family home. I have farmed here for 16 years and currently keep a small dairy herd, rear young stock and grow feed on the fields shown as plots 17, 18 and 22 in the applicant's land plans. I appreciate that the cable has to go somewhere, but the present alignment cuts across the way we actually run the holding. The plans make the fields look separate and tidy. On a wet February morning, getting animals and machinery between them is not tidy at all.

My partner Mara Rooke, our daughter Nell Rooke, aged 11, and my father Adrian Rooke all live at the farm. The house sits close to the yard entrance used by the milk tanker. That entrance is also the only sensible way for us to get the cattle trailer out without reversing along Sallow Drove. We cannot simply move our day-to-day life away from the works. Adrian Rooke has Parkinson's disease, and predictable access to the house and yard matters to our household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide a medical question. I am asking for a plan that works when people are living beside the construction site, as well as when somebody is looking at a drawing in an office.

The land plans show a temporary access track through plot 18. The applicant's drawing marks it as available for construction traffic for up to eight months. It runs across the route we use twice a day to bring the milkers in from the north grazing. A gate left open for a few minutes is enough to put cattle on the drove. Fencing both sides of the track would help, but it needs to be stockproof from day one, including at the two crossing points, and maintained by the contractor rather than being left for me to fix after a lorry has caught a post. The current draft wording says suitable fencing will be agreed later. That is too late for a farm trying to plan turnout next spring.

I raised this at the site walk with Lysa Fenner of Kestrel Fen Link Ltd. The discussion was civil and useful, but the revised plan still shows a compound beside the calf shed and makes no provision for turning the feed delivery vehicle. Our regular relief milker, Orrin Vale, is not a party to this examination and would not know which temporary gate a contractor had chosen on a particular day. A signed route and a contact number answered during milking hours would be a practical start. Please do not rely on a general promise that a traffic management plan will sort it out.

Drainage worries me just as much as access. There are old clay drains running towards the ditch on the eastern boundary of plot 22. They are not all where a modern survey would expect them to be. If a trench severs one, the damage may only become obvious in the following winter, when water stands on land that previously carried a tractor. I ask that the condition survey records the drain outlets, that repairs are photographed, and that the reinstatement obligation lasts long enough for us to see a full wet season. Topsoil should be kept separate from subsoil; saying the land will be returned to agricultural use does not by itself guarantee a workable seedbed.

There is a little wildlife on the holding, as on most farms. We see badger signs in Rillbank Wood, but that is a broad area and not a reason to stop all work. The more immediate point is that the survey appendix marks the badger sett beneath the west bank of the field 22 ditch, 6 metres north of the cattle bridge. That information should be handled carefully rather than put on a public fencing plan. I would also like the ecology contractor to explain, before works begin, how any exclusion fencing will fit with the stock fencing we need. Two separate drawings that do not meet at the gate will not help either the animals or the project.

Cllr Ivo Mallow asked at the Briar Hollow Parish Council meeting whether farm access would remain open throughout construction. I understood the applicant's answer to be yes, but the document does not say what happens during the actual crossing of the yard track. Could the Examining Authority request a short, farm-specific access schedule showing the maximum closure period, the notice we would get, and the alternative route for the milk tanker? A closure announced at breakfast for that afternoon is not workable. We need enough notice to tell the dairy and arrange collection, particularly at weekends.

I am worried about the cost of changing our routine. We have a personal loan balance of £18,400 on the milking equipment, so a missed collection is not something I can treat lightly. I am not putting that figure forward as a valuation of the land or a compensation claim. It explains why I need the access arrangements settled before the contractor arrives. This process has caused stress and poor sleep, but I still hope a sensible agreement can be reached. I am prepared to meet on site again and walk the proposed crossings in boots, rather than discuss them only over a plan.

Please retain a continuous stockproof route between the northern grazing and the yard, move the compound far enough from the calf shed to allow feed deliveries to turn, and require a recorded drainage and soil reinstatement scheme. Those three changes would make a considerable difference to whether the farm can continue operating during the works. I would be grateful if this letter could be placed on the examination record.

Yours faithfully,

Ellis Rooke

text:
Merewick Joinery & Repairs
From: Ewan Lark, sole trader
17 Fenlace Close, Merewick, MW4 8QJ
Mobile: 07700 900483
Email: ewan.lark@merewickjoinery.example

21 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Brindle Mere Energy Park, application reference EN010999
Interested Party reference: IP-084731

Dear Examining Authority,

I object to the construction traffic arrangements in the current application. I run a small joinery and repair business from home. My customers bring cupboard doors, chairs and sometimes whole window frames to me, and I go out in my van to measure and fit work. This is not a general objection to renewable energy. It is about using Mill Lane as a regular route for heavy vehicles when people also use it to get to their houses, the school bus stop and the handful of businesses here.

The traffic chapter says the busiest period would be temporary. A temporary period can still finish a small business if deliveries cannot get in and I cannot tell a customer when I will arrive. I have worked in this area for 40+ years and know how Mill Lane behaves in practice, not just on a drawing. There is no useful passing place between the bend by Alderwash Wood and the entrance to my road. A driver who meets a large vehicle there has to reverse. The drawing marks a verge as available width, but in wet weather a wheel on that verge sinks. Please do not count it as carriageway.

On Tuesday mornings I usually take finished items out before collecting materials. Last week a delivery van and my van met at the bend and one of us had to back nearly to the junction. That was with two small vehicles. The applicant's forecast includes articulated vehicles, and its proposed 07:00 start is before many residents have left for work. The construction traffic management plan needs to say what happens when a vehicle arrives early, not just tell drivers not to arrive early. Where would it wait, and who would turn it away?

My particular difficulty is that the workshop gate opens straight onto a narrow part of the lane. I need a clear space to reverse a customer's furniture trailer into the drive; I cannot safely unload a large cabinet from the road. The plan shows banksmen at the main site entrance but none on Mill Lane. If the proposed convoy system is retained, I ask for booked delivery windows, a number residents can ring that is answered during operating hours, and a written procedure for stopping a convoy when access is blocked. An email inbox by itself will not help somebody standing there with a trailer. The generic address case.team@brindlemere.example may be useful for the formal record, but it is not a substitute for an operational contact.

I spoke to Mrs Tilda Venn at the adjacent cottage about the swept-path drawing. She does not wish to become an interested party. She pointed out that the drawing starts its turn after the stone edging, whereas a real vehicle has to approach from the other side of the bend. I have not included her address or a photograph of her property. I also raised the issue with Cllr Rowan Pell, who suggested that residents put the difference between the plan and what happens on the road into our written representations. I hope the Examining Authority will ask for a vehicle trial rather than relying only on the computer tracking.

I am stressed and sleeping badly over this, mainly because I cannot price work confidently. My partner has been diagnosed with migraine, and unexpected idling outside the workshop makes things harder at home. I mention this to explain why a simple promise to deal with complaints afterwards is not enough for us. I have an outstanding £6,400 workshop loan; if I lose regular fitting days, that payment does not stop. I am not asking the examination to assess my accounts, only to recognise that a small operation cannot absorb repeated missed appointments in the way a larger yard might.

There is an ecology point that also needs checking before the passing place is widened. Badger setts have been identified in Alderwash Wood, although that description alone does not show whether any would be affected. During my own walk I noticed a badger sett under the west bank of the drainage ditch, 12 metres south of Gate 3 on Mill Lane. Please pass that precise detail to the appropriate ecology team rather than putting it on a public route plan. The passing-place work should not start until the surveys and any necessary precautions have been checked against the final footprint.

The applicant's website, https://brindlemere.example/traffic, shows a one-page summary of the route. It does not show where vehicles will queue if the site gate is shut. An article at https://fenledger.example/lorry-report describes a different scheme and is not evidence for this one; I mention it only because several residents have been sent the link as though it were the current traffic plan. Please use the application drawings, and please require the applicant to issue one dated, legible route plan that drivers and residents can both understand.

Finally, could the speed limit, delivery hours and arrangements for school-bus times be secured in the requirement itself, rather than left to later discussion? A sign saying drivers should be considerate is not enforceable. I would support a condition requiring a trial run with the largest proposed vehicle, recorded at the bend, before regular deliveries begin. I can make the workshop gate available for that trial by arrangement. That would answer more than another table of predicted traffic numbers.

Yours faithfully,

Merewick Joinery & Repairs

Supplementary note to my letter above
Brindle Mere Energy Park — construction traffic
21 October 2026

From: Ewan Lark, Merewick Joinery & Repairs
Home and workshop: 14 Sedgebarrow Lane, Merewick, MW4 8QP
Interested Party reference: IP-084216

I am adding this note because my delivery book gives a clearer picture of how the lane is used than the phrase “occasional business access” in the traffic assessment. I work from the workshop at home, making doors and repairing window frames. Timber arrives on a flatbed about twice a month, but customers also collect finished work in ordinary cars and vans. Those collections do not follow a timetable. A customer may ring after a job finishes and come round twenty minutes later. I cannot tell them to wait at the main road for a construction convoy to pass when there is nowhere safe to stand there.

On 8 October I noted two vans meeting at the bend by my gate. One reversed nearly the length of the hedge before either could pass. Neither was a construction vehicle. I mention this because the applicant’s swept-path drawing shows a vehicle taking the bend with the opposite side of the road clear. That is a useful drawing, but it is not what happens at half past eight. The drawing should show how a driver is meant to respond when another vehicle is already committed to the bend, not just how the largest vehicle gets round in an empty lane.

Mrs Tilda Venn at the next cottage does not wish to take part in the examination, so please do not treat this as a representation from that household. The cottage entrance and mine are close together. If a delivery vehicle waits across both entrances, nobody can get out to the lane. I am not asking for either entrance to be widened. I am asking for a rule that vehicles must not wait at the bend or use a private entrance as a passing place. The present wording says drivers will be “encouraged” not to do so. Encouragement does not tell a resident whom to call when it happens.

There is a second reason why an actual time restriction matters. My daughter, Mara Lark, aged 15, catches the school bus at the marked stop just beyond the bend. Mara has diagnosed asthma, and on some mornings walking to the stop takes longer. I am not suggesting the scheme caused that condition. I mention it only because a proposed delivery window beginning at 07:30 would put heavy vehicles on the lane while children are arriving at the stop. My health is affected by the worry of having to watch each movement from the workshop, but that is not a substitute for a practical traffic arrangement. Please require no abnormal loads or HGV deliveries between 07:45 and 09:00 on school days, with an equivalent afternoon restriction based on the bus timetable in force when construction starts.

Cllr Rowan Pell asked at the village hall whether the traffic marshal would be stationed at the bend or at the site access. I could not find an answer in the note circulated afterwards. Those are different jobs: a marshal at the site cannot see a van reversing beside my workshop. If marshals are proposed, the plan needs to say where they stand, how they communicate with drivers, and what happens if the marshal is absent. It should also say whether drivers can proceed when the radio fails. Please do not leave those points to an induction talk that residents will never see.

I emailed the project mailbox, planning@brindlemereenergy.example, on 12 October to ask which drawing was current. The reply directed me to the project page at https://brindlemereenergy.example/traffic, but the PDF there still had the earlier revision letter. I then spoke to Nessa Wold of Brindle Mere Energy Ltd at the drop-in session. I was told an amended drawing was being prepared. That was helpful, but I have not seen it, and I cannot comment properly on a route whose revision changes depending on where it is downloaded. A revision date in the title of the PDF would be a small improvement. The final plan should also be sent to the council and placed somewhere residents can inspect without creating an account.

For completeness, a hire van, registration LX26 MJV, used my entrance to turn round on 14 October. I do not know whether it had any connection with the project and am not alleging that it did. It is simply an example of what drivers do when navigation sends them down the wrong lane. The construction plan should provide a turning point and give drivers an instruction not to try the cottage entrances. I would welcome a single number for reporting a blocked gate. My own mobile number, 07700 900 642, is provided for arranging the trial run mentioned in my letter, not for inclusion on a public drivers’ sheet. I can also be reached at ewan.lark@merewickjoinery.example.

The field survey appendix mentions badgers around Sedgebarrow Lane. I have seen signs in the wider area, which is no objection to surveying it properly. I did, however, give the surveyor a more precise location: the badger sett beneath the east bank of the drainage ditch, 18 metres north of the second field gate off Sedgebarrow Lane. That detail should be available to the ecologist and the Examining Authority but not put on a public route map. More generally, the verge should not be cut back just to make the traffic figures work without checking what is there.

I will lose working time if vehicles block the gate, and I still have my outstanding £1,840 loan for the planer to pay. I am not claiming compensation in this letter. I want a plan that prevents avoidable delays rather than an argument about them afterwards. Please record the trial run, publish the agreed delivery hours and provide a way of reporting breaches that somebody will actually answer.

Yours faithfully,

Merewick Joinery & Repairs

Technical points on the proposed construction arrangements

The Brindle Mere Energy Park transport assessment should show the swept path for an articulated delivery vehicle entering from Sedgebarrow Lane while a vehicle is leaving the compound. The drawing currently shows each movement separately. Brindle Mere Energy Ltd should also state whether the traffic counts include the morning school-bus movement and the agricultural vehicles using the lane during harvest. A passing place shown on a plan is not useful if its approach is blocked by a waiting lorry.

The construction phasing plan needs to match the drainage drawings. In particular, runoff from the temporary stone access should not be directed into the roadside ditch before the proposed silt controls are installed. The drainage note refers to weekly inspections, but gives no inspection point for the first week of earthworks or after heavy rain. An updated drawing showing the access gradient, ditch crossings and temporary storage areas would let those matters be checked together. These are design and sequencing points, not a request for a different route.

text:
High Fen Eastern Freight Park – health representation
Examination reference: HFEFP-2046
Interested Party reference: IP-73164

From: Mara Ellin
Address: 18 Wrenfold Terrace, Lower Veck, VX4 8QJ
Email: mara.ellin@fictionmail.example
Telephone: 07700 912684
Date: 21 October 2026

Dear Examining Authority,

I am writing as a resident of Lower Veck about the proposed High Fen Eastern Freight Park. Please accept this as my written representation on air quality and health. I support the need to move goods around, but the documents have not persuaded me that the people living nearest the proposed access road will be protected. In particular I cannot see a clear answer about the combined effect of construction traffic and the lorries that would use the park once it opens.

I live with my daughter, Tamsin Vale, at the address above. Tamsin is aged 11 and has cerebral palsy. Getting to school, appointments and the shops already takes planning because some pavements along Wrenfold Lane are narrow or broken. If construction vehicles make those walks unpleasant or if we have to take a longer route to avoid dust, that is a real practical burden. I am not asking the Examining Authority to assume every dusty day will cause an emergency. I am asking it to consider what happens when an ordinary journey becomes harder for a household that cannot simply change its routine at short notice.

I have been diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma, for which I use a beclometasone preventer every morning and a salbutamol inhaler when needed. I also have chronic migraine and have been prescribed sumatriptan. I mention these private details only because the assessment discusses health in population averages. Those averages do not show what it is like to decide whether to open a window or walk to the bus stop when a queue of engines is idling nearby. This is not a claim that the development caused my conditions; it has not been built. My concern is about additional exposure and the way the applicant proposes to check it.

The air quality chapter gives annual figures, but I could not find a simple account of the worst hours at the Wrenfold Lane junction. The traffic tables show a morning peak, while the construction programme suggests several activities could happen at the same time. Please could the applicant say whether the model assumes those activities overlap, and whether the monitoring point will be close enough to the homes on our side of the lane to pick up short periods of dust? A monitor near the estate entrance would be useful, but it is not the same as a monitor by the junction where vehicles may wait to turn.

I have felt stress about the proposal and have had poor sleep since the revised drawings were published. My health is affected by worrying about the road, but I know that worry on its own is not a measured pollutant. What would help is a condition that sets out who will respond when residents report visible dust or prolonged idling, how quickly a complaint will be checked, and what can actually be stopped or changed if a limit is exceeded. A promise to investigate at some later point is not enough. The contact details should be available to people who do not use a smartphone.

At the community drop-in on 14 September 2026, Cllr Ivo March asked about the school walking route. I thought the answer concentrated on the crossing beside the site gate rather than the whole route through the village. Mrs Della Pryce, a neighbour who is not taking part in the examination, also asked whether the footway would remain open during drainage works. I have not seen that question answered in the latest plan. It would be helpful to have a drawing that shows each temporary closure, the diversion, and the expected length of time it will be in place. Please do not treat a suggested route on a map as proof that it is usable for everyone.

I checked the information available through https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate and the project updates sent from enquiries@highfenfreight.example. The update says there will be a construction environmental management plan, but much of the practical detail appears to be left until after consent. I would prefer the key controls to be settled now: wheel washing, covering loads, a clear rule on engine idling, and a way of pausing particularly dusty work in dry weather. If those controls are already in a submitted document, please point residents to the relevant page rather than referring generally to an entire chapter.

I have lived in this area for over 20 years. I know there will be some change whichever option is chosen, and I am not asking for a guarantee that no one will ever notice a lorry. I am asking for the health evidence to be understandable at street level. It should explain who may be exposed, when exposure is most likely, how the applicant will know if predictions are wrong, and what residents can do about it. Please also consider whether the construction timetable can avoid the school arrival and leaving times on days when work is closest to Wrenfold Lane.

Finally, I would welcome a plain-language note before the hearing which puts the predicted air quality changes beside the existing measurements for Lower Veck. Percentages without the starting figures are difficult to interpret. I would also like the applicant to explain whether a complaint about dust will be logged separately from a complaint about noise, since the two may happen together but need different responses. I hope these points can be addressed through enforceable requirements rather than a general assurance that contractors will follow good practice.

Yours faithfully,
Mara Ellin

Further health representation concerning High Fen Eastern Freight Park

I am submitting this further note because the health part of my earlier representation may have sounded like a general objection to lorries. It is not. I live at 14 Reedbank Terrace, Lower Veck, LV4 8PN, close enough to Wrenfold Lane that dust from vehicles using the lane can settle on the front window ledge. My interested party reference is IP-47281. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide whether any particular day of coughing was caused by the proposed scheme. I am asking for the assessment to deal properly with people who already have health conditions and with what happens during construction, not only after the freight park opens.

I have been diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma and migraine with aura. I use a salbutamol inhaler when needed and a preventer inhaler containing beclometasone every day. These are not details I would normally put in a public planning document, but they explain why an average annual air-quality figure does not answer my concern. A short spell of dust or diesel fumes outside the house can mean closing the windows and changing what we planned to do that afternoon. I cannot tell from the tables whether the model includes the short periods when several vehicles might queue, move off and idle near the lane junction. I would like the applicant to answer that question directly.

My child, Tamsin Vale, is aged 11 and has been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Tamsin also has sensory processing difficulties. An unexpected change to the usual walk to school, or being told at the last minute that the windows must stay shut because the road is dusty, can be difficult for Tamsin. I do not suggest that the project would cause that disability. The point is that a mitigation measure which relies on residents simply altering their routines may not work equally well for every household. Please do not treat this as a request to identify my child in any public map or household survey.

On some days the air already feels stale along Wrenfold Lane, especially when traffic is stopped at the bend. That is an observation, not a measurement. I understand that the applicant has used monitoring results and forecasts, and that a model cannot predict every minute of a construction day. However, the health chapter should make clear which receptors stand for homes beside the lane, where the existing measurements were taken, and whether the claimed small change is small in absolute terms as well as in percentage terms. If there is no monitor at the closest homes, please say so plainly. I would rather see an honest explanation of uncertainty than another table without the figures behind it.

The construction route is my main concern. Will the wheels of vehicles leaving the work site be cleaned before they reach Wrenfold Lane? Who checks that on a dry, windy morning, and what happens if the equipment is not operating? I would also like to know whether the proposed hours for deliveries allow a burst of HGV movements around school arrival time. Asking parents to use a different route sounds simple on paper, but the alternative footway is narrow and does not continue for the whole distance. A commitment to damp down exposed surfaces would be useful only if it says when the work must stop because dust control has failed.

I attended the community drop-in with Mrs Della Pryce, who lives nearby but has not made a representation. We both left unsure whether complaints about a smell would be recorded as air-quality complaints or only as general site enquiries. Cllr Ivo March asked a useful question there about the length of time between a complaint and a site visit. I am not relying on the drop-in as evidence of a breach; construction has not started. It showed me that residents need a clear contact route and a record of the action taken. A generic mailbox such as planning@highfeneastern.example is fine if someone actually checks it outside office hours during major earthworks.

I feel anxious about the possibility of keeping the house shut through a hot spell, and I sometimes sleep poorly after reading the construction programme. Those feelings are real, but they are different from the diagnoses I have set out above. I do not want them counted as separate medical conditions in an assessment. Equally, the fact that some effects are hard to put in a spreadsheet does not make them irrelevant. A plain-language explanation of what residents should do if visible dust enters a home would be more practical than saying only that impacts are predicted to be negligible.

I ask the Examining Authority to consider a requirement for published dust checks along the residential stretch of Wrenfold Lane, with a named role responsible for responding to exceedances or visible dust. I am not asking for the employee's personal telephone number. A staffed project contact point and a way to see the outcome of a complaint would be enough. The applicant should also explain how it will review the controls if the traffic pattern differs from the one assessed, rather than waiting for an annual report. If monitoring shows a problem, residents should know what will change and how quickly.

Finally, please put the baseline measurements, predicted construction changes and proposed trigger levels together in one accessible note. That would help me understand what protection is actually offered to this household without requiring me to interpret several technical appendices. I support proper testing of the proposal; I am not claiming that every illness or poor night's sleep in Lower Veck would be the applicant's fault. My request is for specific, enforceable measures where people live, and for a response that addresses the circumstances described here rather than a general statement about regional air quality.

Yours faithfully,
Mara Ellin
mara.ellin@postbox.example

I also want to explain why the trigger levels matter to us. I have diagnosed asthma and take a prescribed salbutamol inhaler. During dusty periods I have needed it more often, although I cannot say that the freight park is the cause of any past episode. My child, Tamsin Vale, aged 11, has a diagnosis of autism. Unexpected changes to our routine can be difficult, so advance notice of particularly dusty construction work would help us plan.

At the community drop-in, Mrs Della Pryce asked whether monitoring would continue after the main earthworks. Cllr Ivo March also asked how residents could see the results. I would welcome an answer to both questions. I worry about air quality and sometimes sleep poorly when the windows have to stay shut. Those concerns are about our wellbeing, not a claim that the project has already made us ill. Please explain what High Fen Eastern Freight Park will do if readings exceed the proposed levels near Lower Veck homes.

The transport assessment for High Fen Eastern Freight Park should show separate forecasts for construction traffic and the completed scheme. In particular, the assignment of HGV trips to Veck Moor Road needs to be reconciled with the proposed routing strategy; the two tables currently appear to use different peak-hour assumptions. A sensitivity test for a delayed rail connection would also make the assessment more useful.

Fenreach Logistics Ltd should provide a construction phasing plan that identifies when the eastern bund will be formed relative to the first earthworks. Without that sequence, the landscape assessment cannot demonstrate whether its proposed screening will be effective during construction. The drainage drawings should likewise show where runoff from temporary haul roads will be intercepted before it reaches the Lower Veck ditch.

These points concern compliance with the Veckshire Local Transport Plan 2042 and the draft construction environmental management plan. They are requests for clearer evidence, not objections to freight development in principle.

MEREFOLD TIDAL LINK
Environmental Statement Appendix 9.4: Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey
October 2026 | Revision 2

Prepared by Larchlight Ecology Ltd for Brackenfen Grid Links Ltd

1. Purpose and scope

This appendix records the otter and Schedule 1 bird evidence used in the assessment of the proposed cable crossing and temporary construction access at Velwick Fen. It should be read with ES Chapter 9, the Outline Ecological Management Plan (OEMP) and the confidential receptor plan deposited separately with the Examining Authority. The public plan shows survey compartments and working areas, but not the positions of active resting or breeding places. Grid references below have deliberately different precisions: a two-figure reference identifies a broad survey square, whereas a five-figure reference can identify a feature to approximately one metre. It would be misleading to treat them as interchangeable.

The survey covered Garran Rill, Sallowdene Drain, the reedbed margins and the disused pumping structure beside Quernlow Wood. The general survey area falls within TF 36 64. That reference is supplied so that the extent of the study can be understood; it is not a record of a protected place. The proposed haul route and cable corridor are shown on drawing MTL-ES-9-014. Survey permissions were obtained for the accessible banks only. Land beyond the northern drain was viewed from the public track, so absence of a record there must not be read as absence of a species.

2. Methods and limitations

Walkovers took place on 14 March, 28 April and 19 June 2026. The otter survey looked for spraints, footprints, slides, feeding remains and potential resting places. Bird observations were made from fixed points, with visits timed to avoid prolonged attention at any nest. Mira Pell of Larchlight Ecology Ltd checked the field sheets and photographs after each visit. Water was high in March and several low bank cavities could not then be inspected safely. A dry-weather check in June addressed most, but not all, of that limitation.

Photographs were assigned codes rather than public coordinates. The data sheet can be requested through ecology@brackenfengrid.example by the Examining Authority or relevant statutory adviser. Survey methods follow the approach described in the OEMP and the published guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/protected-species-how-to-review-planning-applications. The contractor must use the final approved plan, not an extract of this appendix, when setting out works.

3. Otter results

Otter activity was confirmed on both watercourses. A spraint was recorded at TF 3624 6417 on an exposed stone below the public footbridge. This is a field sign, not a resting place; its relatively precise reference is retained to make the repeat-survey method clear. Footprints and a slide were also found along Garran Rill, approximately 300 m east of Velwick Fen. That description is intentionally broad and does not locate a holt.

One occupied holt, coded H1 in the restricted record, was confirmed at TF 36427 64083, under the root plate of the western alder on the north bank of Garran Rill. Fresh bedding and repeated use were observed without opening the feature. A second bank cavity was treated as a possible lie-up but was not confirmed occupied; its position is held in the restricted record because contractors may otherwise mistake it for an ordinary erosion void. The public drawing indicates an otter constraint reach rather than showing H1. No conclusion about the number of animals using the watercourse is possible from these signs.

4. Schedule 1 bird results

Marsh harrier was recorded hunting over the reedbed on two visits. The broad location, Quernlow Wood and adjoining Velwick Fen reedbeds, is provided for habitat context and is not the location of a nest. Behaviour on the June visit indicated breeding. The confirmed marsh harrier nest, coded B1, was at TF 36519 64372, in the reed clump immediately south of the old sluice gate. That detailed record is included here for the restricted review copy and must not be transferred to a public constraints plan.

A peregrine was seen passing over the corridor, but no breeding site for that species was identified within the survey area. Barn owl pellets were found in the disused pumping structure. An inspection from its doorway found no eggs or young, and the structure has therefore been treated as a potential roost rather than a confirmed breeding site. These findings do not justify clearance without a pre-works check: bird use can change between the survey and construction. General references to birds at TF 36 64 in earlier consultation replies do not resolve whether any nest was present.

5. Assessment and conservation measures

Trenchless installation beneath Garran Rill is preferred. The launch compound must remain outside the otter constraint reach shown on the confidential plan, and no lighting is to be directed towards either watercourse. If trenchless installation proves impracticable, Brackenfen Grid Links Ltd must submit a revised method statement and assessment before bank works begin. No operative is to investigate H1 or move woody material near it. A suitably qualified ecologist will brief the site team, mark an exclusion area on the ground without displaying the holt coordinates on general site notices, and check for changes immediately before works.

Reedbed cutting and piling near B1 are to be programmed outside the breeding period where practicable. If the programme cannot achieve that, works in the affected compartment must pause until the project ecologist has completed a disturbance assessment and the necessary consents are in place. The restriction applies to access, noise and lighting as well as vegetation removal. It is not satisfied merely by leaving the nest clump standing. The OEMP requires replacement reed growth, retention of a continuous waterside corridor and post-construction checks in the first and third suitable survey seasons.

The precise receptor records will be supplied to the appointed ecological clerk of works through the controlled data register. Public versions of this appendix should retain the methods, broad habitat information and mitigation commitments while withholding the detailed H1 and B1 locations. Queries about the drawing revision can be sent to the shared project mailbox, ecology@brackenfengrid.example.

7.6 Residual effects and implementation

7.6.1 This section draws together the measures in Sections 7.2 to 7.5 for the Merefold Tidal Link. It should be read with the Outline Ecological Management Plan (OEMP), the Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) and Drawing MTL-EC-014 Rev C. Drawing MTL-EC-014 Rev C shows the working limits and broad habitat compartments; it does not show the controlled receptor records referred to above. Those records are not needed to understand the assessment or the commitments set out here.

7.6.2 Brackenfen Grid Links Ltd proposes to install the landward connection in two construction phases. Phase 1 comprises the temporary compound, access improvements and the duct route as far as the Merefold Drain. Phase 2 comprises the drain crossing, reinstatement and removal of temporary surfacing. The programme allows the crossing works to be completed without keeping both banks open to construction traffic at the same time. The sequence may change following detailed design, but a change in sequence will not remove the ecological hold points in the OEMP. The appointed ecological clerk of works will confirm that each hold point has been discharged before the relevant activity starts.

7.6.3 The permanent footprint is predominantly improved grassland and existing hardstanding. Temporary works also affect short lengths of rough grassland and reed-fringed ditch. These habitats are common within the wider Merefold Basin, although the reed edge provides local cover and a movement corridor. For that reason, the assessment treats the continuity of the waterside strip as more important than the area figure alone. Temporary fencing will mark the approved working width. Materials, spoil and fuel will be stored inside the compound, not along the drain margin. If a fenced limit needs moving, the contractor must submit an amended method statement for ecological review rather than moving it informally on site.

7.6.4 Directional task lighting is proposed where works continue after dusk. Lights will be aimed into the working area, fitted with shields where practicable and switched off when the work area is unoccupied. The CEMP will prohibit continuous lighting of the Merefold Drain corridor for security convenience. Noise controls include maintained plant, no idling beside retained vegetation and the use of the quieter available method where it is reasonably practicable. These controls apply to access and set-up activities, not only to vegetation clearance. A weekly site inspection will record whether fencing, lighting and housekeeping remain effective; defects will be corrected before the next affected shift.

7.6.5 At the drain crossing, the design retains a continuous waterside corridor during operation. The temporary interruption during installation will be minimised by completing bank works in sequence and reinstating the first bank before disturbing the second wherever ground conditions permit. Excavated material suitable for reuse will be kept separate from imported stone. Reinstatement will use an agreed local seed and reed mix, with erosion protection limited to locations where it is needed for bank stability. The OEMP sets out watering, replacement planting and control of invasive growth. It also requires checks in the first and third suitable survey seasons, as noted in Section 7.5. Failure of replacement growth to establish will trigger remedial planting rather than a change to the success criterion.

7.6.6 Drainage during construction will be managed through clean-water diversion, settlement measures and inspection after substantial rainfall. No untreated pumped water will be discharged directly to the Merefold Drain. The working method will be agreed with the fictional Merefold Drainage Board before excavation at the crossing. This is a construction-water control, separate from the permanent drainage design described in Chapter 12. The permanent design maintains existing field-drain connections and does not introduce a new routine outfall to the reed-fringed ditch.

7.6.7 Larchlight Ecology Ltd has considered other reasonably foreseeable works in the basin, including the adopted Marshgate Road maintenance scheme and the consented Quay Reach storage yard. These schemes are outside the Merefold Tidal Link working limits but may overlap with its construction period. The cumulative review therefore considers shared access routes, lighting in the wider landscape and the possibility of several short-term interruptions to vegetated corridors. It does not assume that impacts cancel out merely because each scheme has a small footprint. With the phasing, corridor and lighting controls secured in the OEMP and CEMP, no additional cumulative ecological measure is identified at this stage. The review will be revisited if the agreed construction programme changes materially.

7.6.8 The assessment distinguishes an absence of a record from evidence that a receptor is absent. Where pre-start checks are required, the check will take place within the period specified in the OEMP and its result will be entered in the controlled data register. A check does not itself authorise work that would otherwise require consent or a revised method. If conditions differ materially from those assessed, the activity will pause while the ecological clerk of works reviews the finding with the construction manager. The public compliance record will state the decision and any revised mitigation, without reproducing a precise location of a sensitive receptor.

7.6.9 On that basis, the residual construction effect on ordinary grassland is negligible, and the residual effect on the reed-fringed corridor is minor adverse and temporary until reinstatement has established. The operational effect is assessed as negligible, subject to maintenance of the permanent corridor and the absence of routine lighting at the crossing. These conclusions depend on implementation of the specified measures; they are not a prediction for an uncontrolled construction method. The applicant will provide the final CEMP and OEMP for approval before the relevant works commence, and will retain inspection records for audit through construction and the post-construction monitoring period.

7.7 Otters and Schedule 1 birds

7.7.1 This appendix records the evidence used to assess effects of the Merefold Tidal Link on otters and Schedule 1 birds. It should be read with Chapter 7, the outline Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) and the outline Operational Environmental Management Plan (OEMP). Larchlight Ecology Ltd prepared the appendix for Brackenfen Grid Links Ltd. The survey area included the reed-fringed drainage corridor, the proposed crossing and adjoining fields. References beginning ‘MF’ use the project’s local survey grid, not Ordnance Survey coordinates.

7.7.2 Desk records were reviewed before visits in April, June and September 2025. Surveyors walked accessible banks looking for spraints, footprints, slides, resting places and potential holts. Bird observations were made from existing tracks and agreed vantage points, with no entry into reedbeds during the breeding season. Weather, water level and visibility were recorded on the field sheets. High water prevented inspection of part of the southern bank in April; this limitation was addressed by a further visit when levels fell. No conclusion below depends on treating an absence of signs as proof that a species is absent.

7.7.3 Otter activity was recorded across the broad square MF 43 19. Spraints were present on two exposed stones, and prints occurred in soft silt after the June rainfall. These signs indicate regular use of the corridor but cannot establish the number of animals. One occupied holt was confirmed at MF 43827 19643, beneath the north-bank willow root plate at chainage 2+185, 14 m upstream of the proposed temporary bridge. This precise record is held in the restricted survey schedule. The published constraints plan shows only a broad receptor zone; it is not intended to direct anyone to the holt.

7.7.4 The temporary bridge and its approach matting would avoid the watercourse bed, but piling noise, bank access and night-time security lighting could disturb otters. Without controls, disturbance during construction is assessed as a moderate adverse effect at the local level. There is no proposed permanent bank loss at the crossing. The assessment assumes that the contractor will not store materials within the marked exclusion area and that the crossing position will not be moved towards the sensitive bank feature without ecological review. A change to the working width would also require that review.

7.7.5 A pre-start check will be carried out by a suitably experienced ecologist shortly before enabling works. The ecologist will mark the agreed exclusion area on the contractor’s working drawings without distributing the underlying location record in general site briefings. If activity or ground conditions differ materially from those described here, work in the affected area will pause while the method is revised and any necessary licence or advice is obtained. Trenches will be covered overnight or provided with an escape ramp; unattended pipework will be capped. Fuel and concrete controls are set out in the CEMP. The ecologist will record checks and any stop-work instruction in the site log.

7.7.6 Merefold Drainage Board was consulted about the proposed clear-span crossing and requested that the bank profile and maintenance access be reinstated. Its comments concern the crossing method, not confirmation of species occupancy. The reinstatement drawing will retain a continuous vegetated route along both banks. Operational inspection will be undertaken in daylight except where an urgent safety repair is required. Permanent lighting is not proposed.

7.7.7 Breeding-bird observations identified a marsh harrier territory in the wider reedbed. The precise nest record is MF 44109 19176, tree R17 on the east edge of Reedmere Compartment C, 6 m south of the farm access culvert. The observation was made from a track and was not followed by an approach to the nest. A second Schedule 1 species, barn owl, was recorded hunting over the grassland in September, but no nest or occupied roost was found within the works boundary. Records at the coarse scale MF 4 1 are included for landscape context only and do not identify a breeding site.

7.7.8 The bird survey was designed to inform the works programme, rather than to count every bird using the estuary. Marsh harrier observations were separated from records of birds merely passing through. A bird carrying prey towards the reedbed was treated as supporting evidence of breeding; a single hunting pass was not. The distinction matters because the proposed haul route lies beside, but does not enter, the reedbed. Visibility from the western vantage point was partly obscured by tall vegetation in June, and the assessment therefore adopts a precautionary disturbance zone.

7.7.9 Vegetation clearance beside the haul route will take place outside the breeding season where practicable. If that is not possible, an ecologist will check the affected area before clearance and specify a stand-off and programme appropriate to the findings. No contractor is authorised by this appendix to approach, photograph or move a nest. Delivery timing and the use of horns and reversing alarms will be reviewed near the reedbed; broadband alarms will be preferred where safe. The ecologist may require a temporary cessation of work if bird behaviour indicates disturbance. Details of the nest will be supplied only to those who need them to implement these measures.

7.7.10 With these controls, the predicted residual effect on otters is minor adverse and temporary during construction, falling to negligible in operation. The residual effect on breeding marsh harrier is also minor adverse and temporary, provided the programme and stand-off are implemented; effects on hunting barn owl are negligible. These are conditional conclusions, not permission to proceed regardless of later survey findings. The applicant will carry forward the restricted records into the final CEMP, arrange any required update surveys, and report material changes to the relevant consenting body before works in the affected area begin.

7.7.11 This appendix distinguishes the public survey summary from the restricted species record. Records checked by Mira Pell of Larchlight Ecology Ltd include photographs, field sheets and coordinates taken during the 2025 visits. The broad search area is shown as project grid MF 43 21 on Figure 7.7. This coarse reference is suitable for understanding the crossing assessment but must not be used to set out works.

7.7.12 Otter spraint and footprints were recorded along the Merefold Cut, with a well-used path between the channel and rough grassland. A probable active holt was recorded at project grid MF 43822 21647, beneath the eastern bank immediately downstream of culvert C-4. This location is included here for controlled circulation only. An absence of fresh spraint on one visit should not be read as an absence of otters from the catchment. No works affecting the bank may start until the pre-construction check and, if required, the licensing route have been completed.

7.7.13 Marsh harrier was observed carrying food towards the reedbeds in the wider MF 43 21 square. The confirmed nest is in the third reed clump north of inspection peg R-17, at project grid MF 44106 21983. This precise record is not to appear on public construction drawings. Barn owl hunting activity was noted over the western pasture; no nest was confirmed there. The proposed exclusion area and watching brief apply to the marsh harrier breeding period, subject to adjustment if an update survey finds a change.

7.7.14 Brackenfen Grid Links Ltd will issue the restricted drawing to the ecological clerk of works and the relevant consent officers only. Merefold Drainage Board has been consulted on the trenchless crossing and requested that the maintenance access remain available. The final CEMP will record who received the drawing, the survey date relied upon and any change to the stand-off before vegetation clearance.
