text:
Relevant representation: Brackenmere Eastern Link

Submitted by: Mara Fenn
Interested Party reference: IP-482731
Address for correspondence: 14 Wrenfold Lane, Brackenmere, BM4 7QJ

I support the application for the Brackenmere Eastern Link. I have lived in Brackenmere for 40+ years and have watched traffic change from something you noticed mainly at the start and end of the working day to a more or less constant line through the village. This is not a claim that every vehicle is connected with the proposed route. It is simply why I think a proper alternative to the village street is overdue. I ask the Examining Authority to recommend consent, with conditions that make sure the promised relief actually happens.

I agree in particular with the published relevant representations from Nella Voss and Idris Kelm. They have each explained, in rather different ways, why moving through-traffic away from the houses, shops and crossing points matters. I am not speaking for either of them; I mention their representations because they are already part of this examination and because their descriptions ring true to my experience. I also noted Cllr Tavin Rowe's comments at the parish meeting about keeping access to the village centre during construction. That is an important point even for those of us who support the scheme.

My front bedroom faces the existing road. When a heavy vehicle goes over the uneven cover near the junction, I often wake up and then wait for the next one. There are nights when I get back to sleep easily and nights when I do not. The result is poor sleep and a rather worn-out feeling the next day. I worry about my wellbeing when this carries on for several nights, and I have said at home that my health is affected by the noise. I am describing how it feels, not putting forward medical evidence. It would be wrong to promise that the new road will make the village silent, but taking a substantial amount of through-traffic away should give households a better chance of an undisturbed night.

The daytime difference matters too. It can be difficult to have a conversation at the bus stop when traffic is queued and engines are idling. People trying to cross are sometimes left to judge a small gap between vehicles, and drivers coming out of side streets seem to become impatient. I would like the applicant to show clearly how it will check traffic levels after opening, rather than relying only on predictions made before construction. The comparison should include ordinary weekdays, school days and evenings. If the expected reduction does not occur, there ought to be an understandable route for residents to raise it and for the highway authority to consider what can be done.

I spoke with my neighbour, Iona Pell, about the drawings displayed locally. That conversation is not offered as another person's representation. It did remind me that the plans are difficult to follow if you do not already know the plot numbers or the technical names for junctions. Please keep a plain-language plan available at the library and explain any changes to temporary routes before the barriers go up. A notice appearing after a footway has closed is not much use to someone setting off on foot in the morning.

I have read the applicant's outline construction information and understand that building a road is noisy work. My support does not mean that I want construction vehicles sent through the village without controls. The construction traffic routes should be definite, with arrangements for deliveries outside the busiest school arrival and departure periods where practicable. Foot access to shops and bus stops must be kept usable, including for people who walk slowly or use a mobility aid. If there has to be a short closure, the diversion needs to be signed from both ends, not just from the end nearest the works.

The landscaping is also worth getting right. On the plans the new road is set beyond the last group of houses, but sound travels across open ground and young planting will not screen very much at first. I would welcome the proposed earth shaping and planting, provided they are maintained and failed plants replaced. I am not asking for a wall around the village. I am asking for the detail that turns a line on a drawing into something that still works ten years after opening. The same applies to drainage: maintenance responsibilities should be clear before the road is handed over.

The environmental survey mentions badgers in the wider area around Larchmere Wood. I do not know the position of any sett and am not suggesting that the survey maps be made more public. I want the ecological measures checked during the works and explained in the final documents in a way that does not expose sensitive wildlife locations. Protecting habitats and improving the road are not opposing aims if the commitments are practical and followed through.

Some objections say the scheme will encourage more driving. That is a fair concern to examine, but it does not describe what living beside the present route is like. In my view the link should be considered alongside safer crossings, decent bus services and walking routes within Brackenmere, not as a substitute for them. I would support a requirement for the applicant to report on those connections when the detailed design is settled. The parish should be able to see what is planned without having to search through hundreds of pages for one altered drawing.

I therefore support the scheme in principle and ask for enforceable construction arrangements, post-opening traffic monitoring and continuing maintenance of the landscape and drainage measures. I hope the examination will test the forecasts carefully. I also hope it will not lose sight of the ordinary experience behind them: a street that many residents use every day is presently being asked to carry traffic that could take another route.

Mara Fenn

Further technical points for the examination

1. Traffic forecasts and monitoring

The traffic case for the Brackenmere Eastern Link should distinguish between vehicles diverted from the village centre and additional trips arising after the road opens. The two are not interchangeable. The figures in Transport Assessment BMEL-TR-04 appear to compare an opening-year scenario with a single future-year scenario, but the assumptions about committed housing and employment sites are difficult to trace between the tables. I ask the Examining Authority to require one reconciled list of developments used in every traffic model, with a short explanation of any differences from Gablewick Borough Council’s planning trajectory.

The model should also be tested against a slower uptake of the new route. A link that eventually removes through traffic from Market Lane might not do so immediately, particularly if drivers continue to follow familiar routes or navigation systems. Conversely, a large forecast reduction on Market Lane should not be counted as a permanent benefit without checking whether traffic returns as other parts of the network become busier. These are questions about the forecasts, not reasons to abandon the proposal.

Post-opening counts would make the scheme’s claimed benefits testable. I suggest counts on Market Lane, Fenbridge Road and the proposed link before construction, at roughly one year after opening, and again after five years. The monitoring plan should specify weekday peaks, school-term conditions and heavy goods vehicles separately. It should publish the results in a table using the same road sections as the application, rather than only an area-wide percentage change. If the predicted reduction through the centre is not achieved, the applicant should set out what practical traffic-management measures can be considered and who would decide on them.

2. Junctions, buses and active travel

The drawing titled Junction Strategy Plan BMEL-JS-07 shows the main junction layouts, but turning movements should be presented alongside each junction’s capacity results. A junction can appear to work in the aggregate while one minor-road approach experiences a long queue. The examination should also check whether the design vehicle used for the eastern roundabout reflects the vehicles expected to serve the proposed employment area. Swept-path plans would be more useful if the same vehicle type and drawing scale were used throughout.

A new road must not leave walking and cycling connections as disconnected pieces on opposite sides of a carriageway. The crossing near Alder Drove should be assessed as part of a continuous route to the village, including the approach gradients, lighting and winter maintenance. Any bus-stop changes should be shown on a single plan with the final pedestrian routes. I do not think a statement that stops will be ‘relocated as necessary’ provides enough certainty where a stop’s usefulness depends on which side of the junction it ends up.

3. Landscape, noise and lighting

The landscape drawings show useful planting on the western approach, although the visual assessment relies heavily on year-15 illustrations. The examination would benefit from equivalent winter views at opening and year five, when planting is still establishing. This matters most at the raised section beside Hollowbank Fields, where screening cannot be assumed to work at once. The earthworks profile, finished levels and maintenance access should be checked together; an attractive cross-section on one plan is less persuasive if it cannot be built within the proposed land take.

Noise barriers, if required following detailed design, should not be treated as an isolated engineering addition. Their height, finish and effect on views need to be assessed before approval. The same applies to lighting. The Lighting Principles Note BMEL-LP-02 says that columns will be limited to junctions, but the limits are not marked clearly on the general arrangement drawings. A condition or requirement should fix the extent of permanent lighting, with a defined process for approving any later change. Badger activity has been reported in Brackenmere Wood; that broad observation supports careful construction lighting and ecological checks but does not identify a particular sett.

4. Drainage and construction sequence

The outline drainage strategy proposes attenuation basins and controlled discharge towards the Lower Mere catchment. It should explain more plainly what happens during an exceedance event: where water flows once the designed storage is full, and whether those routes remain available if a maintenance access is blocked. The calculation package should use consistent assumptions for climate-change allowance and impermeable area. Drawing BMEL-DR-11 labels one basin by its permanent water level, while the schedule appears to give its maximum operating level; those should be distinguished so the stated storage can be checked.

Long-term maintenance should be secured before the drainage design is signed off. A plan ought to identify the organisation responsible for inspecting inlets, removing sediment and maintaining planting, as well as the access needed for that work. Reliance on an unspecified future arrangement would weaken an otherwise sensible strategy. This request is about the infrastructure as a whole, not any individual property.

Construction phasing is equally important. The draft sequence indicates that the temporary haul connection from Quarry Spur Road may be brought into use before the permanent eastern junction. If so, the Construction Traffic Management Plan should contain a separate route plan for that period and a clear trigger for closing the temporary access. Monthly vehicle totals alone would not show whether a short, intense phase creates avoidable queues. Peak daily movements, delivery hours, wheel-washing arrangements and the procedure for changing routes should be fixed in an approved plan. The plan should also explain how safe crossing routes remain available when works move from one side of a road to the other.

5. Requirements

The final requirements should connect the approved plans, monitoring duties and maintenance plans rather than leaving each in a separate document. The Brackenmere Local Transport Framework 2025 supports removing unnecessary through traffic while improving local travel choices; the scheme’s compliance with that aim should be measured after opening, not simply asserted at consent. I ask for a consolidated schedule showing each commitment, its approving authority, when approval is needed and where the public can find the approved version. That would make technical changes easier to follow and the promised benefits easier to verify.

6. Why I support the link

I support the Brackenmere Eastern Link, subject to the safeguards I have set out above. I am Mara Fenn and I live at 17 Fenward Rise, Brackenmere, BK7 4QN. I have lived in Brackenmere for over 40 years. That does not make me a traffic expert, but it does mean I know the difference between an unusually busy day and the ordinary weekday traffic that now uses the village as a short cut. The morning queue starts before many people are properly up, and in the evening it can still be stop-start when residents are trying to get home.

The route past the village is narrow in places. When a large vehicle brakes outside the houses, then accelerates again, the noise carries further than a traffic count on a page can show. My sleep is broken by it some nights, and my wellbeing is affected when it happens for several days running. I am not suggesting that every vehicle will disappear if the link is built. I do think a usable alternative for through traffic would make a noticeable difference, provided the old route is not left as the easiest way through on a satnav. This is why the traffic measures and the post-opening checks matter just as much to me as the new road itself.

7. Other representations

I have read the published relevant representations from Nella Voss and Idris Kelm and agree with their main points. Nella Voss asks that success be judged on what happens on the existing village streets, rather than simply on the number of vehicles using the link. That is sensible. A scheme could meet its forecast for the new road and still leave residents with almost the same noise if the remaining traffic is badly timed or consists of heavier vehicles. Idris Kelm makes the practical point that walking routes must remain direct. I agree with that too. People will not use a crossing that involves a long detour, however neat it looks on a drawing.

At the parish meeting, Cllr Tavin Rowe said that residents should be able to see the monitoring results without having to ask repeatedly for them. I support that suggestion. The approved monitoring locations, the dates of the counts and the results should be put in one public place in plain language as well as in technical tables. If a count is moved because a road is closed, the reason should be stated. Otherwise it will be difficult to compare the figures before and after opening, and arguments about whether the link has worked will go on indefinitely.

My neighbour Iona Pell mentioned the same difficulty to me after looking at the consultation plans, but is not taking part in this examination. A person reading the drawings should be able to tell which side of each road the footway will be on during the works, and when any temporary crossing will move. That sounds a small detail until you are standing beside traffic with shopping bags and cannot see how to reach the other side. I am mentioning the conversation to explain the practical point, not to speak on my neighbour's behalf.

8. Construction and operation

I recognise that construction will bring disruption before any benefit is felt. My support is not a request to give the contractor a free hand over hours, diversions or deliveries. The construction traffic plan should show the routes to be used by larger vehicles, how drivers will be told not to take the village short cut, and whom residents can contact when a vehicle goes the wrong way. A shared project mailbox, such as enquiries@brackenmerelink.example, would be more useful than a number printed on a notice that is not answered after the site office closes.

There should also be a simple way to check what has happened to a complaint. I do not mean publishing residents' details. A monthly summary saying how many concerns were received, what they were about and what action was taken would show whether a problem is recurring. It would also help distinguish a one-off delivery mistake from a route that is not working. Where a road closure is unavoidable, signs should go up in advance at the point where a driver or pedestrian can still choose another route, not just at the barrier.

After opening, the council and the applicant should check speeds and turning movements as well as overall traffic totals. Veldmere Routes Ltd has presented the link as a way to remove unnecessary through traffic from Brackenmere. I support that aim. If the surveys show the promised change has not happened, the requirements should provide a clear route to consider further measures on the old road. Waiting for residents to collect their own evidence would be unfair when the scheme already has a monitoring programme.

I would particularly like the crossings near the school route and the bus stops to be checked in use, not only certified as complete. A crossing can satisfy a design requirement and still feel awkward if drivers approach it too quickly or the waiting area fills up. The review should ask people who walk and wheel those routes what has changed. Their comments would not replace traffic data, but they would help explain it.

9. Closing point

For those reasons I ask the Examining Authority to retain the link in the proposed scheme and make the commitments on village traffic, safe crossings, construction routes and public reporting enforceable. I am in favour of the Brackenmere Eastern Link because I believe it can give the village some relief. My support depends on the benefits being tested openly once the road is in use, rather than treated as delivered on the day it opens.

Mara Fenn

Supplementary note to my relevant representation
Brackenmere Eastern Link

I am adding this note because my closing point about testing the benefits after opening could be read as a qualification of my support. It is a qualification, but not a change of mind. I want the Brackenmere Eastern Link to go ahead. I have lived in Brackenmere for over 40 years, and the amount of traffic passing through the village is no longer something we can simply put up with and hope will settle down. I support the proposed link because it offers a practical way of taking through traffic out of the centre. I also want the commitments made for the village to mean something after the contractors leave.

The effect of traffic at night is easy to overlook if a survey concentrates on the busiest hour of the working day. A single heavy vehicle coming through late can wake me, and sometimes it takes a while to get back to sleep. On other nights it is the repeated engine noise rather than any one vehicle. Poor sleep makes the following day harder, and the uncertainty about whether it will be a quiet night affects my wellbeing. I am not saying that every disturbance comes from the road, or that the link will make Brackenmere silent. I am saying that the present route puts avoidable noise close to where people live, at times when there is otherwise little going on.

I agree with Nella Voss’s published representation about the need to look at conditions on the village streets, not just whether vehicles have moved onto the new road in the model. I also agree with Idris Kelm’s published point that construction traffic must follow the agreed routes. Those are separate questions, and both matter to my support. A good result in the first year of operation would not excuse unnecessary disruption during construction. Equally, a well-managed building period would not be enough if through traffic gradually returned to the village afterwards. I hope the Examining Authority will read their representations alongside mine rather than treating our concerns as objections to the link itself.

At the parish meeting, Cllr Tavin Rowe asked how residents would know whether the promised reduction in village traffic had actually happened. That is a fair question. The published monitoring should show counts at more than one point, including the streets where drivers might try to avoid a queue at the junctions. It should identify the time of day and distinguish heavy vehicles where that can reasonably be done. A yearly total on its own would hide the very periods that disturb people most. If the applicant proposes a baseline, residents need to be able to see what dates were used and whether roadworks or an unusual closure affected them.

My neighbour Iona Pell said to me recently that she would like to be able to cross the main street without judging the speed of a line of vehicles first. I mention this as an ordinary conversation, not as a representation made by her. It made me think about how the scheme should be judged from the pavement as well as from a traffic counter. When a large vehicle passes the shops, people waiting to cross step back even where the pavement is technically wide enough. Reducing that pressure would be a real benefit. It should be checked by visiting the crossings when people are using them, rather than by recording only that the markings and signs have been installed.

The applicant, Veldmere Routes Ltd, has set out how the link is expected to operate. I do not expect it to guarantee that no driver will ever choose the village route. I do expect a clear process for responding if the figures show that too many still do. A commitment to review the position is useful only if the review has a date, published results and an explanation of what action is available. Where an action depends on another authority, the documents should say who will approach it and how the outcome will be reported. Otherwise everyone can agree there is a problem without anyone being responsible for the next step.

During construction, notices should be put where residents will see them and should say plainly when an access or crossing will change. Not everyone follows project updates online. If a diversion has to alter at short notice, a sign left pointing to the old route is worse than no reassurance at all. I would also ask that complaints about vehicles using the wrong route are logged by location and time and that the response is made public in a form that does not identify the person who reported it. This is not about catching out a particular driver. It is about seeing whether the controls work repeatedly, including early mornings and evenings.

There will be people who disagree with me about the balance of the scheme. I understand why, especially for those nearer the proposed road. My support is based on what I experience in the village and on the possibility of making daily journeys through it less dominated by traffic. It is not a claim that the new road has no effects elsewhere. Those effects need proper mitigation, and the benefits claimed for Brackenmere need proper verification. Neither task should be dropped because the other is difficult.

I therefore ask for the traffic and crossing reviews to be requirements with results available to the public, and for the construction route arrangements to be clear before work starts. If the measured outcome falls short, the response should be explained openly. That would give residents a fair way to judge whether the link has done what was promised. Subject to those points, I remain in favour of the Brackenmere Eastern Link.

Mara Fenn

Supplementary page to my relevant representation — Brackenmere Eastern Link

I have added this page because my earlier comments may have sounded as though I only care about the middle of Brackenmere. I do live here and have done for 40+ years, so naturally I notice what happens on the village street first. But a link road can move a problem as well as relieve one. I support the scheme because I think it gives us a chance to change how the street works, not because traffic on the new route would somehow cease to matter.

I agree with the published representation from Nella Voss, particularly the point about being able to cross the street without waiting for several gaps in a row. I also agree with Idris Kelm's published comments on checking what the traffic forecasts actually deliver after opening. They have each made their own representations in this examination; I am not speaking for either of them. I mention them because their points put into clearer words things I see on ordinary journeys, and because they ought not to be treated as objections to the scheme just because they ask for safeguards.

My main concern remains the difference between the scheme as drawn and the scheme as experienced. A plan may show two crossings and a lower traffic total, but residents will still have to use the crossings in rain, at dusk and when drivers are in a hurry. The review should therefore count whether people can actually cross, not only how many vehicles pass a counter. It should look at the morning and late afternoon, and at times when deliveries make a short queue more awkward. If the crossing is placed where people do not naturally walk, some will continue to cross elsewhere. That is not a reason to blame them; it is a reason to check the design before it is fixed.

Iona Pell, who lives near me and is not taking part in this examination as far as I know, said that she sometimes waits for the traffic noise to ease before opening a window. I have the same sort of reaction. On nights when a vehicle accelerates through the village, I wake and then find it hard to get back to sleep. I feel worn down the next morning. I am not making a medical claim and I cannot say that every disturbed night is caused by the road. I can say that the sound of passing vehicles is one of the things I notice, and that a quieter village street would make a real difference to my wellbeing. The noise assessment should take account of the sharp, occasional events as well as an average figure for a whole period.

At the parish meeting, Cllr Tavin Rowe asked whether the promised changes in the village would happen promptly after the link opened. That was a fair question. If the new road opens but the existing street is left looking and working just as it does now, drivers may carry on using it out of habit. I would like the timetable for the crossings, signs and any speed measures to be tied to the opening arrangements. Otherwise we could spend months being told that the benefit is coming later. I do not expect every bit of village work to be finished on the same day, but the sequence and the person responsible for each step should be plain.

There is also the construction period. I accept that building a road involves lorries and disruption. What I cannot judge from a general assurance is what happens if a delivery vehicle misses the agreed route or if a closure sends ordinary traffic through the village at a busy time. Veldmere Routes Ltd should publish a straightforward route plan that a resident can understand without reading several separate appendices. It should say how a problem is reported, who checks it and when a reply can be expected. A generic project contact would be better than expecting residents to find the right contractor themselves. Reporting should not require someone to prove the cause of a traffic queue from their front window.

I would also ask the Examining Authority to consider how the benefits will be reported after opening. A single survey soon after the link comes into use might catch an unusual week. There should be an initial check and a later one, using comparable days where possible, with the findings put in public view. If traffic through Brackenmere is higher than forecast, the report should say so and explain what action is available. I do not want a promise that every result will be perfect. I want a process that does not disappear when the road is built.

Some neighbours oppose the scheme because of its effect beyond the village. I understand why they ask difficult questions about landscape, drainage and access to fields. Support for the Brackenmere Eastern Link should not be taken to mean that those questions are unimportant. The applicant should answer them on their merits. Equally, the problems on the existing street should not be treated as minor merely because they are familiar. Living with something for a long time does not make it satisfactory.

I remain in favour of the application, subject to enforceable arrangements for the village measures, construction traffic and checking the results. That is a conditional but genuine expression of support. If the examinations of those points produce changes, I would regard that as the process working, rather than as a reason to abandon the link.

Mara Fenn

Further note to my relevant representation
Brackenmere Eastern Link
21 October 2026

I am adding this note because I may not have explained clearly enough why the existing road matters to me. I have lived in Brackenmere for over 40 years. The traffic has changed in that time: it is not just the number of vehicles, but the way the larger ones come through in groups, sometimes quite late. On those evenings I find it hard to get to sleep, and if I wake when a lorry passes I can lie awake listening for the next one. It leaves me tired and affects my wellbeing the following day. I am not saying a new road will make the village silent. I am saying the present arrangement has a real effect on ordinary life here.

I agree with the published representations from Nella Voss and Idris Kelm, particularly their points about making the village traffic measures part of the scheme rather than leaving them as a promise for later. I do not speak for either of them, but I thought their comments put that concern better than I did. At the parish meeting, Cllr Tavin Rowe also asked how the results would be checked after opening. That seems a fair question even for those of us who support the link.

My neighbour Iona Pell mentioned the same difficulty with evening traffic when we spoke by the gate. I include that simply to explain why I do not think my experience is unusual; I have not asked my neighbour to join this examination or to endorse my submission.

Veldmere Routes Ltd should set out who will carry out the traffic counts, when they will happen and what will be done if traffic does not reduce as forecast. Please also make the information easy for residents to find without having to search through several technical reports. I remain supportive of the Brackenmere Eastern Link, provided those practical matters are dealt with properly.

Mara Fenn

Additional technical point – transport and drainage

The transport assessment for the Brackenmere Eastern Link should show the junction results for the morning and evening peaks separately, not just the daily average. In particular, the model should test what happens if the planned employment land opens before the link is fully operational. A sensitivity run with slower-than-forecast traffic growth would also help explain whether the proposed junction layouts remain appropriate.

The drawings show attenuation beside Merefold Road, but the drainage statement is less clear about where exceedance flows would go if the design storm were exceeded. Please show the overland route on a plan and confirm that construction compounds would not interrupt it. The phasing plan should also identify when temporary drainage becomes operational relative to earthworks.

These points appear relevant to the Brackenmere Local Plan Policy T4 and the draft Construction Environmental Management Plan. Resolving them would make the application easier to assess; they do not alter my support in principle.

text:
Relevant representation: Elmswick Eastern Link Development Consent Order

From: Rowan Fenwick
Interested Party reference: IP-482761
Address for correspondence: 17 Lantern Fold, Elmswick, EW4 8PN
Email: rowan.fenwick@postvale.example
Telephone: 07700 614 283

I object to the Elmswick Eastern Link as currently proposed. I understand why a route around the town is being considered, but the application treats Lantern Fold as though it were only a line of houses on a traffic drawing. We are already close to the existing freight road. Adding an elevated junction, lighting and a construction compound beside it will change what it is like to live here, not just what a noise model says it will be like.

I have lived in this part of Elmswick for over 40 years. That is not an argument against any change. It does mean I know when the road is busiest and which windows we have to close when lorries idle at the present junction. The applicant's traffic figures average the day out. On weekdays the difficult period is before school and again when the late deliveries come through. I would like the Examining Authority to ask for an assessment of those periods separately, including vehicles using the service yard at Morrow Quay, 2 Basin Road, Elmswick. That is a commercial site, not anybody's home.

My neighbours Mrs Elspeth Vale and Harun Dace are not making representations, so please do not contact them about this letter. Their back gardens face the proposed slip road and the drawings show a screen which appears to stop short of that row. At the informal drop-in, the applicant's acoustic consultant Dr Tessa Brook MSc of Fenline Acoustics said a revised barrier drawing would be uploaded. I cannot find one in the examination library. The follow-up message came from tessa.brook@fenline-acoustics.example, but it contained the same drawing number. I am not saying the consultant promised an outcome; I am saying we need the correct drawing before being asked to comment on mitigation.

My son, Nico Fenwick (aged 11), has asthma, controlled with a prescribed salbutamol inhaler. We have not been offered any information about dust controls for the compound nearest our street. I have chronic migraine, and irregular night-time noise is difficult for me to manage. I know these circumstances cannot decide the route by themselves, but they explain why a condition saying simply ‘minimise disturbance’ would give us very little reassurance. Please require published limits, monitoring points at the nearest homes and a clear way to report a breach. Even without those conditions, the prospect of several summers of works makes me anxious and I have had poor sleep since the route was announced. That is not a claim that everyone on the street has a medical condition.

The construction plan also needs a proper pedestrian route. The temporary diversion shown on sheet EL-TR-14 sends people across the entrance to Silver Mere Farm and then back along the same verge. The farm name on the plan is useful for finding the entrance; I am not asking for the farm family's details to be published. Children walk that way to the bus stop. I watched two vehicles turn in at once last Tuesday, and there was nowhere obvious for a person on foot to wait. Please ask for a continuous protected path rather than a sign telling pedestrians to take care.

Ecology has been discussed mostly in terms of planting after construction. Badgers have been seen in Robin's Wood, which is a broad area and hardly a secret. I did, however, see an active sett at the base of the split ash immediately east of gate G7, 24 metres north of the culvert marked C3 on the applicant's ecology plan. Please pass that observation to the appropriate ecologist without putting the precise point into a public drawing. Bats also feed over the wider fields north of Elmswick; I do not know of a maternity roost and would not want a guess presented as a survey finding. Replacement planting may be helpful, but it will not screen an elevated road in its first years.

The question of compensation has been left vague. A local estate agent's informal valuation of my house was £238,000 before the preferred route was announced. I am not asking the Examining Authority to settle a claim in this representation. I include it because the applicant's statement that there will be ‘no material residential effect’ does not reflect the concern felt by people who may need to move. If the applicant considers its assessment robust, it should explain the assumptions for the properties closest to the slip road, rather than referring readers to an area-wide average.

Cllr Mira Quill asked at the parish hall session whether construction traffic could use the northern access instead. I would welcome a written answer to that question. I also agree with the point about lighting made in the published representation of Petra Iden, who is already an Interested Party. Neither comment removes the need for a plan that shows the height of the lamps as seen from Lantern Fold.

I sent an earlier query to enquiries@elmswicklink.example and was directed to the project documents. The drawing index there is useful, but several files are labelled ‘indicative’ and the dates of revisions are not easy to follow. An unrelated article at https://regional-roads-review.example/elmswick-traffic-claim has been circulated locally; I have not relied on it, because I cannot check its figures. Please base any answer on the applicant's submitted data and make the version used clear.

I ask that consent is refused unless the applicant supplies a corrected barrier drawing, a realistic construction traffic and walking plan, and enforceable controls for noise, dust and lighting. If those matters can be resolved, residents should have a chance to comment on the actual measures rather than a general promise that details will come later.

Yours faithfully,
Rowan Fenwick

Further technical points on the Elmswick Eastern Link

The traffic case needs a clearer audit trail before the forecast benefits can be given much weight. The transport assessment describes a 2038 design-year model, but the junction appendices appear to mix 2036 and 2038 flows. At the Broom Lane / Eastern Gate roundabout, the morning peak turning totals in Table 7.4 do not equal the totals shown on drawing T-214. The difference may be a simple update that did not reach every document. It should nevertheless be reconciled in one schedule stating the model run, forecast year, peak hour and drawing revision used for each junction. Otherwise it is not possible to tell whether the reported queue reductions follow from the submitted layout.

The proposed access at Kiln Road is another uncertainty. The assessment assumes that most construction vehicles will approach from the east, while the construction strategy allows deliveries from either direction subject to later agreement. Those are not equivalent assumptions for the narrow section between the railway bridge and Mill Cut. The applicant, Brackenmere Routes Ltd, should provide a construction assignment using the highest expected daily and peak-hour HGV movements, not just an annual average. Swept-path plots should cover two HGVs meeting at the bridge approach and the temporary signal arrangement shown on drawing CT-09. If those movements cannot be accommodated without overrunning the footway, the route needs to be changed in the consent documents rather than left to a contractor's method statement.

There is also a gap between the permanent traffic forecast and the proposed walking and cycling network. The shared path on the north side of the link ends at the Kiln Road tie-in, yet the desire-line diagram shows onward movement towards the Eastern Gate employment area. A person travelling in that direction would have to cross the new access road and then cross Kiln Road at an uncontrolled point. The answer should be a continuous, dimensioned route on the general arrangement drawings. The crossing assessment ought to use the same flows as the junction assessment, including the committed West Mere Depot development. A drawing that identifies a possible future connection does not demonstrate that the connection can be delivered.

For landscape assessment, the photomontages should be checked against the final earthworks envelope. Viewpoint LV-06 is illustrated with a shallow planted cutting, whereas the sections accompanying the drainage chapter show a wider maintenance strip and an open swale. Both cannot occupy the same ground without altering the planting width. This matters particularly at the rise east of Ashfold Copse, where the proposed screening would take several growing seasons to establish. The environmental statement should distinguish the opening-year appearance from the year-15 illustration, and should show any safety fence, lighting columns and drainage access track that would actually be visible. The Landscape Management Plan should also specify replacement planting requirements if the first planting fails.

The drainage design needs similar consistency. The preliminary strategy directs runoff to the North Beck outfall and relies on storage within two basins. Its exceedance plan, however, shows overland flow from Basin B towards the Kiln Road underpass when the basin is full. The submitted long-section does not show the underpass threshold, so the direction and depth of that flow cannot be verified. Marlow Fen Drainage Board's ordinary watercourse requirements should be incorporated into the detailed design parameters, but board approval by itself would not resolve the question of what happens above the design event. A simple level schedule for the basins, outfall, carriageway low points and underpass would make this check possible. The maintenance responsibility for the swales and culverts should be identified as well; the strategy currently refers only to a body to be appointed after construction.

Construction phasing is relevant to more than vehicle movements. Phase 2 closes the existing field crossing before the replacement route is shown as open in Phase 3. The construction drawings should state whether a temporary crossing is proposed, its usable width and surfacing, and how it will be kept separate from the earthworks compound. The same set of drawings should show the drainage works required before bulk excavation begins. At present the programme and temporary-works plan describe different sequences. This is not a request for a fixed date for every activity; it is a request for a buildable sequence with no unexplained break in access or surface-water control.

Lighting should be assessed on the basis of the junction arrangement proposed for approval, rather than a generic column layout. The lighting appendix models standard-height columns along the main carriageway but omits the additional units marked at the Eastern Gate splitter island on the highway drawing. Elmswick Borough Council's adopted Dark Corridors Policy identifies Ashfold Copse and the beck corridor as areas where spill should be minimised. An isolux plot including the splitter-island units, the maintenance access and the underpass would allow the effect of shielding and dimming to be tested. The policy does not prohibit lighting; it calls for the necessary lighting to be designed and justified as a whole.

Finally, the draft requirement for detailed design should not allow a materially different road profile, drainage footprint or crossing arrangement to be approved without reference to the assessed limits. Parameters such as maximum earthworks levels, minimum path widths, basin extents and lighting limits can be stated now. Elmswick Borough Council and Marlow Fen Drainage Board can then review the later details against measurable commitments. This would give the decision-maker a reliable basis for judging the Elmswick Eastern Link, while leaving normal engineering tolerances for detailed design.

Relevant Representation – further comments on the Elmswick Eastern Link

I am Rowan Fenwick and I object to the application as it stands. My earlier points about the road profile, drainage footprint and lighting are not just requests for nicer drawings. They go to whether the effects on the people living along the eastern edge of Elmswick have been assessed at all. I have lived in this part of the borough for 40+ years, and the lane and its ditches work as one system when it rains hard. The submitted plans split that system between highway drawings, landscape drawings and a drainage strategy, with slightly different assumptions in each. Please do not leave residents to find out at the detailed design stage which drawing was meant to govern.

Our home is at 7 Wrenfold Close, Elmswick, EW4 7QJ. I give that address to explain why I am particularly concerned about the proposed raised section south of the underpass, not to suggest that only this street is affected. The noise tables appear to use the present ground level at our end of the gardens, whereas the sections show a higher running surface. A modest change in level could put traffic in view above the hedge and make the proposed earth bank much less useful. I ask the Examining Authority to require an assessed worst-case road height, with a corresponding worst-case noise assessment, before consent is granted. A condition saying that the final design will be ‘substantially in accordance’ with the drawings is too elastic here.

I have asthma, and fumes from queuing traffic are a particular worry for me. I am not claiming that every vehicle on the link will worsen my condition, but the application ought to show how traffic will behave at the two new junctions, including when a lane is closed or the school run meets a delivery peak. My child, Nico Fenwick, aged 11, has been diagnosed with epilepsy. The drawings show the shared path emerging close to moving traffic, but do not explain whether the path will have a continuous barrier or how a parent and child are meant to cross when the lights fail. These are practical questions for our household. I also sleep badly when traffic is heavy and feel anxious about what construction will be like; those feelings are not a substitute for proper measured evidence.

At the parish hall session, Mrs Elspeth Vale, who lives next door and is not making her own representation, explained that water from the field already reaches her back step after prolonged rain. She did not say the new road caused that existing problem. Her point was that a basin placed uphill from the houses should be specified and maintained properly, with an accessible overflow route. Another neighbour, Harun Dace, asked where the temporary pumps would discharge during construction; he was shown an indicative arrow rather than an outfall drawing. I repeat these conversations because the applicant's response to the drainage questions in its consultation report says the matter was resolved with residents. From what I saw, it was not. The Marlow Fen Drainage Board should be asked for a specific response to the proposed temporary works as well as the permanent scheme.

Cllr Mira Quill also attended the session and suggested that a walkover in wet weather would help everyone understand the low point by the gate. I agree, although a walkover cannot replace calculations. Petra Iden's published representation raises a similar issue about the culvert capacity farther east; I support the request there for the assumptions to be provided in a readable table. These comments are not a complaint about the people doing the design. They are a request that Brackenmere Routes Ltd put one set of figures before the examination, rather than promising that Elmswick Borough Council will sort out the details afterwards. The council will need clear limits to enforce, not another series of diagrams marked illustrative.

There is also an ecology point which may be easy to miss if the underpass is looked at only as a pedestrian connection. Badger signs have been recorded in Brindle Coppice and bats use the trees along the old ditch; that is a broad description, not a request to publish every survey record. However, the confidential ecological note supplied to residents marks a badger sett in the bank 14 metres east of the north end of Footpath 8, immediately below the second ash tree from the stile. That location should not appear on a public plan or be repeated in the open examination library. It does need to be considered when the contractor chooses a haul route and any fencing. A drawing that moves the haul route by a few metres could be the difference between a workable precaution and a disturbance. The same care should be applied to night lighting during works, not only to the finished road.

I have read the noise summary attributed to Dr Tessa Brook MSc of Fenline Acoustics. I am not asking for the consultant's personal details to be published, and I would prefer questions to go through the examination rather than to an individual inbox. The public address tessa.brook@fenline-acoustics.example.invalid was included in a circulated slide, but the relevant material should instead be lodged as a numbered examination document, showing the receptor heights, assumed road surface and uncertainty. If there is a revised model, residents need to be able to compare it with the earlier one. A headline statement that the change is negligible is not enough when the view and the physical barrier have also changed.

For completeness, my Interested Party number is IP-483729 and my contact email is rowan.fenwick@example.invalid. I put these here so that any request for clarification can reach me, not because I want my contact details repeated in the published representation. I have also looked at https://fen-watch.example.invalid/maps/underpass, which shows an informal photograph taken from the path; it may help explain my concern about sightlines, but it is not a substitute for a verified survey. I would be content to attend an accompanied site visit if one is arranged.

I ask the Examining Authority to seek revised, joined-up sections for the road, path and drainage features; to test the highest permitted road level and construction arrangements; and to secure measurable limits in the requirements. If those matters cannot be resolved during examination, my objection remains. The link may offer a journey-time benefit, but that does not justify transferring unresolved noise, water and safety risks onto the neighbouring streets.

Rowan Fenwick

Further comments on the Elmswick Eastern Link
Relevant representation addendum, 21 October 2026
From: Rowan Fenwick
Address for correspondence: 14 Reedglass Close, Elmswick, EW4 2QT
Email: rowan.fenwick@personalmail.example.invalid
Interested Party reference: IP-EL-07429

I am adding this because, after sending my representation, I realised that I had described the underpass as though it were separate from the drainage proposals. On the drawings they meet at almost the same point. I am not withdrawing the earlier points. I object to the application by Brackenmere Routes Ltd unless the Examining Authority can see a workable design for all three things together, not a promise that the detail will be sorted later.

The proposed path is our practical way to the shops and the bus stop. It is not just a leisure route. My child Nico Fenwick uses it with me, and at aged 11 cannot be expected to judge whether water on the approach is shallow enough to cross or whether a lorry will turn across the temporary path. I am not suggesting that every puddle closes a path. I am asking who will inspect it, who has authority to close it, and what usable alternative will be provided when it is closed. A sign telling people to use a road with no pavement is not an alternative.

My concern about standing water is based on what happens now, not a prediction made from a map. Mrs Elspeth Vale, who lives at 7 Sedge Turn, Elmswick, EW4 2QN and is not making a representation, has had water up to the front step after prolonged rain. Harun Dace, another neighbour who is not involved in the examination, helped move belongings out of the ground-floor room on that occasion. I do not have a surveyed level for either property and would not want this account treated as one. It is a reason to ask the Marlow Fen Drainage Board and the applicant to reconcile their levels and to explain where water goes if the new culvert is partially blocked during a storm. Saying that maintenance will be agreed is not enough without an identified party and an access route.

The noise tables also need to say what happens during construction, particularly the evening movements. I have chronic migraine, and unexpected reversing alarms can make an attack worse. That is a statement about my circumstances, not a request to give my house a different noise limit. Nico has asthma, so I also want to know whether dust monitoring will cover the path beside the compound rather than only the nearest fixed house. The disruption is already causing stress and poor sleep in our household, but I recognise those words are not a medical assessment. Please assess the ordinary users of the path as well as people behind closed windows.

I attended the parish hall session at which Cllr Mira Quill asked whether the temporary crossing would be lit. The answer I heard was that lighting was still under review. Petra Iden has already made a representation about the crossing and I support the request in that published representation for a drawing showing the actual diversion width. At the session, Dr Tessa Brook MSc of Fenline Acoustics talked through the operational noise figures. My difficulty is not with that explanation of the figures; it is that the figures do not show the combination of construction traffic, a wet underpass approach and people being sent around a compound fence. I appreciate these may sit in different assessment chapters, but they will occur in the same place.

There is also an ecology point which I have not seen addressed clearly. Badgers have been recorded in Willowhook Wood; that is a broad area and I do not claim that the whole wood should be closed. During the walk I mentioned previously, I saw fresh digging at the sett beneath the north bank of Drain 4, immediately beside the third timber post east of the footbridge at grid reference TL 48231 70642. I have not entered the site or disturbed it. I give the location so that the appropriate ecologist can check it before any fence posts or drainage works are set out. Any public version of this comment should avoid directing visitors to the spot.

For completeness, my own address is provided for correspondence, not as a surveyed receptor point. I have lived in this part of Elmswick for over 20 years, but that does not make my recollection of flood depths a substitute for measurements. Equally, the absence of a measurement from a resident should not be taken to mean the problem did not happen. The applicant could usefully publish a single section showing the road embankment, drain, path level, fencing and flood exceedance route at the crossing, with the assumptions printed on it in ordinary units. I could then check whether I have misunderstood the drawings.

I have read the material posted by Elmswick Borough Council at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects as a general guide to the examination process. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide a private boundary dispute. I am asking it to require an answer that can be inspected and enforced: levels, a safe diversion before the existing path is closed, a named maintenance responsibility, and monitoring locations that include the people walking past the works. If those can be secured, I will consider the revised material. Until then I maintain my objection.

Rowan Fenwick

Further technical comments on the Elmswick Eastern Link

The following points concern the assessment method and the wording of the proposed requirements. They do not depend on a particular property boundary. Brackenmere Routes Ltd should provide a single drawing schedule identifying which traffic, drainage and landscape drawings supersede earlier versions. At present the traffic appendix uses a different junction numbering sequence from the general arrangement plans. That makes it unnecessarily difficult to check whether the same junction has been assessed throughout. A table giving each junction's plan reference, model reference and construction-phase reference would resolve this fairly simply.

The traffic assessment relies on an opening-year forecast for the junction of Alderbank Road and Mere Cut Lane, but the queue plots appear to show only an average weekday peak hour. The construction programme places the heaviest earthworks movements in a shorter period, when temporary signals would also be operating. Those are different conditions. The applicant should show a sensitivity test with the temporary signal stages, the stated maximum number of construction vehicles and the background traffic forecast all applied together. It should give the resulting queue length in metres, not just a ratio of flow to capacity, so the result can be compared with the available road space.

The proposed diversion along Reed Ferry Road also needs to be modelled as a route rather than as an isolated junction movement. The Transport Assessment assumes that displaced traffic will spread across several roads. The Construction Traffic Management Plan, however, directs vehicles to one signed route. Both assumptions cannot describe the same period without an explanation. Please publish the turning counts used at the three access points, the assumed share using the signed diversion and the method used to prevent vehicles from taking the shorter route through Market Fold. An advisory sign alone would not establish compliance with a route restriction.

There is a similar mismatch in the proposed monitoring. A commitment to review traffic 'where necessary' gives no trigger, timescale or person responsible for acting on the result. The requirement should specify counts before the diversion begins, counts during each traffic-management stage and a published comparison against the forecast. If a stated threshold is exceeded for two consecutive survey periods, the applicant should have to submit a remedial plan to Elmswick Borough Council before continuing the affected stage. The threshold must be expressed as a measurable number, not left to a later management plan with no examination of its terms.

On drainage, the drawings show the eastern cutting draining towards the Fenreach Outfall. The hydraulic calculations seem to assume that the outfall can discharge freely at the same time as the receiving channel is at its design water level. The Flood Risk Assessment should test a restricted outfall case and explain whether the proposed storage volume remains adequate. The calculation sheet should state the rainfall duration, climate-change allowance, antecedent water level and discharge control setting on one page. These inputs are scattered across the current appendices, and it is not clear which combination produces the maximum water level within the cutting.

The maintenance interface with Marlow Fen Drainage Board is also material. The plans identify an access strip beside the channel, while the landscaping sheets put hedge planting and a shallow swale within what appears to be the same strip. A dimensioned cross-section is needed to demonstrate that machinery can still reach the channel and that excavated material can be placed without blocking the swale. The relevant requirement should secure the final cross-section and the party responsible for keeping both the swale and the access strip clear. That is an operational matter, not merely a detail of planting species.

For landscape and visual assessment, the Year 1 and Year 15 photomontages should be accompanied by a plan of the assumed planting heights and locations. The current images indicate substantial screening on the eastern embankment, but the planting schedule describes small stock at installation and allows losses to be replaced in the next planting season. The assessment should say what happens to the claimed mitigation if establishment is delayed or the soil on the embankment does not support the forecast growth. A five-year replacement obligation would not, by itself, demonstrate that the Year 15 view will match the assessment.

Lighting is treated as a permanent operational effect in the Environmental Statement, yet temporary compounds are shown close to the edge of the same assessment area. The construction lighting plan should include mounting heights, beam direction, hours of use and an isolux plot for the compound at the Saltmarsh Gate worksite. It should also explain whether any security lighting remains on overnight when no activity is taking place. This can be dealt with through a requirement, provided the limits and the approved drawing are identified now rather than determined entirely after consent.

Finally, the draft requirements should be checked against the National Policy Statement for National Networks on mitigation and the need for clear, enforceable controls. A requirement to submit a plan is not a substitute for specifying the outcome that plan must achieve. For each of the matters above, the examination would benefit from a short schedule listing the assessed assumption, the drawing or table where it appears, the proposed control and the authority that would approve any change. This is a practical request for consistency between the assessments and the works that could actually be built. Until those links are clear, the transport, drainage and landscape conclusions cannot be independently checked.

I object to the Elmswick Eastern Link as presently drafted. I have lived near the proposed haul route for 40+ years, and the traffic assessment does not reflect school-run queues or tractors turning at the drain bridge. I am worried about noise and poor sleep; that is not the same as saying the scheme's impacts are acceptable. I have diagnosed asthma, and dust from trial works has already made it harder to use the garden. My child Nico Fenwick, aged 11, has epilepsy and needs a predictable journey to school. Please do not treat the school bus as a minor receptor.

Mrs Elspeth Vale at 18 Reedbell Close, Elmswick, EW4 7QJ told me she will not submit evidence because the online forms are confusing. Harun Dace, another neighbour, described the same queues. Neither has agreed to have their details published. At the parish hall Cllr Mira Quill asked about drainage, and Petra Iden's published representation raises the same point. The Marlow Fen Drainage Board should be given drawings showing the outfall capacity.

The note by Dr Tessa Brook MSc of Fenline Acoustics assumes closed windows, which is not reasonable in summer. I ask Brackenmere Routes Ltd to provide enforceable limits, not another promise to review matters after approval.

Rowan Fenwick

The transport assessment for the Elmswick Eastern Link needs a clearer account of how the construction traffic model has been tested. The forecast for the Reedbell Road and Cinderbank Lane junction uses an average weekday, but the submitted drawings show temporary lane closures during the culvert works. The assessment should model those closures separately and state whether its queue estimates include vehicles turning into the works compound.

The drainage strategy also needs a check against the construction programme. Drawing EL-DR-214 shows the permanent attenuation basin available before the eastern embankment is completed, while the phasing table places basin excavation later. Brackenmere Routes Ltd should explain where runoff will be held in the intervening period and provide the temporary discharge rate to the Marlow Fen Drainage Board.

I also ask the Examining Authority to secure a landscape maintenance period through the requirements. Replacement planting beside Cinderbank Lane is useful, but the visual assessment appears to assume established screening from the first year of operation.

From: Ms Ari Denslow <ari.denslow@post.example>
To: Bellmere Marsh Project Team <bellmere-marsh@examinations.example>
Date: 14 October 2026, 21:06
Subject: Bellmere Marsh Link / question about the drainage drawing

Dear case team,

I am an interested party in the Bellmere Marsh Link examination (IP reference BM-48271). I am writing from 18 Reedlark Close, Bellmere, BM4 6QN. Please use email for replies if possible, as the phone signal inside the house is hopeless. My mobile is 07700 814263.

The revised drainage drawing uploaded on Tuesday appears to move the temporary outfall towards the back of Reedlark Close. The key calls it a construction measure, but the accompanying note says it may remain for up to eighteen months. I have lived here for 40+ years and have seen that ditch come over its banks after ordinary winter rain. I am worried about more water standing in the gardens, rather than objecting to drainage work in principle. Is there a drawing that shows where the outfall goes once construction is finished? I looked under the documents tab and may have missed it.

I also wanted to flag something without putting it in a public comment. Mrs Belin Korr at 20 Reedlark Close, Bellmere, BM4 6QP showed me photographs of water against the kitchen step. Mrs Belin Korr is not taking part in the examination and asked that the address not be circulated. Please don't contact her on the strength of my email. A white van, registration KX26 ULP, was parked over the ditch inspection cover when I went to look, though I cannot say whose van it was.

My daughter Nessa Denslow, aged 11, has diagnosed epilepsy. The flashing amber lamps used during the earlier survey were difficult for our household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to resolve a medical issue; I would just like the construction lighting question passed to whoever is answering it. This has left me anxious about the next works. A reply before the 23 October deadline would help me decide whether to submit a further written representation.

Regards,
Ari Denslow

To: Ari Denslow <ari.denslow@post.example>

Dear Ari,

Thank you for your email. I am Iona Vell, one of the case officers supporting this examination. We have recorded your query under correspondence reference BM-EX-1042. That number is for tracking the email; it is not a new interested-party reference.

The case team cannot interpret the applicant's engineering drawings or confirm what arrangement will eventually be approved. We can ask Larchfen Infrastructure Ltd, the applicant, to identify the relevant drawing and explain whether the outfall is temporary. We will also ask for the response to address construction lighting. An answer provided during the examination will normally be placed on the project page so that all parties can see it. We will not include the information about your neighbour or household in the question sent to the applicant.

If you want the Examining Authority to consider your own account of flooding, please submit it by the deadline using the project mailbox above. Your concern about water at the rear gardens and your concern about lighting can be described without identifying another resident. I have asked my colleague Merrin Saye to check which drainage documents were accepted at the last deadline; Merrin will reply if there is a newer drawing I have overlooked.

For general submission queries you may use bellmere-marsh@examinations.example or the case team switchboard on 0300 790 4628. My direct work number is 0300 790 4639. Please note that a telephone conversation is not a substitute for a written submission.

Kind regards,
Bellmere Marsh Project Team
National Infrastructure Examination Case Service
