text:
Relevant representation: Merewick Northern Relief Road

Applicant: Merewick Transport Authority
From: Ms Elinor Fennick
Address: 14 Orchard Row, Hathercombe, HC4 7QN
Email: elinor.fennick@letter.example
Interested Party reference: IP-842617

I support the application for the Merewick Northern Relief Road. I have lived in Hathercombe for over 40 years, and I would like the Examining Authority to know why a proper route around the village matters to people who live here. My support is not a claim that every detail is perfect, or that construction will be easy. It is a request to look at what happens now, as well as what may happen while the road is built.

At present, vehicles coming through on the B4178 pass the houses on Orchard Row before reaching the narrow bend by the old pump house. I cannot tell from my window which vehicles are making local deliveries and which are avoiding the longer route through Merewick. What I can say is that large vehicles come through early and late, and the sound carries into our bedrooms. If one hits the uneven drain cover at the bend, there is a sharp noise followed by the rattle of whatever it is carrying. On some nights my sleep is broken several times. I feel worn down the next day and worry about whether I will get a decent night's sleep. This affects my wellbeing, even though it is hard to put a number on it in a traffic assessment.

I agree with the published representation by Nadia Peverell, especially the point that the village is being used as a through route rather than just for access. I also agree with Owen Mallow's published representation about the difficulty of crossing the road near the village shop. They are both Interested Parties in this examination and have put their own views on the record; I am not speaking for either of them. I mention their submissions because they describe two sides of the same problem. Vehicles are passing through a place where people need to walk across the road, collect shopping and get home safely.

The proposed relief road would give through traffic a route that does not require it to pass the shop and Orchard Row. That seems to me a substantial public benefit. The application documents include forecasts, but residents are also able to describe the everyday pattern those figures represent. A quieter main street would make it easier to open a window in the evening and to hear somebody talking at the front door. Those may sound like small things compared with a major road scheme. They are not small when the present conditions are experienced every day.

I understand that some people are concerned that traffic might simply move from one group of houses to another. The final design should therefore keep the proposed barriers and planting where they have been shown, rather than treating them as optional extras after consent. I would like the construction traffic plan to include clear permitted routes for heavy vehicles, hours for the noisiest work and a way for residents to report a problem and get an answer. The project mailbox, planning@merewicktransport.example, is useful, but an acknowledgement on its own would not tell us what will be done. If a temporary closure is needed, notice should go up at the shop as well as online; not everyone checks a website before leaving home.

I have heard concerns about the loss of land by Larch Spinney. I walk there sometimes and I do not dismiss those concerns. There have been badger signs in the wider spinney, and the planting and habitat measures ought to be checked after the road opens, not only promised beforehand. At the same time, I do not think the possibility of change at that site means the existing village road should remain the main through route indefinitely. Both matters deserve proper conditions and follow-up.

At a recent drop-in, Mrs Clara Densley, who lives nearby but is not taking part in this examination, asked whether the diversion signs would send lorries past the school during construction. I did not know the answer. It would help if the applicant put the proposed diversion route on a simple village map, with any changes explained before they happen. That is a practical question, not a reason in itself to refuse the scheme.

Cllr Iona Bellwick said at the parish hall discussion that access for emergency vehicles must be maintained. I agree. Access to the shop and homes must be maintained too, with particular care for people walking along the B4178. I turned 69 this summer and I am still happy to walk into the village, but the speed and volume of traffic can make even a short crossing unpleasant. Over the years I have seen plenty of proposals put forward and then quietly disappear. This one should not be lost without weighing what the present road is doing to the village.

I ask the Examining Authority to recommend consent, subject to enforceable arrangements for construction traffic, noise controls, safe crossings and the promised landscaping. Please do not assume that because I support the road, I am content with unlimited disturbance while it is built. I accept that there will be an awkward period. I support the scheme because I believe the longer-term change for Hathercombe will be worth it, provided those commitments are kept and residents can find out whom to contact when something goes wrong.

Elinor Fennick

Supplementary note to my relevant representation

I am adding this note because I want to explain why my support for the Merewick Northern Relief Road is not just a general wish for less traffic. I have lived in Hathercombe for over 40 years. The main road has always carried vehicles, but it now feels as though there is hardly a pause between them at the times when people need to get about on foot. I do not expect a new road to make the village silent. I do think it could make the ordinary business of living here easier.

I agree with the published representations from Nadia Peverell and Owen Mallow, both of whom have registered as Interested Parties. Nadia’s point about being able to cross the road without watching for a gap that never quite comes reflects my experience. Owen is also right to ask what will happen on the existing road once through traffic has somewhere else to go. If the speed and layout are simply left as they are, some of the benefit of the scheme will be missed. I would like the Examining Authority to consider the relief road and the promised village measures together, rather than treating the latter as an optional extra.

The effect of noise is difficult to put into a table. Lorries passing late in the evening can wake me, and after a broken night I feel worn out and less able to concentrate the next day. My sleep has been poor when traffic is especially heavy. That is an account of what it is like to live here, not a claim that every vehicle can be heard in every house. I also worry about my wellbeing when I cannot open a bedroom window in warm weather without hearing engines and the repeated rattle from the road. A predicted reduction in traffic would be welcome, but I hope the applicant will explain in plain language what its noise figures mean for homes along the present route.

At a discussion in the parish hall, Cllr Iona Bellwick said that residents should be able to see how the before-and-after traffic counts will be checked. I agree. A count taken on an unusually quiet day would not tell us much. It would be useful to publish the survey dates, the types of vehicles counted and a short explanation of any seasonal differences. The results should be made available somewhere residents can find them without having to work through a large set of technical appendices. I have no objection to proper technical evidence; I simply want to be able to tell whether the change we were promised has happened.

Mrs Clara Densley, who lives at 7 Sedgecroft Lane, Hathercombe, HX0 4ZZ, mentioned to me that deliveries sometimes stop near the bend because drivers cannot easily see a safe place to pull in. She is not making a representation herself, and I do not speak for her. I mention the example because the scheme should be accompanied by practical thought about servicing the village, not just the movement of cars on a drawing. A narrower or calmer main road would be a good outcome, but loading and access need to work too. The same applies to the bus stops: people should not have to choose between a long detour and an uncomfortable crossing.

I would also ask for care during construction. Supporters of a road can still be affected by it being built. If construction lorries are meant to use designated routes, those routes ought to be clear to drivers and residents, with a way of reporting departures from them. I have seen references to a community contact arrangement, but I would prefer one clearly advertised project mailbox, such as enquiries@merewickroad.example, and a commitment to acknowledge reports within a stated period. It is frustrating when a complaint is passed from one contractor to another and nobody seems responsible for giving an answer. A summary of complaints and what was done about them would help build confidence, provided personal details are removed.

Landscaping matters as well. Newly planted trees cannot provide the screening shown in an illustration on the day they go into the ground. I would like the requirements to say who must look after them, how failures will be replaced and when residents can expect an update. I am not asking for instant results. I am asking that the planting should still be there and growing after the contractors have left. Footpaths affected by the works should likewise be easy to follow and usable, with any temporary diversions properly signed before the original route is closed.

Some neighbours are opposed to the road, and I understand why land take and construction worry them. My support should not be read as dismissing those concerns. Merewick Transport Authority needs to show that the detailed arrangements are fair to people close to the proposed route as well as to those of us beside the existing road. In particular, I would welcome a straightforward map showing which local roads construction vehicles may use, where temporary restrictions are proposed and how emergency access will be maintained. Changes to those arrangements should be communicated before they happen, not discovered when a sign appears at the end of a lane.

For me, the central question remains whether Hathercombe can have a main street that works better for people walking, using the bus and visiting local shops. The relief road offers a real opportunity, but consent should carry conditions that make its benefits more than an aspiration. I therefore continue to support the application, with firm requirements for construction management, monitoring, crossings, village-road measures and planting. I hope the Examining Authority will take these points as constructive comments from somebody who wants the scheme to succeed, and who will still be here to see how it works in practice.

Elinor Fennick

Further points on the submitted technical material

The support expressed above is subject to the detailed design doing what the application says it will do. The following points concern the traffic, drainage and landscape information for the Merewick Northern Relief Road. They do not alter the overall position on the scheme, but they are matters that ought to be settled through requirements rather than left for discussion after construction.

Traffic modelling and monitoring

The traffic assessment shows a reduction in through traffic on Hathercombe Main Street, but its forecast year figures should be read alongside the assumptions about which routes drivers will actually choose. In particular, the model should show separately the vehicles joining at the Far Barrow junction, those continuing towards Merewick, and those using Alderfold Lane as a short cut. A single total for traffic crossing the village cordon will not show whether one residential approach has become busier while the main street has become quieter.

Merewick Transport Authority should publish turning counts for the same junctions before opening and at agreed intervals afterwards. The counts should cover a normal school week and a Saturday, with any roadworks or unusual closures recorded alongside them. The proposed monitoring in MNRR-TR-04 appears to concentrate on the relief road itself. It needs a corresponding set of counts on the existing roads if the claimed village benefit is to be tested. The trigger for corrective measures should be stated in numbers, not described simply as a material change. Otherwise there may be disagreement about what the monitoring has found.

The drawings for the Far Barrow junction should also be checked against the swept paths for the largest vehicles expected during construction and operation. The concern is not whether a vehicle can turn once under ideal conditions, but whether it can turn without mounting the footway when another vehicle is waiting. The final design should retain the indicated pedestrian refuge and should not narrow it later to obtain additional carriageway width. Signal timings, if signals are selected at detailed design, need to allow a crossing in one movement for the forecast pedestrian demand.

Drainage and water quality

The drainage strategy proposes attenuation before discharge towards Fenmarsh Beck. That is preferable to an unrestricted outfall, but the submitted material is less clear about how the system will perform if a maintenance access is blocked or a basin is already partly full following successive storms. The detailed drainage design should give storage volumes, assumed infiltration rates and exceedance routes for each catchment. An exceedance route marked only as following existing levels is not sufficiently informative where the road is on embankment and nearby field drains are being intercepted.

The temporary drainage arrangements deserve equal attention. During the earthworks phase, bare ground, stockpiles and haul-road crossings will be present before permanent swales are established. The construction environmental management plan should identify where settlement measures will be installed, how they will be inspected after heavy rain and where water will go while individual drainage sections are being connected. A drawing at the appropriate scale would make this much easier to check than a general commitment to good practice.

The long-term maintenance schedule should name the body responsible for the basins, swales, outfalls and any oil-control equipment. It should include access arrangements that work without repeatedly closing the shared-use path. It would be helpful for the as-built drainage drawings and inspection records to be available to Merewick District Council, rather than held only within the contractor's handover file.

Landscape and construction phasing

The photomontages show planting at establishment and at a later year, but the later views rely on a fairly continuous screen. The requirement should therefore specify replacement of failed trees and hedgerow sections for a defined establishment period, together with a measurable standard for successful cover. Planting on a drawing is not the same thing as planting that survives beside an exposed road. The sections near Ternfield Copse also need to show the final height of the earthworks, safety barrier and lighting columns together, so their combined appearance can be assessed.

Construction phasing matters to the landscape as well as to traffic. If the western embankment is built early but planted only at the end of the whole contract, it will remain exposed for longer than the visual assessment seems to assume. The programme should allow planting in the first suitable season after each completed section, where that will not be damaged by later works. Temporary compounds and lighting should be removed promptly when they are no longer required, rather than retained until the last phase has closed.

The shared-use path is an important part of the scheme, not a finishing item. The programme should show when its connections at Hathercombe Green and Far Barrow become usable and what signed route will be available until then. A length of new path ending at a working area or at an uncrossed junction would not deliver the active-travel benefit described in the application.

Policy and requirements

These points are consistent with the aims in the Merewick Local Transport Plan 2042 and the West Merewick Spatial Framework: reducing unnecessary traffic through settlements, managing surface water at source and making walking and cycling routes continuous. The application gives reasons for the relief road in each of those areas. The draft requirements now need to provide a way of checking the outcomes.

Before the relevant works begin, the final traffic-monitoring schedule, drainage drawings, planting specification and phased path plan should be submitted for approval. Each should identify what will be measured, when it will be checked and what happens if the approved standard is not met. That would turn the scheme's intended benefits for Hathercombe into commitments that can be followed through after the road opens.

Further points on the draft requirements

The monitoring schedule should use the same count locations and peak-hour definitions as the Transport Assessment. Otherwise it will be difficult to tell whether any change is due to the Merewick Northern Relief Road or to a change in the method of counting. The baseline should cover a normal school term and should distinguish through traffic from local trips where the model permits. Counts on Hathercombe High Street and the B6148 should be repeated at six months, one year and three years after opening. Merewick Transport Authority should publish the results alongside the forecast figures, including any difference between weekday and weekend flows. I am not asking for a guarantee that every street will be quieter on every day, but the requirement ought to say what review is triggered if the forecast reduction is not achieved.

The construction traffic plan also needs to be settled before the first substantial earthworks, rather than left to individual contractors to interpret. The haul route shown via East Merewick Link is sensible in principle, provided deliveries do not divert through the centre of Hathercombe when that route is congested. A record of delivery hours, vehicle numbers and any authorised diversion would allow this to be checked. The plan should explain how the temporary crossing of the existing cycle route will be managed during each phase, including the period when the new bridge is being finished but is not yet open for use. A line on a drawing marked ‘temporary route’ is not enough if the line cannot be used in wet weather.

On drainage, the outfall drawings and the maintenance schedule should be read together. The Drainage Strategy describes attenuation and treatment before discharge to the Merewick Brook, but the draft requirement is less clear about who will inspect the swales once the highway is in use. It should require a handover record, inspection intervals and a procedure for removing silt without damaging the planting. The drawings should also show how exceedance flows are directed away from the shared-use path. This is a design and maintenance point, not an objection to the principle of the outfall.

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment identifies the cutting and its proposed planting as the main means of limiting views from the western approach to Hathercombe. The final planting specification should therefore include replacement thresholds, watering arrangements and an establishment period long enough to test whether the screening actually takes. The photographs used for monitoring should be taken from agreed public viewpoints in comparable seasons. That would make the results much easier to understand than a statement that planting has been completed. Where a temporary compound is removed, its reinstatement should be checked separately from the permanent highway verge.

Finally, the phased path plan should show a usable connection at each stage, not simply the completed network. This matters particularly at Quarry Lane, where a short missing section would send users back onto the carriageway. The West Merewick Spatial Framework supports continuous routes, and the draft requirements should make continuity a condition of opening the relevant part of the road. Subject to those checks, the proposal remains consistent with the transport and environmental aims set out in the application.

I support the Merewick Northern Relief Road, subject to the path and planting checks set out above. I have lived in Hathercombe for over 40 years, and the traffic through the village is noticeably worse than it used to be. On some nights the lorries wake me, and I find the broken sleep affects my wellbeing the following day. I am not claiming that the new road will remove every vehicle, but a proper through route should make a real difference.

I agree with the published representations of Nadia Peverell and Owen Mallow on the need to keep village access practical during construction. Their points about the temporary diversions should not be lost just because they support the scheme overall. Mrs Clara Densley, who lives nearby but is not taking part in the examination, has also asked me when the works would start. Clear notices for residents would help. As Cllr Iona Bellwick said at the parish hall discussion, people need to know what will happen street by street.

text:
Relevant representation: proposed Bracken Fold Solar and Battery Scheme
Application reference: BF-NSIP-2026-04
From: Mara Venn
Interested Party reference: IP-608217
Address for correspondence: 18 Tern Close, Sundermere, HL4 8QJ
Email: mara.venn@posthaven.example

I object to the Bracken Fold Solar and Battery Scheme as presently proposed. I live at the above address and have looked at the plans and the applicant's consultation summary. My objection is not to renewable power in principle. It is to putting the battery compound, construction access and lighting so close to homes, while treating the lane as if it were an empty line on a drawing. Please register this as my relevant representation. I would like to speak at a hearing if there is one about access or noise.

Our end of Tern Close backs onto the fields. At the consultation event, the board showed the battery containers behind an earth bund. The board did not show what the bund would look like from an upstairs window, or how the cooling fans would sound at night when traffic has stopped. I have lived in Sundermere for 40+ years and know that noise carries across the hollow. That is not a technical measurement, but it should be a reason to measure it properly rather than rely only on a daytime visit. I am already stressed about it and sleep badly when there is heavy traffic. I have been diagnosed with asthma, and dust from the proposed months of groundworks is a particular concern for me. I am not asking the Examining Authority to accept my prediction as medical evidence; I am asking for a proper assessment at the houses that will receive the dust.

My son, Tavi Venn, is aged 11 and has epilepsy. The construction route passes the stop used for the school bus. The route drawing counts cars at the main junction but not children crossing from Tern Close on winter mornings, when the bend is dark. Please require a supervised crossing or a different route before works start, not a promise to sort it out in a later traffic plan. My mother has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and sometimes stays with us. I do not think the air-quality chapter explains how short bursts of dust would be dealt with when several lorries arrive together. The statement that there are no sensitive receptors on this side of the road is simply wrong.

I spoke to my neighbour Mrs Nella Brist, who lives at 20 Tern Close, Sundermere, HL4 8QJ. The neighbour has not made a representation and did not ask to be named in a public document; I mention the conversation because it made me check the drawing again. Another resident, Mr Oswin Keel, pointed out that the swept-path line crosses the verge beside the bus stop. Neither conversation is a substitute for the applicant checking the road in person. I wrote down the registration ZT26 RKL after a survey van mounted the pavement there on 12 September 2026, in case the road-safety team wanted to identify the visit. I am not alleging that the driver did anything deliberate.

The scheme boundary is also confusing. Sheet 7 marks Alder Wash Farm as a named property, but the access arrows on the same sheet appear to send HGVs past its entrance. I understand that Plot 14 and the works at Bracken Fold Lane are part of this application, not a separate highway scheme. The farm name on the plan is not an invitation to assume that everyone living nearby accepts the route. At the drop-in, Jorin Pell of Fallowmere Renewables Ltd told me that detailed lorry timings would come later. If timings matter to whether the lane can safely be used, residents need to see them during the examination. The generic project address, planning@fallowmere.example, sent me a link to the consultation material, but the link did not include an updated swept-path drawing.

There is wildlife information missing as well. The environmental statement says there are badger signs in Alder Wash Wood; that broad description is fine for public discussion. However, the confidential survey sheet I was accidentally shown identifies a sett under the third oak on the eastern bank of Drain 4, 18 metres north of the Bracken Fold Lane culvert. That position is directly beside the proposed temporary haul route. I have not copied the sheet or photographed it. Please ensure the ecological advisers check the route against their confidential records and do not publish a precise sett map in an ordinary hearing document. I have also seen bats over the fields, but cannot say where they roost. The presence of bats is a reason for careful surveys, not a reason to guess at a roost on a public map.

Cllr Iona Rusk has asked for a pedestrian count at the Tern Close bend. I support that request. It would also help if the applicant provided a readable plan of the construction entrance, showing where vehicles wait when another lorry is coming out. The applicant's project webpage says deliveries will be managed, but it gives no maximum queue length. A traffic marshal cannot remove a blind bend. The proposed planting may screen the panels eventually; it will not screen headlights or make the road wider during construction.

Finally, the noise assessment should use evening and weekend baseline readings as well as weekday daytime ones. My garden is quietest after the last bus, which is exactly when a continuously running fan would stand out. Please consider a more distant battery location, enforceable fan-noise limits and a construction route that does not use the school-bus bend. If the scheme cannot meet those conditions, I ask that consent be refused. I am willing to answer questions about what I have personally observed, but I do not want my family or neighbours treated as having signed up to give evidence merely because I have mentioned them here.

Mara Venn

Supplementary note to my relevant representation — 21 October 2026
Bracken Fold Solar and Battery Scheme

I am adding this note because, after signing my representation, I checked the revised access drawing and realised it still assumes that two vehicles can pass beside the school-bus bend. My objection is not to renewable energy in principle. It is to putting the battery compound and construction traffic where the submitted drawings put them, without showing how the road will work for the people who use it now.

I live at 14 Tern Close, Merecross, MC4 7QP. The entrance to the close is not on the proposed haul route, but the route is the way we reach the bus stop and the small shops. On a school morning there are children waiting on the pavement, cars pulling away from the close and a delivery van often stopped by the bend. None of those movements appears to be in the swept-path drawing. The drawing shows a clear road, a clear pavement and a vehicle entering at a steady angle. That is not the situation I see.

I asked at the consultation whether an observer had actually stood there at bus time. Jorin Pell of Fallowmere Renewables Ltd said the traffic team had used counts, but I did not get a date or the hours counted. This is not a complaint about the person at the event; it is a request for the underlying observations. The address I was given afterwards was jorin.pell@fallowmere.example, though I would rather any response went through the examination than to me privately. The generic project mailbox, planning@fallowmere.example, is printed on the leaflet. Please do not treat a leaflet contact as evidence that the bend has been checked.

Cllr Iona Rusk requested a pedestrian count at the junction, as I understand it. I support that request. A count should include the fifteen minutes before and after each school bus and should distinguish people crossing the road from those walking along it. It should also record when a vehicle occupies the opposite lane to get round a parked van. If the applicant has already done this work, please publish the results with the times and dates, not just a daily total. The count from Tuesday afternoon in the transport appendix does not answer the question about mornings.

My son Tavi Venn, who is 11, uses that bus stop. Tavi Venn has a diagnosis of autism and an unexpected reversing alarm or a sudden instruction to move back can make the journey particularly difficult. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide access arrangements on the basis of one family's circumstances. I am asking for a route that does not rely on children noticing and responding instantly when a lorry needs more room. A temporary marshal may help, but the draft traffic plan does not say where the marshal would stand or whether one would be present when deliveries run late.

Mrs Nella Brist lives near the bend and has not made a representation. At a doorstep conversation the neighbour described seeing a tractor reverse when a bus approached; she did not ask me to pass on an account as evidence, so please do not list the neighbour as a witness. Mr Oswin Keel also pointed out to me that the arrow on the revised swept-path drawing seems to start beyond the narrowest part. Mr Oswin Keel has not registered as an Interested Party. I mention those conversations only to explain why I looked again at the drawing. My own observations are that vehicles wait opposite the field gate and pedestrians step into a driveway to let other pedestrians pass.

The battery compound is a separate concern. My garden is behind the houses facing the eastern field. I have diagnosed asthma, and I would like the dust-control plan to say what happens when dry earth is being moved on a windy day, rather than merely promising 'best practicable means'. That diagnosis is not a claim that the scheme will cause a particular illness. For the proposed fans, I am concerned about noise and poor sleep, especially in summer when bedroom windows are open. The assessment should compare the fans with the quiet periods actually experienced at the rear of the houses. It should give a limit that can be checked after installation, including at night.

There is an ecological point which should not be lost in the argument about access. The ecology summary says there are badger signs in Bracken Fold Wood. That is a broad description and I do not object to it being public. During the walkover I noted a badger sett directly under the east bank of the disused lime pit, 18 metres north of the stile on Footpath 6. Please keep that exact location out of the public copy and have the ecological advisers check it before any fencing or trenching is fixed. A plan that simply marks the whole wood as habitat would not tell a contractor where extra care is needed.

For completeness, the reference on my acknowledgement is IP-48271. I tried to check the revised drawing through the applicant's project page and also found a local photograph at https://merecross-observer.example/bend-photo; the photograph is not a measured survey and I do not rely on it for road widths. The Planning Inspectorate guidance at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate was clearer about how to submit this note than the consultation leaflet. I have lived in this area for over 20 years, but length of residence does not substitute for a proper traffic assessment either.

Please require the applicant to test an alternative construction route and a battery position farther from the houses. If those options are rejected, the reasons should be set out against actual bus-time observations, night-time background readings and enforceable conditions. I would welcome a written answer to those points through the examination. I do not consent to my household or the neighbours named above being contacted simply because I have referred to them.

Mara Venn

The remaining points concern the adequacy of the assessment rather than opposition to renewable generation in principle. Bracken Fold Solar and Battery Scheme could make a useful contribution to electricity supply, but the examination needs to be able to distinguish effects that can be controlled by a requirement from effects which have simply not been measured. At present several important conclusions in the Environmental Statement depend on assumptions that are not carried through into the draft Construction Traffic Management Plan or the drainage drawings.

First, the construction traffic figures should be reconciled in one table. The transport chapter gives a daily average for heavy goods vehicles, while the outline programme shows deliveries concentrated in the piling and battery installation periods. An average spread across the whole construction programme conceals the busiest weeks. Fallowmere Renewables Ltd should provide the maximum number of two-way HGV movements expected on any day and in any hour, broken down by phase, vehicle type and access. That schedule should include abnormal loads, concrete deliveries, spoil movements and return journeys. It should also say whether empty vehicles will follow the same route. Without those details it is difficult to test the junction capacity work or the proposed limits on deliveries.

The model of the Moorwick Road and East Mere Lane junction appears to use turning counts from a neutral weekday. The assessment should explain how those counts were adjusted for the school-term peak and seasonal agricultural traffic. A sensitivity test is needed for the busiest construction hour coinciding with the morning bus period, not just the highway network's conventional peak. This is a narrow-road issue as well as a junction-capacity issue: the traffic report predicts little queueing, but it does not demonstrate where opposing vehicles can pass between the junction and the site gate. The swept-path plans should show the full route, including bends and passing places, with a clear statement of what land must be available before deliveries begin. Any reliance on temporary traffic control needs to appear in the draft management plan as an enforceable measure, with responsibility for inspection and maintenance.

I also ask for a route comparison rather than a statement that the proposed route is preferred. The alternative via Hollowbank Way may have its own constraints, including a longer journey and works at the western junction, but those matters can be tested. A comparison should cover road geometry, vulnerable road users, surface condition, bus operation, total vehicle-kilometres and the practicality of temporary improvements. If either route requires vegetation clearance or alteration to a ditch, that should be assessed in the relevant environmental chapter. The examination should not have to infer the reasons for rejecting an option from scattered drawings.

For landscape and visual effects, the viewpoints provide a useful starting point but do not show a consistent worst-case scenario. Some photomontages assume established screening even though the planting schedule indicates that replacement hedges will take several growing seasons to provide meaningful cover. The visual assessment should separate the construction condition, the first operational year and the mature planting condition. It should also show winter views where leaf cover has been used to support a finding of limited effect. A wireline from the eastern edge of Mere Rise would help explain the combined appearance of panels, security fencing, cameras and the battery compound. Those elements should be assessed together rather than as separate small additions to the landscape.

The battery compound deserves a more explicit alternatives assessment. The current layout leaves little room for landform or planting between the equipment and the nearest residential edge, while the supporting text suggests that equipment could be moved within the wider site. A plan comparing the present location with a position farther into the development area should give dimensions, access implications, cable lengths and any drainage constraints. If the present location is retained, the acoustic assessment must use the final equipment specification or a binding maximum sound-power level. It should state how tonal or intermittent characteristics have been allowed for and show the predicted night-time level at the assessment positions. A promise to confirm equipment after consent is not a substitute for testing the envelope now.

On drainage, the flood-risk material describes a broadly unchanged rate of runoff, but the detailed drawings show several new tracks, inverter pads and compacted working areas. The calculations should identify the area treated as impermeable or partly impermeable and explain the assumptions made for compacted ground beneath and between panels. The outfall towards Willow Drain needs a drawing showing levels, capacity and the proposed means of controlling sediment during construction. Maintenance of swales and the attenuation basin should be secured for the operational life of the scheme, with an inspection schedule and a procedure for dealing with blockage. It is not enough to leave those matters to a future management document without stating the performance standard it must meet.

The ecological mitigation should likewise be tied to the construction sequence. The documents refer generally to badger activity in Bracken Wood and to bat foraging along boundary hedges; these are reasons for proportionate controls, not for assuming that every field has the same constraint. The final lighting strategy should identify working hours, the circumstances in which temporary lighting may be used, and limits on light spill at retained hedges. The vegetation plan should specify when new planting will be installed relative to any removal of existing cover. Monitoring should have a stated trigger for remedial work if planting fails, rather than relying on a broad commitment to review it.

Finally, the draft requirements should be checked against the conclusions claimed in the Environmental Statement and the policy balance under National Policy Statement EN-1. Where an effect is described as acceptable only because deliveries will avoid particular periods, screening will be established or runoff will be controlled, the corresponding requirement should state the limit or outcome clearly. Fenwick Vale Council and the examining authority should be able to see which measures are fixed at consent, which details can properly be approved later, and what happens if monitoring shows that a measure is not working. A single commitments register, cross-referenced to the final plans and requirements, would make that exercise much easier.

The transport assessment also needs a clearer account of what happens when the construction programme and the highway model are read together. The weekday peak-hour junction tests use a single construction traffic figure, but the programme shows overlapping periods for panel deliveries, cable installation and battery compound works. It is not clear whether the tested figure represents that overlap or an average across the whole build. Fallowmere Renewables Ltd should provide a weekly profile of two-way heavy goods vehicle movements, identify the highest plausible delivery week, and rerun the Bracken Lane/Alder Bank junction assessment using that week rather than the construction-period average.

The proposed access drawings show vehicles entering from Bracken Lane, but the swept-path envelope appears to cross the hatched area at the bend. The plans should confirm whether that area is adopted highway, and whether any temporary works or vegetation clearance are needed outside the order limits. This is a point about the land and the geometry, not simply driver instructions. If the access cannot operate as drawn, the alternative should be assessed before consent rather than left to the construction traffic management plan.

On drainage, the Environmental Statement describes infiltration as the preferred approach while the outline surface water strategy retains an attenuation basin and controlled outfall as a fallback. Those are materially different arrangements. The final strategy should set out the ground-testing threshold that decides between them, the design storm and climate-change allowance for each option, and a drawing showing exceedance routes away from the battery compound. Approval of detailed calculations by Fenwick Vale Council would then be tied to an assessed design envelope, not an open choice of drainage method.

The landscape drawings should likewise distinguish planting assumed in the year-one visualisations from screening that will take years to establish. A five-year replacement and maintenance period may not address losses that occur immediately afterwards. The requirement should specify measurable establishment criteria and continuing replacement where a screen is relied upon for the assessed visual effect. None of these requests changes the principle of the Bracken Fold Solar and Battery Scheme; they are needed so that the limits of its assessed effects can actually be checked on the ground.

I remain opposed to the Bracken Fold Solar and Battery Scheme. The proposed requirements do not resolve what the construction traffic will mean for people on Tern Close. From my home at 17 Tern Close, Fenwick Vale, FV4 2QN, I see children crossing the lane where the swept-path drawing shows lorries turning. My son Tavi Venn, aged 11, uses that crossing for school. Mrs Nella Brist next door is also worried, although she has not submitted a representation. Mr Oswin Keel pointed out the same problem on the drawing but has not registered as an Interested Party.

At the consultation event, Jorin Pell of Fallowmere Renewables Ltd said the route could be managed, but I still cannot find a pedestrian count for school hours. Cllr Iona Rusk asked for one too. I have asthma and worry about dust during construction; I also feel anxious about the traffic. Please do not approve the scheme without a properly assessed route and enforceable limits.

Mara Venn

KESTREL QUAY LEGAL LLP
Suite 4, Rialto House, 17 Canal Quay, Bellmarsh, BM2 6QT
Direct dial: 01632 960 478 | nina.orrel@kestrelquay.example

21 October 2026

By email to the Examination

Bellmarsh Water Transfer Order
PINS reference: EN040218
Interested Party reference: IP-200418
Written representation on behalf of Ada Fenlow

Dear Examining Authority,

We act for Ada Fenlow in relation to the proposed compulsory acquisition of land at Hollowbank Farm. This letter responds to the Applicant’s revised Book of Reference and its note on temporary possession, both uploaded on 9 October. Our client supports the need for a reliable water supply in principle. The objection is to the extent and duration of the powers sought by Weycross Water Infrastructure Ltd over working land, and to the suggestion that the farm can continue operating normally while the works take place.

The land shown as Plot 17b is used for access between the yard and the eastern fields. It is not a spare margin. Machinery uses it during harvest, and the stock trailer must be able to turn there without reversing onto Sedge Lane. The current order limits show fencing across that turning space. Although the Applicant’s response says access will be maintained, its drawing BM-WT-AC-014 shows only a narrow pedestrian gate. Please confirm whether a vehicle gate is proposed, its clear width, and who will be responsible for opening it during working hours. An assurance in a meeting is not an enforceable access arrangement.

We have supplied the Applicant with a marked-up plan showing the route used by the farm’s larger vehicles. The route is different from the track indicated in the Environmental Statement because the indicated track floods after ordinary winter rain. A trial visit on 2 October was useful, but no revised access drawing has followed. Our client asks for a requirement securing an agreed construction traffic and farm-access plan before entry onto Plot 17b. It should cover harvest movements, emergency access, temporary surfacing and the reinstatement standard. If agreement cannot be reached, the matter should go to an independent surveyor rather than being left to the contractor’s discretion.

We are also concerned about the permanent easement proposed across Plot 18a. The Book of Reference describes it as a right for a buried main, yet the draft Order would permit apparatus, inspection and vegetation clearance without a stated width. The explanatory note refers to a corridor of 12 metres; the plan appears to show something wider at the bend. The Examining Authority is asked to require a dimensioned plan and a narrower power tied to the apparatus actually authorised. The farm should not lose the practical use of additional land simply because a contractor may find a generous corridor convenient.

The Applicant has suggested compensation can resolve any difficulty. It cannot substitute for a workable access route. Nor does the public statement that the holding will be ‘unaffected’ reflect the information given at the site visit. Our client has a personal mortgage balance of £186,400, and an extended interruption to the farm business would affect the ability to meet repayments. We include that figure to explain why the timing of possession matters, not as a compensation claim for the Examination to determine. Our client is aged 71 and has rheumatoid arthritis; repeated last-minute changes to the agreed route would make day-to-day arrangements particularly difficult. We ask that any notice of entry specify a named contact role and give at least 28 days’ warning of changes, save in a genuine emergency.

There is a separate ecological point. The Environmental Statement records badger activity in Bellmarsh Spinney but does not identify how the compound boundary was checked following the September survey. During the site visit, the farm manager pointed out a sett in the bank 14 metres south of the north-east corner of Plot 17b, beneath the split ash beside Gate 3. We ask for confirmation that the ecological clerk of works has reviewed this feature before any fence line is fixed. This concern is not an objection to appropriate surveys; it is a request that their results inform the final working area.

At the meeting, Cllr Emmet Sorrel asked whether the temporary haul road could be moved towards the existing drainage ditch. That option deserves a proper response in the alternatives table. Leon Tarver, who works land next to the proposed compound but has not submitted a representation, also raised the loss of the turning head. We mention that point because the Applicant’s meeting note records only ‘general concerns about access’. It was a specific operational question, and the note should be corrected. We do not speak for that neighbouring holding.

For correspondence only, our client’s residential address is 8 Sedge Lane, Fenwick Mere, FM4 7QJ. Please do not treat that address as the site access: the proposed works and the relevant gate are on the land identified in the Order plans as Hollowbank Farm, Plot 17b. The firm’s office address above may be used for formal notices to us. Routine examination updates can be sent to the general enquiries mailbox, but any request for instructions should come through the direct contact shown in this letterhead.

In summary, we request a dimensioned easement plan, a secured farm-access plan and an updated response to the ecological and haul-road points. We would welcome a short issue-specific hearing if these matters remain unresolved after the Applicant’s next deadline. The project documents cited above are available through the Examination library at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate, and the Applicant’s general project information is at https://bellmarsh-transfer.example/project. Neither website resolves the discrepancy on the access drawing.

Yours faithfully,

Nina Orrel
Solicitor | Kestrel Quay Legal LLP

Direct dial: 01632 960 478

Bellmarsh Water Transfer Order
Further written submission on behalf of Ada Fenlow
Access drawings and compulsory acquisition of rights

Dear Examining Authority,

Further to our summary at the end of the previous submission, we have checked the Applicant’s latest access drawing against the rights proposed over Ternfold Farm. This note is submitted on behalf of Ada Fenlow. It does not withdraw the objections already made to Plot TF-07 or suggest that an informal assurance from the Applicant is an adequate substitute for an enforceable provision in the Order.

The landowner’s immediate problem is quite practical. Drawing BWT-AC-214 Rev C shows a maintained route from Stile Lane to the western field, but its key describes the same strip as a temporary construction access. The Book of Reference then seeks permanent rights to pass and repass over it for inspection and maintenance. Those descriptions cannot all mean the same thing. If the strip is permanent, its width, turning head, drainage and responsibility for repair should be fixed now. If it is temporary, the Order should say when it will be reinstated and how access to the field will be maintained thereafter. A promise to agree those matters with a future occupier leaves too much to chance.

The point is not answered by the Applicant’s reference to an existing farm track. That track is only usable in dry weather and does not connect to the field entrance shown on Rev C. A loaded trailer cannot make the turn at gate TF-3 without entering the proposed fenced compound. Please provide a swept-path drawing using the agricultural vehicles identified in our earlier representation, with the fence and drainage ditch shown at their proposed finished positions. We would also like the Applicant to state whether the compound gate will be locked during ordinary farm operations, who will hold keys and how access will work when a contractor is not present.

There was some confusion at the site meeting. Cllr Emmet Sorrel asked whether the western field would remain accessible throughout construction; the answer given was that a route would be available, not that the route on the deposited drawing would be available. Leon Tarver, a neighbouring land worker who was present but has not made a representation, pointed out the narrow turning area. He was not speaking for Ada Fenlow, and the Applicant should not treat that exchange as agreement to the drawing. We ask that the meeting note distinguish an observation made on site from an undertaking by the landowner.

The proposed haul route raises a separate timing issue. The programme describes approximately twelve weeks of trenching, whereas the draft access schedule permits use of the temporary strip until all reinstatement is certified. Those are different end points. Ternfold Farm has been worked for over 40 years, and the seasonal use of the western field cannot simply be moved to a convenient week after construction. A secured access plan should identify the route available during each stage, the maximum period of closure at gate TF-3 and the person authorised to resolve a blockage on the day. A generic emergency number will not help if a vehicle is waiting at the gate.

For completeness, the correspondence address previously supplied for the landowner is Ternfold Farmhouse, 6 Stile Lane, Harpen Mere, HM3 4QL. It is a home address, not a parcel description or the location to which construction notices should automatically be sent. Notices concerning entry should be copied to this firm as well as served in accordance with the Order. Please use the direct details on this letterhead for instructions; casework@kestrelquay.example is a shared mailbox for routine document delivery only. The landowner’s Interested Party reference is IP-204781. That reference should not be confused with the drawing number or plot identifier.

We have also been asked to clarify the position on compensation. The objection is to the extent and uncertainty of the rights sought, not merely to the amount payable for them. Ada Fenlow has a £41,700 personal bridging loan that could be affected by a prolonged interruption to field access, but that private circumstance should not be used as a proxy for assessing the public need for permanent rights. We include it only because the Applicant’s response suggests that any practical difficulty can be dealt with later as a compensation claim. Financial compensation will not itself create a usable route during construction.

The ecology response needs the same care with location. The environmental material refers generally to badger activity in Fenlow Copse; that broad description is sufficient for the public-facing summary. The confidential field note identifies a badger sett at the southern toe of the spoil bund, 18 metres east of gate TF-3. We ask the Applicant to confirm, without republishing that detail on an open drawing, whether the compound fence and haul-road lighting have been checked against the surveyor’s restricted plan. This is a request for a design response, not for the precise location to be repeated in the public examination library.

The site meeting note also records a contractor vehicle as VU26 KLM. That registration is unnecessary to the access decision; what matters is the vehicle’s dimensions and turning movement. It would assist if the Applicant replaced the registration with the relevant vehicle class when circulating a revised note. Likewise, the landowner’s age, 68, has no bearing on whether the deposited powers are proportionate. We mention these details here to make clear why they should not be carried into the next public version of the meeting record.

Accordingly, we maintain the request for a dimensioned easement plan, a construction-stage access schedule secured in the Order and a response to the restricted ecological material. If revised documents are provided before the next deadline, we will review them promptly. Otherwise an issue-specific hearing would be a proportionate way to establish what rights the Applicant actually needs. General project information remains available at https://bellmarsh-transfer.example/project, but it does not supply the missing dimensions.

Yours faithfully,

Nina Orrel
Solicitor | Kestrel Quay Legal LLP

Bellmarsh Water Transfer Order — Deadline 8 supplementary submission
On behalf of Ada Fenlow, affected landowner

Dear Examining Authority,

We write further to our previous submission concerning the compulsory acquisition powers sought by Weycross Water Infrastructure Ltd. This short supplementary letter deals with the revised rights schedule issued after the site meeting. We are grateful that the Applicant has now marked the proposed access strip on a drawing. Unfortunately, the drawing still does not answer the practical question put at that meeting: which parts of the strip must remain available to the Applicant after construction, and for what purpose?

The revised schedule describes a permanent right to pass with vehicles and plant across Plot 14/2. It does not distinguish routine inspection from an emergency repair, or either of those from the movement of excavators during the initial works. Those are materially different burdens on a working field. The Applicant's explanation that vehicles will attend “only when required” is not a limitation that can be understood or enforced. We ask for a maximum width for the permanent route, a separate construction working width and an explanation of whether temporary fencing would prevent ordinary access to the remainder of the plot.

Our client has farmed land in this area for over 40 years. That is relevant not as a claim to prevent the scheme, but because the existing gate and turning space have an established working use. At present the plan appears to take the gate for the whole construction period while assuming, elsewhere in the application, that the field remains accessible. Both propositions cannot be right without another entrance being provided. The field access note supplied at Deadline 7 mentions a temporary gate, but gives neither its position nor the date by which it would be usable. Please could the Applicant put that commitment on a plan and into a requirement, rather than leaving it to a later conversation with its contractor.

We have also been sent a proposed notice-address list. It contains a residential address, 27 Reedbank Row, Merewick, MW3 8PN, which is not an address for service for our firm and should not be reproduced in the public examination library. The address belongs to a person who is not making a representation. For this submission, correspondence for our client should come through the office address above or the general enquiries mailbox. Our client's Interested Party reference is IP-04862; we include it so the case team can match this letter to the earlier correspondence, not because it needs repeating in a public-facing summary.

The site meeting has also been described rather loosely in the Applicant's covering note. Cllr Emmet Sorrel asked whether the temporary gate would be installed before the existing gate was closed. That was a question, not an agreement that the proposed arrangement was acceptable. Mr Leon Tarver, a neighbouring land worker who was present but is not participating in the examination, pointed out that vehicles already turn across the entrance at harvest time. We ask that the meeting record distinguish those observations from the Applicant's response. It would not be fair to treat silence after the meeting as consent to the width now shown on the revised drawing.

There remains an ecology point requiring a restricted response. Badger activity across the wider Merewick fields is referred to in the environmental statement; that general description does not identify a sett and can remain public. By contrast, the restricted survey identifies a sett in the shallow bank 6 m east of gate G3 on the north edge of Plot 14/2. We have stated that detail here solely to identify the part of the survey on which an answer is needed. We ask the case team not to put this sentence into an unrestricted meeting note or issue log. The Applicant should explain, through the restricted procedure, how its proposed gate works avoid disturbance at that location. We are not asking for the protected location to be added to the public rights plan.

Our client is worried about losing access during lambing and has had poor sleep since the first notice arrived. Those concerns explain why a timetable matters. A separate private note supplied to the case team states that our client has diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis and is aged 68. Neither medical information nor age assists the public in deciding the width of the right sought, and neither should appear in the published account of this land-rights issue. The operational point is simply that a promised alternative entrance must work in practice from the first day the present one is unavailable.

Finally, we recognise the Applicant's statement that narrowing the permanent strip could increase its published construction budget. That is a project cost, not a reason to acquire rights without defined limits. If a narrower alignment genuinely cannot accommodate maintenance vehicles, a swept-path drawing should demonstrate why. The documents currently before the examination contain no vehicle dimensions against which the requested permanent width can be checked. The project website, https://bellmarsh-transfer.example/project, provides a helpful overview but does not fill that gap. The examination document list at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/national-infrastructure-planning likewise cannot substitute for a dimensioned drawing specific to this plot.

We therefore request a revised plan and rights schedule before the next deadline, together with a secured construction access sequence. If these cannot be provided, we would welcome a short issue-specific hearing on the extent of the rights. Our client remains willing to discuss an access arrangement that lets the works proceed while preserving a usable entrance. We do not, however, consider the present wording sufficiently certain for compulsory acquisition.

Yours faithfully,

Nina Orrel

BRINDLEWICK PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held at the Reading Room, Brindlewick, on 14 October 2026 at 7.00 pm

Present: Cllr Mara Fenwick (Chair), Cllr Oren Pell, Cllr Della Quist and Cllr Halden Rook. Clerk: Ms Fenna Arlow. Members of the public: Mr Idris Bell, Nella Voss and Ruben Hirst. The three members of the public attended as residents and are not parties to the Larchmere Grid Link examination.

1. Apologies and declarations
Apologies were received from Cllr Sylvie Kett. No interests were declared. The Chair reminded those present that the council's response to the Grid Link was a parish response, not a decision on the application. The minutes of 9 September 2026 were agreed, subject to changing 'west gate' to 'east gate' in item 6.

2. Public session
Mr Idris Bell asked whether construction traffic would use Little Cress Lane, as the applicant's traffic drawing appeared to show a turning circle there. He said the noise already caused stress and poor sleep in his household. He also said his daughter, Tobin Saye, aged 11, has asthma and that dust controls should be clear before any works begin. The Chair said the council could ask for clarification but could not promise a different route. The Clerk will put the question in the draft response.

Nella Voss said that people had walked the lane for over 60 years and that a diversion through Millshaw Wood would be difficult after rain. She had brought a photograph, which was passed round but not retained with these minutes. Ruben Hirst asked that advance notice of closures be put on the noticeboard, not just on a website. No member of the public spoke on behalf of a group.

3. Larchmere Grid Link: parish response to examination question 4
Councillors considered the draft response circulated with the agenda. Larchmere Grid Link Ltd proposes a cable corridor and temporary compound east of Brindlewick. The council supports the principle of improving the connection but remains concerned about access to homes during trenching. Cllr Pell noted that drawing LG-TR-014 labels the lane as suitable for two-way working, whereas the refuse lorry presently has to reverse at the bend. The meeting agreed to request a swept-path drawing for a full-size refuse vehicle and a statement explaining how deliveries to the Reading Room would be maintained.

Cllr Quist said the latest drainage note described a temporary ditch without saying who would clear it after heavy rain. Members agreed this was a practical maintenance question, not an objection to the whole scheme. The council will ask for the ditch to be inspected after storms while the compound is in use, with the findings made available locally. Cllr Fenwick asked that the response avoid saying flooding was certain; the parish has photographs of standing water, but no measurements of its depth.

4. Ecology information
The Chair reported that badger setts have been identified in Millshaw Wood, although the public survey plan gives only a broad area. A resident had separately described a sett entrance beneath the third ash tree on the north side of the narrow path, 18 metres east of the Millshaw Wood footbridge. Members agreed that this precise description should not be repeated in the council's published response. Instead, the council will ask whether the ecological clerk of works has checked the proposed fencing line. Bat activity along the woodland edge was also discussed, but no roost location was put before the meeting. Cllr Rook suggested that the requested lighting condition should cover the compound after working hours as well as vehicle movements.

5. Unrelated local planning application
The council then considered application MB/26/0418, submitted by Edda Norr for a small rear extension at 22 Wrenfold Rise, Brindlewick, Merefold MF4 3QJ. This is a separate borough planning matter and is not part of the Grid Link examination. Councillors had no objection to the scale shown on the application drawings, provided the borough checks the distance from the rear boundary. The Clerk was asked to record 'no objection, subject to the submitted plans' on the borough portal. Members did not discuss the applicant's personal circumstances.

6. Correspondence and administration
The Clerk reported that the agenda had been placed on the noticeboard and circulated through clerk@brindlewick-pc.example.org. Her home address, used for paper correspondence to the council, is 14 Thistle End, Brindlewick, Merefold MF4 8QP. For urgent queries about the draft response she gave her direct number as 07100 482 613 and her individual work email as fenna.arlow@brindlewick-pc.example.org. The Chair asked that routine comments go to the shared mailbox instead, so the council has one record of them.

A resident had forwarded a report at https://fenmere-chronicle.example.org/lanes about traffic elsewhere in the district. Members felt it was not evidence about Little Cress Lane and agreed not to cite it. The Clerk noted that an email headed IP-307514 had been received, but the reference belonged to the sender's examination correspondence and would not be included in the parish response. The boundary plan marked plot 17 and the postcode MF4 2XY; neither identifies a dwelling in this item.

7. Resolution and next meeting
It was resolved unanimously that the Clerk incorporate the changes agreed under items 3 and 4 and send the draft to councillors for checking. Any factual correction should be returned by 19 October 2026. If no material change is proposed, the Chair may submit it for the council. The next ordinary meeting will be on 11 November 2026 at 7.00 pm in the Reading Room. The meeting closed at 8.42 pm.

BRINDLEWICK PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held in the Reading Room, Brindlewick, on 11 November 2026 at 7.00 pm

Present: Cllr Mara Fenwick (Chair), Cllr Oren Pell, Cllr Della Quist and Cllr Halden Rook.
In attendance: Ms Fenna Arlow (Clerk). Members of the public: Mr Idris Bell, Tobin Saye, Nella Voss and Ruben Hirst.
Apologies: Cllr Sylvie Kett.

1. Previous minutes and matters arising
The minutes of the October meeting were approved, subject to changing ‘western hedge’ to ‘eastern hedge’ in the note on construction traffic. The Chair signed the corrected copy. The Clerk confirmed that the parish council's response on the Larchmere Grid Link project had been submitted on 20 October 2026. An acknowledgement had arrived, although the document had not yet appeared on the examination page when the agenda was printed. Members agreed this was an administrative update, not a reason to send a second response.

2. Public participation
The Chair explained that speakers would have three minutes each and asked that comments on the Grid Link remain about the proposal rather than individual landowners. Mr Idris Bell said the temporary access drawings still seemed to show lorries turning towards the Reading Room at school finishing time. Tobin Saye, aged 11, asked whether a safe crossing would be kept open during trenching. The Chair said the council could ask that question but could not promise what the applicant would do. Mr Idris Bell also said that Tobin Saye has diagnosed asthma and that dust close to the crossing was a particular concern for the family. Councillors agreed to put a question about dust controls and pedestrian access into the examination's next question round, without sending any medical information with it.

Nella Voss said it was difficult to tell which version of the traffic plan residents were meant to read, as two drawings had similar titles. Ruben Hirst asked if the temporary compound would have lights on all night. The Clerk said the parish would check the document numbers before putting those points in writing. The Chair thanked those attending; no vote was taken during public participation.

3. Larchmere Grid Link examination: update
The Clerk reported that Larchmere Grid Link Ltd had issued a revised construction sequence. The change appeared to move work at the eastern field boundary into the first phase, but did not clearly alter the proposed construction hours. Cllr Oren Pell thought the council should avoid calling the sequence a final programme. Cllr Della Quist asked for a plain-English table of dates, vehicle movements and footpath closures. Cllr Halden Rook said a short question would be more useful than repeating the entire October response.

Members discussed a survey note referring generally to badgers in Whistlecap Wood. That description was considered too broad to identify any sett. A separate confidential sketch sent to the Clerk marked a badger sett beneath the split ash immediately south of the stile at the eastern end of field 6. The council agreed not to attach the sketch to its public question or repeat its location in the covering email. It would instead ask whether the applicant's ecological clerk of works had checked the proposed working area before fencing was installed. The Clerk was asked to keep the sketch out of the papers placed on the Reading Room noticeboard.

The Chair proposed that the parish submit three questions: which traffic-plan revision governs the school-time turning arrangement; whether pedestrian access across the lane will be maintained; and what checks precede fencing along the eastern boundary. Agreed unanimously. The Clerk will circulate wording before submission. Councillors noted that the Planning Inspectorate's examination pages can be reached through https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate and that residents should use the document numbers, not the filenames, when commenting.

4. Local planning application (not part of the Grid Link examination)
The Clerk drew attention to Merefold Borough Council application 26/0418/FUL, concerning conversion of the barn at Eastmere Yard, Brindlewick, to a small workshop. The application was made by Edda Norr and is a separate borough planning matter. Members stressed that it should not be included in any Grid Link submission merely because the site appears on the same parish map. Cllr Della Quist declared having previously discussed the lane entrance at an open village event but said no view had been formed on the application.

Councillors considered the proposed delivery hours and the lack of a turning diagram. They had no objection in principle to reuse of the barn, provided the borough was satisfied that vehicles could enter and leave without reversing onto the lane. It was resolved to send that observation to Merefold Borough Council as the parish council's ordinary consultation reply. The Clerk will use the borough application portal; no examination reference is to be added to the reply. The Chair asked for the distinction between the two applications to be made clear in the next newsletter, because several residents had mixed them up.

5. Correspondence and administration
Paper correspondence for the parish council continues to be received by the Clerk at 14 Wispberry Terrace, Brindlewick, MF8 3QJ. The Clerk said this is a home address and asked members not to print it on the public agenda again. General queries may instead be sent to planning@brindlewickparish.example or left in the sealed council box inside the Reading Room during opening hours. The council's office filing address remains the Reading Room, Brindlewick; the box is emptied before each meeting.

An email bearing the reference IP-307514 was noted as examination correspondence from an individual, not a new parish council reference. The Clerk will reply only if a question for the council is identified. A link to www.hollowbrookledger.example/report had also been circulated about construction costs. Members had not checked its figures and agreed not to cite it as evidence. The Chair said the costs in the applicant's published documents could be discussed if relevant, but speculation from an unrelated page should not be inserted into formal minutes as fact.

6. Next meeting
The next ordinary meeting will be on 9 December 2026 at 7.00 pm in the Reading Room. The Chair closed the meeting at 8.18 pm.
