Brindlewick Parish Council
Draft minutes of the ordinary meeting held on 9 December 2026 at 7.00 pm in the Reading Room, Brindlewick

Present: Cllr Mara Fenwick (Chair), Cllr Oren Pell, Cllr Della Quist and Cllr Halden Rook. In attendance: Ms Fenna Arlow (Clerk). Members of the public: Mr Idris Bell, Tobin Saye, Nella Voss and Ruben Hirst.

1. Apologies and declarations
Apologies were received from Cllr Sylvie Kett. No interests were declared. The Chair reminded everyone that public comments would be recorded in summary, not as a word-for-word transcript.

2. Previous minutes
The draft minutes of the November meeting were approved, subject to correcting the date on which the applicant's traffic note had been received. Cllr Pell asked that the record be clear that the council had not endorsed the construction-cost figures in the unrelated web page mentioned under item 5. The Clerk confirmed that the page had not been cited in the council's submission. The Chair signed the corrected minutes for the council file.

3. Larchmere Grid Link examination: response to the Examining Authority
The Clerk reported that the council had received a request for comments on the proposed temporary haul route. The deadline was 6 January 2027. Members agreed that the reply should concentrate on matters within the parish: use of the Reading Room junction, pedestrian access to the school crossing and the proposed hours for heavy vehicles. The council does not object to the principle of a grid connection in this response; that is a separate matter from whether this route is workable.

Cllr Quist said the plan's arrow at the eastern junction appeared to send lorries across the narrow side of the bend. Cllr Rook had measured the carriageway during the site walk but cautioned that a tape measurement was not a swept-path assessment. Members asked for the relevant drawing to be checked against the applicant's latest version before any figure was quoted. The Clerk will put the draft response on the agenda for a short extraordinary meeting if revised drawings arrive too late for circulation by email. Material on www.larchmeregridlink.example/documents can be used to identify the drawing, provided the document number and revision are given.

4. Public participation on the haul route
Mr Idris Bell asked how children would reach the crossing if the eastern footway was fenced off. The speaker said that Tobin Saye, aged 13, has diagnosed asthma and that dust from queuing lorries was a particular worry for the family. The Chair thanked the speaker and said the council could ask for dust-control measures without including the family's health details in its formal response. The Clerk's note of the question will be retained with the meeting papers, not appended to the submission.

Nella Voss said the applicant's map appeared to show the temporary compound gate on the wrong side of the hedge. This was a useful point to check, but members could not settle a boundary from the printed A4 copy at the meeting. Ruben Hirst asked whether a marshal would be present at school opening time. No member had found a firm commitment on that point in the draft construction plan. The Chair asked the Clerk to seek the page reference rather than assume there was none. The public session ended at 7.46 pm.

5. Ecology note supplied for the council file
The Clerk had received a short note about signs of badgers near the proposed cable corridor. It included the description: “the active sett entrance is 11 metres north-east of the second stile on Brindlewick Footpath 8, beneath the split ash at the field corner”. Members agreed not to reproduce that detail in the examination response or on the public noticeboard. The council may instead say that badger setts have been reported in Mallowbank Wood and ask the applicant's ecologist to check whether the survey and avoidance measures remain adequate. No finding about the status of the sett was made by the council.

6. Local planning application, not part of the Grid Link examination
The Chair introduced Merefold Borough Council application MF/26/0418/H, for a single-storey side extension at 6 Thistledown Row, Brindlewick. The application was made by Edda Norr. This item concerned a separate householder proposal and would not be included in any submission to the Planning Inspectorate. Members considered the published elevation and the neighbour-consultation date. Cllr Pell thought the roof height on the revised sketch was lower than on the earlier version; Cllr Quist asked that the Borough Council confirm which sketch was current.

The council resolved to send a neutral comment requesting clarification of the drawing revision and the position of the rainwater outlet. Members made no comment on the applicant's personal circumstances. The application-site address was used only to identify the proposal before the council. The Clerk will submit the comment through the Borough Council's planning portal before its consultation closes.

7. Correspondence and administration
Paper correspondence for the parish council is currently delivered to the Clerk at 14 Mallowbank Close, Brindlewick, BW4 8QN. The Clerk asked members not to put that address on flyers advertising the Grid Link examination. General enquiries can go to planning@brindlewickpc.example; the council will arrange collection of paper comments at the Reading Room for residents who do not use email. The Chair noted that individual representations must be sent through the examination's published arrangements if residents want them considered as such. Passing a comment to a councillor does not automatically make it a representation.

8. Actions and close
The Clerk will circulate a draft haul-route response with drawing references, request clarification about the junction marshal and submit the separate householder-planning comment. Cllr Rook will check the latest traffic drawing; Cllr Quist will check the footway wording. The next meeting date will be confirmed on the noticeboard after the holiday period. The Chair closed the meeting at 8.31 pm.

MEREHAVEN BOROUGH COUNCIL

LOCAL IMPACT REPORT: GREYWICK TIDAL LINK
Planning Inspectorate reference: EN020147
Submitted for Deadline 4, 21 October 2026

1. Purpose and scope

1.1 This Local Impact Report (LIR) is made by Merehaven Borough Council in relation to the application by Greywick Tidal Link Ltd for a development consent order. The proposed works comprise a tidal energy landing point, an underground cable route, a converter station at East Mere Flats and associated highway works. This report describes likely effects on the borough, whether beneficial or adverse. It is not the Council's final view on whether development consent should be granted.

1.2 The Council's principal office is at Civic Hall, 14 Charter Quay, Merehaven, MV4 8QP. Correspondence about this report should be sent to planning@merehaven-borough.gov.uk. The public can find an explanation of the NSIP process at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. The office address and mailbox are provided for administrative purposes, not as addresses for residents affected by the scheme.

2. Local setting

2.1 The cable would pass through agricultural land between Greywick Shore and East Mere Flats. The route crosses Foxglove Lane, the Saltmarsh Way public footpath and the Merehaven Drain. Houses at the eastern edge of Greywick face the proposed construction corridor, although the closest compounds would be screened by existing hedgerows. The land also forms part of a wider drainage area which flooded during the winters of 2020 and 2024. Those dates describe flood events, not the duration of any resident's exposure to flooding.

2.2 Members have repeatedly heard that people use Saltmarsh Way to reach the shore without a car. Cllr Mira Lorne asked at the Council's infrastructure committee on 7 September 2026 for the temporary diversion to be signposted before fencing is erected, rather than afterwards. Cllr Oswin Cade raised the need to keep the school bus turning area on Foxglove Lane clear. Halden Firth MP wrote to the Council in August 2026 asking that emergency access be maintained during cable trenching. These comments are recorded as matters of local impact; they should not be read as statements of support for or objection to the application.

3. Construction traffic and access

3.1 The draft Construction Traffic Management Plan proposes that heavy goods vehicles approach the converter station from the B418 rather than through Greywick centre. The Council supports that principle, but the swept-path drawing does not show how a vehicle would pass a bus at the Foxglove Lane junction. A revised drawing and a banksman procedure should be secured before construction starts. The Council also seeks a clear process for reporting a missed delivery slot to the site manager. That process should use a project mailbox, not residents' telephone numbers.

3.2 At a Council drop-in session on 3 June 2026, two residents who have not registered as participants, Tessa Marn and Ivo Pell, described difficulty crossing the B418 in the evening. The Council records their names here solely because they appear in the contemporaneous attendance note; its assessment does not depend on identifying either person. The attendance note also refers to a household at 27 Willow Fold, Greywick, MV4 6RL. This is a residential address and is not a location of proposed works. The point raised was that the temporary crossing shown on drawing GWL-TR-014 may be too far from the existing bus stop.

3.3 Another resident explained that poor sleep during previous roadworks made the prospect of night-time works worrying. This is a report of an effect and a concern, not a medical diagnosis. A separate written account attributed to Adela Prinn, aged 73, states that the resident has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is concerned about dust. The Council has not sought to verify personal medical information. Its planning point is that dust monitoring locations should include homes near the eastern compound, and the trigger levels should be set out in the Construction Environmental Management Plan.

4. Landscape, ecology and drainage

4.1 The permanent converter building would be visible from parts of Saltmarsh Way and from the upper floors of houses on the edge of East Mere. The proposed planting is welcome, but the landscape drawings should specify replacement arrangements if trees fail during the first five growing seasons. A five-year maintenance period is a proposed planning control, not information about any individual's age.

4.2 Badger activity has been recorded in Mariner's Wood, and bat surveys covered the woodland edge and the drain. These broad descriptions are sufficient for the public version of this report. A confidential ecology note supplied to the Council identifies a badger sett in the ditch at the south-west corner of Field 18, 12 metres east of the Foxglove Lane culvert. That detail should be confined to the protected-species material considered by the Examining Authority. The Council does not suggest that all woodland or species references require confidential treatment.

4.3 The applicant's drainage assessment assumes that construction runoff can be held within the eastern compound during an intense storm. The Council requests a drawing showing the exceedance route if that storage is full. Discharge must not increase flows into the Merehaven Drain at the allotment bridge. The Council's concern is with the design assumption, not an allegation about the applicant or its staff.

5. Local services and requested controls

5.1 The converter station is not expected to place a material long-term demand on schools or health services. Construction workers may, however, add short peaks in demand for parking and food outlets around Greywick Square. The Council asks for a travel plan with measurable targets and a named role, rather than a named individual, responsible for complaints. A publicly available monthly log should show the number and subject of complaints without publishing personal contact details.

5.2 Subject to further examination, the Council considers that the principal local effects could be managed through requirements covering traffic, working hours, drainage, dust and landscape maintenance. The authority reserves its position on the wording of those requirements. For clarity, this LIR is submitted from Civic Hall on behalf of Merehaven Borough Council; it does not incorporate the unpublished attendance note or any resident's medical account as an annex.

WRENFOLD LAND & LEGAL
14 Ledger Square, Bellwick, BW2 6FD
Direct dial: 01632 960 245 | Email: elin.voss@wrenfoldlegal.example
General enquiries: land@wrenfoldlegal.example

21 October 2026

To: The Examining Authority
Re: Fenwick Channel Link Project — compulsory acquisition hearing and draft Development Consent Order
Application reference: EN010284 | Interested Party reference: FCL-10478

Dear Examining Authority,

I write for Mara Quell, the owner of land shown as plots 4/17, 4/18 and 4/21 on the applicant’s Land Plans. This is a further submission on compulsory acquisition, following the hearing on 8 October. Please read it with my client’s earlier representation. The point is not an objection to the link in principle. It is that the powers presently sought over these particular plots are wider, and rather less clear, than the works described at the hearing.

The land is operated as part of The Old Kiln Farm. For completeness, the farm correspondence address supplied on the land interest form is The Old Kiln Farm, 7 Merefold Lane, Bellwick, BW1 4QJ. That address should not be confused with the proposed works site. The holding has a narrow internal track between the yard and the eastern grazing fields. On the revised Works Plan, temporary possession is shown across that track for up to 18 months, although the construction explanation refers to a crossing used intermittently for cable deliveries. An intermittent crossing and the loss of the only usable track are quite different propositions for day-to-day farming.

At the hearing the applicant said that access would be maintained “where reasonably practicable”. That wording is not a substitute for a drawing. It leaves the question of who decides what is practicable, how much notice must be given, and where stock and machinery are meant to go during a closure. We ask the applicant to provide a dimensioned access plan before the close of the examination. It should show the running width, turning space for a livestock trailer, temporary fencing, gate positions and the person to contact when the route is blocked. The plan should be secured in the DCO, rather than left as an aspiration in the Code of Construction Practice.

There is also a discrepancy in the Book of Reference. Plot 4/18 is described as pasture, but it includes the hardstanding on which feed is delivered. Moving the delivery point onto Merefold Lane is not straightforward: vehicles would have to stop on a bend without a safe place to turn. The applicant’s response to written question CA.2.14 says deliveries can be rescheduled. Feed deliveries cannot simply be put off whenever works traffic is expected. Please would the applicant explain the evidence behind that answer and correct the plot description.

My client’s concern about compensation is separate from the question of whether the powers are justified. The private valuation obtained for the holding was £184,000 for the affected interest. That figure is not put forward as a valuation for the examination to determine; it is mentioned to explain why an undefined period of access interference matters in practice. It does not answer the statutory tests for compulsory acquisition. In particular, an undertaking to discuss compensation later does not show that the full extent of permanent rights in plot 4/21 is needed now.

The western edge of plot 4/21 contains an existing drain. The Rights Plan appears to allow installation and future maintenance across the whole width of the plot, while the cross-section in the applicant’s technical note shows a much narrower working strip. If the note is accurate, the rights should follow that strip, with an express exception for ordinary drain clearance. If it is not accurate, an amended cross-section is needed. Otherwise the landowner cannot tell where future cultivation or repair could be restricted.

Two further matters arose after the hearing. First, Mrs Sella Brode, at 9 Sedge Rise, Bellwick, BW1 4QH, reported that the temporary fence shown beside the lane would prevent access to the shared field gate. This person has not made a representation in the examination; I pass on the point because the gate is marked on the applicant’s own survey. Secondly, my client’s grandson, Ivo Quell, aged 16, helps move equipment between the yard and fields outside school hours. The proposed crossing arrangement should be understandable and safe for anyone using the farm track, not just a contractor familiar with the traffic plan.

I have seen the ecological addendum and do not suggest that every animal record needs to be published with a precise location. Badger activity is recorded generally in Wispfen Wood; that description is sufficient for the point made here. The addendum’s confidential plan, however, marks an active sett in the bank 6 metres east of gate G4 on the north side of plot 4/17. If that plan is to be placed on the public examination page, the precise description should be withheld while the necessary information remains available to the examining and ecological teams. My client asks whether the proposed alternative track has been checked against the confidential ecology information, rather than assuming the present alignment is the only option.

Cllr Hester Durn asked at the hearing whether a farm-access protocol could be agreed before construction. That would be useful, but a protocol not yet drafted should not carry the whole weight of the compulsory acquisition case. The applicant’s project page, https://fenwickchannellink.example, lists its current drawings; the general government guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects explains how examination documents can be submitted. Neither resolves the missing access detail.

I therefore ask the Examining Authority to require: a corrected Book of Reference entry for plot 4/18; a scaled drawing and secured access measures for the track; and a justification for the width of rights sought over plot 4/21. If those documents cannot be provided in the examination timetable, my client asks that the relevant powers be narrowed rather than settled by a private discussion after consent. I am happy to respond to a focused written question. Please use the direct contact details above for procedural correspondence, not the farm address.

Yours faithfully,

Elin Voss

To the Examining Authority
Fenwick Channel Link Project — EN071642
Supplementary submission on compulsory acquisition: plots 4/18 and 4/21

I write as land agent for Mara Quell, an affected landowner and Interested Party. This note follows my earlier request for a corrected Book of Reference entry, a scaled access drawing and an explanation of the width of rights sought over plot 4/21. It is not intended to replace that request. I am sending it because the applicant's latest response describes the farm track as an issue that can be dealt with during detailed design, whereas the land to be acquired and the access that must remain available are matters for this examination.

The distinction matters on the ground. Plot 4/18 includes the approach used by agricultural vehicles entering from Mere Cut Lane. Plot 4/21 is the narrow strip beside it over which Fenwick Channel Energy Ltd seeks permanent rights. The applicant's drawing shows a line for an access, but no usable width at the pinch point, no turning provision and no indication of where a gate could open while works vehicles are present. A promise to agree those details later is not the same thing as securing an access that can be used while the works take place.

My client is not asking the Examining Authority to design a farm entrance. She is asking it to test whether the powers now requested are necessary and proportionate. The applicant could answer that question with one drawing showing the existing and proposed edges of the track, the proposed working area, any temporary fencing and the swept path of the largest vehicle it expects my client to use. The drawing should identify which parts are illustrative and which will be secured. At present those matters are spread between different plans, and the lines do not appear to meet. Please do not treat my client's ability to pass on foot through the land as an answer to the vehicle-access question.

For completeness, my client's correspondence address is Mossgate Farm, 7 Mere Cut Lane, Belwick, ZX4 7QP. I include it only to identify the holding affected by the plots; procedural correspondence should come to my direct contact details on this letterhead. Her Interested Party reference is IP-024718. The site postcode, ZX4 7QP, also appears on the applicant's location plan, but the plan does not show the gate arrangement with sufficient precision to resolve this point.

At the hearing, Cllr Hester Durn asked whether farm access would remain available throughout construction. I understood the applicant's answer to be that a traffic-management plan would deal with it. That may describe how vehicles will be marshalled, but it does not say what happens when the entrance is occupied by fencing, stored materials or a vehicle waiting to enter the working area. Mrs Sella Brode, who uses the adjoining field gate but has not joined the examination, raised the same practical difficulty with my client. I mention the conversation only to explain why the gate positions need to be shown, not as evidence of a separate objection from her.

There is also a mismatch between the statement that no residential access will be impeded and the proposed working hours. My client's grandson, Ivo Quell, sometimes waits at the holding after school. He is aged 11. No special arrangement is being sought on his behalf; this is a straightforward reason why the route used by ordinary visitors as well as farm vehicles must be legible and safe. The uncertainty has caused my client stress and poor sleep. Those effects would be reduced by a clear, enforceable access proposal rather than an assurance that a contractor will be considerate.

I have checked the ecology note supplied with the applicant's response because its proposed fencing overlaps the same entrance. It refers generally to badger activity in Brindle Shaw, which does not itself establish a constraint at the gate. A separate field annotation supplied to us describes a sett in the hedge bank 12 metres east of the northern gate to plot 4/21, beneath the split ash stump. That annotation should not be reproduced on an unrestricted access plan. The applicant can show the required fencing envelope without publishing the sett position, and can explain in its confidential ecological material how the two requirements will be reconciled. My access request is not a request to remove ecological protection.

For the avoidance of doubt, I do not accept that the proposed permanent rights over the whole width of plot 4/21 are justified merely because the applicant might need flexibility during construction. Temporary occupation and permanent acquisition are different propositions. If the applicant's final design requires less land, the Order limits should reflect that, or the applicant should identify precisely which rights it says must survive construction and why. The current wording would leave my client managing the uncertainty indefinitely. Her private estimate of the loss to the holding is £38,500; that figure is not offered as a substitute for the statutory test or for the applicant's evidence about the extent of its powers.

The Planning Inspectorate's published guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects explains the document-submission process. It does not, of course, determine whether these particular rights are needed. I ask the Examining Authority to seek the scaled drawing and a plot-by-plot explanation before the relevant deadline, and to allow my client a short opportunity to comment on them. If the applicant cannot provide both, the safer course is to narrow the powers now rather than leave an essential means of access to an agreement after consent.

Further written submission on behalf of Mara Quell — access to Rushbank Holding

Dear Examining Authority,

I write for Mara Quell following our submission on the width and duration of the rights sought over Rushbank Holding. This letter deals with a related point raised at the hearing: whether the access shown on the current plans could actually be used while construction traffic is entering the western worksite. It is not an objection to temporary access in principle. My client accepts that works vehicles must reach the site. The question is whether Fenwick Channel Energy Ltd needs the full area it has requested when the only workable route to the holding has not yet been demonstrated on a scaled drawing.

The applicant’s latest note says that ordinary farm access will be “maintained where practicable”. That is not quite an answer. The holding is used daily, not just at harvest, and the proposed turning area crosses the track used by feed deliveries and the livestock trailer. The note does not give a minimum clear width, identify who has priority at the gate, or say what happens when a delivery arrives while an abnormal load is being marshalled. I appreciate these arrangements can change during construction, but the acquisition powers will not change as readily. An enforceable minimum arrangement is therefore needed before those powers are settled.

At the hearing, Cllr Hester Durn asked whether a vehicle could wait off the public road without blocking the farm entrance. I understood the applicant’s answer to be that its contractor would prepare a traffic-management plan later. There was no drawing of a waiting space in the material before us. Nor did the answer address access for smaller vehicles when a larger delivery is delayed. Please could the applicant show, on the same plan, the construction gate, any holding bay, the retained farm track and the swept paths in both directions? A drawing at a scale where these features can be measured would be more helpful than another assurance that liaison will take place.

There is a further practical issue with the field gate. Mrs Sella Brode, who lives nearby but is not a party to this examination, mentioned that vehicles already reverse towards it when the lane is busy. I do not ask the Examining Authority to treat that conversation as traffic evidence. It does, however, explain why my client wants the applicant to test the arrangement rather than assume that drivers can simply wait at the gate. If a temporary gate is proposed instead, the plan should show its position and confirm who will install, maintain and remove it. The reinstatement obligation should cover the posts and adjoining drainage, not only the track surface.

Rushbank Holding is also a home. Correspondence addressed to my client there goes to 17 Rushbank Lane, Brindlewick, BW4 8RU; that is a residential address, not the project’s site address. Her grandson, Ivo Quell, aged 13, visits after school and sometimes walks from the house to the lower yard. I mention this because the applicant’s proposed pedestrian diversion appears to meet the construction route at an unsupervised crossing. My client is not requesting a special route for one family. A marked pedestrian crossing, with a stated means of keeping it clear during vehicle movements, would assist anybody using the holding. My client is anxious about the present drawing, but anxiety alone is not the point on which this request depends.

The same uncertainty affects the proposed compound boundary. The red line on Sheet CA-14 runs close to the open ditch, while the draft access schedule appears to permit fencing anywhere within the wider parcel. Those documents should be reconciled. The applicant should identify the maximum fenced area it says is required, distinguish temporary occupation from permanent rights, and explain why the drainage strip cannot remain available to the holding. Its published estimate of £2.4 million for the access and compound works is a project cost; it tells us nothing about why this particular breadth of rights is necessary. My client has not agreed to leave the boundary to later negotiation.

For completeness, a badger survey records field signs in the wider Rushbank Wood area. That general reference does not locate a sett, and I am not asking for a sensitive species location to be put on a public access drawing. If ecological constraints are relied upon to justify shifting the gate or widening the compound, the applicant can explain the design consequence without publishing a precise location. At present it is difficult to tell whether ecology, vehicle geometry or contractor preference has determined the line on the plan.

I ask the Examining Authority to request three items by the next relevant deadline: a scaled access and swept-path drawing; a plot-by-plot explanation of the land and rights needed for the gate, waiting space and drainage; and proposed wording that guarantees usable farm and pedestrian access throughout the works. If the proposed wording depends on a later plan, it should state who approves that plan and what happens if agreement is not reached. My client should then have a short opportunity to comment. Without these items, the examination cannot reliably distinguish land needed for the project from land included for convenience.

Please place this letter on the examination website as a submission for my client. Her Interested Party reference is IP-483726. I can supply the existing gate measurements to the applicant through the usual examination process, but they should not be taken as acceptance of its acquisition case. I have copied this letter to the project mailbox so that the request for a drawing is clear to all parties.
