6. ECOLOGY AND NATURE CONSERVATION
Merevale Link Energy Park Environmental Statement, Volume 2
Prepared by Dr Nessa Varn MSc MCIEEM of Barlowe Ecology Ltd for Valequay Renewables Ltd

6.1 Scope and approach
This chapter considers the construction, operation and decommissioning of the proposed solar arrays, cable route and access improvements at Mothwick Farm. It should be read with the habitat plans and the restricted ecological records in Appendix 6C. The survey area includes arable fields, drainage grips, two blocks of plantation woodland and a group of redundant agricultural buildings. Surveys were undertaken between April and September 2025, with a walkover update in March 2026. Weather, access and survey limitations are set out below rather than being treated as evidence that a species is absent. The proposed layout has changed since the first survey; the assessment uses Revision P04, dated 12 June 2026.

6.2 Baseline habitats
Most of the development footprint is regularly cultivated land of low botanical interest. Gorseglass Wood and the hedgerows north of Bramblefen Lane provide more continuous cover and are used by commuting bats. Several field margins contain tussocky grass, and a wet ditch connects the western fields to the larger drainage network. There are badger field signs across Mothwick Farm, but signs alone do not establish where an occupied sett is located. The woodland edge will remain outside the fenced array, although temporary working areas are proposed beside it. Figure 6.3 shows broad habitat parcels; it is not intended to show entrances, nests or roost access points.

6.3 Badgers
A check of suitable banks, spoil heaps and woodland margins found two active setts and one group of disused holes. The restricted survey record gives the following locators: Sett B1 is in the east bank of the disused drainage grip, 6 m north of gate G3 in Plot 14, at local survey coordinates E 438.6 / N 211.2. Sett B2 lies beneath the western root plate of the forked ash immediately behind the southern end of the old cart shed, Plot 9; its principal entrance faces the shed's rear wall. These details are included here for technical review, not for display on a public constraints map. More generally, badger setts were recorded in and around Gorseglass Wood. No sett entrance would be directly filled under Revision P04. Trenching, night working and storage of excavated material could nevertheless obstruct established routes or disturb animals if controls are not followed. A pre-construction check will confirm activity before groundworks begin; any necessary licence and exclusion measures will be agreed with the appropriate authority.

6.4 Bats
Activity transects and static detectors recorded common pipistrelle, soprano pipistrelle and occasional barbastelle passes. Bat activity was greatest along the connected hedges; it was substantially lower in the centre of the open arable fields. Buildings and trees were inspected where access was safe. A small common pipistrelle day roost was identified under a loose tile on the north roof slope of the cart shed at Mothwick Farm. This is not a maternity roost, and the building is retained. A maternity roost was confirmed at the north-east corner of the upper hayloft in Building H2, where the roof plate meets the brick gable directly above the second loading-door hinge. A separate, large barbastelle roost occupies the hollow on the inward-facing limb of tree T47, 4.2 m above ground and immediately east of culvert C5 in Plot 11. These two locators are held on the restricted drawing EC-07. Bat roosts were also found within the Mothwick Farm building group; that description is sufficient for the non-restricted plan. Further emergence surveys are required if the detailed cable design changes the proposed tree-retention area.

6.5 Birds and other fauna
Breeding-bird visits recorded skylark in the open fields and a range of common hedge-nesting birds. A barn owl nest was confirmed inside the boarded recess above the western feed hatch of Building H3, 1.5 m south of the internal ladder and opposite the yard entrance. The precise nest position is relevant to the construction method but should not appear on drawings issued to the general site workforce. Barn owls have been observed around the Mothwick Farm buildings; this broader description does not identify the nest. No works to Building H3 are currently proposed. The wet ditch provides possible foraging habitat for otters, although no holt was identified during the accessible-bank inspection. No conclusion is drawn about inaccessible lengths beyond the survey boundary.

6.6 Assessment of effects
Without mitigation, construction could cause temporary loss of field-margin habitat, interruption of commuting routes, disturbance from lighting and a risk of harm where vehicles cross animal paths. The principal operational change would be conversion of cultivated land to managed grassland beneath and between panels. This may increase some foraging opportunities, but it does not remove the need to protect existing roosts and nesting places. The buried cable would pass near the woodland edge rather than through Gorseglass Wood. The assessment assumes that the hedgerow gaps shown on Drawing L-12 are the maximum extent of removal. If the contractor requires wider gaps, the effects must be reviewed before clearance. References to approximately 40 years of farming at Mothwick Farm describe land management history, not the age of any individual.

6.7 Mitigation and monitoring
A suitably qualified ecologist will mark sensitive working zones on a controlled site plan and brief the principal contractor before vegetation clearance. Restricted location data will be supplied only to staff who need it for that work. The ecological clerk of works will inspect open excavations daily, confirm that escape ramps remain in place and halt activity where unexpected evidence of an occupied sett, roost or nest is found. Lighting will face away from retained hedges and buildings, with task lighting switched off when not required. Tree protection fencing will be installed before compounds are established. Any replacement roost features will be specified after the final building and tree schedule is approved; boxes are not assumed to compensate automatically for the loss of a maternity or large rare-species roost. Monitoring in years 1, 3 and 5 will review habitat establishment and the effectiveness of the working-zone controls. General project enquiries may be sent to ecology@barlowe-ecology.example.

9.8 Residual ecological effects and information for detailed design

9.8.1 This section should be read with the construction controls set out above. The assessment covers the cable corridor, inverter compounds, temporary haul route and land needed for reinstatement at Merevale Link Energy Park. It has been prepared for Valequay Renewables Ltd by Barlowe Ecology Ltd. The field record was compiled by Dr Nessa Varn of Barlowe Ecology Ltd in April 2026. Survey sheets distinguish a confirmed breeding site from signs of occasional use; a record of activity is not, on its own, evidence that an animal will be present when works start. The protected-site details below are provided to explain the assessment and should be held in a restricted ecological working drawing rather than placed on a public-facing constraints plan.

9.8.2 Badger activity was recorded along the western boundary and in Merevale Wood. Those descriptions are deliberately broad and should not be used to set out exclusion fencing. The main sett entrance was recorded at grid reference MZ 18437 62814, beneath the north bank of the ditch 23 m east of gate G4. A second, apparently subsidiary entrance lies in the hedge-root plate immediately behind pole P17 on the eastern edge of Parcel 6. Fresh spoil and bedding were present at the first entrance in the September visit; the second showed spoil but no fresh bedding. Camera observations cannot establish the number of badgers using either entrance. The nearest proposed excavation can be shifted within the agreed working width, and the final peg-out must be checked against both entrances before vegetation clearance. No assumption is made here that a licence will be granted merely because an application is submitted.

9.8.3 Bat transects found activity along the retained hedgerows, particularly near the watercourse north of the village. This is a useful description of the commuting habitat, not a roost location. Inspection of buildings identified a common pipistrelle day roost in the roof void of Old Mill Store; the proposed works do not affect that building. A maternity roost was confirmed in the gap behind the third weatherboard from the left on the south gable of Brindle Barn (grid reference MZ 18502 62776). Emergence counts varied across the season, and the count reported in Appendix 9C is a minimum, not an estimate of the whole local population. A large roost of the locally scarce grey long-eared bat was also located in the cavity 2.4 m above ground on the west face of veteran oak T38, at MZ 18391 62852. The oak is to be retained with its root protection area fenced before plant arrives. These two records require separate checks at detailed design stage: a standard box on a new pole would not replace the function of either feature.

9.8.4 Bat activity across the wider site does not justify lighting every access point throughout the night. The lighting schedule will use shielded fittings and a shut-off arrangement at the temporary crossing, subject to construction safety requirements. Where evening working is unavoidable, the ecological clerk of works will review the actual beam spread on site rather than rely solely on the manufacturer's drawing. Monitoring should record whether the unlit hedge connection remains usable, including after the haul route surface has been taken up. A change in flight activity at one detector may reflect weather or season, so the results will be interpreted alongside the pre-construction baseline.

9.8.5 Barn owl was observed hunting across the eastern grazing fields. That observation is not itself a nest record. The occupied nest was identified on the rear beam of the north-east bay of Cresswell Pump Shed, at MZ 18721 62644. The shed is outside the permanent land take but close enough to the temporary vehicle route for disturbance to be possible if traffic queuing is allowed beside it. Deliveries will therefore be scheduled to avoid stationary vehicles on that section of route during the breeding period, with the precise restriction confirmed by a pre-start check. Other farmland birds, including skylark and yellowhammer, were recorded in the wider survey area. Their individual song posts have not been treated as fixed nest positions; vegetation removal will be timed or preceded by a competent check as appropriate.

9.8.6 The watercourse and adjacent rough grassland may support otter foraging. Footprints on a muddy bar were recorded, but no holt was confirmed in the survey area. The description “along the Merevale Beck corridor” is intentionally approximate. No new permanent culvert is proposed. Temporary crossing details must allow the banks to be restored without leaving a steep-sided trap, and any pollution incident will be reported under the construction environmental management plan. Bat and badger survey results will also be reviewed after any material change to the working footprint; the absence of a record on an earlier visit is not a guarantee of absence later.

9.8.7 Subject to the avoidance measures and the further checks above, residual effects on the retained hedgerow network are assessed as not significant at the project scale. That conclusion is conditional: if the route moves towards an occupied sett or either sensitive bat roost, the design and effects assessment must be revisited before the relevant works proceed. Habitat creation on the restored margins is expected to improve connectivity in the medium term, but it is not counted as an immediate substitute for existing roost structures. The public register may refer to badger setts in Merevale Wood and bats around Brindle Barn without repeating the restricted field coordinates. The applicant's project correspondence can be sent to ecology@barlowe-ecology.example; that shared mailbox is not a substitute for notifying the site ecologist of an unexpected find on the day.

8.9 Protected species: survey findings and design response

8.9.1 This section continues the assessment of the retained hedgerow network and sets out the locations used for the construction-stage constraints plan. It has been prepared by Dr Nessa Varn of Barlowe Ecology Ltd for Valequay Renewables Ltd in relation to Merevale Link Energy Park. The locations below are included so that the limits of the assessment can be checked against the final working drawings. They should not be reproduced on the public site notice. References to Field M17, Building B6 and Track R3 are construction-plan identifiers, not survey dates.

8.9.2 Walkover surveys took place in April, June and September 2025, with supplementary emergence and re-entry visits in suitable weather. Access to the western bank was restricted on one June visit by standing water; this was recorded as a limitation rather than treated as evidence that species were absent. The results describe conditions at the time of survey. An animal may move into a suitable feature between that visit and the start of works, particularly where clearance is delayed into a later season.

Badger

8.9.3 Badger activity was recorded throughout Merevale Wood. That broad description is sufficient for the public register, but not for setting out an exclusion area on the works plan. The principal occupied sett is in the north bank of Ditch D4, 6 m east of Culvert C2, at site grid E 248216 N 371304. Fresh spoil, bedding and regularly used entrances were present on both April and September visits. A subsidiary sett was recorded under the east root plate of the ash at the south end of Field M18, site grid E 248307 N 371118. Its entrances appeared inactive in September, although inactivity on one visit must not be taken as permanent abandonment. Badger paths also crossed the proposed cable corridor west of the compound; paths alone do not establish another sett location.

8.9.4 No excavation, tracking of heavy plant or storage of spoil is proposed within the stand-off areas shown on the confidential constraints drawing. The fencing line will be checked in the field by the site ecologist before it is pegged out. If trenching or drainage levels need to change, the construction manager must refer the revision back for ecological review rather than relying on a distance measured from a small-scale figure. Night working near retained habitat is to be avoided, and open trenches will be covered or provided with a means of escape at the end of each shift.

Bats

8.9.5 Activity transects recorded common pipistrelle along the eastern hedge and occasional passes by other bats around Brindle Barn. The presence of bats in that general area does not, by itself, identify a roost. Emergence surveys did, however, confirm a maternity roost behind the third timber weatherboard from the left on the north gable of Brindle Barn, site grid E 248659 N 370902. A separate, large barbastelle roost was confirmed within the split oak marked T42 at site grid E 248776 N 370755, immediately beside Track R3. The two features have different sensitivities and must not be combined as a single dot on a general arrangement plan.

8.9.6 A small, non-maternity common pipistrelle roost was also found under the south eaves of the pump shed (Building B6). This feature is shown on the ordinary ecological features plan and will be retained. Its description should not be confused with the restricted maternity-roost record above. Several other trees have potential roost features but no confirmed occupation. The assessment assumes that these trees remain unless a later drawing expressly identifies removal and is reviewed by the project ecologist.

8.9.7 The lighting schedule requires directional fittings at the compound, with no permanent illumination of the barn gable, the retained split oak or the connecting hedgerow. Temporary security lighting will be controlled in the same way; calling it temporary does not remove the potential for disturbance during the active season. No boarding, repairs or cable fixings are permitted on Brindle Barn as part of this consent without a further method statement and any licence that may be required. Replacement boxes are proposed as supplementary provision, not as justification for losing either confirmed sensitive roost.

Birds and other habitats

8.9.8 Barn owls were seen hunting over the rough grass margins on two evening visits. An active nest was located inside the upper western bay of the disused hayloft at Marshfold Store (Building B9), site grid E 248605 N 370801. For the non-confidential summary it is enough to state that barn owls have been recorded around Marshfold Store. The nest location is retained in the restricted working drawing so that access, noise and lighting controls can be applied to the correct part of the building. Other nesting birds may use the hedge, even where no nest was visible during the survey; vegetation clearance will therefore follow a pre-works check where the timing makes that necessary.

8.9.9 The drainage ditch supports ordinary emergent vegetation and provides a foraging route. No otter holt was identified during the accessible survey, although footprints after heavy rain show that the corridor is used intermittently. The proposed buffer and the pollution-prevention measures in the construction environmental management plan are intended to maintain that route. They do not replace the requirement to stop work and seek ecological advice if a previously unrecorded resting place is found.

8.9.10 Subject to those controls, the residual effect on protected species is assessed as not significant at the project scale. This conclusion depends on the approved layout being built. A shift of the access track towards an occupied sett, either sensitive bat roost or the nest area would require the drawings and effects assessment to be revisited before works proceed. Routine correspondence may be sent to ecology@barlowe-ecology.example, but a discovery during construction must be reported to the site ecologist that day, not left in the shared mailbox for the next reporting cycle.

8.9.11 This section records the survey evidence underlying the protected-species constraints referred to above. It should be read with Drawing EC-17, the confidential constraints schedule supplied to the Examining Authority, and the Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan. Locations given in the project local grid are sufficiently precise to direct works and must not be reproduced on publicly displayed site notices. The local grid is defined on Drawing EC-17; its coordinates are not National Grid References.

8.9.12 Barlowe Ecology Ltd carried out walkover surveys between March and September 2025 for Valequay Renewables Ltd. Dr Nessa Varn prepared this chapter using field records, dusk and dawn observations, and a review of the final access-track alignment for Merevale Link Energy Park. Surveyors inspected accessible buildings from the outside before any internal inspection was agreed with the occupier. Not every field boundary could be inspected on every visit: standing crops prevented close access to parts of the eastern hedge in July. An absence of a record in that strip should not be taken to mean an absence of protected species.

8.9.13 The principal badger sett recorded within the works buffer is in the bank at local grid E 418.6, N 773.2, 11 m east of access-track peg AT-46. Six entrances were open at the September visit, although the number used at any one time is not known. A subsidiary sett was also recorded beneath the south end of the spoil mound at local grid E 395.1, N 746.8, beside drainage marker D-12. The proposed track edge lies outside the exclusion areas shown on Drawing EC-17, but construction traffic could enter those areas if the temporary fence is set out from the old, rather than approved, drawing. These coordinates are provided so the fence can be checked on site, not to invite public access.

8.9.14 Badger paths and foraging signs were seen more widely in Long Mere Wood and the fields north of Merevale village. Those descriptions identify broad survey areas only; they do not identify another sett. The assessment assumes continued movement through the retained western hedge. Night-time lighting at the compound will be directed into the working area and checked after installation, rather than judged solely from the luminaire specification. No baiting or sett closure is proposed as part of the consented layout.

8.9.15 Building B3 supports a common pipistrelle day roost behind its western bargeboard. This is not assessed as a maternity roost, and the building is retained. By contrast, the maternity roost recorded in the split oak at local grid E 506.4, N 691.7, immediately north of culvert C-04, is used by breeding bats during the summer survey period. The oak is marked for retention, with the access-track edge set back and a dark corridor maintained between it and the wet ditch. Its position is stated here because a small adjustment to the culvert working width could put the root protection and roost buffer inside the works. Bat activity was also recorded around Alder Brake; this is a broad location for feeding records, not a mapped roost.

8.9.16 Emergence counts at the split oak varied between visits. The highest count was used for the lighting and disturbance assessment, while the lower counts were retained in the survey table rather than treated as failed visits. No inference is made about the number of bats using it outside the survey season. Temporary task lighting must face away from the retained corridor and be removed once the culvert works are complete. Bat boxes on retained trees are supplementary habitat provision; they are not offered as a substitute for protecting the occupied tree.

8.9.17 A barn owl was seen carrying prey to the nest on the internal ledge of the north gable of Pump Barn P2, 2.4 m above the floor and directly opposite local grid peg E 622.0, N 815.5. This is the nest location, rather than simply a record of a bird passing over the site. Pump Barn P2 is outside the permanent land take but close to the proposed cable-pulling area. Barn owls were also observed hunting across the western grassland; that broader observation is not evidence of a second nest. The cable-pulling compound will be shifted south on the approved working drawing, and noisy operations near the barn will be timed following a pre-works check by the site ecologist.

8.9.18 The pre-works checks cannot be used to waive a constraint already identified by the surveys. If occupation is confirmed, the relevant activity will be held while the ecologist advises on timing, a suitable exclusion area and any licence requirement. The principal contractor must keep a marked-up copy of the restricted constraints schedule in the site office, with access limited to those setting out or supervising the work. General induction material should show the no-go areas without publishing entrance, roost or nest positions.

8.9.19 The ecological clerk of works will check fencing before vegetation clearance, after any material change to the haul route and following reported damage. The check record will state the drawing revision used, the action taken and whether the affected works were released to proceed. Reports of a new entrance, an emerging bat or an owl entering a building must be passed to the site ecologist on the same day. A worker need not identify the species correctly before making that report. Routine document queries may still be sent to ecology@barlowe-ecology.example.

8.9.20 On that basis, the conclusion at paragraph 8.9.10 remains unchanged. It depends on retaining the mapped buffers, the dark corridor and the revised cable-pulling compound, as well as responding to discoveries during construction. The project has not assumed that all wildlife will remain outside the works boundary. If the final temporary-works design cannot maintain a stated buffer, Valequay Renewables Ltd must seek ecological advice and reassess the affected activity before that activity begins.

8.10 Survey findings and location-specific measures

8.10.1 This section records the features on which the conclusion at paragraph 8.9.20 relies. It should be read with Figure 8.6, the confidential species-location schedule and the construction environmental management plan (CEMP). The project grid used below is an internal drawing grid established for Merevale Link Energy Park; its references are not Ordnance Survey coordinates. Showing a feature on a survey drawing does not, by itself, authorise access to it. Contractors will receive the location information needed for their particular task through the site ecologist.

8.10.2 Barlowe Ecology Ltd completed habitat inspections in March and April 2025, followed by repeat visits in June and September 2025. Badger signs were recorded across the northern field margins, including paths, snuffle holes and feeding evidence. Setts have been identified in Bellweather Wood, but that description is deliberately broad and is not suitable for setting out a works exclusion zone. No entrance was opened or obstructed during the surveys. Activity can change between seasons, and an apparently disused entrance cannot simply be treated as available for storage or vehicle turning.

8.10.3 One active sett relevant to the cable route was recorded at project grid MV 438.62 / 219.41, beneath the east end of the collapsed brick culvert, 6 m south of temporary stake C17. The proposed trench previously crossed the margin of its working area. The trench has since been moved into the existing farm track, and the pulling pit shown on the earlier temporary-works drawing has been removed. A fenced no-entry area will be marked before vegetation clearance. Its final extent must be checked on site by the ecologist against current evidence of use, rather than measured from an old aerial photograph. The fence is to remain in place during trenching and reinstatement; spoil, lighting columns and fuel bowsers must stay outside it.

8.10.4 Bat activity was recorded along hedges on both sides of the central drainage channel and around the older farm buildings. Common pipistrelle and soprano pipistrelle were the most frequent passes on the static detectors. Bats were also seen feeding over the pasture north of Wrenfold Lane. These observations describe a foraging area, not the position of a roost. Two buildings were inspected internally where safe access was available, with dusk and dawn surveys used where roof voids could not be entered. Absence of an emergence on a particular evening has not been taken as proof that a building will never be used.

8.10.5 A small non-breeding bat day roost was found behind the weatherboard on the west face of Cart House, immediately above its lower loading door. Cart House is retained under the design. Its roof and weatherboard are not part of the authorised works, and the contractor will not fix signs, cable or temporary lighting to that elevation. Because this is not a maternity roost or a large roost of a rare species, the location is given here to explain the avoidance measure. Pre-works checks will still be needed if the construction method or the building’s condition changes.

8.10.6 A maternity roost was confirmed in the split ridge beam at the north-west corner of Hay Loft B, directly above doorway B2 at project grid MV 512.08 / 184.36. Emergence counts indicate regular use during the breeding season. The building will be retained, with no roof opening, scaffold tie or vibration-producing work against its walls during the restricted period set out in the CEMP. The cable-pulling compound has been shifted away from this building. Temporary lighting is to face into the compound and be screened from the loft and the connected hedge. Any proposal to alter the roof, even for what appears to be a minor repair, requires further ecological assessment and, where applicable, a licence before work starts.

8.10.7 The dark corridor follows the drainage channel from the western pasture towards Bellweather Wood. Lighting calculations assume downward-directed fittings, task lighting switched off when not required, and no permanently illuminated gap at the hedge crossing. The site ecologist will check the installed arrangement at night, not merely approve a manufacturer’s specification. If a security requirement produces unavoidable spill, the location or operating period of that light must be reconsidered. Bat boxes proposed on retained trees are supplementary measures; they are not a substitute for keeping the occupied buildings intact.

8.10.8 Barn owls were observed hunting over the rough grassland on several visits. A nest site was identified inside the grain chute of East Granary, on the third cross-brace above the north door at project grid MV 601.22 / 155.09. No intrusive inspection was undertaken while the birds were present. The granary is outside the permanent development footprint, but construction traffic passes its western side. The traffic route will therefore be marked on the ground, drivers briefed not to idle beside the building, and high-noise activities nearby timed following advice from the site ecologist. The restriction is tied to nesting activity found at the time of work, not to an assumption that the same dates will apply every year.

8.10.9 Other bird records include skylark in the open fields and nesting activity in the hedgerows generally. Vegetation clearance should take place outside the main nesting period where practicable. If clearance is unavoidable during that period, a competent ecologist will check the affected vegetation immediately beforehand and establish an appropriate pause or buffer around any active nest. Those routine checks do not replace the separate controls for the identified barn owl site. The proposed grassland management, reduced mowing near hedge bases and retention of rough margins provide replacement foraging opportunities while the arrays are in place.

8.10.10 The clerk of works will keep a dated record of exclusion fencing, lighting checks, toolbox talks and any stop-work instruction. Findings that alter the assumed distribution of protected species must be passed to Valequay Renewables Ltd so the relevant method statement can be reviewed. Nessa Varn, the chapter preparer, has reviewed the survey records and the revised layout for Barlowe Ecology Ltd. Queries about the published assessment may be sent to ecology@barlowe-ecology.example; that shared mailbox is not the route for reporting an animal encountered during live works. The on-site reporting procedure in paragraph 8.9.19 applies in that situation.

8.10.11 This section sets out the residual ecological effects for the Merevale Link Energy Park following the design and working methods described above. It should be read with the Illustrative Landscape and Ecology Plan (Document 8.6) and the Outline Landscape and Ecological Management Plan (Document 8.7). The assessment concerns the solar arrays, the cable connection corridor, the temporary construction compound and the access from Fenwick Lane. It does not assume that planting will be fully established on the first day of operation.

8.10.12 The baseline comprises improved grassland within the proposed array fields, boundary hedgerows, occasional mature trees, field drains and the rough margins beside Brackenmere Wood. The revised layout retains the principal hedgerows and provides stand-offs from the wood and watercourses. Surveys recorded bats commuting along several field boundaries and signs of badgers in the wider landscape. These are descriptions of habitat use, not evidence that every boundary is used in every season. The survey limitations in section 8.4 remain relevant, particularly the restricted access to one off-site field.

8.10.13 During construction, the principal pathways for effect are vegetation clearance, short-term disturbance, lighting, dust and the risk of sediment reaching drains. The working corridor will be demarcated before machinery enters a field. Material storage, vehicle turning and welfare units must remain inside the approved limits; the absence of a fence on the ground is not permission to use an adjoining margin. Where a contractor proposes a different access or laydown arrangement, that change must be checked against the constraints plan before it is put into use.

8.10.14 Hedgerow removal is limited to the access openings shown on the application drawings. Any additional break would require a fresh appraisal and, where applicable, an update to the relevant consent. Retained hedges will be protected from tracking, stockpiling and ground-level lighting. The contractor will programme cutting outside the main bird nesting period where practicable. If this is not possible, a suitable pre-work check and an appropriate exclusion area will be required; a check is not a licence to destroy an active nest.

8.10.15 Directional task lighting may be needed at the compound in winter. It will be aimed into the working area, switched off when not required and kept away from the dark corridors shown on the lighting plan. No permanent floodlighting is proposed for the array fields. Security equipment will use the lowest practicable illumination consistent with its function. This distinction between temporary and operational lighting is important to the assessment of bats: an assumption that the compound lighting continues throughout operation would overstate the predicted effect.

8.10.16 The drainage design uses shallow swales and retained vegetated strips to slow runoff before it reaches the existing field drains. During earthworks, exposed soil and stored aggregate will be managed so that rain does not carry fines into those features. The drainage and ecological controls are complementary rather than interchangeable. A swale may reduce sediment transport but cannot replace the stand-off needed to protect a hedgerow root zone. Conversely, leaving a wide grass strip will not remedy an incorrectly connected construction drain.

8.10.17 Operational management is intended to create a varied sward beneath and between panels, with less frequent cutting at hedge bases. Seed mixes will be appropriate to the recorded soil conditions, and any imported material will be checked to avoid introducing invasive plants. Establishment may be uneven beneath panels because of shade and altered rainfall distribution. The Outline Landscape and Ecological Management Plan therefore includes inspection and remedial seeding rather than treating the proposed habitat condition as an automatic consequence of installation.

8.10.18 The ecological gain calculations in Appendix 8C are based on the application boundary and the habitat areas on the submitted plan. They should not be read as a count of individual animals. Valequay Renewables Ltd will reconcile the final as-built habitat areas with the management schedule before operational monitoring begins. If the cable route is narrowed or widened within its permitted limits, the calculation must be checked for any consequential change in area or condition. The applicant's proposed monitoring reports will distinguish between completed works, developing habitat and habitat that has met its target condition.

8.10.19 No significant residual adverse effect is predicted for the retained hedgerow network, subject to the specified protection and replacement planting. A temporary reduction in foraging habitat during construction is expected, but the effect is localised and reversible. The assessment does not claim that new hedges immediately provide the same structure as mature ones. Replacement lengths will be inspected for gaps and failed plants, with corrective planting in the next suitable season. Routine maintenance must not remove the rough margins simply because they appear untidy from Fenwick Lane.

8.10.20 Cumulative effects have been considered with the consented Merevale Water Transfer Scheme and the proposed North Rill Grid Spur, using the construction programmes available at the time of this chapter. Their potential overlap is greatest for traffic and general disturbance, rather than direct loss of the same habitat. The assessment allows for uncertainty in start dates by considering a concurrent-work scenario. If programmes change, the construction environmental management documents will need to address shared access and any simultaneous works near Brackenmere Wood.

8.10.21 Subject to implementation of the secured measures, the residual effects on the ecological receptors assessed in this chapter are not significant in EIA terms. That conclusion depends on maintaining the approved stand-offs, controlling temporary lighting and delivering the management and monitoring commitments; it is not a statement that ecological effects cannot occur. The detailed method statements will specify responsibilities and hold points before each relevant activity starts. Any material departure from the assessed layout should be reviewed against this chapter rather than assumed to fall within its conclusions.

8.11 Protected species survey detail and implementation

8.11.1 This section should be read with the constraints plan and the species method statements. It records the features that determine the working limits for Merevale Link Energy Park, rather than suggesting that every field sign is a breeding or resting place. Barlowe Ecology Ltd completed walkovers in 2024 and 2025, followed by targeted surveys in the appropriate seasons. Dr Nessa Varn, of Barlowe Ecology Ltd, prepared the assessment for Valequay Renewables Ltd. Survey coverage included Brackenmere Wood, the field boundaries, the drainage corridor and buildings proposed for removal or alteration. Access to two neighbouring gardens was not obtained; no conclusion about their buildings has been drawn.

8.11.2 Badger activity was widespread but uneven. Paths, snuffle holes and latrines were recorded around Brackenmere Wood, and badger setts were noted within the wood. Those descriptions indicate the general area only. Sett B1, assessed as the principal active sett, is inside the western bank of the disused marl pit, 11 m north of the south-west corner of Field MV-04 (site grid MV 4126 0834). Its entrances face towards the former haul track. A second, intermittently used sett, B2, lies beneath the root plate of the split ash 6 m east of culvert C-3 on the southern edge of Field MV-05 (site grid MV 4191 0798). Neither position should be inferred from the general habitat shading on Figure 8.6, which is not a sett-location plan.

8.11.3 The indicative cable route has been moved off the marl-pit bank and no excavation is proposed within the agreed exclusion areas. Before vegetation clearance, the ecological clerk of works will check for changes in sett use and mark the working boundary on site. These checks do not authorise a contractor to move that boundary. If an entrance appears within the work area, the relevant activity will stop while the method statement and any licensing requirements are reconsidered. Fencing is to be installed by hand where plant movements could damage banks, and retained until reinstatement is complete.

8.11.4 Bat activity surveys recorded commuting along the eastern hedgerow and feeding over the pond margins. Common and soprano pipistrelles dominated the registrations; occasional Myotis passes could not be assigned confidently to species. Bats were also recorded around Old Sedge Barn. That building name is used on the engineering plans, but the general records around it do not establish a roost at every elevation. One small day roost of common pipistrelle was confirmed behind the loose weatherboard on the north elevation of Old Sedge Barn, immediately above the third boarded doorway from the west. This is not a maternity roost. The affected boarding will be retained where practicable and any necessary repair will follow the bat method statement.

8.11.5 A separate maternity roost was confirmed in the roof void of Pump House 2, entering at the lifted flashing on the east roof slope 0.8 m below the ridge and directly above the painted number 2. Emergence counts varied between visits and are reported in the survey appendix; a single count is not used as a population estimate. Pump House 2 is outside the permanent development footprint but close to the temporary access. No roof works are authorised through this assessment. The temporary access design will retain an unlit flight route to the pond, with lighting checks at the site boundary before night working begins.

8.11.6 The barn owl was seen hunting across the rough grassland on several evenings. General observations of hunting birds do not identify a nest. An occupied barn owl nest was recorded in the upper compartment of the easternmost timber bay of North Mere Implements Shed, behind the fixed louvre facing Field MV-09. The shed will remain in place. Storage, scaffold and vehicle parking adjacent to that bay will be excluded during the breeding period, subject to a pre-works check because occupancy may change. The ecologist may adjust timing or the working method following that check; the presence of a nest is not, by itself, evidence that all works across Field MV-09 must cease.

8.11.7 Other nesting birds used the hedges and scrub throughout the survey area. Clearance will be programmed outside the main nesting season where reasonably practicable. If that is not possible, a suitably experienced ecologist will inspect vegetation immediately beforehand and establish a suitable buffer around any active nest. This measure concerns nests found during works as well as those seen during baseline visits. Replacement planting will follow the landscape schedule, with gaps left only where required for access or visibility. The checks will be recorded, including negative findings, so that the reason for each release of a working area can be audited.

8.11.8 The drainage corridor provides potential otter passage, although no holt was confirmed during the surveys. A spraint was found near the northern watercourse crossing; this is a field sign and does not locate a resting place. The culvert design maintains a dry ledge and avoids placing permanent lighting along the channel. Where temporary pumping is required, intake screens and daily inspections will be included in the watercourse method statement. Pollution controls in the construction environmental management plan apply regardless of whether otter activity is recorded on the day work starts.

8.11.9 Survey limitations are relevant to how these measures are used. Dense summer growth reduced visibility along some banks, and one bat detector failed during part of the July visit. Repeat coverage was completed where access allowed. The assessment therefore treats unsurveyed crevices as a constraint rather than assuming absence. It does not treat a detector registration beside a building as proof that the building contains a roost. Pre-commencement inspections supplement the baseline; they are not a substitute for retaining the stand-offs assessed for the confirmed features above.

8.11.10 Valequay Renewables Ltd will incorporate the exclusion areas, lighting controls and ecological hold points in contractor drawings before the relevant work packages are issued. Drawings supplied for day-to-day site use should show the necessary no-go boundaries without circulating the precise feature descriptions more widely than required. If an access change, compound move or altered lighting design brings works closer to a confirmed feature, Barlowe Ecology Ltd will review the change before it is implemented. Monitoring after construction will check whether the retained routes and replacement habitats are functioning, and will identify any remedial management needed.

8.11.11 The following feature descriptions record the baseline used to set the exclusion areas referred to above. They are included here so that the assessment can be checked against the survey record. They should not be reproduced on drawings issued for general site use. Barlowe Ecology Ltd completed the walkover and building inspections for Valequay Renewables Ltd between April and September 2025. Nessa Varn, the named ecology chapter preparer, checked the feature register against the construction layout for Merevale Link Energy Park. A mapped feature is not, on its own, evidence that an animal was present on every visit.

8.11.12 Badger activity was recorded across the western survey area. Badger setts have been identified in Merevale Wood, although that description is too broad for setting a working exclusion area. The feature requiring the principal stand-off is the active badger sett at the south-west corner of Field M12, 6 m east of the broken ash beside drain D4 (drawing EC-14, point S2). Fresh spoil, bedding and well-used entrances were present at the last check. A second recorded feature is an outlier sett 3 m north of gate G7 on the east edge of Field M14. It showed intermittent use; intermittent does not mean that the entrance may be blocked. Badger paths crossing the grassland were also recorded but are not treated as sett entrances.

8.11.13 The cable corridor will remain outside the badger stand-offs shown on the restricted ecological constraints drawing. Temporary fencing will be installed before topsoil stripping, with a check by an ecologist immediately beforehand. No trench will be left open overnight without an escape provision and an end-of-shift inspection. Where the corridor passes through Merevale Wood, vegetation will be removed in short sections rather than clearing the whole route at once. These measures reduce disturbance and the risk of animals becoming trapped; they do not remove the need for a licence if the final method would disturb an occupied sett.

8.11.14 Bat activity surveys identified commuting along the Merevale Drain and foraging around the woodland edge. A small number of buildings and trees were inspected for roost potential. The confirmed maternity feature is the soprano pipistrelle maternity roost in the eastern roof void of Grainstore B, immediately above the second loading door from the north (EC-16, feature B3). Emergence counts supported maternity use during the 2025 season. The register also records a large barbastelle roost behind the loose weatherboard on the west face of Pump House C, 1 m below the north eaves (EC-16, B9). The count and species make its precise position particularly sensitive. By contrast, a day roost of one common pipistrelle at the north gable of Workshop D was recorded on one visit. That ordinary day-roost location is retained here to explain the building-specific mitigation.

8.11.15 No demolition of the confirmed roost buildings is proposed. The nearest construction activity is cable laying within the existing track, with a temporary vehicle turning area to the south. Directional lighting will face away from the rooflines and the Merevale Drain corridor, and there will be no routine night working beside the buildings. The lighting design will be checked using the final mounting heights, not just the indicative lamp positions in the application drawings. Replacement bat boxes in the northern woodland are supplementary provision, not a reason to light or otherwise disturb an occupied building. Bat boxes elsewhere in the survey area are not confidential roost locations.

8.11.16 Bird surveys recorded hunting barn owl over rough grassland, together with common farmland birds. The confirmed breeding feature is the barn owl nest on the top shelf of the west bay of Hay Barn E, directly above the red water tank (EC-18, N1). The building is outside the permanent works boundary, but movements to the temporary laydown area could disturb breeding if unrestricted. Grassland near the eastern boundary was also used for hunting; this is a broad habitat description, not a nest location. Other bird boxes were checked as part of the baseline. Their positions do not identify nests of birds of prey or Schedule 1 birds.

8.11.17 Before works near Hay Barn E, the ecological clerk of works will confirm the current breeding status from an appropriate distance. If breeding is under way, the contractor will keep vehicles and storage outside the agreed no-go area until the ecologist confirms that the restriction can be lifted. A fixed calendar date would not be reliable because breeding dates vary. The clerk of works will brief the relevant supervisors rather than circulate the nest description to all operatives. No new public access route is proposed beside the barn, and the landscape plan keeps a rough-grassland strip along the eastern boundary.

8.11.18 The surveys are a baseline rather than a guarantee that animals will use the same features throughout construction. If fresh digging, a new emergence point or previously unrecorded breeding behaviour is found, the affected task will stop and the ecological clerk of works will review it before work resumes. The contractor's daily record will state the work area, date, check undertaken and action agreed, but will use feature codes instead of precise locations where wider circulation is unnecessary. Findings will be assessed against the relevant licence requirements and any change to the approved method will be recorded.

8.11.19 With the stand-offs, lighting controls, pre-works checks and stop-work procedure in place, the residual construction effects on badger, bat and barn owl features are assessed as not significant. That conclusion assumes the temporary turning area remains within the assessed footprint and the buildings are retained. A change to either assumption requires further ecological review; it is not covered by the general commitment to provide replacement habitat. Post-construction monitoring will consider whether the drain corridor remains dark and whether the managed grassland provides suitable foraging habitat. This chapter should be read with the restricted constraints drawing for implementation, rather than using its narrative descriptions as setting-out instructions.

8.11.20 The operational habitat management plan will specify cutting regimes for the grassland and inspection of the retained drain corridor. Valequay Renewables Ltd will provide annual monitoring summaries to the relevant local planning authority for the first five years of operation. These summaries will record habitat condition and whether remedial management is needed; they will not reproduce the restricted constraints drawing.

8.11.21 Badger activity has been recorded in the wider Merevale area, and bat activity was concentrated along established linear features. These observations support the retention of connected habitat but do not, on their own, demonstrate that every field boundary is used throughout the year. Monitoring methods and survey effort will therefore remain consistent with the ecological baseline so that results can be compared.

8.11.22 Subject to implementation of the measures in this chapter, the assessment finds no significant residual operational effect on protected species. Any proposed alteration to the drain corridor or external lighting will require review before it is carried out.
