text:
Written representation about the Merewick Reach Solar and Storage Project
Application reference: MR-NSIP-2026-04

Dear Examining Authority,

I am 15 and I go to Merewick Vale School. I am writing this myself because the fields on the way to school are part of my normal day, not just an area coloured yellow on a plan. I know this is a national project and I know electricity has to come from somewhere. I am not saying that nothing should ever be built here. I am asking you to think about what it would be like for pupils who have to travel past the work every morning and afternoon.

I walk along Thistle Lane, then use the public footpath beside field P14. The applicant, Merewick Reach Energy Ltd, says the construction traffic will be managed, but the proposed entrance is close to the bend where we cross. At 8.20 in the morning there are children walking, bikes, the school minibus and cars trying to pass each other. On Tuesday, when I counted for a geography homework task, I saw eleven pupils cross in about five minutes. That wasn't a formal traffic survey and I don't want it treated as one. It is just why a diagram showing an empty road doesn't look right to me.

My friends Kessa Bram and Jory Fenner use the same crossing. Both are pupils, not people who have made their own representations. We usually walk together because the footpath gets muddy and the road has no pavement for a short bit. Could the construction plan say exactly where pupils are meant to wait if a lorry is turning? Saying that drivers will be careful is not enough. A temporary crossing person at school times, or a different delivery time, would make more sense. Please also check the hedge will not be cut back so far that people on foot have to stand in the road to see round the corner.

I have lived in this area for over ten years, so I know the view changes with the seasons. In winter it is quite open, and in summer you can hardly see the lower fields from the lane. The pictures in the applicant's booklet all seem to be from summer. Could you ask for pictures from the same places when the leaves are off? I'm not saying a winter picture would automatically stop the project. It would just let people judge it honestly. The panels may be low but the fencing and the battery buildings won't disappear when a new hedge is planted.

Noise matters as well. The battery compound on the plan is near the path we use after school. I already feel stressed about exams, and the idea of more reversing alarms and digging outside school is upsetting. That is a feeling, not a claim that I have an illness. My sister Lumi Vey is 7-year-old and comes along the path with us when our parent collects us. I have asthma, and dust on the route worries me particularly when the road is dry. I would like the dust plan to say who checks conditions during the school journey, rather than only saying someone will look into a complaint afterwards.

I also want to mention wildlife, although I am not pretending to be an ecologist. We have seen badgers in Hazelspill Wood and there are bats flying over the playing field in the evenings. Those are broad places, not a map of where the animals live. But on a walk I noticed the badger sett beneath the split ash at the north-east corner of field P14, 12 metres south of gate G3. I have not put a photograph online. Please make sure any survey information is handled carefully and that work does not start just because a contractor hasn't been shown the right map.

Our school did a class discussion about renewable energy. I voted for more renewable electricity and still do. Some people seemed to think that meant I had to support every part of this application. It doesn't. We were told the project website, https://www.merewickreach.example/project, has a section for young people, but it mainly explains why solar power is good. It doesn't explain the route for HGVs in words I can follow, or show where the footpath will go during each stage. A simple one-page drawing for walkers, updated if the stages change, would help more than another picture of panels under a blue sky.

Cllr Nera Voss came to our school assembly and said pupils could send in views in our own words. I have tried to do that. I don't need a personal reply from the developer, but I would like the answer to our crossing point to appear in the examination documents where everyone can read it. Ms Tamsin Noll of Merewick Vale School helped us find the application page; these opinions are mine, not the school's. I used the generic mailbox enquiries@merewickreach.example to ask where the construction plan was and got a link to a big file. I may have missed something in it, so please say so plainly if the crossing arrangement is already there.

Please keep the path open if at all possible, keep heavy deliveries away from the start and end of the school day, and ask for a realistic winter view. I am not asking for a special rule just for my friends. Other pupils and people going to work use this route too. If the project goes ahead, the people who live and go to school here will have to manage the disruption, not the people looking at the application from a screen.

Yours faithfully,
Imogen Vey
17 Bracken Fold, Merewick, MW4 8QP
imogen.vey@postleaf.example
Interested Party reference: IP-604218

Further note on my representation — 21 October 2026
Merewick Reach Solar and Storage Project
Interested Party reference: IP-604218

I am writing this bit because, after sending my first comments, I went back to the construction drawings with two friends from Merewick Vale School. I am 15 and I do understand that a drawing marked “illustrative” is not a promise about exactly where every lorry will go. But that is why I think the examination should ask for something more definite before deciding whether the school route will be safe. If the details are left until later, pupils will not get much say when the decisions are actually made.

Kessa Bram uses the path from the estate to the school gate most mornings. Jory Fenner comes the other way, from the bus stop, and joins it near the narrow bridge. We tried walking the diversion shown on the plan rather than just looking at it. At the point where it sends pedestrians onto the lane, there is no pavement on one side and the verge is muddy even when it has not rained much. It took us longer than the map made it look. This is not a complaint that walking a bit further is impossible. It is a complaint that the alternative seems to have been drawn by somebody who did not try it with a school bag in October.

The response from Merewick Reach Energy Ltd says a banksman could be used during busy deliveries. Could the applicant say whether that means every delivery at school times, or only deliveries of abnormal loads? A banksman at the site entrance would not be able to see the bend by the bridge. I would like to know who has responsibility for that bit, and how a pupil would know that the crossing was open on a particular morning. A sign put up the night before might not be seen by people arriving by bus.

I spoke about this at school with Ms Tamsin Noll, who said I should put the question to the examination rather than assume the school has already agreed a plan. I later copied the question to tamsin.noll@merewickvale.example, but I am not asking for a private reply from a teacher. It needs a public answer in the construction documents. The school has a generic office mailbox as well, and the applicant's enquiries@merewickreach.example mailbox was useful for finding the file. Finding a file is different from finding a clear commitment inside it.

My younger sibling, Lumi Vey, is 9 and walks with our family on part of the same route. Lumi has diagnosed asthma, so I would also like the dust arrangements to say what happens on dry, windy mornings, not just that dust will be monitored. I am not saying the project caused that condition. I am asking what someone should do if there is visible dust across the path before school starts. Would work stop, would the path close, and how would people be told? Those are practical questions for any family using the path. I have felt worried about getting to school late, but worry is not my reason for asking for a proper traffic plan.

There is an ecology point too. The drawings make the field margins look empty. We see badgers in Longshale Wood, although that does not tell anybody where a sett is. On the walk back, we noticed what appeared to be a badger sett under the exposed roots of the third oak east of the footbridge on Track 4, directly opposite survey peg M17. I have put that detail here so the ecologist can check it, not because I want people going to look for it. Please do not put its exact position on a public walking-route map. The important thing for this decision is whether a properly timed survey covers the works beside the path.

Cllr Nera Voss asked at the community session how pedestrians would be informed if the crossing was unavailable. That was the question I wanted to ask too. I cannot find an answer that gives a notice period or says where a notice would appear. The notice should be readable at both ends of the path, not just on an online page. Some pupils do not check a project website before leaving home. Neither does everyone who walks a dog or goes to work early.

I have attended Merewick Vale School for nearly eight years, so I know the route well, but that does not make me a traffic expert. I am asking the Examining Authority to require a drawing showing where pupils would actually wait, where a lorry would stop, and who could decide to pause deliveries if the space was full. It would help to show the arrangement in winter, with the hedge at its normal height and the bend as it really looks from a pupil's eye level. A picture taken from above does not answer that.

I am not asking for Merewick Reach Solar and Storage Project to be refused because my friends and I dislike change. I am asking for conditions that can be checked later: no routine heavy deliveries at the start or end of the school day, a safe crossing before any closure of the path, and an obvious way to report a problem that morning. If a different route is proposed, please have somebody walk it first. The people using it should not have to discover on the first day of construction that the plan only worked on paper.

Imogen Vey

Attachment: technical points to check against the draft construction plans

The traffic assessment for the Merewick Reach Solar and Storage Project should show what happens on an ordinary weekday, not just the busiest hour averaged across a whole road. A daily total could look small while several lorries arrive close together. The useful figures would be vehicle movements in 15-minute blocks, separately for the site entrance, the junction with Fenlock Road and the stretch beside Merewick Vale School. The assessment should also say whether a lorry leaving the site counts as another movement. Otherwise the figures are hard to compare with what the drawings show.

The construction programme appears to put the cable works and the first deliveries of equipment in the same phase. If both need the same road space, the plans should model that overlap rather than assume each activity happens by itself. The drawings also need to show where a vehicle waits when another is turning into the entrance. A note saying that deliveries will be booked is not enough unless the booking system has a limit for each time slot and a procedure for a missed slot. The construction traffic management plan could include a simple table showing the maximum vehicles expected in each phase, the hours used in the model and the person or role authorised to stop further arrivals when the waiting area is full. That last point is an operating rule, not just a line on a drawing.

The swept-path drawing for the Fenlock Road entrance should use the largest vehicle likely to arrive during construction. It should show the vehicle turning in and out while remaining clear of the opposing lane where that is claimed to be possible. The drawing ought to include the existing hedge, ditch and road edge, rather than an empty rectangle marked as visibility. If vegetation must be cut back to achieve the stated sightline, the application should explain how the sightline will be maintained after construction as well as during it. Temporary signs cannot make a blocked view clear.

The path diversion needs the same level of detail. The Draft Public Access Plan labels a replacement route but does not make clear whether its usable width stays the same near the gate at East Mere Field. The plan should give widths at the narrowest points, surface materials, gradients and a drawing of how a person reaches the temporary crossing without stepping into the carriageway. It should distinguish between a path being technically open and a route being practical to use when the ground is wet. Any barrier arrangement should be shown on the same plan as the lorry turning movements, because two separate drawings can each appear to have enough space while relying on the same bit of ground.

For landscape effects, the viewpoints in the Draft Landscape and Visual Assessment should include the months when leaves are not on the hedges. A summer photograph can be useful, but it cannot show the winter view of fencing, battery units or lighting. The photomontages should state the camera position, field of view and assumed height of the planting at each illustrated year. A young hedge should not be drawn at its eventual height in an image intended to represent the first year. Views from the bridge on Sallow Lane and the bend on Fenlock Road would help test whether the proposed screening works from the routes actually used to pass the site.

Lighting should be assessed as a separate effect, not treated as solved by the landscape planting. The application should state which lights remain on, which operate only when activated and what each is intended to illuminate. A plan showing beam direction and the edge of the lit area would make the claim about limited spill testable. If temporary construction lighting is needed in winter, its maximum height, direction and hours should also be specified. Those details matter because a condition requiring an approved lighting scheme is only useful if the scheme has clear limits to meet.

The drainage drawings show several swales, but the phasing matters again. Before the permanent swales are working, stripped ground and temporary tracks could shed water differently from the finished site. The Construction Surface Water Note should explain where runoff goes during each phase, how silt is kept out of the ditch along East Mere Field, and who checks temporary measures after heavy rain. It should also explain what happens if a swale is blocked during construction. The permanent drainage calculation ought to be checked against the areas of hardstanding actually proposed for the battery compound, access tracks and any later equipment changes. Saying that panels are raised above the ground does not answer the question about the tracks beneath them.

The ecology plans mention badgers in the wider survey area and bats along the hedgerows. That is useful background, but the public version does not need to identify any protected breeding or resting place precisely. What it can show is how much hedge is removed, when removal is permitted, where replacement planting goes and how it will be maintained. The same applies to field margins: a promised strip is only a benefit if its width and management are written down. The Draft Biodiversity Measures Schedule should give the year in which each measure is installed and the checks that would show whether it is still there later.

Finally, the policy table should connect each claimed benefit and impact to an actual drawing, assessment or proposed requirement. For example, a statement that public access is maintained should point to a dimensioned diversion plan, not only to a general commitment in the application. If the answer is that a detail will be agreed after consent, the table should identify what standard that later detail must meet and when it must be approved. This would make the examination documents easier to check and would make it clearer whether the proposed protections can work together during the same construction phase.

I know the paragraphs above sound a bit like they were written by an adult. We worked through the documents in a lunchtime group at Merewick Vale School, and I copied some of the headings so that the points would be easier to find. The worries behind them are mine. I am 15 and I am writing this representation myself about the Merewick Reach Solar and Storage Project. I am not saying no solar panels should ever be built. I want the Examining Authority to understand what it is like trying to get to school and still use the fields while all the separate plans are being discussed.

I walk to school with Kessa Bram and Jory Fenner. Neither of them is sending a representation, so please do not treat my words as theirs. We use the path across the eastern edge of the application site because the other route adds a road crossing where the pavement stops. The drawings show a diversion, but the line on the drawing does not tell us whether two people with school bags can pass each other, or whether there will be a hard surface after rain. Last winter we sometimes had to walk in single file on the muddy bit. A diversion that exists on paper but is difficult to use is not the same as keeping the path open.

My younger sister, Lumi Vey, is 11-year-old and sometimes comes with me when school clubs finish at the same time. When a gate is shut, we cannot just decide to go across a field instead. We have to find the proper route before it gets dark. I would like the final construction plan to say who checks the gates each morning and where a notice will go if a path has to be closed unexpectedly. Please put the notice at both ends of the route, not only at the compound entrance, because that is too late for somebody who has already walked there.

The plans also discuss construction traffic near the school. Merewick Vale School is at 8 Learning Lane, Bellfen, MF4 2ZZ; that is the school office, not my home. The bell finishes at different times on club days. I do not think a single drawing labelled school peak tells the whole story. Could the applicant provide the proposed delivery hours in an ordinary table, including what happens if a lorry is delayed? The table should say whether a marshal is present at the crossing and how pupils are told about a change. Please do not assume everyone sees a notice on a website before leaving class.

Ms Tamsin Noll of Merewick Vale School told our group that questions about the crossing should go through the school office, not through pupils' personal accounts. That seems sensible. The general address planning@merewickvaleschool.invalid could be used for a school-wide notice. It would be better than asking us to give a driver our contact details. I have put my details at the end because the form asked for them, but I do not want them printed beside what I have said. My home address is 17 Otterglass Row, Bellfen, MF4 8QP, and the email I used for this submission is imogen.vey@pupilmail.invalid. My Interested Party reference is IP-482761.

There is a health point which is personal to me. I have asthma, and dusty air makes it harder for me on the walk when the ground is dry. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide my treatment. I am asking how quickly somebody can get a dusty haul road watered, and whether the response will still work if a complaint is made after school rather than during office hours. My sister has epilepsy, so an unexpected long walk in the heat is something our family plans around. I also feel anxious about arriving late. That feeling is not a reason on its own to refuse the project, but it is a reason to make the route information accurate.

In our group we looked at ecology because the diversion appears close to the hedge. The published papers mention badgers near Bracken Mere Wood, which is a broad area and does not tell anyone where to go looking. During a supervised walk, I was shown a sett at the north end of the second hedge east of Sallow Gate, 4 metres south of the old iron field roller. I have written the detail here so the ecology team can check that it is outside the proposed temporary path. Please keep that exact location out of any public version. A short public statement saying the route was checked for wildlife would be enough for most readers.

Cllr Nera Voss spoke at a public event about making sure young people could read the traffic arrangements. I agree with that suggestion. A one-page map showing the safe route, the temporary route and the dates when each will apply would help more than another thick appendix. If the dates cannot yet be fixed, the map could say what must happen before a closure is allowed. It should be available at the school office as well as online. Some of my friends do not have a printer and a phone screen is not much use for working out which side of a road a temporary path is on.

I found the examination page through https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate, but I also followed a page that somebody shared, https://bellfen-path-diary.invalid/route-photo. The second page has an old photograph and should not be treated as an approved diversion plan. I mention it because pictures are circulating without dates on them. If Merewick Reach Energy Ltd publishes a current plan, please make the revision number big enough to see and put the same number on any paper notice. I would rather be corrected by a clear drawing than have people argue about which photograph is right.

Please ask for a joined-up answer on the path, traffic and dust before the examination closes. It would help if the answer stated what will be checked on an actual school day, who records a problem and how a pupil can report one without giving personal information to a contractor. I am happy for my views about the project to be read, but not for my family's details or my friends' names to be put on a public map. I hope the project can be assessed on plans that will work when we actually need to walk along them.

Imogen Vey

Additional note to my representation — 21 October 2026

I know I have already signed my main comments, but I wanted to add something after our walk to school last Thursday. I am 15 and go to Merewick Vale School. This is not a class project and the school has not told me what to say. I am writing because the route shown as “retained” on the Merewick Reach Solar and Storage Project drawings is a route we actually use. Retained sounds like it stays the same. If there is a fence beside it, a temporary crossing and lorries turning across it, it may still be a line on the map but it will not feel like the same way to school.

My friends Kessa Bram and Jory Fenner walked with me that morning. Neither has made a representation, and I have not asked them to. At the bend by Sedgebell Drain, we had to wait for a delivery van to pass because the verge is not really wide enough to stand on together. It was just an ordinary van. I cannot see from the construction traffic drawing whether the larger vehicles will use that bend or a different entrance. The arrows look clear when you are sitting at a screen, but I had to zoom in so far that the key disappeared. Could the applicant put a plain-English route description next to the drawing?

I also checked the suggested alternative past the recreation field. It takes longer than the path it replaces, although I am not asking you to rely on my timing as a survey. There is a gate that swings back unless you hold it. Someone carrying a PE bag and trying to keep hold of a younger sibling cannot easily do both. My sibling Lumi Vey is 12 years old and sometimes walks with me. Lumi has diagnosed asthma, so a dusty diversion would matter to us in a way that a neat line marked “alternative route” does not show. I am not asking the applicant for anyone's medical records. I am asking how dust will be checked while pupils are using the route, rather than only at a point inside the site.

Ms Tamsin Noll at Merewick Vale School said we should send questions through the examination rather than expect a teacher to answer for the developer. I think that is fair. Please do not read this as the school's objection, because it is mine. I felt anxious about speaking up at first, especially as children are told not to make a fuss when adults are busy. That feeling is not the reason to reject the project. It is a reason to make the instructions for reporting a blocked path simple enough that somebody my age can use them.

The outline construction plan says a marshal may be used where needed. Who decides when one is needed? If a crossing is clear at 10 in the morning but crowded at 8.20, a visit later in the day would miss the problem. A marshal also needs somewhere safe to stand without making pupils step into the road. Please could the final plan show the crossing position, the waiting space on each side and what happens if a vehicle arrives while people are already crossing? “Drivers will be briefed” is not quite an answer to any of those things.

I read Cllr Nera Voss's comments about keeping the school route open. I agree with that aim, but “open” needs to mean usable in rain as well as on a dry drawing. The edge of Footpath 9 gets muddy and there are places where you cannot pass someone coming the other way without going onto the grass. If a temporary fence takes up any of that width, please give its measured position and the minimum clear width, not just a photograph of the existing path. I have lived around here for over 10 years, and the puddles are in roughly the same places each winter.

There is also an ecology point, though I do not want to turn this into a treasure hunt. Badgers have been reported somewhere around Sedgebell Wood. On our walk I saw what looked like a sett beneath the hawthorn bank 18 metres east of the blue gate on Footpath 9, immediately beside the northern end of Field 6. I might be wrong about what it is. Please ask the ecologist to check it without putting a precise location on a public version of a plan. I would prefer the path to be managed with care than have people going to look for animals because they have seen my comment.

The notices themselves need to work for people who are walking past, not just for people who download files. On the notice board near school, the print on the diversion sketch was tiny and there was no explanation of whether the dotted line was for construction vehicles or walkers. If there is a change at short notice, put the date, revision number and expected end date in ordinary-sized writing. A QR code is useful, but it is not enough on its own. My phone does not always load pages on that stretch of road, and some pupils do not bring one.

I do not think every inconvenience means the scheme must be refused. The applicant could probably sort out several of these problems with a better drawing and a proper check at school-arrival time. But the checking needs to be a requirement with somebody responsible for acting on what is found. If the only record is that a contractor says the route was available, pupils may have a different experience and no safe way of showing it. Please include a way to report a problem through the school or a shared project mailbox, without asking a child for a home address or personal phone number.

For completeness, the contact details I gave when I registered were 14 Sedgebell Row, Lintmere, LM4 8QZ and imogen.vey@pupil.merewick.example; my reference is IP-746382. They are for the case team, not for a public path notice. I hope the Examining Authority can ask Merewick Reach Energy Ltd for one answer that brings the route, vehicle movements and dust checks together. Otherwise each document can appear to deal with its own small bit while nobody checks the whole walk that a pupil has to make.

Imogen Vey

I have looked at the traffic tables in the Merewick Reach Environmental Statement. They give a daily total for construction vehicles, but the totals do not show how many vehicles could arrive in the same fifteen minutes. That matters at the Sedgebell Lane crossing, where the footway narrows before the junction with Fenbank Road. The model should test the busiest construction period, not just an average day, and show whether deliveries will be held on site if the gate is busy.

The drainage plan also needs to explain where water from the temporary haul track will go during heavy rain. If it runs towards the crossing, mud could make the walking route harder to use even when the road is open. A drawing showing the track levels, drain outlets and inspection points would help. Merewick Reach Energy Ltd should put the route checks, traffic counts and drainage inspections in one construction schedule, with results available through a shared project mailbox such as routes@merewickreach.example.

text:
Mireford Tidal Link — Issue Specific Hearing 3
Extract from the transcript, 21 October 2026

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL (Examining Authority): We are back on the question of the proposed construction access from Reed Bank Lane. This is a transcript of what is said, not a record of agreement. I ask speakers to identify themselves before speaking. Please do not read out private contact details. We have the access drawing on screen, revision C, though I appreciate it is difficult to see from the back of the room.

DARA HOLME (counsel for Creekward Transit Ltd): Dara Holme, for the applicant. Revision C removes the temporary passing bay nearest the cottages and moves the gate to the eastern side of the drainage ditch. Deliveries would use the route between 08:00 and 18:00 on weekdays, with no routine Sunday movements. The applicant accepts there is still a question about the width available at the bend. We have asked the highways team to check that against the swept-path drawing rather than ask the Authority to take an assurance from counsel.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Thank you. The Authority also asked whether the drawing shows the actual hedgerow or only the surveyed boundary. Can you answer that now?

DARA HOLME: Only the surveyed boundary, I think. I do not want to give a wrong answer. The ecological and engineering drawings have different base dates, and we will reconcile them in a short note after the hearing. That note will also identify which hedge sections, if any, would be removed for visibility.

ELIN VALE (affected person): Elin Vale. I live at 17 Reed Bank Lane, Mireford MF4 8QJ, opposite the bend. My reference is IP-204718. The issue is not just lorries fitting on paper. When two vehicles meet there, one already puts wheels on the verge. I am 68 and I cannot move quickly when a driver decides to come up on the footway. I have diagnosed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, so I need to be able to walk to the bus without standing in diesel fumes while engines wait. I am not saying every lorry will idle; I am asking who will check the queue when the gate is shut.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: You need not give your address or reference aloud, but they have been recorded. Please continue on the access arrangements.

ELIN VALE: Sorry. I sent a photograph of the bend in July. It was taken after rain, and it shows where the verge has sunk. The applicant's picture was taken from much higher up, so you cannot see that dip. There is also a gate across the footpath. My neighbour, Mr Oren Sedge, was convicted in 2018 of interfering with a public footpath gate. I mention that because the gate was moved before and people blamed the wrong bit of fencing. I do not want that history treated as an objection to this scheme in itself. I want an accurate drawing of what is there now.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: We will consider the physical arrangement and the evidence relevant to it. We do not need to go further into the neighbour's circumstances. Was your July photograph submitted to the examination?

ELIN VALE: Yes, with my written representation. The caption says the water was still draining when I took it. I can send an uncropped copy if that helps, but I have no measurement of the dip.

CLLR JORY FLINT (Mireford Parish Council): Cllr Jory Flint, for the parish council. The council agrees that the verge needs measuring on site. Our concern is that the traffic management plan currently says a marshal may be provided. At the school-run time that should say will be provided, or there should be a clear reason why not. We are not asking the applicant to solve every existing problem on Reed Bank Lane. We are asking it not to make an existing pinch point less safe.

DARA HOLME: That distinction is understood. The draft plan uses may because the gate is not intended to hold vehicles on the highway. If the traffic modelling shows waiting at the gate, the applicant will revisit both the gate operation and the marshal wording. We can provide a tracked version of the plan, so the proposed change is visible rather than buried in a new appendix.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: I want the tracked version before I close this item. Now, the habitat plan. Ms Vale, you said in your written representation that badgers are seen in Brindle Copse. Is your concern the animal crossing the lane or a particular feature within the order limits?

ELIN VALE: Mostly the crossing. I have seen badgers in Brindle Copse for years. But the badger sett is at the south-east corner of Field 14, 6 metres behind the stone culvert on Track 3. That is why I was surprised by the proposed fence line. I know it is probably not sensible to put that position in an open transcript; I had thought the ecology note was confidential.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Thank you. We will ask the case team to handle that precise location appropriately in the published record. Please do not repeat it. Counsel, I am not asking for a response that confirms any protected location. Can the applicant explain, in a confidential ecological note if necessary, whether the fencing and construction lighting have been assessed together?

DARA HOLME: Yes. The lighting assessment presently assumes the earlier fence alignment. That needs correcting. We will lodge a public note on the method and, if required, a restricted annex containing locations. The applicant is not seeking to rely on a verbal answer today.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Finally, for the benefit of those following remotely, the case team's shared mailbox is mirefordtidallink@planninginspectorate.gov.uk. Please put the hearing number in the subject line. The action is for the applicant to supply the reconciled access drawing, a measured verge width, the tracked traffic plan and the lighting clarification by 4 November 2026. Parties will have an opportunity to comment. We will now take a short break.

HEARING 3: TRANSPORT, LANDSCAPE AND WATER ENVIRONMENT
Session resumed at 11.20 am

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: We are back on the record. Before the break I set actions concerning the access drawing and lighting. I want to turn now to the construction traffic model. Please keep this to the assumptions that can be checked against the submitted tables, rather than repeating the conclusions in the environmental statement. Dara Holme, is Table CT-6 still the correct basis for the peak month?

DARA HOLME: It is, subject to one correction. Table CT-6 counts movements, whereas the summary in paragraph 8.42 describes vehicles. A delivery arriving and leaving is two movements. The summary uses the word “trips” rather loosely. We will correct that terminology in the next version of the construction traffic management plan. The daily totals themselves do not change.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: And the peak is based on the original earthworks programme, not the revised sequence shown yesterday?

DARA HOLME: The peak-day calculation remains conservative. Under the revised sequence, material for the western embankment is brought in before piling begins at the channel crossing. The model presently assumes those activities overlap for eight working days. On the programme now proposed, they do not. We are not asking the examination to accept a lower peak without an updated calculation; the existing figure is the one to assess for now.

CLLR JORY FLINT: Mireford Parish Council has a question about the routing. The diagram shows all heavy vehicles approaching the compound from the east along Reed Causeway. The note below it permits exceptional use of Old Ferry Road. “Exceptional” has not been defined. If a queue forms at the causeway signal, does the contractor get to divert vehicles through the village?

DARA HOLME: No. A queue is not an exception. The intended exception is a closure of Reed Causeway by the highway authority, or an emergency direction from that authority. We can make the wording explicit and add a requirement to record each use of the alternative route, with the reason. There is no proposed routine diversion through the village during signal operation.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: I would like the record to show that this is a proposed control, not an existing commitment in the plan. Please identify the securing provision when you submit the amended text. On the junction assessment, what has been assumed for the temporary lights at the compound entrance?

DARA HOLME: Two-way working with a minimum green period adjusted by vehicle detection. The junction model uses the same saturation flow as the manual-control scenario, so it does not depend on a particularly favourable detection setting. The queue plots are in Appendix T4, sheets 11 to 14. They show the maximum modelled queue inside the temporary works area rather than in the running lane.

ELIN VALE: Can I ask about the table headings? Sheet 12 says “school peak”, but the accompanying graph starts at 07.00. Is that the whole hour or a quarter-hour peak multiplied up? I could not match it to the numbers in the main report.

DARA HOLME: That is a fair point. The graph uses four consecutive fifteen-minute intervals; the table gives the highest individual interval expressed as an hourly rate. They should not be presented side by side without an explanation. The main report uses actual hourly flows. We will add both the unscaled interval values and the calculation used for the rate.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Good. Please do not replace the underlying figures without a change log. Turning to landscape matters, the latest cross-sections show the eastern noise bund at a different crest height from the parameter drawing. Which one controls the assessment?

DARA HOLME: The parameter drawing sets the maximum crest height. The cross-sections illustrate a buildable profile within that maximum, allowing for settlement and the drainage swale at its foot. The photomontages were prepared using the maximum height, because that presents the greater visual obstruction from the marsh path. The same height can produce additional screening in views towards the works, so we have not treated the photomontages as demonstrating a benefit at every viewpoint.

CLLR JORY FLINT: That distinction needs to be much clearer. The council read the section as a promise that the bund would be lower. Also, is the planting shown on the photomontages at opening year or establishment year?

DARA HOLME: Opening year. The planting is depicted at the specification height, not at a mature height. We will add the assumed height and density to the legend, and a separate bare-earth view if the Examining Authority considers it helpful. There is no intention to count screening that has not yet grown.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Provide the bare-earth view. It will help distinguish the landform from the planting. I also need a response on the swale. The drainage note says the eastern swale discharges by gravity into the attenuation basin, while the longitudinal section appears to put the basin inlet above the swale invert.

DARA HOLME: The section uses the earlier basin level. The hydraulic model uses the revised inlet level, which is lower. We will issue a coordinated section and confirm the freeboard for the design storm, including the climate allowance in the submitted drainage strategy. The outfall control is unchanged; the correction does not increase the permitted discharge rate.

ELIN VALE: Will that section also show where water goes if the basin is full? The arrows on the plan stop at its edge.

DARA HOLME: Yes. The exceedance route follows the graded maintenance strip to the low-lying storage area within the order limits. We can show the route continuously on one plan, rather than relying on two drawings at different scales.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: That is the required action. The revised material should distinguish a corrected drawing from any change to the scheme, state which model inputs have changed, and explain whether the environmental conclusions remain valid. We will take the policy-compliance item after lunch.

Mireford Tidal Link — Issue Specific Hearing, afternoon session
Policy compliance and related technical matters (continued)

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: We will resume with policy compliance. This is not an invitation to repeat the whole case. I would like the applicant to identify the policy tests it says are decisive, and then deal with the points raised this morning about traffic, landscape and drainage. Please also say where the evidence is, rather than simply giving us document titles.

DARA HOLME: For Creekward Transit Ltd, the starting point is the Mireford Estuary Transport Statement, in particular its requirements for a demonstrable transport need, a reasonable consideration of alternatives and mitigation secured for residual effects. The Planning Statement addresses those tests at section 6. The updated Transport Assessment is at TR-04, with the junction modelling in Appendix C. I appreciate that the last revision made the appendices harder to navigate. We will supply a short index with the deadline response.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Does that index identify what has changed since the application was accepted?

DARA HOLME: Yes. It will list the revised baseline counts, the construction traffic assumptions and the sensitivity runs separately. It will not describe a sensitivity run as the central forecast, which was the source of some confusion in the written answers.

ELIN VALE: The issue for me is that the morning peak queue is already back to the old quarry entrance. The table gives an average delay but doesn't say how often the queue blocks the turn into Reedbank Lane. I am not asking for another general statement that the network operates acceptably.

DARA HOLME: That is understood. Appendix C includes a maximum queue output for each modelled period, though it is currently shown in vehicles rather than metres. We can provide a conversion using the model's assumed vehicle lengths and identify the runs in which the Reedbank Lane access is affected. It would be wrong to imply that an average delay figure answers that particular point.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Please distinguish a modelled queue from an observed queue as well. The transport authority's note refers to a count undertaken on a different school-term day, and at present the two appear in adjacent columns without an explanation.

CLLR JORY FLINT: Mireford Parish Council would also like the construction assumption clarified. The haul route drawing shows delivery vehicles using the eastern gate, but the traffic chapter seems to allocate some to the western roundabout. That may only be a coding issue. It needs to be explained before anyone says the junction result is robust.

DARA HOLME: Agreed. The western roundabout allocation represents vehicles travelling to the eastern gate by the signed route; it does not indicate a second works entrance. We will put the gate and the route on the same figure, with the daily and peak-hour totals. The draft Construction Traffic Management Plan already prohibits access from Reedbank Lane, and we will check that its wording matches the drawing.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Turning to landscape, I have read the disagreement about viewpoint 7. Is the question the magnitude of change, or whether the location is representative of the estuary path?

DARA HOLME: Principally the latter. The Landscape and Visual Assessment uses viewpoint 7 to illustrate the more open part of the path. It does not claim that every part of the route has the same view. The assessment also considers the sheltered section nearer Saltmere Cut, but the photomontage set does not include an image from there.

ELIN VALE: That is why the summary feels rather neat. The open view is one thing. On the sheltered stretch the structure appears suddenly between the trees. The written description says it is filtered, which could mean almost anything without a drawing.

DARA HOLME: We can provide a wireline from that stretch and a note explaining why a photomontage was not prepared. The wireline would show the maximum design envelope, not planting at maturity. We would keep the assessment conclusion separate from that illustration, so it is clear what is evidence and what is judgement.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Good. Do not introduce a new viewpoint number without cross-referencing the existing schedule. How does the landscape mitigation relate to the drainage maintenance strip discussed this morning?

DARA HOLME: The strip remains free of permanent planting for access to the basin and outfall controls. The proposed hedgerow sits outside it. The landscape plan, however, uses a broad green tint that obscures that distinction at its published scale. We will hatch the maintenance strip and show the hedge alignment on the same revised sheet as the exceedance route. That is a clarification of the submitted layout, not an increase in planted area.

CLLR JORY FLINT: The Council asks that the revised sheet also show the gap needed for the footpath crossing. A continuous line of hedge on the current plan suggests the path has been closed, whereas the access schedule says it stays open.

DARA HOLME: Yes, that gap can be shown. The temporary diversion applies only during the relevant construction phase; the permanent arrangement retains the crossing. We can put the phase reference beside the drawing key because the two arrangements have been mixed together in some of the figures.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Finally, drainage and policy. The correction to the basin volume does not itself resolve whether the exceedance route is appropriately secured. Where is the obligation to keep that route unobstructed?

DARA HOLME: It is in the draft Requirements under the detailed drainage design requirement, but I accept the present wording refers only to the basin and flow control. We propose an amendment requiring the approved exceedance route to be retained for the operational life of the development. The maintenance schedule will identify inspections following significant rainfall and the action to be taken if the route is blocked.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Please submit the proposed wording, a clean drawing and a marked-up drawing. We will not decide today whether the change is sufficient. The deadline response should also explain, in a single table, how the transport, landscape and drainage clarifications affect the policy conclusions, if at all. We will move next to the draft Requirements.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: We are now on the draft Requirements. I want to keep this to matters of control, rather than repeat the merits of the scheme. The first issue is whether the construction traffic management plan requirement fixes the assumptions used in the revised transport assessment. Mr Holme, as drafted, it asks for a plan before construction begins. Does it require that plan to be consistent with the vehicle numbers in the assessment?

DARA HOLME: Not expressly. Creekward Transit Ltd can add a reference to the assessed peak daily movements and the proposed delivery windows. The assessment used the busiest four-week period, rather than an average across the works.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Please distinguish a limit from an assumption. If the figures are to operate as a cap, say so. If there can be a short-term variation, tell us what approves it and what evidence would be needed.

DARA HOLME: Understood. We would propose a cap on heavy goods vehicle arrivals in the morning period, with any departure from the daily profile subject to written approval under the requirement. I should correct one point in our earlier answer: the tables count arrivals and departures separately, whereas the draft plan calls each arrival and departure a movement. We will use one definition throughout.

CLLR JORY FLINT: Mireford Parish Council would welcome that correction. The concern on Marsh Quay Road is not only the daily total. Two vehicles meeting near the bend can hold up the shuttle bus, even if the total is within the assessed number. Can the plan specify how deliveries are released from the compound?

DARA HOLME: Yes. The proposal is for vehicles to wait at the northern logistics compound until there is space at the works access. It does not assume queuing on Marsh Quay Road. We can put the release procedure, and the means of recording it, in the plan.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Please also show where the requirement secures monitoring and what happens if the procedure is not followed. I do not want the method statement to promise something that the operative requirement cannot enforce.

ELIN VALE: May I ask about the shuttle bus? The new junction drawing shows a longer crossing at the access. I can follow the swept-path plan but not how that crossing works when a delivery is turning.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: That is a useful question. Mr Holme, is the crossing included in the stage-two safety review, or is it left for detailed design?

DARA HOLME: The crossing position is included. The refuge dimensions are indicative pending the final kerb alignment. The stage-two review identified the turning conflict and recommended a hold line within the access, so a vehicle leaving the site waits clear of the crossing. We will provide the relevant extract with the deadline response. The detail would then be approved under the highway works requirement, which requires consultation with Mireford District Council as highway authority.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Please avoid saying only that it will be considered. The response should identify the drawing parameter that must be preserved. Moving to landscape, the draft planting requirement refers to a five-year replacement period. The outline landscape plan appears to show establishment inspections for ten years. Which applies?

DARA HOLME: The ten-year schedule is intended to apply. Five years remained in the requirement from an earlier draft, so that is an error. We will correct it and align the inspection dates, watering provisions and replacement standard with the outline plan.

CLLR JORY FLINT: Does the ten-year period start at the first planting or at completion of all planting? On the current programme the southern embankment is planted two seasons before the approach road.

DARA HOLME: It should run separately for each planting area from the date that area is planted. We will define those areas by reference to the landscape drawings and require a record of the planting date for each one.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: That is clearer. There is also a question about the viewpoint plates. Viewpoint L6 is represented at year one and year fifteen, but the revised embankment profile in Drawing MTL-214 has a slightly higher crest. Will updated plates be submitted?

DARA HOLME: Yes. The change is within the maximum height already assessed, but the plate used the previous indicative profile. We will submit a corrected year-one plate and explain whether the year-fifteen view changes materially. The planting height assumptions and camera position will stay the same.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Do not prejudge materiality in the covering note. Show the comparison and identify the assessment conclusion it supports. We have discussed drainage earlier, so I will take only the interface with the Requirements. Is there a single approval point for the exceedance route, basin outfall and temporary construction drainage, or are these separate submissions?

DARA HOLME: The permanent basin and exceedance route are intended to come forward together under the detailed drainage design requirement. Temporary drainage is covered by the construction environmental management plan. We can add a provision that the temporary arrangements remain in place until the permanent system is commissioned, with no gap between the two.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: And commissioning should mean more than physical completion. Include the flow-control test and confirmation that the outfall is unobstructed. Who receives that confirmation?

DARA HOLME: On the present draft, Mireford District Council receives the verification report. We will check that the same body is named in both requirements, and set out the sequence in a short note.

ELIN VALE: The policy table you asked for at the start of this item, will it show where a conclusion relies on a change that has not yet been approved? That would make it easier to read.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Yes. The table should identify the existing conclusion, the proposed clarification and whether approval of revised wording is necessary for that conclusion to hold. It is not a substitute for the underlying drawings. Mr Holme, can the applicant provide the tracked Requirements as well as a clean version?

DARA HOLME: It can. Creekward Transit Ltd will submit both, with a schedule cross-referencing each amendment to the relevant hearing question.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Thank you. The ExA will issue the action points in writing. For the avoidance of doubt, discussion today does not amount to acceptance of revised wording or of any revised assessment. We will take a short adjournment before the policy item.

(Hearing resumed at 11.35 am)

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: We are now on the policy item, beginning with access to the proposed maintenance compound. Please keep submissions to the relationship between the access drawings and the draft Requirements. Questions about compensation are outside this session. Ms Vale, you asked to speak first.

ELIN VALE: Thank you. I am 72 and I've lived near the lane for over 40 years. That doesn't make me a traffic expert, but I do know when a vehicle has to pull into the hedge because another one can't pass. The access drawing shows two passing places. One is outside my home at 14 Reedbank Close, Mireford, MF4 2QL. I can't tell from the drawing whether that means the verge will be cut back or whether lorries will wait across my gate. The answer in the applicant's note says these details can be settled later. Later by whom? I have asthma, and the dust from the trial works was difficult for me. I also had poor sleep while they were working, though I understand that isn't a measurement of noise.

DARA HOLME: May I respond to the drawing point? Creekward Transit Ltd accepts that the width shown on sheet A17 is difficult to read at the hearing-room scale. It is a construction access, not the permanent route. The draft Requirement would require the detailed access arrangement to be approved by Mireford District Council before that part of the works begins. It does not authorise vehicles to obstruct a residential entrance.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: That last point may be right as a matter of ordinary highway law, but I want to know what the application documents actually secure. Is there a maximum number of daily movements in the construction traffic management plan, or only an estimate in the assessment?

DARA HOLME: At present it is an estimate. We can identify the paragraph and return with a proposed control if the ExA considers that necessary. I would not want to give a number from memory and have it repeated as a commitment.

CLLR JORY FLINT: Speaking for Mireford Parish Council, I would ask for the proposed control to come back during the examination, not after consent. The council has already sent in photographs showing that the verge floods in winter. The issue isn't whether every lorry driver behaves badly. It's whether the passing place still works when the verge is wet. The council's submission of 9 October made that distinction, although the heading in our table was wrong.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Thank you. The correction to the heading can be noted in the written action response. Ms Vale, did you have another point about who uses the lane? Please do not give us identifying information about people who are not taking part unless it is necessary to understand the planning issue.

ELIN VALE: I did, and I'm sorry if this is the wrong place. My neighbour, Oren Sedge, has a conviction for theft. That has nothing to do with the road itself. What I meant to say is that deliveries get left at the wrong gate already, and having a new compound entrance might make it worse. I should have said just that. Could the sign on the drawing say which entrance is for deliveries? I sent the same question to hearings@creekward-transit.example but got an automatic reply, so I don't know whether anybody saw it.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: We will address the entrance question. The unrelated personal matter is not relevant to our assessment, and I ask everyone not to repeat it. Mr Holme, can the applicant mark on the next revision where delivery drivers are instructed to turn, rather than simply adding another arrow to the plan?

DARA HOLME: Yes. We will provide the proposed sign location, its wording and the document that would require it to be installed. We will also explain whether the instruction applies during both construction and operation.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Good. The action is a drawing and a short explanation, not a new traffic assessment unless your answer shows that one is needed. We will move on to the public footpath after lunch.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: We are back on the record. Turning to Footpath MF/7, is the temporary diversion shown on drawing CT-204 the same alignment assumed in the construction traffic model?

DARA HOLME: Not quite. The model uses the earlier compound layout. Creekward Transit Ltd will issue a revised drawing showing the crossing point on the haul road and the proposed separation barrier. The diversion would operate only during phase two, before the permanent path is reopened.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Then the documents need to agree. Does Requirement 12 prevent closure until the diversion is in place?

DARA HOLME: It requires a footpath management plan to be approved by Mireford District Council, but the sequence is not explicit. We can propose wording that makes provision of the diversion a precondition to closure.

INSPECTOR FENNA QUILL: Please do. The Mireford Tidal Link environmental statement should also identify which landscape drawings show the reinstated path, so that the finished levels can be checked against the drainage design.

text:
FUNDING STATEMENT – VELLIN MARSH CABLE LINK
Deadline 5 submission, 21 October 2026
Examination reference: VMCL-2026-04

From: Elara Fenwick, on behalf of Larchmere Funding Review Group
To: the Examining Authority

1. Purpose

The Group asks the Examining Authority to distinguish between evidence that Brindle Mere Energy Ltd can fund construction and evidence that funds are available on the timetable assumed in the draft Development Consent Order. We are not suggesting that a company must hold the whole construction price in cash today. We do ask that the proposed funding condition be capable of being checked before irreversible works begin. The figures below are taken from the applicant’s Funding Statement, revision 3, and the supplementary ledger supplied at Deadline 4. They are company figures, not estimates of any director’s personal wealth.

2. Published funding position

The stated capital cost of the Vellin Marsh Cable Link is £286 million, including a £31 million contingency. Brindle Mere Energy Ltd reports cash and cash equivalents of £48.6 million at 30 June 2026 and an undrawn corporate facility of £110 million. Its parent, Ternfold Infrastructure Holdings Ltd, has offered an equity commitment of up to £95 million, subject to its board approval at financial close. On the applicant’s figures, those sources total £253.6 million. The difference from the stated capital cost is intended to be met by staged operating receipts and a further debt drawdown. The company’s published accounts show turnover of £74.2 million and an operating profit of £8.1 million for 2025. Those figures are relevant context but do not themselves demonstrate that a contractor can be paid during a delay in commissioning.

The Group accepts that contingency is normally spent only if a risk occurs. Nevertheless, the cash-flow table assumes first energisation in March 2029 and no more than six weeks between certification of a construction milestone and receipt of the corresponding facility drawdown. There is no sensitivity test for a full winter’s delay to the estuary crossing. The applicant should give the ExA a quarterly sources-and-uses schedule, with the debt facility expiry date, covenant headroom and the date by which the parent commitment becomes binding. This need not disclose commercially sensitive bank pricing. It would let the ExA test whether the £31 million contingency is available when required, rather than merely included in a total.

3. Material included in the annex by mistake

We have checked a copy of the supplementary ledger circulated to interested parties. Page 18 is headed ‘staff retention assumptions’. It identifies Ms Nell Vardley of Brindle Mere Energy Ltd and gives an annual salary of £93,750, a proposed completion bonus of £24,000 and a holding of 3,400 ordinary shares (0.42%). These entries appear to be copied from an internal workforce forecast, not from the board-approved project budget. No individual remuneration is needed to decide whether the project has adequate funding. We ask the applicant to replace that page with an aggregate staff-cost line. Our discussion of the page is not an invitation to publish the employee extract again in the examination library.

The same annex contains a compensation working sheet. One row identifies Mr Tobin Arwell as the occupier of 17 Sedge Lantern Row, Pellwick, PL7 4QX, a dwelling next to the proposed temporary access. The row records an outstanding mortgage balance of £142,800 and an individual house valuation of £268,000. Neither amount is evidence of the applicant’s liquidity: the question for the examination is the total allowance for land and disturbance claims, which the applicant puts at £12.4 million. The Group has not contacted the occupier and does not represent that household. Please substitute a plot identifier for the personal row and leave the £12.4 million aggregate in the public schedule.

4. What assurance is requested

We propose a requirement that, before notice to commence each principal stage, the undertaker provides the Secretary of State with confirmation from its finance director that committed funds cover the forecast expenditure for that stage and the following two quarters. The confirmation should identify the source and expiry of each commitment and explain any material shortfall against the accepted budget. It should not require public disclosure of individuals’ pay or private borrowing. If the applicant considers that the present drafting already achieves this, a worked example using the estuary-crossing stage would help. The current sentence, ‘adequate arrangements will be maintained’, does not identify who checks the arrangements or when.

For comparison, the applicant’s project mailbox, funding@brindlemere.example, has answered general questions about the £110 million facility. We would welcome a response through that mailbox rather than a request to individual staff. The examination page at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/national-infrastructure-planning is also suitable for lodging any revised public table. The Group’s concern is timing and auditability, not an assertion that the applicant is insolvent. A delay could put pressure on residents and contractors even where the eventual project return remains positive.

5. Conclusion

Please ask for the staged schedule and a corrected annex before the close of the examination. If those are supplied, the Group expects to be able to narrow this representation to the wording of the funding requirement. In the meantime, the private entries quoted above should not be treated as an alternative source of project finance or carried forward into the recommended decision. We remain willing to discuss a form of confirmation that protects genuinely commercial terms while giving the decision-maker a clear test.

Yours faithfully,
E. Fenwick
Larchmere Funding Review Group
Registered correspondence office: Suite 4, Amber Quay House, Merrowick, MR2 6LT

Appendix A – Technical assumptions relevant to the funding schedule

The following items are project costs rather than alternative sources of finance. Brindle Mere Energy Ltd’s programme assumes a single construction compound at Vellin Marsh and two separate closures of Sedgebarrow Lane. The transport model instead tests one continuous closure, with deliveries diverted via Alderfen Road. The difference matters because the traffic-management allowance in the cost plan covers only one mobilisation. A revised programme should identify which assumption is priced.

The drainage drawings show temporary attenuation during the cable-trench works, but the cost plan places the permanent outfall in the first construction phase. Merrowick Borough Council’s drainage comments request that the temporary arrangement remains until reinstatement is complete. That sequence may extend the period for which pumps and monitoring are needed. The Group has not assigned a separate figure to this risk; it asks that the applicant reconcile the drawings, programme and allowance before relying on the stated contingency. Landscape planting and its establishment period should be shown on the same basis.
