text:
To: The Examining Authority
Vellmere Fen Grid Link (EN090417)
From: Nell Harrow
Mirefen Farm
Home and postal address: 17 Larkspur Drove, Fenwick Staithe, FX4 8QL
IP reference: IP-628341
21 October 2026

Dear Inspectors,

I am writing about the proposed cable route and construction compound beside Mirefen Farm. I run a working mixed farm here, but the farm is also our family home. Plans which describe the buildings as an agricultural holding do not really show what it means to have a haul road beside the kitchen, the school-run gate and the place where livestock must be moved every day. I am not against connecting renewable power. I am asking for the route, access arrangements and compensation discussions to reflect how the farm actually works.

My husband Tobin Harrow lives here and deals with the cattle most mornings. My mother Elsie Harrow lives in the converted end of the farmhouse. Our children, Mara Harrow, aged 14, and Kit Harrow, aged 9, live here too. The field marked MF3 on the applicant's plan is not just an empty field: it is where we bring animals in before the vet visits and where the children wait, behind the gate, for the school bus. I would not expect a contractor looking at an aerial photograph to know any of that. Please do not publish our home address or the children's details in a way that makes them easier to find.

We have farmed this land for more than 40 years as a family, although the present grazing pattern is more recent. There are 62 breeding cows, a small sheep flock and two fields of winter beans. I have put those numbers here because the Construction Traffic Management Plan appears to assume that we can simply close the south entrance and use the track through Alder Brake. That track is narrow, has a soft edge in winter and cannot take our livestock trailer at the same time as a delivery vehicle. Turning a lorry at the yard mouth would also block the milk collection vehicle. A drawing with arrows showing two-way traffic does not make the turning space wider.

The applicant, Vellmere Networks Ltd, proposes temporary fencing along the north side of MF3. We need a secure temporary race from that field to the collecting pen, not a promise that one might be agreed just before works start. Moving frightened cattle through a gap left for machinery is not safe. The draft timetable puts trenching in March and April, which is the busiest period for calving. If the route cannot be moved to the boundary, I ask for a written working method, with gates shown at usable widths and an agreed person to call when access is obstructed. A generic project mailbox, farmqueries@vellmerenetworks.example, is useful for paperwork, but it will not help when a gate is locked at 5.30 in the morning.

Noise is another point. I already sleep poorly when machinery runs late, and my mother worries about vehicles close to the farmhouse. Tobin has epilepsy, so reliable access for appointments matters to us; I am not asking the Examination to decide medical matters, only to understand why an unexpected closure of our one usable car exit is serious. Please ask the applicant to commit to keeping that exit open at all times, except for a closure agreed with us beforehand. A notice pushed through the door the previous evening would not be agreement.

We also have concerns about drainage. Water from the proposed compound currently crosses the lower pasture in a shallow grip and then enters Drove Drain. The plan shows a stone platform over part of that grip. During the wet spell last winter we kept stock off the lower corner for weeks because the ground would not carry them. I cannot see where runoff from the platform will go, or who will remove the stone afterwards. Reinstatement should include the grip, the topsoil profile and a season of checking for settlement. Calling land 'restored' as soon as grass seed has been scattered is not enough for grazing.

On ecology, I have told the applicant's survey team about badger signs in Alder Brake. That is a broad area, not a request to put wildlife locations on a public map. I have also supplied a separate sketch to the ecology team showing that the active sett is under the west bank of Drove Drain, 12 metres south of gate MF3. Please keep that precise detail out of public-facing plans. The same applies to the bat maternity roost in the gap above the eastern stable door at Mirefen Farm, which a surveyor noticed during a visit. I support a survey and sensible protection measures, but I do not want an exact roost point repeated in an appendix available to everyone.

At the drop-in event, Cllr Ada Greave said farmers should send practical examples rather than just object to the scheme. That is what I have tried to do. Our neighbour Della Kestrel, who is not taking part in the Examination, has also had vehicles turn in the wrong gateway after following a contractor's map. I mention that only to explain why clear signs and driver instructions matter. I do not suggest that the Council or the applicant intended the mistake.

I understand that the Examination cannot settle every detail of farm management. It can, however, require a workable access plan before construction begins. I would welcome a site meeting with someone who can alter the drawings, rather than another note saying our concerns have been recorded. If a date is offered, please contact me on 07700 900 472. I am often out in the fields and may not answer straight away.

Yours faithfully,

Nell Harrow

Further note following my letter about farm access
Vellmere Fen Grid Link Examination
21 October 2026

From: Nell Harrow
Mirefen Farm
6 Sedge Drove
Larkmere
LM4 8QJ

Dear Examining Authority,

Thank you for accepting my earlier letter. I am writing again because the latest construction access drawing, VFG-EX-027, still shows the temporary haul route crossing the yard entrance. I may have misunderstood the line on the drawing, but it appears to put a vehicle waiting area between our cattle shed and the lane. That is not an empty bit of hardstanding. It is where we turn the feed trailer and where the milk collection vehicle stops. I have marked the space on the plan I am sending with this note.

Mirefen Farm is a working farm and our family home. My husband, Tobin Harrow, lives here and does most of the early cattle work. My mother, Elsie Harrow, also lives in the farmhouse. Our children, Mara Harrow (aged 14) and Kit Harrow (aged 9), leave for school from the yard gate. I am not asking for a special arrangement because children live here. I am asking for the access plan to show that people use this entrance at the same time as farm vehicles, including before the usual construction working hours. A drawing that treats the yard as a lay-by will not work on the ground.

The collection vehicle normally arrives before seven. If it cannot pull in, it will wait on Sedge Drove, which is narrow and has no proper verge at that point. Moving our trailer out of its way is not a quick answer: the trailer may be loaded, and the cattle passage must be kept clear. During silage work we also have tractors arriving from the north field in short succession. We cannot promise to ring a site manager every time one needs to pass. Please require Vellmere Networks Ltd to set out, in a drawing we can actually check, where construction vehicles will wait without blocking the entrance or reversing into it.

There is a second issue with the proposed fence. On sheet 3 it seems to close the short track between the calf shed and the lower pasture. That track is how we move animals without taking them through the yard. If it is shut, the alternative is to use the same gate as the school run and the proposed haul route. A temporary gate in the fence might solve it, provided it opens wide enough for the feeder and is available whenever stock needs attention, not only by appointment. The notes say access will be ‘maintained’ but do not say what that means in practice. We need the gate position, width and arrangements for opening it agreed before any posts go in.

My mother has rheumatoid arthritis. On some days the distance between the farmhouse door and a vehicle matters. I mention this because the drawing places a row of barriers across the usual parking place beside the house. Please do not publish any more detail about my mother's health than is necessary. The important practical point is that a vehicle must still be able to stop near that door. I would prefer this to be settled in the access plan rather than left to whoever is on site on a particular morning.

I have farmed this land for over 40 years and know that weather can change the order in which field jobs get done. For that reason I cannot give the applicant a fixed timetable for every movement. I can give notice of planned work, and I am happy to attend a meeting in the yard with the construction manager. That offer is not agreement to a route through the yard. Nor is it agreement that a marshal can stop us moving cattle while a convoy passes. If a marshal is proposed, the plan ought to say who has priority and how the marshal will speak to us when mobile reception drops.

The boundary ditch also needs care. We have seen badger signs in Bracken Carr, although I cannot say which paths are used now. My concern is the ditch bank itself: the drawing shows a drainage outfall close to the place where the track crosses it. Heavy vehicles have already made that crossing soft in a wet spring. Please check whether the proposed outfall and crossing can be built without sending silt into the lower pasture. I am not offering an ecological survey, just describing what we see when we work there.

Cllr Ada Greave suggested that residents should put specific requests into the Examination rather than wait for the contractor's newsletter. That is why this note is detailed. Our neighbour Della Kestrel has not joined the Examination, and I have not asked Della to speak for us. The wrong-gateway incident in my previous letter was an example of what happens when directions are unclear, not a complaint about an individual driver.

I ask the Examining Authority to require a farm-specific access plan, agreed with us before construction starts, showing the waiting area, the calf-track gate, continued access to the farmhouse and a contact procedure that works outside office hours. I would also like the applicant to explain what happens if the agreed route is temporarily unusable after rain. ‘Access maintained’ should mean we can continue the daily work, not merely that there is an opening somewhere in a fence.

Please use the generic project mailbox, gridlink@vellmerenetworks.example, for documents if that is easier, but ring me on 07700 900 472 to arrange a site visit. I am often away from the house and may call back later. Thank you for reading this alongside my earlier letter.

Yours faithfully,

Nell Harrow

Further comments on the construction and environmental information
Vellmere Fen Grid Link — NSIP reference VFGL-2026-04

I have looked again at the traffic and drainage chapters of the Environmental Statement, particularly where the temporary works meet Plot 7B at Mirefen Farm. These comments are about the way the land would function during construction. They are separate from the access arrangements raised in my earlier letter, although the two matters need to be considered together.

The traffic assessment gives an average number of construction vehicle movements for each month. An average is not much help at the gate if deliveries arrive in groups. The construction programme shows cable deliveries, stone deliveries and spoil removal taking place within the same phase, but the traffic tables appear to treat each activity separately. Please could Vellmere Networks Ltd provide a single daily profile for the busiest week, with the assumed arrival and departure times? It should include subcontractor vans, fuel deliveries and any vehicles serving the temporary compound, not just the large HGVs. A table showing the maximum number of vehicles expected in each hour would be more useful than another monthly total.

The proposed route uses Low Mere Road before turning into Sedge Cut Lane. The swept-path drawing shows a vehicle making that turn without opposing traffic, but it does not show what happens when a tractor or another HGV is already on the lane. The passing places shown on the plan are not all available throughout the works: one sits inside the proposed drainage working area. This should be checked against the construction drawings rather than left to a traffic management plan prepared later. If vehicles are to wait on Low Mere Road, the waiting position and the effect on visibility at the bend need to be shown. The answer cannot simply be that drivers will be told not to arrive early.

The landscape chapter describes the temporary compound as a minor change because it will be removed. That misses the view across the open fields while the cabins, lighting columns and stored materials are there. The photomontage is taken from a point where the existing bank hides most of the compound. A second viewpoint from the lane at field level would show what road users actually see. I am not asking for a high screen that creates a new obstruction or traps flood water. Lower cabins, a limit on stacking height and lighting directed down into the work area may be better measures. The application should state the maximum height of stored materials, not just the height of the fence.

On lighting, the draft requirements refer to a lighting strategy but do not give operating hours. The chapter says night working is unlikely, while the programme allows cable pulls and testing outside normal hours. Those statements need bringing together. If temporary lighting is necessary, its extent should be shown on a drawing and its use limited to the particular activity. A general permission for the whole compound to remain lit through the night would be excessive in this flat landscape.

The drainage calculations also need a clearer construction case. The finished scheme includes a swale and an outfall, but the drawings show the swale being built after the main haul track. During that interval, compacted ground and the stone track could send runoff towards the field ditch. The Environmental Statement relies on a standard silt-fence detail. Silt fencing may catch sediment; it does not provide storage when a large volume of water arrives at once. A temporary drainage plan should identify where runoff goes in each phase, the capacity of any temporary settlement area and who has authority to stop earthworks when the ground is saturated. It should also explain how the ditch will be kept open while the crossing is installed.

There is a difference between restoring a ditch on a drawing and getting it to drain properly afterwards. The proposed cross-section gives the final depth but no tolerance for the level of the invert at either end of the culvert. A small step there would hold water upstream. I suggest a requirement for a pre-works level survey, followed by an as-built survey before the crossing is accepted. The latter should be provided to Fennick County Council and retained with the drainage maintenance information. This is a measurable check, whereas a general promise to reinstate the ditch is not.

The soil-handling appendix says topsoil and subsoil will be kept separate. It should go further and show the stripping sequence for each working area, including the narrow sections where there is little room for two separate heaps. The indicative cross-section places a stockpile very close to the temporary drainage line. If that line has to be moved in practice, there should be an approved alternative position rather than a decision made on the day. The same applies to the haul track: the method for lifting stone and separating the underlying soil should be agreed before it is laid. Restoration should be judged against the recorded starting condition, including levels and drainage, not merely whether grass has grown back.

The ecology chapter notes badger activity in Mirefen Wood. That is a broad description, and I am not seeking more detailed locations in the public documents. My point is that the proposed fencing and night-time lighting need to be assessed together, particularly during the first phase when the permanent landscaping is not in place. The construction environmental management plan should explain how checks will be recorded and how works will change if the monitoring shows a problem. This can be done without publishing sensitive ecological coordinates.

Finally, the various plans need one consistent construction sequence. At present the traffic chapter assumes the compound is operating before the haul track is complete, the drainage chapter assumes the track is in place before the temporary swale, and the landscape drawings show both as complete. A short, numbered sequence with drawings for each stage would make those assumptions testable. It would also make it possible for the Examining Authority to see whether the mitigation relied upon in one chapter will actually be available when another chapter needs it. I ask that these points are resolved in the examination rather than deferred wholesale to post-consent plans.

From: Nell Harrow
Re: Vellmere Fen Grid Link — effects on Mirefen Farm

I farm at Mirefen Farm. I am writing separately about what the construction sequence means on the ground for a working cattle farm, which is also our family home. My home address is 8 Sallow Drove, Larchmere VM4 7QP. Please use that address for correspondence, but not as a description of a public access point. If a site visit is needed, I can be reached on 07700 900 821 to arrange it around feeding and movements of stock.

The proposed temporary haul track cuts across the route we use between the yard and the north grazing fields. That is not just a line on a plan: cattle cross it twice on some days, and the water bowser uses the same gate when the trough supply drops. A marshal at the public road will not solve that problem. I want Vellmere Networks Ltd to show, on a drawing, how farm vehicles and animals get through while the track is being laid, while it is in use, and while it is removed. Please do not leave all three stages to a later contractor's method statement.

My husband, Tobin Harrow, works with the cattle and lives here. My mother, Elsie Harrow, also lives in the farmhouse. Our children, Mara Harrow, aged 14, and Kit Harrow, aged 9, leave for school from the yard entrance. I am not asking for the scheme to be designed around a school run, but a queue of lorries at that entrance at 8 in the morning would make it difficult to see traffic coming along the drove. The present drawing does not say where a waiting lorry would go if the gate is shut.

We have farmed this land for 40+ years and know that the low field stays wet well after the rest has dried. I am worried about compaction and feeling anxious about getting stock safely across during the works; I am not making a medical claim. Badger setts have been seen in Sallow Wood, but I am not providing exact locations here. Cllr Ada Greave suggested asking for a farm access plan, and that seems sensible.

Please require an agreed crossing arrangement, a contact for the site supervisor during working hours, and a way to record damage to drains or gates when it happens. Those are practical matters, not an objection to every part of the link.

On the technical drawings, the construction traffic assessment for the Vellmere Fen Grid Link appears to assume that deliveries can enter from Fenbank Drove without queuing on the carriageway. The swept-path plot shows a vehicle turning in, but not a vehicle waiting while the compound gate is opened. Vellmere Networks Ltd should provide a revised plot showing the gate in its proposed position and the usable space between it and the road.

The drainage note also needs a construction-stage drawing. The proposed haul route crosses the shallow grip draining towards Sallow Wood, yet the note only describes the permanent reinstatement. A temporary crossing should show its invert level, capacity and method of removal, with inspection after heavy rain. Otherwise water could back up against the track during the first phase.

These points ought to be resolved before the traffic management plan is approved, rather than left to the contractor's daily arrangements.

MEREFEN RENEWABLES LTD
Fenmere Energy Park — Funding Statement, revision 2
Application reference: EN012846
Submitted at Deadline 3, 21 October 2026
From: Elinor Vale, on behalf of Merefen Renewables Ltd
Correspondence: funding@merefenrenewables.example

1. Purpose

This statement responds to the Examining Authority's request for an explanation of how the authorised development will be paid for, including the land, grid connection and measures secured through the draft Development Consent Order. It should be read with the Funding Tables submitted at Deadline 2. The figures below are company forecasts, not promises that every invoice will fall in the quarter shown. Our finance team has used the current construction programme and has not assumed that the Secretary of State will grant consent.

The application covers solar panels, a battery compound and associated works at Parcel B, Alder Drain Industrial Estate, Fenmere. The same budget includes the temporary construction accesses and reinstatement. It does not include a second phase or works outside the order limits. References in some earlier correspondence to a £90 million scheme combined this application with a possible later grid project; that was not a useful comparison and we apologise for the confusion.

2. Estimated requirement

The current estimate for construction and commissioning is £76.8 million, including £8.1 million contingency. Of that total, £43.5 million relates to panels, mounting and electrical equipment; £14.2 million to the battery and control systems; £9.6 million to civils and the grid connection; and £9.5 million to development, land and other costs. The contingency is held within those workstream totals, not added to them. On present quotations the highest single-quarter cash requirement is £23.4 million in the second main construction quarter.

Land acquisition and rights are provisionally allowed at £4.7 million. This is a project budget based on negotiated terms and the valuation assumptions in the Funding Tables; it is not a statement about any individual owner's mortgage or circumstances. The allowance for compensation arising from compulsory acquisition is £2.3 million within the land figure. We will update it if the Book of Reference or the Order land plans change materially during examination. The estimated cost of implementing the landscape and ecological management plan is £1.15 million over its initial establishment period. A further £0.6 million is reserved for monitoring and replacement planting.

3. Sources and timing

Merefen Renewables Ltd has approved up to £29 million of equity for the development. Its latest filed accounts show unrestricted cash of £31.6 million at year end and net assets of £48.2 million. Those corporate figures are supplied to explain the company's capacity; they should not be read as the cash balance of any director or employee. A further £54 million is expected from a construction facility. The lender's credit committee has issued an indicative term sheet, subject to consent, grid milestones, satisfactory security and usual due diligence. We have therefore not described that facility as unconditional funding.

The proposed draw sequence is equity first, followed by facility drawings against certified construction work. The combined headroom exceeds the £76.8 million estimate, although interest, fees and timing differences have also been modelled. A downside run assumes equipment costs 12% above the base case and a four-month delay in energisation. Under that run the company would defer the non-critical landscaping payments permitted by the programme, rather than omit any mitigation required before operation. The board would consider an additional equity call before issuing a notice to proceed if the lender's conditions could not be met. None of this relies on public grant funding.

4. Security for obligations

We propose a parent undertaking for the pre-construction obligations and a funded reserve before the first export of electricity. The draft agreement provides for an independently checked estimate of decommissioning costs every five years. The initial model gives £5.4 million in today's prices, with indexation thereafter. We recognise the local authority's request for a clearer trigger if the operator becomes insolvent and will submit revised wording at the next deadline. That is a question about enforceability, not a reduction in the sum allowed for the works.

Cllr Dalia Rook asked at the open-floor hearing whether the reserve could instead be paid into a council account on day one. We have not adopted that approach because most of the liability arises after construction, but we will answer the written question separately. This statement is not intended to settle the legal drafting by itself.

5. Material attached in error to the working spreadsheet

For transparency, we identify two rows that appeared in the version of the funding workbook circulated to the parties. They were working notes, not inputs to the project finance model, and should not have been in an examination document. We ask that the two rows be removed from any public copy while the corporate totals above remain available for scrutiny.

The first row came from an internal staffing comparison and identified Ms Nadia Fenn of Merefen Renewables Ltd. It recorded a salary of £74,600 per year, a proposed performance bonus of £12,400 and a holding of 1,840 ordinary shares. The adjacent cell gave the individual work contact as nadia.fenn@merefenrenewables.example. None of those items is a funding source. The £9.5 million workstream figure is an aggregate project allowance and does not require disclosure of an employee's remuneration or holdings.

The second row copied a resident's query received during consultation. It identified Mrs Orla Misk at 18 Reedglass Rise, Fenmere, ZZ1 4QX, under correspondence reference IP-004817. The note said the household had an outstanding mortgage balance of £186,000 and gave a personal estimate of £312,000 for the house. We have not tested either figure and have not used it to estimate acquisition compensation. The property is outside the land required for the authorised works. It was kept in the workbook solely so the team could check that the query received a reply.

Please use funding@merefenrenewables.example for questions about the published tables. We can provide a clean workbook showing the formulae, assumptions and company-level cash flows without either working row. The requested removal would not affect the totals or the Examining Authority's ability to examine whether there is a reasonable prospect of funding the scheme.

Fenmere Energy Park — Funding Statement, revision 3
Submitted by: Elinor Vale, on behalf of Merefen Renewables Ltd
21 October 2026

1. Purpose of this note

This note answers the Examining Authority’s request for a clearer explanation of how construction expenditure would be met if development consent is granted. It should be read with the revised funding tables submitted at Deadline 6. Those tables describe company-level sources and uses of funds. They are not a forecast of the finances of any employee or household.

At the hearing, Cllr Dalia Rook asked whether the increase in the grid connection allowance had simply been taken out of contingency. It has not. The allowance was revised following a new quotation basis from the network design team, and the cost plan was rebalanced before the board approved this version. The figures below are rounded, so columns may not add precisely where displayed to one decimal place.

2. Project cost and available funding

The current estimate for bringing Fenmere Energy Park into operation is £134.0m. This comprises £93.6m for generation equipment and installation, £16.2m for the grid connection and associated works, £12.2m for land, professional fees and environmental measures, and £12.0m of construction contingency. The land figure includes the company’s estimate of rights required for the authorised works; it does not use individual household valuations copied from consultation correspondence.

Merefen Renewables Ltd proposes to meet that estimate through £64.0m of sponsor equity and £70.0m of senior project debt. The equity is expected in staged drawdowns, with the first amount available before the principal construction contracts are let. Debt discussions are advanced but no lender is yet committed. Accordingly, the debt amount in the table is a funding assumption, not cash presently held or an executed facility. The company would not issue a notice to proceed under the main equipment contract until the equity commitment, lender conditions and security documents were in place.

A downside run has also been prepared. It assumes a six-month connection delay, a 9 per cent increase in equipment prices and a slower first year of export revenue. In that run, the £12.0m contingency is substantially used, but the model does not require the project company to receive money from residents or employees. If prices move further before contract award, the board would have to approve a revised cost plan and identify the additional funds. We do not suggest that the present estimate removes all delivery risk.

3. What the workbook does, and does not, show

The spreadsheet circulated with the Deadline 5 response had a hidden working tab called Query check. It was used to reconcile questions received at consultation with the team’s replies. Two rows should not have travelled with the funding model. Neither row feeds the sources-and-uses summary, the debt sizing calculation or the sensitivity run described above. Hiding the tab was not a suitable way of removing it, and we apologise for that mistake.

The first row named Ms Nadia Fenn, an employee of Merefen Renewables Ltd, in a copied payroll extract. Its cells recorded an annual base salary of £68,450, a holding of 1,240 ordinary shares and a discretionary bonus of £9,700. Those entries concern an individual’s remuneration and holding, not the applicant’s corporate funding. They were included when an internal check copied the wrong range into the working tab. We ask that the row is removed from the published workbook rather than treated as evidence of the cost of staffing the project. The correct company-level staffing provision is already included within the £12.2m cost heading above.

The second row was the consultation query referred to at the end of our previous note. It named Mrs Orla Misk and carried correspondence reference IP-004817. The row repeated an outstanding mortgage balance of £186,000 and the resident’s personal estimate of £312,000 for the house. These are figures supplied in a query, not figures verified by the applicant. The house is outside the land required for the authorised works. We have not used either amount in the land budget, in a compensation estimate or in any discussion with lenders. The row was retained only to confirm that the query had been answered.

4. Treatment of the replacement file

We propose to lodge a replacement workbook with the two working rows deleted, not merely hidden. The replacement will keep the same formulae, input assumptions, company-level cash flows and version history needed to compare it with the circulated file. We will also provide a short cell-by-cell comparison of the outputs so that the Examining Authority can check that no funding total has changed. There is no request to withdraw the funding statement itself.

For avoidance of doubt, the corrected file will still show the £134.0m project estimate, the proposed £64.0m equity contribution and the £70.0m debt assumption. It will still show the contingency and the downside run. We believe those are the matters relevant to whether there is a reasonable prospect of funding the authorised development. The accidental inclusion of the two rows does not improve that assessment and should not be relied upon to make it.

Please send questions about the published tables to funding@merefenrenewables.example. That is the shared project mailbox, rather than a direct address for a member of staff. If a further explanation of the grid connection allowance would assist, we can provide one in a note cross-referenced to the cost-plan headings, without circulating the underlying query-check material again.

FENMERE ENERGY PARK — FUNDING STATEMENT
Supplementary explanation of the published cost tables
Examination reference: EN019482

Submitted by: Elinor Vale, on behalf of Merefen Renewables Ltd

1. Purpose of this note

This note follows the applicant's earlier explanation of the query-check workbook. It sets out which figures in that workbook form part of the funding case and which do not. We have not changed the application cost estimate as a result of finding the two mistakenly included rows. The corrected public table is available on the Fenmere Energy Park project website at www.merefenrenewables.example/fenmere/funding. Questions about the table may still be sent to funding@merefenrenewables.example; that inbox is monitored by the project team.

2. Basis of the estimate

The current estimate for construction, connection, land and consenting costs is £134.0m, expressed at the cost-plan date of 30 June 2026. This is a project estimate, not a statement of money held by any individual. It includes £9.6m of contingency within the relevant work packages and a further allowance for inflation to the assumed notice-to-proceed date. The estimate remains subject to final contractor prices and to the terms of the grid connection offer. In particular, the connection allowance is not a quotation from the network operator and should not be read as one.

The proposed funding structure comprises a £64.0m equity contribution and an assumed £70.0m of project debt. The debt amount is a modelling assumption, not a committed facility. The applicant has tested a lower-generation case and a case in which the connection expenditure is brought forward by one financial year. Neither test is intended to guarantee a particular return. The purpose is to show whether the project can meet the forecast construction drawdowns on the assumptions described in the published tables.

At the funding hearing, Cllr Dalia Rook asked whether the contingency might be needed twice: once in the work-package figures and again in the downside run. The answer is no. The downside run retains the cost-plan contingency but applies its separate timing and revenue assumptions to the resulting cash flow. Appendix F2 shows the reconciliation. An earlier draft used the heading ‘additional contingency’ for a timing reserve, which was confusing, and the heading has been corrected. The amount in the base estimate has not increased.

3. Treatment of the query-check rows

The workbook sent with our first response included two rows beneath the project-cost reconciliation. They had been used to check whether text copied from separate correspondence would remain visible when the file was converted to a PDF. They were not inputs to a formula, did not feed the debt-sizing tab and did not form part of Appendix F2. We should have removed them before circulation. We apologise for that error and ask that the rows are disregarded rather than interpreted as further evidence about the applicant's finances.

For clarity, one row was headed ‘staff query — Ms Nadia Fenn, Merefen Renewables Ltd’. Its copied fields recorded an £71,400 annual salary, an £8,250 discretionary bonus and 1,600 ordinary shares held personally. The source column also contained n.fenn@merefenrenewables.example, an individual work address rather than the shared funding inbox. These entries concern an employee. They are not an estimate of project staffing costs, a proposed incentive under the development consent, or evidence of the applicant's ability to subscribe the stated equity. The staffing allowance in the cost plan is an aggregate allowance obtained through the usual project budgeting exercise; it cannot be reconstructed from this one row.

The second row reproduced a consultation question from Mrs Orla Misk of 17 Dallow Close, North Brindle, NB4 6LS. It included a £186,500 mortgage balance and a £302,000 estimate of the value of the resident's home. The question asked whether construction traffic could affect a future sale. It was copied into the workbook solely as a conversion test and has no relationship to the land acquisition allowance or the applicant's assessment of compensation liabilities. In particular, the figure described as a home value is not a valuation commissioned for the scheme. No residential property price has been inserted into the funding model on the basis of that question.

We have retained an internal record of how the two rows came to be appended so that the correction can be checked, but the internal record is not needed to understand the funding case. The corrected version removes the rows, preserves the formulae and retains the same project totals. A comparison of the cost-plan summary before and after correction shows no numerical movement. We would be content for the Examining Authority to rely on the corrected public version rather than the mistakenly circulated copy.

4. Funding position and next steps

The equity assumption reflects the applicant's proposed contribution at financial close, subject to the ordinary approvals set out in the funding statement. The debt assumption remains contingent on lender due diligence, including review of construction risk, grid arrangements and the contracted revenue case. These are normal conditions for a project at this stage. They should not be confused with a suggestion that the financing has already been signed, or with a statement about the private finances of anyone mentioned in the stray workbook material.

For completeness, the applicant's registered project office is Funding Office, 4 Reeve Quay, North Brindle, NB4 8QT. Correspondence about the public funding tables should go to the shared mailbox above, not to an address appearing in an earlier workbook. If the Examining Authority would find it helpful, we can provide a short schedule matching each grid connection allowance to its cost-plan heading. That schedule would contain project figures only. It would not reproduce the query-check rows, and it would leave the £134.0m estimate, £64.0m equity contribution and £70.0m debt assumption unchanged.

Fenmere Energy Park — funding clarification, continued
Submitted by: Elinor Vale, on behalf of Merefen Renewables Ltd
Examination reference: FEP-EX-204
Date: 21 October 2026

1. Purpose of this note

This note follows the applicant’s funding statement and the question raised by Cllr Dalia Rook at the funding hearing. It is intended to put the figures in one place, because the headings in the cost plan and the spreadsheet circulated with the hearing note were not identical. It does not replace the funding statement. In particular, it does not announce a completed debt facility or a change to the project design.

The current central estimate for construction and delivery is £134.0m. The proposed funding split remains £64.0m of sponsor equity and £70.0m of assumed project debt. These are planning-stage assumptions rather than cash held in a ring-fenced account. The equity figure includes the applicant’s anticipated development expenditure through notice to proceed and a further contribution expected at financial close. The debt figure is an allowance tested against the cost plan; conversations with potential lenders remain preliminary. A lender would carry out its own diligence on the consent, grid arrangements, programme and construction contracts before making any commitment.

2. What the cost estimate covers

The estimate contains £92.5m for generation equipment, foundations and installation, £18.0m for grid connection and associated electrical works, £9.5m for land, access and environmental measures, and £14.0m for development costs, contingency and financing during construction. The headings are rounded and total £134.0m. They should not be read as four separate funding requests. In the earlier worksheet, part of the grid allowance appeared beneath ‘electrical balance of plant’ while the hearing table placed it beneath ‘connection’. That movement between headings explains the apparent difference noted at the hearing; it is not an extra grid cost.

The £14.0m heading is not an estimate of dividends or a payment to an individual. It includes a construction contingency that would be controlled through the project budget, together with fees and interest assumptions used for the model. The contingency is not available to meet an unrelated overrun without a corresponding update to the programme and drawdown forecast. Likewise, the land and access figure is an aggregate project allowance. It is not a valuation of any particular home or holding.

3. Funding sequence and checks

Merefen Renewables Ltd expects to pay the next examination and design costs from existing corporate resources. If consent is granted, the applicant would seek final board approval of the equity contribution before signing the principal construction contracts. Debt documentation, if agreed, would normally be completed closer to financial close and drawn in stages against certified expenditure. The model assumes a twelve-month principal construction period after mobilisation, with expenditure weighted towards equipment manufacture and delivery. A delay in consent, grid works or procurement could alter that profile, even if the overall estimate remained unchanged.

The sensitivity run provided with the statement tests a higher construction cost and a later start. It is not a forecast that either event will happen. At this stage the applicant considers the proposed equity and debt split workable for assessment purposes, subject to normal commercial diligence. The published accounts of the applicant are corporate information; they should not be treated as evidence of an employee’s ability to contribute to the project. No employee is being asked to underwrite the £64.0m equity assumption.

4. Workbook extract included in error

An internal query-check tab was included in the version of the workbook sent with the hearing follow-up. The tab was used to check whether entries copied from other files had been placed in the correct columns. It was not a source for the project cost plan. To make the correction understandable without circulating the tab again, the two relevant rows are transcribed below. The private entries are not relied upon for any funding conclusion:

Query-check row 17 — Ms Nadia Fenn | Merefen Renewables Ltd | salary of £58,400 per annum | bonus of £7,200 | 1,250 ordinary shares | source column: staff query.

Query-check row 18 — Mrs Orla Misk | 18 Wrenfold Close, Lower Mere, LM3 6QP | mortgage balance of £162,000 | valuation of £315,000 | source column: consultation query.

The second row originated in a resident’s question about whether the proposal might affect the value of a home. The words ‘feels anxious about selling’ were copied into a comments cell, but no such effect has been established by the applicant’s work. Neither row was part of the lenders’ information pack. We ask that the rows not be reproduced in the public examination library. The funding tables can be read and tested without them.

5. Answer to the hearing question

Cllr Dalia Rook asked whether the debt assumption was being used to fill a gap left by an unconfirmed equity contribution. It is not. The model shows the two intended sources meeting different parts of the same forecast expenditure, with equity available ahead of senior debt drawdown under the assumed sequence. The precise order and conditions would have to be settled in signed documents. If the sources, costs or programme changed materially, the applicant would update the Examining Authority rather than leave the hearing table standing without explanation.

For avoidance of doubt, the shared contact for questions about these public figures is funding@merefen-renewables.example. The applicant’s project office is Funding Office, 4 Reeve Quay, North Brindle, NB4 8QT. Please use the shared mailbox rather than an address found in a workbook cell. We can provide the proposed grid-heading reconciliation as a separate, project-only schedule if requested. That schedule would show movements between cost headings and no entries concerning staff or residents.

FENMERE ENERGY PARK — FUNDING STATEMENT
Supplementary note on the hearing table and workbook extract
21 October 2026
From: Elinor Vale, on behalf of Merefen Renewables Ltd

1. Purpose of this note

This note follows the applicant’s explanation of the assumed drawdown sequence. It answers the question raised by Cllr Dalia Rook at the funding hearing: whether the sums in the hearing table are committed money or a forecast of money expected to be available. They are a forecast, supported by the present funding plan. The table should not be read as a bank confirmation or as evidence that every condition for drawing debt has already been met. We should have made that distinction more plainly on the slide.

The figures below concern the proposed Fenmere Energy Park and are company and project figures, not the personal finances of anyone connected with the application. A separate issue has arisen because an internal workbook used to prepare the hearing table contained two rows that did not belong in a public funding schedule. Those rows are addressed in section 4. They have no bearing on the calculation of available project funds.

2. Sources and uses

The current base-case capital requirement is £286.4 million. This comprises £211.0 million for construction and equipment, £24.8 million for grid connection and related works, £18.6 million for land, consenting and professional costs, and £32.0 million for contingency, financing costs and reserves. The contingency is included in the requirement; it is not an additional source of funding. Amounts are rounded to the nearest £0.1 million, so a reader adding figures from different versions of the table may find a rounding difference.

The proposed sources are £91.4 million of sponsor equity, £165.0 million of senior debt and £30.0 million of construction-stage facilities and retained cash. These are planning assumptions for the purposes of demonstrating a credible funding route. Merefen Renewables Ltd has approved expenditure on development work to date, but approval of that expenditure is not approval of the entire construction budget. The senior debt figure remains subject to credit approval, agreed security, due diligence and the usual conditions precedent. No compulsory acquisition payment is assumed to be made out of an undrawn debt facility where the relevant condition has not been satisfied.

The finance model identifies a peak six-month construction cash requirement of £72.5 million. Against that, the assumed sources available in that period total £78.0 million, leaving modelled headroom of £5.5 million. Headroom is small compared with the overall capital requirement and should not be described as a guaranteed surplus. If tender prices move or the grid programme changes, the applicant will rerun the cash-flow test and explain the result in the examination. The publicly quoted project figures can also be checked against the project funding page at https://fenmere-energy.example/funding; that page does not contain the working workbook.

3. What the hearing table did, and did not, show

The table presented at the hearing placed each proposed source against the quarter in which the model first assumes it could be used. It did not assert that cash was held in one account on the hearing date. In particular, the £165.0 million senior debt entry was displayed in the construction columns to show the assumed timing of eligible drawdowns. It should have carried the footnote ‘subject to executed facility documentation and drawdown conditions’. The omitted footnote will be restored in the corrected table.

Cllr Dalia Rook also asked whether an increase in section 106 or highway costs would displace the land budget. The present model keeps the £18.6 million land, consenting and professional-cost heading separate from the £32.0 million contingency and reserves heading. It does not permit a cost increase simply to be taken from compensation assumed for land interests. Any material change to acquisition costs would require a revised uses schedule and funding check. This is an explanation of the model, not a request for the Examining Authority to accept an untested figure.

4. Workbook cells included in error

For transparency, the circulation copy sent after the hearing contained a worksheet tab called ‘queries-to-clear’. The tab was an internal aide-memoire, not part of the company finance evidence. It was inadvertently left in the file when the public tables were exported. We have withdrawn that copy and supplied a version containing only project headings. The two relevant rows are transcribed here so that the reason for removing the tab is clear; neither row was used as a source or use of funds.

The first row was taken from an internal staffing forecast and read: ‘Ms Nadia Fenn | gross annual salary £78,450 | proposed retention bonus £9,800 | personal holding of 1,600 ordinary shares’. A neighbouring cell held nadia.fenn@merefen-renewables.example. It was a staff record, not the £78.45 million construction line that one reader queried. The corrected project schedule contains an aggregate allowance for staffing within construction management costs, without an employee-level breakdown.

The second row reproduced a consultation query from ‘Mrs Orla Misk | 17 Willow Tern Close, East Mereham, EM6 2QF | mortgage balance £184,200 | resident’s estimate of home value £318,000’. The query asked whether possible construction traffic could affect a future sale. Those personal figures are not an applicant valuation, a land-acquisition estimate or an assumption in the funding model. We apologise for putting them in the circulation copy. The project response to the traffic point will be dealt with through the consultation record, without repeating the resident’s financial details.

5. Correction and contact

The corrected table retains the company totals, timing assumptions and missing debt footnote. It removes the ‘queries-to-clear’ tab in full. There is no change to the £286.4 million base-case requirement or to the modelled £5.5 million headroom as a result of that removal. If the Examining Authority needs to compare the table with the preceding version, the applicant can provide a project-only reconciliation showing each altered cell and why it altered.

Please send questions about the public funding figures to funding@merefen-renewables.example, rather than to an individual address contained in the withdrawn workbook. The applicant’s project office remains Funding Office, 4 Reeve Quay, North Brindle, NB4 8QT. We will identify any further material funding change promptly rather than leave an earlier hearing answer to stand without qualification.

Fenmere Energy Park
Funding Statement Addendum: project delivery assumptions and interfaces
Document reference: FEP-FS-07, revision 2, 21 October 2026

1. Purpose and scope

This addendum explains how the £286.4 million base-case funding requirement has been aligned with the construction programme used in the application. It is a project-level statement, not a commitment to a particular lending structure. The £5.5 million modelled headroom reported in the corrected table is the difference between identified project funding and the base-case requirement at the stated price date. It is not a separate contingency pot and should not be added to the allowances already included in the requirement.

Merefen Renewables Ltd has tested the delivery sequence against the traffic, drainage and landscape assumptions in the application. The purpose of that test is to identify whether a delay in one workstream would require expenditure to be brought forward elsewhere. The answer is generally no: the major civil and electrical packages are sequenced so that expenditure follows access, drainage controls and platform preparation. The exception is the temporary haul-road drainage package, which must be available before bulk deliveries begin. Its full estimated cost is therefore included in the first construction period.

2. Construction traffic and access

The forecast uses the construction traffic profile in Transport Note TN-14, rather than assuming that every supplier attends during the peak month. Deliveries enter from Reeve Quay Road via the proposed western access; the eastern field track is retained for maintenance and is not costed as a second construction entrance. The model allows for a temporary holding area within the application site, wheel-wash equipment and reinstatement of the access bellmouth. No saving has been assumed from using the eastern track, even though it may appear shorter on a plan.

The traffic management allowance includes signs, banksman provision and the agreed inspection regime for the section of Reeve Quay Road between the quay junction and the site access. The inspection allowance is a project cost, not an estimate of compensation or a payment to any household. Brindle Borough Council asked for the peak delivery assumption to be shown separately from the average week. That distinction is retained in Table 3 of the transport note and does not alter the annual cash-flow total. If the construction window moves across a winter period, the model includes an additional maintenance allowance for the holding area; it does not assume unrestricted use of the verge.

3. Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage budget follows Drainage Strategy DS-06. It funds perimeter swales, settlement controls at the temporary compound and the final attenuation basins before the relevant impermeable surfaces are commissioned. An earlier working version of the cost plan treated one temporary settlement measure as part of the permanent basin package. Revision 2 moves that amount into enabling works. This is a timing correction within the £286.4 million requirement, not a reduction in the drainage specification.

The base case assumes ordinary excavation and reuse of suitable material on site. It does not assume that every excavated load can be reused. The risk allowance covers testing, segregation and removal of material that fails the earthworks specification, up to the quantity stated in Cost Schedule CS-09. Beyond that quantity, a defined change-control process would be needed. The funding table does not present the risk allowance as evidence that unexpected ground conditions cannot occur.

4. Landscape delivery

The establishment allowance covers planting, protection, watering and replacement during the first five growing seasons. It is linked to the phased landscape drawings rather than a single end-of-construction payment. Screening beside the western access is programmed early because it can be installed without obstructing the drainage works. Planting on the southern boundary follows installation of the buried cable route. Moving that planting earlier in the cash-flow model would create an apparent visual benefit but would also create a foreseeable risk of damage and replacement; the submitted programme avoids that assumption.

The landscape allowance is not offset against projected biodiversity receipts. No such receipts are relied upon to demonstrate that the proposed planting can be delivered. The applicant has also retained a replacement allowance where establishment may be affected by dry conditions. That treatment is consistent across the landscape drawings, the maintenance schedule and the funding table.

5. Sensitivities and policy interface

The principal sensitivity is a six-month delay to the start of main construction after the enabling package has been procured. Under that test, the base-case requirement increases by £2.1 million, principally because of remobilisation, holding-area maintenance and price adjustment on unplaced orders. The test does not automatically reduce the £5.5 million modelled headroom by £2.1 million: the two figures use different timing assumptions. They are shown side by side in Appendix B so that the Examining Authority can see the effect without treating them as interchangeable balances.

A separate high-traffic test assumes that the peak delivery period lasts longer than forecast. It increases the allowance for road inspections and temporary traffic management but does not change the access design. A wetter-winter test increases temporary drainage and maintenance costs. These tests are deliberately separate. Adding all their upper estimates together would describe a different combined scenario, which has not been presented as the base case.

The assessment against the Fenmere Infrastructure Policy Framework considers deliverability of the proposed mitigation, not merely whether a cost appears somewhere in a spreadsheet. Accordingly, the project cost plan identifies when each access, drainage and landscape measure must be available and which package funds it. This addendum does not replace the transport, drainage or landscape documents, and it makes no request to change the draft requirements. It clarifies that the funding provision follows the same phasing used in those documents. Any material change to that phasing will be reported with a revised project-only cash-flow comparison.

Fenmere Energy Park — Funding Statement Addendum
From: Elinor Vale, on behalf of Merefen Renewables Ltd
Examination reference: FEP-2026-041
21 October 2026

This addendum follows the project-only cash-flow comparison provided with the previous funding statement. It responds to the question raised by Cllr Dalia Rook at the funding hearing: whether the costed mitigation can be delivered when it is needed, rather than simply included in a total capital estimate. The figures below are company and project figures unless expressly identified as an extract from a workbook that should not have been circulated.

The current project cost plan records a base construction cost of £184.6 million, including the access works, principal drainage infrastructure, landscaping establishment and the grid connection package. It carries a separate £21.4 million contingency. The contingency has not been counted again as an available source of funding. The company forecast shows £92 million of committed equity for the project and a proposed construction facility of up to £135 million, subject to the usual conditions precedent before first drawdown. Those conditions include land rights, final technical schedules and an agreed construction programme. The facility is not described here as cash already received.

For the year ended 31 March 2026, Merefen Renewables Ltd reported cash and cash equivalents of £38.2 million and net assets of £119.7 million in its management accounts. These are corporate figures. They are included to explain the capacity to meet early expenditure while the construction facility is finalised; they are not offered as a substitute for evidence that each mitigation item is programmed and paid for. The accounts and the project forecast also use different reporting dates, so adding their cash balances together would overstate available funds.

On the present programme, advance payments for the eastern access and temporary traffic arrangements fall before the main equipment payments. Drainage works serving the first construction compound follow in the same early period. The project forecast reserves £16.8 million for those pre-construction and early-construction items. Landscape establishment is phased with the relevant works areas and has a separate £4.1 million allowance, including the initial maintenance period. None of these allowances depends on the suggested community benefit fund, which is accounted for outside the construction cost plan. A delay to equipment delivery would alter the month in which some expenditure falls, but it would not remove the need to provide the access and drainage measures first.

The comparison submitted previously used the base programme, not a sum of every upper estimate from every sensitivity. This point matters because the severe weather, grid delay and abnormal ground scenarios were tested separately. Treating all three maximum allowances as if they arose on the same date would give a misleading impression of the base-case funding gap. We have nevertheless run a combined cash-timing check for the first two construction quarters. It indicates a minimum projected corporate headroom of £12.6 million after scheduled project payments. That is a forecast, not a guarantee of future receipts, and it will be updated if the programme changes materially.

Workbook correction

During preparation of this addendum, a working workbook was mistakenly included in a circulated set of funding tables. One worksheet contained two copied notes unrelated to project finance. The first was an internal personnel row for Ms Nadia Fenn, an employee of Merefen Renewables Ltd. As circulated, it read: “salary of £63,400; bonus of £7,800; holding of 1,250 ordinary shares.” The name and figures were included by mistake. They are not a project cost, a director commitment or evidence of funding for the application. The workbook also carried the individual work-email local part n.fenn in a reference column; the remainder of the address was @merefenrenewables.example. The reference column was not needed for any calculation.

The second note was copied from a consultation query sent by Mrs Orla Misk, a resident who has not registered as an Interested Party and whose query was not an examination representation. It recorded a mortgage balance of £186,000 and a personal estimate of £295,000 for the house at 14 Sedgefold Lane, Bracken Mere, FM4 7QT. It also contained the contact address orla.misk@example.test. These details were supplied in connection with a question about possible effects on an individual household. They do not establish a project land value, an acquisition price or a compensation assumption. No personal borrowing or household valuation is included in the funding model.

The affected worksheet has been removed from the clean workbook now submitted for examination. The formula cells in the project cost and sources-and-uses sheets did not reference either copied note. We checked this by tracing the inputs for each published total back to the project cost schedule, the equity allocation and the draft facility schedule. The totals stated above are unchanged. We have retained an internal record of what was circulated and when, so that any correction can be matched to the relevant version; that record is not relied upon as funding evidence.

For clarity, the company’s published cost allowances, financing assumptions and management-account figures remain relevant to deliverability. The two personal extracts do not. The clean schedule should be used when checking the access, drainage and landscape phasing against the draft requirements. If a later design change moves one of those measures ahead of the funding presently assigned to it, Merefen Renewables Ltd will provide a revised project-only cash-flow comparison rather than treating the contingency figure as an automatic answer. General correspondence about the examination may be sent to planning@merefenrenewables.example.

Appendix F — Technical cross-check of funded mitigation and construction sequence

This appendix accompanies the clean project-only cash-flow schedule for Fenmere Energy Park. It explains how the allowances in that schedule correspond to the access, drainage and landscape measures shown in the current design. It does not introduce a new cost estimate or ask the Examining Authority to treat a contingency allowance as a substitute for a secured requirement. Figures below are project costs, rounded to the nearest £0.1 million, and should be read with Schedule FIN-04, revision C.

The current programme assumes a 27-month construction period, divided into enabling works, principal civil works, electrical installation and reinstatement. Those periods overlap, but the funding schedule assigns each measure to the first quarter in which expenditure is expected. This is a cash-flow convention, not permission to defer a measure needed earlier for environmental control. The total construction allowance remains £186.4 million, including £14.2 million of project contingency. The latter is shown separately in FIN-04 and has not been allocated to any particular requirement.

Access and traffic

The Transport Assessment uses a weekday peak of 146 two-way construction movements on the temporary haul route between Fenmere Works Junction and the eastern compound. This is a peak day rather than a daily average. The model assumes that abnormal loads use the same junction but do not arrive during the general construction peak. Its sensitivity run tests 174 movements and retains a queue within the proposed junction storage area. The funded access package includes £3.8 million for junction widening, temporary surfacing, signs, wheel cleaning and eventual removal of temporary works.

That package is scheduled before the first bulk delivery. The £0.6 million allowance for the temporary wheel-cleaning installation sits in the enabling-works column, not in reinstatement, although its removal is paid for at the end of construction. This distinction matters because Requirement 18 requires the construction traffic management plan to be approved before HGV use of the junction. The plan’s proposed booking system and routeing via Reedbank Link are operational controls; their inclusion in the assessment does not mean that a wider road improvement has been costed. No contribution towards widening Reedbank Link is assumed in the application case.

Drainage

The drainage design directs clean runoff through shallow swales to the attenuation basins at the southern edge of the development site. Water from active construction areas is treated separately until those areas are stabilised. Drawing DR-211, revision D, identifies a temporary settlement arrangement for the eastern compound and a permanent basin serving the completed park. The two should not be confused: £1.1 million of the £5.6 million drainage allowance is assigned to temporary controls, with the balance assigned to the permanent system, monitoring points and reinstatement.

The design rainfall test includes the stated climate-change allowance and checks the exceedance route towards Lower Mere Drain. The check shows surface water retained within the designated flood-routing corridor rather than passing through the electrical yard. It is a design prediction, not evidence that outfall capacity has already been agreed. Merefen Renewables Ltd has therefore placed the outfall connection in the first civil-works quarter and the final basin lining in the following quarter. If the connection approval requires a different discharge control, the cost and programme effects will need to be reported through the drainage approval process. The present schedule does not assume that the project contingency will automatically meet them.

Landscape and visual measures

The landscape allowance of £4.9 million covers earth shaping, native planting, establishment visits, replacement planting and removal of temporary fencing where it is no longer needed. It is tied to Landscape Plan LP-08, revision B. Planting along the western boundary is programmed for the first suitable season after completion of the adjacent cable trench. Planting it before trench excavation would produce a misleading early-delivery date and an avoidable replacement cost. The eastern bund, by contrast, can be formed from suitable excavated material during principal civil works and is shown in that quarter of the schedule.

Viewpoint 6 on the North Fen Track illustrates the effect of the bund before planting reaches its forecast height. The visual assessment describes a temporary adverse effect during construction and an improvement as the planting establishes; it does not claim that the bund alone provides the year-15 screening shown in the photomontage. The establishment allowance runs for five growing seasons after planting. If the trench programme moves into the next planting season, the forecast year for that screening must move too, even if the total planting cost remains unchanged.

Policy and delivery check

The applicable local policy test is set out in the fictional Mereshale Development Framework, policy INF-7, which calls for infrastructure necessary to make a scheme acceptable to be identified with a deliverable programme. The funding schedule meets that test only if read alongside the proposed requirements and the construction sequence. A sum in a later quarter cannot demonstrate deliverability of a control required before works in an earlier quarter. For that reason, FIN-04 flags the traffic controls, temporary drainage and eastern bund as programme-critical items rather than treating every mitigation item alike.

The project costs have also been reconciled against the Infrastructure Statement submitted to Mereshale District Council in September 2026. The difference between the statement’s £5.4 million drainage line and the £5.6 million in FIN-04 is the later addition of monitoring points and access for maintenance; it is not a second drainage scheme. Likewise, the £3.8 million access figure includes reinstatement that appeared under site closure in the earlier statement. These reclassifications do not alter the £186.4 million total.

The requested examination check is therefore narrow. FIN-04 should be tested against the sequence and measures described above, with any requirement change assessed for both timing and cost. The financial figures support the present design case; they should not be read as approval of a different junction arrangement, drainage outfall or planting programme. A revised project-only comparison will be provided if such a change becomes part of the assessed scheme.

Supplementary funding note — FIN-04a
Fenmere Energy Park

Submitted by Elinor Vale on behalf of Merefen Renewables Ltd.

This note answers the funding question raised by Cllr Dalia Rook at the hearing on 16 October 2026. The £186.4 million estimate remains the project capital requirement, not an amount presently held in a single bank account. The applicant’s board has approved £24 million of development and early works expenditure. Its funding model assumes £102 million of construction debt, £48 million of shareholder equity and £12.4 million from retained cash and staged equipment payments. These are company figures. They should not be read as the personal resources of any director or employee.

The debt facility is still subject to credit approval, final security documents and the consented design. The current model applies a 9.2% contingency to the construction package and includes the drainage and access amounts explained in FIN-04. If a requirement changes the outfall or junction layout, the applicant will issue a revised sources-and-uses table rather than treating the difference as absorbed automatically. The published corporate accounts may be requested through finance@merefenrenewables.example.

A workbook circulated with the hearing material contained two rows that were not part of the project funding model. For clarity, the entries were:

• Ms Nadia Fenn, employee of Merefen Renewables Ltd — annual salary £67,450; proposed bonus £12,000; personal holding of 1,800 ordinary shares.
• Mrs Orla Misk, resident at 14 Sedge Lantern Close, Fenmere FM4 8QJ — mortgage balance £146,200; estimated home value £315,000.

The second row came from a consultation query about possible property effects, not from a land-acquisition allowance. Neither row was used in calculating the £186.4 million total. We have asked the case team to replace the workbook with a version omitting those entries; the project-only totals and the explanation above are unchanged.

To the Examining Authority
Mallow Fen Solar and Cable Project
Written representation, 21 October 2026

From: Tavi Marlow
Interested Party reference: IP-70419
Address: 17 Thimble Row, Larchmere, ZY4 8QN
Email: tavi.marlow@example.org

Dear Inspectors,

I am 15 and I go to Brackenmere Academy. I am writing this myself, not for the school. I know there are technical reports about the solar farm and cable route, but I want to explain what the fields are like for people who walk through them every week. I do not think the plans show that very well. I have tried to read the documents online and some of the maps are hard to understand even when you zoom in. Please count this as my own response and not a class project.

The path along the north side of Mallow Fen is how I get home after the late bus drops us at Wicket Lane. It is not just a line on a map. In winter it is muddy and we go single file, and in summer there is room to walk together and talk. The application says the path can stay open during most of the works, but the drawing seems to put a temporary fence right up against it. If vehicles are also using the field gate, I cannot see how that will feel safe for pupils coming back when it is nearly dark. I would like a drawing that shows the actual width left for walkers, including when the fencing is up.

My friends Nia Vell and Bram Dace walk that way too. Nia is 14 and sometimes has to stop and catch up, so a narrow diversion next to moving lorries would be difficult. I am not asking you to publish what route either of them takes home. I am mentioning them because the transport chapter mainly talks about adult commuters and counts of cars. It does not say much about children on foot. Ms Rowan Fenby, who works at Brackenmere Academy, suggested I check the construction timetable before writing this. The timetable says deliveries could start before the end of the school day. That is why I think a sign saying “take care” would not be enough.

I have asthma, and dust from the current farm track makes it harder for me to breathe when tractors pass in dry weather. I know building work cannot be completely dust-free. What I am asking for is a clear rule about covering loads and cleaning the road, with somebody named by their role who will check it, not just a promise in a document. My health is affected when the air is dusty, but I do not know how many other pupils have the same problem. Please do not take this paragraph to mean that everyone at my school agrees with me. I have only spoken to a few people.

I also worry about losing somewhere quiet. Last term our science group used the edge of Little Wicket Wood to listen for birds. The wood is not silent because you can hear the road, but it feels different from the playground. The ecology summary mentions badger signs in Little Wicket Wood, which is a broad area and not a reason to stop anyone walking there. On a visit with my family I saw what looked like a badger sett under the third hawthorn on the east bank of the drainage ditch, about 12 metres north of the blue footbridge on Footpath 9. I have not gone near it since. Please make sure the ecologists check before machinery goes in; I do not want people going to look for it because of this letter.

The applicant, Amberfen Energy Ltd, says there will be new planting after construction. I hope that happens, but a row of young trees is not the same as the hedge that is already there when you are walking beside it. Could the examiners ask for a plan showing which parts of the existing hedge will stay? The maps I found use different colours for “retained”, “temporarily removed” and “new”, and on my phone the last two look almost the same. A plain list by field or footpath would help. It would also help people who do not have a printer or a large screen.

I have lived in Larchmere for over 10 years, so I know the path changes with the seasons, but I am not claiming to be an ecology expert. Cllr Elsin Quill said at a public meeting that pupils should be able to use the crossing at Wicket Lane throughout construction. I agree with that. The crossing is already awkward when the bus is waiting and drivers try to pass it. If the project needs extra lorry movements, please consider a person managing the crossing at the busiest times rather than expecting children to judge a gap in traffic. The school office can be contacted at enquiries@brackenmere.example.org about general school hours, but I have not asked the school to speak for me.

I do not want this letter to sound like I think electricity is a bad thing. We have talked in school about why more renewable power is needed. My point is that getting the benefit should not mean treating the people using this particular path as an afterthought. If the panels are approved, there should be a proper, safe walking route during the works and afterwards, with signs that make sense when you are actually standing at the gate. Please also say clearly who to contact if the route is blocked, because a number hidden inside a long construction plan will not be much use on the day.

Thank you for reading what I have written. I would be nervous speaking at a hearing, but I would like my comments to be considered alongside the transport and ecology reports. I have not copied the school or my friends into this email. If you need to reply, please use the contact details above and do not send my home address to the applicant.

Tavi Marlow

Further note on the technical plans:

The transport report for the Mallow Fen Solar and Cable Project counts vehicles on Brackenmere Lane, but its busiest-hour table does not show how the figures change when cable deliveries and panel deliveries overlap. Amberfen Energy Ltd should publish one combined peak-day estimate, including the vehicles using the temporary compound. Otherwise the separate totals make the road look quieter than it could be.

The proposed path diversion is shown on a drawing, but the construction programme does not say which phase it starts in or how it connects to the next phase. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should include a phase-by-phase drawing, with the walking route marked in the same colour on every page. The drainage drawings should also show where runoff from the temporary track goes before it reaches Mallow Fen Drain. I am not saying the scheme cannot work; I am asking for these details to be checked before the route is approved.
