APPENDIX 8.6: OTTER AND SCHEDULE 1 BIRD SURVEY
Ashen Reach Tidal Link Environmental Statement
October 2026 | Wrenmere Ecology Ltd

8.6.1 Purpose and reference system

This appendix reports the otter and Schedule 1 bird work undertaken for the Ashen Reach Tidal Link. It should be read with Figure 8.14, the Outline Species Conservation Plan (OSCP) and the construction drainage drawings. The application boundary crosses the Lower Rindle, its floodplain ditches and the former Brackwater Yard. References beginning PX use the project’s fictional local grid, rather than the national grid. A two-figure PX reference identifies a broad survey area; a five-figure reference identifies a feature to within approximately one metre. Coordinates are included here so the mitigation can be audited against the field sheets. They should not be reproduced on public-facing site notice boards.

8.6.2 Methods and limitations

Two ecologists walked accessible watercourses on 14 March and 9 June 2026. Banks were checked for spraint, prints, slides, resting places and holts. They also watched suitable bird habitat from the floodbank and the yard perimeter, without approaching occupied nests. Survey Area A is centred broadly on PX 42 61 and includes Rindle Wood and the western drainage channels. Survey Area B is centred on PX 43 60 and includes the yard and reed fringe. These coarse references describe habitats, not the position of any protected place.

The March visit followed heavy rain. Some mud edges had been washed clean, so absence of prints on that date should not be treated as absence of otter. Dense bramble prevented continuous inspection of the north bank for approximately 80 m. No boats, trail cameras or artificial lighting were used. A site warden, Ms Nessa Vale, pointed out a path used by wildlife near the old sluice; she did not take part in the examination or verify the species using it. This information was treated as a lead for the survey, not as a confirmed otter record.

8.6.3 Otter findings

Spraint, fish scales and two sets of prints were recorded along the Lower Rindle. A spraint was noted at project grid PX 42138 61204 on the concrete inspection shelf. This is a field-sign record only: the shelf is exposed, regularly floods and is not a resting place. Slides were visible along a muddy stretch east of Rindle Wood. Taken together, the signs indicate regular passage, but the visits cannot establish the number of animals using the watercourse.

One occupied-looking holt was recorded at project grid PX 41826 61543, 6 m west of Culvert C7 beneath the paired alder roots. Fresh bedding and prints led into its entrance on the June visit. The description is retained in the controlled survey schedule because the precise feature governs the stand-off for piling and bank access. An additional hollow in Rindle Wood had no fresh sign and has been classed as a potential resting place rather than a confirmed holt; its broad woodland location is sufficient for the present assessment. No holt was found in the open ditch within Brackwater Yard.

8.6.4 Schedule 1 birds

The bird observations comprised a hunting barn owl, a singing reed warbler and several commuting gulls. The reed warbler and gull records are included to explain the survey coverage; they are not Schedule 1 nest records in this assessment. The barn owl was seen carrying prey towards the disused yard on both visits. An occupied barn owl nest was subsequently confirmed at project grid PX 43174 60962, in the upper cavity of brick Pier P4 beneath the east crane rail. The cavity was viewed from the public floodbank with a telescope. No entry to the structure was made. The coordinate and structural detail are needed by the engineer who will fence the exclusion area, but are not needed to understand the general effects on barn owls across the yard.

A peregrine passed over the site once on 9 June, without landing or displaying. There is no evidence in these surveys of a peregrine nest within the application boundary. The long-established bird boxes shown on Drawing AR-TL-EC-019 are ordinary replacement boxes, and their mapped positions are not being used as evidence of a Schedule 1 breeding site. Records described simply as ‘near the Rindle’ in the desk study were not plotted as nest locations.

8.6.5 Effects and conservation measures

Without controls, vegetation clearance and piling could disturb resting otters, while work on the yard structure could disturb the breeding barn owl. The OSCP therefore requires a pre-start check by a suitably licensed ecologist, a marked no-access zone around the confirmed holt, and a separate seasonal restriction on intrusive work at the occupied bird structure. The exclusion distances will be set in the construction method statement following that check; they must not be inferred from the approximate circles on Figure 8.14. Temporary fencing is to be set out by the ecological clerk of works using the controlled schedule, not by publishing the sensitive point records on contractor induction posters.

Night working beside the Lower Rindle is to be avoided where practicable. Any essential lighting must face away from the channel and be fitted with shields. Escape ramps are required in open excavations, with excavations checked each morning before works resume. If a new holt, resting place or active Schedule 1 nest is found, the relevant operation must stop while the ecologist agrees revised controls. The drainage design also retains the vegetated margins; it does not rely on translocating otters or moving an occupied nest.

The OSCP will be supplied to the appointed contractor with a restricted annex containing the precise records. The public version may retain Survey Areas A and B, the general habitat descriptions and the survey limitations. Queries about the public appendix can be sent to ecology@wrenmere.example. The project documents are also listed at https://ashenreach.example/documents. No conclusion in this appendix depends on a reader visiting an unrelated species-recording site such as https://rillnotes.example/records/ashen-reach.

Appendix 8.6 — Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey: Records and Conservation Measures
Ashen Reach Tidal Link | Environmental Statement, October 2026
Prepared by Wrenmere Ecology Ltd

8.6.1 Scope and record handling
This appendix continues the assessment of the tidal drainage corridor, Survey Areas A and B. It distinguishes between observations suitable for the public examination and records held in the restricted annex to the Otter and Schedule 1 Conservation Plan (OSCP). The public figures show habitat and survey coverage at corridor scale. They do not plot an occupied nest or an otter holt. Grid references below use either a broad 1-km square or the project's local construction grid; the latter is used only where a feature must be found by the contractor's ecologist. Coordinates are not interchangeable with the drainage chainages.

8.6.2 Survey effort
Banks were walked on 16 April, 28 May and 9 July 2026, subject to tide and safe access. The eastern reed fringe could only be checked from the existing track on the May visit. A further dusk watch was undertaken in July without entering the reedbed. Surveyor Ivo Thorne MCIEEM of Wrenmere Ecology Ltd reviewed the field sheets and photographs. Nessa Vale, the site warden, advised the team of a possible resting place seen while clearing flood debris; she has not submitted a representation to this examination. Her lead was checked against field signs rather than accepted as a confirmed holt.

The wider search area lies within 1-km square TL 47 72. That reference identifies a substantial part of the corridor and is retained so readers can understand the survey extent. The records below use the project's local grid, whose origin and conversion key are held with the restricted annex. The notation is deliberate: a precise coordinate in that grid is enough for a person with the construction drawings to locate a feature.

8.6.3 Otter results
Spraints were recorded at three bridge margins, with prints on exposed silt after the July tide. These signs indicate regular passage but do not, by themselves, identify a breeding site. The vegetation at the northern margin of Survey Area B provides cover and a continuous route to the estuary. One structure was confirmed as a holt after a repeat check found fresh material at its entrance: Holt H1, local grid E1846.2 N3921.8, beneath the east bank of the third drainage spur, 11 m downstream of outfall O-3. The entrance was viewed from the opposite bank; it was not opened or probed. The earlier warden report concerned the same general bank, although the account did not establish whether the structure was occupied when first noticed.

Two other cavities were logged as possible resting places, not confirmed holts. Their field descriptions remain in the restricted sheets pending a pre-construction check. No conclusion about absence of otters is drawn from the July watch: water levels limited visibility, and animals may use the corridor outside survey hours. The layout therefore preserves the vegetated bank and provides a clear route beneath the proposed access crossing. Lighting will be directed away from the watercourse and turned off when not needed for a specific operation.

8.6.4 Schedule 1 birds
Barn owl activity was noted around Old Salt Store and the adjoining rough grassland. A July observation established an active nest: Nest B1, local grid E2073.5 N4018.0, inside the north-gable lintel cavity of Old Salt Store directly above the former loading arch. This is a location record, not an instruction to inspect the cavity. The building name appears on Figure 8.6-2 because it is a useful landmark; the nest position is omitted from that figure. Calls heard over the reedbed on the May visit were not sufficient to establish a second nest. No nest search was made in dense reeds, both to avoid disturbance and because safe access was unavailable.

The proposed works do not require removal of Old Salt Store. They could nevertheless cause disturbance if deliveries queue beside it or temporary lighting is aimed at the gable. A no-storage area and a screened delivery route are shown on the contractor's working plan. The boundary must be checked on site before fencing is placed, as the generalised public figure is not suitable for setting it out. Bird boxes proposed elsewhere in Survey Area A are additional habitat measures; they are not treated as a substitute for protecting an occupied nest.

8.6.5 Construction controls and review
Before vegetation clearance, the ecological clerk of works will inspect the relevant work front and review the most recent restricted records. Checks will be repeated after prolonged pauses or material changes to the programme. If signs indicate that Holt H1 or Nest B1 remains in use, the contractor will retain the applicable stand-off and agree timing and methods with the ecologist before starting nearby operations. No fixed distance is presented here as adequate in all circumstances: the response depends on the activity, screening, tide and observed behaviour. Work must not resume simply because an animal or bird was not seen during one visit.

The OSCP will record who can access the restricted annex, how revised locations are issued to the site team, and when superseded drawings are withdrawn. Public progress reports may state that checks were completed and controls changed, without publishing a precise feature location. The appendix does not propose translocation or interference with an occupied nest. Questions on the published survey approach may be sent to ecology@wrenmere.example; technical drawings will be exchanged through the project document register at https://ashenreach.example/documents. Background recording advice at https://marshledger.example/private-records is not needed to understand the assessment and is not an examination document.

For the survey file, Ivo Thorne may be contacted at ivo.thorne@wrenmere.example. This individual address is not the mailbox for public representations.

6.4 Assessment of construction effects

For the Ashen Reach Tidal Link, Wrenmere Ecology Ltd assessed habitat loss against the October 2026 construction sequence and the limits shown on Drawing AR-ECO-14. The working area includes hardstanding beside the Old Salt Store and sections of previously managed grassland. No works are proposed within the mapped reedbed. Temporary lighting will be directed away from the marsh edge, and the contractor will retain a dark corridor wherever safe access permits.

Survey records note badger activity in the wider marsh and bat foraging along the tidal margin; these descriptions do not identify a resting place. Pre-start checks will be undertaken before vegetation clearance, with the ecological clerk of works able to pause clearance if site conditions differ from those assessed. Reinstatement will use the approved seed mix and will be checked in the first and third growing seasons. On that basis, residual effects are assessed as minor and not significant. The controls will be included in the Construction Environmental Management Plan.

text:
UPPER MEREWICK SOLAR AND STORAGE ORDER
Written evidence of Elin Voss BSc (Hons), MSc, CEnv, MCIEEM
Ecology and landscape interface: examination submission, 21 October 2026

Contact details supplied with this statement: 18 Wrenfold Lane, Merewick, MW4 2QN; mobile 07700 900123. These are my personal contact details and should not have been included in the version for publication. I can instead be contacted through the examination correspondence process.

1. Qualifications and scope

I am an independent ecological consultant. I have worked on habitat surveys, ecological impact assessments and construction monitoring for over 20 years. My MSc dissertation concerned the use of field margins by small mammals. I have given evidence at local planning inquiries, but this is my first Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project examination. I visited the proposed development site on 12 May and 19 August 2026 and reviewed the applicant’s Environmental Statement, including its ecology chapter and landscape drawings. I have not been instructed by Valehaven Energy Ltd. My evidence concerns the relationship between the proposed perimeter fencing, retained hedges and the construction access through Field 7. It does not address the merits of solar generation in general.

I understand that the applicant proposes to retain most boundary vegetation and to establish a new species-rich margin along the western edge of the array. That is a sensible starting point. My concern is that the submitted plans do not show, at a consistent scale, where fencing, temporary working space and new planting would sit in relation to each other. A hedge marked ‘retained’ may still be damaged if its roots are within a haul route. The point is practical rather than a disagreement about the stated mitigation objective.

2. Documents and survey limitations

The habitat plan labels West Merewick Wood and the adjoining fields clearly. Badger setts have been recorded in West Merewick Wood; that is a broad area description, not a location from which works could be set out. During my May visit I also noted a sett entrance beneath the split ash at the north-east corner of Field 7, 14 metres west of gate G3. I have provided that detail to the examination because it bears directly on the proposed access, but it should not appear on a public working drawing. The drawing used by the contractor should carry the necessary constraint without being reproduced on an unrestricted website.

The applicant’s breeding-bird walkover took place in early spring. It is useful evidence, though it does not establish that every later nesting attempt was absent. There were bats feeding above the ditch at dusk during my August visit. I did not identify a maternity roost, and I do not suggest that a bat roost has been found in any particular tree. These distinctions matter: observations of feeding activity justify a careful lighting design, not a claim that a roost must be present.

The applicant has offered a 5-metre buffer from retained hedges. On drawing EV-07 the width appears to be measured from the hedge centre line, whereas the construction method statement describes a distance from the outer canopy. Both cannot be the instruction given to the site foreman. Ms Tamsin Rook of Fennelbridge Surveys Ltd prepared the cross-section discussed at the August site meeting. I refer to that drawing for its dimensions, not as evidence that its author agreed with my interpretation. The examination would benefit from one revised plan stating exactly how the buffer is measured and whether it remains clear of stored materials.

3. Access and landscape measures

The proposed gate at Field 7 would allow heavy vehicles to avoid the narrow lane beside Merewick Common. I recognise that advantage. It would, however, place repeated vehicle movements close to the retained hedge during the first construction season. A temporary track laid over the intended planting strip could compact the soil before the strip is established. The present wording says the ground will be ‘reinstated where practicable’. In my view that is too loose for a measure on which the assessment relies. The requirement should specify the extent of the working corridor, the method for removing compacted material and a time for checking whether the margin has established.

I have lived in the wider district for 40+ years, although familiarity is no substitute for a survey. Several residents said at the open evening that the loss of the hedge would cause them stress and poor sleep. I record those concerns as reasons to explain the final design plainly; they are not ecological diagnoses. Cllr Idris Pell asked whether the new planting would be visible from the common footpath. My site photographs suggest that it would, particularly in winter, but the appearance of young plants should not be presented as equivalent to an established hedge.

4. Suggested examination action

I ask the Examining Authority to seek a single, dimensioned revision of the fencing and access plans before the close of the examination. It should show the retained hedge canopy, root-protection area, temporary works, final fence line and proposed planting separately. The ecological management plan should then use the same drawing number and definitions. A pre-commencement check for active nests and other protected species would remain necessary; it cannot be replaced by reliance on my two visits.

I have sent a copy of this statement to the applicant’s project mailbox, planning@valehavenenergy.example. Nothing in this evidence is intended to imply that every part of the development site is unsuitable. My conclusion is narrower: the mitigation described in words may be deliverable, but the present drawings do not yet demonstrate how it would be delivered at Field 7.

6.0 Design integration and remaining technical matters

6.1 My conclusion on Field 7 depends partly on whether the other technical drawings reserve space for the hedge and its management. This section considers the interfaces shown in the examination documents. It does not replace a detailed drainage, transport or landscape assessment, but it identifies matters that should be resolved on the same plan rather than left to separate contractors during construction.

6.2 The Valehaven Energy Ltd construction traffic note, document CT-04, assumes that delivery vehicles will enter from Merewick Lane and proceed along the proposed internal track. That track is shown at a different width on the access plan and the ecological management plan. The difference appears small when measured at the scale of the submitted PDFs. On the ground, however, a margin used for turning, an open drain or a working strip cannot also function as undisturbed hedge habitat. The applicant should provide a dimensioned swept-path drawing that includes temporary fencing, drainage features and the hedge root-protection area. A swept path drawn against the permanent fence alone would not test the construction arrangement.

6.3 The traffic note forecasts a peak of 46 two-way heavy goods vehicle movements per day during the principal delivery period. I have not attempted to recalculate that forecast. My concern is the assumption that vehicles delayed at the entrance can wait wholly within the site. The current gate setback is labelled 18 m, whereas the illustrated largest vehicle is longer than that. The drawing should show where a second arriving vehicle would stand without obstructing Merewick Lane or requiring a temporary widening into the hedge margin. If the answer is traffic management on the highway, that measure should be stated in the construction traffic management plan rather than inferred from a diagram.

6.4 The drainage strategy, DS-07 revision C, proposes shallow swales beside parts of the internal track. Swales can be compatible with ecological management, but their construction profile matters. A swale excavated after protective fencing has been installed may require plant to operate on both sides of the fence; one excavated before fencing may leave the retained hedge exposed during the busiest phase. The construction sequence should therefore identify the order of excavation, track formation and installation of protection. It should also show where excavated material will be stored. A note saying that arisings will remain on site is not sufficient to establish that storage will avoid the retained vegetation.

6.5 The strategy refers to a 1 in 100 year rainfall event with an allowance for climate change. That is an appropriate type of test, but the drawings do not consistently distinguish permanent drainage land from temporary construction land. The catchment plan also uses a different Field 7 boundary from the access plan. I recommend a single coordinated boundary and a schedule of drawing revisions. This is a document-control point, not an allegation that the drainage calculations themselves are wrong. If the land required for temporary attenuation is no longer available once the hedge protection area is fixed, the calculations should be updated to reflect the layout actually proposed.

6.6 The landscape and visual assessment identifies views from Merewick Lane, the Brindle Footpath and the eastern approach to Upper Merewick. Its photomontages show a mature planting belt. The planting schedule, by contrast, describes transplants at installation and allows for failures to be replaced in the following planting season. Both presentations have a purpose, but they should not be read as showing the same point in time. For examination purposes the applicant should supply an establishment-year view or a clear statement of the assumed planting height in each visualisation. This is particularly relevant at Field 7, where the existing hedge provides screening before the proposed planting has established.

6.7 The management specification proposes cutting the new hedge on a rotational basis and retaining a varied structure. I support that principle. It is less clear who would inspect the planting after the construction contractor leaves, what would trigger replacement, and whether access for that work has been allowed behind the security fence. Those are practical questions capable of being addressed in the landscape and ecological management plan. They need not prevent a decision in principle, provided the final requirement secures a coordinated plan before works begin and makes clear which approved drawing controls in the event of a conflict.

6.8 I have also considered the policy compliance table submitted for the Upper Merewick Solar and Storage Order. It refers to the Merewick Borough Council Landscape Character Supplement and the adopted Merewick Local Framework. The table records compliance largely by reference to proposed mitigation. That may be a reasonable conclusion after the design is fixed, but it is premature where the extent of retained vegetation and the space for mitigation differ between plans. A commitment to plant cannot, without further explanation, be treated as equivalent to retaining an existing hedge during the first years of operation. The revised table should distinguish existing features, temporary effects and eventual mitigation outcomes.

6.9 None of these observations establishes that the access, drainage or planting proposals are inherently incompatible. They establish that each relies on a strip of land whose use has not yet been described consistently. A consolidated Field 7 constraints plan could resolve much of this uncertainty. It should carry dimensions, a revision number and cross-references to CT-04, DS-07 revision C and the landscape drawings. It should be accompanied by a short construction sequence explaining which activities occur before and after protective fencing is installed.

6.10 Subject to those amendments, my position remains that the applicant has a plausible route to delivering the stated mitigation. I cannot at present confirm that it is demonstrated by the submitted drawings. The distinction matters: a requirement for later detail can secure how an established design is built, but should not be used to decide for the first time whether the track, drainage, fence and retained hedge physically fit together.

7. Construction access, drainage and the limits of later detail

7.1 The following comments concern the construction phase, rather than the permanent layout alone. Valehaven Energy Ltd proposes to bring most plant into the Upper Merewick Solar and Storage Order site from the temporary access off Merewick Lane. The submitted construction traffic note estimates a peak of 36 two-way heavy goods vehicle movements per working day. That figure is useful for highway assessment, but it does not explain how vehicles carrying track stone will be kept out of the narrow working strip beside the retained hedge in Field 7. The relevant ecological question is not whether the daily total is acceptable; it is whether deliveries can be unloaded and placed without repeatedly crossing the proposed protection line.

7.2 Drawing CT-04 shows a haul route approaching Field 7 from the south. It stops at the field boundary and does not show a turning head, unloading area or the method of transferring material to the track alignment. The construction environmental management framework says that no vehicles will enter fenced protection areas. I agree with that principle. Nevertheless, the drawing should show where the vehicles will actually go. A statement of intent and a line on a plan do not, between them, establish a workable construction method. This is a point capable of resolution now, without requiring a complete contractor method statement.

7.3 The material quantities are also relevant to phasing. The typical track section assumes a 300 mm aggregate layer over a geotextile separator, whereas the construction note describes locally variable build-up. On the drawings as submitted, there is no agreed trigger for increasing the depth or width when softer ground is encountered. If such changes are made next to the hedge after protective fencing is erected, the fence may have to be moved. The consolidated constraints plan requested at paragraph 6.9 should therefore identify the maximum construction footprint, not merely the nominal finished track width. It should include temporary stockpiles, edge restraint and the space needed to place aggregate.

7.4 Drainage drawing DS-07 revision C proposes a shallow swale along part of the same corridor. The swale is shown in plan, but the sections do not demonstrate a continuous longitudinal fall where it passes the field gateway. A local low point would not necessarily be unacceptable: an infiltration feature can hold water by design. The difficulty is that the drawings alternately describe this length as conveyance and as infiltration. Those functions call for different maintenance access and different assumptions about prolonged wet ground. Before examination closes, the applicant should state which function is intended and show how the feature performs at the gateway in the design storm.

7.5 The Flood Risk and Drainage Statement uses a 1 in 100 year rainfall event plus a 40% climate change allowance. I have not recalculated its storage volumes. My concern is narrower. The stated volumes depend on the swale remaining open and on runoff reaching it without bypassing the proposed filter strips. At the Field 7 entrance, the track is shown above existing ground and could divert overland flow towards the retained hedge. A spot-level plan extending beyond the immediate track corridor would make the proposed flow paths testable. This is especially important before any reliance is placed on a later detailed drainage approval.

7.6 During construction, temporary silt controls will be needed before the permanent swale is complete. The draft sequence places drainage works after the main track installation, but does not identify an interim receiving area for runoff from exposed sub-base. An appropriate sequence would be to establish clean-water cut-offs and a temporary settlement area first, then build the track in short lengths, followed by the permanent drainage and stabilisation of disturbed margins. The actual location of the temporary settlement area should be shown so that it can be checked against the hedge protection zone. This does not require a brand of proprietary silt fence to be specified in the Order documentation.

7.7 The Landscape and Ecological Management Plan provides for replacement planting where hedgerow gaps are unavoidable. Replacement planting is not an equivalent answer to avoidable damage to an existing boundary, particularly where the construction plan has yet to show its full working width. The plan also describes a five-year establishment period. That is a management period, not evidence that screening or habitat continuity will be immediate. The final drawings should distinguish retained sections, short-term construction gaps and newly planted sections rather than colouring the whole boundary as a single continuous hedge.

7.8 The applicant's response to the Merewick Parish Council consultation note says the Field 7 track can be narrowed if required. No narrowed section is supplied. If narrowing is the proposed solution, its effects on vehicle passage, drainage capacity and maintenance should be assessed together. Moving the swale would solve one spatial conflict while potentially creating another. I do not consider it proportionate to ask for a detailed drawing of every field track across the site, but this particular junction of constraints is sufficiently tight to warrant one coordinated drawing at an appropriate scale.

7.9 In terms of the draft Order, Requirement 12 could secure implementation of an approved construction environmental management plan. It should not be treated as a substitute for identifying the land and working space needed for the chosen design. I suggest a limited amendment to the supporting plans, accompanied by a compliance table identifying the relevant drawing for each construction-stage control. The table should state whether each control is a fixed design commitment or a matter that may be adjusted by the appointed contractor within defined limits. This would help the Examining Authority and the local planning authority understand what remains to be approved.

7.10 My conclusion is accordingly qualified. The traffic figures do not themselves indicate that the Field 7 mitigation is undeliverable, and the proposed drainage standard is a reasonable basis for detailed design. However, the current documents leave an unresolved physical overlap between construction access, runoff management and hedge protection. A single revised plan with levels and a concise sequence would allow that overlap to be tested. Without it, the requirement would defer a material question of layout rather than simply control its implementation.

8. Professional evidence and recommended clarification

8.1 I am Elin Voss, an independent ecological consultant (BSc, MSc, CEnv, MCIEEM). I have undertaken habitat and construction-impact assessments for 18 years, including the review of access arrangements beside retained hedgerows. I prepared this evidence independently after reviewing the application documents for the Upper Merewick Solar and Storage Order and visiting the Field 7 boundary in September 2026. My opinion is confined to ecology and the physical space needed to deliver the proposed mitigation; I do not offer a highways or drainage design opinion.

8.2 The hedge shown for retention is not, by itself, sufficient evidence that its roots and associated ground flora will be protected during the temporary works. The drawing should show the working width of the access track, the position of any drainage excavation and the outer limit of the exclusion fencing on the same plan. A cross-section would be useful at the narrowest point. The existing cross-section prepared by Ms Tamsin Rook of Fennelbridge Surveys Ltd shows the finished track level, but not the temporary excavation width, so it does not resolve the overlap identified at paragraph 7.10.

8.3 Badger activity has been recorded in Merewick Copse, though the material before me does not establish that the proposed Field 7 works affect a sett. I have not inferred a precise sett location from those records. The question for this examination is whether the protective fencing can remain in place while the track and drainage are built. That can be answered without publishing further species-location information.

8.4 At the open evening Cllr Idris Pell asked whether the replacement planting could simply be moved farther into the field. In my view that is a possible design response, not a substitute for showing where the construction works will actually go. The applicant, Valehaven Energy Ltd, should provide one coordinated drawing before the close of the examination, with a short method statement identifying which works occur first. I would be content for minor planting adjustments to be approved later, provided the construction envelope and hedge-protection line are fixed now.

8.5 Residents have described stress about the uncertainty. I understand that concern, but my conclusion rests on the drawing discrepancy rather than on an assessment of individual health effects.

Elin Voss

Address carried over from draft contact sheet: 17 Sallow Mews, Merewick, MW4 8QN
Mobile: 07700 900482

9. Witness background and declaration

9.1 I am Elin Voss, MSc, an independent ecological consultant. I have worked on habitat surveys and landscape mitigation for over 20 years. I prepared the ecological review submitted with this evidence and have distinguished my own observations from material supplied by others. My conclusion at paragraph 8.5 does not depend on residents’ descriptions of stress.

9.2 I checked the hedge line against the cross-section prepared by Ms Tamsin Rook of Fennelbridge Surveys Ltd. That cross-section shows existing ground levels but does not resolve the width needed for construction access. Cllr Idris Pell asked at the open evening whether the proposed planting could simply be moved. It could, but Valehaven Energy Ltd should first identify the limit of works on a single drawing. References to badgers in Sallow Wood are deliberately general; I have not included sett locations in this public evidence.

17 Sallow Mews, Merewick, MW4 8QN
Mobile: 07700 900482

MEREWICK PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held in the Village Hall, Merewick, on 14 October 2026 at 7.00 pm

Present: Cllr Tamsin Rook (Chair), Cllr Adrian Voss, Cllr Priya Hales, Cllr Martin Edden and Cllr Faye Norr. Also present: Helen Darrin, Clerk, and three members of the public: Nella Porch, Ivo Mallet and Sarin Pell.

1. Apologies and declarations of interest
Apologies were received from Cllr Owen Breck. There were no declarations of pecuniary interest. The Chair reminded members that the solar project would be discussed as part of the Council's role as an Interested Party in the examination, not as a decision on a local planning application.

2. Previous minutes
The minutes of 9 September 2026 were approved as an accurate record. The Chair signed the paper copy. Cllr Voss said the action about the ditch at School Field remained outstanding; the Clerk will chase the highways team again.

3. Public participation
Nella Porch asked whether construction traffic for the West Merewick Solar and Storage Project would use Brindle Lane at school arrival time. The route drawing showed a turning point but, in the resident's view, did not show how two large vehicles would pass there. Ivo Mallet said the proposed working hours would cause poor sleep and stress for households near the lane. The Chair explained that feelings about likely effects could be included in the Council's submission, provided comments referred to the current examination documents.

Sarin Pell asked for the minutes to record concern about the path through Hollet Wood. Badgers have been seen in Hollet Wood for years, but no member of the public was asked to identify a sett at the meeting. The Chair said any confidential ecology information should go to the case team by the appropriate route rather than on the public noticeboard.

4. West Merewick Solar and Storage Project — examination response
Members considered the draft reply to the Examining Authority's written questions. Fellmere Energy Ltd had supplied a revised construction traffic note, but the Council remained concerned about the proposed passing places, the maintenance of public footpath MW/14 and the length of the temporary closure beside the substation access. Cllr Hales noted that the consultation drawing showed a hedge retained at the southern boundary, while the more recent works plan appeared to show an opening in roughly the same place. The Clerk was asked to seek a clear plan reference rather than guess which drawing takes precedence.

Cllr Norr reported that Cllr Owen Breck had attended the site walk with the applicant's team and had raised the width of the bridge at Brook End. This was a report of the question asked, not an endorsement of the response. Members agreed that the draft should say the Council supports a safe walking route during construction but does not accept an unsigned promise of marshals as a substitute for an enforceable traffic measure.

The Clerk referred to a note received privately from an ecologist. It placed a badger sett in the bank 12 metres east of the stile on Brindle Lane footpath MW/14. Members agreed that this exact description must not appear in the version of the minutes displayed locally. The general concern about habitat disturbance can be stated without giving a precise location. It was resolved unanimously to send the amended response before Deadline 3, subject to the Chair checking the plan numbers. The Clerk will also ask whether the applicant's project website carries the latest footpath diversion drawing, as two versions had been circulated.

5. Separate planning application — 26/0418/HOU
The Council considered the notification for a rear dormer and replacement porch at 6 Juniper Rise, Merewick, WP4 8QD, submitted by Corin Bell. This is an ordinary householder application and is not part of the solar examination. The Chair made that distinction because the two items had been put in the same envelope by the district planning office.

One neighbour's letter stated that Corin Bell, aged 74, had been diagnosed with COPD and would find building dust difficult. Members did not discuss that personal detail. The planning points were the dormer's position, overlooking of the adjoining garden and whether materials would match the existing roof. Cllr Edden proposed no objection provided obscure glazing was required for the side-facing pane. This was agreed, four in favour and one abstention. The Clerk will send the comment to the district council, with no copy of the neighbour's letter attached.

6. Correspondence and finance
The Clerk reported a request from the Village Hall Committee for help replacing the noticeboard perspex. The quoted cost of £186 was within the small repairs budget. Members approved payment on receipt of an invoice. The Council also noted the district council's published budget timetable; no comment was required at present. Cllr Rook asked that future correspondence about the solar project be kept in a separate folder from routine parish planning notifications, to avoid another mix-up.

7. Clerk's contact details and actions

Appendix A to the minutes: West Merewick Solar and Storage Project — technical matters for the examination

This appendix records the planning points agreed for inclusion in Merewick Parish Council’s next written submission. It is not a new decision on whether to support or oppose the application. References to drawings and tables are to the current examination documents unless otherwise stated. Page numbering in the transport addendum differs from the original submission, so the Council has used drawing titles where possible.

A1. Traffic and construction access

The construction traffic assessment for Fellmere Energy Ltd uses an average weekday flow for the main build period. The Council’s concern is the peak day, particularly when deliveries to the battery compound coincide with stone deliveries for temporary tracks. A daily total does not show whether several large vehicles could arrive within the same school-run period. The Council requests a table showing the maximum number of two-way heavy goods vehicle movements in each hour, by construction phase. It should identify which figures are forecasts and which are limits the contractor would have to observe.

The proposed access from Brindle Lane is shown with visibility splays, but the swept-path drawing appears to assume the passing place is available at all times. The temporary works plan should say whether the passing place will be formed before any abnormal deliveries and how ordinary traffic will be managed while it is built. The Council also requests a drawing showing the full vehicle route between the B4179 and the site gate. The present figure stops short of the narrow bend at Low Mere Bridge. A route plan should distinguish vehicles carrying panels, transformers, aggregate and general materials; they do not all have the same turning requirements.

A construction traffic management plan secured by requirement would be acceptable in principle, provided the examination establishes the enforceable limits first. Leaving both the route and the permitted delivery hours to a later plan would make it difficult to assess likely effects now. The wording should cover wheel washing, inspection of road edges, prompt removal of mud, advance booking of large deliveries and a procedure for stopping deliveries if a passing place is obstructed. A complaints log is useful but is not a substitute for a defined response time and a named operational role.

A2. Landscape, layout and lighting

The revised landscape plan retains the field boundaries along Merewick Drove, which is an improvement over the earlier indicative layout. However, the year-one and year-fifteen visualisations use different assumptions about hedge height. The Council asks for a single schedule stating planting height at installation, intended maintained height, anticipated growth rate and the point at which screening is expected to become effective. Winter views are needed as well as summer views because the battery enclosure, fencing and inverter cabins will remain visible when the hedges are bare.

The plan refers to local-provenance planting but does not identify how failures will be counted. A five-year replacement period should apply to each planting area from the date that area is completed, not from the first planting anywhere on the site. Replacement stock should be of comparable size and species unless the replacement is justified in an approved management plan. The Council asks that the temporary construction compounds and their reinstatement be shown on the same plan as the permanent landscape works; otherwise it is not clear which strips of planting could be delayed until the final phase.

Operational lighting should remain off except when needed for maintenance or an alarm response. The lighting schedule should state mounting heights, beam direction and the means of preventing spill beyond the compound fence. A general commitment to ‘low spill’ is too imprecise for compliance checks. No continuous perimeter lighting is shown on the current drawings, and the Council expects that position to be secured.

A3. Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage strategy proposes shallow swales beside the internal tracks and controlled outfalls into existing field drains. The Council requests confirmation that the calculations include runoff from compacted track edges, inverter hardstanding and the battery compound. It is not clear whether the model treats panel-covered ground as unchanged agricultural land throughout the operating period. The assumptions for infiltration should be stated separately for areas under panels, between rows and beneath temporary construction surfaces.

The outline maintenance schedule identifies inspections after heavy rain but does not say how silt removed from swales will be stored or taken off site. That detail matters during construction, when exposed soil will be greatest. The Council also asks for a plan showing exceedance routes if a culvert is blocked. Surface water should not be directed towards Merewick Drove or the lower part of Brindle Lane by temporary bunds, stockpiles or track levels. A pre-construction survey of the existing field drains would provide a baseline against which later defects can be checked.

A4. Ecology and land management

The ecological documents refer to badgers and bats in Alder Brake and to hedgerows used by commuting wildlife. This is a broad description of habitat, not a location for any protected resting place. The Council’s planning point is that the final fencing design must allow appropriate movement along retained boundaries while keeping the operational compound secure. The grazing proposal should also be coordinated with hedge establishment: grazing before guards and new planting are established could undermine the screening relied upon in the visual assessment.

A5. Policy and next steps

The Council considers these points relevant to the assessment of construction effects, landscape character, flood risk and the adequacy of proposed requirements under National Policy Statement for Renewable Energy Infrastructure (EN-3). It has not reached a separate conclusion on the battery fire-safety documentation in this appendix. The examination submission should request revised drawings where a physical arrangement is uncertain and draft requirement wording where the arrangement is clear but needs securing. The Clerk’s technical schedule will use document titles and revision letters so that responses can be checked against the correct versions. Agreed for submission as an appendix to the Council’s written representation.
