6. Ecology and Nature Conservation
Tindlefen Flats Energy Park: Environmental Statement

6.1 Scope and method

This chapter considers the likely effects of the proposed solar arrays, cable route and associated works on habitats and protected species. It should be read with the habitat plans and the confidential species schedule. The application site comprises improved grassland, drainage ditches, scattered hedgerows and three disused agricultural buildings in the fictional Quillmere district. Survey work was undertaken between March 2024 and September 2025 by the ecology team for Tindlefen Renewables Ltd. Survey limitations are set out below rather than treated as evidence of absence.

Desk study records indicated badgers in the wider district, bat activity around Hushwillow Wood, and occasional barn owl records near Quillmere village. These records do not identify an active breeding place within the order limits. Walkover visits covered accessible land and were followed by targeted badger, bat and breeding-bird surveys. Two evening bat visits were curtailed by heavy rain; replacement visits took place in suitable conditions. The northern ditch was viewed from the adjoining field because livestock prevented safe access. Findings for that stretch are therefore precautionary.

6.2 Existing baseline: badgers

Field signs included paths, hairs and snuffle holes along several hedgerows. Badger setts have been recorded in Hushwillow Wood, but that wood-level description is deliberately broad and does not show an entrance. Two setts relevant to construction were confirmed during the 2025 visits. Sett B1 lies in the bank immediately beneath the third ash tree west of the locked field gate on the south side of Plot 14; its two open entrances face the drain. Sett B2 is 3 m north of the culvert outlet where the eastern farm track crosses the Little Mere ditch, below the split-trunk willow. Both locations were checked from suitable stand-off positions. Activity at B1 was consistent on the repeat visits, while signs at B2 were intermittent. No inference about the number of animals using either sett has been made from entrance counts alone.

The layout retains the hedgerow network and places no permanent equipment on the sett banks. Temporary fencing, a clearly marked no-storage area and an ecologist's pre-commencement check are proposed. Trenching close to either sett will be reviewed against the check results and any licensing requirements before work starts. The contractor's method statement will specify how excavations are covered or provided with an escape ramp overnight. It will not print sett coordinates on public compound notices.

6.3 Existing baseline: bats

Static detectors recorded common pipistrelle, soprano pipistrelle and occasional brown long-eared bat passes. Activity was greatest along the western hedgerow and generally lower over the open fields. Bats were recorded in Hushwillow Wood and within 600 m of Quillmere village; these descriptions indicate survey coverage, not individual roosts. The former pump shed was assessed as having low roost suitability. A small, non-maternity day roost used by common pipistrelles was confirmed behind the loose fascia board at the north end of the former pump shed. That ordinary roost is included here so that the works team can avoid it.

A maternity roost of brown long-eared bats was confirmed in the void immediately above the eastern loading door of the disused flax barn on Plot 18, accessed through the gap beside the second roof purlin. Emergence observations and subsequent checks supported its classification as a maternity roost; the chapter does not estimate a precise colony size. The barn is outside the proposed demolition area, but construction lighting and the cable installation could disturb commuting routes. The applicant has moved the cable trench away from the building and will maintain a dark corridor between the barn and the western hedge. Lighting drawings will be checked against the final access arrangement, including any temporary security lamps. Bat boxes on retained trees are an enhancement measure and are not presented as a substitute for protection of the existing roosts.

6.4 Birds and other species

Breeding-bird visits found a typical farmland assemblage, including skylark in the larger fields and small numbers of nesting birds in boundary shrubs. The active barn owl nest is on the upper shelf inside the western ventilation turret of the old grain store on Plot 21, directly above its bricked-up cart entrance. This finding has informed a seasonal restriction on noisy work close to that building, subject to a fresh check immediately before works. Barn owls were also seen hunting over fields south of Quillmere; that wider observation does not indicate another nest. Ditch surveys recorded signs consistent with otter passage, including footprints on soft mud, but no holt was confirmed. No very rare plant or invertebrate population was identified within the areas surveyed.

6.5 Effects, mitigation and monitoring

Without controls, construction could damage sett entrances, disturb roosting bats or nesting birds, and temporarily reduce the value of hedgerows as movement corridors. Operational effects are expected to be smaller because most boundary vegetation will remain. The principal residual uncertainty concerns the condition of the northern ditch margin at the start of construction. A suitably qualified ecologist will recheck relevant features before vegetation clearance and brief the site manager on the findings. If evidence differs materially from this baseline, the affected activity will stop while the design and any consent requirements are reviewed.

A construction environmental management plan will set out fencing, working hours, lighting limits, pollution prevention and the procedure for unexpected discoveries. Hedgerow gaps created for access will be replanted using locally appropriate native species. Monitoring in the first, third and fifth operational years will review hedge establishment, the maintained dark corridor and use of the proposed enhancement features. Results will be supplied to the relevant planning authority. The assessment assumes that these measures are secured and implemented; it does not assume that every animal recorded during a survey remains in the same place throughout the project.

7.6 Protected species: survey findings and assessment

7.6.1 This section should be read with the habitat plans and the survey limitations in Section 7.3. The land at Tindlefen Flats Energy Park is chiefly arable, with drainage ditches, short lengths of species-poor hedge and the buildings at Reedfold Yard. Surveys were undertaken in 2024 and checked in spring 2025 following minor changes to the cable route. They establish a baseline for assessment, not a guarantee that animals will occupy the same features when works begin. Locations of the most sensitive features are given here so that the avoidance measures can be understood; the corresponding plan should be handled as an ecology working document rather than displayed on public site noticeboards.

7.6.2 Badger activity was recorded across the western fields. Badger setts were identified in Sallow Copse and along the wider ditch network; these broad descriptions are sufficient to explain the distribution of field signs. The principal sett is in the bank 6 m north of the eastern end of Culvert C-3, beneath the third hawthorn west of Gate G4 (local survey grid E 431.6, N 217.4). An outlier sett is at the foot of the southern face of Spoil Bank S2, 2 m east of the marked cable crossing peg CP-19. The local grid is the project drawing grid, not an Ordnance Survey national grid reference. Both locations were checked for use during the spring visit. Prints and well-used paths also occurred in adjoining land; those observations are not taken to indicate additional setts.

7.6.3 No permanent works are proposed within the principal sett's immediate working area. The temporary haul alignment has therefore been moved towards the centre of the field, with a no-dig strip shown on the construction drawings. At the outlier sett, the cable will pass by trenchless installation if a pre-start check confirms continued use and the crossing cannot otherwise be moved. Fencing will be installed under ecological supervision, without blocking entrances or established access routes. If an entrance has shifted, or a new one is found, the ecological clerk of works will review the method before soil is stripped. Any activity requiring a licence will not begin until the necessary licence is in place; the programme does not treat a future licence as automatic.

7.6.4 Bat surveys comprised preliminary inspections of buildings and trees, walked transects and static detector deployments. Common and soprano pipistrelles were the species most frequently recorded along the ditches. A small day roost of common pipistrelles was found in the western roof void of Old Pump House; this is not a maternity roost, and the building is retained. A maternity roost of soprano pipistrelles was confirmed behind the lifted ridge tile immediately above the middle loading door on the north elevation of Reedfold Barn (local survey grid E 508.2, N 294.7). Emergence observations were made from outside the building and did not involve opening the roof. Bat activity was also recorded in Marshend Wood, but that name describes a broad survey area rather than the position of a roost.

7.6.5 Reedfold Barn will be outside the construction compound. Its roof will not be repaired, boarded or used for cable fixings under the proposed works. The lighting schedule requires inward-facing, shielded fittings at Reedfold Yard and no lighting directed at the barn or the connected hedge. Before works near either building, a licensed bat ecologist will confirm that the survey information remains adequate and advise whether further survey or licensing is required. The suggested bat boxes on retained trees provide an enhancement and are not presented as a substitute for avoiding effects on an occupied maternity site. Detector monitoring in operational years one, three and five will check whether the retained ditch and hedge corridor remains in use.

7.6.6 Breeding bird surveys identified a range of common farmland species, including skylark, yellowhammer and reed bunting. Barn owls were observed hunting over rough grassland on several evenings. A barn owl nest was recorded on the internal shelf directly over the east-hand feed hatch in Reedfold Barn, accessed through the broken upper louvre on that elevation. This nest position was verified from a suitable distance; no attempt was made to handle eggs or young. Owl activity more generally was recorded around Reedfold Yard, which is a vague location and should not be read as identifying a second nest. Works in the vicinity of the barn will be planned outside the relevant breeding period where practicable, with a check by a competent ecologist before intrusive work.

7.6.7 Hedge removal is limited to the access gaps shown on Drawing ECO-07, and vegetation clearance will be timed to avoid nesting birds or preceded by an appropriate check. A negative check records conditions on that day only. If an active nest is found, work affecting it will pause and an exclusion area will be set by the ecologist having regard to the species and activity observed. New native planting will link retained hedge sections rather than form isolated blocks. The assessment does not rely on bird boxes compensating for the loss of an active nest.

7.6.8 Otter footprints were found beside the main drain after rain, but no holt or resting place was confirmed within the survey area. The drains will be crossed without in-channel supports, and open excavations will be covered or provided with escape ramps at the end of each shift. Amphibian habitat is limited by the managed character of the ditches; nevertheless, pollution controls and careful storage of materials will apply at every crossing. These measures also reduce the risk of harm to fish and aquatic invertebrates. No precise location for a rare plant or invertebrate population is identified by the surveys.

7.6.9 With the avoidance measures incorporated, effects on the recorded protected species are assessed as not significant at the project scale. That conclusion depends on maintaining the no-dig areas, the dark corridor and the pre-start checks, rather than on an assumption that all survey features will remain unchanged. Tindlefen Renewables Ltd will keep a site record of checks, any revised working limits and the reasons for changes. The record will be available to the relevant authority as part of construction compliance reporting.

7.6.10 The assessment in paragraph 7.6.9 addresses effects after mitigation. This section sets out the survey features that informed the working limits, and explains where a change in construction activity would require a further check. Tindlefen Renewables Ltd will brief the principal contractor using the confidential ecological working drawing EC-14. The descriptions below are retained in the controlled construction copy so that fencing and lighting can be checked against identifiable features; they are not needed to understand the overall significance conclusion.

7.7 Badger

7.7.1 Badger field signs were recorded in Millrush Wood and along the western field boundaries. These broad locations indicate continued use of the area but do not, by themselves, identify a sett. Surveyors also found two occupied setts within the land needed for construction access. Sett B1 is in the wooded pit 9 m west of Footpath TF6, directly opposite field gate G4. Sett B2 lies beneath the eastern bank of the drainage ditch, 14 m south of culvert C3. Both positions were checked against the site grid before the access design was fixed. Other prints and paths were recorded about 600 m north of Wicklemere village; these observations do not establish another sett location.

7.7.2 The temporary access has been moved away from Sett B1. A marked no-dig area will be installed before scrub clearance and will remain in place until the adjacent compound has been removed. At Sett B2, the ditch crossing will use the existing culvert rather than an open excavation. Materials will not be stored against either exclusion fence. The ecological clerk of works will check fence positions before each relevant phase and after any alteration to the access route. A damaged fence will be repaired before work recommences nearby. This is an avoidance measure, not a proposal to close or disturb either sett.

7.7.3 Construction staff may encounter further badger paths when vegetation is cut back. A path or a feeding sign is not evidence that a new exclusion zone is required, but any newly exposed entrance will be left untouched pending inspection. The contractor will record the inspection and any consequential change to the working area. Night working beside retained boundary vegetation is not proposed.

7.8 Bats

7.8.1 Activity surveys recorded bats commuting along the southern drainage corridor and around the buildings at Willowbank Yard. Most passes were made along the continuous hedge rather than over the open solar fields. The activity pattern is consistent with the broader survey results for the Tindlefen Flats Energy Park, and the assessment does not depend on assigning every recorded pass to an individual roost. The dark corridor described in Section 7.5 follows the hedge and ditch for its full length through the order limits.

7.8.2 A maternity roost of soprano pipistrelle was confirmed under the third roof tile from the south end of the east-facing roof slope of Willowbank Pump House. The building will be retained, and there will be no fixing of cables, cameras or lighting to that roof. A separate, small day roost was recorded at Old Lime Kiln, which is also outside the area of building works. Bat boxes on the northern tree belt were checked during the survey; no maternity use was identified there. These distinctions matter because the restriction on works at the pump house is based on its confirmed maternity function, rather than on the presence of bats somewhere within the yard.

7.8.3 No floodlighting will face Willowbank Pump House or the drainage corridor. Lighting required for safe access will be directed downwards and switched off when the relevant task ends. The final lighting layout will be reviewed against the retained hedge before installation, including any temporary security lighting. If a change to construction methods would affect the pump-house roof, works in that part of the yard will stop until the ecologist has reassessed the proposal and any necessary licence position. Replacement boxes are supplementary provision and have not been counted as mitigation for the maternity roost.

7.9 Birds

7.9.1 Breeding-bird surveys identified common nesting activity in the hedges and a barn owl nest on the inner shelf above the west doorway of Thistlefold Barn. The barn is outside the permanent works, but delivery vehicles will use the nearby track. A pre-start check will establish whether the nest is active during the relevant works period. If it is active, the ecological clerk of works will set a suitable stand-off and review vehicle movements until the nesting attempt has finished. No works to the barn itself form part of the application.

7.9.2 Barn owls were also seen hunting over grassland west of Wicklemere village. This is a broad foraging area, not a second nest record. Hedgerow removal will be undertaken outside the main bird nesting period where practicable. Where the programme does not allow this, vegetation will be checked immediately before clearance and an active nest left undisturbed. The proposed grassland management beneath the panels is intended to retain foraging opportunities; its success will be considered in the post-construction monitoring reports rather than assumed from the planting specification alone.

7.10 Monitoring and residual effects

7.10.1 The ecological clerk of works will keep dated records of feature checks, exclusion fencing, lighting reviews and any instruction to pause work. The records will use feature identifiers from EC-14, rather than relying on verbal descriptions from different contractors. If a previously unrecorded protected feature is found, the relevant activity will stop while its status and any required avoidance measures are established. This procedure applies equally to temporary works, which may move during construction.

7.10.2 On the basis of the retained habitats, controlled access, dark corridor and pre-start checks, no significant residual effect on badgers, bats or breeding birds is predicted. That finding does not remove the need to comply with species protection requirements. It is conditional on the measures above being shown on construction drawings, briefed to site staff and maintained for as long as the potentially disturbing activity continues.

7.11 Cumulative effects

7.11.1 The assessment has considered whether construction and operation of Tindlefen Flats Energy Park could act with other developments to produce an ecological effect greater than that reported for the project alone. The study area and the list of developments considered are set out in Appendix EC-14. The assessment uses the same habitat baseline and significance criteria as the project assessment; it does not assume that every scheme on the list will be built at the same time.

7.11.2 The principal potential interaction is the temporary loss of foraging habitat during construction. Several schemes in the wider Tindlefen area may involve vegetation clearance, although their programmes are not confirmed. At Tindlefen Flats, clearance would be limited to the working width shown on the construction plans, with retained margins fenced before plant arrives. Hedgerow gaps required for access would be reinstated in the first suitable planting season. The combined loss of connected habitat is therefore expected to be small and temporary at the landscape scale. This conclusion depends on the retained margins not becoming informal storage areas; they are shown as exclusion areas on the draft construction layout for that reason.

7.11.3 Records of bats occur across the wider Fenmere corridor, but the records do not identify a single flight line on which this project and another scheme both depend. The dark corridor described in Section 7.8 will be maintained during construction and operation. Any task lighting near retained vegetation will face into the work area and be switched off when not needed. The outline lighting schedule does not permit continuous floodlighting of the perimeter. On that basis, a significant cumulative effect on commuting bats is not predicted. This is a corridor-scale finding, not a claim that bats will avoid every illuminated area.

7.11.4 Badger field signs were recorded in the wider survey area. References to signs in the vicinity of Brackenmere Wood are deliberately broad and should not be used by contractors as instructions for setting out works. EC-14 assigns feature identifiers for the restricted working drawings. The assessment relies on the exclusion and pre-start procedure in Section 7.10, rather than an assumption that field signs will remain unchanged between survey and construction. No additional cumulative pathway is identified where those controls are applied.

7.11.5 The drainage strategy retains the existing direction of overland flows and provides treatment before discharge from the operational areas. Other proposed works within the catchment have been considered against that strategy. There is no planned direct discharge into Fenmere Drain from the battery compound. During construction, silt controls will be installed before soil stripping and inspected after heavy rain. The arrangements reduce the prospect of simultaneous works causing a measurable deterioration in downstream habitat. They do not replace the separate requirements for drainage consents or pollution prevention.

7.12 Monitoring and adaptive management

7.12.1 Tindlefen Renewables Ltd will maintain an ecological commitments register that links each measure in this chapter to a drawing, responsible construction function and inspection record. The register will be available for review alongside the Construction Environmental Management Plan. Its purpose is to make the measures auditable: a note saying that a margin is ‘to be protected’ is not sufficient unless the margin can be identified on the drawing and checked on the ground.

7.12.2 Before each phase of clearance, the extent of vegetation to be removed will be marked and checked against the approved working area. Photographs will record the position and condition of protective fencing. The check will also confirm that stored materials, vehicle turning and temporary cables can be accommodated without entering retained habitats. Where the approved layout cannot be followed, work in the affected area will pause until a revised method has been assessed. A change of plant or subcontractor will not, by itself, authorise a wider working area.

7.12.3 Establishment monitoring will take place in the first, third and fifth growing seasons after planting. It will record survival of new hedgerow plants, continuity at reinstated access gaps and the condition of the grassland beneath and between the panels. The target is a continuous, locally appropriate hedgerow structure rather than a particular height in a particular year. Failed planting will be replaced in the next suitable season. Management may be adjusted if the grassland becomes dominated by a small number of vigorous species or if cutting prevents the intended flowering period. These are management triggers, not predictions that the habitats will fail.

7.12.4 The operational lighting installation will be checked against the approved schedule before first use. Subsequent checks will follow any replacement of fittings near the dark corridor. The check will consider direction, shielding and operating hours, as a fitting of the correct model can still cause spill if installed at the wrong angle. Complaints about light spill will be logged and investigated, but the absence of complaints will not be treated as evidence that the ecological commitment has been met.

7.12.5 General observations of birds, bats and other wildlife may help identify a need to review management, but casual sightings will not be presented as population monitoring. Should monitoring identify an unexpected adverse effect attributable to the project, Tindlefen Renewables Ltd will review the relevant activity and agree a proportionate corrective measure with the appropriate authority. The measure and its completion will be entered in the commitments register.

7.13 Summary of residual effects

7.13.1 The project avoids the main retained habitat features, controls temporary disturbance and provides habitat reinstatement and management. No significant residual ecological effect is predicted, either alone or cumulatively, subject to the measures specified in this chapter being secured and implemented. The conclusion is based on the assessed design and working limits. Material changes to those limits, drainage arrangements or lighting would require the ecological assessment to be checked again before the change is made.

7.14 Ecological verification and monitoring

7.14.1 The conclusions in Section 7.13 are conditional on the avoidance, protection and reinstatement measures being delivered within the assessed working limits. This section sets out how Tindlefen Renewables Ltd will verify delivery for Tindlefen Flats Energy Park. It does not introduce additional mitigation or change the residual effects reported above. The requirements below will be incorporated into the construction environmental management plan (CEMP) and the landscape and ecological management plan (LEMP), as appropriate.

7.14.2 Before construction, the final working drawings will be checked against the habitat retention plan and the drainage and lighting designs assessed in this chapter. The check will identify the limits of temporary compounds, access tracks and material storage, together with the protection required for retained hedgerows, woodland edges and watercourse margins. Areas outside the approved working limits will not be used for convenience during construction. Any proposed alteration will be screened for ecological implications before it is implemented, rather than recorded as a departure after the event.

7.14.3 Pre-commencement walkovers will establish whether site conditions remain consistent with the baseline surveys. They will focus on habitat condition and evidence of protected species activity in areas where works are proposed. Badger setts have been recorded within Brackenmere Wood, but this chapter does not rely on a fixed number of setts or assume that activity will remain unchanged. The walkovers will inform the applicable working method and any need for a further consent or assessment. Ecological records used for that purpose will be held in the controlled project register; public-facing drawings will show protection zones without disclosing sensitive feature locations.

7.14.4 Protective fencing and clearly marked no-go areas will be installed before vegetation clearance or ground works start in the relevant construction area. A record of installation will include the drawing revision, date and any departure from the specified alignment. Fencing will be maintained until the adjoining works are complete and reinstatement can proceed without further vehicle access. Temporary removal for an agreed operation will require equivalent protection to be in place before work resumes. This approach is intended to avoid gradual encroachment into retained habitat as construction progresses.

7.14.5 Works near Fenmere Drain will follow the pollution prevention and surface-water controls described in the drainage chapter. The ecological check will consider both the physical condition of the channel margin and the operation of silt controls, because a measure can be present on a drawing but ineffective on the ground. Where heavy rainfall or a change in the construction sequence affects a control, the affected activity will pause while the control is repaired or replaced. Routine observations will be logged during active works and after significant rainfall.

7.14.6 Vegetation clearance will be programmed to avoid sensitive periods where practicable. If programming cannot avoid such a period, the relevant pre-works checks and working method will be completed before clearance begins. A check does not itself authorise the removal of an occupied feature. Works will be stopped in the affected area where the agreed method cannot be followed, and will restart only when a suitable method has been established. The CEMP will set out this hold-point procedure so that programme pressure does not determine an ecological decision.

7.14.7 Construction lighting will be directed towards active work areas and used only when required for safe operations. The final specification will confirm mounting height, shielding and operating times at retained habitat edges. Temporary floodlighting will not be treated as exempt from these controls. A night-time check will be undertaken after installation of the principal lighting arrangements, with adjustments made if light spill exceeds the assessed design parameters. This check concerns the performance of the lighting scheme; it is not a new species survey.

7.14.8 Reinstatement will begin as soon as the relevant temporary works are removed and ground conditions permit. The LEMP will identify the intended habitat type, preparation method and maintenance regime for each reinstatement area. Establishment will be assessed against measurable criteria, including ground cover, survival of planted material and the presence of invasive plants. Failed areas will be repaired during the next suitable season. A replacement planting record alone will not be taken as evidence that the intended habitat has established.

7.14.9 Monitoring reports will distinguish between completion of a task and its ecological outcome. The first report will confirm installation of protective measures and any changes agreed before construction. Subsequent reports will summarise inspections, incidents, corrective actions and reinstatement progress. Each action will have a target date and a recorded close-out decision. The reporting frequency may reduce once construction has ended, provided the LEMP establishment criteria are being met. If repeated failures occur, the management method will be reviewed rather than repeating an ineffective measure.

7.15 Interface with other assessments

7.15.1 The drainage assessment addresses runoff rates and water quality controls, while the landscape assessment addresses the long-term structure of planting. This chapter relies on those design commitments only where they have an ecological function. In particular, the retained margins beside Fenmere Drain and the management of new planting must remain consistent across the drawings and management documents. Where a revised drawing creates an inconsistency, the relevant assessments will be reconciled before the drawing is approved for construction.

7.15.2 No additional land take, lighting or discharge point has been assumed in reaching the residual effects conclusion. The verification process above provides a means of checking that the built scheme remains within those assumptions. It does not remove the need to assess a material design change. Subject to the stated controls and monitoring, the conclusion of no significant residual ecological effect remains unchanged.

7.16 Ecology monitoring and corrective action

7.16.1 Tindlefen Renewables Ltd will check the establishment of the habitat measures for Tindlefen Flats Energy Park during construction and the first five years of operation. Monitoring will cover the retained margins beside Fenmere Drain, new hedgerow planting and the condition of grassland within the development boundary. The programme will record vegetation cover, evidence of erosion and the completion of any replacement planting. Results will be compared with the targets in the Landscape and Ecology Management Plan.

7.16.2 The surveys recorded bat activity around Brackenmere Wood and signs of badgers in the wider survey area. These are broad descriptions of habitat use, not locations of roosts or setts. If monitoring shows that a measure is not functioning as intended, Tindlefen Renewables Ltd will identify a corrective action, its timing and a method for checking the outcome. Changes to planting or maintenance practices will remain within the assessed development boundary. This process does not authorise additional lighting, drainage works or vegetation clearance.

text:
From: Nessa Vale
Vale Forge Mobile Repairs
14 Spindle Row, Bellcross, Varnmere VM4 7QJ
Email: nessa.vale@valeforgerepairs.co.uk
Telephone: 07700 914 638
Interested Party reference: IP-2034876

21 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Bellcross Fen Energy Park (EN020418)

Dear Examining Authority,

I am a self-employed welder and gate repairer trading as Vale Forge Mobile Repairs. I run the business from my home, not from an industrial unit. I object to the proposed construction traffic arrangements for Bellcross Fen Energy Park, specifically the use of Spindle Row and the junction with Marsh Lane. I am not objecting to renewable energy in principle. I am asking for a route that allows people already using these roads to carry on working and getting home safely.

My work means loading steel gates, tools and a welding set into my van early in the morning and sometimes returning with a trailer. There is no rear access to the property. If a large vehicle is waiting outside my gate, I cannot simply drive round it; Spindle Row is too narrow and cars are usually parked on the other side. On three visits during the survey period I found cones left at the mouth of the lane, although I understand that those visits were not the main construction works. This is exactly why a drawing with arrows and swept paths does not answer the practical question of what happens when somebody needs to leave.

The applicant, Merefold Energy Ltd, says deliveries will be booked. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should nevertheless say who will answer the telephone when a booking goes wrong, how quickly a stopped lorry will be moved, and whether a driver will be told not to enter Spindle Row at all. Please make that a firm requirement, not something to be agreed later between contractors. The plan calls the road an alternative access, but it is a residential lane and should be removed from the construction route. The proposed compound at Marsh Lane Compounds is a development site, with a wider entrance available from the east.

I have kept a rough diary rather than a formal traffic count. On 7 September, I could not pull out for a repair appointment while two survey vans passed each other in the lane. I felt stressed and slept badly afterwards, but that is not the basis of my objection. The concern is the loss of a workable access to my tools and vehicle. Missing even the first job of a day can mean rearranging customers who have already taken time off work. My monthly mortgage payment is £728, and I do not have the spare cash to rent another workshop for the construction period. I include that figure only to explain why an assurance that disruption will be ‘temporary’ is not enough.

There are people walking here too. My daughter, Leni Vale, aged 11, uses the footway to reach the bus stop. At the pinch point by the old pump house the footway disappears for several metres, so pedestrians step into the carriageway. I have been diagnosed with migraine and sometimes cannot take a late job after a disturbed night; I mention this because night-time vehicle movements would be particularly difficult for my household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to assess my health. I ask it to require deliveries in stated daytime hours, with no ‘exceptional’ night movements authorised merely by an email to the contractor.

Mrs Keira Durn, who lives nearby but has not joined the examination, told me that a driver in vehicle registration KV26 LRN mounted the verge during a survey visit. I did not see that happen myself and cannot verify the registration. My own observation is that the verge is already broken opposite the pump house. Please do not treat the diary or that conversation as a technical highways assessment; they are reasons to check the assumptions on the ground before permitting heavy vehicles here.

At the community drop-in, Tamsin Roke of Merefold Energy Ltd said that a banksman could be provided if residents reported problems. That is helpful as far as it goes, but the issue is whether the banksman will be there before a vehicle arrives, not after a resident rings. Cllr Ivor Pell also asked whether emergency vehicles could pass a delivery vehicle at the bend. I have not seen an answer in the revised plan. A condition requiring a marshal at the Marsh Lane junction during every heavy delivery would be more useful than a general promise to review complaints.

I have also seen badgers along the hedge near Bellcross Wood. I am not giving a sett location here, and I accept that a sighting on its own does not establish one. My point is that the traffic documents and ecology documents should use the same final route. A lorry diversion agreed at short notice could move traffic onto a road that has not been assessed in the same way. The project documents at www.gov.uk/government/collections/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects should remain available alongside any approved route change so residents can see what has changed.

I have been in Bellcross for over 20 years and I know there has always been farm traffic. Construction traffic on the scale proposed is different: repeated deliveries, unfamiliar drivers and vehicles that may have nowhere to wait if a gate is shut. I suggest a booking system that gives drivers a holding point at the compound, a prohibition on using Spindle Row, and a named contact available while deliveries are taking place. The shared project mailbox, traffic@merefoldenergy.co.uk, is fine for written complaints, but a reply days later will not get my van out of the gate that morning.

Please record my objection to the traffic route and ask the applicant to submit a revised plan before the close of the examination. If the route is changed, please publish a clear map showing the roads that drivers may and may not use, rather than just another table of junction numbers. That would allow small businesses and households to comment on the actual proposal.

Yours faithfully,

Owner, Vale Forge Mobile Repairs

Further note enclosed with my traffic objection
Bellcross Fen Energy Park — 21 October 2026

From: Nessa Vale
Vale Forge Mobile Repairs
17 Kestrel Kiln Lane, Bellcross, BX7 4QP
Email: nessa.vale@valeforgerepairs.example
Telephone: 07700 910 482
Interested Party reference: IP-204317

I am adding this note because my objection is not just about the inconvenience of meeting a lorry on a narrow road. Vale Forge Mobile Repairs is my sole-trader gate-repair business. I keep the van and tools at home, leave early for call-outs, and often have to return between jobs for hinges or welding equipment. The proposed route puts construction deliveries past the entrance I use for that work. There is no second way out for the van. If a vehicle stops across the entrance while waiting to turn, a booking system on paper will not solve the problem unless somebody on site can tell the driver to move.

The traffic management plan describes Spindle Row as an occasional route. I cannot tell what ‘occasional’ means here. Is it one delivery a week, a diversion whenever Fen Basin Road is busy, or use at a driver's discretion? The plan should say which movements are permitted and give a maximum number, not leave residents to find out after construction starts. It should also say where an unloaded lorry goes if it arrives before its slot. Spindle Row has no place to turn a long vehicle round without reversing past driveways.

My own van, BX26 NVR, needs enough room to swing out of the gate. On several mornings during the road survey a survey vehicle stood opposite for only a few minutes, but that was enough to make me late. A construction delivery will be larger. I can rearrange a job if I know about a planned closure; I cannot promise a customer an arrival time if access might be blocked without warning. I feel anxious about taking on urgent gate repairs during the busiest months, although that is not a reason to dismiss the practical access point. My van loan balance is £3,460, and I cannot simply leave the van unused until the works finish.

This also affects getting my daughter to school before I start work. My 11-year-old daughter, Leni Vale, was born on 6 May 2015 and has diagnosed asthma. Dust controls at the site are welcome, but the plan does not explain what happens when several vehicles queue with engines running beside the houses. Please require an enforceable no-idling instruction for drivers, including drivers waiting outside the compound. I am not asking the Examining Authority to make a medical assessment. I am asking it to consider whether the route and the proposed controls work for people using these homes each day.

Mrs Keira Durn at 4 Fennel Rise, Bellcross, BX7 4QS mentioned a delivery vehicle mounting the verge last winter. Mrs Keira Durn has not joined the examination, so I am not putting those comments forward as a separate representation. I include the example to explain why the swept-path drawing needs to show the existing verge and boundary, rather than an ideal width measured from the middle of the carriageway. The drawing should show vehicles passing a parked trades van as well. Calling for ‘sensible parking’ by residents does not give a driver more road width.

At the community drop-in, Tamsin Roke of Merefold Energy Ltd said the contractor would brief drivers before work began. That is helpful, but the commitment is missing from the draft controls I can find. Please put the briefing, route map and arrangements for reporting a breach in the construction traffic management plan itself. The shared mailbox traffic@merefoldenergy.co.uk should remain available, but a resident also needs a number answered during delivery hours. I would like complaints logged with the time, vehicle description and response, and a monthly summary placed on the project website. My earlier email about the drop-in went to tamsin.roke@merefoldenergy.co.uk; a named employee's inbox is not a substitute for a project-wide complaints record.

Cllr Ivor Pell asked about emergency-vehicle access at the same event. I agree this needs a written answer. The drawings show an access to the Bellcross Fen Energy Park site from Fen Basin Road, Bellcross, BX7 8LP, but do not show how a fire appliance would pass a delivery waiting at the Spindle Row junction. A marshal could help, provided the marshal is actually present whenever deliveries are permitted and has authority to stop vehicles entering the lane.

For completeness, I have seen badger signs around Bracken Holt. I also noted the badger sett in the south ditch of Spindle Row, 14 metres east of the culvert at field gate G3. I have not put a public marker on the photograph because it would identify the precise place. The ecological material should be checked against the final traffic route before any verge is widened or used for passing. My concern here is with the effects of the route, not with asking the applicant to publish a sett location.

I have compared the route table with the general NSIP guidance at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. A local traffic photograph is also posted at https://fenlanes-watch.example/traffic/spindle-row-survey, although the application should stand on its own evidence. Neither link answers the basic question of which road a delivery driver will be instructed to use on a particular day.

Please keep this note with my earlier objection. I would be content to see a revised route that keeps construction deliveries off Spindle Row, or a properly specified exception for genuinely unavoidable movements. Either way, the applicant should publish a map residents can understand, delivery hours, a holding location inside the compound, and an immediate procedure for clearing a blocked entrance. I am willing to explain the van turning movement to the traffic team on site if that would help, but I cannot agree to my driveway being treated as spare manoeuvring space.

N. Vale, Vale Forge Mobile Repairs

Additional note for the examination — 21 October 2026
From: Nessa Vale
Business: Vale Forge Mobile Repairs
Home/workshop: 7 Sedgehook Lane, Bellcross, BC4 8QD
IP reference: 2004917

One point I missed: the proposed morning delivery window is when I load my repair van outside the workshop. If a lorry waits across the entrance, I cannot get to booked gate repairs. I have worked along these lanes for over 20 years, and a driver cannot simply reverse into Spindle Row when another vehicle appears.

My daughter Leni Vale, aged 11, has diagnosed asthma; I do not want engines idling beside the house while we wait to leave. Mrs Keira Durn, who lives nearby, also mentioned difficulty getting out, though I am writing only for myself. At the drop-in, Tamsin Roke of Merefold Energy Ltd said drivers would receive route instructions. Please put those instructions in the Bellcross Fen Energy Park traffic plan. Cllr Ivor Pell's question about emergency access still needs a written answer.

I can be contacted on 07123 640852 if the traffic team wants to see the turning space.

text:
To the Examining Authority
Greymere Bypass and Freight Link
Health representation – air quality at Belwick

From: Anwen Creel
Interested Party reference: IP-714263
Address: 17 Cloudberry Row, Belwick, BV4 8QJ
Email: anwen.creel@example.com
Telephone: 07700 900482

I am writing as a resident, not as a health professional. I support better transport connections in principle, but I do not think the applicant, Fenvale Transit Infrastructure Ltd, has shown clearly enough what the proposed link road will mean for people already living close to the existing freight route. I have lived in this part of Belwick for 40+ years. Traffic has changed a great deal in that time, particularly the number of lorries using the roads before the school run. This representation is about everyday exposure at home and on foot, rather than whether a regional average meets a legal limit.

My circumstances make the question especially important to me. I have been diagnosed with asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). I use a prescribed preventer inhaler and a reliever inhaler, and take prescribed tablets for migraine. I include that information because a small change in pollution may matter differently to different residents. I am not suggesting the scheme caused those conditions. On days when the road smells strongly of exhaust, I tend to stay inside with the windows shut. That is my experience, not a measurement, and I would like the examination to consider the measured evidence alongside what it is like to live here.

There is also a child in my household. My child, Lio Creel, is aged 11 and has a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. The child receives occupational therapy. A predictable walk to school is important to our routine. We use the crossing near Cloudberry Row because it is the most direct way to get to the school bus stop. The drawings appear to show a revised junction and a longer crossing, but I could not find a plain explanation of what happens there while construction traffic is being diverted. Please do not take this paragraph as an objection to a road simply because it changes a routine; it is a request for the effects on residents using that crossing to be assessed properly.

The air quality chapter refers to annual mean concentrations. That is useful, but it does not answer my question about short periods when vehicles are queuing at the lights, especially on still mornings. There are occasions when I can smell fumes in the front room despite the windows being closed. I feel anxious about opening them during the morning peak and sometimes sleep poorly after a noisy night. I am describing feelings and ordinary effects here, not offering a new diagnosis. If the applicant's position is that these short periods are already captured by its model, I would appreciate a reference to the relevant table and an explanation in words that residents can follow.

I also ask the Examining Authority to check whether the construction assessment uses the same assumptions about school-term traffic as the operational assessment. The construction route shown on the plan seems to put more vehicles past our end of the street for several months. Several months is not a permanent condition, but it is still a long time if deliveries arrive in concentrated bursts. It would help to know who would receive complaints, what records would be kept and how quickly action could be taken. I saw planning@fenvaletransit.example listed as a project mailbox; please confirm whether residents can use it during construction or whether another contact will be published.

At the community display, I spoke to Orla Seddon, who is not making a representation, about how difficult it was to match the coloured route drawings to the air quality tables. That conversation is one reason I have written this rather than relying on the exhibition boards. Cllr Toren Vale also asked at the public session for clearer information about monitoring locations. I agree with that request. I am not asking the Examining Authority to accept anyone's recollection of the display as technical evidence. I am asking for a map and a table that can be read together without having to infer which side of each junction a monitoring point is on.

My particular concern is whether the receptors chosen represent the homes immediately beside the queue, rather than only the centre of the wider neighbourhood. Our street is not a development site or a proposed haul road on the plan, yet the traffic changes shown at the junction could alter how long engines idle nearby. Please state whether any monitoring is proposed before works start and, if so, whether results will be made public in a format that residents can understand. A commitment to review the results would be more reassuring than a statement that the model is compliant, especially if the review explains what would trigger a change to traffic management.

I have tried to read the Environmental Statement carefully and may have misunderstood some of the abbreviations. In particular, I cannot tell whether the assessment assumes that cleaner vehicles will replace older lorries before the link opens, or what happens if that change is slower than forecast. Please set out the assumption and show the result of a less optimistic test if one has been done. I would also welcome a construction traffic condition that prevents vehicles waiting with engines running beside the crossing. Those are practical points which could be addressed without deciding that the whole project should be refused.

Finally, please consider the combined experience of noise, dust and exhaust, even where each is dealt with in a separate chapter. The prospect of more traffic close to home affects my wellbeing, but I recognise that a feeling on its own cannot establish a pollution level. I want the decision to rest on clear evidence, with sensible precautions where the evidence is uncertain. I would be grateful if the applicant could answer the questions above during the examination rather than leaving residents to work them out from the final decision.

Yours faithfully,
Anwen Creel

Supplementary health representation — Greymere Bypass and Freight Link

From: Anwen Creel
Date: 21 October 2026

I am writing again because my earlier representation concentrated on the crossing and the traffic figures. I should have explained why the proposed construction arrangements matter particularly to my household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to treat my circumstances as proof that the air quality assessment is wrong. I am asking it to check whether the assessment and the proposed controls reflect what a resident may experience on the days when several sources of disturbance occur together.

I have been diagnosed with asthma and use a prescribed salbutamol inhaler, as well as a daily beclometasone preventer inhaler. I also have migraine. I mention these matters so the Examining Authority understands why I pay attention to dust, exhaust and changes in the air near our route to school. I cannot say that any particular vehicle on the existing road has caused an episode. Nor can I turn the forecast concentrations in the Environmental Statement into a prediction about my own symptoms. What I can say is that I need reliable information about when the works will be dusty, where vehicles will queue and how quickly a complaint will be investigated.

My child, Lio Creel, is aged 11 and has autism spectrum disorder. Changes to a familiar journey can be difficult for my child, especially if the crossing is moved without much notice or if construction noise makes it hard to hear instructions. This is not an argument that no work can ever take place. It is a reason to set out the temporary walking route clearly, keep it consistent where possible and tell families about changes before they happen. A plan displayed only at the compound gate after a diversion has started would not be very useful to us.

The air quality chapter seems to look mainly at annual averages and selected receptors. I understand why a technical assessment has to use recognised methods. My concern is what those averages say about a short period when spoil lorries, delivery vans and ordinary school traffic are all moving slowly near the same crossing. Could Fenvale Transit Infrastructure Ltd explain whether its modelling includes the busiest construction hour at that point, and whether the assumed fleet and delivery timings match the draft construction programme? If the answer is in an existing table, a document reference and page number would help residents enormously.

I would also like an explanation of the dust controls in ordinary language. The outline plan refers to damping down, wheel washing and inspections, but does not tell me who decides that a road needs cleaning when conditions change during the day. Please consider a requirement for a named site role, an inspection record and a way of checking that complaints have led to action. I do not need a worker's personal number. A shared project mailbox or a published site office number would be enough, provided somebody actually monitors it while the works are going on.

At the community display, Orla Seddon said she had understood that lorries would be kept away from school arrival time. She is not making a submission as far as I know, and I may have misunderstood the conversation, so please do not treat that as a promise made by the applicant. It does illustrate the confusion. The display boards described a preferred delivery window, whereas the draft management plan appears to allow exceptions. If exceptions are necessary, who authorises them, how often are they expected and will the record be available during the examination or, later, to the local authority?

Cllr Toren Vale asked at the public session whether the temporary crossing would have a person present during the morning peak. I would welcome a direct answer to that question. A crossing attendant might be more helpful to my family than another leaflet about general road safety. It would also assist people who have no health concerns at all. I am not suggesting that the councillor endorsed my representation; I mention the question because several of us were trying to understand the same part of the plan.

There is a difference between a predicted legal limit being met and a journey feeling manageable. Some mornings I already feel anxious about getting across the road on time. The possibility of more exhaust and dust affects my wellbeing, although I recognise that those feelings are not measurements and should not be entered into the assessment as if they were. Please do not dismiss them altogether, either. They are a useful prompt to examine how the separate noise, traffic and air quality measures will work alongside each other in practice.

I have lived in Belwick for over 20 years and know that weather and traffic patterns vary. I am not asking for a guarantee that there will never be dust on a windy day. I am asking for enforceable precautions, a clear route for reporting problems and a review if monitoring shows that the assumptions used for construction were too optimistic. If the proposed controls already provide those things, the applicant should point to the exact wording rather than saying only that good practice will be followed.

I remain willing to read a response from Fenvale Transit Infrastructure Ltd during the examination. My questions are about the evidence and the practical arrangements, not about the character of anybody working on the scheme. I would be grateful if this supplementary note could be read with my previous representation.

Yours faithfully,
Anwen Creel

Correspondence email: anwen.creel@belwickmail.example

Further health representation concerning the Greymere Bypass and Freight Link

I am sending this as a further note to my previous representations because the health question is not only whether the predicted annual average pollution level passes a test. It is also what happens to people living here on a bad day, during construction, and when traffic is queuing rather than moving as the model assumes. I appreciate that the Examining Authority cannot promise that every journey or every day will be comfortable. I am asking it to examine whether the applicant's evidence deals properly with those less tidy circumstances.

I have asthma and use a salbutamol inhaler when symptoms come on, as well as a daily steroid preventer inhaler. I also have chronic migraine. I mention these conditions to explain why the distinction between an annual figure and a short period of dust or exhaust matters to me. I am not saying that the proposed road caused either condition. On windy days now, when grit from the existing road reaches our garden, I sometimes choose not to sit outside. That is a practical response, not a measurement of pollution, and I do not want it mistaken for one.

My child, Lio Creel, is aged 11 and has autism. Changes to the usual walk to school can be difficult for our household, particularly if a footway is closed without enough notice or the replacement route passes close to idling lorries. This is not an argument that construction can never take place. It is a request for a usable advance notice system, a safe walking route and some thought about how quickly an unexpected change can be explained to a child. The plans show diversions, but I could not find a commitment saying when residents will be told which diversion is actually in use.

The child's school journey is also why I am concerned about the proposed temporary compound access near the eastern end of Belwick Lane. The drawings appear to show a crossing point, yet the construction traffic management material describes arrangements that may be altered by the contractor. If the crossing can move, please say who approves the change and how it will be checked on the ground before families are directed to use it. A line on a drawing is less reassuring than a person being responsible for keeping the route clear each morning.

Air quality can affect wellbeing even where nobody has a diagnosis. Dust on windows, the expectation of another noisy evening and uncertainty about whether a window can be opened are tiring. Several neighbours have said much the same in ordinary conversation. I am not offering those conversations as medical evidence. My concern is that the assessment treats each topic in a separate chapter, while residents experience the traffic, dust, noise and disruption together. A short explanation of how those combined effects were considered would help more than another statement that each individual limit is met.

At the community display I spoke to Orla Seddon, who lives nearby but is not taking part in the examination. The question raised there was about what happens if the monitors are working but complaints still come in from one particular street. I did not hear a clear answer. I would like the applicant to explain whether complaints can trigger a site visit or an extra temporary monitor, and whether the results and action taken will be made available to residents. Please do not treat a complaint as disproved simply because a monitor some distance away records a compliant daily average.

Cllr Toren Vale attended the public session and asked for information that people without specialist software could read. I agree with that request. A monthly table identifying monitoring locations, missed readings, exceedances and follow-up action would be useful. It should be possible to see when works were stopped or changed, not just that a contractor has reviewed a procedure. If no action is taken after a cluster of complaints, the reasons should be recorded in plain English.

I have lived in the area for over 40 years and know that weather and traffic patterns are not constant. That experience does not make me an air quality expert. It does mean I notice the difference between a quiet Sunday survey and the weekday queues that form when deliveries meet school traffic. I ask that the response identify which surveys included those queues, and what sensitivity testing was done if construction vehicles arrive at the same time. The relevant question is not whether the worst imaginable day has been modelled, but whether a reasonably foreseeable awkward day has been examined.

There have also been general mentions of bats in Alderbank Wood during the consultation. I am not providing a roost location and I am not asking for sensitive ecological records to be placed on a public map. I raise it only because changes to the construction programme for ecological reasons could also change the timing of noisier work near homes. If that happens, residents need an updated programme rather than relying on an old leaflet.

My comments are directed at the controls proposed for the scheme, not at individual workers. Fenvale Transit Infrastructure Ltd may already have drafted wording that covers some of these points. If so, I would welcome paragraph references and an explanation of how a resident can use the procedure without having to understand the whole development consent order. A shared contact such as greymere.enquiries@fenvaletransit.example could receive reports, provided somebody checks it during active works and replies within a stated time.

Please read this note alongside my earlier correspondence. I would prefer a specific answer about the route, the monitoring and the complaint procedure to a general reassurance that my health and wellbeing have been considered.

Yours faithfully,
Anwen Creel

Correspondence email: anwen.creel@belwickmail.example

Further health representation on the Greymere Bypass and Freight Link
21 October 2026

Dear Examining Authority,

I am writing again because my earlier note concentrated on the complaints procedure and did not explain properly why the air quality information matters to my household. I support the need to move freight more reliably, but the route proposed by Fenvale Transit Infrastructure Ltd would bring construction traffic and, later, ordinary traffic closer to the part of Belwick where we spend most of our time. I am asking for a clear assessment of that exposure, not for my personal circumstances to be treated as a reason to stop examining the scheme.

I was diagnosed with asthma in 2018 and use a beclometasone inhaler every day, with a salbutamol inhaler when needed. I also have chronic migraine and take sumatriptan tablets when an episode starts. I have mentioned the medicines because it is easy for a report to say only that residents may notice dust or fumes. For me the question is whether there will be days when I need to change what I do, and whether I will know about those days in time. I am not claiming that the proposed road caused either condition. The road has not been built, and I do not want my comments recorded as evidence of a health effect that has already happened.

My child, Lio Creel, aged 11, has autism spectrum disorder. Changes to the usual walk and unexpected loud activity can be difficult for my child to manage. We can plan around a known closure or a particularly noisy operation much better than we can deal with a surprise at the end of the school day. That is why advance notices need to say what is happening, on which street, and for roughly how long. A general notice saying that works are taking place ‘in the vicinity’ is not much use to us. Please do not take this to mean that every child in Belwick would have the same difficulty; I am describing our household.

The air quality chapter discusses annual averages, but I could not find a plain explanation of what the figures mean during the weeks when soil is being moved and heavy vehicles are queuing. I have lived in this area for over 20 years, and the lane already feels different when several lorries arrive together. That is an observation, not a set of measurements. I would like the applicant to explain whether its construction assessment includes vehicles waiting with engines running at temporary signals, how often the haul route may change, and whether monitors will be placed where people actually walk rather than only at the edge of the works. If monitors are proposed, please say who will publish the readings and how quickly they will be available.

At the community display I spoke with Orla Seddon, who lives nearby but is not making a representation. We disagreed about whether the drawings showed a continuous footway through the temporary junction. This is not evidence about air quality, but it shows why the material needs to be readable without somebody from the project standing beside it. Cllr Toren Vale also asked at the public session how residents would hear about a changed construction route. I would welcome a written answer in the examination documents so that everyone gets the same information.

I am concerned about the combined effect of dust, traffic noise and uncertainty on our wellbeing. Some nights I sleep poorly after reading another update, although that feeling is not a diagnosis and I am not asking the Examining Authority to treat it as one. I would still like to know what practical steps are proposed: covered loads, wheel washing that is checked rather than merely promised, limits on idling, and a way to report a visible plume without having to decide first which contractor caused it. If there is a trigger level for changing working methods, the level and the action following it should be set out together.

There should also be a simple way to receive warnings. A message to a shared address such as greymere.enquiries@fenvaletransit.example would be useful if residents can choose email notices instead of relying on a board at the site gate. The scheme website could carry a dated notice, but I would not want online publication to be the only method for a sudden change. Please explain how households without regular internet access would be told about a closure or an unusually dusty activity. Notices should give a contact for the works team and say when somebody will respond, including outside office hours if work is permitted then.

I do not expect anyone to promise that there will be no disruption. I am asking the applicant to distinguish what it can predict from what it will check once works start. If a forecast proves wrong, residents need to know who can alter the arrangements and how that decision will be communicated. I would also be grateful if the response identified the relevant plan or requirement by its document reference, because I have struggled to follow changes between versions. A short table linking the commitment, the person responsible for carrying it out and the place where results will be published would help considerably.

Please read this as an addition to my earlier correspondence, particularly the request for a usable complaint procedure. My medical details are included only to explain why timely, specific information matters to us. My request is for the air quality assessment and the construction controls to be tested against what residents will experience on the ground, with clear answers before any final decision is made.

Yours faithfully,
Anwen Creel

Correspondence email: anwen.creel@belwickmail.example

Technical appendix: assessment assumptions and proposed controls

This appendix concerns the Greymere Bypass and Freight Link and the supporting material submitted by Fenvale Transit Infrastructure Ltd. It deals with the modelling and proposed controls rather than individual circumstances. The principal issue is whether the forecasts and the measures intended to secure them are expressed consistently across the Transport Assessment, the Environmental Statement and the draft requirements.

Traffic forecasts

The Transport Assessment presents an opening-year and a design-year comparison, but the description of the reference case does not make clear whether the proposed North Fen Distribution Yard is included as committed development. That distinction matters because its vehicle movements would use the same approach to Greymere Junction as the freight link. The Examining Authority should request a schedule of committed developments used in each model run, with the assumed trip generation, opening year and access route for each. A statement that such developments are “included where relevant” is not enough to reproduce the result.

The submitted junction tables show average weekday peak hours. They do not provide a comparable assessment of the Saturday late-morning period, when traffic to the Greymere retail area is highest. Nor is it clear whether the freight forecasts include empty running. These are modelling questions, not arguments for applying a general uplift to every flow. The applicant should provide turning movements for the relevant periods and explain which movements are forecast from observed counts, which are assigned from development assumptions and which are transferred from the strategic model.

For construction traffic, the Construction Traffic Management Plan should state a maximum number of heavy goods vehicle movements per day and per hour for each phase. A single scheme-wide maximum could conceal substantial differences between earthworks and surfacing. The plan should also distinguish vehicles entering the site from vehicles leaving it; otherwise the published figure can be read in two ways. Any commitment to avoid school arrival and departure periods needs defined clock times and an identified approval mechanism for exceptions.

Air quality and monitoring

The air quality chapter uses annual-average concentrations to assess operational effects. That is appropriate for the stated assessment method, but it does not by itself explain how short, intensive construction activities near the temporary haul-road access have informed the control measures. The location and duration of stockpiles, wheel-washing and unsealed running surfaces should be shown on the same phase drawings used for the dust-risk assessment. If these features are left to a later contractor plan, the requirement should specify the minimum controls and the authority that must approve any changes.

The proposed monitoring schedule refers to “representative locations”. It should identify the selection criteria: proximity to haul roads and junctions, prevailing wind, existing background concentrations and the ability to distinguish scheme effects from other sources. Results should be published at a stated interval, including periods when no exceedance is recorded. A register should record equipment downtime, calibration checks, complaints received through the project procedure and the response to any trigger level. A trigger without a specified action is not a control.

Drainage and water environment

The drainage drawings indicate attenuation beside the eastern cutting and an outfall to the Middle Rill. The Flood Risk Assessment describes storage for the design storm, but the drawing notes appear to use a different impermeable-area figure from the one in the calculations. This may be a drawing revision issue. It should nevertheless be reconciled before the requirement is discharged, because changes to the paved area affect both storage volume and the expected frequency of discharge. The calculation sheet, drawing revision and maintenance specification should carry a common reference.

The outfall detail should show the proposed erosion protection and the means of safely inspecting it after high flows. The drainage strategy should also say who maintains the interceptors and sediment traps during construction and after handover. Responsibility should not depend on an informal arrangement between contractors. A maintenance schedule, inspection frequency and reporting destination would make the commitment testable.

Landscape, ecology and phasing

The landscape assessment describes the year-one and year-fifteen views from Belwick Ridge, but the planting specification does not identify how failed planting will be replaced during the establishment period. The height and density assumed in the visualisations should be traceable to species, spacing and maintenance commitments in the Landscape and Ecology Management Plan. If the screening relies on growth beyond the secured establishment period, that dependency should be stated plainly.

The ecology chapter records badger activity in the wider Greymere area and bat use of the woodland corridor. Those broad descriptions do not identify a protected breeding or resting site. The request here is for a workable pre-construction survey procedure: the permitted survey window, who receives the results, how a change in findings affects the work programme, and the point at which clearance may begin. Sensitive survey records need not be included in a public monitoring table for those procedural commitments to be enforceable.

Requirements and verification

The draft Development Consent Order should link each mitigation commitment to a named plan and its revision. Where a plan is to be approved later, the requirement should specify the minimum contents and prevent the relevant works from beginning before approval. This is especially important for construction routes, dust controls, drainage maintenance and replacement planting. Greymere District Council should have a defined opportunity to review monitoring results, rather than merely receiving an annual summary after the opportunity to respond has passed.

A consolidated commitments table would resolve several avoidable ambiguities. For each item it could show the source assessment, the secured requirement, the party responsible for delivery, the monitoring frequency, the trigger for corrective action and the place where results will be published. This would allow the final decision to be checked against the assumptions on which the assessment rests.

Further health representation – Greymere Bypass and Freight Link
From: Anwen Creel

I am writing further to my comments on the commitments table. It is useful to know who will check the dust and traffic figures, but a table will not by itself make the air outside our homes any easier to breathe. Please consider this alongside my earlier representations, rather than as a new objection to the principle of the scheme.

I have been diagnosed with asthma and take a prescribed salbutamol inhaler. I also have chronic migraine, for which I take sumatriptan. I mention these details because the assessment tends to describe residents as if a short period of poor air quality would affect everybody in the same way. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide what causes any particular episode of illness. I am asking for the likely dust and exhaust exposure at the Belwick end of the route to be assessed properly, including during construction and when vehicles are queuing.

My child, Lio Creel, aged 11, has diagnosed autism. Changes to the usual walk to school can be difficult to manage, so a construction diversion with little notice is not just a minor inconvenience for our household. I appreciate that this does not mean works cannot take place. It does mean the proposed notice arrangements need to say how families will find out about a changed crossing or a dusty working period before it happens.

At the community display, Orla Seddon asked where complaints about dust would actually go. That seems a fair practical question. Cllr Toren Vale also asked whether monitoring information would be available while works were happening, not months afterwards. I felt anxious after reading the current proposals and have had poor sleep, but I do not suggest that those feelings are a medical diagnosis.

Could Fenvale Transit Infrastructure Ltd be required to publish the monitoring locations, the action levels and a simple route for reporting problems? The generic mailbox, consultations@fenvale-transit.example, could be used if somebody is responsible for checking it promptly. I would also welcome a clear explanation of what happens if a limit is exceeded on more than one day.

Turning to the technical evidence, the traffic forecasts for the Greymere Bypass and Freight Link should show the same construction peak in the air-quality and noise assessments. At present, the Environmental Statement appears to use a daily average for haul movements, while the junction assessment tests the busiest hour. That makes it difficult to see whether the predicted dust and noise levels at Belwick reflect the actual construction programme.

Fenvale Transit Infrastructure Ltd should provide a single table setting out vehicle numbers by phase, route and hour, including movements along Merebank Lane and Low Fen Road. The Construction Environmental Management Plan should then link those figures to monitoring frequency and the action levels mentioned above. If a haul route changes, the revised assessment ought to be available before that change starts, rather than recorded afterwards. Greymere District Council should also receive the monitoring returns during each phase so that exceedances can be checked against the traffic actually recorded.
