text:
DUNWICK FEN PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held on 15 October 2026 at 7.00 pm in the Council Room, Dunwick Fen Village Hall, Mere Lane, Dunwick Fen, DF3 7AA.

Present: Cllr Tessa Morland (Chair), Cllr Idris Pell, Cllr Lenna Quist, Cllr Arun Bellam and Cllr Neve Dall. Clerk: Oriel Dast. Members of the public: Faylin Odrick, Nessa Brindle and Dr Harlan Vest. Apologies were received from Cllr Sela Wint. These minutes are a record of the council's discussion, not a transcript of every remark.

1. Declarations and previous minutes
No interests were declared. The minutes of 17 September 2026 were agreed as a fair record and signed by the Chair. The clerk noted that the damaged noticeboard latch had finally been replaced. The contractor's invoice will come to the next meeting, as it had not arrived in time for this agenda.

2. Hallowmere East Solar Park Development Consent Order examination
The Chair explained that Fen Vale Renewables Ltd had submitted revised access drawings to the Planning Inspectorate. The council's Interested Party reference is IP-704218. Councillors had received copies of the drawings, although the large-scale sheet was not available in paper form until just before the meeting. It was agreed that comments should deal with the change to the construction route rather than repeat the council's earlier general objection to the scheme. The examination documents can be found via https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate, and the council's submission will be sent from clerk@dunwickfenparish.example.

Cllr Pell said the swept-path drawing appeared to assume that two lorries would never meet on the bend beside the village hall. Cllr Quist asked whether the temporary passing place was inside the land shown on the order plans. The clerk will put both questions to the applicant at the next open-floor hearing, if there is an opportunity, and otherwise send them in writing. Councillors did not want to suggest that the hall car park could be used as an informal waiting area. It is used for school drop-off and for the Thursday lunch club, and there is no agreement with the hall trustees for construction traffic to enter it.

During the public session, Faylin Odrick asked whether the proposed working hours included vehicle movements before 7 am. Nessa Brindle said traffic already made sleep difficult and described feeling anxious about a longer construction period. These comments were noted as concerns about the proposal; the council has not checked the applicant's traffic totals. Dr Harlan Vest said that dust near the footpath was a particular worry because of a diagnosis of asthma. The Chair advised that members of the public could also make their own submissions to the examination. No vote was taken on the personal accounts given during public session.

The council discussed ecology information sent separately by residents. A note referred generally to badgers in Marrow Copse; members agreed that this was too broad to identify a particular sett. A second sketch, however, marked a sett at the south end of drainage culvert D4, 18 metres east of Gate 3 on parcel 42. The clerk was asked to pass that sketch to the applicant's ecologist through the examination process, but not to reproduce its marked location in the council's public representation. Cllr Bellam also asked for confirmation that the replacement hedgerow would be planted before the temporary compound was removed, rather than left to an unspecified later phase.

It was RESOLVED unanimously that the Chair and clerk prepare a short response covering construction routing, the status of the passing place, working hours and the timing of hedgerow planting. A draft is to be circulated to councillors before the deadline. The council will use the adopted minutes as evidence of the points raised, but the response should distinguish councillors' observations from unverified reports made at the meeting. Cllr Morland asked that a plain-English copy be put on the noticeboard for residents without internet access.

3. Other planning business: 26/01482/FUL
The council considered the separate householder application by Mr Pelham Soot for a rear extension at 4 Reeve Close, Dunwick Fen, DF3 7QB. This is a district council application and is not part of the solar park examination. Members noted the neighbour consultation plan and the roof-height measurement. Cllr Dall proposed no objection, provided the district planning officer checked the relationship with the adjoining first-floor window. The motion was seconded by Cllr Pell and carried, four in favour and one abstention. The council did not discuss the applicant's circumstances. The clerk will enter the decision on the district portal under the council's name, without attaching these minutes.

4. Correspondence and parish matters
The Chair reported a reply from Maris Venn MP about drainage maintenance. It had been forwarded to the council's shared mailbox, planning@dunwickfenparish.example, and councillors agreed to await the drainage board's site visit before requesting another meeting. A member of the public mentioned photographs at https://fen-watch.example.org/photo-set; councillors had not reviewed the site and did not rely on it when reaching any decision. The clerk reminded members that requests for council records should go to the shared mailbox, not to a councillor's private account.

For the record, the clerk's correspondence address remains 17 Alderwick Fold, Dunwick Fen, DF3 7QJ while the village hall office is being refurbished. Urgent meeting-day calls may be made to 07700 900 326. The clerk's individual work email is oriel.dast@dunwickfenparish.example, but ordinary enquiries should still go to the shared mailbox so they are not missed during leave. The office arrangements will be reviewed in December; no change to the council's registered meeting place is proposed.

5. Next meeting
The next ordinary meeting will be on 19 November 2026 at 7.00 pm, subject to confirmation that the hall heating is working. The Chair thanked the public for attending and closed the meeting at 8.48 pm. Any correction to these draft minutes should be sent to the clerk before the next meeting.

Prepared by Oriel Dast, Clerk, Dunwick Fen Parish Council.

text:
RELEVANT REPRESENTATION
Merebrook Link Road Development Consent Order

From: Nadia Fenwick
Interested Party reference: MBLR-IPA-00481
Address: 14 Copper Mere Lane, Larchmere, LM4 7QF
Email: nadia.fenwick@example.net

I support the Merebrook Link Road and would like to be registered as an interested party. I live in Larchmere, close enough to the present road through the village to hear traffic from the front bedroom. I have lived in the village for over 40 years. During that time the amount and type of traffic using the street has changed, but the street itself has not got any wider. It still has houses with doors close to the pavement and a crossing which people use to get to the village shop. The scheme is not perfect, but I believe it would make day-to-day life here better.

I agree in particular with the published representations from Tamsin Vell and Orin Dace. Both are interested parties in this examination, and both make the point that a link road should take through-traffic out of the centre rather than simply moving a queue from one end of the village to the other. I also agree with their request for the applicant, Merebrook Corridor Partnership, to explain clearly how the junctions will work when the road first opens, not only at the end of a forecast period. It is sometimes difficult for a resident to connect the figures in a traffic table with what happens outside their own window. Their comments put that practical question plainly.

At present, vehicles braking and accelerating outside my house can wake me up, particularly when a line of traffic forms early in the morning. Once awake I find it hard to get back to sleep. I feel tired and cross the next day, and the uncertainty about whether it will be a quiet night affects my wellbeing. I am not saying that every vehicle causes a problem or that the road will remove all noise. I am saying that a proper alternative for traffic which has no reason to stop in Larchmere would give the village a chance of being quieter. It would also make walking along the main street more pleasant. On some evenings I wait for a gap before crossing even though the shop is just on the other side.

I know that other residents are worried about construction and about the landscape where the new road would run. Those concerns should be answered, not brushed aside because the eventual result may be beneficial. I would ask for working hours to be stated in a way that residents can understand, with a clear route for reporting problems and a requirement to put them right. Dust controls matter as well as noise controls. A commitment in a document is only useful if somebody checks what is happening on the ground. The applicant should publish a simple timetable before each main phase, including any nights when work cannot be avoided, so people are not left guessing.

The plans also need to make sense for people who do not drive. The proposed paths near Hollowgate Field ought to join up with existing village routes without making someone walk a long way round to find a safe crossing. I have seen people with pushchairs turn back at the present junction because they could not judge the traffic. A quieter main street will help, but it should not be the only walking benefit claimed for the scheme. I would like the Examining Authority to check that the crossings, lighting and maintenance arrangements are secured in the final requirements, rather than left as an intention on an illustrative plan.

I support the approach to planting shown in the application, provided the new hedges are looked after long enough to establish. There have been general reports of badgers in Brindle Wood and bats around the village. I mention those as reasons to take the ecology measures seriously, not as a claim about any particular nest or roost. The same applies to drainage. The applicant should show how water from the road will be managed during heavy rain and who will maintain the drains later. Support for a scheme does not mean accepting an avoidable problem for someone else.

Cllr Hester Quill said at a public meeting that the village needs a usable route during the works as well as a better one afterwards. I thought that was a fair way of putting it. I have also spoken informally with my neighbour, Mr Pellan Rusk, who is not making a representation. Our conversations reminded me that advance notice needs to reach people who do not check a project website every week. Notices at the shop and clear signs at affected paths would help, alongside online updates. The project mailbox, merebrooklink@merebrookcorridor.example, is useful, but it should not be the only way to find out about a sudden closure.

For these reasons I ask the Examining Authority to recommend consent, subject to enforceable arrangements for construction traffic, noise, safe walking routes, drainage and aftercare of planting. Please do not read my support as a request to relax those arrangements. A well-managed link road could take the worst of the through-traffic away from homes while keeping Larchmere connected to the places its residents use. That is the outcome I hope the examination can secure.

Nadia Fenwick

Supplementary technical points on the Merebrook Link Road

I add the following points to explain what I mean by enforceable arrangements. They concern the material that the Merebrook Corridor Partnership has submitted, rather than the principle of providing a link road. I support the aim of removing through-traffic from Larchmere, but the predicted benefit depends on how the junctions, construction accesses and drainage are actually delivered. These matters should be settled in the requirements, not left as aspirations in a management plan.

Traffic modelling

The Transport Assessment reports an overall reduction in traffic through the centre of Larchmere. The headline figure is encouraging, but it combines ordinary weekdays with periods when queues form at the East Weir Roundabout. The examination would benefit from a separate table showing turning movements and queue lengths for each junction in the weekday morning and afternoon peaks, both with and without the scheme. In particular, the model should show whether traffic diverts onto Merebank Lane when the new road meets Fenward Road. A network-wide benefit would not answer a local problem if the side-road junction then becomes difficult to cross.

The assessment should also explain how the 2025 counts were adjusted for seasonal use of the Barrowmere Works site. The counts and the forecast are not the same thing, and the difference ought to be visible. I am not asking for another general traffic survey if the existing data are adequate. I am asking for a clear audit trail from observed flows to the figures used for the design year, including the assumptions about committed development. The most useful output would be a short comparison table, not another set of coloured network plots without the numbers behind them.

Walking and cycling

Drawing MB-LR-TR-017 shows a shared path beside part of the link road, but the route appears to stop short of the Fenward Road crossing. The final connection matters more than the length shown in the middle of the drawing. Please require a continuous, surfaced route between the Larchmere Greenway and the existing path at Weirfield Common, with the crossing arrangement approved before that section of road opens. A note saying that details will be agreed later is not sufficient if the space needed for the crossing has already been fixed by earthworks and drainage.

The proposed underpass near Chainage 2+400 is shown without much information about gradients, lighting or visibility through it. Its usability after dark and in wet weather should be checked against a section drawing, rather than inferred from the plan view. During construction, any temporary diversion should be signed from both ends of the affected route and kept separate from plant movements. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should state who checks the signs and how quickly missing signs are replaced. This is a practical issue: a diversion is only useful if it can be followed from the point where the usual path closes.

Drainage and water

The Flood Risk Assessment identifies attenuation near Lower Mere Field. It would help to see a single schedule matching each outfall to its contributing paved area, discharge limit, maintenance access and proposed adopting body. At present those details sit in different drawings and chapters, making it difficult to check whether the swales shown on the landscape plans are the same features relied on in the hydraulic calculations. The final drainage design should retain the stated discharge limits and should not substitute underground storage for the visible swales without a recorded explanation of the consequences for maintenance and landscape design.

There should also be a hold point before works begin at the Brindle Beck crossing. The contractor should submit the temporary drainage and sediment-control layout for that phase, including where clean runoff is diverted and how heavily silted water will be contained. A general commitment to good practice is welcome but cannot show whether the measures fit within the land available beside the crossing. The requirement should make clear that the temporary layout must be in place before excavation starts, not merely included in a document submitted around the same time.

Landscape and construction phasing

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment treats the proposed planting as established in the later-year views. That is a reasonable way to illustrate the intended result, provided the consent secures the work needed to get there. The planting schedule should specify replacement of failed trees and shrubs over a defined establishment period, with annual records of losses and replacements. It should also identify who maintains the planting where it crosses the boundary between highway land and the attenuation area. Otherwise a gap in responsibility could become a gap in the screen.

Construction compounds should be shown on a phasing plan with their anticipated periods of use and the routes serving them. The draft plan marks a broad area near Barrowmere Works but does not distinguish storage, parking and soil stockpiles. Those uses have different effects on drainage and on views from Weirfield Common. I would like the final plan to identify a maximum stockpile height and show how the compounds will be restored before the last section of road is brought into use. Restoration should not wait indefinitely for completion of unrelated finishing works elsewhere on the scheme.

Requested outcome

These points could be addressed through amended drawings, a short modelling note and carefully worded requirements. They do not require a different route. I ask the Examining Authority to test whether each promised measure has an approval stage, a delivery trigger and a means of checking it afterwards. If those links are made clear, the Merebrook Link Road is more likely to deliver the traffic relief described in the application without leaving avoidable problems at its edges.

Further comments on why I support the road

I want to be clear, following my comments about the construction compounds, that I support the Merebrook Link Road. My concerns about stockpiles and restoration are requests to get the details right, not objections to the route. I have lived in Larchmere for over 40 years, and the amount of traffic passing through the village has changed a great deal in that time. The road through the centre is still treated as a through route, even though people have to cross it to reach the shop, the hall and the paths towards Weirfield Common.

I agree in particular with the published representations from Tamsin Vell and Orin Dace. Tamsin Vell's point about the village needing a useful road, rather than just a road that looks satisfactory on a traffic diagram, is well made. Orin Dace also asks what will actually happen to the existing route once the link opens. Those are not reasons to hold up the scheme indefinitely. They are reasons to make sure that the benefits described in the application are secured and can be checked afterwards. I understand that both have made their own representations in this examination; I am not trying to speak for either of them.

Most days I can hear vehicles building up speed before they reach the bend into the village. At night it is not a continuous noise. It is one lorry, then a gap, then another, which makes it harder to settle back to sleep. I sometimes lie awake listening for the next one and feel tired the following morning. That affects my wellbeing, but I am not claiming that a new road will make Larchmere silent. Farming vehicles, deliveries and ordinary journeys will still use the village road. What I hope for is fewer of the vehicles that have no reason to come into the village at all.

I know some people worry that a link road simply moves noise from one set of homes to another. That concern deserves a proper answer. The drawings and noise information should be understandable to residents beside the new alignment as well as those of us on the old route. Where the applicant has allowed for a bund, planting or a particular road surface, the final documents ought to say when it will be provided and what happens if it does not perform as expected. It would be no comfort to somebody near the new road to be told that traffic has improved in Larchmere. Equally, uncertainty about those details should not obscure the problems on the existing road.

My neighbour, Pellan Rusk, is not taking part in this examination. We have talked generally about the difficulty of crossing the road when vehicles arrive in groups. I mention the conversation only to explain why I do not think the issue can be reduced to an average daily traffic figure. A person waiting at the kerb experiences the gaps between vehicles, the speed at which they approach and whether it is possible to tell what is coming round the bend. The assessment should therefore consider what the village road will feel like to use after opening, not only how many vehicles are predicted to leave it.

I support a clear plan for the old route alongside the new road. That need not mean closing it or making access awkward for residents and businesses. It could mean appropriate speed management, safer places to cross and signs that direct through traffic onto the link. The order of works matters: if these measures are left until long after the link opens, drivers may simply carry on using the road they know. There should also be a sensible way of reviewing the traffic figures after opening, with an explanation of what action could follow if the forecast relief does not occur.

Cllr Hester Quill has spoken about the need for the village to remain accessible during construction. I agree. A route on a drawing is not much help if the temporary diversions send unfamiliar traffic past the hall without clear signs, or if a crossing is shut with little notice. Information about changes should be put where people will see it, not only in a technical document. A shared project mailbox, such as questions@merebrooklink.example, would be useful if someone is responsible for reading it and replying while the works are under way. That is a practical request, not a suggestion that every short-term inconvenience can be avoided.

I also ask the Merebrook Corridor Partnership to keep the description of likely benefits modest and precise. The link may take through traffic out of the centre; it will not remove every delivery van or solve every parking problem. Claims about quieter nights should say which roads and periods they refer to. This would make it easier for residents to judge the scheme fairly and for the Examining Authority to decide whether the proposed requirements match what is being promised.

In conclusion, I remain in favour of consent for the Merebrook Link Road, subject to the safeguards and clarifications I have raised. I would rather see a workable scheme with its construction effects controlled and its village benefits followed through than lose the opportunity for relief because some of the present wording is too vague. Please treat this as support for the scheme, while asking the applicant to make those commitments firm enough to mean something after the examination has ended.

Nadia Fenwick

Supplementary note to my relevant representation — Merebrook Link Road

I am adding this note because my support for the scheme may have sounded more qualified than I intended. I support the Merebrook Link Road. The qualifications matter, but they are requests to make a useful scheme work properly, not reasons to refuse it.

I have lived in Larchmere for over 40 years. Traffic was never absent, but there are now evenings when I wait for a gap before opening the front window. Heavy vehicles make a different sort of noise from cars: you hear one approaching, then the rattle as it passes, and sometimes another follows before the road has gone quiet. If that happens after I have gone to bed, I often lie awake listening for the next one. On some mornings I feel worn out before the day has started. It affects my sleep and wellbeing, which is why the promise of taking through traffic out of the village means something practical to me.

I agree with the published representations from Tamsin Vell and Orin Dace. Tamsin Vell is right to ask how the predicted reduction in village traffic will be checked once the road opens. Orin Dace makes a fair point about drivers still being able to choose the old route. Both comments are consistent with supporting the scheme. If the Merebrook Corridor Partnership expects a substantial change, residents ought to be able to see the counts before and after opening, including evening and night-time figures, rather than only a single daily total.

I also listened to Cllr Hester Quill at the parish meeting. The point about keeping access to local shops during construction was well made. A diversion sign on its own will not tell a visitor whether a shop can still be reached, and it would be a shame if the works damaged the very village the road is meant to help. I ask for clear advance notices, updated when arrangements change, and a way for residents and businesses to report a problem that is actually monitored. A generic contact such as enquiries@merebrooklink.example would be more useful if the applicant also published when people should expect a reply.

Pellan Rusk, a neighbour who has not made a representation, described being woken when a vehicle stopped with its engine running near our houses. I mention this only to explain why averages cannot tell the whole story. One short but loud event can interrupt a night even if the figures for that hour look acceptable. I would like the applicant to explain how its noise assessment accounts for that sort of event, and what residents can do if the position after opening is different from what was forecast.

I appreciate that construction itself will be noisy. That is not an argument for pretending there will be no disturbance. It is an argument for saying plainly which operations might take place at night, how many nights are expected and what notice nearby households will receive. Phrases such as ‘where practicable’ leave too much room for misunderstanding unless someone has to record why an exception was needed.

For clarity, this supplementary note does not change my conclusion. I favour consent, provided the traffic monitoring, construction communication and night-time noise commitments are secured in a form that can be checked. People in Larchmere have waited a long time for through traffic to have another route. I hope the examination can improve the details without losing that opportunity.

Nadia Fenwick

Further comment on the relevant representation

I have lived in Larchmere for 40+ years and still support the Merebrook Link Road. I agree with the published representations of Tamsin Vell and Orin Dace, especially their request for proper monitoring at the village end, rather than relying only on modelled traffic figures. Cllr Hester Quill also raised the difficulty of getting across the main road at school finishing time; that is exactly what I see.

At present the lorries wake me some mornings and, when there is a late run of them, I find it hard to get back to sleep. It leaves me tired and worried about the next night, but I am not saying construction must be silent. My neighbour Mrs Pellan Rusk mentioned the same early noise to me, although she is not making a representation. Please keep the promised night-work notices in plain language and tell us whom to contact if the agreed hours slip.

Nadia Fenwick

text:
A. Vale
Vale & Lantern Heating
14 Mallow Croft, Ellowmere, LM4 8TW
Telephone: 01632 960418
Email: arden.vale@valelantern.example

21 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Ellowmere Freight Link Development Consent Order
Interested Party reference: IP-048219

Dear Examining Authority,

I am a self-employed heating engineer trading as Vale & Lantern Heating. I work from my home in Ellowmere, and I object to the construction traffic arrangements put forward by Fenspan Link Ltd. I am not objecting to every part of the freight link. My concern is the proposal to send heavy vehicles along Mallow Lane and past the small row of houses where I keep my van and tools. The traffic management plan calls this a suitable local route, but it reads as though nobody has tried to load a van there at half past seven in the morning.

My work takes me to customers across the district. On a normal day I leave with cylinders, fittings and sometimes a replacement boiler, and may return between jobs for a part. The van is not an optional extra: without it I cannot do the work. The entrance to Mallow Croft is narrow, and a vehicle coming downhill on Mallow Lane can be at the turning before a driver has a clear view. If construction lorries are arriving in groups, waiting to get out will be difficult. If they queue across the turning, it will be impossible. My van registration is LM26 VDX, in case the applicant needs to distinguish it in the photographs I have submitted.

The drawings show a swept path for a single articulated lorry. They do not show that lorry meeting a delivery van, a bin wagon or another lorry at the bend by the old pump house. There is no pavement for part of that stretch. Drivers currently slow or stop to let people through; that informal arrangement will not work with the number of HGV movements proposed. I ask that the applicant supply a drawing showing two-way movements and explain where a vehicle would wait without blocking a driveway. A statement that drivers will be told to take care is not enough.

I have lived and worked in Ellowmere for more than 20 years. This is not a claim that nothing should change. I have had roadworks outside my gate before and managed. What worries me here is the combination of early starts, a long construction period and no reliable way for residents or small businesses to find out what is coming on a particular day. I already sleep badly when I know a large delivery is due, because I have to allow time to get the van out. That is an effect of uncertainty, not an objection to workers doing their jobs.

At the consultation event, I asked whether the first vehicles could be held at the compound until after the school run. The answer I remember was that deliveries would be scheduled 'where practicable'. Please say what that means. Is the proposed 07:00 start a firm restriction on movements along Mallow Lane, or just the opening time at the compound? A lorry travelling to the compound before seven is still a lorry on our road. I would support a restriction on HGV movements past Mallow Croft between 07:45 and 09:00, with an exception only for an emergency agreed in advance with the highway authority.

My daughter, Mila Vale, is 9 years old and walks to the school bus stop with me. My daughter's asthma means I am particularly concerned about engines idling near the turning, although I understand that the air-quality chapter considers the wider area. I am asking for an enforceable no-idling rule at the holding point, not making a claim that every passing vehicle will cause harm. The bus stop should also be shown on the construction route plan. At present it is marked only as part of a general footway line, which misses where people actually wait.

Mrs Nella Firth, who lives further along the lane and is not making a representation, asked me whether access for the weekly care visit would be maintained. I cannot answer that from the submitted plan. Please do not treat my mentioning this as permission to contact the neighbour; it is an example of the uncertainty for people who depend on a vehicle reaching the door. Cllr Sera Menwick also asked at the public meeting how residents would report a blocked access. I could not find a response in the event notes.

I have seen the applicant's project updates at https://fenspan.example/ellowmere and the contact address planning@fenspan.example. A generic inbox is useful, but it is not a traffic controller. The draft construction traffic management plan should give residents one telephone number answered during delivery hours, a maximum response time, and a procedure for stopping arrivals if the bend is blocked. It should also require advance notice of unusually large loads. Please specify how complaints will be logged and reported to the highway authority, rather than leaving the detail to be agreed after consent.

I was told that badger signs had been seen in Ellowmere Copse. I am not trying to identify a sett, and I appreciate that the ecology documents deal with that separately. My point is that moving a queue from Mallow Lane to the copse entrance would create a different problem. The applicant should show the proposed holding area clearly before deciding that vehicles can simply wait off the residential stretch. The compound postcode, LM4 9NN, is not a substitute for a drawing of its entrance and available space.

Finally, delay has a real cost for a sole trader. My personal take-home income last year was £21,400, and missing even one booked visit can mean rearranging several customers. I am not asking the Examining Authority to calculate compensation from that figure. I am asking for a workable route and hours that let me leave home to earn a living. Please require Fenspan Link Ltd to revise the traffic management plan before the examination closes, or impose a requirement preventing HGV use of Mallow Lane until the junction and access arrangements have been checked on site.

Yours sincerely,

Arden Vale | proprietor, Vale & Lantern Heating

Enclosure to my letter: examples from the morning peak
Ellowmere Freight Link examination — construction traffic on Mallow Lane

I have put this on a separate sheet because the traffic plan speaks about vehicle movements in a day, whereas my problem is getting a work van out of one gate at a particular time. Vale & Lantern Heating is run from my home at 17 Mallow Lane, Ellowmere, LM4 8QJ. That is a residential address, not a depot, although my tools and the van have to leave from there. The drawings show the compound by its postcode, LM4 9NN, but they do not show what happens to a queue when the gate is shut.

On 14 October 2026 I left for a boiler appointment just after 7.30 am. A delivery lorry serving the existing works was waiting opposite my drive. There was room for a car to squeeze past but not for me to swing the van out without mounting the footway. I waited rather than do that. This was one lorry, not the proposed sequence of HGVs. I have worked in this area for 40+ years and know that the lane's usable width changes with parked cars and bins. The swept-path drawing appears to assume that nobody else is there.

My van registration is LM26 VHL. I give it only so the case team can recognise the vehicle in the photographs I have sent separately, not because I want it published. At 7.45 I am often carrying a gas test kit and parts that cannot sensibly be transferred to a bicycle. Saying that tradespeople could use another mode is not an answer to the access problem. I do not need an exemption from traffic rules; I need a plan that works when somebody actually lives along the route.

There is a school walk along the same pavement. My daughter, Mila Vale, is 9 and leaves by that gate most weekdays. Mila has asthma, and diesel fumes close to the waiting vehicles make the walk difficult. I mention this because the proposed marshal position is directly beside the pedestrian pinch point, not to suggest that every passing lorry will cause an emergency. It would help to put the waiting area inside the compound and keep the pavement clear. I feel anxious about the morning crossing, but that is a description of how I feel, not a medical diagnosis.

Ms Nella Firth, who lives further along Mallow Lane and is not taking part in this examination, told me that a lorry had reversed as far as the bend last week. I cannot verify its operator and I have not put that down as a breach by Fenspan Link Ltd. It is a reason to check the visibility before approving a route, rather than just relying on the route plan. At the public meeting Cllr Sera Menwick asked whether the driver instructions would include a prohibition on reversing along the residential stretch. The answer recorded in my notes was that this would be dealt with later. Later is too late if it is left outside an enforceable construction traffic management plan.

For completeness, my Interested Party reference is IP-594213. I sent the case team an email from arden.vale@valelantern.example on 15 October 2026. The reply can go to that address, but I ask that the personal part of it is removed from any public copy. The project mailbox, ellowmerefreightlink@planning-inspectorate.gov.uk, is fine to publish. My direct number is 07700 900472; please use that only if a photograph will not open. There is no need for the number to appear on the examination website.

I looked at the ecology sheet because an alternative holding place has been suggested near Alder Stitch Wood. The sheet records badgers in Alder Stitch Wood, which is a broad area and does not tell drivers where to go. I have seen a sett entrance under the eastern bank of the drainage ditch 14 metres south of gate G3 at plot 17B. Please do not put that description in a public traffic drawing. It needs checking by the ecologist before anyone marks out a holding bay. I am not asking for a bay in the wood; the point is that shifting the queue away from houses without checking the proposed spot could create another problem.

The land plan labels Wren Fold as a building and plot 17B as part of the works area. I have used those labels because they let the applicant find the place on its own drawings. They are not anyone's contact details. Likewise, the address shown for the site office, Unit 6, Copper Quay Trade Park, Ellowmere, LM4 9NN, is a workplace address, not my house. Those distinctions matter when the documents are put online. My own address above should not be copied into a public response just because it is also where I keep the business records.

I would accept a condition requiring a site visit with a van and an HGV present, at the actual morning hour, before Mallow Lane is used for construction deliveries. The visit should record whether a vehicle can wait fully within the compound, whether the footway remains passable and who has authority to stop a delivery at the previous junction. It should also say who residents contact when the gate is blocked. A generic promise to monitor traffic does not give me a number to ring at 7.30 on a working morning. My photographs are numbered 1 to 4, with the date and direction written on the back; I can provide the originals if the Examining Authority needs them. Please treat this enclosure as part of my objection, not as a request to withdraw the points in my letter.

Technical enclosure — access, drainage and phasing

The construction traffic assessment for the Ellowmere Freight Link uses an hourly average at the Mallow Lane junction. That is not enough to test the gate arrangement. Fenspan Link Ltd should provide a peak fifteen-minute arrival profile, including vehicles turned away from the compound, and show the queue length on the submitted access drawing. The drawing should also identify the swept path for an HGV entering while another vehicle is waiting to leave; the two movements should not be assumed to occur separately.

The drainage drawings appear to place the temporary haul-road outfall upstream of the permanent attenuation basin. Please confirm where runoff goes during the first construction phase, before that basin is operational, and give the design rainfall event used for the temporary works. A phasing condition could require both the gate layout and temporary drainage to be approved before deliveries start. Without those details, the assessment does not demonstrate that the proposed construction sequence will work.

text:
Relevant representation – Brambleford Vale Solar and Storage Project
Application reference: EN009876
From: Nora Bellamy
Address for correspondence: 14 Cinder Lane, Eldermere, EL7 4QX
Email: nora.bellamy@example.net
Telephone: 07700 900 381
Interested Party reference: 20049816

I object to the proposed development. I am not against renewable energy, but this is the wrong place for a scheme of this size, particularly with the battery compound so close to houses. I have lived in Eldermere for more than 30 years and use the paths across the valley most weeks. The land looks very different on a plan from how it feels when you walk through it. It is open, quiet countryside at present, not spare land waiting to be filled up.

The documents describe the view from Cinder Lane as partly screened. That is not my experience in winter, when the hedges are thin and you can see straight across the fields. Field 7 rises towards the lane. Panels, fencing, cameras and the access track would be visible together, not as separate small features. The applicant’s photomontage in APP-014 seems to have been taken from further down the road than the point outside our houses. Please could the Examining Authority ask for a winter view from the bend by the old water trough? That is where people actually stop to look across the valley.

Noise is my other main concern. The battery units and inverters may meet a calculated limit and still be unpleasant at night. The existing background sound is mostly wind and the occasional vehicle. My neighbour, Mrs Tessa Harrow, lives at 16 Cinder Lane, Eldermere, EL7 4QX, immediately beside the proposed access. Mrs Tessa Harrow is not making a representation, as far as I know. I mention the house because the traffic drawings show vehicles passing its front window, but the noise assessment calls it a ‘farm access’. It is a home. Another neighbour, Mr Ivo Pellen, asked at the drop-in whether reversing alarms would be used during construction. The answer given was that this would be settled with the contractor. That is not reassuring when deliveries could begin early in the morning.

I have type 2 diabetes and poor sleep makes managing it more difficult. My 11-year-old daughter, Lila Bellamy, has been diagnosed with asthma. Dust from the haul route concerns me, particularly if the road is dry for several weeks. I am not saying that the project caused these conditions; I am asking for proper controls before work starts, rather than a promise to decide them later. My mother, Mrs Esme Bellamy, has rheumatoid arthritis and sometimes stays with us. Walking the level part of Footpath 12 is one of the few outings we can comfortably do together. The suggested diversion would take us along a narrow road without a pavement. I am 47 and I find that road uncomfortable to walk on myself, especially when a large vehicle is coming the other way.

The traffic chapter says that construction vehicles will avoid school arrival times. It does not say what happens when a delivery is delayed or when two lorries meet at the Cinder Lane bridge. There is no passing place on that stretch. Last month I waited behind a tractor while a van reversed almost to the junction. This is ordinary farm traffic, not a line of construction lorries. I would like a binding route, hours and a person residents can contact when something goes wrong. A general complaints procedure is not enough if a vehicle is blocking the road there and then.

I also disagree with the suggestion that the public paths will remain available in any meaningful sense. A path between high security fences is not the same walk across open fields. The drawings mark a new planting strip, but that planting will take years to establish and may not survive dry summers. Please do not count future screening as though it exists on the first day of operation. Cllr Orla Fenwick raised a similar point at the parish discussion in September. Jonah Crewe has also made a representation about the loss of the valley view, which I support.

There is wildlife here beyond the list in the non-technical summary. I have seen badger paths in Brackenfold Wood, although I cannot say where the animals live from those signs alone. During a walk with the surveyor I pointed out a badger sett in the west bank of the drainage ditch, 18 metres north of the stile on Footpath 12 beside Field 7. I give that detail so it can be checked and protected, not put on a public map. Bats also feed over the hedge line in summer. I am not claiming to know their roost. It would help to see a clear explanation of how the fencing, lighting and vegetation removal have been considered together rather than in separate chapters.

At the consultation event, Pavel Dorr of Larkmere Renewables Ltd said residents could send questions to pavel.dorr@larkmererenewables.example. I sent a question about the access width but have not had a substantive answer. The project mailbox, planning@larkmererenewables.example, sent an acknowledgement. The project website, https://bramblefordvale.example/project, still shows the same general access diagram. I kept a short account of what was said at the event at https://vale-notes.example/noise-log, in case it helps explain why I am asking again.

I am worried about what a prolonged construction period would mean for daily life. I also have an outstanding mortgage of £83,400, so moving away is not a simple answer to these concerns. That is not a request for compensation. It is a request that the impacts on existing households be assessed honestly. Please refuse consent in the present form, or at minimum require a different access, enforceable noise and dust limits, and a path diversion that is safe for people walking rather than just a line on a drawing.

Nora Bellamy

Further comments to my relevant representation
Brambleford Vale Solar and Storage Project

I am adding this note because I realised, after sending my representation, that I had not explained how the proposed access would work in practice for our lane. I remain opposed to consent in the present form. I am not against solar power; I am against treating the lanes between Eldermere and Brambleford as if they are spare construction roads. This is a residential and walking route, and the access diagram does not show the occasions when two vehicles cannot pass without one reversing.

The applicant's drawing marks a passing place beside the entrance to Mill Orchard. On the ground that space is where people step off the lane when a tractor comes through. It is also where the school walking group waits before crossing. My daughter, Lila Bellamy, uses that route. She is 11, and I do not think the assessment should assume children will always have an adult beside them. There is no pavement from that point to the village noticeboard. A condition saying drivers must take care does not make a safe walking route.

Mrs Tessa Harrow lives at 14 Orchard Fold, Eldermere, EL4 7QP, immediately opposite the bend shown as Access Point C. Mrs Harrow is not making a representation, as far as I know, and I mention her only because her front gate opens almost onto the carriageway. During the survey visit she asked whether the gate had been included in the swept-path drawing. The answer she got was about the width of the highway, which isn't the same question. Mr Ivo Pellen, at 6 Orchard Fold, Eldermere, EL4 7QP, has the same difficulty getting out when a delivery van stops at the bend. Neither neighbour has asked me to speak for them. I am describing what I have seen from the lane.

The construction traffic estimate appears to be an average. It would help residents to have the busiest day and busiest hour shown plainly, including movements to the battery compound. If deliveries are spread over a longer period to reduce the peak, that also has an impact: months more of reversing alarms, dust on windows and uncertainty about when it is safe to walk. I have lived here for 40+ years and know that the lane looks wider on a plan than it feels beside a moving lorry. My health is affected by poor sleep when there is sustained noise, but I understand that is not itself a technical noise measurement.

I should have made the health point more clearly in the first part. I have been diagnosed with asthma, and dust from repeated heavy vehicle movements is a particular concern for me. My mother, Mrs Esme Bellamy, stays with us on some weekdays. She has rheumatoid arthritis and walks slowly, so a suggested diversion involving a steep stile would not be usable for her. Lila has no safe alternative route to the stop if the existing path is closed at the same time as the lane is busy. These are ordinary household circumstances, not reasons to disregard the needs of everyone else using the route. I ask for the diversion to be walked by the examining team, rather than assessed only from its length on a map.

At the applicant's drop-in, Pavel Dorr of Larkmere Renewables Ltd said that details of the crossing could be dealt with later. I accept that some details do come later, but the position of a safe crossing is central to whether this access is acceptable. The leaflet gave a contact email of consultation@larkmererenewables.example, which is useful for questions, but an answer by email will not bind a future contractor. I would like a requirement setting out where walkers go before the first vehicle uses Access Point C, with no gap between the closure of the old path and opening of the new one.

I agree with Jonah Crewe's published representation about the need to check the turning assumptions on site. Cllr Orla Fenwick also asked at the public session for a drawing that showed the road edge and the gates, not just the carriageway centreline. Those seem reasonable requests. I am concerned that the applicant calls the change minor because it is a short stretch of road, when for those of us on foot it is the most difficult stretch of the whole journey.

There is an ecology point as well. Badger signs have been recorded in Hawthorn Spinney and I am not asking for the public plans to mark every animal location. However, the survey sheet left on the table at the event marked an active badger sett beneath the eastern bank of drainage ditch D4, 23 metres south of field gate FG-19. That level of detail should not be in an unrestricted document. I raise it here so the team can check whether the survey material needs a confidential version, and so that fencing and ground works near the ditch receive proper scrutiny. My objection does not depend on publishing the sett's position.

For correspondence about this addendum, my address is 28 Willow Rise, Eldermere, EL4 7QJ and my email is nora.bellamy@posthaven.example. Please do not put either on a public copy. My Interested Party reference is IP-78426; I include it to help match this note to what I sent earlier. The project page at https://bramblefordvale.example/project still has the general diagram, but I could not find a revised pedestrian plan there when I checked on 19 October 2026.

I would be grateful if the Examining Authority could ask for a properly dimensioned access and walking-route plan, a construction traffic profile showing peak days, and a clear explanation of who checks compliance if the route becomes unsafe. Until those matters are resolved I ask that consent be refused. If changes are proposed, residents need a chance to see and comment on the actual drawings, not simply be told that the problem can be managed later.

Nora Bellamy

Further comments to my relevant representation — Brambleford Vale Solar and Storage Project

I am adding this note because, after signing the previous page, I realised that I had described the walking route mainly as a line on the applicant's drawing. It is also the way people get to the bus stop and the small playing field. My objection is not to solar power in principle. It is to placing construction traffic and temporary fencing so close to a route used every day, without showing how anyone will pass safely when a delivery is turning.

I live at 14 Thistle Row, Eldermere, EM4 8QT. This is my home, not a site address. From our front window the proposed construction entrance is visible across the lane. I have lived in Eldermere for 40+ years, but I have not seen the lane carry vehicles of the size illustrated in the construction statement. The drawings show a passing place but not what happens when a person with a pushchair is already between that place and the bend. Saying that drivers will be briefed does not answer it.

My daughter, Lila Bellamy, aged 11, uses the lane after school. Lila has asthma and carries a reliever inhaler. I am not suggesting that the project caused that condition; I am explaining why dust control and a usable walking route matter particularly to our household. My mother, Mrs Esme Bellamy, lives with us and has rheumatoid arthritis. Mrs Esme Bellamy cannot simply step onto the uneven verge to let a lorry pass. Please do not publish the medical details as part of an unredacted public version of this letter. I have diagnosed chronic migraine myself and take sumatriptan when an attack starts. Poor sleep and worry about the scheme are separate matters, but the likelihood of an early start outside our windows makes those worries worse.

Two neighbours have spoken to me but are not making representations. Mrs Tessa Harrow at 16 Thistle Row, Eldermere, EM4 8QU says the existing hedge makes the corner difficult to see round. Mr Ivo Pellen, whose home is 3 Cartwheel Cottages, Eldermere, EM4 7JP, has also noticed vans mounting the verge. These are ordinary observations, not a traffic count, and I would rather the applicant tested the corner properly than rely on my account of conversations. Neither neighbour has agreed to have contact details put online. By contrast, Jonah Crewe has submitted a representation to this examination about the same bend, and the photograph attached to that representation shows why a swept-path line by itself is not enough.

At the community drop-in, Pavel Dorr of Larkmere Renewables Ltd showed me a diagram with an access gate further east than the one on the current drawing. I asked whether it was a replacement plan or just an option. The reply was that a revised plan might follow. My notes are not a record agreed with the applicant, so I ask the Examining Authority to obtain the actual plan rather than treat my recollection as evidence of a change. An email later arrived from pavel.dorr@larkmererenewables.example, but its attachment was the same general diagram already on the project page. A project mailbox such as consultation@larkmererenewables.example would be a better way to circulate any new drawing to everyone.

There is also an ecological point which may need handling outside the public document library. I saw signs of badgers in Alderwash Wood, a broad area that the ecology chapter already discusses. More specifically, a badger sett entrance is beneath the fallen ash immediately west of the second stile on Footpath 6, at grid reference EM 43127 68294. I have not disturbed it. That location should be passed to the relevant ecologist without publishing a pinpoint that could put the sett at risk. I have seen bats along the lane as well, but I do not know where they roost and would not claim otherwise. My objection on this point is that the lighting plan still gives no clear hours for the gate lights or an explanation of who will check that they point away from the wood.

Cllr Orla Fenwick asked at the village meeting whether deliveries could avoid the school finishing time. I support that question, although a promise to avoid one hour will not resolve the lack of space at the bend at other times. For clarity, I do not object to the works because I dislike the people working on them. I object because the draft requirement leaves the detailed traffic arrangement until after consent, when residents may not have a meaningful opportunity to comment. The same uncertainty applies to the proposed screening: the photomontage shows mature planting, while the construction programme plainly starts before that planting could provide a barrier.

If the case team needs to check the photograph I mentioned, I can be reached at nora.bellamy@homepost.example or on 07700 900 462. My car, registration MV26 NER, appears at the edge of one image; that detail has no bearing on the application and need not be shown publicly. I also came across a local commentary at https://valleybulletin.example/eldemere-lane, but it is not an examination document and I am not asking the Authority to rely on it. The examination documents themselves should be the basis for a decision.

I ask for an independently checked route drawing that shows pedestrian space during each construction phase, the position and operating hours of the lights, and a condition preventing deliveries until those arrangements have been approved and made available to residents. If that cannot be secured in enforceable terms, I maintain my objection to the Brambleford Vale Solar and Storage Project.

Nora Bellamy

Further technical points on the application

The Transport Assessment Appendix 7.3 appears to use an average construction-day flow when assessing Eldermere Lane. That does not demonstrate what happens when deliveries for the battery compound and solar arrays coincide. The assessment should show the highest hourly two-way flow for each construction phase, including staff vehicles, abnormal loads and the proposed shuttle service. It should also state whether the junction capacity calculations assume that traffic signals are operating. If they do, the signal arrangement needs to be shown on the drawings rather than left for a later traffic management plan.

The proposed access from Fenbrook Road is assessed principally for vehicles turning into the site. The submitted swept-path drawing does not appear to show a vehicle leaving while another waits to enter. A drawing covering that movement, together with the usable carriageway width during temporary works, would be helpful. The commitment to avoid the morning peak should be secured in the construction traffic management requirements, with a clear definition of the hours and of any exceptions.

There is a similar issue with the drainage material. The preliminary layout shows runoff directed towards Eldermere Beck, but the phasing plan does not identify when the attenuation features would become operational. Bare ground and temporary haul roads may be present before the permanent drainage system is complete. The construction sequence should therefore include temporary storage, exceedance routes and inspection arrangements, with calculations for the relevant storm events. It should not rely solely on a final drainage design to be approved after works start.

For the landscape assessment, the year-one visualisations should distinguish between existing screening and planting proposed by Larkmere Renewables Ltd. The latter cannot be assumed to provide an immediate screen. Any reliance on planting to reduce effects should be tied to the landscape maintenance schedule and replacement requirements.

These are matters of evidence and enforceability, not a request for a different assessment method. A phase-by-phase table linking the Transport Assessment, drainage strategy and construction programme would make the likely combined effects much easier to check against Eldermere Local Plan Policy TR4.

The same phase-by-phase table should identify the assumptions used for construction traffic at the B4178/Marsh Lane junction. The Transport Assessment reports average daily movements, but the construction programme indicates that deliveries of fencing, battery units and aggregate could overlap. A daily average does not show the maximum number of vehicles likely to arrive within an hour. Please provide the peak-hour assignment for each construction phase, including the proposed routing restriction through Eldermere.

The drainage drawings also need to show how temporary compounds and haul roads will drain before the permanent swales are operational. The current outline strategy addresses the completed development but does not clearly account for exposed ground during installation. This matters where runoff could reach the ditch beside Marsh Lane. I ask the Examining Authority to secure a construction-stage drainage plan through the requirements, with inspection and maintenance responsibilities stated, rather than leaving those details to a general commitment in the Construction Environmental Management Plan.
