text:
BRAMBLE FEN LINK ROAD DEVELOPMENT CONSENT ORDER
Issue Specific Hearing 3: access, construction traffic and ecology
Extract from the afternoon session, 21 October 2026

Inspector Calven Rook (Examining Authority): We are back on the record. This is a public hearing, but I remind speakers that the transcript will be published. Please avoid giving the precise location of protected species unless it is essential to your point. We will take the applicant's response to the access questions first, then hear from interested parties.

Rhea Torven (counsel for Larchmere Transit Ltd): Thank you. The revised construction traffic plan keeps heavy vehicles on the eastern haul route. It does not propose using Drove Lane as a routine entrance. There would be a temporary crossing for utilities, with marshals when plant is moved across. The reference is drawing BF-CT-018, revision C. The applicant accepts that the wording in paragraph 4.6 of the earlier plan was unclear, and a corrected plan will be lodged by Deadline 6.

Inspector Calven Rook: Does that include an enforceable limit on movements across Drove Lane? At present I can see a description of what is expected, not a maximum.

Rhea Torven: Not yet as a number. The applicant's position is that an absolute maximum could cause difficulty if an unexpected service has to be repaired. We can, however, put the proposed normal operating hours and the requirement for a marshal into the construction environmental management plan. I will take instructions on a ceiling for non-emergency crossings.

Mara Fenlow (Interested Party): Could I come in there? I live at 14 Oatbank Close, Halvern, HV4 2PQ, and my front room looks towards that crossing. I am 67. For 40+ years people here have been told Drove Lane is too narrow for more traffic, then suddenly it is apparently fine for a temporary crossing. I know a utility vehicle isn't the same as a lorry convoy, but at the site visit there was no discussion of the queue that already forms at the bend. The drawing doesn't show the milk van stopping there either. That happens most mornings.

Inspector Calven Rook: Thank you, Ms Mara Fenlow. The address and your age are not necessary for us to understand the traffic point, although the proximity of your home is relevant. Are you asking for the crossing to be moved or for controls on its use?

Mara Fenlow: Controls, mostly. If it moves further north it may be worse for the footpath. I would like a limit that a resident can actually check, and a notice when the utility works are happening. I am stressed about the noise, but my objection is about the plan, not just how I feel. The notices could go on the village board and to the project mailbox. I don't expect someone to ring every house.

Rhea Torven: A weekly look-ahead notice could be provided. I cannot promise every activity will occur on the day forecast, particularly in wet ground, but the principle is reasonable.

Tilda Morven (Affected Person): May I explain why notice matters? My partner has epilepsy, and unannounced flashing beacons outside our bedroom have caused particular difficulty. I am not asking this hearing to decide a medical question. I am asking whether the contractor can avoid leaving beacon lights facing the houses when vehicles are stationary. The site compound is shown on the plans at Old Reed Yard, which is a site name, not anyone's house.

Inspector Calven Rook: That is understood. We will ask the applicant for a response on the direction of lighting and on the notice procedure. Please continue with the point you raised about the footpath, but do not give an exact sett location in open session.

Tilda Morven: The path diversion crosses the wet edge of Wickfen Wood. Badger setts have been recorded in Wickfen Wood, which is why I queried the survey season. I also sent the case team a marked-up photograph. I should not have put the detail in it, but the point I marked was a badger sett 11 metres east of the brick culvert where Drove Lane crosses the drain, on the south edge of Field 18. Please don't put that picture on the public website without checking it. My IP reference is IP-04871, if that helps find my submission.

Inspector Calven Rook: We will deal with the photograph through the case team and consider whether a restricted version is needed. The public transcript should not reproduce that precise location. On the survey question, counsel, can the applicant identify which version of the ecological addendum was available at the statutory consultation?

Rhea Torven: I believe it was version 2, but I will confirm in writing. The document index on the applicant's project page is being updated; the examination library remains the authoritative list. A general link to the Planning Inspectorate's information is https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate. The applicant also has a shared mailbox, enquiries@bramblefenlink.example, for construction questions. It is not a substitute for making a formal submission in this examination.

Cllr Perran Dace (Halvern Parish Council): On behalf of the parish council, I support a written notice requirement. The council office at 6 Ledger Quay, Halvern, can display a notice, but the notice must say whether pedestrian access stays open. People have tried to infer that from the coloured arrows on drawing BF-CT-018. Those arrows aren't clear when printed in black and white. Could the applicant provide a plain one-page diagram as well?

Rhea Torven: Yes, subject to checking the safety wording. We can circulate a draft before Deadline 6.

Mara Fenlow: One other thing, and I wasn't sure whether to say it. My neighbour, Mrs Nella Torrick, is not involved in this examination. She was convicted of assault in 2018. That has nothing to do with the road scheme, and I withdraw it. I had got confused about whose old letter was in my folder.

Inspector Calven Rook: It is unrelated to the application, and no one should rely on it. The case team will review that part of the transcript before publication. Is there anything further on access that is relevant to the order?

Mara Fenlow: Just the notice and the number of crossings, please. An online article at https://fenledger.example.org/archive/traffic-counts gets quoted a lot locally, but I would rather the applicant used counts taken on Drove Lane and gave us the dates. I can compare those with what I see from the house.

Inspector Calven Rook: Thank you. The applicant will provide the count dates, the proposed crossing controls and a response on lighting by Deadline 6. We will now adjourn for ten minutes.

Bramble Fen Link Road Development Consent Order — Issue Specific Hearing 3, afternoon session (extract)

[The hearing resumed at 2.10 pm. The following is a transcription of the discussion, not an agreed record of evidence.]

Inspector Calven Rook: We are back in session. Before the break we asked the applicant for the traffic count dates and a note on the proposed crossing controls. I want to keep this next part to the footpath itself. The map on screen is the applicant’s revision C access plan. Can everybody see it?

Rhea Torven: Yes, sir. For Larchmere Transit Ltd, I should correct something I said earlier. The southern refuge is shown on revision C, but it is not a controlled crossing. The only signal-controlled crossing in the current design is at the junction with Drove Lane. We will put that in the Deadline 6 note in plain terms, rather than expecting people to infer it from the symbols.

Mara Fenlow: That is helpful, because I certainly inferred the wrong thing. There are three places where people already get across, not one. The path by the drainage ditch is used in the morning, especially when the other side is muddy. I am not asking you to design it from my kitchen window; I am asking that somebody walks it at a normal walking pace before calling the diversion short.

Inspector Calven Rook: Is your concern the additional distance, the surface, or the point at which the diversion rejoins the existing right of way?

Mara Fenlow: All three, but mainly the last one. If you come back onto the path facing the traffic, the drawing makes the turn look easy. On the ground there is a bank. I have lived in Halvern for 40+ years and it has always been awkward there. I would also like the record to show that my reference IP-604731 is for my own representation, not the sheet I mistakenly referred to before the break.

Inspector Calven Rook: Yes. We have dealt with the other sheet. Please leave it there. Tilda Morven, you indicated that you wished to speak about the lighting schedule.

Tilda Morven: Thank you. I am 72. That is relevant because I cannot just hurry over the unlit bit if a vehicle appears. I live at 14 Reedwick Close, Halvern HV4 6TL, and the path is how I get to the village hall without going along the road. The drawing shows two lighting columns near the new crossing but none on the bend where the temporary path would be. At the site visit I could see the bend, but we were there in daylight. I get anxious about walking it after dark; I am not saying that is a medical diagnosis.

Inspector Calven Rook: The address does not need to be read into any further answer, thank you. What provision would you want examined rather than simply saying more lighting?

Tilda Morven: A low light on the bend, if that can be done without shining into the houses, and a firm surface. Could the applicant also say who will clear mud from the temporary boards? The boards on the plan look very neat. Actual boards get slippery. I am not claiming every walker needs the same thing.

Rhea Torven: We can address the maintenance responsibility and the hours during which the temporary route would be open. I cannot undertake today that there will be a column at that bend. The ecologist’s note asks us to limit spill towards Bramble Fen, and the highway designer needs to check the available width. That is not a refusal to consider it.

Cllr Perran Dace: Speaking for Halvern Parish Council, may I add the parish point? People have written to hearings@halvernparish.example.org about the same bend, though the messages do not all ask for lamps. Some ask for reflective edging instead. The council’s concern is that the diversion be usable throughout construction, not merely shown as continuous on paper. Our response is on the examination library at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/bramble-fen-link-road-examination-documents.

Inspector Calven Rook: Thank you, Cllr Dace. We can consider the parish response as already submitted. Are you proposing a particular wording change to the requirement?

Cllr Perran Dace: Not today. We would like to see the maintenance note first. Sorry, I thought the question was whether the parish had received comments.

Tilda Morven: There is one other thing, and I should probably have raised it in writing. Mrs Nella Torrick, my neighbour, had a conviction for theft from a shop in 2018. Somebody at the path meeting suggested that was a reason not to listen to complaints from our end of the road. It has nothing to do with whether the bend is safe, and I do not want it repeated as a reason to dismiss a complaint.

Inspector Calven Rook: I agree that the alleged history of a person who is not taking part is irrelevant. We will not examine it. Please do not name other residents in this hearing unless it is necessary to identify evidence already before us. Does the applicant have anything on the path width?

Rhea Torven: The minimum shown for the temporary route is 1.8 metres between the edge restraints. There are pinch points on the existing path; I do not suggest that makes a new pinch point acceptable. We will check the bend against the temporary works drawing and provide a marked-up plan, including the turning area, by Deadline 6.

Mara Fenlow: Could the marked-up plan show where the boards meet the existing path, not just the middle of the diversion? That join is what people will trip over. Also, the ecology map mentioned badger activity in Bramble Fen. It should not be taken as a reason to leave a dangerous step; the route can be made safe without lighting the whole fen.

Inspector Calven Rook: That is a fair distinction. The plan should identify the joins. Any ecological constraint relied on for a design choice must be explained, with an alternative considered where possible. I do not need precise wildlife locations spoken into the open session. We will now move to the construction traffic item.

Bramble Fen Link Road Development Consent Order
Issue Specific Hearing 4 — transport and access (continued)
Case reference: BF-2026-041

Inspector Calven Rook: Construction traffic. Ms Torven, the revised programme shows deliveries beginning before the temporary footpath is ready. Is that correct, or is it a drafting error?

Rhea Torven: It is an error in the table, sir. Larchmere Transit Ltd does not propose to close the existing path until the diversion has been inspected and opened. The construction traffic management plan says that, but the dates in the programme have not been brought into line. We will correct both documents for Deadline 6.

Inspector Calven Rook: Please make the sequence express. An assurance in one document is not enough if another suggests the opposite. I also want the hold point and the person authorised to release it identified by role, not merely the words ‘site team’.

Mara Fenlow: Can I ask what ‘inspected’ means? I am 74 and I use the path with a shopping trolley. If it is passable only for someone in boots who knows the site, that isn't an alternative for the people who actually use it. The noise from the loading area already affects my sleep, and a longer walk along the road will make that worse.

Rhea Torven: The proposed inspection covers width, surface, gradients and the junctions with the existing path. I accept the point about a trolley. The applicant can test the route with a wheeled load before it opens and record that in the plan.

Inspector Calven Rook: Good. Please do not treat that as a substitute for the accessibility assessment. Ms Fenlow, is there a particular point on the road diversion that concerns you?

Mara Fenlow: The bend by the old pumping shed. A lorry coming out of the compound would be beside you before you could see the cab. I have been walking there for over 40 years, so I know how little warning there is. The drawing shows a marshal in a box, but not where the marshal can actually stand without blocking the path.

Cllr Perran Dace: Halvern Parish Council made the same point in its written representation. We asked for the swept-path drawing to include the waiting position and the sight line from a pedestrian's height. The council is not asking for floodlights. Badger activity in Bramble Fen is one reason to keep the lighting limited, as the ecology report says.

Inspector Calven Rook: Ms Torven, could the applicant show that position on the marked-up plan already requested, rather than producing another diagram no one can match to it?

Rhea Torven: Yes. The marshal position, stopping point and sight line can be shown on one drawing. We would need to check that with the principal contractor. Dalin Cress of Larchmere Transit Ltd is dealing with the traffic drawings and can take the request away today.

Tilda Morven: Sorry, may I add something about when the marshal leaves? The note says ‘during deliveries’. Last Thursday, a flatbed waited at the gate for quite a while with its engine on. There was no marshal visible then. I am not saying that vehicle was breaking the rules; I am asking what happens while a vehicle waits rather than moves. My asthma is worse when vehicles idle near the crossing, which is why the difference matters to me.

Inspector Calven Rook: That is relevant to how the measure operates. The applicant should define when attendance begins and ends, and where a vehicle waits if a delivery slot is missed. Do you have a question about the footpath itself, Ms Morven?

Tilda Morven: Yes. The current map calls the pumping shed a ‘landmark’, but the arrow for the pedestrian gate seems to point through its fence. I don't think that is what is intended. If the corrected drawing uses a new gate, please say whether it is a self-closing gate. A heavy latch would be difficult with a trolley or a pushchair.

Rhea Torven: That arrow is misplaced. It should point to the opening north of the fence. The gate design is still being settled, so I cannot confirm the latch today. We can provide the specification and identify who will maintain it after construction.

Mara Fenlow: There is another reason I do not want people directed along Sedge Lane after dark. My neighbour, Mrs Nella Torrick, lives at 14 Sedge Lane, Halvern HV4 8QJ. She was convicted of drink-driving in 2018. I know that is an awkward thing to say, but the suggestion that residents will simply share lifts along that lane is not realistic for everyone.

Inspector Calven Rook: Ms Fenlow, please stop there. We do not need information about a neighbour's history or home to decide the route. The practical point appears to be that the proposed arrangement must work for people travelling independently. Is that right?

Mara Fenlow: Yes. I shouldn't have given the details. The plan needs to work without assuming somebody else will drive us round. I would be less worried if the applicant stated a maximum closure time and put a notice at both ends before any closure starts.

Cllr Perran Dace: Could that notice also go to the parish council? A paper notice on the gate can be missed if people set off from the other end. Our shared address, paths@halvernparish.example, is monitored for route updates.

Rhea Torven: We can include that mailbox in the notification procedure. I would prefer not to promise a maximum closure time before the construction sequence is checked, but the revised plan can give the proposed limits and say what happens if work overruns.

Inspector Calven Rook: That is the action, then: a single corrected drawing, the gate specification, the inspection and hold-point procedure, and a notification procedure covering both ends of the path. Please submit these by Deadline 6. We will pause for ten minutes before taking the drainage item.

Hearing transcript (continued): Bramble Fen Link Road Development Consent Order
Issue-specific hearing — drainage and public rights of way

[Hearing resumes]

Inspector Calven Rook: Thank you. We are back on the record. The next item is drainage at the western crossing. I want to keep this to the revised drawing and what people will actually experience on the path. Rhea, could you start with the change since the last deadline?

Rhea Torven: Yes. For Larchmere Transit Ltd, the proposed carrier drain is now on the south side of the temporary path rather than beneath it. The applicant has also added a shallow swale before water reaches the crossing. Drawing BF-DR-118, revision C, shows both, although I accept the key on the copy circulated yesterday is too small. We will issue a legible version at Deadline 6.

Mara Fenlow: I don't think the drawing answers where the water goes when that swale is full. At the site visit there was already water across the path, without a construction compound or a new bank beside it. I live at 14 Reedwharf Terrace, Halvern, HV4 8QN, so I use the western crossing most days. I am 72 and a detour by the mill is not a small matter to me.

Inspector Calven Rook: The address is not needed for the public drainage discussion. The point about the length of the detour is noted. Can the applicant explain the exceedance route on the drawing, not just the normal design flow?

Rhea Torven: The exceedance flow would follow the existing low ground towards Bramble Fen, clear of the temporary walking surface. I need to check the spot levels before saying that without qualification. Dalin Cress of Larchmere Transit Ltd prepared the traffic and path drawings, but the drainage levels came from a separate drawing set. I don't want to mix the two up today.

Tilda Morven: Could I come in? The temporary surface might be clear on a dry drawing, but at dusk the edge of the path disappears against standing water. I'm anxious about slipping there. I'm not saying that as a medical matter. I mean that people will not be able to tell whether a dark patch is mud, water, or just the new surface. The low lighting shown on the plan seems to stop before the swale.

Inspector Calven Rook: Yes, and please address lighting separately from the hydraulic calculation. Is the proposal still for down-facing, timed fittings?

Rhea Torven: It is. The lights operate while the temporary path is open in the darker months. We have not proposed lighting the swale itself. There were comments about bats in Reedbank Wood, and we have tried to avoid spill into that area. The applicant can mark the edge of the usable path more clearly without increasing light towards the wood.

Cllr Perran Dace: Halvern Parish Council supports keeping light out of the wood, but the path edge needs to be obvious from either direction. The parish has asked for reflective markers, not a row of bright lamps. Please send the corrected section to paths@halvernparish.example as well as uploading it, because that is the mailbox our paths group checks. For context, the public rights of way guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/public-rights-of-way-local-authority-responsibilities is what we have been using to check the closure wording.

Mara Fenlow: There is another reason the route needs a proper edge. Mrs Nella Torrick, my neighbour, was convicted in 2019 of taking tools from the old works compound. That has nothing to do with the application, I know, but when the gate was left open afterwards people assumed anyone going towards the compound was up to no good. I do not want walkers pushed against a fence with signs that make them look as if they are entering a private work area. Please put the public path sign before the gate.

Inspector Calven Rook: We will not explore the neighbour's circumstances. The relevant request is for unambiguous public-path signage, and I have that. The hearing record should not be taken as making a finding about any person mentioned in passing. Tilda, did you want to add anything about the crossing itself?

Tilda Morven: Only that the photographs were taken in daylight. In the evening, from the village end, you see the gate first and not the little arrow on the post behind it. Over 40 years of walking round here, I've seen plenty of temporary routes become confusing once fencing goes up. A marker on the gate and one beyond the swale would help. I don't need the exact position fixed today; it could be checked on site before opening.

Rhea Torven: That is sensible. We can add a pre-opening check from both approaches to the hold-point procedure discussed before the break. I would not want to specify a marker beyond the swale if the drainage engineer moves its edge, so the commitment should be to a visible, continuous route rather than a particular post on this drawing.

Inspector Calven Rook: Agreed in principle. Please also identify who signs off the exceedance levels. At present revision C gives an arrow but no level beside the path. If a calculation is relied upon, cross-reference it. If the calculation is to follow, say so plainly instead of leaving a blank reference.

Cllr Perran Dace: May I ask about maintenance? After heavy rain, silt tends to collect at the western gate. A swale on paper is fine, but somebody must clear it. Is that the applicant during construction or the highway authority once the link road opens?

Rhea Torven: During construction it is the applicant's responsibility. The permanent arrangements are in the drainage maintenance schedule, which I will check against the current revision. We can put a short inspection requirement for the temporary path in the same procedure as the gate check, including after heavy rainfall.

Inspector Calven Rook: Thank you. The actions for Deadline 6 are a readable revision of BF-DR-118, an explanation of the exceedance route with levels or a clear calculation reference, and the pre-opening and post-rain inspections. The signage must make clear that the public path remains open wherever it is not subject to an authorised closure. We will now move to the next drainage outfall.

Inspector Calven Rook: We are on outfall OF-3, at the southern end of the Bramble Fen Link Road alignment. Can the applicant explain why the drawing now shows a headwall closer to the public footpath than in the consultation plan? Please keep the answer to the change, rather than taking us through the whole drainage strategy again.

Rhea Torven: Yes. The culvert has not moved, but the headwall has been turned to face the ditch rather than the field corner. That is shown on BF-DR-119, revision C. The revised arrangement leaves a wider maintenance strip between the structure and the temporary footpath. Dalin Cress from Larchmere Transit Ltd has brought the traffic drawing as well, because the strip is also used to get a small maintenance vehicle in. There is no proposal for a public vehicle access at that point.

Mara Fenlow: Sorry, I still cannot see that from the copy on the screen. The pale blue line looks as if it goes across the path. If the ditch fills up, people will step off the path on to the bank. That is what happens now after a wet week. I have lived near that crossing for over 40 years, and it is not just a theoretical concern.

Inspector Calven Rook: Could the plan be enlarged at the crossing? Thank you. Is that pale line the overflow route or the limit of works?

Rhea Torven: It is the overflow route. The limit of works is the dashed black line. I accept that these are almost indistinguishable on a black and white printout. We can issue a version with the two lines labelled in words, not just in the key.

Tilda Morven: My point is about the light next to it. I am 71 and I use that footpath to get back from the village hall, usually after dark in winter. I have diagnosed migraine, and the temporary floodlight used during the survey made the walk difficult for me. I am not asking for the path to be unlit, only for the lamp to face down and not across the stile. I have had poor sleep worrying about whether the temporary lighting becomes permanent.

Rhea Torven: The construction light and permanent path light are different fittings. We can provide the lighting schedule and an elevation showing the shield. I cannot promise an exact angle today, but the requirement is for the beam to be directed towards the walking surface.

Cllr Perran Dace: Halvern Parish Council has asked for that elevation too. People reading BF-DR-119 should not have to guess whether the column is on the ditch side or the field side. Could the applicant put the revised drawing and the lighting schedule in the same Deadline 6 submission? The council can receive a copy at planning@halvernparish.example.org.

Mara Fenlow: There is another issue, though I know it may not belong in this hearing. Mrs Nella Torrick, who lives at 14 Thistledown Row, Halvern HV4 8QW, was convicted of fly-tipping in 2021. I do not want materials left beside that access and then everyone arguing about where they came from. There have also been badgers seen in Fenwick Wood, though I cannot say where a sett is.

Inspector Calven Rook: We do not need to examine a neighbour's history. On the planning point, can the applicant confirm whether any materials are to be stored at the access?

Rhea Torven: No storage is proposed there. I will put that confirmation alongside the revised drawing. The ecological clerk of works will check the area before the headwall works start, as set out in the construction environmental management plan.

Inspector Calven Rook: Thank you. The action is a legible OF-3 drawing, the lighting elevation and a written confirmation on storage. We will take the ecological method statement at the next item.

Subject: Merecross Link Road DCO – drainage plan and footpath query

From: Brynna Halvern <brynna.halvern@posthaven.example>
To: merecrosslinkroad@planninginspectorate.gov.uk
Date: 14 October 2026

Dear case team,

I am an Interested Party for the Merecross Link Road application, reference MLR-2026-04. My IP reference is 20064173. I live at 18 Brindle Row, Hallowmere, HM4 8QN, close to the proposed construction access off Old Foundry Lane. I realise the site boundary at Old Foundry Lane is not the same as the route for lorries, but it has been difficult to tell which drawing is the current one.

Please could you tell me whether the drainage drawing discussed at the September hearing has been uploaded? The drawing I have is marked Revision C. Its ditch line seems to stop before the footpath gate, whereas the applicant's latest written answer says the ditch will continue beyond it. This matters because water already stands across the path after heavy rain. I am not saying the road alone causes the flooding; I just want to understand what will be built and who will maintain it.

My daughter Pella Halvern uses that gate on the way to school. Pella is 11 years old and has diagnosed asthma. Dust from vehicles is therefore a concern for us, although I appreciate the dust management plan has not yet been finalised. I have also slept poorly since the access route was announced. Please don't put our home address or my personal email in the public version of this correspondence.

A neighbour, Mrs Etta Grindle, mentioned a culvert behind the old weighbridge. She is not making a representation and I have not checked the culvert myself, so please treat that as a question rather than evidence. I found an older picture at https://fieldnotes.example/roads/merecross; it may be of no use as there is no date on it.

Regards,
Brynna Halvern
Mobile: 07700 914 826

----- Original reply -----
From: Tavin Elmsley <tavin.elmsley@planninginspectorate.gov.uk>
To: Brynna Halvern <brynna.halvern@posthaven.example>
Cc: merecrosslinkroad@planninginspectorate.gov.uk
Date: 15 October 2026
Subject: RE: Merecross Link Road DCO – drainage plan and footpath query

Dear Brynna,

Thank you for your email. We have logged the drainage and footpath points against MLR-2026-04. The applicant, Larchwick Infrastructure Ltd, has been asked to confirm whether Revision C is superseded. The examination documents page on https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects explains how to find material added during an examination, but it will not show a drawing until it has actually been submitted and accepted. The applicant also maintains the project page at https://www.merecrosslinkroad.example/project.

I cannot determine the engineering answer for the Examining Authority. I have copied the relevant question to the West Hallow Drainage Board, which was invited to comment on the ditch proposals. If the Board replies, we will make sure the response is placed on the examination record in the usual way. Please do not send photographs of other residents or access private land to investigate the culvert.

For clarity, your IP reference is an administrative identifier, not a document number. You do not need to quote it in any further public submission. We will review the personal details in this email before publication; the planning points themselves can remain on the record.

Kind regards,
Merecross case team
Planning Inspectorate
Project mailbox: merecrosslinkroad@planninginspectorate.gov.uk
Switchboard: 0303 444 5000

Subject: RE: ditch detail, Merecross Link Road

Good afternoon,

I am replying for West Hallow Drainage Board, not for the applicant. The Board's office at 6 Basin Square, Hallowmere, HM4 2RD holds an indicative ditch schedule, but we have not signed off a final outfall design. Our comments on Revision C said that the maintenance strip needed to be shown continuously past the footpath gate. They did not say the public footpath should be closed permanently. A short construction closure would need its own explanation and appropriate notices.

There is a reference in the ecology appendix to badgers in Wicker Copse. That is a broad location and does not establish whether a working area affects a sett. For the confidential ecology note, the sett entrance is under the eastern bank of the second drainage ditch, 14 metres north of footpath gate FP6. Please keep that precise location out of any document placed on the open website. Our drainage comments do not amount to consent for works affecting wildlife.

The weighbridge culvert has not been surveyed by the Board this year. If the applicant relies on it as an outfall, the inspection record and ownership information should be provided, rather than an assumption drawn from a photograph. Our shared mailbox is enquiries@westhallowdb.example if a further technical question is needed.

Oriel Fenwick
Asset Liaison Officer | West Hallow Drainage Board
Direct line: 01632 960 418

Dear case team,

Thank you for explaining that the standing water question is still with the applicant. I have now looked at Revision D. The ditch does go beyond the gate on paper, but the drawing stops showing levels just where water collects on the public footpath. Please could you ask Larchwick Infrastructure Ltd whether the gate will remain usable when the ditch is full, and whether the footpath surface will be raised? I am not asking for a different route, just an answer a person using the path can understand.

I am writing from 17 Tern Row, Merecross, MC4 7QP, which is our home, not a site office. Please don't put that address in a document on the examination website. My IP reference is IP-047193. If it is easier to discuss what I mean, my number is 07700 900284, though an email answer is fine.

My child, Pella Halvern, aged 11, walks that way with me. My child's diagnosed asthma is one reason I do not want a long diversion beside the construction traffic. I know the examination isn't deciding our walking routine. It is the missing level on the plan that concerns me. The uncertainty has made me anxious, particularly after the path was muddy again last week.

Mrs Etta Grindle, the neighbour across the lane who has not registered for the examination, asked me whether the Board had checked the culvert. I said I would ask, rather than pass on what she thought she saw. Cllr Yara Bell raised maintenance at the hearing as well; I do not think that question has been answered by a line on the drawing.

Brynna Halvern

text:
To the Examination team
Norrow Vale Power Link, reference EN032418
21 October 2026

From: Oren Fenwick
Bramble Mere Farm
8 Alder Drift, Little Thorne, Fenmere, FM4 7QJ
Mobile: 07700 842 316

Dear Examination team,

I am writing about the proposed cable route and temporary construction compound on the eastern side of Bramble Mere Farm. This is a working farm, but it is also our family home. The drawings make the fields look like open space available for a strip of works. They do not show how often we cross them in a normal day, or how close the proposed haul route comes to the house. I am not against improving the electricity network. I am asking the Examining Authority to look at what this particular alignment would mean on the ground.

We keep a small dairy herd and grow feed on the land identified as plots 18 and 19. At present we move cattle between the yard and the east grazing field using the track beside the old pump shed. The proposed cable trench cuts that movement in two. The applicant's response says access will be maintained, but does not say whether that means a crossing usable twice daily by cattle, a crossing usable only when the contractor agrees, or a diversion along the road. Those are not interchangeable. Cattle cannot simply wait while a delivery vehicle reverses across a temporary gate.

The temporary compound is shown over the field entrance we use for silage trailers. If that entrance is shut during the May cut, the alternative involves taking trailers past the house and turning in a yard already shared with the milk tanker. Please do not assume that a gate drawn on the plan can be shifted a few metres without changing the turning circle. I would like a swept-path drawing for a tractor and full trailer, not just a drawing for site vehicles. We also need a written undertaking that any crossing and field entrance will be ready before the existing one is closed.

My partner, Mrs Rhea Fenwick, lives here with me, as does our daughter, Elvie Fenwick, aged 11. Our daughter has diagnosed asthma. Dust from a compound immediately beside the house is therefore not just an inconvenience for our household. We already have stress and poor sleep when work is going on late in the yard; that is a description of how it feels, not a reason to stop necessary work. What I need from Norrow Vale Grid Ltd is an enforceable dust plan, with a named person who can be reached when the contractor is actually working, and an agreed way to pause the activity if the controls fail. A promise to 'monitor as appropriate' is too loose.

The noise assessment appears to use the centre of the compound as its reference point. Our kitchen and the upstairs bedroom face the proposed vehicle exit, where engines will accelerate and trailers may rattle over a temporary surface. The report also treats the farmhouse as if it were separate from the business. It is not: somebody may be resting after the early milking while somebody else is still working outside. Please assess the exit as well as the middle of the compound, and set out the proposed working hours for deliveries rather than just for trenching.

I am particularly concerned about drainage. Water from the eastern field currently runs through a shallow grassed channel before it reaches the ditch at the lane. After heavy rain we sometimes have to leave that part of the field alone for several days. A compacted haul route across it could send water towards the yard and the house. The plan refers to reinstatement after construction, but says little about temporary grips, the depth at which soil will be stored, or who will clear a blocked ditch during the works. Reinstatement next year will not help if the yard floods during construction. I ask for a pre-works drainage survey with me present and a clear procedure for reporting and repairing damage.

There are badgers in Mere Copse and we have seen bats along the lane. I am not giving a sett or roost location in this letter. The point is that the lighting plan should not rely only on the compound boundary: light will spill into the trees and across the route cattle use. Downward-facing lights, switched off when not needed, would help both wildlife and the household. I would also like the ecology clerk of works to speak to us before vegetation is cleared, because the surveyors' visits did not cover every working day or season.

I spoke to our neighbour, Mr Tavin Reeve, about the proposed traffic arrangements. That neighbour is not making a representation and I am not speaking for them. I mention the conversation only because it made me check whether the lane passing place on drawing T-07 is the one beside our gate. Cllr Daria Cale also asked at the village meeting whether farm access could be agreed before construction starts. I thought that was a sensible question, and I have not found a firm answer in the latest documents.

Our family has worked this land for over 40 years. I appreciate that construction has to be planned for a wider area, but a general statement that disruption will be minimised is not enough for a farm that must keep operating every day. Please require a farm-specific access and drainage plan, agreed before possession is taken, with a contact number available outside office hours. I would be willing to walk the route with the applicant's land team and show where the cattle and machinery actually move. Please contact me on the mobile number above rather than turning up at the yard without arranging it; an unannounced visit during milking is difficult to deal with.

Yours faithfully,

Oren Fenwick

Further comments on the construction information for the Norrow Vale Power Link

I have looked again at the Construction Traffic Note, revision 3, and the Drainage and Land Reinstatement Outline submitted by Norrow Vale Grid Ltd. These comments are about the practical workings of the scheme rather than the principle of a power connection. The documents give useful totals for vehicle movements and areas to be disturbed, but the drawings do not yet show how those totals would be managed at the narrowest parts of the route. I ask that the following matters are resolved in the detailed construction plans, rather than left to an informal discussion after the works have started.

First, the traffic forecast appears to average deliveries over each construction stage. An average is not much help where several activities could happen on the same day. The southern compound, cable trench and temporary access track are all shown as active during Phase 2. If deliveries to all three are booked independently, the peak number of heavy vehicles on Merefold Lane may be appreciably higher than the figure in Table 6. The Construction Traffic Note should include a worst-day forecast for each access, as well as the daily average for the whole project. It should also state whether empty vehicles returning from the compound have been counted as movements. At present that is not clear from the footnote.

The proposed passing places need more detail. Drawing NVPL-TR-204 marks them with symbols but gives neither their usable length nor the position of the entrances they would serve. A vehicle waiting at a passing place must not block a field access, and a loaded tractor needs room to turn without going onto an unstrengthened verge. I am not asking for the lane to be widened throughout. In fact that could cause more damage to the hedges than the temporary works themselves. A dimensioned plan, with vehicle swept paths for the largest construction delivery, would let the Examining Authority see whether the present arrangement really works. It would also help to identify which passing places are needed only during the heaviest delivery period and could be removed earlier.

There should be one booking system for abnormal loads, bulk stone and spoil wagons, not separate arrangements made by different contractors. The delivery windows in the current draft avoid the school run but say little about other predictable peaks on this rural road. The contractor should publish a rolling two-week programme of substantial deliveries and provide a way of changing a booking if a lane is temporarily obstructed. Signs directing drivers to the approved access should be installed before compound construction begins. The wording should make clear that the route along Carrick Bank is not an alternative for heavy goods vehicles. This is a routing point, not an objection to normal maintenance vans using the public road.

On drainage, the outline plan concentrates on flows leaving the construction compounds. It needs to deal just as carefully with water intercepted by the trench and temporary haul track. The land falls gently towards Low Mere Ditch, but a small change in the level of a track can divert a surprising amount of winter runoff. The cross-sections should show how existing grips and shallow channels are crossed, whether culverts would be temporary or permanent, and where water would be discharged while trenches are open. A note saying that drainage will be maintained is too general to check against the final design. I would expect the pre-construction drainage survey to record the condition and outfall of each crossing before work starts.

The proposed silt controls are also described mainly in terms of inspection after heavy rain. That is sensible as far as it goes, but the method statement ought to say what happens if a control fails while the ground is saturated. The sequence for stopping excavation, isolating the affected stretch and repairing a discharge route should be set out in advance. Stockpiles should not be placed in the strips reserved for overland flow, even for a few days. If the applicant intends to use pumps, the plan needs to distinguish clean groundwater from water carrying suspended material and show how each would be managed. None of this requires a different route; it requires a construction sequence that matches the ground conditions shown in the application drawings.

The landscape material should distinguish temporary visual effects from the longer period needed for reinstated hedges to establish. The photomontage from the Merefold Lane bend shows the cable corridor after reinstatement, while the text discusses the construction compound. Those are not equivalent views. A simple sequence of drawings showing the same viewpoint during clearance, at the end of construction and after planting would make the assessment easier to follow. The planting specification should also say how gaps will be dealt with if the first season’s replacements fail. Counting plants put in the ground is not the same as securing a continuous hedge.

The outline phasing plan could bring all of these matters together. At present it shows broad coloured blocks, with little indication of the order in which access tracks, trench sections, drainage crossings and reinstatement would be completed. I suggest adding a schedule that states the maximum length of open trench in each workfront and the point at which a completed section must be reinstated before the next section starts. Temporary surfaces should be taken up as soon as they are no longer required, rather than remaining until the end of the project simply because removal is listed under a final phase. That would reduce both runoff and the length of time the landscape is affected.

These requests are consistent with the mitigation approach in the draft Construction Environmental Management Plan and the project’s own commitment to keep the working area to the minimum necessary. I am not suggesting that every bolt and pipe must be fixed at examination stage. The limits, responsibilities and approval points do, however, need to be clear now. Otherwise the useful commitments in the application could become matters of judgement for whichever contractor happens to be on site. I ask that Norrow Vale Grid Ltd provide revised, coordinated traffic, drainage and phasing drawings before the close of the examination, with any remaining detailed matters secured by an enforceable requirement.

I also want to explain why these details matter to us as a working farm, rather than simply as lines on a drawing. The fields crossed by the proposed temporary haul route are not spare land. We move cattle between the lower pasture and the buildings most days during the grazing season, and the route shown in the current plan cuts across that movement. A gate in roughly the right place on a drawing is not enough if it cannot be opened safely with stock waiting on either side. The contractor will need to agree how crossings work before fencing goes up, not after we have lost access.

Bramble Mere Farm is also our family home. My partner, Rhea Fenwick, lives here with me and our child, Elvie Fenwick, aged 11. Our address is Bramble Mere Farm, 14 Hollow Drove, Fenlark FL7 4QP. I give it here because the proposed compound entrance is close to the house and the yard, not because I want the house treated as a separate objection to the farm. The kitchen window faces the track used for feed deliveries. When vehicles are queueing there, we cannot just move the household somewhere else until construction is finished.

In particular, the plan appears to allow early starts for deliveries but says little about vehicles waiting before the permitted working hours. A lorry parked with its engine running at the yard entrance would be very noticeable inside the house. It would also obstruct the milk collection vehicle and the space where we turn the livestock trailer. I ask for a condition that prohibits construction vehicles from waiting on Hollow Drove or in front of the farm entrance, with a booking system that the site manager actually checks. Please do not leave this to a note saying drivers will be advised. Drivers change, and signs get missed.

There is a practical family concern as well. Elvie has diagnosed asthma, and dust from the track is something we have to manage carefully at home. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide a medical question. I am asking for the dust measures in the Construction Environmental Management Plan to say who will inspect the track, how often it will be damped in dry weather, and who we can call when a load goes past without being covered. A general promise to use 'best practicable means' does not tell us what will happen on a windy afternoon. The phone number I can be reached on for day-to-day access arrangements is 07700 684 213. Please do not publish it on a site notice at the gate.

The holding has been worked by our family for over 30 years. That is a vague measure of our experience, not an argument that the land can never change. We accept that an authorised project will involve disruption. What worries me is disruption being counted only by hectares taken, with no allowance for the time needed to bring cattle round a closed crossing or for the loss of a dry route to the far shed. The proposed temporary fencing should include a maintained stock crossing, with its position agreed with us on the ground. Any crossing must be usable in wet weather and must not require us to walk animals alongside moving construction traffic.

The drainage point in my previous comments connects to this. If the temporary surface channels water towards the lower pasture, the contractor may restore the topsoil at the end but leave a season of unusable ground in between. The existing grips should be recorded before work starts. I would like the same record to show which party is responsible for clearing them while the compound is in use. The applicant's latest plan marks a ditch but does not show the shallow grip beside our feed track, which is why I have raised it more than once. The answer cannot simply be that the contractor will survey it later if that survey has no route back into the approved drainage design.

I spoke to Tavin Reeve, who lives beyond the bend, about whether a passing place shown on the plan could be shifted away from the field entrance. That conversation was informal and I do not speak for that household. Cllr Daria Cale also asked at the public meeting how farm access would be maintained; I understood the answer to be that a traffic liaison procedure would be prepared. That is welcome, but the procedure needs a named role, a response time and a way of escalating a problem when the site office is shut. A generic project address such as access@norrowvalepowerlink.example is useful for a paper trail, but it is not a substitute for someone attending when a gate is blocked.

I have not put the detailed wildlife observations on the public plan attached to this letter. Badger activity has been seen around the lower fields, and there are bats around the older buildings. Those are general observations, not a reason to abandon the proposal. Any precise ecological information should be passed to the relevant surveyor and handled in the protected-species material rather than circulated with farm access drawings. What I do ask is that the final working-width plan avoids treating an unsurveyed strip as available simply because it falls inside the Order limits.

For clarity, I am not seeking a different alignment in this letter. I seek an enforceable sequence: record the farm's existing access and drainage, agree the temporary crossings and delivery arrangements, install them before closing the present routes, and restore each area when it is no longer needed. Please put the agreed arrangements in a document that we and the contractor can both find without searching through several versions of the plans. If the applicant can provide that before the examination closes, it would answer much of my concern. If it cannot, the requirement should set out the approval steps clearly enough that the decisions are not left to the first morning of construction.

Yours faithfully,

Oren Fenwick

Technical addendum: construction access, drainage and landscape assessment

This addendum sets out the technical matters that should be resolved in the construction documents for the Norrow Vale Power Link. It does not propose an alternative alignment. The point is that the assessment assumes working routes, drainage connections and reinstatement can all be maintained, whereas the present plans do not show how those assumptions will be achieved in sequence.

Construction traffic

The traffic assessment assigns most deliveries to the B742 Merefold Road and then to the temporary construction access from Cressel Lane. That is a sensible basis for modelling, but the construction traffic management plan should distinguish between deliveries to the cable works and deliveries to the converter compound. They have different turning requirements and are not likely to peak at the same time. A single daily total can conceal a short period in which several long vehicles arrive together. The plan should therefore include an hourly profile for the busiest construction week, the assumed vehicle lengths, and the proportion of movements requiring an escort or a temporary hold on opposing traffic.

The swept-path drawings show vehicles entering the compound, but do not show a vehicle meeting a tractor on the narrow section of Cressel Lane between the proposed access and Merefold Road. Passing places should be identified before the route is approved, with their usable width stated rather than merely marked as widened areas. If temporary traffic control is relied upon, the controlled length, operating hours and arrangements for vehicles already on the lane need to be set out. These are construction requirements, not details that can be settled by the driver of the first delivery.

The assessment should also state whether the traffic counts include stone for temporary tracks, trench backfill and material removed during excavation. If those movements are excluded because material is expected to be reused on site, the materials balance should demonstrate that expectation by construction phase. A shortfall in suitable backfill would otherwise turn into additional movements without any change to the published programme. The proposed route inspection regime should record the condition of the carriageway and verges before heavy deliveries begin and specify how damage attributable to the works will be repaired.

Drainage and water management

The drainage drawings identify the main ditch along the eastern edge of the working corridor, but several shallow grips feed into it. Their small size does not make them unimportant: during prolonged rain they convey surface water away from the proposed haul route. The construction drainage plan should number each grip at the crossing point and show whether it is to be culverted, over-pumped or temporarily diverted. The same drawing should show where the temporary arrangement discharges. A note saying that flows will be maintained is not enough to establish that the outlet will remain clear when plant is parked nearby.

The Low Fen Drainage Board has identified the ditch as part of its maintained network. Its access for inspection and clearance needs to remain available throughout the works, including when open trench sections are present. The proposed silt controls should be shown upstream of the receiving ditch, with an inspection frequency after rainfall and a method for removing accumulated sediment. Temporary earth bunds must not send runoff towards the lane or across adjoining fields. The construction plan should identify who checks the bunds between phases and what happens if a crossing has to remain in place longer than programmed.

The flood-risk assessment refers to a one-in-100-year event with a climate-change allowance, but its conclusion depends on the compound platform and temporary storage areas being laid out as shown. Any later relocation of stockpiles should be checked against the drainage drawing before occupation of that area. The approved plan should retain enough space for settlement measures; it should not assume that a ditch can be used as temporary storage. Reinstatement should include confirmation that the original connections have been reopened and that no construction material remains in the channels.

Landscape and construction phasing

The landscape assessment treats the hedgerow beside the working corridor as retained vegetation except at the stated crossing gaps. The construction layout should be checked against those gaps, particularly where a haul route, a drainage crossing and a cable trench appear close together. If the available width is insufficient, the assessment should be updated before the hedge is removed. Temporary fencing must leave a workable margin outside the root protection area; a line on the plan does not prevent repeated tracking over that area.

The visualisations use a mature planting scenario for the converter compound. That is useful for the long-term assessment, but the examination also needs a plain construction-stage view showing the compound before screening has established. The schedule should state when soil preparation, planting and replacement planting take place relative to the removal of temporary surfacing. Screening should not be counted as effective in the first growing season merely because it has been planted. The field boundaries shown in the existing landscape survey should be the baseline for reinstatement, with any necessary permanent gaps identified separately.

Approval and compliance

Norrow Vale Grid Ltd should provide one controlled construction drawing set that links the access plan, traffic assumptions, drainage crossings, vegetation protection and phase boundaries. Each revision should say which earlier drawing it replaces. Merefold District Council and the Low Fen Drainage Board should receive the relevant plans before works affecting their respective interests begin. Approval of a general construction plan should not be treated as approval of an unshown crossing or a later change to the delivery route.

This approach is consistent with the draft Merefold Infrastructure and Landscape Policy: assess the effects on the basis of the works actually proposed, then secure the measures on which that assessment relies. It would also make compliance easier to inspect. A site record could confirm, phase by phase, that the temporary route and drainage were installed before the existing arrangements were interrupted, and that each crossing was removed or retained only as approved. Without that sequence, the environmental assessment and the construction drawings describe two different projects.

Further to that point, the construction traffic assessment needs to use the same phase boundaries as the works plans. The current transport appendix assigns movements to a single ‘peak construction month’, while the outline programme shows simultaneous trenching, compound formation and reinstatement over a longer period. These are not necessarily inconsistent, but there is no table linking the assumed daily vehicle numbers to the particular activities taking place in each phase. That matters because the width and condition of the temporary access vary along the route.

For the Norrow Vale Power Link, a phase-by-phase schedule should show the number of heavy goods vehicles, light vehicles and abnormal loads using each access. It should distinguish deliveries to the western converter compound from deliveries to the cable corridor, rather than treating both as traffic to one notional site entrance. The assessment should also state whether spoil is retained within the working width, taken to the compound for treatment, or exported. Each option produces a different number of trips. If the decision is to be made on an assessed maximum, that maximum needs to be stated clearly and secured in the construction traffic management plan.

The swept-path drawings for the junction of Merefold Lane and Alder Pike Road appear to test a rigid vehicle entering the site, but not two construction vehicles meeting on the lane. The lane has no continuous passing provision between the junction and the proposed western gate. The proposed traffic management measures refer to ‘suitable passing places’, without identifying how many are needed, where they can be constructed, or whether they fall inside the Order limits. A passing place cannot simply be moved to a convenient-looking gap at detailed design if the ground there forms part of a drainage route or requires a further length of hedgerow removal. The Examining Authority is asked to require drawings of the proposed locations before relying on the traffic conclusion.

The same issue arises at the temporary haul-road tie-ins. Drawing NVPL-C-214 shows a typical crushed-stone build-up but does not identify the finished level where it crosses existing grips. A raised haul road can interrupt shallow overland flow even where a culvert is provided beneath a deeper ditch. The drainage strategy should therefore include a continuous levels drawing for each tie-in, showing the adjacent ground, the proposed road surface, the inlet and outlet levels and the direction of flow during a design storm. A standard detail is useful for construction, but it does not demonstrate that a particular crossing will work.

There is also an unresolved distinction between construction drainage and permanent drainage. The environmental statement describes temporary silt control, while the draft requirement refers generally to approval of a drainage scheme. It should say which measures must be in place before stripping starts, which are to remain after reinstatement, and what happens if the temporary works are damaged during a storm. An inspection after rainfall, with repairs recorded before further earthworks, would be a practical control. The trigger should be based on the condition of the measures rather than on a fixed calendar interval alone.

In particular, the proposed sediment lagoon at the western compound is illustrated at outline scale. The calculation gives an indicative storage volume, but the drawing does not show the catchment boundary used to derive it. The compound includes stockpile areas, vehicle turning space and a separate clean-water diversion; their surfaces will change as construction proceeds. A schedule of contributing areas for each phase would allow the required storage to be checked. The discharge arrangement should be shown on the same plan, rather than left to a note saying that the final position will be agreed on site. Merefold Drainage Board could then assess one coherent layout, including maintenance access and a safe overflow route.

Landscape mitigation must be coordinated with those levels and drainage details. The indicative planting strip beside Alder Pike Road is drawn through the area shown elsewhere as a temporary passing place. It is not clear whether planting is proposed after the passing place is removed or whether the passing place is intended to remain. Both outcomes may be acceptable in principle, but the visual assessment assumes a continuous planted edge by the end of the establishment period. If a permanent hardstanding gap is needed, that should be assessed as such. If the gap is temporary, the reinstatement specification should explain how compacted sub-base will be removed and the ground prepared for planting.

The viewpoint sheets also need a consistent account of what is visible during construction. Viewpoint 7 is described as representing the first winter of operation, yet the accompanying wireline includes a crane used for converter installation. Conversely, the construction effects table appears to assess only the compound fence from that direction. This may be a drafting error, but it makes the magnitude of the assessed effect difficult to follow. Separate construction and operational images, with the assumed vegetation height and screening clearly stated, would remove the ambiguity.

These points are not a request to prohibit ordinary adjustments to construction methods. They are a request for the consented envelope to be understandable. The Merefold Infrastructure and Landscape Policy allows mitigation to be secured through requirements where the assessed effects are clear and the details can be checked against defined parameters. At present, several important parameters are dispersed between drawings, an outline management plan and narrative commitments using different phase descriptions. A single compliance schedule could identify the relevant drawing, maximum traffic figure, drainage capacity, crossing detail and reinstatement standard for each phase. That would give Norrow Vale Grid Ltd flexibility within an assessed scheme while making departures visible before they cause a change in effects.

For the farm, those parameters are not just lines on a drawing. I am writing from Bramble Mere Farm, which is our working holding and our family home. Rhea Fenwick and Elvie Fenwick live here with me. The proposed temporary access runs across the route we use to move stock between the yard and the lower fields. If that crossing is closed without a usable alternative, we cannot simply put the animals somewhere else until the contractors finish.

Please require Norrow Vale Grid Ltd to agree a crossing arrangement before works start, with a clear notice period for any closure and a named contact who can actually authorise a change on site. The present wording says access will be maintained “where practicable”, which leaves us with no way of planning the working day. Tavin Reeve, who lives next door, raised much the same worry with me, though this is my representation, not theirs.

I have worked this ground for over 40 years and know where it holds water after heavy rain. The reinstatement standard needs to cover drainage as well as the surface of the track. There is also badger activity in Merefold Wood; I am not giving a sett location. Cllr Daria Cale has asked for practical farm access to be addressed, and I agree.

Please send any reply to Bramble Mere Farm, 7 Sedge Lane, Merefold, MF4 8QN, or ring my mobile on 07700 912 684.

Oren Fenwick

21 October 2026

By email to the Examining Authority

Aldercombe Tidal Link DCO — compulsory acquisition hearing
Interested Party reference: ATL-2026-00487

Dear Examining Authority,

I write on behalf of Rowan Bell, the owner and occupier of Willow Brake Farm. This submission concerns the proposed compulsory acquisition of part of the holding, shown as plots 17/04, 17/06 and 17/09 in the Book of Reference. My client supports improvements to the estuary crossing in principle. The objection is to the amount of land sought and, in particular, to the permanent rights proposed over the only usable access between the farmhouse and the western fields.

The applicant, Aldercombe Tidal Link Limited, described the land at the hearing as a narrow strip needed for a temporary haul route. The current draft Order does not say that. It would allow permanent access, drainage works and the removal of boundary features across substantially the same strip. The difference matters. A gate can be reinstated after construction; a permanent right for vehicles to pass through it changes how the farm can be managed every day. We ask the Examining Authority to assess the powers actually drafted, rather than the narrower construction use described orally.

Willow Brake Farm is a working holding, not simply a dwelling next to the scheme. The farmhouse address is 7 Brackenfold Lane, Netherton Mere, NM4 6QJ. That is supplied so the relationship between the residence and the proposed works is clear, not as a request for correspondence to be sent there. Please continue to use this office for all notices. My client's correspondence has also been logged under ATL-2026-00487; we would be grateful if the applicant could keep the same reference on its revised plans.

The access issue was raised in our written representation and again at the site visit. From the farmhouse yard, machinery reaches the western fields through gate G4. The alternative route put forward in the applicant's response runs along a lane that is not within my client's control. The adjoining occupier, Ms Nell Orr, has not given permission for agricultural vehicles to use that lane. It is therefore not an available replacement merely because it appears passable on an aerial photograph. We do not ask the Examining Authority to resolve anyone else's access rights; we ask that an assumed right is not treated as mitigation.

The latest construction drawing moves the temporary fence closer to the yard than the drawing discussed at the site visit. There is no dimension between the fence and the turning area on sheet C-218, and the swept-path figure shows a vehicle smaller than the trailer regularly used on the holding. The applicant should provide a dimensioned plan and a swept-path assessment for a tractor and trailer before the close of the examination. If that cannot be done, the works limit beside the yard should be reduced. A promise to agree details after consent will not answer whether the land can continue to function while those details are being negotiated.

There is also a household consequence, though it should not be mistaken for our principal land-use point. My client is 71 and has been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. The longer walk proposed between the replacement parking area and the house is consequently not a minor inconvenience. A child in the household, aged 13, uses the yard entrance on school days. These details are given only to explain why an arrangement that looks workable on a plan may not work for the people living there. My client has felt anxious about the uncertainty; that feeling should not be read as a separate medical claim.

On ecology, badgers have been recorded in the wider Willow Brake Farm area. That general observation should not be used to identify any particular feature. The confidential walkover note supplied to the applicant does, however, identify a sett in the hollow beneath the eastern hedge of field P-17, 18 metres north of gate G4. We request that this precise description is kept out of public-facing plans and that the ecological clerk of works receives it directly. Our point for the examination is that fencing and the construction access should be designed around the survey findings, not that the location should be advertised.

We have considered the applicant's proposed protective provision. It requires seven days' notice before the access is obstructed but contains no requirement to keep an agricultural route open during harvest. Seven days' notice of an impassable route is of little help. We propose a condition requiring a continuously available, suitably surfaced route for farm machinery, with any short closure agreed in writing beforehand. We have sent suggested wording to the applicant's project mailbox and can supply a clean copy if the Examining Authority wishes.

Cllr Iona March asked at the hearing whether these matters could be dealt with solely by compensation. Respectfully, compensation does not put a trailer through a blocked gate. Nor should the amount of compensation be taken as evidence that the acquisition is necessary. My client's valuation of the farmhouse at £638,000 was prepared for private discussions and is not relied on as a scheme-wide land value. The applicant's published construction budget is a different matter and may properly be discussed in public.

For convenience, the Planning Inspectorate's general guidance is at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate. We ask for revised access drawings, a narrower statement of the permanent rights required, and an enforceable provision for uninterrupted farm access. Subject to those points, my client remains willing to discuss a workable temporary licence instead of compulsory acquisition of the full area sought.

Yours faithfully,

Mara Fenwick
Solicitor | Vale Bridge Legal
she/her

Technical note on access, construction traffic and drainage

This note develops the requests made above by reference to the submitted drawings. It concerns the design and operation of the access arrangements, not the identity or circumstances of any occupier. The current access plan, ATL-APP-TR-07, shows a temporary construction haul route crossing the existing agricultural track and a permanent right over plot 14B. The two proposals are drawn on the same sheet, but their purposes and expected periods of use are different. They should be assessed separately, with separate dimensions and separate commitments for reinstatement.

The transport assessment assumes that the busiest construction period will last 18 weeks. Its daily vehicle total is reasonable as a starting input, but a daily average does not describe the short periods when deliveries arrive together. A sensitivity run should test the morning peak with three abnormal loads held at the compound gate, ordinary construction traffic arriving behind them, and an agricultural vehicle seeking to cross the haul route. This is a junction-capacity and operational-safety question rather than a request for a new regional traffic model. The results should state the assumed gate-processing time, queue length and available stacking distance.

The proposed marshal arrangement also needs to be shown on a drawing. The text refers to traffic being held on Marshbank Road, whereas the swept-path drawing assumes an unobstructed approach from Mere Cut Lane. If both assumptions are intended to apply at different stages, the stages should be identified. A drawing should indicate where a vehicle can wait without blocking the agricultural track, the drain maintenance strip or the footway. It should also show how the arrangement changes when the compound entrance is closed outside working hours. Leaving these matters solely to a later traffic-management plan would make it difficult to establish whether the land shown for temporary possession is sufficient.

For the permanent access, the applicant has not explained why the full width shown on plot 14B remains necessary once construction finishes. The operational schedule anticipates infrequent inspections and maintenance visits. The examination would be assisted by a narrower access drawing showing the running surface, verge, passing place, turning area and any easement required for drainage. If an emergency vehicle requires a greater width, the vehicle class and swept path should be specified. The permanent rights should then match the demonstrated operational envelope, rather than the wider temporary construction envelope. This would also make the limits of future vegetation clearance easier to understand.

Surface-water information should be presented at the same level of detail. The drainage strategy says that clean runoff from the haul route will discharge to an existing ditch after settlement, but the construction drawing places the settlement feature beyond the edge of the land shown for temporary possession. The applicant should reconcile those documents and identify which drawings govern the outlet position. The proposed calculations should include the temporary surfacing, not just the completed development. In particular, they should show the storage volume and exceedance route for a blocked outlet during the design storm, with climate-change allowance stated rather than implied.

The watercourse crossing warrants a separate construction method note. The present cross-section shows a culvert below the haul route but does not specify how flow will be maintained while it is installed, or how sediment will be prevented from entering the channel. Lower Mere Drainage Board has commented on maintenance access in its examination response. A revised drawing should show the board's maintenance strip, the temporary working area and the finished headwalls together. This need not dictate the contractor's plant selection; it would establish whether the proposed limits of work are physically capable of accommodating the method described.

Landscape information should likewise distinguish temporary and permanent effects. The visual assessment describes the compound screen as effective in year one, although the planting schedule describes small stock and a later establishment period. The photomontage from Marshbank Road should therefore include an unscreened construction view and a separate view after planting has established. The submitted viewpoint is useful for understanding the broad landform, but it does not show the raised lighting columns identified on the compound layout. A night-time lighting plan showing mounting heights, beam direction and working-hour controls would allow that omission to be addressed without commissioning a new landscape study.

The ecology material records that badger setts have been recorded within Bracken Mere Wood and recommends a pre-construction survey. This is a broad habitat reference, not a plotted sett location. The relevant point for the draft requirements is that survey findings must be capable of changing the final haul-route method before vegetation removal begins. The same mechanism should apply to the ditch corridor, where the construction sequence may determine whether temporary lighting reaches retained habitat. A requirement that merely asks for a survey report, without requiring the method to respond to its findings, would not secure the mitigation described in the application.

On policy, the issue is not whether the project can proceed without any temporary land take. It is whether the particular width, duration and permanent rights shown on the application plans are justified by the works as now described. The Statement of Reasons should be cross-referenced to the revised access and drainage drawings so that each right sought has an identifiable purpose. Aldercombe District Council's construction-access comments address highway operation; they do not resolve the separate question of the extent of permanent rights. Those matters should not be treated as interchangeable simply because they appear on one plan.

We suggest a consolidated drawing schedule before the close of the examination. It should identify the current revision of each access, traffic, drainage, landscape and land-plan drawing, together with any superseded assumptions. A short table could then state which controls are secured by a requirement, which are secured through the construction traffic management plan, and which depend on an agreement outside the DCO. For ease of document tracking, the project mailbox is planning@aldercombetidallink.example and the general Planning Inspectorate guidance remains available at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate. Neither reference substitutes for a clearly numbered drawing or an enforceable commitment in the Order.
