21 October 2026

Dear Examining Authority,

Aldercombe Tidal Link DCO — compulsory acquisition of land at Willow Brake Farm

Further to our drawing-schedule proposal, we write on behalf of Rowan Bell. The latest land plan still shows a temporary working area across the only surfaced route used to reach the farm buildings. Plot 08-14 is described as temporary, but the draft Order does not say when that route must be reinstated or how access will be maintained while works are under way.

At the hearing, Cllr Iona March asked whether an alternative route had been agreed. It has not. Ms Nell Orr, the adjoining occupier, has also raised a practical concern about vehicles turning at the boundary; she is not participating in this examination. We ask Aldercombe Tidal Link Limited to identify the relevant drawing and propose a binding access requirement before the close of the examination.

Yours faithfully,

Mara Fenwick
Solicitor | Vale Bridge Legal

text:
Relevant Representation: Marnwick Eastern Freight Interchange
Application reference: EN012345
From: Nora Pellam
Address for correspondence: 14 Sedgeglass Close, Marnwick, MW4 7QT
Email: nora.pellam@example.org
Interested Party reference: IP-048271

I am writing as a resident of Marnwick, not as a medical expert. I object to the proposal by Marnwick Logistics Ltd in its present form because I do not think the assessment explains what the extra traffic, dust and emissions will mean for people living beside the proposed construction route. I have read the air quality chapter and the non-technical summary, but the figures in them do not sound like the road outside my house on an ordinary weekday. My comments are about that gap, rather than an argument that all development should stop.

I have been diagnosed with asthma. I use a salbutamol inhaler and a daily beclometasone inhaler. I mention this because changes in air quality are not an abstract issue for me, although I understand that my own experience cannot replace proper monitoring. On days when traffic queues on Reedbank Lane, I sometimes have chest tightness by the time I have walked back from the shops. That is what happens now, before any construction lorries are added. I am anxious about what the proposed works could do to the air at the front of the house, and I have slept poorly while trying to understand the plans. Anxiety and poor sleep are not the basis of my objection; the missing local evidence is.

My child, Ivo Pellam, is aged 11 and has autism spectrum disorder. My child receives occupational therapy. The walk to school follows Reedbank Lane because the other route has no continuous pavement. A predictable journey matters in our household, and a long diversion past idling lorries would be difficult. I am not asking the Examining Authority to assume that every child will respond in the same way. I am asking for the assessment to recognise that telling families to change their route is not a simple answer for everyone. Please do not publish my child's details in a version of this letter available to the public.

The transport chapter appears to rely on average daily movements. An average hides the short period around school drop-off, when delivery vans, buses and cars already compete for the bend near the old pump house. If a construction vehicle waits there for a gap, other vehicles tend to idle behind it. I would like the applicant to show a separate forecast for the morning and afternoon school periods, including the days when earthworks and deliveries overlap. The forecast should say which junctions were counted, on what dates, and whether the counts included the delivery traffic from the existing yards.

The dust measures read like standard promises rather than a site-specific plan. The proposed wheel wash is shown within the application site at Gate C, but the drawings do not explain who checks the public road after a vehicle leaves. The site address given in the notices is Gate C, Eastern Yard, Marnwick, MV3 6QP; that is not a residential address. I would welcome a named responsibility in the construction environmental management plan, an inspection log available to residents, and a clear trigger for stopping dusty work when the measures fail. These requests would make the controls easier to understand and enforce, not just longer on paper.

I have lived in this area for over 40 years and know that wind direction makes a difference here. Some afternoons the road dust hangs near the houses; on others it blows away quickly. The assessment's chosen receptor points seem to miss the front gardens on the short stretch between the pump house and the lane junction. Please add a receptor there or explain, in ordinary language, why the existing points represent it. A postcode alone, MW4 7QT, does not tell you which side of the road a person is on or whether a garden faces the traffic.

I also ask for a straightforward complaints process during construction. A web form is useful, but it should not be the only route when somebody wants to report dust while it is happening. The applicant has published consultation@marnwicklogistics.example as a shared project mailbox. Could the examination confirm that this address, or an equivalent monitored contact, will remain in use during the works and that reports will receive a reference number? I do not want residents to have to work out which subcontractor happens to be on shift before a concern can be logged.

At a ward meeting Cllr Eleri Dovant said the main question for the examination was whether the mitigation could be checked in practice. I agree. My concern is not that the air quality consultants have deliberately ignored residents. It is that the submission gives us predicted annual numbers without showing clearly what happens during the busiest hours outside the homes closest to the route. The non-technical summary ought to set out the likely worst construction period and what a resident should do if the stated controls are not being followed.

Please ask Marnwick Logistics Ltd for revised peak-hour information, receptor mapping for Reedbank Lane, and an enforceable monitoring and response plan before deciding whether the air quality effects are acceptable. If the scheme is approved, I ask that HGV movements past the school be restricted at opening and closing times unless a properly evidenced alternative is provided. I would also like any later changes to the route to be advertised locally, rather than appearing only in a technical document. The Planning Inspectorate's general information page, https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate, is helpful, but it cannot substitute for clear notices about this particular scheme.

Thank you for considering this representation. I would be willing to answer written questions about what I have observed, but I do not consent to my personal contact details or my child's information being put on the public register.

Nora Pellam

Supplementary technical note: transport, air quality and construction controls

This note sets out the technical points that I think should be resolved before the examination closes. It concerns the modelling and enforceable controls for Marnwick Eastern Freight Interchange, rather than individual circumstances. In particular, the assessment should show whether the proposed routing arrangement works when the network is congested, not only when vehicles follow an unconstrained modelled route.

The transport assessment uses an average weekday to describe HGV movements. That is a useful starting point, but it can conceal short periods when several vehicles arrive together. The applicant should provide hourly arrival and departure profiles for the construction phase and each operational phase, with the assumptions about gate capacity and booking slots stated. If the model assumes that a vehicle delayed at the entrance will wait inside the site, the drawings should demonstrate sufficient internal stacking space without obstructing the access junction. A swept-path drawing does not, by itself, demonstrate that a queue can be accommodated.

The assessment also needs a sensitivity test for disruption on East Bypass. A closure, roadworks or recurring peak-hour delay could cause drivers approaching from the south to use Old Quarry Lane. It is not enough to label that road an unsuitable route on a plan. The examination should establish how vehicles will be directed, how compliance will be checked and what happens when the designated route is unavailable. The same test should cover vehicles arriving without a booking and vehicles sent by subcontracted hauliers who may not receive the applicant's routing instructions directly.

The traffic figures should be reconciled across the transport assessment, the air quality chapter and the construction programme. At present, the reader cannot easily tell whether the maximum daily HGV figure includes spoil export, deliveries for drainage works and staff-related servicing. A single table, using consistent vehicle definitions, would make the worst-case assumptions auditable. Where different chapters use different years or growth factors, the reason should be explained rather than left to a footnote. The peak construction month is the relevant case for short-term effects; an annual average cannot replace it.

For air quality, I ask for the model inputs at each assessment receptor, including the assumed road speed, fleet mix, background concentration and distance from the carriageway. The receptor schedule should identify why each point was selected and whether it represents the highest likely concentration on that stretch. If a receptor has been placed at a building façade while a public footway is closer to the running lane, that distinction should be clear. The modelling should also test queuing at the site access and at the East Bypass roundabout, since a free-flow speed assumption may understate emissions where vehicles repeatedly stop and start.

The Marnwick Air Quality Action Plan 2025 identifies traffic emissions as an existing concern in the eastern corridor. Compliance with a numerical objective is important, but the decision should also consider the size and distribution of any additional exposure. The applicant should present changes attributable to the development separately from changes expected through fleet turnover. Otherwise an improvement in background conditions could mask a local increase caused by the scheme. The uncertainty discussion should address both the traffic forecast and the emissions factors, not just the dispersion model.

Construction dust controls should be tied to activities and weather conditions. The proposed commitment to damp down exposed ground is too general unless it specifies responsibility, inspection frequency and a trigger for extra action during dry or windy periods. Wheel-washing arrangements should show where vehicles stop, where wash water drains and how mud deposited beyond the access will be removed. The construction management plan should also distinguish ordinary earthworks from periods of intensive material handling. Complaints and inspection records should be reviewed together so that a repeated problem leads to a change in working practice, rather than simply being logged.

Drainage matters because standing water and runoff can affect the operation of dust controls and the condition of adjoining roads. The drainage strategy should confirm the capacity available during each construction phase, before the permanent system is complete. It should identify the route for runoff from temporary stockpiles and the controls that prevent silt reaching the roadside ditch. The maintenance schedule needs to cover temporary as well as permanent features. An outline promise to agree details later would leave a material part of the construction effects untested.

The landscape drawings show proposed planting along the eastern boundary, but mature screening should not be used to describe the appearance at opening. The visual assessment should include the first winter after construction, with lighting and fencing shown at their proposed heights. Planting may soften views over time; it will not immediately screen high-level vehicle movements or illuminated yard equipment. Any lighting condition should specify measurable limits, operating hours and a process for checking the installed scheme against the approved design.

Finally, the draft requirements should be read against the evidence in document TR-07 and the corresponding environmental chapters. Where an assessment relies on a booking system, routing rule, vehicle limit or particular sequence of works, that measure should appear in an enforceable requirement or approved management plan. Monitoring should have a defined start date, reporting interval and corrective-action procedure. Marnwick Borough Council should receive the reports in a form that allows the forecast and recorded vehicle movements to be compared. These are practical checks on the conclusions presented in the application, not a request for another general statement that impacts will be managed.

Health representation – Marnwick Eastern Freight Interchange

I am writing as a resident of Marnwick, following my comments on the draft requirements. I have diagnosed asthma and use a prescribed salbutamol inhaler. My concern is not that every passing lorry will cause a medical emergency, but that the assessment treats the average air-quality figure as if it describes what happens outside our homes during the busiest hours. Dust during construction matters too, particularly if the site entrance and haul routes operate before the road has been cleaned.

My child, Ivo Pellam, has cerebral palsy and is prescribed baclofen. He does not take part in this examination, but the practical effect on our household should still count. On days when the air smells of exhaust, we keep the windows shut. I feel anxious about what the proposed longer operating hours may mean for our wellbeing and sleep. I have lived in Marnwick for over 20 years; this is not a concern based on a single bad afternoon.

I ask Marnwick Logistics Ltd to publish monitoring results at regular intervals and explain what action follows an exceedance. Marnwick Borough Council should receive those results, not just a year-end summary. Cllr Eleri Dovant has also asked for clearer reporting. Please attach an enforceable response procedure to the relevant requirement.

Nora Pellam

text:
RILLFEN SOLAR AND STORAGE PROJECT
Written ecological evidence on hedgerow and night-time lighting effects
Deadline 5 submission | Examination reference EN011247

From: Dr Maren Tallow
Interested Party reference: IP-201376

1. Scope and independence

I submit this evidence in my own capacity as an independent ecologist. It concerns the revised lighting strategy and hedgerow plans lodged by Fellmere Current Energy Ltd at Deadline 4. I support renewable generation in principle. My concern is that the drawings do not yet show how the western access track can be built and operated without interrupting a continuous dark corridor. This is an assessment of the proposal, not of the motives of its designers.

I hold a PhD in landscape ecology and have carried out habitat surveys and lighting reviews for more than 20 years. My fieldwork has included solar sites, roads and wetland restoration schemes. I have lived in the Fallowden area for over 40 years, although local familiarity is no substitute for survey evidence. My age is recorded as aged 48 in the CV supplied with my original representation; that detail has no bearing on my opinion. I have not been instructed or paid by the applicant or by an objectors' group. I have read Oren Pell's filed technical note on bat activity, and agree with its recommendation for a measurable lighting limit rather than an aspiration to minimise spill.

My address and mobile were copied into this version from an earlier covering sheet in error: 17 Wicker Row, Fallowden, FD4 8QN; 07700 900 482. Please use the examination portal for correspondence. The applicant's general ecology mailbox, ecology@fellmerecurrent.example, is suitable for sending questions about the drawings, but it is not my contact address.

2. Material considered and method

I have considered the Environmental Statement ecology chapter, the Deadline 4 Hedgerow Retention Plan (revision C), and the applicant's Lighting Note LN-04. On 8 September 2026 I walked the public rights of way around the western boundary shortly before dusk. I did not enter the application land. Observations from a public path cannot establish occupancy of a roost or a sett, and I have not represented them as doing so. I used a handheld light meter to compare existing conditions along the path; these readings are indicative only because cloud cover changed during the visit.

The plan shows a break in the hedge beside the proposed western access track. On the ground, the hedge links Rillfen Wood with the ditch running north of the former pump house. Bats were seen crossing that link on my visit, but I cannot identify them to species from those observations. The broad statement that there are bat records in Rillfen Wood is useful context, not a location for a particular roost. Equally, the statement in the ecology chapter that badgers use the wider area should not be treated as proof that any one entrance is active.

A separate field note supplied to me for checking contains two locations that should not be reproduced on a public plan. It describes the badger sett as being 18 metres east of the southern gate of Cinder Lane allotments, beneath the second ash from that gate. It also identifies a bat maternity roost in the north attic of the old pump house, behind the easternmost louvre. I mention those details here so the Examining Authority can see why the unedited field note needs restricted handling. They are not necessary to understand the mitigation requested below. The publicly circulated version can say that protected sites have been recorded near the western access corridor, without plotting them.

3. Lighting and construction

LN-04 proposes directional fittings and states that unnecessary lighting will be avoided. It does not give a maximum illuminance at the retained hedge, the hours during which temporary lamps may operate, or the method for checking the completed installation. Those omissions matter more than the choice of fitting shown in the schedule. Headlights from delivery vehicles may also sweep across the gap even when fixed lamps are off. A drawing showing only permanent luminaires will not answer that point.

I recommend a pre-construction lighting plan with a stated limit at the hedge face, a vehicle movement assessment and a commissioning survey after dark. The plan should cover compound lighting as well as the finished development. If a hedge opening is unavoidable, the applicant should identify its width and show how a continuous vegetated link will be restored. Replacement planting is not an immediate substitute for an established hedge, so a temporary dark route should be considered during establishment. The commitment should be secured in the requirements, with a procedure for correcting any exceedance found during operation.

I feel anxious about the possibility of light shining towards homes, and poor sleep has been mentioned at local meetings. Those concerns are relevant to good design, but I do not rely on them as evidence of an ecological effect. I have diagnosed asthma, which can make dusty construction visits difficult for me; that personal circumstance does not change my survey conclusions. The appropriate tests here are the predicted light levels and the effectiveness of the proposed controls.

4. Responses and conclusion

At the community session Cllr Ivo Keld asked whether a post-construction check would be public. I support that suggestion. A resident, Sella Mirk, who is not participating in the examination, pointed out the vehicle turning area to me. She was describing what could be seen from the path, not providing a bat survey, and I have not treated her account as one.

The applicant has made revisions which reduce the likely extent of hedge removal. Nevertheless, an enforceable lighting limit and monitoring arrangement are needed before the western access design can be regarded as settled. A link to the examination library is available through https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate. My earlier, informal photographs were placed at https://fieldnotes.example.org/rillfen-2026; they are background material, not a substitute for the survey reports.

Submitted by Maren Tallow
21 October 2026

RILLFEN SOLAR AND STORAGE PROJECT
Supplementary written evidence on western access and ecology
Maren Tallow, independent ecological witness
21 October 2026

1. Purpose and expertise

This note follows my earlier evidence on the proposed western construction access. It deals with the distinction between a route that is passable on a drawing and one that can be used without changing the ecological effects assessed in the Environmental Statement. I am an independent ecologist with an MSc in Applied Ecology and MCIEEM accreditation. My work for more than 20 years has included bat activity surveys, habitat management plans and examination evidence for infrastructure schemes. I have walked the publicly accessible routes around the Rillfen site on four occasions in 2026 and reviewed the applicant's revised access drawing, lighting schedule and ecology addendum. I have not entered private land without permission.

I am giving this evidence in my own professional capacity. My conclusions concern the information available to the Examining Authority, rather than whether any particular resident supports the project. The matters raised by Sella Mirk at the community walk, as described in my earlier note, prompted me to check the turning geometry. They did not supply survey evidence. Similarly, Cllr Ivo Keld's question at the community session about emergency access was a useful question, not evidence that emergency vehicles will use the western gate routinely.

2. Points on which the documents now agree

Fellmere Current Energy Ltd has moved the temporary compound further from the western hedge and proposes to retain a greater length of the hedge at Gate W3. That is a material improvement. The revised swept-path drawing also shows that an articulated delivery vehicle can turn within the hardstanding if the waiting bay is kept clear. These conclusions can be accepted without accepting that the present lighting commitment is adequate. A line on a drawing marked 'temporary lighting if required' does not identify the height, direction, operating hours or maximum spill of the equipment that might actually be brought to site.

Oren Pell's technical note, submitted separately to this examination, makes a similar point about the difference between the designed arrangement and its operation. I agree with the note's recommendation for a pre-commencement lighting plan. My concern is narrower: the plan needs an enforceable limit at the retained hedge, not merely a promise that fittings will be sensitive. For clarity, I do not suggest that every movement after dusk would have a significant effect. The risk is a succession of small changes, including a relocated lamp or a delivery queuing beside the hedge, which may not be captured by the present drawings.

3. Surveys and protected-species information

The applicant's activity surveys record bats along the western boundary. Bats were also noted around Alderwick Copse; that is a broad habitat description and should not be read as identifying a roost. No conclusion about the use of any individual tree can be drawn from those activity records alone. The ecology addendum proposes a check before vegetation clearance, which I support, but does not say who will approve a change in the access layout if the check finds a constraint. That decision route should be written into the requirement.

One item in my working survey schedule should have been transferred to the restricted ecology annex rather than the publicly available table: the bat maternity roost is in the split ash at grid reference FX 42716 61304, 12 metres south-east of Gate W3. I request that this precise location be withheld from the public version of the table. It is not necessary to publish it to understand my conclusion. The public document can say that a roost constraint has been identified close to the access and that the detailed record has been supplied to the relevant examining and ecological authorities. Badger field signs in the wider Rillfen fields are likewise a reason to maintain a precautionary check, not a reason to publish the position of every feature found during construction.

4. Proposed control

I recommend that the requirement for the construction environmental management plan expressly cover temporary and mobile lighting. Before the western access is used, the undertaker should submit a plan showing fitting positions and heights, beam direction, hours of use, an agreed maximum spill at the retained hedge, and the method of checking compliance on site. The approved plan should apply to replacement fittings as well as the initial installation. A named ecological clerk of works, identified by role in the plan, should be able to require a lamp to be turned or screened immediately if measurements show an exceedance.

The same requirement should provide for a short written record after the first two weeks of access use and after any substantial change to the layout. Photographs are helpful, but a photograph alone will not show whether a lamp met an illuminance limit. If the applicant considers the measurements unnecessary, it should explain how the limit will otherwise be demonstrated. This is a proportionate control for a temporary operation; it does not require a fresh ecological assessment for every delivery.

For comparison, the examination library index is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate. A general account of my earlier site walk is at https://wetlands-diary.example.net/rillfen/western-gate. The latter is an external field-notes page, not an examination document and not the basis of the recommendation above.

5. Conclusion and administrative correction

The western access can, in my opinion, be made acceptable in ecological terms if the lighting and change-control measures are secured before use. I therefore ask the Examining Authority to treat my objection as one to the present wording of the requirement, rather than to the principle of an access at this location. Nothing in this note changes my view that the applicant's reduction in proposed hedge removal is welcome.

My contact sheet was attached to the evidence bundle in error. The home address on it is 17 Wispbarrow Lane, Clovenhush, FH4 8QJ and the personal mobile is 07700 900 487. Neither is needed for publication. Examination correspondence can instead be sent through the case team's generic mailbox, rillfen.case@planning-inspectorate.gov.uk.

Submitted by Maren Tallow

Further evidence: construction drainage and western access

1. Scope of this note

This note considers whether the drainage and construction-phasing material submitted by Fellmere Current Energy Ltd is sufficiently coordinated with the revised western access. It does not reopen the principle of the Rillfen Solar and Storage Project. The issue is whether the proposed controls can be understood, implemented and checked at the point when works move from the access corridor into the adjoining fields. My review concerns the Construction Drainage Strategy, revision C, the Access Arrangement Plan, revision D, and draft Requirement 14 as submitted for the current examination deadline.

2. Existing drainage pattern

The western access crosses a shallow fall towards the Rillfen Cut. The published levels show a local high point near the field gate, with surface water then moving along the southern verge of Wispbarrow Lane before entering the existing ditch network. This is not a steep catchment, but it is one in which a small obstruction can change the direction of overland flow. The strategy acknowledges that possibility; the drawings do not yet show how the temporary haul-road edge will be graded to avoid it.

The applicant’s calculations use the same contributing area for the permanent access and the initial construction compound. That is a conservative starting point for the permanent design, but it does not describe every construction stage. During topsoil stripping, the compacted working width may extend beyond the finished carriageway. Until the permanent swale is connected, runoff from that width will need an identified temporary route. The statement that it will be ‘managed on site’ is not, by itself, a workable construction instruction.

I recommend a drawing showing temporary drainage for each stage in which the western access is in use: formation, utilities installation, panel delivery and reinstatement. It should identify the flow direction, any temporary bunds, the discharge point and the inspection arrangement after heavy rain. This need not be four separate drawings if a single plan distinguishes the stages clearly. The important point is that a site supervisor can identify which arrangement applies on a given day without interpreting an outline strategy.

3. Interface with construction traffic

The Construction Traffic Management Plan assumes that most heavy deliveries will enter from Fenbarrow Road and leave by the same route. The western access is described as available for lighter vehicles and occasional abnormal movements. However, the swept-path sheet depicts a larger vehicle using it without stating whether that movement is exceptional or part of the normal delivery programme. That difference matters to drainage: repeated trafficking at the verge may compress the ground intended to function as an infiltration strip.

The applicant should either confirm a vehicle class and maximum frequency for the western access or demonstrate that the temporary drainage design accommodates the broader use shown on the swept-path sheet. I am not suggesting an arbitrary cap on movements. A clear design assumption would allow the detailed plan, the contractor’s instructions and subsequent monitoring to be checked against the same baseline. It would also avoid treating a change in routing as merely an administrative traffic matter when it could alter the condition of the drainage edge.

There is a related sequencing point. Drawing RFS-TR-204 shows the access wearing course complete before the adjacent swale is planted. If that sequence is retained, a temporary sediment control is needed at the downstream end until vegetation has established. The current note proposes straw bales ‘where required’, but gives no trigger for their use and no indication of how trapped material would be removed without disturbing the swale profile. A simple inspection schedule and removal method would resolve this.

4. Landscape and ecological coordination

The western boundary hedge is retained on the revised plans except at the access opening. That is a welcome reduction in removal, but it leaves little space between the hedge base, the drainage feature and the construction running surface. Detail RFS-LV-118 should therefore show these elements together on one cross-section. At present they appear on separate landscape and engineering sheets with different assumed verge widths. Neither drawing establishes that the intended hedge protection zone will remain outside the area needed for ditch maintenance.

The field margins around Rillfen Cut are used by bats and other wildlife. That broad observation does not identify a roost or establish a reason to exclude works across the whole corridor. It does support retaining an unlit margin, limiting unnecessary night working and ensuring that any temporary water-control installation does not become a permanent break in the boundary vegetation. These matters can be addressed through coordinated detail rather than a further general survey condition.

5. Policy and recommended control

The approach set out above is consistent with the fictional Clovenhush Infrastructure Landscape Policy CLP-7, which requires construction effects to be addressed alongside the final layout, and with the Rillfen Drainage Board’s Technical Standard 2024 on identifiable exceedance routes. Neither document prevents the access. Both point towards drawings that explain what happens before the permanent works are functioning, not solely what the completed development will look like.

I suggest that Requirement 14 be amended so that the detailed construction drainage plan is approved before formation of the western access, rather than before first operation of the solar panels. The plan should include staged drainage arrangements, the agreed traffic-design assumption, inspection and sediment-removal procedures, and a combined cross-section showing the hedge, swale and running surface. Any subsequent change to vehicle use that affects the drainage design should be assessed against that approved plan before the change is made.

Subject to those points, I consider the drainage issue capable of resolution through detailed design. My concern is with the present gap between the strategy, drawings and proposed timing of approval. It should not be read as an objection to the revised access location or to the applicant’s decision to retain more of the western hedge.

4.6 Construction-stage verification

The remaining question is whether the proposed drainage can function while the western access is being formed, before the permanent swale and hedge-edge levels are complete. Drawing RF-DR-214 shows the finished arrangement but does not identify a temporary outfall or the point at which construction traffic ceases to use the compacted strip beside the swale. This is a sequencing issue, not evidence that the final design is unworkable.

Fellmere Current Energy Ltd has indicated that the principal cable deliveries would enter from Merefold Road during Phase 2. The Construction Traffic Management Plan, revision C, assumes a maximum of 24 two-way HGV movements on a peak delivery day. The drainage calculations use a trafficked width of 3.5 metres, whereas the swept-path drawing includes a locally widened passing area. The two drawings should be reconciled: otherwise the impermeable area used in the runoff calculation may be understated. A revised calculation should distinguish the permanent running surface from any temporary stone working area that will be removed and reinstated.

For the Rillfen Solar and Storage Project, I recommend a hold point before bulk delivery traffic begins using the western access. At that point the temporary drainage route should be shown on an as-built plan, with photographs of the silt controls and confirmation that flow cannot discharge directly towards the ditch at the southern field boundary. Inspection after a significant rainfall event would provide a practical check on the assumed flow direction. The approved maintenance schedule should also say who records sediment depth and what threshold triggers removal; a general requirement to 'inspect regularly' is insufficient.

These matters can be secured without altering the access alignment. They are consistent with Policy W3 of the Moorwick Local Infrastructure Plan, which requires construction effects to be addressed as well as the operational design. I therefore maintain the qualified conclusion in paragraph 4.5: detailed approval is needed before formation of the access, with verification before its first substantial use.

5. Qualifications and declaration

5.1 I am Maren Tallow MSc MCIEEM, an independent ecologist instructed to provide evidence on the Rillfen Solar and Storage Project. I have worked on habitat and drainage interfaces for over 20 years and visited the site in September 2025 and March 2026. My conclusions above are my own; I have not undertaken the detailed culvert design. Oren Pell's filed technical note provides the hydraulic calculations, which I have considered but not independently recalculated.

5.2 At the community session Cllr Ivo Keld asked whether the maintenance trigger would be enforceable. My recommendation in paragraph 4.5 addresses that question. Sella Mirk, who lives near the southern field but is not an examination participant, described water standing beside the lane. I have treated this as an observation, not a measured baseline.

Environmental Statement, Appendix 8.4: Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey
Lorn Beck Solar and Storage Project
Prepared by Brindlefield Ecology for Merefen Renewables Ltd, September 2026

8.4.1 Scope and treatment of records
This appendix reports the 2025–26 walkover surveys of the Lorn Beck corridor and adjacent buildings within the proposed Order Limits. The purpose is to inform the crossing design, construction timing and the outline species conservation plan. Survey coverage comprised both banks between the old ford and the southern drainage outfall, together with views of the kiln and pump house from publicly accessible land. Access was not available to every interior space. Absence of a record in those spaces must not be read as absence of a species.

Records below use the project grid, rather than National Grid references, because the survey drawings were prepared on the engineering base. The grid is tied to Drawing 8.4A, which is held separately as a confidential ecological plan. References at different precisions are deliberate: the public habitat overview uses the coarse square SP 42 68, whereas precise field-sign records are supplied for audit. A precise coordinate does not, by itself, mean a breeding or resting place has been found. Copies of the non-confidential survey method can be requested from ecology@brindlefield-ecology.example.

8.4.2 Otter
Otter activity was recorded on three of four visits. Spraint was found on a flat stone at PG 184461 072604, and a second, weathered spraint was found near the drainage outfall. These are field signs only; neither point is described as a holt. Footprints in soft silt and a regularly used bank path were also noted, though heavy rain had removed some impressions before the February visit. Otters may travel the whole beck, including reaches outside the Order Limits. The broad description ‘along Lorn Beck north of Pellwick’ is used in the public figure and is not intended to identify a resting site.

One occupied resting place, recorded as OH-1, was identified at PG 184228 072413, beneath the root plate of the leaning ash on the left bank, 14 m downstream of the old ford. Fresh bedding material and repeated entries were recorded without inserting equipment into the cavity. A second place, OH-2, was assessed as a probable holt at PG 184391 072558, under the west abutment of Cresset Farm footbridge. Its status remains uncertain because the opening could not be watched through a complete dusk period. Both places are treated as active for the impact assessment. References to OH-1 and OH-2 elsewhere in this appendix are record identifiers, not additional location information.

The proposed cable crossing has been moved from an open-cut alignment to a trenchless one. Entry and exit compounds are shown beyond the vegetated banks on Drawing 8.4B. The construction method statement must prohibit lighting directed at the channel and prevent storage of fuel, spoil or fencing materials against the bank. A pre-start check is required because flood events can create new resting places. If a new holt is found, work in the affected reach should stop while the ecological clerk of works advises on a revised method and any necessary consent. These controls apply whether or not a particular sign was recorded on a survey day.

8.4.3 Schedule 1 birds
The survey considered breeding opportunities as well as incidental sightings. Kingfisher was seen travelling along the lower beck on two mornings. An occupied nest tunnel, coded KB-1, was confirmed in the vertical bank at PG 184507 072681, 6 m upstream of the timber sluice on the east bank. Observation was from the opposite bank, and no attempt was made to measure the tunnel. The wider reach is shown as potential foraging habitat at SP 42 68 on the public constraints figure. That coarse square should not be substituted for the confidential nest record when setting out works.

Barn owl pellets were found on a beam in Fenward Pump House at PG 184556 072705. Pellets are evidence of use, not evidence of nesting, and the visit could not establish when they were deposited. A barn owl nest was, however, confirmed in the second ventilation opening from the east on the north wall of Fenward Pump House, at PG 184574 072719. The building is outside the permanent development footprint but within the area potentially affected by temporary night lighting. The design must therefore use cowled fittings, with the light-facing side of the building checked before the final compound layout is approved.

For comparison, a robin nest was noted in a hedge at PG 184801 072936. It is included in the ordinary nesting-bird constraint, not the Schedule 1 register. Bird activity was also reported around Cradlewood Copse, about a kilometre north-west of Pellwick; that account is too imprecise to establish a nest location. Mr Devlin Wray, who lives at Hushacre Farm, said he had watched kingfishers on the beck for 40+ years. His account is useful context but does not replace the dated survey records. His correspondence address, 4 Ford Fold, Pellwick, PN4 8QJ, is not needed to understand the ecological conclusion. Cllr Orla Fenwick also asked at the community meeting whether the footbridge would remain open during works; access arrangements are addressed in Chapter 11.

8.4.4 Conservation plan and limitations
No bank reprofiling is proposed within the otter corridor. The trenchless crossing, retained marginal vegetation and a no-night-working rule beside the beck are the principal avoidance measures. Temporary fencing is to leave a continuous route along the watercourse, without loose netting that might trap wildlife. The contractor's induction should distinguish an otter spraint point from a holt: treating every sign as a resting place would make the drawings misleading, but ignoring signs would make the pre-start check ineffective.

Work close to the confirmed bird nesting features is to be programmed outside the breeding period where practicable. Where that is not possible, the ecological clerk of works will inspect the affected area before work begins and specify a stand-off appropriate to the activity observed. No fixed distance is offered here as a substitute for that assessment. The measures will be carried into the detailed construction environmental management plan and reviewed if the final design changes. The records represent conditions during the survey visits, not a guarantee that the same individual animals or nesting features will be present throughout construction.

Appendix E7: Otter and Schedule 1 bird survey note
Lorn Beck Solar and Storage Project

E7.1 Scope and recording convention

Brindlefield Ecology prepared this note for Merefen Renewables Ltd to explain the survey records behind the ecological constraints drawings. It should be read with the watercourse plan and the construction environmental management plan, rather than used as a clearance certificate. The walkovers covered Lorn Beck, its connected ditches and the proposed cable crossing. Surveyors recorded signs visible from lawful access points; steep banks and high water prevented close inspection of some reaches. A blank record therefore means no sign was confirmed on that visit, not that the reach cannot be used.

The location references below use the project's local survey grid, not the National Grid. A two-figure pair such as LB 42 63 identifies an approximately 1 km square and is suitable for discussing general distribution. Five-figure pairs are plotted positions from the field tablet, checked against the surveyed bank line. They should not be converted into public wayfinding directions. Photograph numbers and habitat descriptions in the working survey sheets are retained so that the ecological clerk of works can relocate a feature without circulating its position more widely.

E7.2 Otter evidence

Otter signs occurred on both sides of the proposed crossing within LB 42 63. Two spraints were found on exposed stones, one with fish remains, and a short run of prints crossed soft silt after rain. These are field signs, not proof of a breeding site. An older slide on the western bank could not be attributed confidently because livestock use the same gap. Survey conditions were better in September than in the May visit, when the beck was running high and several bankside ledges were under water.

One enclosed feature was assessed as a probable otter holt: local survey grid LB 42186 63974, beneath the south-bank rootplate of the second alder upstream of the old sluice. Loose bedding was visible just inside the opening; no camera or intrusive inspection was used. Its status could change, and the absence of an animal during a daytime visit must not be read as abandonment. A possible lie-up recorded elsewhere in the beck corridor is shown only at watercourse-reach level on the public constraints plan because the evidence there was less certain.

The cable design currently avoids excavation within the beck banks. Before temporary fencing or vegetation clearance, the ecological clerk of works should check the relevant reach for fresh prints, spraint and entrances, then agree the working limit with the site manager. No lighting is to face the bank overnight. If an occupied resting place could be affected, work in that part of the corridor must stop while the ecologist reviews the method and any licensing requirement. The drawings deliberately do not turn every spraint point into a fixed exclusion zone.

E7.3 Birds

Kingfishers were seen along Lorn Beck during two visits, but a bird flying along a channel does not, by itself, establish a nest. Devlin Wray's account of regular kingfisher sightings from Little Sallow Farm is consistent with the survey record; it does not fix a breeding location or establish that the same pair was present on each occasion. The general flight corridor is described as the beck through LB 42 63. Reedbed at Fenmarsh Pool also supported calling water rails, for which the survey found no nest. These observations should remain in the broad habitat schedule, not on a point-feature map.

A fresh kingfisher nesting tunnel was confirmed at local survey grid LB 42611 63502, in the vertical face of the eastern drainage cutting opposite marker post C17. Adults entered the tunnel carrying fish during the June visit. This is a Schedule 1 nesting feature and its plotted position is provided in the restricted construction copy only. The face appeared intact at the final visit, although the surveyors could not determine when use ended. No other confirmed Schedule 1 nest was recorded within the working area. An old hole farther downstream was not treated as occupied: it lacked fresh spoil and no bird entered it during the observation period.

The current layout leaves the drainage cutting outside the permanent works. That separation does not remove the risk from temporary compounds, piling noise or people using the bank as a shortcut. Work close to the confirmed feature should be scheduled outside the breeding period where practicable. If that is not possible, a competent ecologist must inspect before activity starts and set an activity-specific stand-off. There must be no attempt to block or probe a tunnel to establish whether it is in use. Any change to the access route or compound boundary requires the bird record to be checked again.

E7.4 Public access and follow-up

Cllr Orla Fenwick asked whether the proposed footbridge diversion would bring walkers nearer the beck during construction. The present diversion follows the existing surfaced path and does not require entry to either surveyed bank. The contractor should mark that route clearly; an informal path forming at the water's edge would need prompt review. This is an access-management measure as well as an ecological one, and it can be implemented without displaying sensitive point locations on public notices.

The pre-start checks, stop-work procedure and record of any revised stand-offs will be included in the detailed construction environmental management plan. Merefen Renewables Ltd should retain the restricted feature sheet for the site team and publish only the reach-level version with general habitat measures. If the programme slips into a later breeding season, the bird checks must be repeated. Likewise, a change to the crossing method requires a fresh assessment of otter resting-place risk. The survey records describe what was observed on particular days; they are not a prediction that individual animals will remain in, or stay away from, the same locations.

6.8 Residual effects and monitoring

Brindlefield Ecology has reviewed the reach-level records alongside the revised construction sequence for the Lorn Beck Solar and Storage Project. The temporary crossing is now programmed before cable trenching, so the bankside working area can be reinstated before the wider haul route is removed. No change is proposed to the permanent drainage outfalls.

Badger activity was recorded in the wider Brindle Copse survey area, but the public ecology plan shows only habitat compartments, not individual field signs. Bat activity along Lorn Beck was highest at the tree-lined margins; low-spill lighting and a no-lighting buffer remain embedded measures. The proposed replacement planting is intended to strengthen that corridor, rather than compensate for a confirmed loss of roost habitat.

Merefen Renewables Ltd will report any departure from the approved working method through the construction environmental management plan. On that basis, residual effects are assessed as not significant, subject to the pre-start checks and the agreed stop-work procedure.
