MEREFIELD BOROUGH COUNCIL
Local Impact Report: Larch Fen Link Development Consent Order
Planning Inspectorate reference: EN020487
Submitted 21 October 2026

1. Purpose and status

This Local Impact Report is submitted by Merefield Borough Council in relation to the proposed Larch Fen Link, promoted by Veymere Infrastructure Ltd. It describes likely effects within the borough, rather than setting out a final view on whether development consent should be granted. The Council’s postal address is Civic Offices, 14 Lantern Square, Merefield, MF4 8QN. General correspondence can be sent to planning@merefield.gov.uk; documents for this examination may be sent to larchfen@merefield.gov.uk. The Council has used the guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects when preparing this report.

The assessment draws on the Environmental Statement, the applicant’s September 2026 traffic note, ward-level evidence and comments received by the Council up to 14 October 2026. It should be read with the Council’s written representation. Matters capable of being secured through requirements or the draft development consent order are identified below. The Council has not treated every construction inconvenience as a reason to oppose the scheme, but the cumulative effect on the eastern villages needs a clearer account.

2. Local setting

The route crosses the low fields between Merefield and Little Broom, runs alongside Dray Brook and joins the existing carriageway near Lantern Junction. Plot 19 is presently used as a temporary compound in the application drawings. Much of the land is agricultural, with narrow lanes, informal walking routes and open views across the floodplain. The settlements are small, so a modest increase in heavy vehicle movements may be noticeable even where forecast traffic remains below the capacity of a junction.

Cllr Perran Wyle, ward member for Little Broom, told the Council’s public committee that access to the school and surgery must remain practical during the works. Cllr Juno Hartwell asked whether the proposed diversion of Bridleway 4 could be signed before the existing route closes. Marin Dalby MP has also written to the Council asking that construction information be available in paper form, as not all households use the project website. These points are reported as local concerns; they are not substitutes for the technical assessments.

3. Construction traffic and amenity

The principal construction access is proposed from Lantern Junction. The Council welcomes the removal of through-HGV movements from Marsh Lane in the revised construction traffic management plan. However, the plan still describes deliveries as occurring in ‘normal working hours’ without stating how vehicles arriving early will be held off the public highway. The nearest suitable holding area should be identified before construction starts, with a complaint route that does not rely solely on a web form.

One resident, Ms Elira Voss, lives at 7 Alder Cottages, Merefield, MF4 6RX and is not a participant in the examination. The resident reported chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and described difficulty keeping windows open during dry-weather dust from existing traffic. The Council includes the account to explain why enforceable dust monitoring and prompt responses to complaints matter locally; it does not suggest that the scheme caused the condition. The resident is aged 74. Other residents have described poor sleep and stress about the prospect of night works. Those descriptions should be understood as reported effects, not medical diagnoses.

The Council has heard from people who have lived in the area for over 40 years and recall standing water on Marsh Lane after heavy rain. Their observations are useful context but do not replace the flood modelling. A condition requiring advance notice of abnormal loads, with a telephone option for reporting blocked access, would be proportionate. The applicant should also state whether temporary traffic lights will be staffed at school start and finish times.

4. Ecology and water

Dray Brook and its adjoining hedges form a continuous corridor through the application site. The Council does not dispute that the proposed drainage ponds could provide habitat in time, but asks for a maintenance schedule and a clear trigger for remedial planting where new hedges fail. Badger activity has been recorded in Robin’s Copse; this is a broad location and is included here to explain the need for an updated pre-construction survey.

For the confidential ecology schedule only, the Council’s survey records a badger sett in the bank immediately behind gate F2 on Plot 18, at the eastern end of Dray Brook crossing. This detail must not appear on publicly available mapping. A possible bat maternity roost was also recorded in the hollow ash 12 metres south of Culvert C3 on the eastern boundary of Plot 18. The Council asks the Examining Authority to consider whether the proposed ecological management requirement gives enough time for repeat surveys and any necessary licence applications. General references to bats using the Dray Brook corridor do not establish the location of a roost.

5. Community facilities and recommended action

The playing field at Little Broom is used for weekend fixtures and as an informal meeting place. Dust suppression near the field, protection of pedestrian access and reinstatement of the boundary path should be expressly included in the construction environmental management plan. Temporary closures should be shown on a single, dated plan, rather than being dispersed across contractor notices. The Council also requests a quarterly report of complaints, responses and unresolved actions during the main earthworks period.

Nerys Pell MRTPI, Senior Planning Officer, Merefield Borough Council, compiled the officer evidence for this report. For technical queries the direct number is 01632 960418 and the individual work address is nerys.pell@merefield.gov.uk; general examination correspondence should instead use larchfen@merefield.gov.uk. The Council’s Interested Party reference is IP-204817.

Subject to satisfactory controls on construction traffic, drainage, dust and ecological survey work, the Council considers that a number of the local impacts could be managed. It asks the Examining Authority to test the wording of those controls with the applicant, particularly the arrangements for early deliveries and the procedure for notifying residents without internet access.

Merefield Borough Council
21 October 2026

6. Technical assessment of local effects

6.1 Scope and evidence

This part of the Local Impact Report records the Council’s assessment of the effects likely to arise within Merefield Borough from the Larch Fen Link. It is based on the application drawings, the Transport Assessment (document APP-061), the Environmental Statement and the draft Construction Environmental Management Plan. References to proposed controls describe the application as submitted; they should not be read as confirmation that the wording is adequate. The Council has concentrated on effects at the construction compounds, the eastern junction and the low-lying land beside Larch Fen Drain.

6.2 Traffic and access

Veymere Infrastructure Ltd proposes to bring most heavy goods vehicles to the main compound from the B472 Fenway, with a smaller number using the A616 Merefield Road for the eastern works. The submitted assignment places the highest construction flow in month 11. The Transport Assessment gives a daily total but does not consistently distinguish loaded trips from return movements in its junction tables. This matters because the B472/Fenway Lane priority junction has limited storage between the give-way line and the level crossing approach. A short queue could therefore affect through traffic even where the model reports an acceptable average delay.

The Council’s review of the junction model finds that the base-year turning counts are broadly representative of a typical weekday. They do not, however, capture the seasonal movement of agricultural vehicles during the autumn harvest. The Council does not suggest that a further year of counts is necessary. A sensitivity run using the higher construction peak and an allowance for slow-moving vehicles would provide a proportionate check before the examination closes. The same run should report maximum queue lengths, not only mean delay.

The proposed Construction Traffic Management Plan identifies delivery routes and signage, but its current version leaves the start time for abnormal loads to agreement after consent. The Council seeks a defined booking procedure, limits on simultaneous arrivals at the B472 access, and a requirement to keep the public highway clear while vehicles wait for admission. These measures can sit within the plan, provided the relevant requirement makes approval and subsequent compliance enforceable. The Council also seeks a drawing showing how temporary access to the Fenway Lane maintenance track would be retained during surfacing works.

6.3 Landscape and visual effects

The route crosses an open area of reclaimed pasture between Merefield Ridge and Larch Fen Drain. Existing hedges contain views from the west, while the eastern embankment is visible over longer distances because the land falls towards the drain. The photomontages use appropriate winter viewpoints, although viewpoint LF-07 appears to have been taken before the existing reed margin was cut. That difference should be noted in the final viewpoint schedule rather than treated as evidence of additional screening.

The Environmental Statement identifies a moderate adverse operational effect at the eastern embankment in year 1, reducing as planting establishes. The Council considers that conclusion reasonable if the proposed hedge belt is delivered in full. The landscape plan currently shows a maintenance strip between the planting and the drainage swale but does not state its width. This should be fixed on an approved plan so that future maintenance does not progressively remove the hedge. Replacement planting should be secured for five growing seasons, with an inspection at the end of that period. The Council does not seek continuous tree cover across the open fen, which would itself alter the character identified in the Merefield Landscape Character Study 2022.

6.4 Drainage and flood risk

Surface water from the paved sections would discharge through attenuation basins to Larch Fen Drain. The submitted calculations use the 1 in 100 year event with a climate-change allowance and show no increase in the modelled peak discharge. On that basis, the principle of restricted discharge is acceptable. There is, however, an inconsistency between the basin volumes in drainage drawing LF-D-104 and those in the hydraulic calculation appendix. The Council requests one reconciled schedule identifying storage volume, outlet size, exceedance route and the body responsible for maintenance at each outfall.

Ground levels around the eastern compound are close to the mapped floodplain. The proposed temporary stockpile area is shown outside the design flood extent, but the plans do not identify a safe location for excavated material during a prolonged wet period. The final construction drainage plan should require stockpiles to remain clear of the swale, the drain easement and the overland flow path marked on drawing LF-D-109. A simple inspection record following heavy rainfall would assist in demonstrating that the controls are being followed. These are construction-management matters and do not, in the Council’s view, require a change to the permanent drainage strategy.

6.5 Phasing and policy conclusion

The programme divides construction into western earthworks, the central crossing and eastern tie-in. Its narrative says these phases may overlap, whereas the traffic assessment models a sequence with only limited overlap. The draft Construction Environmental Management Plan should specify the activities that can operate concurrently and the trigger for revisiting the traffic assumptions if the programme changes. It should also identify when temporary drainage must be in place relative to vegetation clearance and topsoil stripping. Approval of a programme alone would not provide that control.

The relevant development-plan tests are set out in Policies MLP-T4, MLP-L2 and MLP-W6 of the Merefield Local Plan 2024. The scheme is capable of meeting those policies in respect of transport safety, landscape integration and water management, subject to the clarifications above and appropriately worded requirements. This is a conditional assessment of local effects, not a finding that the application documents already contain every necessary detail. The Council asks the Examining Authority to examine the outstanding drawings and controls together so that an improvement in one discipline does not create an avoidable effect in another.

4.3 Transport and access

The Council has reviewed the junction modelling submitted by Veymere Infrastructure Ltd for the Larch Fen Link against the 2024 base and the proposed opening-year scenario. The model shows a reduction in through traffic on Little Broom Road, but the forecast increase at the Broom Cross junction is sensitive to the assumed proportion of construction vehicles arriving from the east. The transport assessment uses a single average daily profile for deliveries. That is useful for identifying broad capacity effects, but it does not demonstrate how the junction would operate during the overlapping peak of earthworks and bridge-component deliveries. The Council requests a sensitivity run using the maximum weekly delivery schedule in the construction programme. This is a request for a further test, not a conclusion that the junction is unsafe.

The proposed temporary access from Fen Lane would require widening at the bend immediately north of the application site. The swept-path drawings show the design vehicle entering and leaving, although they do not show two such vehicles passing or the position of temporary traffic signals during verge works. Requirement 12 should therefore prevent use of that access until a detailed layout, signal arrangement and reinstatement scheme have been approved. The submitted Construction Traffic Management Plan should also distinguish deliveries to the eastern compound from deliveries to the bridge works. Routing all vehicles by reference to one compound risks understating movements across the village section of Fen Lane.

4.4 Public rights of way

The permanent diversion of Bridleway LB/7 is shown on drawing LFL-TR-014 Rev C. Its gradient appears acceptable on the longitudinal section, but the drawing does not establish the usable width beside the proposed drainage ditch. The ditch could become a practical constraint if fencing or maintenance access were subsequently added between it and the bridleway. A dimensioned cross-section should be secured before the relevant works commence. The Council also seeks a clear trigger for opening the replacement route before the existing section closes. A general commitment to maintain access throughout construction would not resolve a short gap between those operations.

4.5 Landscape and visual effects

The Council agrees with the landscape assessment that the most pronounced operational change would be seen from the western approach to Little Broom, where the embankment would interrupt the present open view across Larch Fen. Planting could soften that effect over time but would not screen the upper part of the embankment at opening. The photomontage labelled Viewpoint 8 usefully illustrates the year-15 condition; it should not be treated as representative of the first years of operation. The Council asks for an additional winter opening-year view, prepared using the finished ground levels and the proposed safety barrier.

The landscape drawings identify a mixed native hedge along the southern boundary. In the Council’s view, its continuity matters more than the precise mix shown at this stage, provided the species schedule remains appropriate to the site. The draft landscape requirement should specify replacement of failed planting for five years after completion and identify who will maintain the planted areas during that period. It should also require approval of the final landform at the western tie-in. These details would make the proposed mitigation capable of being delivered and assessed; they would not remove the underlying change in the character of the fen-edge landscape.

4.6 Water and ground conditions

The drainage strategy proposes attenuation before discharge to the existing field-drain network. Its calculations use the impermeable area of the completed highway. They do not separately quantify the area that may be exposed during the first earthworks phase, when temporary haul roads, stripped ground and stockpiles could coincide. As noted above, the timing of temporary drainage is therefore material. The Council recommends that the relevant requirement identify the controls that must be operating before each phase of stripping begins, rather than relying only on approval of an overall programme.

The outfall detail on drawing LFL-DR-022 Rev B shows an energy-dissipation apron but leaves its final level subject to survey. That is a reasonable approach to detailed design if the permitted discharge rate and the location of the outfall remain fixed. It would not be reasonable for a later approval to move the outfall into a different receiving ditch without an assessment of the changed effects. The Council asks that the drainage requirement draw that distinction expressly. The maintenance schedule should also cover access to the attenuation basin after completion, including removal of accumulated sediment, without assuming that routine access can take place from the bridleway.

4.7 Ecology and construction phasing

The ecological baseline records badger activity in Larch Fen Wood and bat foraging along the wider hedge network. These are broad habitat observations, not evidence that the planting proposals can be deferred until the end of the entire project. Where a hedge is removed to form a temporary access, the drawings should show whether it will be reinstated when that access closes or only when the last compound is cleared. The Council favours reinstatement at the earliest practicable phase, subject to safe construction access and seasonal planting conditions.

The application proposes three main construction phases. Several management plans, however, define their own work areas and do not use the same phase boundaries. This makes it difficult to check whether noise screening, temporary drainage and route diversions will be in place together. A single phase plan, with consistent boundaries and hold points cross-referenced in the relevant requirements, would assist both implementation and enforcement.

Overall, the Council considers the scheme capable of complying with Policies MLP-T4, MLP-L2 and MLP-W6, subject to the further modelling, drawings and controls identified in this report. That conclusion concerns the management of local impacts. It does not depend on every detailed design decision being made now, but it does require the draft requirements to set enforceable limits on the decisions left for later approval.

6. Matters requiring further definition

6.1 This section sets out the technical information which Merefield Borough Council considers necessary before the local effects of the Larch Fen Link can be adequately controlled. It should be read alongside the preceding conclusion on phase boundaries. Veymere Infrastructure Ltd has provided an outline design envelope, rather than a final construction layout. That approach is reasonable for a project of this scale, provided the limits of deviation and the approval requirements work together. At present, several drawings show the maximum land take but not the circumstances in which that land would be used.

Traffic and access

6.2 The transport assessment assigns construction traffic to the B2147 Fenway Road and the A6182 Merefield Road. Its weekday peak-hour forecasts are based on an average delivery profile. The busiest forecast month of earthworks, however, includes deliveries of imported granular material and removal of unsuitable soils. Those movements may overlap with bridge-deck deliveries. The Council requests a sensitivity test for that combined month, using the proposed daily cap on heavy goods vehicles rather than the average daily flow. The test should report queue lengths at Fenway Roundabout and the two temporary site-access junctions, as well as journey-time changes along the bus corridor. A daily cap alone will not control a concentration of vehicles within the school-run period.

6.3 The draft Construction Traffic Management Plan proposes booking slots but does not state how early arrivals will be handled if a delivery is refused entry. The Council does not support informal waiting on Fenway Road. A defined off-highway holding arrangement should be approved before the first bulk-material movement, with a record of booked and actual arrival times made available for monitoring. The plan should also identify who can stop deliveries when queues extend beyond the site access. This is an operational control, not a request for a further highway design option. The swept-path drawings should be updated to reflect the same vehicle lengths used in the traffic assessment; the current drawings and assessment use different design vehicles.

Landscape and visual effects

6.4 The landscape figures show the permanent embankment against a single, mature planting scenario. They do not adequately illustrate the first five years after opening, when replacement hedgerows will provide limited screening. The Council asks for additional winter viewpoints from the public rights of way around East Mere and the approach to Larch Fen Wood. The viewpoints should use a consistent eye level and show both the proposed earthworks and any lighting columns. The Council does not seek to remove all views of the link. It seeks an assessment which distinguishes the temporary exposure caused by construction from the longer-term change in landform.

6.5 Policy MLP-L2 requires the scheme to respond to the local pattern of field boundaries. In the submitted parameter plan, a planting strip ends at the edge of the bridge works, leaving an unexplained gap between two proposed hedgerows. The detailed landscape scheme should show how that gap is treated without compromising visibility splays or maintenance access. Species schedules, establishment periods and replacement obligations should be secured by a requirement that applies to every phase, including any phase delivered after the main carriageway opens. An illustrative planting drawing should not be the sole measure of compliance.

Drainage and water environment

6.6 The flood-risk assessment models the completed attenuation basins, but the temporary drainage note assumes that excavated areas will discharge through settlement measures selected by the contractor. The note gives no maximum disturbed area for each phase. As a result, it is not possible to verify whether the proposed temporary measures have sufficient capacity during the period before the permanent basins become operational. The Council requests a construction-phase drainage schedule showing the contributing area, discharge point, treatment measure and exceedance route for each phase. These matters should be approved before topsoil stripping within that phase, rather than after the relevant earthworks have begun.

6.7 The permanent design proposes a controlled discharge to Merefield Drain. The modelling should confirm that the stated restriction applies to all outfalls serving the highway, including drainage from the bridge approaches. It should also explain how flows will be managed when an outfall is temporarily unavailable for maintenance. Policy MLP-W6 does not require the Council to select the detailed proprietary equipment, but it does require a demonstrable means of limiting runoff and maintaining treatment over the life of the scheme. The maintenance schedule should therefore identify inspection frequencies, access arrangements and the body responsible for keeping the basins functional.

Ecology and construction interface

6.8 The environmental statement records badger activity in the wider Larch Fen Wood area. This is a broad description of habitat use, not a location for construction setting-out. The Council's concern is that the ecological protection measures, haul-road layout and temporary drainage drawings have been prepared at different stages. A coordinated pre-commencement drawing should show working limits, retained vegetation, exclusion fencing and drainage controls together. It should be updated following the required pre-construction surveys, with any necessary changes approved before works begin in the affected phase.

Requirements and monitoring

6.9 The draft requirements refer variously to ‘substantial accordance’, ‘general accordance’ and approval of details. Where a parameter plan sets a measurable limit, the relevant requirement should say so expressly. Where a document is illustrative, the requirement should identify the outcome that the later design must achieve. This distinction matters particularly for access geometry, drainage discharge and the continuity of landscape planting. The Council recommends a compliance table linking each mitigation commitment to its drawing, requirement, delivery phase and proposed monitoring record.

6.10 Subject to those changes, the Council does not identify a technical reason why the outstanding details must all be fixed before a decision on the application. It does consider that the examination should establish the worst-case traffic position and a workable sequence for temporary and permanent drainage. Leaving either matter wholly to post-consent approval would make it difficult to judge compliance with Policy MLP-T4 or Policy MLP-W6. The requested information is proportionate to the identified local effects and can be supplied without changing the principal alignment of the Larch Fen Link.

7. Transport and access

7.1 The Council has reviewed the Transport Assessment Addendum submitted by Veymere Infrastructure Ltd for the Larch Fen Link. The principal local effect is the redistribution of traffic between Fenbank Road, the B4176 Merefield Road and the proposed western junction. The model predicts a reduction in through-traffic on Fenbank Road after opening, but the morning peak results at the western junction remain sensitive to the assumed proportion of heavy goods vehicles. The Council requests a sensitivity run using the upper end of the applicant's construction-traffic estimate alongside forecast operational traffic. Although these flows would not ordinarily occur at the same intensity, the run would test the resilience of the junction during the transition between construction and opening.

7.2 The submitted queue plots use five-minute intervals. These are suitable for comparison between options but can obscure short periods in which a right-turn queue blocks the ahead lane. The Council recommends that the applicant provide maximum queue lengths, rather than averages alone, for the B4176 Merefield Road western approach and the Fenbank Road arm. The results should be compared with the available stacking lengths shown on the junction drawings. A change to the junction layout is not requested at this stage; the purpose is to establish whether the design envelope assessed in the Environmental Statement remains adequate.

7.3 The proposed temporary closure of Willow Drove is shown for 14 weeks in the indicative programme. The diversion has sufficient width for general traffic, but the submitted drawings do not show how farm machinery would pass the temporary signal equipment at the southern tie-in. The construction traffic management plan should include a swept-path drawing for the largest vehicle reasonably expected on the route and identify how signal positions will be adjusted if the temporary carriageway is narrowed. Signs for the closure should be installed before the first works affect the existing carriageway, not merely before the formal closure date.

8. Landscape and visual effects

8.1 The Council accepts the landscape character areas used in the Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment. However, the assessment of the cutting north of Alder Mere appears to rely on planting at its mature height when describing the year-one effect. The Council asks for the year-one and year-15 conclusions to be presented separately in the next schedule of effects. In particular, the visual effect from the permissive path along the eastern embankment should not be described as screened until the proposed hedgerow and woodland edge have established.

8.2 The planting schedule provides a reasonable mix of native woodland-edge and wet-ground species. Its delivery would depend on the drainage design retaining suitable rooting conditions at the toe of the embankment. The Council therefore recommends one coordinated drawing showing the swale profile, maintenance access and planting zones at a common scale. This would avoid a later conflict in which the access strip is kept clear by removing part of the planting relied upon for visual mitigation. Replacement planting should be assessed at the end of each growing season for the first five years, with failures replaced in the following planting season.

8.3 At the East Mere Overbridge, the proposed parapet finish is described only as a muted colour. The Council does not seek a particular product, but a requirement should secure approval of a colour and finish sample before installation. The sample should be considered with the adjoining retaining panels and safety fencing, because these elements will be seen together from the open fen to the east. The lighting drawings should also confirm that no permanent column lighting is proposed along the elevated section. Task lighting needed for maintenance can be controlled separately.

9. Drainage and water environment

9.1 The drainage strategy identifies separate catchments for the northern cutting, central embankment and southern tie-in. This approach is appropriate in principle. The remaining issue is the order in which temporary interception ditches, settlement measures and permanent outfalls will become operational. The submitted programme shows earthworks beginning in the northern cutting before the permanent outfall to Larch Drain is complete. A phase-specific water management drawing is needed to demonstrate that runoff from exposed ground will not be discharged directly to the drain during this interval.

9.2 The Council's review of the hydraulic note found that the modelled design event includes a climate-change allowance, but the storage table does not distinguish between available volume and the volume occupied by permanent water. The applicant should provide a reconciled table for each basin, using the same basin identifiers as the general arrangement drawings. The table should state the design-event inflow, restricted discharge, usable storage and freeboard. This is a request for clarity about the assessed scheme rather than for additional land or a different discharge destination.

9.3 The maintenance schedule assigns inspection of culverts and trash screens but does not explain access when the southern basin is at its design water level. The detailed drainage design should show a safe maintenance route and a turning area outside the basin's active storage volume. Where an access track crosses a swale, its crossing should maintain the swale's conveyance capacity. These matters can be addressed through the detailed design requirement, provided the requirement expressly preserves the storage and treatment performance assessed in the application.

10. Construction phasing and policy conclusion

10.1 The Council recommends a single construction phasing plan which identifies the opening of haul routes, temporary drainage controls, installation of landscape earthworks and removal of temporary compounds. The plan should distinguish works needed before each road closure from works that can follow it. It should also identify hold points for inspection of drainage controls before large-scale excavation begins. This would make the sequence enforceable without preventing reasonable adjustments to the contractor's programme.

10.2 Subject to the further transport information and the controls described above, the Council considers the scheme capable of compliance with Policy MLP-T4 and Policy MLP-W6. The examination should test the junction's worst-case operation and the temporary drainage sequence before the requirements are finalised. Detailed materials, planting zones and maintenance access may then be approved under those requirements, provided they remain within the environmental effects assessed for the Larch Fen Link.

11. Community effects and conclusion

11.1 Merefield Borough Council, Civic Offices, 14 Lantern Square, Merefield MF4 8QJ, has reviewed the applicant’s updated construction programme. Cllr Perran Wyle reported continuing concern about access to Little Broom during weekend works. Cllr Juno Hartwell asked whether the proposed bridleway diversion would be signed before the existing route closes. Marin Dalby MP has written to the Council seeking a clear public timetable. These points should be addressed in the construction traffic management plan, rather than left to informal contractor notices.

11.2 A resident, Ms Elira Voss, described poor sleep during earlier survey works. The Council records this as a concern about potential disturbance, not evidence of an assessed health effect. Comments on this report may be sent to planning@merefield.gov.uk. General guidance on the examination process is available at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects.

Prepared for Merefield Borough Council by Nerys Pell MRTPI, Senior Planning Officer.

text:
Relevant representation concerning the Alderfen East Link DCO
Application reference: XX010947

From: Nera Pell
Interested Party reference: IP-482716
Address: 14 Reedcap Row, Lower Vey, ZX4 7QP
Email: nera.pell@personalmail.example

I object to the proposed link road in its present form. I am not against improving the junction, and I know the existing road can be difficult at school times. But the plans put a new embankment much closer to homes than the consultation leaflet led us to expect. The drawings are hard to compare because the house numbers are missing from some sheets. I have lived here for over 20 years and had to go to the library to print the plans at a size where I could read them.

My home faces the proposed construction access. The applicant says deliveries will usually happen during normal working hours, but ‘usually’ leaves a lot of room for early lorries and weekend work. The turning area appears directly opposite our front windows. At present we hear traffic from the old road mainly when the wind is in our direction. A standing queue of engines, reversing alarms and lights at the new entrance would be a different thing. Please ask Merehaven Linkways Ltd to provide a drawing showing the access and lighting in relation to each occupied house, not only the edge of the highway.

I raised this at the drop-in event with Pavin Rusk of Merehaven Linkways Ltd. The response was that the compound layout was ‘indicative’ and might move. An indicative layout cannot be used to reassure residents about effects which depend on precisely where the gate ends up. The follow-up email from pavin.rusk@merehaven-linkways.example gave no revised plan. The project mailbox, consultations@merehaven-linkways.example, sent me another copy of the same overview drawing. I am not criticising the staff for answering as best they could; I am asking for information that can actually be checked.

Our neighbour, Mrs Vela Morwick, lives at 16 Reedcap Row, Lower Vey, ZX4 7QP and is not making a representation. She has already moved a bedroom downstairs to get away from the old road noise. I mention this because the assessment treats this short row as if every bedroom faces the same way. Another neighbour, Mr Soren Fells, at 12 Reedcap Row, Lower Vey, ZX4 7QP, showed me how headlights from vehicles using the temporary track would sweep across the row. Neither neighbour has asked to be contacted about my submission, so please do not publish their details in an unredacted copy.

My son, Lio Pell, is 11-year-old and has autism. He needs a predictable journey to school; the proposed closure of the footway by the Mill Sluice junction would require us to cross the old road twice. The diversion shown on sheet 6 looks short on paper but it passes the compound gate. I also have chronic migraine and take sumatriptan. I am not saying the road caused that condition. I am saying that extended night-time lighting and unpredictable banging during construction would make it harder to manage at home. Even without those medical issues, the uncertainty has caused stress and poor sleep. Please do not treat that last sentence as a diagnosis.

My mother, Tarin Pell, stays with us regularly and has rheumatoid arthritis. The applicant’s suggested alternative walking route includes the steps at Fenfold Bridge. That is not a usable alternative for everyone. There is a ramp farther along, but the extra distance matters when someone is walking slowly. The access plan should show a step-free route maintained throughout each construction phase, with clear signs on the ground rather than a note hidden in an appendix.

I am also worried about the ecology survey. Badgers have been seen in Alderfen Wood, which is a general observation and not a reason to stop all work. However, the plan supplied to residents marks a badger sett in the bank 9 metres east of the northern stile on Footpath 14, beneath the split ash tree. That level of detail should not have been on a public drawing. Likewise, a bat maternity roost is recorded inside the west-facing roof void of the abandoned pump hut, immediately beside survey peg P17. These locations should go to the appropriate people securely, while the public documents explain the protection measures without pointing anyone straight to the sites.

The transport appendix counts vehicles at the school turn but does not seem to include traffic diverted by the planned drainage works. Cllr Iven Dorr said at the public meeting that the two programmes should be looked at together. I agree. Please require a combined construction traffic plan and a binding limit on movements through Lower Vey during school arrival and collection. An email saying that drivers will be ‘encouraged’ to use another route is not a restriction.

For completeness, my car is registered QX26 NPV and I use the space in front of my house because there is no rear access. If that space becomes unusable, I cannot simply pay for parking elsewhere: I have £18,400 remaining on my mortgage and no spare budget for a daily charge. I realise parking arrangements are a small part of a large scheme, but they are part of how the design will work for actual residents. The document at www.fenwatch-review.example/bridge has a photograph of the narrow section, though the applicant’s own site photographs should be sufficient if the Examining Authority prefers those.

I ask the Examining Authority to require an accurate house-by-house construction plan, a safe step-free walking route, and enforceable limits on working hours and traffic before deciding whether the claimed benefits outweigh these effects. I would welcome a site visit. I do not consent to my personal contact details being placed on the public register.

Nera Pell

Further to the above, I also question whether the transport and drainage assessments use the same construction programme. Merehaven Linkways Ltd models the peak tipper movements as occurring over 18 weeks, but the drainage drawings show the temporary haul road remaining beside Alderfen Ditch through two winter periods. The traffic assessment should explain what happens if earthworks are delayed by wet ground and the peak movements coincide with the school-term morning peak on Veybank Road.

The proposed attenuation basin is shown at the low point of Parcel AF-07. Its outfall appears to depend on a culvert beneath the existing track, yet the submitted drawings do not give that culvert's capacity or a maintenance arrangement during construction. I am not saying the basin cannot work; the information is simply not sufficient to check it. I ask the Examining Authority to require a combined phasing drawing, revised junction counts and a drainage exceedance plan before the construction traffic limits are settled.

text:
6. ECOLOGY AND NATURE CONSERVATION

6.1 Scope and method

This chapter reports the terrestrial ecology assessment for the proposed Larkmere Crossing, promoted by Larkmere Crossing Infrastructure Ltd. It should be read with Figure 6.4 (Habitat Plan) and the confidential protected-species schedule. Fenward Ecology Ltd completed desk study, habitat walkover and targeted surveys between April 2024 and September 2025. Surveyors covered the application site and accessible land within 250 m. Where access was refused, the assessment uses views from public rights of way and identifies the resulting uncertainty. The survey area includes Marshend Wood, the Wickerfold farm buildings and the proposed eastern haul route. These names identify broad survey areas; they do not, by themselves, identify protected-species resting places.

6.2 Baseline habitats

Most land within the Order limits is improved grassland or arable field margin. The hedgerows beside the eastern haul route provide the best continuous commuting habitat. Marshend Wood contains mature ash and oak, fallen timber and a wet ditch. No tree removal is proposed within its central compartment, although temporary lighting could affect its edge. Two ponds were assessed for amphibians; neither is directly filled by the scheme. The drainage design retains a vegetated buffer along the main ditch. Habitat figures are based on the 2025 survey and should not be treated as a prediction that every field boundary will remain unchanged before construction.

6.3 Badger

Field signs, including paths and snuffle holes, were recorded across the Marshend Wood survey area. Badger setts have also been identified in the wider Wickerfold fields. Those broad descriptions are provided so that the assessment can be understood without relying on the confidential schedule. The sett requiring the closest construction control is Sett B1, in the south bank of the drainage ditch, 6 m east of the wooden footbridge on Field Track 2. Its nearest entrance faces the working strip. A second sett, Sett B2, is beneath the hawthorn at the north-west corner of Plot 18, immediately behind the blue field gate. Both locations were checked on the final survey visit; activity at individual entrances may vary seasonally. The absence of fresh spoil on one visit must not be taken to mean a sett is disused.

Open trenches will be covered or provided with escape ramps each evening, and stored pipes will be checked before capping. No excavation, piling or heavy vehicle standing is permitted within the species-specific exclusion area shown in the contractor's restricted working plan until the ecological clerk of works has confirmed the method. If the final design cannot avoid interference with a sett, Larkmere Crossing Infrastructure Ltd will obtain the necessary licence before the relevant works. Pre-commencement checks will update the baseline, not substitute for the controls assessed here.

6.4 Bats

Activity transects recorded common pipistrelle and soprano pipistrelle along the woodland edge, with occasional passes above the pasture. Bat activity was generally higher beside hedgerows than across the open centre of the proposed compound. A small, non-maternity day roost of common pipistrelle was found under the west fascia of the old pump house. That location is reported in the main chapter because it is not a maternity roost or a large roost of a rare species. The pump house is outside the demolition footprint, but vibration and lighting still need managing.

The survey also confirmed a soprano pipistrelle maternity roost in the cavity directly above the middle window on the south elevation of Wickerfold Barn. Emergence counts and repeated observation support the maternity classification. The surveyors did not enter the cavity. Wickerfold Barn is retained, although the current construction lighting layout would illuminate its south elevation unless amended. A separate large greater horseshoe bat roost was recorded inside the blocked brick culvert 12 m downstream of the eastern haul-route crossing, at the chamber reached through its upstream inspection hatch. This feature is not on the proposed excavation line, but the haul route passes close enough for disturbance to require assessment.

The lighting strategy will avoid direct light onto roost access points, retain dark links along the hedgerow network and use directional fittings where site safety lighting is essential. Works affecting a roost will follow a method approved under any required licence. Replacement roost features are proposed as contingency rather than justification for avoidable loss. Post-construction monitoring will check whether the retained commuting route remains functional.

6.5 Birds and other fauna

Barn owl was seen hunting over the rough grassland west of Marshend Wood. This observation does not identify a nest. A later building inspection located the barn owl nest on the upper shelf of the eastern feed store in Wickerfold Barn, immediately above the second doorway from the yard. The barn is retained, but construction traffic and lighting near the yard could disturb breeding birds. The contractor will establish a no-work buffer during any active nesting period, with its extent and duration set by the ecological clerk of works following a current check. The check must be made before intrusive work rather than assumed from the 2025 result.

Other nesting birds may use hedges throughout the site. Vegetation clearance should take place outside the main nesting season where practicable; otherwise a competent ecologist will check the affected vegetation immediately beforehand. Otter footprints were noted beside the main ditch, but no holt was confirmed during the accessible surveys. The record supports precautionary ditch-side working methods and does not establish an otter breeding site. Invertebrate survey found typical grassland and wet-margin assemblages, with no population of a very rare or specially protected species located.

6.6 Effects, commitments and residual position

Without mitigation, construction could cause disturbance to setts and roosts, interruption of bat flight lines and displacement of nesting birds. The principal avoidance measures are retention of Wickerfold Barn, reduced lighting, fenced working limits and checks immediately before works. They will be secured through the Construction Environmental Management Plan and reviewed if the detailed layout changes. The restricted schedule should be supplied only to those designing and implementing the relevant controls; reproducing exact resting-place locations on publicly displayed contractor drawings is unnecessary. Subject to those measures, the residual effects on badger, bats and breeding birds are assessed as not significant at the local population scale. This conclusion depends on the lighting amendment being carried through to the final design, rather than left as a general aspiration. Ecology queries may be sent to ecology@larkmere-crossing.example.

8.6 Assessment of ecological effects

8.6.1 This section considers the construction and operational effects of the Larkmere Crossing following the avoidance measures described in Section 8.5. It should be read with the habitat drawings and the restricted species schedule. The public drawings show the extent of survey areas and proposed habitat works but do not reproduce the exact positions of protected resting places. Larkmere Crossing Infrastructure Ltd has confirmed that the lighting amendment referred to above is included in the design parameters used for this assessment. If that amendment is not incorporated into the final lighting scheme, the conclusions for commuting bats will need to be revisited.

8.6.2 Fenward Ecology Ltd completed the baseline habitat walkover in March 2025 and follow-up visits between April and September 2025. Survey coverage included the proposed crossing, temporary compounds, access routes and a buffer proportionate to likely effects. Access to one small parcel east of Wickerfold Barn was not available during the first visit. Its field margins were viewed from the adjoining public route, and the parcel was subsequently inspected in July. This is not considered a material limitation for the habitat assessment. Weather and survey effort are set out in Appendix 8-C, rather than repeated here.

8.6.3 The working area is principally improved grassland and arable land, crossed by drainage ditches and bounded in places by hedgerows. The most connected habitat is the chain of ditch banks and mature boundary vegetation between Wickerfold Wood and the low ground at Merefold Drain. Individual trees provide local foraging opportunities, although the survey did not identify a continuous canopy route across the existing road. Wickerfold Barn is retained. No part of the proposed carriageway lies within the designated Alderfen Meadows Local Wildlife Site; the nearest permanent works are separated from it by existing farmland and Merefold Lane. The absence of direct land take does not remove the need to control sediment and lighting during construction.

8.6.4 Approximately 0.74 hectares of improved grassland and 0.31 hectares of arable margin will be lost to permanent works. These habitats are common in the study area and the effect, considered alone, is not significant. A short length of species-poor hedgerow must be removed to form the eastern access. The replacement planting shown on Drawing LC-EC-08 is longer than the section removed, but it will not function as a mature linear feature immediately. The assessment therefore treats the construction-stage interruption as a temporary adverse effect, rather than counting the planting as an instant like-for-like replacement. Gaps at the ditch crossings will be kept as narrow as practicable.

8.6.5 Badger activity was recorded in the wider Wickerfold Wood area. No exact resting-place location is given in this public chapter. The likely construction effects are disturbance from excavation, vibration and uncontrolled night working; operational traffic is a separate risk where animals may continue to follow established field boundaries. Fenced working limits, pre-start checks and a prohibition on storing materials outside approved compounds reduce the construction risk. Where checks identify a change in activity, the ecological method statement must be reviewed before work in that area proceeds. The proposed mammal passage beneath the eastern approach will be kept clear of service runs, and its entrances will connect to boundary vegetation. These measures are requirements of the assessment, not optional enhancements.

8.6.6 Bat activity was concentrated along the darker ditch and hedgerow corridors, with lower activity over the open fields. The assessment does not rely on a claim that bats will immediately adopt the newly planted verge. Instead, it assumes retention of the existing western boundary vegetation and a lighting design that limits spill towards Wickerfold Barn and Merefold Drain. Columns will use downward-directed fittings, with shielding where the final photometric model shows spill beyond the approved limits. The detailed model must be checked against the as-built column positions before the road opens. Subject to that check, fragmentation and disturbance effects are assessed as minor and not significant at the local population scale.

8.6.7 Breeding birds may use hedgerows, ditch vegetation and scattered scrub within the construction corridor. Vegetation clearance will be programmed outside the main nesting period where reasonably practicable. If clearance cannot be deferred, a competent ecologist will check the relevant vegetation immediately beforehand and specify an exclusion area where an active nest is found. This does not authorise removal of an active nest. General references to birds using Wickerfold Wood are sufficient for this chapter; individual nest positions have not been placed on public plans. Replacement scrub and hedgerow planting should increase the area of suitable habitat once established, although the first few growing seasons will provide less cover than the vegetation removed.

8.6.8 The principal water-related pathway is runoff carrying fine sediment to Merefold Drain. The drainage design separates clean catchment flows from construction runoff and provides temporary settlement capacity before controlled discharge. Works beside ditches will use marked stand-off areas, and fuel storage will be confined to the compound on the higher ground. The Construction Environmental Management Plan must state inspection frequencies and what happens if a control fails; simply listing silt fencing will not be adequate. During operation, planted treatment swales and maintainable outfalls form part of the permanent drainage system. Their performance depends on routine clearance, particularly after the first winter of operation.

8.6.9 Cumulative effects have been considered with the separately proposed Merefield North Employment Site, using its published layout dated 14 August 2025. The main shared pathway is additional lighting along the southern field boundary, not combined loss of designated habitat. The Larkmere Crossing lighting limits have therefore been assessed on the conservative assumption that background light at that boundary increases. West Fen District Council requested that this assumption be made explicit. No reliance is placed on planting proposed by the other scheme, since its delivery and establishment are outside the applicant's control.

8.6.10 Monitoring will test whether the retained corridors remain usable and whether replacement planting establishes as intended. The first review will take place after the initial full growing season, followed by reviews in years three and five. A failed planting area will be replanted in the next suitable season; repeated failure will trigger a review of soil preparation and maintenance, not further replacement on the same basis. With the specified controls secured and maintained, the residual ecological effects of the Larkmere Crossing are not significant. This conclusion does not dispense with any separate protected-species requirements that may apply when works commence.

8.7 Implementation and verification

8.7.1 The conclusion in paragraph 8.6.10 depends on the mitigation being delivered as part of the Larkmere Crossing, rather than being treated as an aspiration for later detailed design. This section identifies the ecological controls to be carried into the construction environmental management plan (CEMP), the landscape and ecological management plan (LEMP), and the relevant construction drawings. It does not introduce additional land take or rely on planting proposed by the other scheme.

8.7.2 Before vegetation clearance, the contractor will mark the limits of working on the ground and install protective fencing around retained habitat. The fencing line will follow the approved drawings, subject to minor adjustments where a pre-construction walkover identifies a practicable way to retain more existing vegetation without moving works outside the authorised limits. No storage, vehicle tracking, lighting columns or temporary drainage outfalls will be permitted beyond the marked working area. Any proposed change to a retained corridor will be reviewed against the assessment in this chapter before work proceeds.

8.7.3 Clearance will be programmed to avoid the main bird-breeding period where reasonably practicable. Where that cannot be achieved, vegetation will be checked immediately before removal and an appropriate exclusion area maintained around any active nest until it is no longer in use. The check is a construction safeguard, not a substitute for the habitat-retention measures. Records will identify the area checked, the clearance authorised and any delay required, without publishing the precise position of a nest.

8.7.4 Fenward Ecology Ltd recorded evidence of badgers in the wider Larkmere survey area and bat activity along several connected hedgerows. These findings informed the corridor design and the construction controls; they do not indicate that every length of hedgerow is equally sensitive. A pre-commencement check will confirm whether the baseline remains current in the areas affected by the first phase of works. If conditions have materially changed, the contractor will pause the relevant activity while the implications for the method of working and any separate licensing requirement are resolved. No assumption about the availability of a licence has been used to reduce the significance of an effect in this assessment.

8.7.5 Temporary lighting will be directed into the working area and used only where needed for safe operations. At the retained north-eastern corridor, shields and inward-facing fittings will prevent direct illumination of the vegetation edge. The lighting schedule will specify mounting height, direction and operating hours; a site check after installation will confirm that the installed arrangement matches the schedule. Permanent lighting has been assessed on the basis of the submitted design. A later substitution of fittings with a wider beam or higher output would require an ecological review, even if it met the highway lighting standard.

8.7.6 The drainage design keeps untreated construction runoff out of retained ditches. Temporary settlement measures will be installed before earthworks begin, inspected after heavy rainfall and maintained until exposed ground is stabilised. The design also retains shallow vegetated margins beside the replacement drainage channels, where these can be formed without compromising hydraulic capacity. These margins are not counted as an immediate like-for-like replacement for established habitat. Their anticipated contribution is therefore treated as a longer-term benefit, subject to successful establishment and the maintenance set out in the LEMP.

8.7.7 Planting will use the species schedule in the submitted landscape drawings and will connect, rather than terminate short of, the retained hedgerow sections. The LEMP will state stock sizes, soil preparation, watering arrangements, weed control and the criteria for replacing failed plants. It will also identify who is responsible for each management area after construction. An area will not be reported as established merely because planting has taken place: the monitoring record will distinguish installation, survival and development of continuous cover.

8.7.8 The monitoring reviews described in paragraph 8.6.10 will use fixed photographic viewpoints and a consistent condition checklist. The checklist will consider gaps in planting, damage to protective features, excessive shading of new margins, evidence of repeated disturbance and whether the intended habitat connections remain physically open. Observations of species may help interpret the results but will not, by themselves, determine success or failure: an animal not recorded during a visit may still use the corridor at another time. The year-five review will recommend whether routine LEMP management can continue unchanged or whether a targeted adjustment is needed.

8.7.9 Larkmere Crossing Infrastructure Ltd will provide the monitoring reports to West Fen District Council in accordance with the proposed requirement. Where a remedial measure is recommended, the report will set out its purpose, location by management area, delivery timetable and method for checking the result. This reporting route is intended to make corrective action auditable; it does not transfer responsibility for delivery to the council. The CEMP and LEMP will use matching management-area identifiers so that an issue identified on site can be traced to a drawing, an action and a subsequent inspection.

8.7.10 The assessment has considered construction disturbance, permanent habitat loss, changes in lighting and drainage, and the time required for replacement vegetation to develop. It has also considered the potential overlap with the other scheme on the information available at the assessment date. No ecological credit is taken for measures that the other scheme might deliver. On that basis, and with the controls above secured, the predicted residual effects remain not significant. If the detailed design materially changes the footprint, severs a retained connection or alters the drainage or lighting assumptions, that change must be assessed before implementation rather than recorded retrospectively in a monitoring report.

8.8 Ecology monitoring and adaptive management

8.8.1 The conclusion at paragraph 8.7.10 depends on the mitigation being installed in the correct sequence and maintained while the new habitats establish. This section sets out the checks required for the Larkmere Crossing. It does not introduce a further mitigation measure or assume that monitoring can make an otherwise significant effect acceptable. The purpose is to identify a departure from the assessed design early enough for it to be corrected.

8.8.2 Larkmere Crossing Infrastructure Ltd will maintain an Ecology Implementation Schedule alongside the construction programme. The schedule will identify the relevant drawing revision, the area to which each measure applies, the required completion point and the evidence needed to close it out. It will be updated when the programme changes, but a programme update will not itself authorise a change to a retained habitat boundary. Fenward Ecology Ltd will review the schedule before works begin in each construction area. The principal contractor will provide a short record of completed works, including dated photographs where these can demonstrate the position and condition of a measure.

8.8.3 Before vegetation clearance, the limits of working will be marked on site and checked against the approved drawings. The check will include the temporary access strips, soil storage areas and the exclusion fencing beside Cinderbank Wood. An access route that appears minor on a compound plan may still interrupt the retained hedgerow connection if it is used repeatedly. Plant movements outside the marked limits will therefore be treated as a non-compliance, rather than absorbed into the next monthly progress drawing. Damaged fencing will be repaired before work resumes in the affected area.

8.8.4 The pre-construction walkover will verify whether the assumptions used in the baseline remain reasonable. The survey information describes badger activity in Cinderbank Wood and bat activity along the Bracken Mere corridor; these are broad descriptions of use, not directions to individual resting places. The walkover will also check for newly established habitats in areas scheduled for clearance. If a material change is found, the relevant activity will pause while its implications and any licensing requirements are reviewed. The outcome will be recorded before that activity recommences. The walkover is not a substitute for the seasonal surveys already relied upon in the assessment.

8.8.5 Drainage controls will be inspected at installation and following the first substantial rainfall during each relevant phase. Particular attention will be paid to the outfall serving the eastern approach and to the swale adjoining Briar Cut. The inspection will check for erosion, sediment accumulation and any evidence that runoff is bypassing the designed treatment route. The location of a temporary silt barrier may need adjustment as the works advance, but its removal will require confirmation that the permanent control is operating. These checks address both water quality and the condition of the habitats receiving the discharge.

8.8.6 Lighting will be checked against the submitted lighting drawings once the permanent fittings can be operated at night. The check will confirm column positions, shielding, controls and the extent of spill towards retained vegetation. The assessment assumes that the crossing beneath the eastern embankment remains unlit. If operational requirements produce a different arrangement, an ecological review will be needed before the fittings are commissioned. A claim that the lamps are energy efficient would not, on its own, demonstrate that the assessed effect on the dark corridor remains unchanged.

8.8.7 New hedgerow, grassland and wet-margin planting will be inspected at the end of the first growing season and annually for five years. The record will distinguish between planting that is alive, planting that is establishing but underperforming, and areas where the intended habitat has not developed. Replacement of failed plants will use the approved species mix unless the recorded site conditions show that a change is necessary. The inspection will also identify compaction, invasive species and inappropriate mowing. Success is measured by a functioning continuous habitat, not solely by the number of plants initially delivered.

8.8.8 The habitat drawings show several narrow links between larger retained areas. These links must remain usable during construction as well as at completion. At the Rill Lane crossing, for example, the inspection will consider the combined effect of temporary fencing, stored materials and the finished verge profile. If access for maintenance is required through a link, its timing and duration will be recorded. A link will not be described as retained merely because its eventual planting is shown on the final layout.

8.8.9 Results will be issued in an annual ecology note to West Fen District Council for the five-year establishment period. Each note will identify the inspection dates, outstanding actions, changes from the preceding year and whether the assessed mitigation is functioning. Where an action remains open, the note will state what is to be done and when it will be checked again. A summary table alone would not explain why a planting area has failed or whether a change to the drainage has altered the receiving habitat.

8.8.10 Monitoring has practical limits. Seasonal variation may affect what is seen on a particular visit, and a single absence of recorded activity will not be treated as proof that a species no longer uses an area. Conversely, a new record will not automatically mean that the scheme has caused an adverse effect. Fenward Ecology Ltd will review the observation in the context of the baseline, weather, construction activity and the condition of the mitigation. Any material departure from the assumptions in this chapter will be reported through the project change procedure.

8.8.11 On the information presently available, the proposed inspection and response arrangements provide a means of verifying the measures on which the residual-effects conclusion relies. They do not alter the conclusion reached in Section 8.7. The residual effects remain not significant, provided that the secured design and construction controls are implemented and any material change is assessed before it takes effect.

8.9 Cumulative effects

8.9.1 This section considers whether the ecological effects of the Larkmere Crossing would combine with those of other reasonably foreseeable developments. It should be read with the traffic assumptions in Chapter 6 and the construction programme in Chapter 3. The assessment uses the same study area and significance criteria as Sections 8.3 and 8.7; it does not treat every scheme appearing on a planning register as if it will necessarily be built.

8.9.2 The long list was compiled from the development schedules supplied by West Fen District Council and the adjoining authority, together with schemes identified in the transport model. Projects were screened in where their construction or operation could affect a receptor addressed in this chapter and where there is sufficient information to assess a plausible interaction. Small householder works and schemes wholly outside a shared pathway were screened out. The screening record is set out in Appendix 8C, including the reason for each exclusion.

8.9.3 The retained projects include the consented Merrowbank Business Park extension, the proposed Fenward Relief Link and the permitted storage compounds at South Mere. Their programmes are indicative. For the purpose of assessment, construction of the business park and relief link has been assumed to overlap with the busiest year of crossing works. This is a precautionary assumption, not a prediction that the programmes will coincide. The compounds have been considered principally in the operational assessment because the permitted earthworks are substantially complete.

8.9.4 The main shared pathways are temporary construction disturbance, the combined loss of ordinary grassland and the potential for changes to surface-water quality in the Mere Drain catchment. There is no identified direct land take from the same hedgerow sections by more than one retained project. The habitat totals in Table 8.18 therefore distinguish losses within the Order limits from losses shown on other schemes' approved drawings. They should not be added together without allowance for differences in survey method and the possibility of later design changes.

8.9.5 Badgers and bats were recorded across the wider survey area, including around North Fen Wood. That is a broad description of habitat use, not a plotted location of a sett or roost. On the information available, the retained projects would not remove a continuous corridor between the wood and the drain. The crossing design retains the principal vegetated margins, with temporary lighting directed away from them. Similar controls are proposed for the relief link, although its final lighting specification has not yet been issued. The cumulative conclusion accordingly assumes that each project's approved lighting limits are implemented and maintained.

8.9.6 For water quality, simultaneous soil stripping could increase the amount of exposed ground within the catchment. The schemes drain to separate construction outfalls before reaching Mere Drain. Each will require its own sediment-control measures; the controls for one project cannot be relied on to manage runoff from another. Larkmere Crossing Infrastructure Ltd will provide temporary settlement capacity within its construction footprint and will suspend discharge from an affected work area if inspection identifies a failed control. With these measures operating alongside the consented controls for other schemes, a significant cumulative effect on aquatic habitats is not predicted.

8.9.7 Operational traffic from the retained projects is included in the future-year traffic model. The resulting change in traffic on Fenward Road has been used in the air-quality assessment, rather than adding separate estimates from each planning application. The ecological interpretation of those results is given in Table 8.19. Predicted changes at the assessed habitat edges are below the level at which a measurable change in vegetation condition is expected. This finding depends on the traffic scenario described in Chapter 6 and would be reviewed if that scenario materially changes.

8.9.8 There is uncertainty about the timing and detailed planting proposals for the Fenward Relief Link. This does not prevent an assessment of the likely combined effect, but it limits the weight that can be placed on proposed off-site planting as mitigation. The cumulative assessment therefore credits only habitat measures secured for the Larkmere Crossing and measures already required by an existing consent. It does not claim an ecological benefit from unapproved drawings.

8.10 Summary and commitments

8.10.1 The embedded design avoids the highest-value habitats identified during the baseline surveys. Remaining effects arise mainly from temporary works areas, vegetation removal and the risk of disturbance or polluted runoff during construction. The measures described in this chapter include demarcation of retained habitat, a pre-works check where required, controlled lighting, surface-water treatment and reinstatement of temporary land take. These are delivery requirements, rather than suggestions for a later design stage.

8.10.2 Fenward Ecology Ltd will verify the ecological components of the detailed construction method statements before the relevant works start. The inspection schedule described in Section 8.8 provides a route for identifying and correcting damage to fencing, drainage controls or newly established planting. West Fen District Council will receive the annual monitoring summary through the environmental reporting process. Reporting a corrective action will not, by itself, establish that a significant effect has occurred; the nature, extent and duration of the event will be considered against the assessment criteria.

8.10.3 Subject to implementation of the secured measures, no significant residual ecological effect is predicted, either for the project alone or in combination with the retained projects. If a material design or programme change alters an assessed pathway, the relevant assessment will be revisited before that change is implemented. This conclusion does not remove the need to comply with the applicable environmental permits and species protection requirements during construction.
