CHAPTER 8: ECOLOGY AND BIODIVERSITY
Baymere Link Energy Project — Environmental Statement, Volume 1

8.1 Scope and approach
This chapter reports the terrestrial ecology assessment for the proposed cable corridor, converter compound and temporary construction areas. It has been prepared for Baymere Link Energy Ltd using the survey work of Hedgerow Metric Ecology LLP. The assessment considers habitat loss, construction disturbance, lighting and the effects of operation and maintenance. Marine ecology is addressed separately. Survey results are presented here at a level sufficient to explain the assessment; sensitive records would be supplied to the examining authority in a restricted appendix rather than shown on the public habitat plans.

The study area comprised the application boundary and accessible land up to 250 m beyond it. Walkovers took place between March 2024 and September 2025. Badger activity checks, bat emergence and re-entry surveys, and breeding bird visits followed the methods set out in Appendix 8.2. Some access was refused in the northern fields, so absence of a species there cannot be assumed. Weather was suitable for the visits except for one bat survey in June 2025, which was repeated. The impact assessment takes a precautionary approach where survey coverage remains incomplete.

8.2 Existing habitats
The corridor crosses improved grassland, arable fields, three species-rich hedges and the eastern edge of Brindlefen Wood. The wood is not within the permanent footprint. Ditches beside Marsh Lane hold water seasonally and connect to the larger Sallow Drain. These features provide commuting and foraging habitat even where the adjoining fields have low botanical value. Two mature willows at the proposed access bellmouth have cavities; one is to be retained and the other requires further inspection before pruning. No ancient woodland is proposed for removal. The revised alignment also avoids the wet meadow at Long Mere, although temporary works would approach its western boundary.

8.3 Badgers
Field signs, including paths, snuffle holes and latrines, were recorded across the southern half of the study area. Badger setts have been identified in Brindlefen Wood; this broad location is given to explain the local pattern of activity and does not identify an entrance. Two setts within the construction influence area were mapped for the purposes of licensing and method design. Sett BS01 is in the earth bank 14 m east of the southern stile on Footpath 8, beneath the twin ash trees at the north edge of Parcel P17. Sett BS02 is beneath the western end of the fallen willow, 6 m north of the field gate between Parcels P22 and P23. Both remained active on the final check, although the number of occupied entrances varied between visits. A disused outlier was also noted in the wider survey area, away from any proposed excavation.

There would be no permanent land take at either active sett. Open excavations could nevertheless present a trapping risk, and vibration from trenching would require control where works pass nearby. The contractor will mark an exclusion zone before mobilisation, brief the site team and provide escape ramps in trenches left open overnight. Any works requiring sett interference would be subject to the appropriate licence and seasonal constraints. These commitments are included in the outline Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP); they are not a substitute for a pre-construction check, as occupation may change.

8.4 Bats
Activity surveys recorded common pipistrelle, soprano pipistrelle and occasional passes by a rarer woodland bat species. The highest activity was along the hedge adjoining Brindlefen Wood, not in the open arable fields. A small, non-breeding common pipistrelle day roost was confirmed behind the loose fascia on the north elevation of the disused pump house in Parcel P09. The pump house is to be retained, and its roof and fascia will not be altered. This ordinary roost is described here to distinguish it from the breeding record below.

A soprano pipistrelle maternity roost was confirmed behind the fourth weatherboard from the left on the south gable of the old cart shed in Parcel P18. Emergence counts indicate a breeding group, although the count should not be read as a fixed colony size. The cart shed itself is outside the works footprint, but the temporary haul route as originally drawn passed close to it. The route has been shifted into the adjoining field, and no floodlights will face the gable. Temporary task lighting will be shielded, directed downwards and switched off when not needed. A further check before construction will establish whether the roost remains occupied and inform any licence application. Bat boxes on retained trees are proposed as enhancement, not as justification for disturbing the maternity roost.

8.5 Birds and other fauna
Breeding bird surveys recorded skylark in open fields and several common hedge-nesting species. A barn owl nest was observed inside the upper hayloft, on the shelf immediately above the east-facing ventilation slit of East Fold Barn in Parcel P26. The barn will not be demolished, but vehicle movements on the adjacent track could disturb nesting birds. Construction traffic will use the alternative southern access during the breeding period, subject to a check by the ecological clerk of works. The assessment does not assume the nest will be occupied every year. Barn owls have also been seen hunting near Brindlefen Wood; that wider observation does not locate a nest.

Otter footprints were found along Sallow Drain, but no holt was confirmed. Amphibian survey work identified common species at ponds outside the permanent footprint. Habitat connectivity along the drain will be maintained through a clear-span crossing, with bankside vegetation reinstated after the temporary works. General precautionary measures for nesting birds, reptiles and small mammals are set out in the CEMP.

8.6 Residual effects and monitoring
With the alignment change, lighting controls, licensed procedures where necessary and ecological supervision, no significant adverse residual effect on the recorded badger, bat or barn owl populations is predicted. This conclusion depends on the stated measures being implemented, not merely being shown on drawings. The appointed ecologist will check sensitive features immediately before nearby works and keep a confidential record of any change. Public reporting will give outcomes and any corrective actions without reproducing precise locations of protected breeding or resting sites.

8.7 Survey evidence and treatment of sensitive records

This section should be read with the restricted ecology plan. It explains the basis for the conclusions in section 8.6 but is not intended to be used as a works instruction. The field sheets contain exact positions because the alignment and working widths had to be checked against them. Those positions will be carried forward into the confidential construction constraints plan, not into public site notices. Baymere Link Energy Ltd has confirmed that the plan will be issued only to the principal contractor, the ecological clerk of works and the relevant licensing authority. Hedgerow Metric Ecology LLP completed the walkover and dusk surveys between April and September 2025; a further check is required where vegetation clearance has not commenced within the survey validity period.

8.7.1 Badger

Evidence of badger activity was recorded across the wider survey area, including paths through Brindle Copse and snuffle holes along the western field margins. These observations alone do not identify a resting place. A sett was also recorded in the northern part of Brindle Copse; this is a broad description for the public survey summary and does not allow an entrance to be found. The restricted plan records Sett B1 at the base of the third ash south of the disused Limekiln Track gate, 6 m east of the proposed temporary haul-road fence. Four entrances were open at the June visit, although occupation could not be established from that visit alone. Sett B2 is in the south-facing bank of Drain D4, directly below the eastern end of the field bridge marked FB-2. Its two entrances were partly obscured by bramble. Neither record is evidence that all the entrances have the same status throughout the construction period.

The revised haul-road edge is outside the stand-off agreed for the current design. There will be no lighting directed into the copse, and excavation close to either recorded feature will be subject to an ecological check and, if needed, a method agreed under licence before work starts. The contractor's drawing will show a fenced exclusion area rather than entrance coordinates. If an entrance is found beyond the surveyed area, works in its immediate vicinity will stop pending advice; an absence of fresh spoil on a single day must not be treated as proof of abandonment.

8.7.2 Bats

Transects identified commuting activity along the old orchard boundary and the Drain D4 corridor. Low numbers of bats were recorded over the open arable fields, which is consistent with the limited foraging habitat there. The desk study refers to bats in Brindle Copse, but gives no tree or roost position. Those broad records have informed the lighting assessment rather than the calculation of direct roost loss.

A small, non-breeding day roost was found behind the loose bargeboard on the west elevation of Pump House 2. This feature is outside the demolition area. It is recorded here to make clear why no alteration to that building is included in the works specification. By contrast, the maternity roost is in the split trunk of oak T47, 11 m north of the centreline at chainage 2+340 and immediately west of the orchard access gap. Emergence counts in June and July confirmed use by breeding females. The tree is retained, and the access gap has been moved so that vehicles do not pass beneath its crown. A second sensitive record concerns a large roost of the rare marsh pipistrelle in the roof void above bay 4 of the unused East Sluice Store, entered through the missing tile directly above the south gutter outlet. The store is outside the order limits, but temporary floodlighting from the compound could otherwise illuminate its approach. The lighting schedule therefore specifies low-level, inward-facing fittings and a pre-occupation check of the compound arrangement.

Tree inspections cannot establish that every suitable crevice is unoccupied. Where pruning is unavoidable, the appointed ecologist will review the tree immediately beforehand and specify soft-felling or licensed procedures as appropriate. Replacement boxes are precautionary provision, not a substitute for retaining the recorded maternity tree. Monitoring will compare post-construction activity with the survey baseline, with results reported by habitat corridor rather than by individual roost location.

8.7.3 Birds and other fauna

Barn owls were seen hunting over the rough grassland east of the converter site. A nest was confirmed inside the top drawer of the timber feed cabinet fixed to the north wall of Old Reed Barn, 2.4 m above the floor beside the western ventilation opening. This is an exact breeding-site record and will be omitted from the publicly circulated figure. Old Reed Barn will not be used for storage or contractor access. The temporary cable route has also been pulled away from the barn yard to reduce disturbance. Any work affecting the barn structure would require a separate assessment; it is not authorised by the general nesting-bird checks in the CEMP.

Other nesting birds were noted in hedges throughout the route corridor, without any individual nest being used to set the permanent alignment. Vegetation removal should take place outside the main breeding season where practicable; otherwise a competent ecologist will check the area before clearance. Otter footprints at a culvert were treated as evidence of passage, not as confirmation of a holt. The reinstated bankside strip and the open culvert design provide continuity for animals moving along the drain. No protected plant population was identified in the construction footprint.

8.8 Verification

The ecological clerk of works will maintain a dated log of checks, decisions, licences and any departure from the approved method. A discovery that changes a stand-off or working method must be passed to the site manager before the relevant activity resumes. The first monitoring report will distinguish measures installed from measures shown to be effective. References to Brindle Copse or the orchard in that public report are sufficiently broad for scrutiny; the confidential plan remains the proper source for locating the recorded resting and breeding sites.

8.9 Monitoring and residual effects

Baymere Link Energy Ltd will commission post-construction checks in the first, third and fifth growing seasons. Hedgerow Metric Ecology LLP will compare the reinstated drain margins, hedgerow connections and replacement planting against the approved landscape and ecological management plan. Checks will record establishment, gaps, invasive species and evidence of use by wildlife; a record of an animal passing through the corridor will not, on its own, demonstrate that the corridor is functioning throughout the year.

Where planting fails to meet the specified establishment standard, replacement will take place in the next suitable season. The monitoring report will identify the action needed, the responsible contractor and the date for a further check. Observations concerning bats around Brindle Copse and badgers in the wider survey area will be reported at a broad scale in the public version. Subject to implementation of these measures, no significant residual effect on ecological connectivity is anticipated.

NORTH MERE ENERGY LINK
Application reference: EN009842
Written evidence of Dr Elin Voss, independent ecological witness
21 October 2026

1. Qualifications and scope

I am Elin Voss, an independent field ecologist. I hold a PhD in conservation ecology and have worked on habitat surveys, linear infrastructure and ecological impact assessments for 18 years. My curriculum vitae was submitted as Appendix EV1. I have given evidence in two previous infrastructure examinations and have carried out fieldwork for local authorities, landowners and applicants. Those commissions do not affect my duty to give independent evidence here.

I was instructed by the Merewick Habitat Forum, an Interested Party, to review the ecological material submitted by Halewick Transmission Ltd for the North Mere Energy Link. My instructions were to examine the proposed access route through West Tern Wood, the treatment of hedgerows at Parcel P14, and the reliability of the applicant's bat and badger survey conclusions. I inspected publicly accessible parts of the route on 3 September 2026 and reviewed the Environmental Statement, its survey appendices and the applicant's response to the first written questions. I did not enter private land. Where I refer to features beyond the public path, I rely on survey records, photographs or observations made from the path, as stated below.

For completeness, the Forum supplied my contact sheet to the examination team. It appears the version attached to this evidence includes my home correspondence address, 18 Glassfern Close, Merewick, QV7 4LN, and my personal mobile, 07700 900 684. These are not fieldwork locations. My work correspondence can instead go through ecology@merewickhabitat.org.uk. My individual work email is elin.voss@merewickhabitat.org.uk.

2. Main opinion

The Environmental Statement identifies the broad constraints correctly, but the proposed working width is not yet supported by a sufficiently clear plan of retained vegetation. Drawing NL-EC-014 shows a 12 m strip beside West Tern Wood. Drawing NL-CW-031 shows a wider temporary turning area in what appears to be the same place. The applicant should reconcile those drawings before the relevant requirement is discharged. The difference matters because the narrower strip could retain the western hedge, whereas the turning area as drawn would remove it for approximately 46 m.

I do not say that every hedge section must remain untouched. My concern is that the assessment treats reinstatement after construction as equivalent to retaining a mature hedge. It is not equivalent for commuting bats during the construction period or while replacement planting establishes. A plan showing protective fencing, the precise temporary access width and a fallback route would allow that effect to be assessed. A commitment to agree details later is not, by itself, an assessment of the likely worst case.

3. Survey records and limitations

I have seen the note prepared by Ms Rilla Fenwick of Brackenfold Field Services following the April 2026 walkover. That note records one possible badger path but does not give the conditions at the time of inspection. The applicant's later survey records badger activity in West Tern Wood. These are not necessarily contradictory observations: signs may be easier to detect at some times of year than at others. Badger setts have been identified in West Tern Wood, but that broad description should not be taken as locating a particular sett.

One field annotation in the papers I received gives a much more precise location: Sett B is beneath the split ash 11 m east of the southern gate to Parcel P14, on the north bank of the drainage ditch. That annotation should not have been reproduced in a publicly available version of this evidence. It is relevant to the examination because the indicative haul route passes close to the feature; the precise record should be handled in a restricted ecological schedule rather than used to identify a point in a public response.

The same issue arises with the bat records. Bats were recorded around Merewick and in West Tern Wood, which is a useful general description. A separate survey note identifies the maternity roost of a rare bat species in the upper eastern gable of the disused pump house at Parcel P14, directly above the bricked-up round window. That location is unnecessarily exact for the public version of my evidence. The important planning question is whether lighting, vibration and the duration of works near the building have been assessed on a precautionary basis. The submitted lighting drawing covers permanent equipment but does not show the temporary task lights proposed for the compound.

My September visit was a daytime inspection and cannot verify maternity use or the results of nocturnal activity surveys. I also could not confirm whether the ditch held water throughout the summer. I have therefore not treated my observations as a replacement for the applicant's season-long survey work. They identify points requiring explanation, not a claim that the whole survey effort is invalid.

4. Recommendations

Before works in this part of the Order limits, the applicant should provide a single, scaled vegetation-retention and temporary-access plan; specify the lighting controls for the compound; and set out how current protected-species records will inform the final method statement. The plan should distinguish removal, coppicing and temporary fencing. Monitoring should have named triggers and a means of recording remedial action, rather than only a statement that planting will be checked annually.

I understand why residents feel anxious about the loss of the wood edge. Anxiety about a proposal is not evidence of a diagnosed condition, and it is not the basis of my professional conclusion. My conclusion is narrower: the mitigation may be capable of working, but the drawings and construction controls presently leave material uncertainty about what will happen on the ground. Subject to the clarification requested above, I consider that uncertainty capable of being resolved without revisiting the entire route selection.

I confirm that the opinions expressed are my own, within my ecological expertise, and that I have identified the limits of the material available to me.

Elin Voss
Independent ecological witness

SUPPLEMENTARY WRITTEN EVIDENCE OF ELIN VOSS
North Mere Energy Link — examination reference NME-2026-04
Submitted on behalf of Merewick Habitat Forum, 21 October 2026

1. Purpose and status of this note

This note supplements my written evidence on the woodland-edge mitigation proposed by Halewick Transmission Ltd. It follows the clarification sought at the end of that evidence. I have not undertaken a fresh route appraisal. My purpose is to explain what information would allow the Examining Authority to test whether the proposed construction controls can be delivered, rather than merely described in general terms.

I am Elin Voss, an independent ecological witness instructed by Merewick Habitat Forum, an Interested Party in this examination. I hold an MSc in Applied Ecology and the professional qualifications CEnv and MCIEEM. I have worked on habitat surveys, construction-stage ecological supervision and post-construction monitoring for more than 20 years. My evidence is based on the submitted environmental documents, my visit to the proposed working corridor on 9 September 2026, and the survey note identified below. I have not surveyed every tree or verified the applicant's land-access arrangements. Those limitations matter when considering the precision of the proposed mitigation.

Administrative contact details supplied for the examination record (my home details were included here in error):
14 Sedge Lantern Walk, Merewick, MW8 4QT
Mobile: 07700 900 432
Interested Party reference: IP-902347
The Forum's shared correspondence mailbox is evidence@merewickhabitatforum.org. Please use that mailbox for questions about this submission, not my mobile number.

2. What the construction documents need to show

The applicant's proposed fencing line is shown differently on the general arrangement and the ecological mitigation drawing. At the narrowest point, that difference could affect whether retained roots remain inside the exclusion area. A contractor cannot resolve the discrepancy by being told simply to 'avoid damage where practicable'. Before works begin in this part of the corridor, the final drawing should identify the surveyed edge, the working width and the no-entry line on the same base plan. It should also state who can authorise a change in the field and how that change will be recorded.

The same point applies to storage. The construction narrative says that materials will not be stored beneath retained canopies, but the indicative compound layout shows an unassigned strip beside the wood. I cannot tell from the documents whether that strip is intended for turning, temporary laydown or neither. A hatched exclusion zone on a controlled drawing would remove the ambiguity. This is a practical request, not an argument that all activity near the wood must stop.

I have seen the note dated 16 August 2026 prepared by Ms Rilla Fenwick of Brackenfold Field Services. It records signs of badger activity within the wider survey area and recommends a pre-construction check. The note also records the badger sett at chainage 2+415, 6 m north of peg BF-19 beneath the split ash stump. That location is supplied here so the confidential ecological schedule can be reconciled with the construction plan; it should not appear on a publicly accessible constraints map. References elsewhere in this note to badger activity in Lantern Wood are deliberately less precise and should not be treated as a substitute for the confidential schedule.

The applicant's own bat appendix refers to a bat maternity roost in the hollow lime at chainage 2+608, 4 m east of peg BF-24. I have not independently confirmed its current status. If the tree is to be retained, the method statement should nevertheless explain how lighting, vibration and access will be controlled during the relevant works. If its status changes following a lawful update survey, the decision and supporting evidence should be entered in a revision log available to the ecological clerk of works and the applicant. Simply saying that bats will be considered at detailed design does not identify an accountable decision point.

3. Monitoring and reporting

I suggest one baseline photograph from each agreed fixed point before fencing is installed, followed by photographs after installation, after removal of temporary works and at the first two growing-season inspections. The record should include the drawing revision in force at each visit. Where planting fails, the monitor should record the likely cause—such as compaction, drought or shading—before specifying replacement stock. Counting stems alone may otherwise give a misleading impression that the woodland edge has recovered.

The draft requirement refers to annual monitoring but does not say what happens if an inspection identifies an unapproved encroachment. In my opinion, the ecological clerk of works should have a clear route for requiring an immediate pause in the affected activity, with the incident and corrective action reported to the relevant planning authority. This would make the control auditable without turning every minor field adjustment into an examination matter. I have suggested two growing-season inspections as a minimum reporting interval here, not as a claim that ecological recovery will be complete after two years.

4. Response to matters raised locally

Cllr Tamsin Quill asked at the community session whether replacement planting could be moved farther from the cable easement. That is a reasonable question for the detailed plan, although the available drawings do not let me specify a planting distance. Residents have also described poor sleep and anxiety about construction traffic. I acknowledge those concerns; they are not diagnoses, and I have not used them as ecological evidence. My opinion rests on the identifiable gaps between the drawings, survey constraints and proposed site controls.

The broad area described as Lantern Wood is suitable for public discussion of habitat effects. It is not sufficiently precise to direct a contractor around a protected feature. Conversely, precise protected-feature information need not be reproduced in every public submission to make the mitigation enforceable. A controlled confidential schedule, cross-referenced to the approved construction drawing, would serve that purpose.

5. Conclusion

I remain of the view that the uncertainty identified in my principal evidence can be resolved without reopening the route selection. The essential steps are a consistent final base plan, explicit exclusion and storage areas, a confidential schedule for sensitive ecological constraints, and a monitoring record that captures decisions as well as planting totals. I offer these points within my ecological expertise. I do not express an opinion on the applicant's commercial arrangements or the legal drafting needed to secure the controls.

Elin Voss
Independent ecological witness

6. Supplementary observations on construction drainage and access

6.1 Scope of this note

The ecological controls discussed above will only be effective if the construction drainage and access arrangements shown on the final plans are compatible with them. This section considers those interfaces. It does not introduce a new route option or assess the merits of the North Mere Energy Link as a whole. The comments relate to the temporary works corridor between East Mere Lane and the proposed Halewick switching compound, as depicted on Construction Arrangement Drawing CA-17, revision C.

6.2 Basis of assessment

Halewick Transmission Ltd has submitted a preliminary drainage strategy and a construction traffic management plan. Both use indicative layouts. The drainage strategy assumes that clean runoff from undisturbed land can pass around the working area, while water from stripped ground will be intercepted, settled and released at a controlled rate. That is a reasonable starting principle. It is not yet possible, however, to tell from the drawings which temporary access surfaces will drain to the clean-water system and which will drain to the settlement system. The distinction matters most where the access track crosses a shallow natural fall towards the Merewick Cut.

My assessment has treated the proposed compound footprint as fixed for this purpose, but has not assumed that each temporary stockpile is in its final position. The applicant should identify, on one coordinated plan, the maximum extent of stripped ground, track surfacing, soil storage, drainage channels and ecological exclusion areas. A note stating that the contractor will agree details later would not resolve conflicts between these uses of the same narrow corridor.

6.3 Temporary drainage

The drainage strategy refers to a 1 in 30 year rainfall event for the temporary works. It should explain what happens during a larger event or when a settlement facility is unavailable for maintenance. No elaborate permanent structure is necessarily required: an identified overflow route, kept away from exposed soil and sensitive boundaries, may be sufficient. The route must nevertheless be shown rather than left to site judgment during heavy rain.

The drawings should also distinguish the control of runoff from the control of groundwater encountered in excavations. Water pumped from a trench is not automatically suitable for discharge to an open ditch. Its destination should depend on inspection and, where needed, treatment under an agreed site procedure. The proposed inspection point and the location at which a discharge decision is recorded should appear in the construction method statement. I am not suggesting a fixed pumping rate before ground conditions are confirmed; I am asking for an auditable decision process.

At present, a proposed soil store and a temporary swale occupy overlapping space on CA-17. The overlap could be a drafting error, but it has a practical consequence. A swale cannot function as drawn if it is covered by a stockpile or severed by plant movements. The final plan should show a clear separation between drainage conveyance, soil storage and vehicle turning. If the swale is moved, its revised outfall and maintenance access should be checked against the ecological constraints schedule referred to in section 5.

6.4 Construction access and phasing

The construction traffic management plan identifies East Mere Lane as the principal approach and Fenbridge Road as the onward route for abnormal loads. It gives daily vehicle totals for the main construction period but combines deliveries to the compound with movements associated with cable installation. This is likely to understate short peaks when those activities overlap. A simple phase-by-phase table would make the assumptions testable: anticipated duration, maximum daily heavy vehicle movements, proposed working hours and any period when two work fronts operate concurrently.

There is a related issue at the temporary access bellmouth. The swept-path drawing shows an arriving vehicle passing a stationary vehicle within the access, whereas the traffic plan says that vehicles will be called forward individually. Those are different operating assumptions. If the bellmouth must allow passing, the surfaced width and drainage catchment should reflect that. If it will not allow passing, the traffic plan should specify where vehicles wait without obstructing East Mere Lane. Neither matter should be left to an informal instruction issued after construction starts.

The same clarity is needed for restoration. The current programme places removal of temporary access surfacing in the final construction phase, but does not state whether the temporary drainage remains operational until the exposed ground is stabilised. Removing interception too early would defeat the proposed sediment controls. A sequence drawing, using the same boundaries as the final base plan, should show what remains in service during each restoration stage.

6.5 Policy and secured detail

The Merewick Local Transport Plan 2038 seeks to avoid unnecessary construction traffic on minor lanes, while the Fenfold Surface Water Guidance Note requires drainage measures to remain accessible for inspection. Those documents do not prescribe a particular access design for this project. They do support a coherent, checkable set of drawings rather than separate plans prepared on different assumptions.

I consider the outstanding matters capable of resolution through final construction details, provided the approved requirements specify what those details must contain. In particular, the coordinated plan should carry a revision number shared by the drainage strategy, traffic plan and ecological constraints schedule. Any later change to an access surface, soil store or outfall should be screened against all three documents, with the reason for the change recorded. That approach would allow necessary adjustments on site without treating the controls as optional.

6.6 Overall view

Nothing in this supplementary review alters my conclusion on route selection. The present difficulty is one of interfaces: the same temporary land is assigned different functions in different drawings, and the construction sequence does not yet show when each control begins and ends. A coordinated final plan, a phase table and an inspection record would make the proposed measures capable of verification during construction and restoration.

7. Verification and witness details

7.1 The coordinated plan recommended at paragraph 6.6 should identify who checks each temporary work area before it is used, not merely who signs off its restoration. For example, a soil store may be acceptable on the drainage drawing but still obstruct the ecological exclusion strip. The phase table should record both checks and the date on which the strip can safely be removed.

7.2 I have reviewed the survey note prepared by Rilla Fenwick of Brackenfold Field Services. Its account of badger activity in Sallow Carr is consistent with my site observations. The note also identifies the badger sett in the disused chalk pit 18 metres east of gate G4 on parcel P17. That location should be withheld from the public version of the constraints plan, while remaining available to the appointed ecological clerk of works. The broader reference to Sallow Carr is sufficient for explaining the assessment.

7.3 At the community session, Cllr Tamsin Quill asked whether the inspection record would be available after construction. I agree this is important. Halewick Transmission Ltd should retain dated records of any departure from the approved sequence and provide a summary to the relevant planning authority. I do not suggest that every minor adjustment requires a new consent.

Witness biography

I am Elin Voss, an independent ecological witness instructed by Merewick Habitat Forum for the North Mere Energy Link examination. I hold an MSc in Ecology and am a Chartered Environmentalist (CEnv). I have prepared habitat and construction-monitoring evidence for infrastructure examinations for over 20 years. My opinions above are my own and are limited to the ecological interfaces described in this evidence.

Contact details supplied with my draft in error:
Home address: 14 Sedge Lantern Close, Merewick, MW4 7QP
Personal mobile: 07700 900482
Project correspondence: ecology@merewickhabitatforum.example

Elin Voss

BRACKENWICK PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held at Brackenwick Community Hall, 3 Lantern Yard, Brackenwick, on Monday 12 October 2026 at 7.00 pm

Present: Cllr Imogen Vale (Chair), Cllr Tomas Reed, Cllr Saira Keld and Cllr Bryn Moss. Nora Pell (Clerk to Brackenwick Parish Council) was in attendance. Members of the public present for the open session were Mrs Cora Vell, Farid Tollin and Jo Fenney. The three residents confirmed that they were attending as observers and had not registered as participants in the Hearthwick Fen Link DCO examination.

1. Apologies and declarations
Apologies were received from Cllr Oren Pike. No pecuniary interests were declared. The Chair reminded members that the Council's DCO response was a corporate representation and that individual views expressed during discussion should not be taken as an agreed Council position until the resolution was recorded.

2. Previous minutes
The minutes of 14 September 2026 were approved as a correct record, subject to correcting “east verge” to “west verge” in item 6. The Chair signed the paper copy. There were no matters arising not covered below.

3. Public participation
Mrs Cora Vell asked whether the temporary construction entrance would remain open through the school-run period. The Chair said the traffic management drawing showed proposed hours, not a final condition, and that the Council would ask for a clear restriction. Farid Tollin said the latest plan was difficult to read when printed in black and white. Jo Fenney was worried about poor sleep if evening works went ahead. The Chair thanked the speakers. No vote was taken during public participation.

4. Hearthwick Fen Link Development Consent Order
The Clerk reported that the Planning Inspectorate had invited comments on the applicant's revised access drawings and the draft construction environmental management plan by 30 October 2026. The Council's examination reference, IP-094721, should be quoted on the covering letter. Alderflow Networks Ltd had supplied an updated route diagram, but the legend still did not distinguish permanent fencing from temporary fencing on the copy sent to the Council.

Members discussed the haul route beside Merefold Lane. Cllr Tomas Reed said the swept-path drawing appeared to assume that vehicles could pass at the bend without waiting, whereas the roadside ditch narrowed the usable carriageway. Cllr Saira Keld asked that the Council request a banksman at that point and a published procedure for reporting mud on the road. Cllr Bryn Moss wanted the response to avoid saying that all construction traffic should be prohibited; deliveries for the pumping compound would have to reach the site somehow. The Chair agreed that the request should be for enforceable hours, passing arrangements and a named contact role, rather than a blanket objection.

The ecology appendix was also considered. Members had previously referred generally to badger setts in Lantern Wood; this was not a claim about a particular sett. A confidential note received with the survey material, however, identified one sett as being under the north bank of the drainage ditch, 18 metres east of the stile where Footpath BW6 enters Lantern Wood. Members agreed that this detail should not be repeated in the Council's public response. They asked instead for confirmation that the applicant's ecologist had taken it into account before any ditch clearance. The Clerk will send the confidential note only through the examination team's appropriate channel.

Cllr Imogen Vale said the Council should acknowledge the revised landscaping around the pumping compound, which was an improvement on the earlier bare-earth drawing. Members remained concerned about who would maintain the replacement hedge after the initial establishment period. It was agreed that the Council would ask for a maintenance schedule and a drawing showing where gaps in the existing hedge would be retained for farm access.

RESOLVED: The Clerk is to circulate a draft response to all councillors by 23 October. Subject to any factual corrections returned by 26 October, the Chair is authorised to approve its submission on behalf of Brackenwick Parish Council. The draft should address construction hours, vehicle passing, the drawing legend, hedge maintenance and the handling of confidential ecological information. The Council's general mailbox, planning@brackenwick-pc.org.uk, is to be used for the submitted response, not a councillor's personal account.

5. Planning application not connected with the DCO
The Council considered application BW/26/0418, made by Ms Nell Quist for a single-storey rear extension at 22 Merefold Lane, Brackenwick, BK4 8RF. This was an ordinary householder application and not part of the Hearthwick Fen Link proposal. The Clerk read out the planning authority's consultation deadline. Members noted that the proposed roofline was below the existing first-floor windows and that the submitted plan did not show any change to the front boundary. Cllr Bryn Moss asked whether the rainwater pipe discharged to the existing soakaway; the drawing did not say. RESOLVED: no objection, with a request that drainage details be checked by the planning authority. The Council did not discuss the applicant's personal circumstances.

6. Clerk's report and correspondence
The Clerk advised that the paper examination bundle could be inspected by appointment at Brackenwick Community Hall, 3 Lantern Yard, Brackenwick. Correspondence to the Clerk's home address, 7 Flaxwheel Close, Brackenwick, BK4 8QJ, had caused a delay because two envelopes were delivered to a neighbouring street. Members agreed to put the hall address on future meeting notices. For urgent queries about this meeting's minutes the Clerk supplied nora.pell@brackenwick-pc.org.uk and 07700 900418; the Chair asked that neither direct contact detail appear on public noticeboards.

7. Any other business and close
Cllr Saira Keld reported a broken latch on the hall's side gate. The Clerk will ask the caretaker for a repair estimate. The next ordinary meeting will be on 9 November 2026 at 7.00 pm. The Chair closed the meeting at 8.41 pm.

BRACKENWICK PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held at Brackenwick Community Hall, 3 Lantern Yard, Brackenwick, on Monday 9 November 2026 at 7.00 pm

Present: Cllr Imogen Vale (Chair), Cllr Tomas Reed, Cllr Saira Keld and Cllr Bryn Moss. In attendance: Nora Pell, Clerk to Brackenwick Parish Council. Members of the public: Mrs Cora Vell, Farid Tollin and Jo Fenney.

1. Apologies and declarations
Apologies were received from Cllr Oren Pike, who was away on other business. No interests were declared in the Hearthwick Fen Link item. Cllr Bryn Moss declared that he knew the applicant for the householder application at item 6 through the village gardening club. The Chair agreed he could remain for that item but should not move the response.

2. Previous minutes and matters arising
The minutes of the October meeting were approved as a correct record, subject to changing ‘east’ to ‘west’ in the description of the temporary traffic lights. The Chair signed the paper copy. The Clerk reported that the side-gate latch had been replaced and the caretaker had not charged for the part. Meeting notices now give the hall as the correspondence address rather than the Clerk’s home address. The Clerk reminded members that papers sent to 7 Flaxwheel Close, Brackenwick, BK4 8QJ may not reach the Council promptly; there had been no further mis-deliveries since October.

3. Public participation
Mrs Cora Vell asked whether the construction access shown near the school would be used on Saturdays. She said the uncertainty was making her anxious and that her asthma is worse when dust hangs about after lorries pass. The Chair said the Council could ask for the proposed hours and dust controls to be stated plainly, but could not answer for the applicant. Farid Tollin said drivers already ignore the give-way marking at the hall junction. Jo Fenney asked for any reply to be put on the hall noticeboard as well as online, since not everyone uses the website. The Chair thanked all three speakers. None indicated that they had registered as an Interested Party in the examination.

4. Hearthwick Fen Link DCO: consultation on revised access drawings
The Council considered the drawings issued by Alderflow Networks Ltd on 28 October, together with the Clerk’s comparison sheet. Members agreed that the revised turning head removes one concern about vehicles reversing towards the hall. It does not explain how pedestrians on Lantern Yard will be separated from construction traffic during school arrival time. Cllr Tomas Reed noted that drawing HFL-TR-042 shows a gate but does not say who will supervise it. Cllr Saira Keld asked that the Council avoid saying the gate will be permanently staffed when the document does not promise this.

The Clerk read out the draft response. Members made two changes: ‘must provide’ became ‘should provide’ in the paragraph on advance warning signs, and a request was added for a plan showing where contractors would wait if the gate was shut. Cllr Imogen Vale said this was a practical objection to the present access arrangement, not an objection to the whole scheme. It was RESOLVED unanimously to submit the amended response to the examination and place a copy with the minutes. The Council’s shared mailbox, clerk@brackenwick-pc.org.uk, is to be used for any published reply. The Clerk said the examination documents can be found through https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects-the-examination-stage.

5. Ecology note accompanying the revised drawings
Members had received a short note about the proposed hedge removal. Cllr Bryn Moss asked whether the survey covered the whole of Wickmere Wood. The Clerk said the note refers to badger signs in Wickmere Wood but gives no location for a sett; it should not be taken to mean the entire wood is affected. Members asked for clarification about the timing of hedge works and replacement planting. The Council would not reproduce any detailed protected-species plan on the hall noticeboard if one was later supplied. Cllr Saira Keld proposed adding these points to the response agreed at item 4, and this was carried.

6. Unrelated householder planning application
Application BW/26/118 concerns a proposed rear dormer and replacement porch at 12 Copperfern Rise, Brackenwick, BK4 8RL, the home of Ms Nell Quist. The Chair made clear that this was an ordinary district planning consultation and had no connection with the Hearthwick Fen Link examination. The submitted elevation was difficult to read in the black-and-white copy. Members discussed roof materials and whether the porch would project beyond the existing building line. Cllr Bryn Moss did not take part in the vote, in accordance with the declaration at item 1. It was RESOLVED, three in favour, to make no objection, while asking the district planning officer to check the dormer’s proposed cladding against nearby roofs. The Clerk will send that comment under the planning reference above, not with the DCO response.

7. Finance and correspondence
The Council noted payment of the hall electricity account and an estimate for printing larger-format access drawings. Cllr Tomas Reed said the public copy ought to be legible without someone having to borrow a councillor’s laptop. Members approved printing one set for the hall. The Clerk reported that a further email about the access gate had been sent to her directly at nora.pell@brackenwick-pc.org.uk. For examination correspondence she will reply from the shared mailbox. Her direct number, 07700 900418, remains for urgent Council administration and is not to be printed on the noticeboard.

8. Next meeting and close
The next ordinary meeting will be held on 14 December 2026 at 7.00 pm in the hall. The Chair closed the meeting at 8.36 pm.

BRACKENWICK PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held on Monday 14 December 2026 at 7.00 pm in Brackenwick Village Hall

Present: Cllr Imogen Vale (Chair), Cllr Tomas Reed, Cllr Saira Keld and Cllr Bryn Moss. In attendance: Nora Pell, Clerk to Brackenwick Parish Council. Members of the public: Mrs Cora Vell, Farid Tollin and Jo Fenney.

1. Apologies and declarations
Apologies were received from Cllr Oren Pike and accepted. No interests were declared. The Chair reminded everyone that comments made in the public session would be summarised rather than recorded word for word.

2. Minutes of the previous meeting
The minutes of 16 November 2026 were approved as a correct record and signed by the Chair. The Clerk confirmed that the enlarged access drawings agreed at that meeting had been put in a folder in the hall. Somebody had removed the first notice saying where to find them; a replacement notice is now up.

3. Public session
Mrs Cora Vell asked whether the proposed construction traffic route for the Hearthwick Fen Link DCO had changed since the October exhibition. She said she had trouble sleeping when heavy vehicles used the lane, but did not want the Council to speak for her in the examination. Cllr Imogen Vale explained that the Council could only comment on the plans currently submitted by Alderflow Networks Ltd. The Clerk would check the latest drawing revision before the Council sent its written response.

Farid Tollin said the bend by Low Acre Bridge was already difficult for two vans to pass. He asked for the Council's response to distinguish delivery vehicles from staff cars. Jo Fenney said, “I have diagnosed asthma, so please don't describe dust as just a bit of inconvenience.” The Chair thanked all three speakers and said the Council's comments would address dust controls and the traffic-management plan, without including residents' personal circumstances. The public session ended at 7.19 pm.

4. Hearthwick Fen Link Development Consent Order
The Chair introduced the draft response prepared following the November meeting. This is a parish response to the examination and not a decision on the Development Consent Order. Members agreed that the proposed temporary entrance at Plot 6-14 needed a drawing showing how the gate would operate while farm machinery and construction vehicles were both using the track. Cllr Tomas Reed noted that the drawing displayed in the hall showed the gate but not its swing. The Clerk had asked the applicant for clarification and had not yet received it.

Cllr Saira Keld proposed adding a request for the construction traffic figures to be given separately for school arrival and departure times. Cllr Bryn Moss asked that the response also mention the drainage ditch beside the bridge, which had overflowed after recent rain. Members agreed both additions. They did not agree to say that flooding was caused by the applicant's works, as works had not started.

The Council considered the ecology map circulated with the agenda. It showed badger activity generally in Fenmere Wood, which members agreed could be mentioned in the public response. A separate survey note gave the sett position as “inside the disused lime pit, 18 metres east of the northern stile on Footpath 6, beneath the split ash”. The Clerk said that detail was not needed to explain the Council's request for protective fencing. Members agreed to refer only to the need for the applicant to check its fencing plan against the survey before construction. The survey note will not be attached to the public minutes.

It was resolved, by four votes in favour, that the Clerk submit the amended response to the Planning Inspectorate by the published deadline. The Council's shared mailbox, clerk@brackenwick-pc.org.uk, will be used for any reply. Members asked that the final version be placed in the hall folder and on the Council noticeboard. The examination timetable can also be found at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate.

5. Planning application not connected with the DCO
The Council considered householder application BW/26/0417/H for a single-storey rear extension at 8 Thistle Row, Brackenwick. The application was made by Ms Nell Quist. Cllr Bryn Moss reported that the site notice was difficult to see from the pavement, but members had been able to read the drawings supplied by the planning authority. The Council made no objection, subject to the authority considering the boundary gutter shown on drawing 04B. This item is unrelated to the Hearthwick Fen Link DCO and is recorded here because it was on the ordinary parish agenda.

6. Correspondence and administration
The Clerk reported that two letters about the temporary access arrangements had been delivered to her home rather than sent to the shared mailbox. For clarity, the Clerk's home correspondence address remains 6 Wren Fold, Brackenwick, BW4 8QT; it should not be used for examination submissions. Cllr Imogen Vale asked for the address to be removed from the version of the contact sheet displayed in the hall. The Clerk will update that sheet this week.

Members also considered a request from the village hall committee for help replacing the noticeboard light. The estimate was £86.40 including fittings. It was agreed to pay this from the maintenance budget after the committee confirmed that the proposed fitting was suitable for the hall wall. No decision was made about changing the position of the noticeboard.

7. Next meeting and close
The next ordinary meeting will be held on 11 January 2027 at 7.00 pm in the hall. The Chair closed the meeting at 8.28 pm.

Appendix A – technical points for the Hearthwick Fen Link examination

The Council agreed that the following points should accompany its written response to Alderflow Networks Ltd. These are planning matters only and do not alter the decisions recorded in the minutes above.

Traffic: the construction traffic tables use an average daily HGV figure for the whole works period. The Council asks for a separate peak-week assessment, including simultaneous deliveries to the converter compound and cable corridor. The routeing plan should show how vehicles will avoid the narrow bend on Mere Lane when the temporary access is in use. The Council also asks for a commitment to repair any damage to the highway verge before the access is removed.

Drainage: the submitted outline drainage strategy describes attenuation at the compound but does not clearly show where exceedance flows go during a blocked-outfall event. A drawing showing flow paths towards Hearthwick Fen, together with the proposed maintenance responsibility for the swales, would assist the examination.

Landscape: the photomontages should include a winter view from the public footpath east of Brackenwick. Screening shown at year 15 should not be treated as effective at opening. The Council requests an establishment and replacement schedule for the proposed hedge planting.

The Council considers these requests consistent with the drainage and landscape provisions in the Draft Development Consent Order. No position was taken on the final alignment at this meeting.

text:
Relevant Representation – Larkfen Freight Link (TR030094)

From: Mara Ellory
Interested Party reference: IP-204761
Address: 14 Reedglass Close, Merehallow, QF4 7LP
Email: mara.ellory@example.com
Telephone: 07700 936 481

I am writing about the health and air quality parts of the application. I support better freight connections in principle, but I do not think the documents explain what living beside the proposed route will be like on an ordinary weekday. My home is near the approach to the proposed Marshfold Interchange. The plans show the interchange and its construction compound at Plot 17, Old Silt Works, Marshfold. This is not a remote bit of land to those of us who walk past it to get to the shops and school.

I have a diagnosis of asthma and also live with chronic migraine. I use a salbutamol inhaler and a budesonide preventer inhaler. I mention these facts because a small change in air quality or a period of repeated dust can matter in our household in a way that an annual average figure may not convey. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide whether the scheme caused any illness. I am asking for the assessment and, if consent is granted, the controls to reflect the people who will actually be exposed. Please do not take the absence of a hospital visit in a modelled year as evidence that short episodes do not matter.

My child, Neri Ellory, is 8-year-old and has autism spectrum disorder. The morning journey needs to be predictable. A sudden diversion, idling lorries at the crossing, or a very noisy day can make getting to school difficult. The school has made adjustments, and occupational therapy for sensory processing difficulties has been helpful, but those arrangements are not a substitute for sensible construction management. I have spoken with Mrs Fenna Voss about the usual route to school; this person is not making a representation and should not be contacted about mine.

The Environmental Statement concentrates on receptors at fixed points. Could the applicant explain how the chosen points reflect people waiting at the Merehallow Road crossing, rather than just homes with windows shut? The walking route is used at the same time that deliveries to the site may start. The drawings give broad construction phases, but I could not find a clear commitment about the number of heavy vehicles in the first hour of the school day. If that information is in another document, a page reference in the response would be appreciated. I have tried to follow the examination library, but there are a lot of versions.

The proposed monitoring is also hard to understand. I would like a monitor near the crossing before work begins, with results published in plain language each month. A figure that residents can compare with the agreed trigger levels would be more useful than a statement that everything is compliant. Please say who will check the equipment, what happens when a reading is missed, and who has authority to pause a dusty activity. I am not proposing that every unusual reading stops the whole project. I do want a procedure that works on the day, rather than a promise to review it at the end of a quarter.

Watering a haul road may help with dust, but it will not address every concern about exhaust from queuing vehicles. The construction traffic plan should show where engines will be turned off, how drivers will be told, and what residents can do if the same problem happens repeatedly. Please consider a specific no-idling condition at the interchange entrance. It would also help to know whether temporary generators are expected and, if so, where they will be placed in relation to the footway. These seem like practical details that can be settled without opposing the whole scheme.

For completeness, I have lived in this area for more than 20 years. I already experience stress and poor sleep when the road is particularly busy. My health is affected by the prospect of a lengthy construction period, although I understand that a feeling about a future impact is different from a measured air quality effect. I have no monitoring equipment of my own and do not want my observations presented as measurements. They are reasons for asking that the applicant's predictions be tested against conditions on the ground.

Cllr Tamsin Pelder said at the public drop-in that residents would be able to raise problems during construction. I welcome that, but the draft arrangements should specify a response time and a route for escalating an unresolved complaint. A generic mailbox such as airquality@larkfenlinkways.example is fine for initial reports if somebody actually monitors it outside office hours when night works take place. I found the examination guidance at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate helpful, but it does not answer who will deal with a lorry left running outside our crossing.

I ask the Examining Authority to seek a clearer construction traffic schedule, a monitored dust and air quality plan with public results, and a complaints process with named responsibilities by role rather than relying on a particular employee staying in post. These requests are about making the Larkfen Freight Link workable for nearby households. Thank you for considering this representation.

Mara Ellory

Further health representation — Larkfen Freight Link
Application reference: LF-2026-0041
Interested Party reference: LF-IP-01746
From: Mara Ellory
Address for correspondence: 14 Fenmere Row, Larkfen, LF4 8QJ

I am adding this note because my earlier representation concentrated on the practical problem of lorries waiting at the crossing. It did not properly explain why the proposed traffic and construction arrangements matter to my household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide medical questions. I am asking it to look at whether the applicant has assessed the people who will be breathing the air beside the route, including during the temporary works.

I have been diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma. I use a salbutamol inhaler when needed and a daily beclometasone preventer inhaler. I also have chronic migraine, for which I take prescribed sumatriptan. These are existing conditions, not conditions I am claiming the scheme has caused. They make it important to me that the assessment does not treat a short period of very poor air quality as harmless just because a yearly average remains within a limit. Dust on a dry afternoon or exhaust from a stationary queue can matter even when the annual figure looks acceptable. I sometimes get chest tightness after walking beside queuing traffic. I cannot prove which vehicle, or which pollutant, is responsible for a particular episode, and I do not suggest the applicant should pretend that can be proved.

My child, Neri Ellory, is aged 11 and has an autism spectrum disorder diagnosis. Neri also has sensory processing difficulties and takes prescribed melatonin to help with sleep. The morning route to school is familiar and predictable, which helps. If the pavement is closed with little notice, or we must wait alongside idling vehicles while a marshal changes the crossing arrangement, the difficulty is not only the number of extra minutes. Noise, fumes and a sudden change of route together can make the journey much harder. I ask that the child’s name and health details are withheld from the published version of this note. The point can be understood without identifying my child.

Our home is close enough for us to hear vehicles using the existing lane when the windows are open. We have lived in this part of Larkfen for over 20 years. I am not saying every load will pass our door, and I appreciate that the final routing may alter. What concerns me is that the construction traffic table seems to give daily totals, whereas a parent or carer needs to know what may happen between 8 and 9 in the morning, particularly during the first weeks when arrangements are unfamiliar. A daily average does not describe a queue outside the crossing at that time. Nor does it explain what happens when deliveries arrive together after a road closure elsewhere.

Mrs Fenna Voss, who is not making a representation, spoke to me about the same school route. I mention that conversation only to explain why I checked the drawings again; I am not speaking on behalf of anyone else. At the public drop-in, Cllr Tamsin Pelder asked whether the pedestrian route would stay open during the drainage works. I understood the answer to be that a safe route would be provided, but the material on display did not show how it would work on days when both the crossing and the footway are affected. If a revised drawing exists, it would help to put it in the examination library rather than leaving residents to rely on memories of a conversation.

The environmental statement discusses air quality across the study area, but I would welcome a plainer explanation of the assumptions used at the nearest homes and on the walk to school. Please show where monitoring equipment would actually sit, when readings would be published, and what action would follow a high reading. A monitor placed away from the places where people wait may produce useful background data but will not answer this particular concern. If the proposed trigger level is exceeded on several dry days, would deliveries stop, would the haul road be damped down, or would somebody merely record the result? The answer ought to be in a requirement that can be checked later.

I am worried about dust carried out on tyres as well as exhaust. The wheel-wash proposal sounds sensible, but its operating hours and the arrangements for cleaning the public road are not clear to me. I would also like the applicant to say whether engines must be switched off while a driver waits for access. This is not an objection to freight work in general. It is a request for specific controls at the locations where children and residents actually stand, rather than a general promise to use best practice. My poor sleep and anxiety about the works are real, but I recognise that those feelings alone do not establish a medical effect from a future scheme.

There should be a way to report a problem when it happens. The mailbox airquality@larkfenlinkways.example was mentioned in the earlier material, but a resident needs to know whether anyone checks it at night and what information is required in a report. I do not want to be asked to photograph a driver or identify an individual worker. A time, location and description of the issue should be enough. Please also explain how complaints will be logged, how quickly somebody will respond and whether the anonymised log will be available during construction. The examination guidance at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate is useful for submitting evidence, but it cannot replace a local complaints procedure.

I would be reassured by a construction traffic schedule that identifies likely peak hours, a properly monitored dust plan, and a clearly signed pedestrian diversion before any closure starts. If the applicant changes a route, residents should hear about it before the morning journey, not discover barriers when they arrive. I ask the Examining Authority to consider these points alongside my earlier submission. I support practical mitigation that is written down, measurable and maintained for the whole construction period.

Mara Ellory

Further health representation concerning the Larkfen Freight Link

Submitted by Mara Ellory, Interested Party

I am adding this note to explain the health points behind my request for a reliable construction traffic schedule and dust plan. My earlier comments concentrated on getting to school and on how complaints would be handled. This is not a medical report and I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide whether the road is safe for me personally. I do, however, want the likely effects on residents to be considered as real day-to-day effects, rather than treated only as figures at monitoring points.

I live at 17 Merefold Terrace, Larkfen, LF4 8QP, near the proposed haul route. I have lived in this part of Larkfen for over ten years. On a dry morning the existing road already leaves a film of grit on the front window ledge. That observation is not a measurement of pollution. It is why I would like the applicant's dust predictions to be checked against what is actually happening at homes and along the walking route, particularly when several vehicles pass close together.

I have diagnosed asthma and use a salbutamol inhaler when symptoms flare. I also take a preventer inhaler containing beclometasone as prescribed. In addition, I have migraine with aura, for which I take propranolol tablets. I give these details reluctantly, because a public planning process is not where I would normally put health information. They matter here because a dusty diversion, a long wait beside idling vehicles, or uncertainty about which street is open may affect what I can reasonably manage on a school morning. I am not claiming that the scheme caused any of these conditions, nor that every headache or difficult day can be attributed to traffic.

My child, Neri Ellory, is aged 11 and has autism spectrum disorder. My child attends occupational therapy sessions, and melatonin prescribed at night is part of the current routine. An unexpected change to the walking route can be hard to deal with, especially if a pavement is closed without clear information before we leave home. The issue is not that change must never happen. It is that a diversion should be announced early, drawn on a map that a parent can understand, and kept consistent for as long as reasonably possible. We can plan for a stated closure much more easily than for barriers appearing without warning.

The school route was also raised with me by Mrs Fenna Voss, who is not making a representation in this examination. I mention that conversation only to explain why I checked the drawings again; I do not put forward Mrs Voss as a witness or ask for a response on anyone else's behalf. The drawings show the broad route, but I could not find a straightforward explanation of where pedestrians would stand if the crossing nearest Merefold Terrace is temporarily out of use. If the answer is in a later traffic management plan, I hope the final plan will be available before works begin, not only after the arrangement has changed.

At the public drop-in, Cllr Tamsin Pelder suggested residents should keep a record of dates when access is difficult. I think that is sensible, but a diary should not be the only way a contractor learns about a problem. There needs to be someone on site who can deal with a blocked pavement on the same day. The project mailbox, construction@larkfenlinkways.example, could receive photographs, but the published procedure should say when it will be checked and who will arrange an immediate correction. An automatic acknowledgement alone is not a remedy.

I have had poor sleep while trying to work out what the construction period will mean for us. This is a description of how I feel, not an additional diagnosis. Air quality is a wider concern too. Children, people walking to the shops and anyone waiting for a bus will encounter the works without necessarily knowing the timetable. A monitor placed somewhere convenient for the contractor may not represent the air beside a temporary crossing. Please identify the proposed monitor locations, explain why each was chosen, and publish results in a form residents can read without specialist software.

I would also like the Dust Management Plan to say what happens after a high reading or a credible complaint. For example, will vehicle speeds be reduced, will a surface be damped down, and who checks whether that action worked? It is no use saying that dust will be controlled if the only test is carried out after the event. I recognise that dry weather cannot be prevented and that deliveries must take place. I am asking for a method of responding to foreseeable conditions, including cumulative effects when works and ordinary traffic are both present.

Larkfen Linkways Ltd may have assessed emissions against the relevant standards. My concern is the gap between an assessment over a long period and a particular morning when a family must use a narrow diversion. The information supplied so far has not made that gap clear to me. A short public note showing anticipated busy hours, the pedestrian route and the contact for urgent access issues would help. It should be updated when arrangements change and displayed where people actually start the walk, not just on a project website.

I ask the Examining Authority to consider a requirement for advance notice of closures, accessible pedestrian diversions, monitoring near affected walking routes and a complaints process with recorded actions. Those measures would not remove every worry, but they would make the construction arrangements more predictable and give residents a practical way of reporting a problem. I am willing to provide further detail through the examination process if it would assist, while asking that the personal health information in this note is treated appropriately.

Mara Ellory

Further technical points on the construction assessment

The construction traffic assessment for the Larkfen Freight Link relies on daily vehicle totals, but those totals do not show whether heavy goods vehicle movements will coincide with the busiest pedestrian periods. The Examining Authority should ask Larkfen Linkways Ltd to provide hourly forecasts for each construction phase, including deliveries to the compounds, spoil removal and movements between work areas. The forecasts should identify the assumptions used for vehicle occupancy, route choice and the length of each phase. Without that information, the assessment cannot be checked against the proposed management measures.

The model also treats the junction of Merefold Road and Kiln Reach as having spare capacity. That conclusion appears to depend on traffic spreading evenly through the morning peak. A short queue at this junction can block the crossing approach even when the average delay over an hour remains modest. The assessment should therefore report maximum modelled queues, not only average journey times, and test a sensitivity case in which deliveries arrive in a shorter window. Observed traffic counts should be provided alongside the model inputs so that the difference between existing conditions and the forecast is clear.

The Construction Traffic Management Plan should specify permitted haul routes and the method for checking compliance. A general commitment to instruct drivers is not the same as a route-control measure. The plan should state how movements will be logged, how a departure from an approved route will be investigated and when the results will be reported to Dunmere Borough Council. These details can be secured before each phase begins rather than left to informal agreement once vehicles are operating.

Drainage needs the same phase-by-phase approach. The temporary works drawing shows a compound beside the West Soke drain, while the main drainage strategy describes the completed highway. It is not clear where runoff from the compound will go before the permanent system is connected. The drainage submission should show temporary containment, the proposed discharge point, inspection arrangements and what happens if a sediment control fails during heavy rain. It should also explain how the temporary system will be removed without sending accumulated material into the drain.

The landscape drawings show planting along the finished embankment but do not distinguish between land needed for construction and land available for planting immediately afterwards. A programme showing when each planting strip becomes available would make the visual assessment easier to understand. The assessment should also test views during construction, when stored materials and lighting may be more prominent than the completed link. This is a request for the effects already identified in the application to be assessed at the times when they occur, rather than averaged across the whole programme.

Taken together, these points call for clearer evidence and enforceable phase controls. They do not require a different route to be modelled, but they should be resolved before the final wording of the requirements is settled.

Health representation – Larkfen Freight Link

I support the request for clearer phase controls because the construction period is when air quality matters most to my household. I have diagnosed asthma and use a prescribed salbutamol inhaler. I also have chronic migraine and take prescribed propranolol. I am not saying the link caused either condition; I am asking Larkfen Linkways Ltd to assess what additional dust and vehicle emissions could mean during the earthworks.

My child, Neri Ellory, has autism. Changes to the walk to school are difficult to manage, particularly if the usual crossing is closed without notice. Mrs Fenna Voss has raised the same concern about the school route, although she is not making a representation. Cllr Tamsin Pelder said at the drop-in that construction information should be easy to find.

I feel anxious about poor air quality and sleep badly when work starts early. Those concerns should not be dismissed simply because the completed road is expected to meet the stated standards.

Mara Ellory
