text:
PUBLIC HEARING TRANSCRIPT (extract)
Mereford Vale Energy Link, Issue Specific Hearing 2: access and construction traffic
21 October 2026, afternoon session

CHAIR (Inspector Elin Rave): We are back on the record. This is a transcript of the oral discussion, not an agreed account of the evidence. Please give the document reference when referring to a plan. I will take the applicant first, then the interested parties who asked to speak. We have also allowed time for a person affected by the proposed temporary access, although that person has not made a written representation.

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL (Ms Tamsin Vell, Rillbank Advocacy, for Mereford Vale Energy Link Ltd): Thank you. The revised construction traffic note, document MV-TR-021, shows a maximum of 34 heavy vehicle movements on a weekday during the cable-laying period. That is a two-way figure. The earlier figure of 52 included movements which would use the eastern compound and should not have been attributed to the lane at Fellbridge. I appreciate the confusion this has caused. The applicant proposes a banksman at the compound gate during deliveries and a booking system for larger vehicles.

CHAIR: Is the booking system secured anywhere, rather than simply described in the note?

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL: It is in the draft construction traffic management plan, but I accept the wording says the contractor 'may' stagger arrivals. We can change that to 'shall'. I cannot give an undertaking about the precise wording without instructions, but we will put a marked-up version into the examination library by Friday.

INTERESTED PARTY (Elya Sorn): I live at 18 Bracken Fold, Fellbridge, FB4 7QN, and the gate shown on sheet 6 is across from my front room. I am 73. I know the applicant says the use is temporary, but temporary for somebody sitting there every day is different from temporary on a programme. The lorries already struggle at the bend. My IP reference is MV-2026-00418. I emailed the case team photographs from elya.sorn@fellpost.example because I could not work out the upload form. Please don't treat my photographs as evidence of the number of future lorries; they just show how narrow it is.

CHAIR: Thank you. The case team can confirm whether those photographs are in the library. You referred in your email to a vehicle parked at the bend. Is that something the proposed parking restriction could address?

INTERESTED PARTY (Elya Sorn): Maybe. I should be careful how I put this. My neighbour, Mr Jory Pell, was convicted of fly-tipping in 2019. That is why I do not want the hearing to assume everybody using the lane will follow a polite notice on a gate. I'm not saying he has any connection with this scheme. My actual point is that a sign and a banksman are no substitute for a physical place where a lorry can wait without blocking us in.

CHAIR: We do not need to explore your neighbour's circumstances. Can the applicant answer the point about a waiting place? The hatched area on sheet 6 looks like part of the works site, but the key calls it a turning area.

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL: The contractor intends vehicles to wait at the eastern compound, not on Fellbridge Lane. The hatched area is for turning after admission through the gate. I will ask for a clearer annotation. For completeness, the scheme website is https://www.mereford-vale-link.example/examination; the drawing currently there is superseded by MV-TR-021.

AFFECTED PERSON (Neris Dault): I rent the workshop at the end of the lane. I have not registered as an interested party and am only here because the hearing notice said affected occupiers could ask to speak. My workshop is a business address, Unit 3, Quarry Yard, Fellbridge Industrial Estate. The access is used for deliveries of sheet metal. I am not asking for a private slot in the traffic plan. I am asking who I ring if a booked delivery and one of the applicant's lorries reach the gate together. The generic address traffic@mereford-vale-link.example is on the notice, but will anybody answer it while a vehicle is actually there?

CHAIR: That is a practical question. Could the applicant supply a staffed site contact in the plan, rather than read out an individual's number at this hearing?

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL: Yes. We would prefer a site duty number so that responsibility survives a change of contractor. The plan can also require the gate marshal to keep the workshop entrance clear. I had understood, wrongly it appears, that deliveries to the workshop came from the other end of the estate.

INTERESTED PARTY (Cllr Fara Mott): The parish transport working group has walked the lane. I am speaking as an interested party, not giving a decision of the parish council. For 40+ years residents have used the footway there, and it narrows to almost nothing at the railway bridge. There have been general references to badgers in Alder Mere Wood; those do not resolve the safety issue. Could the traffic plan show a pedestrian holding point on the drawing itself? Otherwise it will be lost in an appendix.

CHAIR: That is a request for the applicant to consider, not a direction to design a crossing this afternoon. Before I close the item, is there an ecology point directly related to the turning area?

INTERESTED PARTY (Elya Sorn): There is. I did not put the precise place in my representation because I was told not to circulate it. The badger sett is in the east bank of the drainage ditch, 12 metres south of the red gate on plot MV-14, beside the hatched turning area. I am concerned about vibration if the turning area is enlarged. I have been stressed about all this and sleeping badly, but my question is whether the ecological clerk of works has been shown the revised drawing.

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL: I cannot confirm that today. I will take the location away for checking, and our response will avoid publishing a more detailed sett plan than is necessary. We are not proposing to enlarge the turning area on the present drawing.

CHAIR: Please provide the marked-up traffic plan and an answer on the ecology check by Friday. The examining panel will then decide whether a further written question is required. We will move to drainage after a short break.

MEREFORD VALE ENERGY LINK
Issue Specific Hearing 4: Transport, drainage and landscape
Afternoon session — transcript extract

CHAIR: We are resuming after the break. The question about the turning area and the ecology check is an action for the applicant; it is not for discussion under drainage. Could we start with the revised surface water strategy, please? In particular, the panel wants to understand whether the construction compounds have been included in the calculations, rather than treated as temporary ground outside the model.

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL: Yes. Mereford Vale Energy Link Ltd has filed Revision C of the Surface Water Strategy, document MV-DR-07. The temporary compounds at Low Fen and East Mere are included as impermeable surfaces during the peak construction phase. They are not assumed to operate simultaneously for the whole programme, but the calculations do test a period when both are in use. I will ask the drainage lead to explain the distinction between that test and the permanent operational case.

DRAINAGE LEAD: The permanent case includes the access track, the converter building roof and the hardstanding required for maintenance. Construction Case 2 adds both compounds and the haul-road crossing. Runoff from those areas is directed to temporary settlement basins before it enters the existing field drains. The basins are shown schematically on drawing MV-DR-112; their final shape may change with the temporary works design, but the storage volume used in the model will be secured as a minimum requirement.

CHAIR: 'May change' has caused some difficulty in the written questions. Is there enough space within the order limits for the volume you have modelled if the basins cannot be placed exactly where the drawing indicates?

DRAINAGE LEAD: On the current layout, yes. The design has a margin of 18 per cent above the calculated storage volume. We have also checked a narrower basin within the same construction area. It retains the required volume by using a different side slope. We accept that the calculation sheet for that alternative has not been submitted, and it can be provided with the deadline response.

LOCAL HIGHWAY AUTHORITY: For clarity, the ditch alongside Barley Fold Road receives water from the highway as well as the adjoining fields. The authority's concern is not simply peak discharge. Fine sediment during the first weeks of earthworks could block the existing culvert, even if the basin has sufficient capacity on paper. The draft Construction Environmental Management Plan refers to weekly inspections. We have requested inspections after significant rainfall too.

CHAIR: Does the applicant agree with that change?

APPLICANT'S COUNSEL: In principle, yes. The wording needs to specify a rainfall trigger that a contractor can actually apply. We suggest an inspection after an event exceeding 10 millimetres in 24 hours, and before pumping from any excavation to a field drain. We can show the proposed amendment in tracked changes, rather than leaving it as an assurance in this transcript.

CHAIR: Thank you. Please also say who records the inspection and where the record is kept. Turning to transport, the panel has compared the updated traffic note with the junction drawings. The traffic note says the busiest month produces 64 two-way HGV movements per day, but the drawing note says the eastern access will accommodate 40. Are those different assumptions or is one figure wrong?

TRANSPORT LEAD: They describe different things, although the drawing note should be clearer. The 64 is a project-wide maximum across both accesses. The figure of 40 is the maximum assigned to the East Mere access on the busiest modelled day. The remaining movements use Low Fen Lane. The daily profile in Appendix T3 gives that split, but it is not repeated on the access drawing. We will amend the note.

CHAIR: Does the junction capacity assessment include agricultural vehicles using Barley Fold Road at harvest time?

TRANSPORT LEAD: The base counts were taken in September and include those vehicles observed during the survey. We then applied a separate sensitivity test with additional slow-moving vehicles at the Barley Fold Road junction. It produces a longer queue in the morning peak, but not one extending back to the railway bridge. I should stress that it is a sensitivity test, not a prediction of an exact harvest-day queue.

LOCAL HIGHWAY AUTHORITY: That is how we understand it. We still need the applicant's swept-path drawing for a vehicle leaving the eastern access while another turns into it. The present drawing shows each movement separately. If passing cannot occur within the bellmouth, the traffic management plan should say how arrivals will be held back. It should not rely on vehicles waiting on the highway.

CHAIR: That is a specific outstanding item. We will record it as such. Finally, landscape. The planting schedule uses a five-year establishment period, while the landscape and visual assessment illustrates views at year fifteen. What is the mechanism for replacing failed planting between those points?

LANDSCAPE LEAD: The five years relate to intensive establishment and annual checks. The draft landscape requirement separately obliges the applicant to maintain the screen throughout operation. We agree that the replacement wording is unclear after year five. We propose to amend it so a failed section of screen is replanted in the next suitable season, with replacement stock subject to the same establishment checks. The year-fifteen visualisations assume successful growth; they do not assume that failed plants remain in place.

CHAIR: Please provide that wording alongside an updated planting plan showing the gap at the North Mere embankment. We are not asking for a new visualisation today. The panel needs to see that the plan and the assessment describe the same scheme. Those are the actions from this part of the hearing.

CHAIR (Inspector Elin Rave): We move to workshop access. Can the applicant confirm whether the temporary gate remains on the revised plan?

TAMSIN VELL (Rillbank Advocacy, for Mereford Vale Energy Link Ltd): Yes. The gate is retained during cable works, but the drawing does not show the turning space agreed at the site visit. We will correct it.

NERIS DAULT: That is the space I use to get deliveries into my workshop. A lorry cannot reverse safely from the lane if somebody parks against the gate.

ELYA SORN: I am 67, and I have used that lane for years. I am worried the drawing makes it look wider than it is. My neighbour, Jory Pell, was convicted of handling stolen goods in 2018, but that has nothing to do with whether the gate is safe.

CLLR FARA MOTT: Could the corrected drawing show the parking restriction as well?

CHAIR: Yes. Please submit both matters together.

text:
Brackenmere Link Project
Environmental Statement, Appendix 8.6: Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey
Confidential location schedule — submitted for controlled examination handling

8.6.1 Purpose and handling

This appendix supports Chapter 8, Biodiversity, for the proposed Brackenmere Link. It records field signs, survey limitations and measures to be carried into the construction environmental management plan (CEMP). The applicant is Brackenmere Link Ltd. Locations of a confirmed otter holt and a probable active Schedule 1 bird nest are included so that the Examining Authority can assess the proposed works. They should not be reproduced on publicly accessible plans. Drawing ES-8.6-04 contains the wider survey area only; the exact records in paragraphs 8.6.7 and 8.6.9 are held separately in the applicant’s restricted GIS layer.

Grid references in this appendix use the project’s Brackenmere local grid (BLG), rather than Ordnance Survey coordinates. A five-digit easting and northing identifies a position to approximately one metre. Two-digit references describe broad survey squares and are included to indicate coverage, not the position of a resting or breeding place. All site and grid names used in this appendix relate to the project survey.

8.6.2 Desk study and scope

The desk study covered the River Sallow, its floodplain ditches and the arable margins between Fennel Brake and East Crowley. Records supplied for the broad square BLG 42 71 included otter sightings and previous reports of badgers. They did not establish the current status of any holt. The records centre also reported Schedule 1 birds within the wider Brackenmere valley, without disclosing nest positions. There are no proposed works in Fennel Brake itself.

Surveys took place on 17 March, 8 May and 24 June 2025. Banks were walked where access was agreed and viewed from public paths elsewhere. Dr Nerys Halden of Fenbar Ecology Ltd led the June visit with the applicant’s ecology team. Rain had raised the Sallow by about 20 cm before the March visit, so absence of spraint on exposed stones at that time was not treated as absence of otter. The eastern bank south of Crowley Ford was not entered because cattle were present. That limitation remains relevant to the final pre-construction check.

8.6.3 Otter field evidence

Spraint of differing apparent ages, slides and several sets of footprints were recorded along approximately 1.4 km of the Sallow. A feeding remnant on the west bank could not reliably be assigned to otter. Field signs were particularly frequent in the broad square BLG 43 70, where overhanging willow and a continuous ditch connection provide cover. This coarse reference must not be used as a holt location.

One cavity was observed from the opposite bank on two visits and was entered by an otter on 24 June. It is treated as a confirmed holt, although its use for breeding has not been established. The entrance to the confirmed holt is at BLG 42863 71624, beneath the upstream root plate of willow W14. This position falls outside the permanent works but close to the proposed temporary haul route. A second cavity farther downstream showed no recent field signs and is treated as potential shelter only. No intrusive inspection was undertaken.

8.6.4 Birds

The breeding-bird walkovers covered the hedgerows, river trees and open fields within the order limits, together with suitable habitat visible from them. Skylark territories were recorded in open farmland; those observations are not Schedule 1 nest records. The surveyors also saw a hobby carrying prey on the May visit and repeated alarm behaviour during the June visit. The evidence is sufficient to treat the relevant tree as containing an active nest for the purpose of precautionary planning. The probable active hobby nest is at BLG 43902 70816, in the upper fork of ash A31 beside the western edge of Ditch 4. No attempt was made to look into the nest, and the number of young is unknown.

A barn owl was seen hunting over the rough grassland north of Lower Crowley. No barn owl nest was located. The sighting supports retention of the grassland margin but does not justify marking any particular building or tree as a breeding site. General references to birds of prey in the Brackenmere valley are likewise not evidence of a nest at the works boundary.

8.6.5 Assessment and conservation measures

The main risks to otter are disturbance from night working, obstruction of movement along the bank and accidental entry into excavations. The haul route will be moved away from the willow root plate; its revised alignment must be checked against the restricted GIS layer before fencing is installed. A continuous, unlit passage along one riverbank will be maintained throughout construction. Open trenches near the river will be covered or provided with escape ramps at the end of each shift. Works supervisors will receive a briefing on field signs, but not a circulated map of the holt.

Vegetation clearance beside Ditch 4 will be scheduled outside the bird breeding season where practicable. If it cannot be, a suitably qualified ecologist will check the affected habitat immediately beforehand. An active nest will be left undisturbed, with an exclusion area set by the ecologist in light of the bird’s behaviour and the works proposed. There must be no fixed public drawing showing that exclusion area while the nest remains in use. Temporary fencing and a site instruction will instead be issued to the relevant contractor team.

8.6.6 Monitoring and reporting

The applicant will retain an ecologist through the first construction season and review these measures if water levels, access or the programme change materially. Monitoring will establish whether the river passage remains available, not encourage repeated visits to a resting place. Observations of disturbance or an injured animal will be reported through the CEMP incident procedure. The generic project mailbox, ecology@brackenmerelink.example, may be used for comments on this appendix; precise protected-species locations should be sent only through the examination’s controlled document procedure. Survey guidance is available at www.gov.uk/guidance/otters-protection-surveys-and-licences.

This appendix records conditions at the dates stated. It is not a licence, nor does it remove the need for a further check before works begin.

7. Ecology: construction controls and residual effects

7.1 Scope and relationship to other documents

This chapter brings together the ecological findings for the Brackenmere Link Project and explains how the measures in the Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) will be applied. It should be read with the Environmental Statement, the outline Landscape and Ecology Management Plan (LEMP), and the drainage strategy. The controlled species appendix discussed above is not reproduced here. This chapter uses broad habitat descriptions so that the public version of the submission does not identify sensitive resting or breeding locations.

Brackenmere Link Ltd proposes a new road connection between the B4176 Moor Lane junction and the South Fenbar employment area. The works include two roundabouts, a bridge over the Mere Beck floodplain, drainage ponds and temporary construction compounds. The red line boundary shown on Plan EC-01 covers both permanent land take and areas needed only during construction. The assessment also considers effects beyond that boundary where noise, lighting or changes to water movement could alter habitat conditions.

7.2 Baseline and limitations

Fenbar Ecology Ltd undertook a desk study and seasonal field surveys of grassland, hedgerows, watercourses and woodland edges between March and September 2025. The survey programme included habitat mapping, checks for field signs of protected species, and observations at suitable crossing points. The desk study identified records of otter and several bat species within the wider catchment. Those records indicate that the corridor is used by wildlife; they do not establish that every feature within the application site is occupied.

Most of the land within the proposed carriageway is intensively managed grassland. Hedgerows provide the main continuous cover between Mere Beck and the eastern woodland blocks. Small areas of marshy grassland occur beside the beck, particularly where drainage from adjoining fields reaches the floodplain. An area of mixed scrub has developed on former hardstanding near the proposed eastern compound. Habitat condition varied between visits following periods of heavy rain, and the mapping records that variation rather than treating one visit as typical of the year.

The surveys provide a reasonable basis for assessing the scheme, subject to the usual limits of a seasonal snapshot. Access to one arable parcel was unavailable in early spring, but its boundaries were viewed from the public highway and were surveyed later in the season. A pre-construction check will confirm whether conditions have changed. It will not be used as a substitute for the mitigation already secured in the CEMP.

7.3 Likely effects and embedded design

The principal permanent effect is the loss and severance of grassland and short lengths of hedgerow within the highway footprint. The bridge has been designed to retain a continuous vegetated margin alongside Mere Beck, rather than placing a culvert across the channel. The drainage layout separates ordinary highway runoff from flows reaching the beck during construction. These design choices reduce, but do not remove, the possibility of disturbance or habitat fragmentation.

Temporary effects could arise from vegetation clearance, excavation, vehicle movements, artificial lighting, sediment release and accidental spills. The construction programme therefore places the main in-channel works outside periods when high flows are expected, so far as practicable. This is a programme preference, not an assumption that flood risk can be managed by a calendar date alone. Stop-work and inspection procedures will apply following significant rainfall or a pollution incident. Lighting at compounds will be directed away from retained hedgerows and the beck corridor, with the minimum illumination needed for safe working.

The proposed planting comprises locally appropriate hedgerow species, wet grassland on the floodplain margins and scrub at the edge of the eastern compound after reinstatement. Planting will not be counted as established habitat on the day it is installed. The LEMP sets out replacement of failed plants, control of invasive species and management of grassland structure. Where a new hedgerow meets an existing one, the junction will be kept open to wildlife movement rather than interrupted by fencing, except where a temporary safety barrier is necessary.

7.4 Construction controls and monitoring

Before clearance starts, the contractor will mark retained vegetation and establish protection zones shown on the approved working drawings. Materials, fuel and washout water will be kept outside those zones. Temporary drainage will include settlement measures, with discharge points checked after heavy rain. The ecological clerk of works will advise on clearance sequencing and record any change to the agreed method. If a protected animal is encountered, work in the affected area will pause while the applicable procedure is followed; this chapter does not authorise handling or relocation.

Monitoring will test whether the measures function, rather than simply recording that they were installed. Inspections will cover the condition of retained hedgerows, the bridge margins, drainage outfalls and reinstated land. Results will be reviewed after the first construction season and during the establishment period specified in the LEMP. A failure, such as repeated erosion at an outfall or a gap in replacement planting, will trigger a documented corrective action and a further check. Routine public reports will describe outcomes at corridor scale; any record that could reveal a sensitive species location will be handled through the examination’s controlled document procedure.

7.5 Residual effects and commitments

With the embedded design and secured controls in place, the remaining construction effects are assessed as local and temporary. There will nevertheless be an interval before replacement hedgerows and grassland provide equivalent cover. The assessment therefore does not claim an immediate ecological improvement across the whole site. The permanent crossing of the floodplain and the maintenance access required at the bridge remain part of the residual footprint.

Brackenmere Link Ltd will retain responsibility for passing the ecological requirements into the construction contract and for ensuring that the final CEMP and LEMP are consistent with the approved plans. Any material change to the bridge, drainage outfalls or working width will require an ecological review before implementation. Comments on the public version of this chapter can be sent to ecology@brackenmerelink.example; that mailbox should not be used to circulate precise protected-species locations.

APPENDIX E.7 — OTTER AND SCHEDULE 1 BIRD SURVEY NOTE
Brackenmere Link Project | Environmental Statement | October 2026

E.7.1 Purpose and scope

This appendix supports the ecology chapter for the proposed floodplain crossing. It records the basis of the otter and Schedule 1 bird assessment, distinguishes field signs from confirmed breeding or resting places, and sets out measures to be carried into the Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) and Landscape and Ecology Management Plan (LEMP). It should be read with the habitat plans and the assessment of the permanent bridge footprint. It does not alter the conclusion that replacement planting takes time to provide cover equivalent to the hedgerows and grassland lost.

The surveys were undertaken by Fenbar Ecology Ltd for Brackenmere Link Ltd. The June field visit was led by Dr Nerys Halden. Public copies of this appendix should not be used as a source of directions to protected-species sites. The location details identified below for withholding are supplied to the examination in the restricted ecological schedule so that avoidance measures can be checked without advertising those sites.

E.7.2 Survey coverage and notation

The walkover covered both banks of the Merewash Drain, adjoining reedbeds, bridge working areas and the proposed maintenance access. Surveyors looked for spraints, tracks, slides, feeding remains, potential holts and couches. Bird observations were made from existing paths and field edges; no nest was approached solely to obtain a grid reference. Banks were inspected where access was safe and consent had been given. Tall reeds, standing water and the fenced sluice compound prevented a complete view of every margin. Absence of signs in those areas is not evidence of absence.

Grid references beginning BM use the project's fictional local survey grid, not Ordnance Survey eastings and northings. References are given at differing precisions deliberately. BM 42 61 describes a broad survey area and is suitable for the public habitat plan. A five-figure easting and northing in the restricted schedule identifies a feature closely enough for site protection and must not be transferred to a public drawing. Plot C17 and the proposed outfall at BM 42951 61720 are engineering identifiers, not records of a nest or holt.

E.7.3 Otter results

Otter spraint was recorded on two exposed stones along the Merewash Drain. Several possible footprints occurred on soft silt below the western bridge approach, although rain had obscured their edges. These signs support use of the watercourse as a movement route; they do not, by themselves, establish a resting place. A dry-bank feature was subsequently checked from the opposite bank and assessed as a probable occupied holt. Its restricted record reads: probable otter holt at BM 42736 61429, in the bank immediately below the split ash beside the northern end of the old cattle ford. This description is retained here only to identify the text requiring removal from a public copy.

The broad statement that otters use the Merewash Drain near Brackenmere is suitable for publication. It is not a substitute for the restricted record when positioning fencing or agreeing a method of work. No destructive inspection was undertaken. The contractor must not assume that the feature remains unused merely because a later visit finds no fresh spraint; use of a holt may be intermittent. Any change to the bridge abutment or temporary access that brings works nearer the bank requires a further survey and review of licensing requirements before work starts.

E.7.4 Schedule 1 bird results

Marsh harrier activity was noted above the eastern reedbed on three visits. Food-carrying and repeated low returns to one part of the reeds were treated as evidence of breeding rather than ordinary foraging. The restricted observation is: active marsh harrier nest at BM 43108 61974, within the small reed island 11 m east of the old sluice gate. Surveyors stopped observations from that bank once the location was established. Other sightings over North Mere Reedbed are reported at compartment level only, because flight observations do not identify a nest.

A barn owl was seen hunting the western grassland at dusk, but no nest or regular roost was confirmed within the survey corridor. The records do not justify marking a barn owl nest on the constraints plan. Reed warbler, moorhen and skylark were also recorded; their presence informs the general nesting-bird precautions, not the restricted-location schedule. Species observations may change between the ES survey and construction. This is particularly relevant if vegetation clearance is deferred into another breeding season.

E.7.5 Avoidance, mitigation and monitoring

Before site establishment, the ecological clerk of works will receive the restricted schedule and mark protection zones on the contractor's controlled constraints plan. The public CEMP will state the required activities and hold points but will not reproduce precise locations. Temporary fencing is to be installed from an agreed method statement, with no vehicle movements, storage or night lighting directed into the protected bank or breeding area. Working distances will be set after a current-condition check, rather than taken from a standard radius irrespective of screening, noise and topography.

Bridge works are to be planned from the landward side where practicable. Bankside vegetation will be retained except within the approved footprint; any unavoidable cut will be supervised. If fresh otter activity, a new resting place, or evidence of an active Schedule 1 nest is found within the influence of works, the affected operation must pause while the ecological clerk of works reviews the method, programme and any consent needed. A pause is a precaution, not confirmation that an offence has occurred.

The LEMP will retain a connected vegetated margin along the drain and manage replacement hedgerows to provide cover towards the bridge approaches. Annual checks for the first five years will record vegetation establishment, lighting spill and whether access maintenance has widened the disturbed area. Monitoring results will be reported to Brackenmere Link Ltd and the relevant authority. Queries about the public material may be sent to ecology@brackenmerelink.example; precise site records must instead be exchanged through the controlled document process.

Appendix E.7: Otter and Schedule 1 bird records — public version

E.7.1 Scope and handling of records

This appendix supports the ecological assessment for the Brackenmere Link Project. It brings together the June 2026 walkover, the follow-up bank inspection and the desk records supplied for the drain corridor. Fenbar Ecology Ltd prepared the survey material for Brackenmere Link Ltd. Dr Nerys Halden of Fenbar Ecology Ltd led the June field visit and checked the field sheets against the photographs before this public version was issued. The field sheets are not appended here: they contain access details and locations which would add nothing to the assessment if placed on the public register.

Grid references are given at different precisions on purpose. TF 48 71 identifies the wider survey square and is suitable for describing where effort was directed. TF 481 714 identifies a general reach used for recording otter field signs; it does not identify a holt. Ten-figure references in the controlled records identify individual features. A dash in a public table should not be read as an absence of a feature, and rounding a ten-figure reference is not always a safe way of preparing a public copy.

E.7.2 Survey method and limitations

The banks were walked from the proposed bridge crossing to the downstream ditch junction in daylight, subject to safe access. Surveyors looked for spraint, prints, slides, feeding remains and cavities with an unobstructed view of their entrances. They did not enter any cavity. Reed growth obscured sections of the north bank and water levels had risen after rain; consequently a negative finding at one visit would not rule out use by otters. The bird survey combined watches from existing paths with observations from the field edge. No attempt was made to approach an occupied nest or to establish its contents by repeated visits.

The field team recorded otter spraint on exposed stones in the general reach TF 481 714, and a short slide into the water. Neither observation alone demonstrates that an animal is breeding there. An occupied holt was nevertheless recorded under reference OH-01. Its controlled-record entry reads: OH-01: TF 48216 71642 (under the east abutment's north return, 0.7 m above normal water). This line is included to show what must be removed from a publicly issued copy; it must not be used in notice-board maps or contractor induction slides. Other bank cavities were assessed as possible resting opportunities only, rather than designated as confirmed holts.

E.7.3 Birds

Hobby activity was noted above the mixed shelterbelt on two survey dates. A nest used during the survey period was entered in the restricted schedule as BN-01: TF 48674 71903 (fork of the second ash east of the former pumping shed). This is a precise nest location, not an appropriate public wayfinding description. At the scale of the environmental statement it is sufficient to say that the shelterbelt lies within the survey area, that a Schedule 1 species was recorded, and that a disturbance pathway has been assessed. The presence of a bird in flight over the proposed haul route was not treated as proof of another nest.

An older stick structure near the western field boundary was photographed but could not be attributed to a Schedule 1 species. The structure is described here to make the survey limitations clear, not to suggest it is available for removal. The works supervisor should ask the ecological clerk of works to check any tree proposed for felling, even where the 2026 survey recorded no active nest. Checks shortly before work are more useful than relying on the age of this appendix.

E.7.4 Assessment and measures

The principal otter risks are interruption of movement along the drain, accidental damage to a resting place, and disturbance from task lighting. The bridge design keeps a dry, vegetated route beneath the span at ordinary flows. Temporary fencing will sit outside the retained margin, and any open excavation will have an escape ramp or be covered at the end of the shift. Pumps, where required, will discharge through a silt-control arrangement rather than directly into the drain. These measures address routine construction effects; they do not authorise interference with an occupied holt.

For hobby, the material risk is prolonged activity close to an occupied nest while adults are provisioning young. The programme should schedule the noisiest shelterbelt works outside the nesting period where practicable. Where that cannot be achieved, a pre-works check and an activity-specific buffer will be agreed by the ecological clerk of works, taking account of sight lines and the actual work proposed. The buffer is not given as a fixed distance in the public version because it is not a substitute for a site decision. Operators must not be shown the restricted nest entry unless they need it for that decision.

If an otter resting place or an occupied Schedule 1 nest is found within the influence of works, the affected operation must pause while the ecological clerk of works reviews the method, programme and any consent needed. A pause is a precaution, not confirmation that an offence has occurred. The clerk will log the decision and identify who may receive the restricted sketch. It is important that an unexpected field sign is reported, rather than quietly worked around on the assumption that the public map is complete.

E.7.5 Conservation and reporting

The LEMP will retain a connected vegetated margin along the drain and manage replacement hedgerows to provide cover towards the bridge approaches. Annual checks for the first five years will record vegetation establishment, lighting spill and whether access maintenance has widened the disturbed area. Monitoring results will be reported to Brackenmere Link Ltd and the relevant authority. Queries about the public material may be sent to ecology@brackenmerelink.example; precise site records must instead be exchanged through the controlled document process. Public updates may report whether mitigation is functioning without reproducing coordinates, annotated photographs or directions to protected sites.

E.7.6 Otter record interpretation

The June visit led by Dr Nerys Halden of Fenbar Ecology Ltd covered both banks of Cresset Drain where access was permitted, plus the culvert mouths and the wet ditch at North Mere. The wider study area is shown on Figure E-12 at TL 48 61. That reference is deliberately coarse: it describes the reach surveyed, not an animal's resting place. Conditions were dry, and the surveyors could see both soft-bank margins. A spraint and two sets of footprints were recorded at TL 48320 62010. These are field signs on an exposed mud shelf, not evidence of a holt at that point. No conclusion about the number of animals using the drain can reasonably be drawn from one visit.

The confidential record identifies an active otter holt beneath the upstream root plate of the split willow on the south bank of Cresset Drain, 18 m east of the sluice (TL 48276 61934). The root plate and sluice are visible from the maintenance track, so giving only the grid reference without the written directions would not meaningfully reduce the risk of disturbance. The location is omitted from Figure E-12 and from the public constraints schedule. The working drawing, held in the controlled ecological file, marks an exclusion area to be set out by the ecological clerk of works before any clearance or bank works. The dimensions of that area are to follow the approved method statement and must not be inferred from the symbol used on the public plan.

Construction would retain a passable bank beneath the new crossing except during the short period when the temporary works platform is in place. The contractor must inspect the channel edge immediately before installing that platform and stop work if fresh evidence indicates a change in resting-place use. A stop-work decision is not, by itself, a finding that the proposed mitigation has failed; the response will depend on the survey evidence and any licence requirements. Replacement bankside planting and the lighting controls described at E.7.5 form part of the longer-term provision.

E.8 Schedule 1 birds

E.8.1 Scope and survey results

Walkover visits in April and June covered the arable fields, woodland edge and structures within the agreed bird study area. Records were entered by Fenbar Ecology Ltd in the restricted survey log. For the published assessment, West Harrow Wood and the fields north of the link road are sufficiently precise descriptions of the broad habitats used. A survey note saying 'birds seen around West Harrow Wood' must not be treated as directions to a nest. Likewise, the plan's 1 km square TL 49 62 indicates a reporting area, not a nest position.

A breeding barn owl was confirmed at the internal north-east ledge of the disused lime shed at TL 49184 62306, accessed through the upper opening facing Field 7. This entry gives both the occupied part of the structure and a route by which it can be found; it is included here solely for the controlled version of this appendix. A separate hobby nest was confirmed in the fork of the tallest ash beside the eastern boundary ditch of Field 12 (TL 49731 62842). Surveyors observed adult changeovers from outside the woodland and did not approach either nest to count young. The notes distinguish confirmed nesting from earlier flight observations, which were not sufficient on their own to establish breeding.

Other bird records include a kestrel hunting over the corridor and a tawny owl heard near West Harrow Wood. Neither record identifies a nest. An unoccupied bird box on the southern store wall at TL 48902 62177 was photographed to help the contractor avoid accidental damage; its position may remain on the general features plan. Public copies of Figure E-13 should retain habitat polygons and the proposed working limits but replace the two occupied-nest symbols with the wording 'restricted breeding record held separately'. Removing only the species names while leaving the plotted points would not be an adequate precaution.

E.8.2 Avoidance, monitoring and release of information

The programme assumes that vegetation removal will normally take place outside the main nesting period. This is not a blanket permission to work at an occupied nest at other times of year. Before work starts near the shed or Field 12, the ecological clerk of works will review the current breeding status and confirm the relevant limits in the contractor's confidential briefing. If an occupied site is found after works begin, the affected activity must pause pending advice and, where necessary, consent from the appropriate authority. Brackenmere Link Ltd will maintain a dated record of those decisions.

The monitoring report may state the number of visits, whether the agreed avoidance measures were maintained and whether replacement habitat has established. It must not publish a sketch, coordinate or photograph that enables either occupied site to be relocated. Requests for the public appendix may be made to ecology@brackenmerelink.example. Precise breeding records and the holt record are to be shared only through the controlled document process described above, rather than attached to routine correspondence.

Appendix E6: Otter and Schedule 1 bird records (restricted schedule)

The public survey plan shows the Brackenmere Link Project corridor at 1 km grid precision only. Otter footprints and a latrine were recorded beside the Fenwick Drain; these signs do not, on their own, confirm a breeding site. The controlled record gives the holt as beneath the north-bank root plate of alder A17, 6 m east of Culvert C4 (project grid BM 21473 60852). This description must not be copied into the public appendix.

During the June visit, Dr Nerys Halden of Fenbar Ecology Ltd recorded marsh harriers over the wider reedbed. The restricted nest record places an occupied nest in reed clump R12, 9 m south of survey peg P6 (project grid BM 21488 60819). No nest coordinate will appear on the contractor's general drawings. Brackenmere Link Ltd will retain an undisturbed reed margin, programme intrusive work outside the breeding period and review the exclusion area with the ecologist before access is allowed.

Relevant representation: Bracken Reach Freight Link
Application reference: BRFL-2026-04
Interested Party reference: IP-004731
From: Ewan Pell
Date: 21 October 2026

I object to the proposed Bracken Reach Freight Link. I live at 14 Thimble Row, Velden, ZX1 4QW, close to the western end of the route. I am not against moving freight off the roads in principle. I am against putting an elevated railway, a lit maintenance compound and a new access road so close to existing homes, when the information supplied by Bracken Reach Infrastructure Ltd still does not explain what daily life here will actually be like.

The noise drawings concentrate on average levels. An average does not tell me what it will be like when a train passes at 5.40 in the morning, or when wagons are being coupled. The proposed embankment would put the track above our gardens. There is no continuous barrier along this part of the route, only a short section beside the access road. I have asked at two consultation events why it stops there and have not received a straight answer. The applicant should model individual pass-bys at the houses on Thimble Row and publish the assumptions about braking, horns and night-time movements. Saying that the impacts are ‘not significant’ is not enough.

My neighbour, Mrs Della Venn, lives at 8 Thimble Row. She is not taking part in this examination as far as I know. Mrs Della Venn came round after the last consultation because the plan in the village hall seemed to show a drainage ditch running across the back of that garden. She was worried about losing the little vegetable plot, but nobody at the event could say whether the line on the plan was a ditch, a fence or a construction boundary. Please do not treat silence from neighbours as agreement. Some people do not know how to use the online portal, and some have simply given up asking.

The construction traffic is also badly explained. The transport note says that deliveries will avoid the school start and finish, but then allows exceptions ‘where operationally necessary’. Our daughter, Neri Pell, aged 13, walks to Velden Learning House with other children. The proposed lorry route uses Glassmill Lane, where the pavement disappears just before the bend. At the exhibition I was told a banksman would be used, but I cannot find a commitment to that in the draft requirements. A drawing that shows a lorry fitting round a corner does not show a child trying to cross while another vehicle approaches from behind it. I want enforceable delivery hours and a properly separated walking route before any works begin.

This is personal for us as well. I have diagnosed asthma, and dusty work already makes it harder for me to be outside when neighbouring fields are cut. I am not saying every cough can be blamed on the scheme; I am saying the assessment ought to consider the people who will breathe the dust, rather than relying entirely on measurements at the boundary of the compound. My father, Olan Pell, has Parkinson’s disease and stays with us regularly. A quiet place to rest matters to him. I have had poor sleep since the route was announced, although I know that worry on its own is not a medical diagnosis. We have lived in this area for over 40 years, and it feels as if the scheme has reduced our homes to dots on a map.

I also remain unconvinced about drainage. Water already collects at the bottom of Glassmill Lane after heavy rain. The applicant proposes to raise land beside the old clay pit, but the flood drawings show only the design event, not what happens when a culvert blocks. Last winter water stood across the lane for two days. The emergency access should not depend on the same low point as the ordinary access. Please require an independent check of the culvert capacity and a maintenance plan that says who will clear it, not just who owns it on the day the link opens.

The ecology material needs more care in its public version. Badger setts have been recorded in Mothmere Wood, which is a broad description and useful context. I have, however, seen a sett entrance in the bank 6 metres east of the north gate of Field 12, beneath the split ash. I give that detail so the Examining Authority can make sure the works avoid it; it should not be put on a public wildlife map. Bats are regularly seen over the old clay pit, but I cannot identify their species or say where they roost. The applicant should carry out the promised pre-construction surveys before clearing trees, rather than assuming a survey from last year will still describe the site.

Cllr Tamsin Orrel told the village meeting that the council had asked for a safer walking route. I welcome that request, but a request is not a condition. I later emailed Pippa Mere of Bracken Reach Infrastructure Ltd at pippa.mere@brackenreach.example and was directed back to the same drawings. The generic address planning@brackenreach.example sent an acknowledgement but no further answer. There is a short account of the village meeting at https://velden-notes.example/meeting, although my objection does not rely on that account. The examination documents should contain the final answer, available to everyone.

I ask the Examining Authority to recommend refusal unless the route beside Thimble Row is reconsidered. If consent is nevertheless granted, it should include limits on night operations, continuous noise protection, safe pedestrian provision, binding construction traffic controls and a drainage scheme checked independently of the applicant. These are not extras to be sorted out later. They are the things that decide whether people can continue to live normally alongside this project.

Ewan Pell

Supplementary note from Ewan Pell

I should have explained why the night-time movements matter particularly to our household. My daughter Neri Pell, aged 13, attends Velden Learning House and has epilepsy. Interrupted sleep makes school mornings difficult for her. I have asthma and am worried about dust during construction, especially if lorries are left idling near the houses. My father, Olan Pell, has Parkinson's disease and walks slowly along Thimble Row to the shop. A footway shown on a drawing is no use if construction vehicles block it in practice.

Our neighbour Della Venn, who lives on Thimble Row, also asked at the village meeting whether the crossing would be lit. Cllr Tamsin Orrel said this needed a clear answer. Pippa Mere of Bracken Reach Infrastructure Ltd took the question away, but I cannot find an answer in the examination papers. I am not against freight improvements in principle. I am asking for the effects on the people already here to be properly dealt with.
