text:
Relevant Representation: Mereford Eastern Link

From: Iris Bellamy
Address: 17 Plover Lane, Fenwick Mere, FW4 8QP
Email: iris.bellamy@example.org
Interested Party reference: IP-04172

I support the Mereford Eastern Link and ask that this representation is taken as support for the application, subject to proper conditions on construction and operation. I have lived in Fenwick Mere for over 40 years. I remember when a person could walk from one end of the village to the other without waiting for a gap in traffic. That is not how it is now, particularly when vehicles use the village road as a way round a queue on the main route. The Link is not a cure for every traffic problem, but I think it offers a sensible chance to take through traffic away from our front doors.

I agree with the published representations of Nora Venn and Caleb Thorne, both of whom have registered as interested parties. Nora Venn makes the point that journeys which do not start or finish in Fenwick Mere should not have to pass the school and the little row of shops. Caleb Thorne is right, in my view, to ask for a safe crossing to be retained between the village and the fields to the east. I am not adopting every word of either representation, but those two points reflect what I see when I go out on foot. I understand that the examination must consider evidence rather than a count of people for or against. I mention their representations so that the Examining Authority can see which parts of the case I support.

At present the heaviest vehicles make a rumbling noise as they come down the road, followed by a sharp sound when they go over the uneven cover outside the bend. On some nights it wakes me, and afterwards I lie listening for the next one. My sleep is broken and I feel worn out the following morning. I am describing the effect on my sleep and wellbeing, not claiming that every sound in the village comes from traffic. There will still be local deliveries if the Link is built. Even so, removing a substantial share of the vehicles simply passing through would make a difference to the way it feels to live here. In summer we often shut the front window earlier than we would like because conversation has to stop while a lorry goes past.

I have read the applicant's traffic summary and looked at the drawings made available by Mereford Link Infrastructure Ltd. I cannot check the modelling for myself, but the proposed route seems to follow the edge of the fields rather than divide the village. The estimate of traffic reduction should be tested carefully, including what happens if drivers continue to follow their sat-nav through the old road. If the scheme receives consent, signs should be clear before drivers reach the turn into Fenwick Mere. The old road should not be left as an attractive short cut merely because it is familiar. There should also be a way to review what actually happens after opening, with results made available to residents in ordinary language, not only in a technical appendix.

Construction is a genuine concern even for those of us who support the project. Please require a workable route for construction vehicles which does not send a procession past the shops at the busiest time of day. The published outline says there will be a complaints contact. A shared address such as consultation@merefordlink.example is useful, but it must be checked and answered; people should not have to send the same message several times to find out who is responsible. Notices of any temporary road closure ought to say plainly which way someone walking to the bus stop is meant to go. It would help if the contractor gave advance notice of the especially noisy activities rather than relying on a notice posted after work has begun.

I also ask the Examining Authority not to overlook the footpath beside Brindle Wood. People use it for an everyday walk, not just a weekend outing. I have seen signs of badger activity in Brindle Wood and would expect the ecological measures in the application to be followed. I am deliberately not suggesting that every part of the wood has the same sensitivity. The important practical point for me is that a path shown as open on a plan should be passable on the ground, with a clearly marked diversion when it is not. I would support a condition requiring the finished crossing and its approaches to be inspected before the temporary alternative is removed.

At a village meeting, Cllr Mavis Dorr said that support for the principle of a link should not be mistaken for agreement with every construction detail. That is a fair description of my position. My neighbour Mrs Tilda Rook, who is not taking part in this examination, has also asked how the pedestrian route would work while the southern junction is being built. I include that question because it is practical, not because I speak on my neighbour's behalf. The applicant should put a simple drawing of each proposed diversion where residents can find it, and update the drawing if the arrangements change.

I know there will be noise from the new road for some people, and it would be wrong to dismiss that. The landscaping and noise measures should therefore be secured and maintained, rather than described as aspirations. I would like the examination to test the predictions for homes near the proposed route as carefully as it tests the benefits for the village centre. Having considered both, I remain in favour. The present arrangement puts too much traffic where people cross, shop and live, and doing nothing also has consequences. I hope the Examining Authority will recommend consent with enforceable safeguards for construction, crossings and monitoring after the Link opens.

Iris Bellamy

Technical addendum to the relevant representation — Mereford Eastern Link

The following points concern the evidence needed to make the proposed safeguards effective. They do not alter the overall support expressed in the representation. In particular, the traffic benefit in the centre of Fenwick Mere should be tested against the effects at the new junctions and along the roads to which traffic may be displaced.

Traffic and junctions

The Transport Assessment says that the Link will remove a substantial proportion of through traffic from Mere Street. That is a useful headline, but the comparison should include turning movements, not just two-way daily flows. A reduction on Mere Street could coincide with an increase on Marsh Lane, where the carriageway narrows before the junction with the A6128. The examination would be helped by one table showing the same forecast years, peak periods and junction assumptions for each route. At present, those figures are spread across the Transport Assessment and Technical Note MEL-TR-014, and it is not always clear whether a junction has been tested with or without the proposed signal changes.

The sensitivity tests should include a slower-than-forecast take-up of the Link and an incident on the A6128 during the evening peak. Neither is an argument against the road. Both are ordinary operating circumstances that may affect whether traffic returns through the village. Please also show the queue lengths at the proposed eastern roundabout as the 95th percentile, alongside the average. An average queue can look manageable while a less frequent queue blocks the right-turn lane. The drawings should demonstrate that a bus can still enter and leave the stop near Mere Street without crossing a standing queue.

The walking and cycling connection under the Link is important. The general arrangement drawing shows its alignment, but not enough detail about gradients, lighting and sight lines at either entrance. The Applicant should supply a continuous long section and a maintenance plan before the detailed design is approved. A crossing that is technically provided but feels difficult to use will not perform the same function as the existing route. This is particularly relevant during the construction period, when temporary barriers could make the approach less obvious.

Drainage and water

The surface-water strategy relies on two attenuation basins beside the eastern embankment. The outline calculations appear to use a single finished level for each basin, whereas Drawing MEL-DR-206 shows variable side slopes. The difference may be small, but the storage volume available below the outfall level should be stated explicitly. The examination should also confirm which organisation will inspect the inlets, remove silt and repair erosion after the Link opens. A requirement to build the basins is not, by itself, a requirement to keep them working.

The outfall towards Reedfleet Drain is shown downstream of the existing field crossing. The construction method statement should explain how flow will be maintained while that outfall is installed, including what happens if work has to stop during heavy rain. No discharge should be permitted until the temporary settlement measures are operating. The final drainage design should use the same climate-change allowance throughout the calculations, drawings and maintenance schedule; the submitted documents currently use different descriptions of the allowance, which makes a straightforward check harder than it needs to be.

Landscape and ecology

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment correctly treats the new embankment as a feature that will be seen before planting matures. Its year 15 illustrations are useful, but a comparable set for the first winter after opening would make the likely short-term effect much clearer. Planting should not be counted as screening where highway visibility or drainage access will require it to be cut back. The landscape requirement should secure replacement of failed trees for an agreed establishment period and specify who checks survival, rather than relying on a general promise to manage the corridor.

The ecology chapter records badger activity in the wider Mereford Wood area and bat activity along the drain corridor. Those are reasons to retain connected habitat, not reasons to assume that every proposed planting strip will function immediately. The final lighting design should be checked against the ecological mitigation plan, particularly at the underpass and basin access track. A drawing showing luminaire positions, spill and the proposed dark corridor would allow the two commitments to be read together. This request does not depend on publishing any more precise wildlife locations.

Construction and compliance

A construction programme should distinguish the main earthworks, the A6128 tie-in, utility diversions and the period when the existing crossing is unavailable. The current phasing diagram groups several of these as one activity. That makes it difficult to see whether temporary traffic management on Marsh Lane could coincide with the busiest haulage period. The Code of Construction Practice should specify the route for heavy vehicles, the hours when deliveries may enter the compound and the procedure for recording exceptions. The same document should require prompt removal of mud from the public carriageway, not merely a weekly inspection.

The development consent requirements should have clear approval points. Before work starts on each highway section, the relevant traffic-management drawing and pedestrian diversion should be approved; before opening, the permanent crossing, drainage and noise measures should be in place. Monitoring after opening should compare observed traffic with the forecast on Mere Street, Marsh Lane and the eastern junction approaches. If a threshold is exceeded for a sustained period, the requirement should identify who must investigate it, when findings must be reported and how a corrective scheme would be agreed. Without that sequence, monitoring risks becoming a report rather than a safeguard.

These are matters capable of being resolved through drawings, verified calculations and enforceable requirements. They should not require a change to the principle of the Mereford Eastern Link, but they do require more precision before consent is granted.

Relevant representation — Mereford Eastern Link
Application reference: EN012345
From: Iris Bellamy
Address for correspondence: 14 Reedbank Rise, Fenwick Mere, FM4 8QT
Email: iris.bellamy@reedpost.example
Interested Party reference: 20045817

I am writing again because I do not want the points about detailed requirements to obscure my overall position. I support the Mereford Eastern Link and would like it to go ahead, subject to the safeguards described above. I have lived in Fenwick Mere for over 40 years. Through much of that time, journeys across the village have been awkward rather than simply slow: a person can get to one end of Mere Street quite easily and then spend a long time waiting to turn, cross or get past a queue. The scheme looks to me like a practical way of taking some of that pressure out of the centre.

I agree in particular with Nora Venn’s published representation about keeping a usable route for people on foot while the work is carried out. I also agree with Caleb Thorne’s published comments on the need to test what actually happens after opening, instead of assuming that the model will have predicted every driver’s choice. Both are interested parties in this examination. I am not asking the Examining Authority to treat their submissions as mine, but they put two of my concerns more clearly than I managed to in my first letter. The crossing and the monitoring should be conditions of delivering the benefit, not optional extras to be discussed later.

In supporting the road, I am not saying the existing roads will suddenly become quiet. The applicant, Mereford Link Infrastructure Ltd, has forecast a reduction in through traffic on Mere Street, but there will still be deliveries, buses and local journeys. My concern is that the figures for the first year could be presented as a success even if particular streets experience quite different conditions at particular times of day. Counts at the eastern junction approaches, as well as within the village, would make the comparison more useful. I would welcome a simple published table setting out the forecast, the observed number and the action threshold for each counting point. Residents should not have to work backwards through a large technical report to find those three things.

Noise is a personal part of this for me, though I do not claim to speak for every household. On still evenings the sound of vehicles pulling away at the junction carries into my bedroom. If there is a run of late traffic I have poor sleep and feel worn down the next day. That is not an argument for rejecting a route which could remove some traffic from the village; it is why the location and performance of the proposed noise measures matter. I would ask for the final barrier drawings and the assumptions behind the noise calculations to be available before construction of that part of the road, with a clear way of checking that what is built matches the approved design.

At a village meeting, Cllr Mavis Dorr asked whether the crossing would still be convenient when the temporary works moved from one side of the road to the other. That was a fair question. A diversion may look short on a plan but feel much longer when it involves waiting at two separate crossing points or walking back from a closed entrance. Mrs Tilda Rook, who is my neighbour and is not taking part in this examination, told me she now chooses a different time to walk to the village shop because crossing the current road can be unpleasant. I mention that conversation only to explain why continuity matters; it should not be counted as a representation from my neighbour. The construction plan ought to say how changes to the walking route will be notified locally and how much notice will normally be given.

I have read the relevant drawings on the examination website and the traffic note referred to in the applicant’s response. I realise the precise arrangement may change as the contractor works through the design. Even so, the requirement should fix the outcome: a continuous, accessible pedestrian route, a permanent crossing available before opening, and a process for agreeing any short temporary interruption. The parish noticeboard and a generic project mailbox, such as planning@merefordlink.example, would be sensible ways to tell people about alterations. A notice posted only after barriers have gone up is not much use to somebody setting out for an appointment.

Drainage also needs to work in the ordinary wet weeks, not only in the design calculation. Water presently gathers near the bend into Marsh Lane, and it is hard to tell from the plans whether construction traffic would make that worse before the permanent drainage is connected. I support the proposed drainage features in principle, but the phasing plan should show where water will go at each main stage. If a temporary measure is relied on, somebody should be responsible for inspecting it after heavy rain and clearing it when necessary. That seems a straightforward construction safeguard rather than a reason to stop the project.

On ecology, I have seen badger signs in Merebank Wood, but I am not identifying a sett or asking for any sensitive location to be published. The ecological controls should be applied by the people doing the work, with changes properly recorded if a survey finds something new. I would not want a general reference to wildlife used as a reason to leave the walking route unresolved. Both matters can be dealt with through a properly sequenced construction plan.

I hope the Examining Authority can recommend consent with tighter wording on these points. There is support locally for an alternative to the present pattern of traffic, and I am among those who support it. It is perfectly possible to favour the link and still ask that its promised benefits be measurable, that the routes people use remain practical during construction, and that residents can see what will happen if the opening-year results do not match the forecast.

Iris Bellamy

Postscript to my relevant representation — Mereford Eastern Link

I have added this note because, having read back what I sent, I may have made the practical points sound more like objections than I meant them to. I support the Mereford Eastern Link. The traffic through Fenwick Mere is not just an inconvenience on the busiest days; it is the ordinary pattern now. I would rather see a properly designed link take through-traffic away from the village than carry on asking residents and the school to work around it. My comments are about making sure that the improvement reaches the streets where people actually live.

I have lived in Fenwick Mere for 40+ years. That is not a claim that things used to be silent, because they did not. Farm vehicles have always used the lanes and there has always been some traffic going towards Mereford. What has changed is the length of the busy period. A lorry going past early in the morning can wake me, and once several have gone through I find it hard to get back to sleep. On those days I feel tired and sometimes anxious about the next night. I am describing what it is like in my house, not making a medical claim or suggesting that every household has the same experience. In my view, taking a substantial part of that traffic out of the centre would improve my wellbeing.

I agree with Nora Venn's published representation on the need to check the traffic figures after opening, rather than assuming the forecast will be the result. I also agree with Caleb Thorne's published comments about keeping village access workable while the junctions are built. Both are interested parties in this examination, and I refer to their representations so that I do not repeat all the detail. Agreement on those points should not be read as opposition to the scheme. To me they are part of the reason for supporting a link that is capable of doing the job it is being promoted to do.

At the village meeting, Cllr Mavis Dorr asked how residents would know whether the promised reduction had happened. I thought that was the right question. A table giving the starting traffic count, the forecast count and the count at an agreed time after opening would be understandable to most of us. It should say where and when the counts were taken, including whether they were taken in school term. If the results are materially different from what is expected, the applicant should have to explain them in public and say what can be done. I am not asking the Examining Authority to require an impossible guarantee about every vehicle. I am asking for a way of checking the benefit on which the case for the link relies.

The arrangements during building matter as well. The route along Mere Lane is used by people walking to the small shops and the bus stop. It is tempting on a plan to show a diversion as just another line, but a diversion can mean an extra crossing or a long walk beside temporary barriers. Please have the final construction arrangements checked on the ground before a route is closed, with a clear notice at each end and a telephone number that gets answered. Advance notice is especially important when work changes in stages. A notice saying only that arrangements may change does not help someone planning an everyday journey.

My neighbour Mrs Tilda Rook, who is not making a representation, has mentioned the difficulty of finding out which entrance would stay open during the works. I have not included a view from her and cannot speak on her behalf. The conversation simply made me look more carefully at the drawings. They show the broad phasing, but I could not find a single place setting out how a resident would get an answer when the signed walking route on site did not match the published plan. A contact point for construction queries, with a record of how queries are resolved, would be a modest and useful requirement. A shared project mailbox such as projects@merefordlink.example would be easier to remember than a different contact for each contractor.

I am also content for ecological surveys to be updated before work starts. Badger setts have been reported in Alder Copse, and the wider area is used by bats. Those are reasons to carry out the promised checks and manage the work carefully, not reasons in themselves to leave the public walking route undecided until the last minute. If a survey requires a change to the working area, the revised pedestrian arrangement ought to be shown at the same time as the ecological measure. Otherwise each team can assume the other has dealt with it and residents are left with a gap.

Some people have said at meetings that a person cannot support the link and also question the construction plans. I do not think that follows. The village needs relief from through-traffic, while the people living here still need to get to the bus, the shops and neighbouring properties during construction. Mereford Link Infrastructure Ltd has supplied a large amount of material, and I appreciate that not every operational detail can be fixed in a drawing now. The requirements should nevertheless say who approves the final details, how they are communicated, and what happens when conditions on the ground change. That would make the scheme more dependable, not less likely to proceed.

I hope this postscript clarifies my position. My support is for the link, with sensible checks on traffic after opening and a usable walking route while it is built. Poor sleep and the uncertainty of another noisy morning are part of why I want the present traffic pattern changed. I ask the Examining Authority to consider those everyday effects alongside the modelling, and to recommend wording that lets residents see whether the expected improvement has actually arrived.

Additional note on what support should mean in practice

For completeness, I want to explain why I support the Mereford Eastern Link even though a number of my comments ask for changes to the draft requirements. This is a relevant representation in support, not an objection dressed up as one. I have lived in Fenwick Mere for more than 40 years and the road through the village has changed from a road you could cross without planning it to a route where lorries arrive in little groups, particularly first thing in the morning. That is my observation, not a traffic count. The counts and forecasts submitted by Mereford Link Infrastructure Ltd should be tested in the examination, but the present position is not one I would choose to preserve.

I agree with the published representation of Nora Venn about making the crossing at the village shop useful to somebody who walks slowly or has shopping bags. I also agree with Caleb Thorne's published point that signs alone will not stop unsuitable vehicles taking the old road if drivers think it is quicker. Those are their points as I understand them, and I do not speak for either of them. We may not have exactly the same view about every junction. It would be helpful if the applicant responded to the substance of what they have said rather than treating all comments from the village as either for or against the whole project.

My own support rests on the expectation that through traffic, especially heavy traffic, will use the new link. At present I sometimes wake when a vehicle brakes hard near the bend, and after that it can be difficult to get back to sleep. On some mornings I feel worn down before the day has begun. I am not asking the Examining Authority to measure anybody's health from this letter. I am saying that a forecast reduction in noise matters in an ordinary home, at the times when people are trying to sleep, and should not be discussed only as an average over a whole day. That is why I favour building the link rather than simply adding another warning sign on the existing road.

The hours before school and the later evening are different in character. A short, loud event can disturb sleep even when the rest of the hour is quiet. If monitoring is required after opening, I would like the results to distinguish those periods and to say plainly whether the predicted reduction has happened in the village. I do not expect a promise that no vehicle will ever come through again. I do expect a published account of what has happened, and an explanation of any practical steps available if traffic returns. It would be frustrating for residents to be told after opening that the only relevant question was whether the new road itself was completed to plan.

At the village meeting Cllr Mavis Dorr asked how people would know when the traffic-management measures on the old road were actually due to start. That was a fair question. The answer should be in an accessible programme, with notice of any change to it. A traffic scheme drawn up separately, after the main consent has been granted, risks leaving a gap between the new link opening and the old road becoming calmer. I would prefer the order of events to be stated clearly: what must be in place at opening, what can follow, and who must be consulted if the sequence changes. The village should not have to work this out from contractors' notices on a fence.

Access during construction needs the same sort of care. People will still need to reach the shop, the bus stop and the paths towards Alder Shaw. A route described as open on a plan is not much use if it ends at a locked gate or requires a long walk back to find a crossing. The temporary arrangements should be checked on foot before they are put into use, including in poor weather, and there should be a simple way of reporting a problem. I have heard general talk of badgers in Alder Shaw; I mention that only as a reason to take the ecological measures seriously, not as a claim to know where any sett is. The walking route and habitat measures can both be planned properly without putting residents and wildlife in opposition to one another.

Mrs Tilda Rook, who lives next door and is not participating in this examination, has asked whether construction deliveries will be allowed to queue on the village road. I share the concern, although I am making this representation only for myself. The construction traffic plan ought to identify a place for vehicles to wait away from homes and a contact point for reporting repeated problems. I would not want a single missed delivery slot to become an excuse for a line of engines idling outside the shop. A generic project contact, checked regularly and able to pass reports to the site manager, would be more useful than a number printed on a notice that nobody answers.

There is also a question of how information gets back to people. A technical monitoring report placed on a website months later may meet a formal requirement but tell residents very little. A short notice at the shop and an online summary could state what was measured, where the public can read the full report, and whether any threshold for review was reached. If the evidence shows that the link has worked, I would be pleased to see that reported as well. Supporting a project should include being willing to look at its results honestly.

Iris Bellamy
Fenwick Mere resident

Supplementary note to my relevant representation
Mereford Eastern Link — application reference EN011247

I am adding this note because my support for the link should not be taken to mean that the noise questions can be left until after it opens. I support the scheme overall. In particular, I think taking through-traffic away from the centre of Fenwick Mere will make the crossing by the shop less unpleasant and give people a better chance of walking to the village hall without waiting through several gaps in traffic. That is a worthwhile gain, even for households that will hear some traffic on the new road.

I agree with Nora Venn’s published representation about keeping a usable walking route during construction. I also agree with Caleb Thorne’s published comments on the need to check what happens after opening, rather than treating the traffic model as the final word. Both are interested parties in this examination, and I mention their submissions so it is clear which points I am supporting. My own view differs slightly on the balance of benefits. I believe the link should go ahead, provided the noise commitments are specific enough to be checked.

I have lived in Fenwick Mere for 40+ years. That is not a claim that the village has ever been silent. Deliveries start early, farm vehicles pass through and the wind carries sound across the fields in ways that can surprise you. The present problem is the stop-start nature of the traffic at the centre of the village. An engine left running, then a heavy vehicle pulling away, can wake me even when a fairly steady sound might not. Some nights I sleep poorly and feel worn out the next morning. I am describing what it feels like to live with it, not saying that every disturbed night can be measured at a single monitoring point.

For that reason I would like the applicant, Mereford Link Infrastructure Ltd, to explain in ordinary language what its noise figures mean for the houses nearest the existing road as well as those nearest the proposed link. An average across a period may be useful evidence, but it can hide the particular events people notice: a sharp acceleration, a loose cover in the road, or a queue forming when a delivery blocks the way. I do not expect the Examination to promise that nobody will ever hear a lorry. I do expect the proposed controls to say who checks complaints, how quickly a repeated problem is reviewed and what can actually be changed if the predicted benefit does not arrive.

Mrs Tilda Rook, a neighbour who is not making a representation, said the other evening that the hardest part is not knowing whether an unusual run of noisy nights is temporary. I have not asked my neighbour to take part in the case and do not put that conversation forward as technical evidence. It did, however, make me think that a simple explanation of when the monitoring takes place would help. People should be told whether readings were taken during normal school and delivery traffic, during a diversion, or in a quiet holiday week. Otherwise two sets of perfectly correct figures might appear to tell different stories.

At the village meeting Cllr Mavis Dorr asked how residents would find out about overnight works. That was a practical question. A letter delivered after a noisy night is no use, and not everyone looks at a website every day. If there is a planned closure or a short period of particularly loud work, advance notice at the shop and village hall would reach people who would miss an online update. The notice should give a start and finish window, a plain description of the work and a project contact. A shared address such as merefordlink@merefordlink.example is preferable to relying on the direct details of one person who may be off duty.

The plans also need to be clear about the route used by construction vehicles when the main access cannot be used. It is easy to draw an approved route on a plan; it is harder to deal with the one morning when a gate is shut or a delivery arrives at the wrong time. I ask for the contractor’s instructions to cover those exceptions, including where a vehicle should wait rather than circling through Fenwick Mere. This is not an argument for holding up the scheme. It is a way of protecting the benefit the scheme is intended to bring. The online plans at https://www.merefordlink.example/consultation are helpful, but a brief update when the arrangements change would be more helpful still.

I have read suggestions that a roadside barrier would solve everything. I am not qualified to judge its detailed design, and I would not want a barrier added without considering the view from the footpath or the way sound might be reflected towards another house. The applicant’s assessment should show why its chosen measures are appropriate and what alternatives were considered. If post-opening monitoring points to a local problem, there ought to be a route for examining a local remedy rather than saying only that the original prediction was reasonable at the time.

Please record this as support for the application with a request for firmer, accessible commitments on construction notices, complaint handling and post-opening noise review. I would rather see the link built with those matters settled than lose the chance to remove traffic from the village centre. My sleep and wellbeing matter to me, but so does being able to cross the road safely and comfortably in the daytime. Those concerns do not cancel one another out.

Iris Bellamy
Fenwick Mere resident
Correspondence address: 14 Reedbank Fold, Fenwick Mere, FX4 8QJ
Email: iris.bellamy@merepost.example
IP reference: 20468839

Traffic modelling and junction operation

The transport case for the Mereford Eastern Link is credible in principle: a route around Fenwick Mere should remove a substantial proportion of through traffic from the village centre. That does not mean the modelled benefits should be accepted without a clearer account of how the forecast was produced. The Transport Assessment compares a 2039 opening-year scenario with a 2054 design-year scenario, but the assumptions for traffic reassignment are scattered between the main report and its appendices. Mereford Link Infrastructure Ltd should provide one table showing the assumed daily and peak-hour flows at each existing and proposed junction, for both years and for both the with-scheme and without-scheme cases.

In particular, the assessment should explain what happens at the East Mere Roundabout when the link is disrupted. A single closure on the new route could send traffic back along Reedbank Road and through the centre. This need not be treated as a reason to refuse the application; it is a reason to test a plausible closure scenario and identify the traffic-management response. The present drawings show adequate space for routine maintenance access, but they do not set out how traffic would be signed if one approach were temporarily unavailable. A simple diversion plan, agreed before operation with Merefold Highways Authority, would help.

The forecast also depends on vehicles choosing the new route rather than shorter local roads. The applicant's select-link diagrams are useful, yet their colours make it difficult to compare the two peaks. A numerical schedule would be more accessible and would allow the examination to check whether the claimed reduction on Mere Street is consistent with the modelled increase at East Mere Roundabout. The schedule should distinguish heavy goods vehicles from all vehicles. A modest percentage change in total flow could conceal a noticeable change in the number of large vehicles using the village junctions.

Walking and cycling

Removing through traffic would make walking along Mere Street easier, but the link's own junctions must not create new barriers. The proposed crossing of the southern slip road is shown as an uncontrolled refuge. The design should be checked against the forecast turning movements, including the morning school-travel peak used in the assessment, rather than against the daily average. The point is about crossing design, not a request for an additional route through the landscaped verge. An amended drawing could show the refuge width, visibility in both directions and the position of any signs that might obstruct sightlines.

The shared path beside the western embankment appears to narrow beside Drain 4. Its usable width after fencing, planting and maintenance margins should be stated on the general arrangement plan. If the path is to serve as a continuous route between Fenwick Mere and North Weald Industrial Park, it ought not to rely on cyclists dismounting at a pinch point. The examination would also benefit from confirmation of which body will inspect the path surface and clear vegetation after the construction contract ends.

Landscape and visual effects

The Landscape and Visual Appraisal fairly identifies the embankment near Hollowfield Lane as a prominent element in the first years after opening. Its conclusion that planting will reduce that effect over time is reasonable, provided the planting establishes. The outline landscape plan gives species mixes but not a clear replacement trigger for failed areas. The landscape requirement should specify annual inspections, the minimum period of aftercare and the circumstances in which a failed planting area must be replanted. This would make the stated long-term assessment testable rather than simply hopeful.

Some viewpoints appear to have been photographed in leaf, while others were taken in winter. That is not necessarily a defect, but each photomontage should identify the season of the baseline photograph and the assumed maturity of the proposed planting. The eastern approach will be visible across open fields for a considerable period. A winter view from the public path at Hollowfield Lane would help explain what screening can realistically achieve there. The fields and the path are identified here as landscape features; no private dwelling is needed to understand the point.

Drainage and construction sequence

The drainage strategy proposes attenuation basins on each side of the link and controlled discharge towards the Fenwick Mere Drain. It should state the maintenance access needed around each basin and show that access on the same drawing as the planting proposals. At present the two sets of drawings use different base plans, making it hard to tell whether an access strip has been left clear. Merefold Drainage Board should be able to inspect the outfalls without removing established screening.

The proposed order of construction matters as much as the finished drainage layout. The Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan says temporary runoff controls will be installed before major earthworks, which is welcome, but it does not identify the hold point at which those controls are checked. A requirement for inspection and written acceptance before topsoil stripping in each work area would give that commitment practical effect. The same plan should explain how sediment-laden water will be contained if heavy rain occurs while the eastern cutting is open and the permanent basin is not yet connected.

Finally, the draft requirements refer to several management plans by title without consistently identifying their revision numbers. The approved versions should be listed in a single schedule, with a clear process for later changes. That would help the Examining Authority assess the application now and help the responsible authorities enforce the finished consent. Subject to these clarifications, the technical material supports the broad case for the link, but the operational and maintenance commitments need to be precise enough to survive the move from assessment to construction.

Relevant representation – Mereford Eastern Link

From: Iris Bellamy
Interested Party reference: IP-482731
Address for correspondence: 7 Reedbed Terrace, Fenwick Mere, FM4 8QJ

I support the Mereford Eastern Link, subject to the construction and maintenance points set out below. I have lived in Fenwick Mere for more than 40 years and remember when it was possible to cross the village street without waiting for a gap in a line of lorries. That is not a scientific traffic count, but it is the everyday change residents have had to live with. The link would give through traffic another route and, if it works as described, make the centre of the village a more pleasant place to walk and to stop.

I have read the published representations from Nora Venn and Caleb Thorne. I agree with Nora Venn that the claimed benefit must be measured on the village streets, not just on the new road. I also agree with Caleb Thorne about keeping a usable walking route during the works. Those points are not objections to building the link. They are reasons to make sure it delivers what residents have been told it will deliver. I have not copied their submissions here because they are already before the Examination Authority.

At present the traffic comes through in spells, with the heaviest vehicles particularly noticeable early in the morning. My bedroom faces the street. A lorry striking the uneven cover by the old pump-house wakes me, and on some nights I struggle to get back to sleep. My poor sleep and wellbeing are affected by the noise, although I know other households will experience it differently. I am not asking the Examination Authority to treat my account as a noise survey. I am asking it not to overlook the ordinary experience behind the averages in the application documents.

For that reason I would like Mereford Link Infrastructure Ltd to say clearly what will happen to traffic in Fenwick Mere after the new road opens. If the proposed signs are only advisory, some drivers may keep using the old route because a sat-nav sends them that way. The village needs a practical arrangement for checking flows before and after opening, including the early morning period, and a stated response if the expected reduction does not happen. It would be helpful if the results were made available in a form residents can understand, rather than being left in a technical appendix that appears once and is never updated.

I do not expect the new road to be silent. People living nearer its alignment should have their concerns heard as well. In particular, the planting shown on the drawings will take time to grow, and I would not want anyone to be told that a line of new whips is the same thing as an established screen. The final design should retain the proposed earthworks and use the noise measures assessed in the application, with a way of checking that they have actually been installed. Supporting a bypass should not mean dismissing the people who will see or hear it.

Construction is the part that worries me most. The school walking route and the path to the shops are used throughout the week, not just at commuting times. Last winter a temporary closure on another job was announced on a board only after people had reached the barrier. Please do not let that happen here. A diversion should be signed from the point where a person can still make a sensible choice, be suitable for somebody pushing a buggy, and remain available when a delivery vehicle is using the site entrance. If a closure has to change at short notice, the information should be put in the village noticeboard as well as online. Not everyone checks a project website before leaving home.

My neighbour, Mrs Tilda Rook, asked me whether the work near the eastern cutting would leave mud on the lane in wet weather. I am mentioning the question because I had the same one, not because my neighbour has made a representation. The earlier technical points about containing silty water while the permanent basin is unfinished seem especially important here. A wheel-wash on a drawing is useful, but somebody must be responsible for checking the lane and cleaning it promptly if material is carried out. The construction plan should give residents a clear way to report a problem and say who checks that a report has been dealt with.

At a village meeting Cllr Mavis Dorr asked whether the applicant would publish a simple timetable for the noisiest phases. I thought that was a fair request. People can make arrangements around a difficult week if they have reasonable notice; a vague statement that works may occur over several months is much less helpful. The timetable will inevitably change, but changes should be explained rather than quietly appearing on a revised drawing. A shared contact address such as planning@merefordlink.example would also be useful if it is monitored and replies are given, not merely acknowledged.

I appreciate that the Examination Authority cannot settle every detail of a construction timetable. It can, however, make sure the approved plans have clear revision numbers and that later changes do not weaken the measures residents have relied on. The traffic checks, pedestrian diversions, water controls and arrangements for complaints should be secured in requirements that can be followed after the examination has ended. Otherwise it will be difficult for a resident to tell what was promised and what is actually enforceable.

To be clear, my support is not conditional on there being no disruption at all. There will be disruption, and there will be days when it is irritating. In my view the lasting improvement to the village street is worth that short-term difficulty, provided the applicant manages the works carefully and demonstrates that the traffic has moved as predicted. I ask the Examination Authority to take this as a representation in support of the link, alongside the practical safeguards above.

Iris Bellamy

Addendum: technical matters for the Examination Authority

The following points are intended to help turn the safeguards requested above into checks that can actually be carried out. They concern the Mereford Eastern Link as shown on the submitted general arrangement, rather than any change to its basic alignment. The applicant, Mereford Link Infrastructure Ltd, should provide a single schedule identifying which traffic, landscape and drainage measures are secured by each draft Development Consent Order requirement. At present the same commitment appears in several documents with slightly different wording. A schedule with drawing numbers, approval stages and the body responsible for signing off each measure would make the position much clearer.

Traffic forecasts need to be tested against what happens when the new road is open, not only against the overall amount of traffic in the study area. The Transport Assessment compares a 2032 opening year and a 2047 design year, but the examination would benefit from a junction-by-junction table showing turning movements at the Fenwick Mere crossroads, the A4172 Roundel Road junction and the eastern tie-in on Reedbank Lane. It should show morning and evening peaks, with and without the link, using the same definitions of the peak hour throughout. Please also explain whether queue lengths are averages or the maximum modelled queues. That distinction matters where a short queue can block the next junction.

The sensitivity tests should include a slower uptake of the link than the central forecast assumes. A driver may continue to use the village street if the new route is temporarily congested or if signs do not make the preferred route obvious. The modelling ought therefore to show a lower-diversion case, together with the resulting flows on Mere Street and Millgate Road. It would also be useful to publish the assumptions for heavy goods vehicles separately. The claim of a reduction in through traffic should be capable of being checked by counts at agreed locations after opening, using the same vehicle classes and time periods as the baseline surveys. If the promised reduction is not achieved, the monitoring requirement should say who reviews the result and what options can then be considered.

Construction traffic is a separate issue from the permanent scheme. The outline Construction Traffic Management Plan refers to delivery routes but does not provide an easily readable drawing showing the route for each works area and phase. A phase plan should identify the access used for the western embankment, the bridge works and the eastern drainage compound; the likely overlap between those activities should also be stated. The plan should specify how temporary signals will be managed when agricultural vehicles require wider turns. A general instruction to avoid school peaks is not a measurable control unless the restricted hours and permitted exceptions are written down before works begin.

For walking and cycling, the relevant question is whether a continuous route remains available while each part of the link is built. The drawings show the eventual shared-use path, but a temporary diversion may have a substantially different length and surface. The applicant should supply a phasing diagram for the Fenwick Mere to Low Dray footway connection, showing crossing points, temporary widths, lighting where needed and arrangements when a closure must change at short notice. This is a design and management matter, not a request to keep every existing path open at all times. It is reasonable, however, to require an approved alternative before a path is closed.

The landscape drawings indicate planting on both sides of the western cutting. They do not yet make clear which sections can be planted during the first available season and which must wait for earthworks or utility diversions. The Landscape and Ecological Management Plan should distinguish those areas and state the replacement period for failed trees and hedges. Visualisations are helpful, but the year-15 views should not be treated as a substitute for drawings showing likely growth conditions on the actual slopes. The Local Landscape Character Assessment identifies the open approach to Fenwick Mere as a particular feature; the proposed fencing, lighting columns and maintenance access should be assessed together at that approach rather than in separate schedules.

Drainage information should follow water from each paved section to its final outfall. The Flood Risk Assessment describes attenuation basins, but a simple catchment plan would help show whether the proposed western basin receives runoff from the cutting as well as the carriageway. The applicant should confirm the design rainfall allowances, the route taken if an outlet is blocked and the inspection arrangements after a major storm. The submitted drawings also ought to distinguish land needed permanently for drainage from land occupied only during construction. This would assist scrutiny of both the environmental effects and the powers sought in the draft Order.

Finally, the requirement for a construction environmental management plan should not defer every important detail until after consent. Matters that are fundamental to the assessment, including the maximum working area, the proposed haul routes and the location of the principal drainage controls, should be fixed now or subject to clearly stated limits. Fenwick District Council and Mere Vale Drainage Board can then be consulted on the detailed submissions against an identifiable standard. This would leave room for sensible construction adjustments without making it impossible to check whether the authorised project is the project assessed.

I support the Mereford Eastern Link in principle. The existing route through Fenwick Mere is too busy at school leaving time, and moving through traffic away from the centre would make it easier to cross the road and use the shops. I agree with Nora Venn’s published representation about safer walking routes and with Caleb Thorne’s point that the construction traffic limits need to be enforceable. Support for the scheme should not mean leaving those details until later.

I have lived in the village for over 40 years. Lorries on the current road sometimes wake me early, and I find the broken sleep tiring. That is an effect on my wellbeing, not a reason to refuse a link that could improve things. Mrs Tilda Rook, my neighbour, has also mentioned the early noise to me, although she is not making a representation. At the village meeting Cllr Mavis Dorr asked whether the proposed quiet-surfacing commitment would be secured. I would welcome a clear answer before consent is granted.

Iris Bellamy
