text:
BRACKENMERE DISTRICT COUNCIL
LOCAL IMPACT REPORT
Larkfen Solar and Storage Project | Examination reference EN012345
Submitted 21 October 2026

Report author: Elin Marr, Head of Strategic Planning
Council office: Civic House, 4 Lantern Square, Alderwick, QV1 4RT
Correspondence: planning@brackenmere-dc.gov.uk

1. Purpose and scope

This Local Impact Report describes the likely effects of the proposed Larkfen Solar and Storage Project within Brackenmere District. It is intended to assist the Examining Authority and is not the Council's final position on the application. The Council has considered the application documents, its own records, site visits and comments received locally. The application site covers agricultural land between Alderwick and Low Mere, with a proposed battery compound beside the existing Mossbank substation. Larkfen Energy Ltd is the applicant.

The Council's assessment follows the local impact report guidance available at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. References to document numbers below are to the examination library unless stated otherwise. Figures and effects may change if the applicant submits revised layouts.

2. Local context and landscape

The land is mainly open, with low hedges, drainage ditches and long views from the raised Alderwick Lane. The submitted visual assessment broadly identifies the most exposed viewpoints, but it gives insufficient weight to the view from the lane's western bend, where panels would appear behind a relatively thin hedge. The proposed planting is welcome; it will not screen equipment immediately, and its success depends on maintenance after establishment. The Council asks for a replacement-planting commitment and drawings showing the mature height of the hedge, rather than just the number of plants.

Members also raised the difference between the temporary construction effect and the long operational period. At the Planning and Environment Committee on 8 September 2026, Cllr Iris Fenlow asked that the landscape plan retain the two established field oaks east of Parcel 4. Cllr Jonah Rusk requested a clearer explanation of how lighting at the battery compound would be controlled outside working hours. These were requests for information, not findings that the present design is unacceptable.

3. Highways and access

Construction traffic would use the proposed access off Mossbank Road. This is preferable to routing heavy vehicles through Alderwick centre, where the carriageway narrows beside the library. Nevertheless, the swept-path drawing in APP-087 does not show a vehicle passing a cyclist near the southern bus stop. The Council recommends a revised drawing and a condition requiring the construction traffic management plan to be agreed before works start. Delivery booking, wheel washing and a named contact for complaints should be included in that plan.

The Council has received comments about noise, dust, poor sleep and general anxiety during construction. These concerns are understandable, although the report does not treat them as evidence of a diagnosed condition. One resident, Mrs Nola Creed of 16 Hawthorn Close, Alderwick, QV1 6LT, said she has diagnosed asthma and was concerned about dust during dry weather. Her comment has been considered as part of the general case for effective dust controls; this report does not attempt to assess individual medical risk. In another response, a resident said they had walked Mossbank Road for more than 40 years. That statement describes experience of the route, not the person's age.

4. Drainage and ecology

Low Mere is prone to standing water after prolonged rain. The drainage strategy proposes attenuation within the red-line boundary, but the maintenance schedule does not say who will clear the ditch beside Parcel 7 if silt accumulates. The Council's drainage engineer, Tessa Venn of Brackenmere District Council, asked for an inspection frequency and a drawing of the proposed outfall. Technical queries may be sent to the shared mailbox drainage@brackenmere-dc.gov.uk; the individual address tessa.venn@brackenmere-dc.gov.uk was used for arranging the site visit, not for formal submissions.

The ecological surveys refer to badger activity in Larkfen Wood and bats commuting along the western hedgerow. These are broad habitat descriptions and do not, by themselves, identify a breeding or resting place. A confidential survey note supplied to the Council identifies a badger sett at grid reference QV 43821 67194, under the east bank of Drain 7 immediately behind gate B3. The Council asks the applicant to confirm that the construction exclusion zone can be secured without displaying this precise location on public working drawings. General references to replacement bat boxes and hedge retention can remain in the public ecological management plan.

5. Community facilities and agricultural use

The nearest public footpath would remain open under the current proposal, but users would walk beside temporary fencing during installation. A short signed diversion may be safer when trenching crosses the route. The applicant should give the Council and Fenwick Parish Council advance notice of any closure request. Its draft community fund is noted, but it does not replace mitigation for an identified planning effect.

The submitted land plan shows temporary use of part of Thistle End Farm for the cable route. The name identifies an agricultural holding, not the occupier's residence. The Council understands that the occupier has been contacted, but it cannot confirm agreement about soil storage or reinstatement. Those matters should be settled before entry onto the land and recorded in the soil management plan.

6. Representations and requested action

Corin Vale MP wrote asking whether emergency services would have access to the battery compound from more than one direction. The Council shares the need for a clear emergency access drawing and awaits the applicant's response. A separate resident supplied photographs through https://fieldnotes.example.org/larkfen-survey; the link is recorded here as received, not endorsed as an examination document.

In summary, the Council seeks further information on landscape establishment, construction vehicle movements, ditch maintenance, confidential ecology safeguards and emergency access. Subject to that information, the effects described above appear capable of being addressed through the detailed plans and requirements. The Council will update its position if revised material materially changes the local impacts.

Brackenmere District Council
Local Impact Report: Larkfen Solar and Storage Project
Technical assessment addendum

1. Purpose and scope

This addendum records the Council's assessment of the local effects most likely to require further examination. It should be read with the preceding sections of the Local Impact Report. The assessment uses the submitted design limits and does not assume that illustrative layouts are fixed. Where an effect depends on the final position of equipment, the Council has identified the control needed at detailed-design stage rather than treating the illustration as a commitment.

2. Construction traffic and highway operation

The proposed construction access from Marshgate Road would concentrate heavy goods vehicle movements on the section between the site gate and the B741 Fenwick Link. That section has a narrow running width and limited opportunities for opposing large vehicles to pass. The Council considers the broad choice of access workable, but the applicant's traffic model should be supplemented by a swept-path drawing for a laden articulated vehicle meeting a farm vehicle at the bend north of Reedmere Bridge. A drawing showing only an unopposed entry into the gate would not answer this point.

The submitted programme assumes that delivery peaks for the solar arrays and battery units will not coincide. This is important because the junction assessment has little spare capacity during the morning peak. A construction traffic management plan should therefore specify a maximum daily and hourly delivery profile, booking arrangements, and how a missed booking would be dealt with. It should also identify a holding area within the Order limits; waiting on Marshgate Road would obstruct ordinary traffic and could interfere with access to adjoining fields. The Council does not seek a blanket restriction on all construction activity during peak hours, but requests that the movements used in the model be made enforceable.

Temporary signs, wheel washing and a carriageway condition survey should be agreed before works begin. The survey should cover the carriageway edge as well as the paved surface, since repeated overrunning is a more plausible local impact than general network congestion. The applicant should distinguish repairs made necessary by the works from routine highway maintenance in its proposed inspection procedure.

3. Landscape and visual effects

The principal local landscape change would be the apparent joining of separate fenced fields into one infrastructure area when viewed across the Fenwick Lowlands. Existing hedgerows would continue to break up some longer views, but the effect would be greater where hedge gaps coincide with security fencing and inverter stations. The proposed planting is capable of reducing this effect over time; it cannot be relied on to screen equipment on the first day of operation.

The Council requests a planting schedule stating minimum stock sizes, establishment inspections, replacement triggers and responsibility for management throughout operation. A requirement for planting to be 'substantially in accordance' with an illustrative landscape plan would be insufficient if it allowed an important hedge link to move or disappear. Along the eastern boundary of Parcel PF-04, the detailed plan should retain enough space between the fence and planting for maintenance without cutting back the screen to fence height. Where visibility at an access requires a lower hedge, that exception should be shown explicitly.

The lighting strategy should confirm the mounting heights, operating circumstances and direction of emergency lighting at the battery compound. No routine overnight illumination is proposed, and the Council's assessment depends on that distinction. A photometric drawing at the final equipment positions would enable the effects beyond the Order limits to be checked.

4. Drainage and water environment

The site drains through field ditches towards the North Mere Drain. The drainage strategy proposes to retain existing flow routes and use shallow storage features rather than a single large attenuation basin. That approach is appropriate in principle, provided construction does not sever the smaller ditches before replacement connections are operating. The phasing plan should show when each crossing, temporary diversion and permanent outfall becomes available. It should also set out the arrangements for removing silt from temporary works before handover.

The Council has not identified a need to redesign the whole drainage system, but the maintenance information remains incomplete. Access to ditch banks should be preserved after fencing is installed, including where a ditch lies between a landscape belt and an array. The final drainage management plan should identify inspection frequency, vegetation control, responsibility for blocked crossings and a route for reporting standing water. The calculations should be checked against the as-built levels: shallow changes in ground profile could redirect runoff towards the edge of an adjoining field even where the total discharge remains within the modelled limit.

5. Ecology and land management

The submitted surveys record badger activity in the wider Fenwick Lowlands and bat activity along established hedgerows. These are broad survey findings, not evidence that the whole site is unsuitable for development. The Council supports retaining connected hedgerows, limiting construction lighting and checking vegetation immediately before clearance. Ecological working drawings should be supplied through the appropriate confidential process where they contain protected-site detail; the public landscape drawings need show only the resulting works exclusions and habitat measures. No precise protected-species locations are set out in this report.

The outline land management plan describes grassland establishment beneath panels but gives less detail on remedial action if bare ground persists. A measurable ground-cover target and a practical reseeding procedure would help avoid erosion and repeated vehicle access during operation. The measures should be compatible with the drainage regime and should not require routine cultivation close to retained hedges.

6. Policy conclusion and further information

The Council has assessed the proposal against the Brackenmere Local Plan Policy LQ6 and the Fenwick Lowlands Landscape Character Supplement. Neither document imposes an absolute prohibition on energy infrastructure in this location. The relevant question is whether the design and secured mitigation keep local effects within acceptable limits. On the information available, the Council considers that outcome achievable, subject to the traffic, planting, drainage, lighting and management details identified above. Its position remains provisional where a submitted outline plan has yet to be translated into an enforceable requirement.

7. Matters raised since the Council's initial assessment

The Council received further comments after the site visit on 14 September 2026. These do not change the policy conclusion at section 6, but they show where the draft requirements need more precision. This part of the Local Impact Report records local effects; it is not a decision on whether development consent should be granted.

Cllr Iris Fenlow asked whether the proposed construction hours would cover deliveries as well as work inside the compound. The current wording is not clear on vehicles waiting at the gate before 07:00. Cllr Jonah Rusk also asked that the final Construction Traffic Management Plan show where drivers will be told to turn around if Fenwick Lane is temporarily blocked. Both points concern enforceability rather than a request to prohibit all construction traffic. The Council asks for a plan agreed with the highway authority before any construction access is used, with a named procedure for recording complaints and correcting repeated breaches.

Corin Vale MP wrote to the Council about the cumulative effect of the scheme and the already approved East Fenwick substation works. The letter raised the prospect of two sets of HGV movements on school days. The Council cannot yet confirm that those programmes will overlap. It asks Larkfen Energy Ltd to provide a combined programme, where the information is available, and to explain what coordination is proposed if overlap occurs. This would assist examination of the local transport effect without assuming that every consented project will be built at the same time.

8. Residential amenity and consultation comments

The nearest homes are affected differently according to their orientation, existing vegetation and the route taken by construction vehicles. For that reason a single distance from the panel fence is not, by itself, an adequate test of impact. The Council recommends that the final layout drawings retain the proposed stand-offs at the western boundary and identify any inverter or battery equipment that could produce a tonal noise. A post-installation check should be capable of being requested if a substantiated noise complaint is received.

One consultation response from Mrs Nola Creed, of 18 Mill Sluice Row, Fenwick, BM4 6QD, described worry about reversing alarms and poor sleep during the early works. The response also said the resident has been diagnosed with chronic migraine. The Council records that information only to explain why advance notice of particularly noisy operations was requested; it has not treated one household's circumstances as a substitute for a scheme-wide noise assessment. The same response gave interested party reference IP-734826. The Council would welcome a condition requiring a construction contact point that can deal with an issue on the day it is reported, rather than merely acknowledge it after the event.

There is concern that security lighting will be visible from upstairs windows across the low fields. No permanent floodlighting is shown on the submitted lighting drawing, which is helpful, but the wording should still prevent later installation of dusk-to-dawn lights without further approval. Lighting required for an emergency is a separate matter. The Council's preferred approach is downward-facing, timed or sensor-controlled lighting, with the reason for any exception recorded in the lighting management plan.

9. Water, ecology and access

Tessa Venn of Brackenmere District Council reviewed the applicant's revised drainage note for the Council. The review found that the proposed shallow swales could be workable, provided the outfall levels are checked against the ordinary watercourse and arrangements for removing silt are secured. The review did not approve discharge rates or establish who would maintain the swales after construction. The Council asks that these details be settled before the relevant works start. Queries about the review may be sent to planning@brackenmere.gov.uk; the reviewer's individual work address is tessa.venn@brackenmere.gov.uk.

Fenwick Parish Council has asked that the permissive path shown east of the array remains usable when hedge maintenance takes place. That is a reasonable local request, although a short closure may sometimes be necessary for safety. The management plan should identify an alternative route or a notice period for such closures. It should also say how muddy sections will be repaired, as a path that exists only on a drawing offers little public benefit.

Badgers have been recorded in Alder Brake Wood, and bats use the wider Fenwick Lowlands for foraging. These are broad survey findings, not locations of protected resting places. A confidential ecology note supplied to the Council identifies a badger sett at the south end of the narrow spoil bank, 12 metres east of field gate FG3 beside the northern drainage ditch. That detail should not appear on a public works drawing. Protective fencing and the working method can instead be shown on a restricted plan provided to those who need it. The Council has not concluded that the proposed planting strip will resolve every ecological effect: establishment checks and replacement of failed plants are still needed.

10. Documents and requested outcome

The Council's correspondence address for this examination is Civic Offices, 4 Sedge Quay, Brackenmere, BM4 8QL. General enquiries should go to planning@brackenmere.gov.uk rather than to an officer's direct address. The Council has used the Planning Inspectorate's published guidance on the examination process at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects when preparing this report.

For the reasons above, Brackenmere District Council does not object to the principle of the Larkfen Solar and Storage Project in this location. It requests clearer controls on construction traffic, drainage maintenance, lighting and the long-term management of planting and the path. The Council would be content to comment on revised draft requirements during the examination. Where a matter is left to a later management plan, the requirement should state who approves that plan and when approval must be obtained; otherwise the local mitigation described in the application may not be delivered.

6. Local effects and proposed controls

6.1 This section identifies the effects that are likely to be experienced within Brackenmere District, rather than repeating the full Environmental Statement. Brackenmere District Council has considered the submitted transport, landscape and drainage material against National Policy Statement EN-1 and National Policy Statement EN-3. The Council's position on the principle of development is set out above. The remaining issue is whether the measures described by Larkfen Energy Ltd are secured with sufficient precision to be effective during construction and for the operational life of the Larkfen Solar and Storage Project.

6.2 The construction programme assumes that the solar arrays, battery compound and grid connection works can proceed partly in parallel. That assumption is important to the traffic assessment: a longer programme might reduce daily vehicle movements, but it could extend disturbance across more growing seasons and school terms. The submitted peak of 68 two-way vehicle movements per day, including 14 heavy goods vehicle movements, should therefore be treated as an assessed limit rather than an indicative average. If overlapping phases produce a higher peak, the traffic assessment will need updating before those phases begin. A requirement should identify the programme to be approved and prevent a material change to its phasing without written approval.

6.3 The proposed access from Marsh Gate Road is preferable to bringing construction vehicles through the centre of Fenwick. However, the swept-path drawing shows that the largest delivery vehicles would use nearly the whole carriageway at the access mouth. The drawing does not demonstrate how a vehicle waiting to turn could be passed safely when farm traffic is also present. Temporary traffic management, the position of the holding area and the method of booking abnormal loads should be settled before the access is first used. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should also prohibit deliveries via Merefold Lane, except for emergency access, and specify how drivers will be informed of the approved route. Signage alone would not be an adequate control.

6.4 Traffic counts in the assessment were undertaken outside the main harvest period. This does not invalidate the modelling, but it makes the stated capacity margins less useful as evidence of the practical operation of the junction. The Council requests a short supplementary note comparing the assumed background flows with a representative harvest-day scenario. It should address vehicle queuing at the proposed access and at the Marsh Gate Road/Fenwick Drove junction. Monitoring during the first six weeks of bulk deliveries would then allow the traffic management arrangements to be adjusted if actual queues differ materially from those modelled. The requirement should state who receives the monitoring returns and the timescale for agreeing any adjustment.

6.5 In landscape terms, the arrays would be most apparent on the rising ground east of the existing drainage corridor. The proposed hedgerow reinforcement would help to filter views, but the planting plans use a single establishment period for sections with markedly different ground conditions. The lower fields are seasonally wet, while the northern boundary is more exposed. The Landscape and Ecological Management Plan should identify replacement rates, watering and protection appropriate to each section, with annual inspections for the first five years. The Council does not seek an instant screen: an enforceable plan should instead describe the intended height and density at establishment and the action required where planting fails. ES Figure 7.4 remains helpful for judging the initial visibility of the works, but it should not be read as evidence that proposed planting has already matured.

6.6 The battery compound introduces a different visual effect from the panels because its buildings, fencing and service equipment would remain visible above the proposed boundary planting. Final colours and finishes should be approved before construction of that compound, using non-reflective materials. The lighting design should be equally specific. The application describes lighting as motion activated but does not state the maximum duration of each activation or show the spill at the site boundary. A condition limited only to a future lighting scheme would leave too much discretion. The approved scheme should specify mounting heights, direction, shielding, hours of routine use and the circumstances in which security lighting may operate.

6.7 The drainage strategy relies on infiltration between panel rows, shallow swales and controlled discharge from the battery compound. These are reasonable components in principle, but the calculations assume that ground levels remain substantially unchanged. The construction method statement should therefore set limits on regrading and compaction, particularly where temporary haul routes cross the lower fields. The outline maintenance schedule does not explain how blocked swales will be identified or how sediment will be removed without damaging established vegetation. A final drainage management plan should include inspection frequencies, access arrangements, a record of repairs and a clear handover process for operation after construction. Approval should be required before any impermeable surface is brought into use.

6.8 The proposed diverted path would maintain a continuous route across the site, although the temporary diversion shown for cable installation is not yet detailed. The Council asks for a plan showing the width, surface, wayfinding and drainage of both the temporary and permanent routes. Any closure should be limited to the period strictly necessary for works at the crossing, with an alternative route available before the closure takes effect. Fenwick Parish Council has raised the practical point that a route can be technically open while difficult to follow; the final plan should consequently be checked on the ground before public access is changed.

6.9 None of these points requires a change to the broad site layout. They do, however, depend on the detailed plans being approved at the right stage. Brackenmere District Council recommends that the draft requirements distinguish works needed before commencement, works needed before first operation and matters subject to continuing maintenance. That distinction would make the mitigation described in the application capable of inspection and enforcement, rather than leaving its delivery to an unspecified later agreement.

7. Landscape, amenity and lighting

7.1 Brackenmere District Council has considered the revised landscape drawings for the Larkfen Solar and Storage Project against the character of the Fenwick Levels. The existing hedges are an important part of that character, but in several places they are low and intermittent. The proposed planting would soften views from the public footpaths over time; it would not screen the panels at the point they are installed. The Council asks that the landscape management plan show the intended height of each retained hedge, the location of replacement planting and who will inspect failed plants. A drawing marked ‘indicative’ will not provide enough certainty for discharge of a requirement.

7.2 At the Council’s site visit on 14 September 2026, Cllr Iris Fenlow asked whether the eastern boundary planting could be brought forward so that it establishes before the battery compound becomes operational. Cllr Jonah Rusk asked for the maintenance period to begin when each planting area is completed, rather than on a single date for the whole scheme. These are practical points which the Council supports. Neither councillor suggested that screening would remove every view of the development.

7.3 Representations received by the Council describe worry about construction noise and poor sleep. Mrs Nola Creed, who is not a participant in this examination, wrote that she has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and that dust from vehicle movements is a particular concern. Her letter gave her address as 7 Merebell Cottages, Fenwick Lane, Brackenmere BM4 7QX. The Council refers to the substance of that concern, not the household circumstances, in recommending a dust monitoring and complaints procedure. It should identify the officer responsible for reviewing readings and the action to be taken when a trigger level is exceeded. The application documents presently describe monitoring but are less clear about what happens next.

7.4 The construction environmental management plan should also include the proposed hours for deliveries, arrangements for exceptional loads and a contact point which remains available while works are taking place. A generic project contact is preferable to directing residents to an individual site worker. Where temporary lighting is necessary, the plan should specify its direction and hours of use. This is particularly relevant at the northern access, where drivers would otherwise approach the village edge with lights facing nearby windows.

8. Drainage and water environment

8.1 The Council’s drainage review does not object in principle to the proposed attenuation basins. It does identify a gap between the submitted outline strategy and the arrangements that will be needed to maintain the grips and culverts after construction. Tessa Venn of Brackenmere District Council attended the technical meeting on 22 September 2026 and explained that the eastern grip has previously backed up when field entrances were blocked. The Council recommends a requirement for a final drainage scheme, with an inspection schedule, access rights for maintenance and a procedure for recording any blockage reported by residents. This would assist both the operator and the enforcing authority.

8.2 Fenwick Parish Council reported standing water along the lane after heavy rain. That observation is consistent with the Council’s highway records, although it does not establish that the development would cause additional flooding. The final design should use surveyed levels rather than the approximate levels on the current overview plan. In particular, the outfall from Basin 3 should be shown in section and its capacity agreed before earthworks begin. The Council does not seek a different drainage concept, only evidence that the proposed concept can be built and maintained without worsening existing problems.

9. Ecology and access to information

9.1 The ecological survey records badgers in the wider Fenwick Levels. The Council has separately supplied the Examining Authority with the confidential location of a sett: in the bank immediately behind the third willow from the south at the west end of field parcel F12, approximately 8 metres from the proposed trench line. This detail should not appear on publicly available construction drawings. The public version can show a suitably broad constraint area and explain how the ecological clerk of works will check it before trenching. The same approach should be taken to any later survey findings that identify a sensitive breeding site.

9.2 More generally, the Council welcomes the proposed hedgerow gaps being kept to the minimum needed for cabling and access. The applicant should confirm whether the temporary working width at each crossing is included in its hedgerow-loss totals. A commitment to reinstate hedges is useful, but it should be supported by a plan showing species mix, planting season and replacement of failures. These matters can be secured without publishing confidential species locations.

10. Consultation, requirements and conclusion

10.1 Corin Vale MP has asked the Council to make clear how residents will know when construction arrangements change. The Council agrees that the approved traffic and environmental plans should be available in a form that residents can find, alongside a short explanation of revisions. Its office at Civic Offices, 18 Reedmarket Square, Brackenmere BM2 4RT can receive written queries, and the shared mailbox planning@brackenmere.gov.uk is available for general planning correspondence. These channels do not replace the applicant’s responsibility to operate a construction complaints process.

10.2 For procedural information about the examination, the Council has directed correspondents to https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects-the-examination. Some residents have lived near the site for 40+ years and are familiar with seasonal conditions which may not be obvious from a single survey visit. Their observations should be checked against the technical evidence, not dismissed because they are expressed informally. Equally, a report of standing water or a difficult footpath does not, by itself, demonstrate that the project is unacceptable.

10.3 Subject to the amendments identified above and in section 6, the Council considers that the main local impacts can be addressed through enforceable requirements. It asks the applicant to provide a consolidated schedule showing the document to be approved, the approving body, the stage at which approval is required and any continuing duty to maintain the measure. Without that schedule, there is a risk that an apparently agreed mitigation measure falls between several plans and is not delivered on site.

11. Technical matters and proposed controls

11.1 This section brings together the matters on which Brackenmere District Council considers a more precise development consent order (DCO) requirement is needed. It does not repeat the project description or suggest that every construction detail must be settled before consent. Rather, the approved plans should establish measurable limits, with a clear route for agreeing details before the relevant works begin. References below to approval by the Council are intended to identify its proposed role as discharging authority; the final allocation of functions will need to be consistent across the draft DCO.

Construction traffic

11.2 The transport assessment for the Larkfen Solar and Storage Project assumes that construction vehicles will approach from the B6142 and enter the site from Fenwick Lane. This is a reasonable basis for assessment, provided the route is secured. The present outline Construction Traffic Management Plan (CTMP) says drivers will be ‘encouraged’ to avoid Moor End Lane. Encouragement is not a sufficient control on a narrow lane with limited passing opportunities. The final CTMP should prohibit construction HGV use of Moor End Lane except for an emergency or a separately approved, time-limited operation. It should specify how that prohibition will be communicated to hauliers and monitored.

11.3 The peak daily HGV figure in the assessment is an average across a construction phase. It may therefore conceal shorter periods of more intense delivery activity, particularly during compound establishment and battery installation. Larkfen Energy Ltd should provide a weekly delivery profile for those activities, identify the maximum number of arrivals within any one-hour period and test that maximum against the capacity of the Fenwick Lane access. A booking system, banksman provision at the access and a procedure for dealing with vehicles arriving early should be included in the final CTMP. The Council does not seek a general ban on deliveries during the school day; it seeks defined controls around the morning and afternoon periods when the route is most constrained.

11.4 A pre-construction condition survey should cover the B6142 junction, Fenwick Lane up to the site access and the passing places proposed for use. The survey method, repair thresholds and post-construction inspection date should be agreed before HGV movements start. These matters should sit in a single highway schedule rather than being dispersed between the CTMP and the Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP). The highway authority will need sufficient time to inspect any proposed temporary signage and access works before they are brought into use.

Drainage and flood risk

11.5 The submitted drainage strategy adopts infiltration as the preferred means of managing runoff from the operational compound. That hierarchy is supported in principle, but the indicative infiltration rates have not been verified at the proposed basin and substation locations. Detailed design should rely on site-specific testing carried out at appropriate depths and in the locations where the drainage features are to be built. If testing shows infiltration is unsuitable, the requirement should oblige the applicant to submit an alternative restricted-discharge design, rather than treating a change of method as a minor drawing amendment.

11.6 The design should account separately for runoff from panel areas, impermeable compound surfaces and temporary construction surfaces. Existing field drains intercepted by cable trenches must be recorded and reinstated or diverted so that flows are not transferred to neighbouring land. The current drawings show a shallow swale beside West Mere Ditch but do not state who will inspect it or remove accumulated sediment. An operational drainage maintenance plan should identify inspection frequency, access for maintenance and the party responsible throughout the project’s life. The CEMP should also set out how temporary stockpiles and vehicle tracks will be kept clear of overland flow routes.

Landscape, lighting and public access

11.7 Views from the B6142, Fenwick Lane and Brackenmere Way will change from open agricultural land to a field pattern containing panels, fencing and the storage compound. Existing hedges provide some screening, but the winter viewpoint photography shows that this effect is uneven. The Landscape and Ecology Management Plan should distinguish hedges to be retained, gaps to be planted and new belts, with minimum planting sizes and a replacement period. It should also secure the proposed setback at the eastern edge of Field 4. That setback is material to the assessment of views from Brackenmere Way and should not be left to detailed design discretion.

11.8 No continuous operational lighting is proposed across the panel fields. The Council supports that approach. Lighting at the storage compound should be controlled by an approved scheme stating mounting heights, orientation, operating triggers and maximum illumination at the site boundary. A requirement that lighting merely be ‘low spill’ would be difficult to enforce. Construction lighting should be addressed separately in the CEMP because winter working and security needs may differ from the operational arrangement.

11.9 Temporary diversions of Footpaths FEN/3 and FEN/7 should be installed and signed before the existing routes are closed. The final access plan should show the diversion widths, surfacing where plant crosses a path and the arrangements for keeping signs legible during successive construction phases. The permanent routes should be reopened as soon as the relevant work area is safe, not at the end of the whole construction programme by default. The Council asks that the plan include an inspection point before each diversion is removed.

Conclusion on technical requirements

11.10 These requests are consistent with the approach to mitigation in the Brackenmere Local Plan 2024 and the submitted Environmental Statement. They do not alter the Council’s assessment of the principle of development. Their purpose is to ensure that the effects assessed in the application remain the effects experienced during construction and operation. A revised requirements schedule should cross-reference the CTMP, CEMP, drainage design, landscape plan, lighting scheme and access plan, and state clearly which document prevails if drawings and written measures conflict. Subject to those changes, the Council considers the identified local technical impacts capable of being managed through the DCO.

12. Residual local effects and monitoring

12.1 This section brings together the Council’s assessment of effects that may remain after the measures discussed above have been secured. Brackenmere District Council has considered the submitted Environmental Statement, the draft Development Consent Order and the outline management plans for the Larkfen Solar and Storage Project. The assessment is made at the local scale: an effect may be acceptable in the overall planning balance while still requiring a clear means of checking whether the proposed mitigation is working. The points below should therefore be read with, rather than in place of, the proposed requirements schedule.

Construction traffic

12.2 The construction traffic assessment uses a peak month rather than an average month, which is appropriate. However, the forecast is sensitive to whether the eastern and western array works overlap. The current programme shows only a limited overlap, while the construction description allows flexibility in the order of installation. Larkfen Energy Ltd should confirm the maximum number of daily heavy goods vehicle movements permitted across the whole site, not simply the indicative numbers for each work area. That limit should apply during any overlapping works and should be capable of verification from gate records.

12.3 The Council’s main concern is the junction of Fenwick Drove and Brackenmere Lane. The submitted swept-path drawing demonstrates that the largest proposed delivery vehicle can make the turn if the corner is kept free of temporary equipment. It does not demonstrate how two opposing delivery vehicles would pass along the narrow section immediately south of the junction. Deliveries should be booked in separate slots, with a holding procedure away from the public highway if a vehicle arrives early. The CTMP should identify who records missed slots and how a repeated failure would be corrected. Signs alone would not provide a sufficient control.

12.4 On the basis of those controls, the Council does not identify an unmitigable highway effect. It does not, however, accept that the absence of a predicted capacity problem removes the need to monitor obstruction or verge damage. A pre-commencement condition survey, monthly inspections during the period of peak deliveries and a final survey would provide a proportionate record. The survey extent should include the full agreed delivery route from the strategic road junction to each construction access. Any repair mechanism should distinguish damage caused by the project from routine highway maintenance.

Landscape and visual matters

12.5 The landscape drawings indicate that existing field boundaries would largely be retained. The proposed hedgerow infill is a useful response to views from the public rights of way around Fenwick Common, but the drawings use different widths for the same planting strip. The final landscape plan should show an agreed minimum width, species mix, protection from construction traffic and a replacement period for failed plants. This is particularly important where the planting sits between security fencing and the edge of an existing hedge: a strip that cannot be maintained is unlikely to achieve the screening shown in the year-10 visualisations.

12.6 During the first years of operation there will be open views of fencing, inverter compounds and the upper parts of panel rows from sections of Moorfold Path. These are localised but genuine adverse effects; the proposed planting will not remove them immediately. The Council considers the residual effect capable of reducing over time, provided the finished ground levels and maximum equipment heights remain within the assessed envelope. Any later substitution of equipment should be checked against those limits before it is installed, rather than treated as a purely operational matter.

Water and ground conditions

12.7 The drainage strategy proposes infiltration where testing permits and controlled discharge elsewhere. The principle is reasonable, but the outline drawings do not yet show a continuous exceedance route for water leaving the battery compound during an event greater than the design storm. The detailed scheme should identify the route on a single plan, including where flow crosses internal tracks and whether those crossings remain effective if a culvert is blocked. It should also confirm that runoff is not directed towards the low point at the southern edge of Fenwick Common.

12.8 Construction-phase drainage merits separate attention. Stripping and temporary track formation could alter the way water reaches ordinary watercourses before the permanent drainage features are complete. The CEMP should set out a sequence for installing temporary interception measures, inspecting them after heavy rainfall and replacing them as works move between fields. The proposed inspection log should be available to the relevant authorities on request. This is a practical measure and should not depend on the final operational drainage scheme having been approved.

12.9 The Council has not identified evidence that the permanent development would increase flood risk off site if the detailed design follows the stated discharge limits. That conclusion is conditional. Approval of the final design should include the results of infiltration testing, calculations for each drainage catchment and a maintenance schedule identifying the features that must remain accessible throughout operation. The schedule should cover the period after construction as well as the establishment of landscape planting, since roots and accumulated sediment can affect shallow conveyance features.

Planning balance at local level

12.10 The Brackenmere Local Plan 2024 supports renewable energy development where local impacts are satisfactorily addressed. The Council’s assessment is that the principal local effects arise from the temporary concentration of construction activity and the initially exposed appearance of the infrastructure, rather than from a permanent change in traffic levels. Neither point is resolved by a general commitment to good practice. Both require measurable limits, approved drawings and a route for remedial action if implementation differs from the assessment.

12.11 Fenwick Parish Council has asked that the final management documents be easy to locate during construction. The Council agrees that a document register would assist compliance. It should list the approved revision of each plan, the relevant DCO requirement and any superseded drawing. The register need not duplicate the technical documents, but it should make clear which approved version governs each work area. This would also reduce the risk of a contractor relying on an earlier access or drainage drawing.

12.12 Subject to the amendments identified in this report, Brackenmere District Council considers that the remaining local impacts can be controlled through the DCO and its certified documents. This conclusion should not be read as agreement to defer the definition of mitigation until after works begin. In particular, the traffic limit, landscape dimensions, drainage exceedance route and construction inspection arrangements must be settled before the activities to which they relate commence.

13.0 Member representations and local delivery

13.1 This section records matters raised by elected representatives and explains how they have informed the Council’s assessment. It is not intended to substitute for the representations made by those individuals in the examination. The Council’s conclusions remain those set out in sections 3 to 12, including the qualifications at paragraph 12.12.

13.2 At the Council’s infrastructure briefing on 8 September 2026, Cllr Iris Fenlow asked whether the proposed construction traffic cap would apply to all deliveries serving the Larkfen Solar and Storage Project, including vehicles travelling directly to the battery compound. Officers confirmed that the current wording does not make that sufficiently clear. The Council therefore seeks a single, auditable daily limit covering both the solar works and the battery works, with a record of vehicle movements available to the highway authority on request. A separate limit for each contractor would not achieve the same protection on the narrow approach roads.

13.3 Cllr Jonah Rusk raised the time between planting the proposed southern screening belt and its becoming effective. The Council agrees that a drawing showing a mature hedge does not establish what residents will see during the first few years of operation. The landscape requirement should specify planting sizes, the timing of the first planting season, replacement of failed stock and a maintenance period. The approved plans should also show the minimum width of the belt where it runs beside Fenwick Bridleway 3; that dimension should not depend on a later contractor drawing.

13.4 Corin Vale MP wrote to the Council on 14 September 2026 asking that local footpaths remain usable wherever it is safe to do so. The letter did not express a view on whether development consent should be granted. The Council shares the concern about avoidable closures. Any temporary diversion should be signed at both ends before the existing route is obstructed, and the applicant should publish a simple map showing the diversion and its expected duration. The Council does not support leaving the choice of an alternative route to be made on the day by a works supervisor.

13.5 Fenwick Parish Council has separately asked for advance notice of noisy works, particularly piling and the unloading of battery units. Notice to the parish council is useful but cannot replace notice to people living beside the access route. The construction management plan should state who is responsible for distributing that information, how much notice will normally be given and what happens when an activity must change at short notice. A generic statement that the contractor will liaise with the community is not sufficient for this purpose.

13.6 One consultation response illustrates why the drainage drawings need to be read together with the access drawings. Mrs Nola Creed, of 7 Reedcutters Lane, Fenwick, BM2 8QT, described surface water reaching the entrance to her home after heavy rain and expressed concern that a raised temporary haul road could redirect it. She also referred to a diagnosed migraine disorder when explaining her concerns about overnight lighting. These are matters reported by a resident, not findings that the proposed development has caused flooding or a health effect. The Council relies on its drainage assessment, rather than that individual account, in seeking an identified exceedance route and a pre-commencement inspection of the temporary works.

13.7 Tessa Venn of Brackenmere District Council’s drainage team reviewed the revised crossing detail received on 30 September 2026. Her technical comment was that the culvert drawing identifies its opening but does not yet show how water would pass over or around the crossing if that opening became blocked. The Council asks for that overland route to be marked on the certified drainage plan before the crossing is built. This would give the inspecting officer and the contractor the same point of reference; it would not require a further general drainage study.

13.8 The Council has considered whether these requests could be dealt with entirely through informal liaison with Larkfen Energy Ltd. In its view they cannot. Liaison is appropriate for matters such as arranging an inspection date or agreeing the wording of a resident notice. It is not an adequate means of fixing a traffic cap, the width of a landscape belt or the location of a drainage exceedance route. Those matters should be secured in the DCO requirements or on the certified plans, with any later approval process confined to details within the stated parameters.

13.9 For clarity, the Council’s office address for examination correspondence is Civic Offices, Meregate Square, Brackenmere, BM1 4ZZ. General planning enquiries may be sent to planning@brackenmere.gov.uk, and the Council switchboard is 01632 960 814. These are shared Council contact details, not the address or direct contact details of any officer or member. Public guidance on the examination process is available at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects.

13.10 Officers have not treated the number of objections or expressions of support as a vote on the application. The local impact assessment instead asks what change would be experienced, where it would occur and whether the proposed control is capable of being checked. In particular, the traffic and drainage concerns arise at identifiable interfaces between construction activity and existing routes. The Council considers that clear drawings and records will be more useful at those interfaces than broad commitments to minimise disruption.

13.11 The Council requests that the applicant provide a consolidated schedule of its proposed changes to requirements and certified drawings before the close of the examination. The schedule should identify the document version, the work area affected and the point at which approval or inspection is required. Subject to those changes and the qualifications in paragraph 12.12, the Council considers that the remaining local impacts can be managed. If the controls are not secured, its concern is not simply that details remain outstanding, but that the activities could begin before the relevant limits and mitigation are settled.

14.0 Overall assessment of local impacts

14.1 This section draws together the Council’s conclusions on transport, landscape, drainage and construction phasing for the Larkfen Solar and Storage Project. It should be read with the qualifications and requests for controls set out in the preceding sections; it is not an assessment of the national need for renewable energy.

14.2 The transport assessment indicates that the B742/Alder Lane junction has capacity for the forecast operational traffic. Construction traffic is a different matter. The peak-hour estimates rely on deliveries being spread across the working day and on the northern compound being brought into use before the southern arrays. Brackenmere District Council considers that the construction traffic management plan must secure that sequence, identify the permitted HGV route and include a mechanism for recording and reviewing vehicle movements. Without those measures, the modelled peak is not a reliable basis for assessing local effects.

14.3 The most noticeable landscape effects would arise from the perimeter fencing, battery enclosure and temporary compounds, particularly in views from the elevated section of Fenwick Way. Proposed hedgerow planting would soften some views but would not provide full screening at the start of operation. The Council therefore seeks a planting specification, replacement obligations and a five-year establishment period. The landscape conclusion remains subject to agreement of the final fence and lighting drawings.

14.4 The drainage strategy proposes attenuation within the development area and controlled discharge to the existing field ditch system. Its principles are acceptable, but the detailed design must demonstrate how runoff from access tracks and the battery enclosure will be managed during construction as well as operation. No discharge should commence before the relevant outfall and maintenance arrangements have been approved.

14.5 On that basis, and subject to the controls identified in paragraph 13.11, the Council does not identify a further local impact requiring a change to the site boundary. This conclusion should not be read as support for discharging detailed requirements on the basis of outline drawings alone.

text:
To the Examining Authority
Merefold Solar Link (EN020674)
Relevant representation from Elsi Hart, aged 15
Interested Party reference: IP-407392
Address: 8 Tern Close, Halewick, HW4 6QP
Email: elsi.hart@pupil.fennmere.example

I am a pupil at Fennmere Academy and I am writing about the proposed Merefold Solar Link. I know this is usually the sort of thing adults write about, but the construction route goes past our school and the fields we use on our walk home. I would like the Examining Authority to consider what it would actually be like for pupils, not just what a traffic table says. I am not against solar power. We have done a project on climate change in geography, and I understand why electricity has to be made differently. I just don't think the current plan shows enough care for people who have to be here every school day.

The main issue for me is the proposed use of Marsh Lane for construction vehicles. At about 3.30 pm, the pavement outside the academy is full, and there are pupils crossing to the bus stop while others are going towards South Dene Field. It is not an orderly line of people as it may look on a plan. Some people stop to talk, some are carrying sports bags, and younger pupils can suddenly step round a group without looking. Marsh Lane has a bend by the old water pump, so we often hear a vehicle before we see it. The transport chapter says the road is suitable for HGVs, but I could not find anything that explains how a pupil waiting on that particular corner is supposed to feel safe.

My friends Orla Dene and Finn Sevor walk that way with me. Finn is 14 and gets the bus from the stop nearest the bend. I am naming them because we talked about whether I should send this in, not because they have agreed to make their own representations. On a wet afternoon the bus shelter is too small and people stand along the edge of the pavement. Our geography teacher, Mrs Imogen Pell, suggested we count the vehicles for a class exercise; she did not tell us what view to take on the application. The count was only one afternoon, so I am not saying it is a proper survey. It did make me wonder why the applicant's drawings show pedestrians as if we all stay in one neat place.

Larkswell Energy Ltd says in the construction traffic plan that deliveries will avoid the busiest school times where practicable. 'Where practicable' is doing a lot of work in that sentence. If a delivery is late, does the driver wait somewhere, and who tells the driver? If the school day changes because of an exam or an event, who updates the timetable? I would like an enforceable restriction on large vehicles using Marsh Lane at school start and finish, with a safe place for lorries to wait. I would also like someone to check the arrangement after work starts, rather than just assuming the plan has worked.

There is a second issue with the footpath across South Dene Field. My friends and I use it to get to Wrenfold Wood, and families use it at weekends. I have lived in Halewick for about seven years, and the path has always felt like a way to get out of the traffic for a bit. The diversion shown on the plan is much longer and puts us back beside the road. I know the construction works cannot leave every path open all the time, but signs should say when a route is shut and where the alternative really begins. They should be readable from both ends of the path. Please do not put a sign at the gate after someone has already walked the whole way there.

I am also worried about dust. I have asthma, and running beside a line of idling lorries is different from walking past ordinary cars. This does not mean I am asking for the whole project to be cancelled because of my health. It means the dust and vehicle controls need to work on the days when it is dry and windy, including when school is open. I sometimes have poor sleep before a busy school week, which is a feeling rather than something I am asking the Examining Authority to assess medically. What would help is knowing whom pupils can contact if a problem happens, and being told what will happen next.

In our class we looked at the ecology drawings as well. Badger signs have been seen around Wrenfold Wood, which is not, by itself, a reason to stop the scheme. I do want to point out that the badger sett in the bank at the eastern end of the narrow ditch immediately behind gate 3 of South Dene Field appears much closer to the working area than the general description suggests. I have not put a photograph online because I do not want people going to look for it. Please ask the ecologist to check the construction boundary there and explain what protection will be in place before any fencing goes up.

Cllr Nessa Varr spoke at the school council meeting and said pupils' comments could be sent in directly. That is why I am writing in my own words. The school council asked me to make clear that this is my view, not an official response from Fennmere Academy. I found the examination page at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate, but some of the document names were difficult to understand. A one-page explanation of changes to the route, available through the school and the project mailbox consultation@merefoldsolar.example, would make it easier for us to follow what is decided.

Please take this seriously even though I am still at school. I support making cleaner electricity, but I ask for a proper school-time lorry restriction, a usable footpath diversion, dust controls that can be checked, and a clear answer about the wildlife near the works. Those changes would make a real difference to whether pupils can keep travelling to school and using the countryside safely while the project is built.

Further technical points about the Merefold Solar Link

I have put the points below separately because they may be easier to check against the application documents. I am not saying that every number in the applicant's reports is wrong. I am asking whether the numbers describe what will actually happen on the roads and paths during construction.

1. Traffic and construction phases

The transport assessment for the Merefold Solar Link gives a daily total for heavy goods vehicles, but the daily total does not show when they will arrive. A road can cope with the same number of lorries quite differently depending on whether they come evenly through the day or in a short group. The examination should ask Larkswell Energy Ltd for an hourly breakdown for each construction phase, including deliveries of panels, transformer equipment and stone for temporary tracks. The breakdown should show both directions of travel, not just arrivals at the site gate.

The route along Brindle Lane joins the wider road at Merefold Cross. The swept-path drawing shows one large vehicle turning there, with no other traffic in the junction. It would be useful to test a lorry meeting a bus or another large vehicle, and to say what happens if vehicles arrive before their allocated slot. An instruction to drivers to wait elsewhere is only useful if the waiting place is identified, has capacity and is included in the construction traffic plan. Otherwise the delay may move to Brindle Lane rather than disappear.

The proposed traffic controls should also be written as requirements that can be checked. A restriction on deliveries during school arrival and departure times needs stated hours and a way to record exceptions. I suggest a monthly table showing booked and actual arrival times, missed slots and complaints, with an explanation of any changes made. Fennmere Borough Council should be able to see the information while works are under way, not only in a final report. I do not think that monitoring alone is enough: the construction traffic plan should say what action follows repeated breaches.

2. Paths and access

The rights-of-way plans show a temporary diversion of Merefold Footpath 6 around the western works compound. On the drawing, the diverted line meets a farm access track at an angle, but the drawing does not make clear whether people on foot have to share the track with construction vehicles. The examination should request a cross-section at that crossing, including the proposed surface, fencing, sight lines and signs. The plan should also show where the diversion reconnects with the existing path. A line on a map does not tell users whether the route will be passable after heavy rain.

The path management plan says that closures will be advertised in advance. It should specify how far in advance, where notices will be placed and what happens if a planned reopening is delayed. The shortest diversion on the plan appears to depend on a temporary gate. If the gate cannot be used outside working hours, an alternative route needs to be shown rather than assumed. These details matter even if each closure is described as temporary.

3. Drainage and ground conditions

The flood risk appendix models runoff after construction, when the permanent layout is in place. I could not find the same clear explanation for the period when soil is stripped and the temporary stone tracks are being laid. That period might have different runoff routes. The drainage drawings should mark the temporary ditches, silt controls and discharge points for each phase, including what is installed before the first area of ground is opened.

The field south of Sedgewash Lane slopes towards Merefold Beck. I am not claiming that the solar panels would themselves cause flooding. The question is whether water carrying disturbed soil could reach the beck during construction, and who checks the controls after a storm. The outline management plan refers to inspection, but does not give an interval or a trigger for an extra inspection following heavy rainfall. The final plan should contain both. It should also say where any collected silt will go, so that it is not simply moved from one part of the site to another.

4. Landscape and ecology

The landscape figures compare views at opening and after planting has grown. The later pictures are helpful, but a planted screen will not have the same effect during its first few years. A winter view from the public path beside Sedgewash Lane would make the early effect easier to judge. The drawings should use the same viewpoint and viewing height in both phases. That would allow the change, rather than a change in the picture's framing, to be compared.

The ecology report refers generally to badger activity in Willowmere Wood and to bats using the wider landscape. Those are useful reasons for careful working methods, not reasons to print precise protected-species locations in the public papers. The requirement should instead explain how the ecological clerk of works will check the relevant area before clearance, how work will stop if protected features are found, and how a necessary change to fencing or lighting will be approved. The public version can report that checks happened without publishing sensitive locations.

5. Requirements and clarity

Several commitments are currently in outline plans that Larkswell Energy Ltd may update later. I would like the final requirements to identify which authority approves each detailed plan and what minimum information the plan must contain. In particular, the traffic hours, usable footpath diversion, construction drainage and early landscape planting should not be left as things to consider after permission is granted.

This is not an objection to producing renewable electricity. It is a request for the examination to test whether the proposed controls are specific enough to work. A short table linking each promise to a drawing, a requirement and a person or body responsible for checking it would help readers follow the decision.

6. Traffic figures and access

The traffic assessment should show what happens on the busiest construction day, not only the average over the whole programme. The Merefold Solar Link would bring deliveries to several work areas, and the same narrow roads are used by buses, farm vehicles and people cycling. If deliveries to the panel fields and cable works overlap, adding their separate daily averages could hide a much busier hour.

I ask the Examining Authority to compare the forecast in the Construction Traffic Assessment, document 7.4, with the delivery timetable in the Outline Construction Programme, document 3.12. A table should give the maximum number of two-way heavy goods vehicle movements for each access and each construction phase. It should say whether an empty vehicle leaving counts as a movement. It should also show the assumed working days, delivery windows and number of abnormal loads. Without those definitions it is difficult to check whether a later traffic plan stays within what has been assessed.

The proposed route along Brindle Lane has two passing places on the access drawing, but the drawing does not say whether both can be used while the temporary cable compound is operating. The swept-path drawings should test two large vehicles meeting near the compound entrance, as well as a bus passing a waiting delivery vehicle. A swept-path line on an empty base map is not enough if the usable road width is reduced by barriers or stored materials. Any change to the delivery route should be checked against the same worst-case assumptions before it is approved.

7. Walking and cycling during works

The diversion for Merefold Footpath 8 appears in different positions on the access plan and the landscape plan. One follows the edge of the temporary working area; the other goes around the proposed planting belt. The final plan should choose a single route and show its width, surface, gates, lighting policy and where it joins the existing path at both ends. It should also explain how the crossing of Brindle Lane will work when delivery traffic is at its busiest.

The Outline Public Rights of Way Management Plan says a closure would be short, but does not define the longest permitted closure or the notice that would be given before one starts. I suggest a requirement that the diversion must be open, inspected and signposted before the existing path is shut. If part of it becomes muddy or blocked, there needs to be a way to put that right promptly rather than waiting for the next scheduled report. This is about whether the route will actually be usable during construction, not just whether it can be drawn on a plan.

8. Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage strategy relies on existing ground soaking up rainfall between the panel rows. That may be reasonable in some parts of the site, but the drawings also show haul routes, cable trenches and areas of temporary storage. Compacted soil and an open trench can change where water runs. The assessment should map the areas likely to be compacted in each phase and explain when they will be restored. It should not assume that all panel-field land has the same infiltration rate throughout the works.

On the eastern side of Merefold Field, the proposed works fall towards Sallow Beck. The outline drainage plan shows silt fencing but gives little detail about what happens during a heavy storm before the permanent grass cover has established. I would like to see the location and capacity of temporary settlement features, how they will be checked after rainfall and where clean water will be kept separate from muddy construction water. The plan should say who can stop a task if a measure fails and what must be repaired before work resumes. This can be written into a requirement without fixing every small construction detail now.

9. Landscape and lighting

The landscape drawings include a planting strip beside the eastern boundary, but the programme seems to place some planting after the main installation. If the intention is to screen the works as well as the finished development, the earliest suitable planting season should be identified in the requirement. The applicant should also show which areas cannot be planted early because of access or underground cables. That would make the promise more testable than simply saying planting will be carried out when practical.

The viewpoints on Figure 6.9 use summer and winter images, which is helpful, but the photomontages should state clearly whether proposed planting is shown at installation height or at an assumed future height. These are different views for someone trying to understand the first years of operation. The assessment should give a reasonable replacement period for failed plants and set out who checks that replacements survive.

Temporary lighting is another detail that could have a large effect without appearing on the permanent layout. The construction plan should identify the areas where lighting might be needed, the hours of use and how fittings will be directed away from the footpath and Sallow Beck. It should not leave a general permission for floodlights across the whole site.

10. A checkable set of controls

For these points, I suggest one compliance table with columns for the assessed limit, the drawing that shows it, the requirement that secures it and the body that approves any detailed plan. Fennmere Borough Council should be able to see the same version of the construction plans as the body giving formal approval. The table should distinguish a change that remains within the assessed limits from one that needs further assessment.

I have tried to check the proposal against the Fennmere Local Plan Policy EN4 and the Merefold Solar Link examination documents, rather than against a general view of solar power. My concern is the gap between the outline measures and the instructions someone will use on site. Clear limits for traffic, an open walking diversion, working drainage measures and a dated planting programme would help close that gap.

From: Elsi Hart
School: Fennmere Academy
Re: Merefold Solar Link — my written representation

I am 15 and I walk from the bus stop past the proposed cable route most school days. I support solar power, but the construction plan still reads like the safe route for walkers will be sorted out later. That isn't enough when pupils will have to use it before and after school.

My friends Orla Dene and Finn Sevor also use the path. Finn is 14 and he sometimes cycles home, so a diversion that works for someone walking may not work for a bike. We tried following the diversion shown on the drawing, but it seems to end at a gate. Is the gate meant to stay open? Please could Larkswell Energy Ltd show the whole route on one plan, including where people cross the access road, before any work starts. I felt anxious when a lorry came round the bend during our site visit; I am not saying the driver did anything wrong.

Mrs Imogen Pell, our geography teacher, helped us read the drainage drawings. They show where the temporary ditch might go, but I couldn't find who checks it after heavy rain. Water already lies on the path by Sedgeglass Wood and I have asthma, so I don't want to have to stand beside idling vehicles while waiting for a dry place to pass. That is a practical issue, not a reason to refuse all the panels.

I wrote in my notebook that the badger sett entrance is under the third oak east of the broken stile on Footpath 9, about four metres inside the hedge. Please do not put that exact detail on a public map. Badgers are also seen generally around Sedgeglass Wood, which I understand is less specific. I am asking for a proper check before fencing is fixed, not asking for pupils to investigate it.

Cllr Nessa Varr said at the school question session that Fennmere Borough Council could ask for clearer construction information. I hope the Council can see the final diversion and drainage plans, not just an earlier version. Fennmere Academy should be told the dates when the access road will be busiest, so the school can let pupils know in good time. Please make the walking route, gate arrangements and rain checks requirements that somebody has to follow, rather than promises in another leaflet.

Thank you for reading this. I can be contacted at elsi.hart@pupilmail.invalid, but please don't publish that address.

P.S. I forgot to say why the diversion matters at the end of the school day. I am 15 and usually walk home from Fennmere Academy with Orla Dene and Finn Sevor, who is 14. We cross near the proposed access road because the other route has no proper pavement. If that crossing closes, please show us an actual map of where pupils should go, not just a line saying “use alternative routes”.

Mrs Imogen Pell asked our geography class to compare the plans, but even the newer drawing did not make the temporary gate clear. This has made me anxious about walking home, although I know construction cannot be completely quiet. We have heard about badgers around Sedgeglass Wood; I am not claiming to know where any sett is. I would like Larkswell Energy Ltd to put the school travel plan on the project website before work starts. Cllr Nessa Varr and Fennmere Borough Council should be able to check that it stays up to date.

Elsi Hart
