text:
LARKFEN LINK ENERGY PARK — WRITTEN REPRESENTATION
Examination reference: EN020247
Deadline 5: ecology and construction access

Elena Voss MSc CEnv, independent ecological witness
21 October 2026

1. Scope and experience

I submit this evidence in my own capacity as an Interested Party. I am an ecologist with 19 years’ experience of habitat surveys, protected-species licensing and the review of environmental statements for energy and transport schemes. My MSc dissertation concerned the interpretation of incomplete bat activity datasets, and I have since prepared or reviewed more than 80 ecological assessments. I have provided a short biography because the point I make below concerns survey interpretation rather than a general objection to renewable energy. My IP reference is IP-40861.

I visited the publicly accessible paths around the proposed cable corridor on 6 May, 18 June and 2 September 2026. I did not enter fenced land, undertake a licensed survey or inspect a building. Where I refer to information supplied by the applicant, I mean the Larkfen Energy Ltd Environmental Statement, principally Chapter 9 and its survey appendices. My observations should not be mistaken for a substitute for those surveys.

2. What the examination needs to resolve

The main difficulty is that the construction access drawing and the ecology drawings do not appear to show the same working width beside Hawthorn Spinney. On the access drawing the temporary haul road has a passing place at chainage 2+140. On Figure 9.7 the habitat-loss shading stops before that passing place. A reader cannot tell whether the shaded edge is the limit of excavation, the limit of vehicles, or simply the limit of permanent works. The distinction matters because the submitted mitigation relies on retaining a strip of scrub as a dark corridor.

I ask for one reconciled plan with a dimensioned construction limit, any lighting columns and the route for abnormal deliveries shown together. It should also identify who can authorise a change in the field. A commitment to ‘minimise disturbance where practicable’ is too open-ended at a pinch point that the applicant already knows about. This is criticism of the submitted design, not an allegation about anybody’s conduct.

The assessment says that badger setts have been identified in Hawthorn Spinney. That is a suitably broad description for the public version of the material. The confidential survey appendix should, however, be checked against the passing-place design. For that purpose I recorded the following location in my field notebook: Sett B occupies the sandy bank 11 m north of marker post FP7/3 at the eastern end of Hawthorn Spinney, grid reference TF 48261 73914. I have put it here so that the Examining Authority can verify that the same feature has been assessed; it should not appear on an unrestricted public plan.

The bat evidence needs a similar reconciliation. The survey tables report activity along the spinney edge, but the proposed temporary lighting is assessed by reference to an indicative layout rather than the access drawing now before the examination. The appendix also identifies a maternity roost in the roof void of the disused pump house on Parcel 18, entered through the west-facing gable at grid reference TF 48104 73792. This precise location is unnecessary to explain the public-facing conclusion. It does matter to the confidential review of lighting direction and the proposed no-work buffer. References elsewhere in this evidence to bats around Fenmere are deliberately general.

3. Survey limitations and suggested requirement

At my June visit the ditch beside Brindleford Lane held water despite several dry weeks. I saw no evidence that the applicant’s invertebrate survey had covered the short reach immediately beside the proposed passing place. Absence from a table should not be treated as evidence of absence from an unsurveyed reach. I recommend a pre-construction check of that reach, with the results provided to the relevant ecological adviser before vegetation clearance. The check should not become a way to defer the basic decision about the width of the works.

Mira Fenwick of Valewick Ecology Ltd advised at the community walkover that the contractor’s final method statement would contain the lighting details. I cannot find a requirement securing that statement before the passing place is built. The applicant could resolve this without changing the principle of the scheme by specifying a maximum illuminated area, a construction boundary and a procedure for recording departures. A generic mailbox for practical queries is planning@larkfen-energy.example; it is not a substitute for an enforceable requirement.

I also note Cllr Jory Ansel’s request at the open session for a plan that residents can read without switching between appendices. I support that request. The Alder Marsh Bird Group has made a separate representation about field margins, and I do not purport to speak for that group. My concern here is the narrower question of whether the access design assessed in Chapter 9 is the one that will actually be constructed.

4. Administrative details copied into this version in error

The following lines were carried over from my evidence-cover sheet. My home address is 27 Wrenfold Mews, Fenmere, FM4 8QL, and my mobile is 07700 900623. They are not needed to test the ecological point. I am 46. I have been diagnosed with migraine, which is why I sometimes request a screen break during long remote hearings; that request does not affect my survey conclusions. The uncertainty about the construction limit has caused me stress, but that is not offered as a medical opinion.

5. Conclusion

I ask the Examining Authority to require a single construction-and-ecology plan and a secured lighting method before works begin beside the spinney. Subject to those changes, my evidence does not oppose the energy park as a whole. I would be content to answer written questions about the discrepancies identified above.

Elena Voss

6. Supplementary technical note: construction controls and drainage interface

6.1 This note sets out the technical wording I consider necessary to make the recommendations in section 5 workable. It does not change my overall conclusion. The relevant drawings are the Construction Limits Plan, revision C, and the Outline Ecological Management Plan, revision B. They show broadly the same area of permanent development, but they do not use the same boundary for temporary works beside Brindle Spinney. That difference matters because a temporary haul route, lighting column or drainage excavation can create effects outside the permanent fence line. A condition referring only to the final layout would not resolve it.

6.2 The documents should be reconciled in a single plan at a legible scale before any site clearance. The plan should distinguish the order limits, permanent works, temporary working areas, ecological exclusion areas and land available for reinstatement. It should also identify which drawing takes precedence if a contractor finds an inconsistency. A general commitment to work 'where practicable' within the construction limits is not an adequate substitute: it gives no measurable boundary against which the works can be checked. This is a drawing-control issue, not an objection to the principle of the Larkfen Link Energy Park.

6.3 The proposed construction access from Thistlebank Road appears capable of separating delivery traffic from the narrow lane serving the eastern fields. However, the Transport Assessment uses an average daily vehicle figure for the busiest phase. Averaging conceals the short periods when aggregate deliveries and staff arrivals would coincide. A revised construction traffic schedule should therefore state the assumed maximum number of movements in each peak hour, the proportion of heavy goods vehicles, and the proposed holding arrangements if vehicles arrive early. The schedule should be tied to the phase in which the access track and cable crossing are constructed, rather than presented as one figure for the whole programme.

6.4 The swept-path drawing demonstrates entry by the design vehicle when the verge is available, but the verge is also shown as a drainage feature on the surface-water plan. The final access detail should confirm its finished level, load-bearing treatment and maintenance responsibility. If it is compacted or strengthened for vehicle overrun, the drainage calculation should use the resulting infiltration value rather than the existing ground assumption. This is a small point on the drawing, but it affects whether runoff is directed towards the roadside ditch during intense rainfall.

6.5 The Flood Risk and Drainage Statement adopts a controlled discharge to Fenmere Cut. The stated allowable rate should be checked against the updated impermeable-area schedule, including the temporary compound if it remains surfaced through more than one construction phase. Calculations for the permanent drainage system do not, by themselves, demonstrate that the compound can operate without silty water entering the Cut. A construction drainage plan should show the sequence of earthworks, temporary interception measures, settlement provision and the point at which permanent attenuation becomes available. It should specify an inspection after heavy rain and a procedure for removing accumulated sediment without placing it on the ditch bank.

6.6 The landscape drawings show native planting along the western boundary. The planting is useful as long-term screening, but its establishment period should not be treated as immediate visual mitigation. From the public route across Merefold Common, the principal construction effect will be the visibility of the compound and crane activity, not the final height of the installed equipment. The Landscape and Visual Appraisal should report that temporary effect separately and explain what, if anything, can be achieved through compound layout. Moving stockpiles behind the existing hedge may be effective; relying on newly planted shrubs will not be effective in the first construction season.

6.7 Lighting requires a similarly specific approach. The submitted outline says that task lighting will be directed away from retained vegetation, but does not identify the maximum mounting height, operating hours or circumstances in which mobile towers could be used. The secured lighting method should include a plan of permitted lighting zones, luminaire specifications and a procedure for checking light spill at the edge of Brindle Spinney. It should address both routine winter working and exceptional safety work. The method need not prohibit every temporary light; it must make clear how unnecessary spill will be avoided and how a non-compliant fitting will be corrected.

6.8 The ecological material records bat activity along the wider Brindle Spinney corridor and refers to badger signs within the wider survey area. Those are appropriate matters for precautionary working methods. Neither statement, on its own, identifies a particular roost or sett, and no such location is needed in the public-facing construction plan. The plan can instead set out the relevant working restrictions, checks before vegetation removal and the process for responding to an unexpected finding. That approach preserves an auditable method without placing sensitive survey detail in a drawing intended for general circulation.

6.9 Alder Marsh Bird Group has asked that the eastern grassland remain available during the first spring after construction starts. The submitted phasing diagram does not establish whether cable installation, soil storage and reinstatement would occur in that order. A short phase-by-phase table would resolve the point. It should list the area occupied, the expected duration of occupation, the reinstatement specification and the criterion for accepting the restored surface. Calendar dates alone would be less useful because the start of works may move; the environmental controls should follow the activity.

6.10 I recommend that the Examining Authority seek one revised construction-and-ecology plan, supported by the traffic schedule, construction drainage sequence and lighting method described above. Each should have a clear approval stage before the relevant works begin. This would allow the detailed contractor design to develop while retaining enforceable limits on where and how construction takes place. In my opinion, those changes would address the present uncertainty without requiring a redesign of the permanent energy park.

7.1 The traffic schedule should distinguish daily average movements from the maximum hourly flow during delivery peaks. Larkfen Energy Ltd has modelled the Meregate Lane junction using an even distribution across the working day, whereas the draft construction programme allows several transformer deliveries in the same morning. The difference matters for queue length and for the time available to clear the junction before school traffic. A revised assessment should test a concentrated delivery scenario, state the assumed vehicle dimensions and identify where vehicles would wait if a delivery slot is missed.

7.2 The proposed routing restriction is useful, but the present wording does not say how compliance will be checked. I recommend a delivery booking register and a monthly summary of route exceptions, submitted to Brackenmere District Council during the main construction phase. These are monitoring measures, not a request for a new highway design. Subject to that clarification, the traffic effects could be controlled within the limits assessed for the Larkfen Link Energy Park.

text:
Representation on the Eldermere Link Road application

I am a pupil at Brackenmere Community School and I am 15. I am writing this myself, not as homework and not for the school. I want the Examining Authority to know what the road would be like for people who have to cross the proposed route every day. I have not been to one of the hearings because they are during lessons, but I read the non-technical summary and looked at the plan in the library. Some of the lines are hard to match up with places on the ground. I hope this still counts as a proper representation.

My journey starts on Merefold Lane. I walk with my friends Orla Fenn and Idris Wye, who also go to Brackenmere Community School. The school postcode is QV4 8LT. A postcode for a school is not where any of us live. We use the lane because the other way round adds a big hill and goes past a junction where drivers do not always stop. On wet mornings the verge is already too narrow for everyone coming towards us. Putting construction lorries there, even for a temporary period, would make walking feel much less safe.

The application says there will be a signed diversion while the bridge is built. The line on the map seems to take pupils behind the playing fields and out at the bus turning area. That is where buses reverse before school. Last Thursday we tried walking the suggested way after lessons, without going onto the fenced land, and it took longer than the drawing makes it look. My friend Leni Pask, who is 14, missed the bus we normally get. I am not saying a bus being missed is the most important planning issue. I am saying the diversion should be tested at the time pupils actually use it, not just on a quiet afternoon.

I have diagnosed asthma. Dust from the works worries me because the current footpath runs beside the proposed earth-moving area. The dust section of the application talks about houses but I could not find anything about the line of people walking to school. I do not want to be told simply to use a different route if that route has no pavement for part of it. I feel anxious about being late and about crossing between big vehicles, though I know those feelings are not measurements of traffic. Please ask the applicant for a drawing showing where a safe walking route will be on each stage of the works, with the gates and bus stops marked.

Our geography teacher, Miss Talia Brindle, showed us how to read the key on a habitat map. This is not a school submission and the teacher did not write it for me. We have seen badger paths in Wrenfold Wood, but I understand that paths alone do not tell you where a sett is. On a walk in September I saw what looked like a sett entrance inside the narrow bank 11 metres east of the kissing gate at the south end of Merefold Lane, beneath the split ash. I am including that detail so the ecology people can check it before that bank is cleared. Please do not put the precise spot on a public walking map.

I also think the replacement planting should be explained in ordinary words. The pictures show mature trees along the finished road, while the schedule says young whips will be planted. Those are not the same thing for pupils walking without shade in summer. Wrenfold Wood is shown as a place for bat surveys, which seems sensible, and I am not claiming to know where bats roost. The footbridge lighting matters as well. If it shines across the field all night, people and wildlife will notice it, even if the drawing looks nice in daylight.

I heard Cllr Soren Ives ask at a public meeting whether the temporary crossing could be open before Merefold Lane closes. I thought that was a fair question. The answer I heard was about the final bridge, not the weeks when there might be no bridge at all. Eldermere Roads Partnership has put a project website at https://www.eldermere-link.example, but I could not find a simple calendar showing which route pupils are meant to take each week. I sent a question to representations@eldermere-link.example and got an automatic reply. A map in the school reception and at the bus stop would reach people who do not check a website every morning.

There are other worries people talk about at school, including noise in exams and mud carried onto the lane. I have lived in this area for about ten years, so I know that the field gets very wet, but that is not the same as having drainage data. I am asking the Examining Authority to look at the applicant's drainage work, not to take my word for it. Please make sure any wheel-washing promise has someone checking it when lorries leave the site. A promise buried in a document is difficult for a pupil to use when the road is muddy on the way home.

I do not think the whole project should be decided just by whether my walk is convenient. Some families want a quicker trip to work. But children should not have to choose between a route beside construction traffic and a diversion that is unsafe around buses. Please require a continuous walking route before works close the present path, publish the stage-by-stage maps, and check the bank by the kissing gate before any clearance. I would like my comments to be considered even though I cannot come to a hearing in school time.

Nessa Valen
IP reference: IP-502741
Contact: nessa.valen@post.example

Further comments on the proposed road

The traffic assessment for the Eldermere Link Road appears to compare the completed scheme with a future year without it, but it is less clear how traffic will be managed during the temporary closures. The construction phasing plan should show the expected number of heavy goods vehicles for each phase and identify which junctions have been tested at school start and finish times. An average daily figure would hide short queues at the crossings.

The drainage drawings show new outfalls towards Brackenmere Brook. Before consent is granted, Eldermere Roads Partnership should explain what happens when a heavy storm coincides with a blocked highway gully. The maintenance arrangements should say who will inspect the silt traps after construction, not just during it.

Finally, the landscape drawings should include winter views from the public path. Screening described as effective in year fifteen will not screen the embankment while the planting is still small.

text:
From: Ellis Venn
Crowglass Farm
17 Mere Lane, Brindlewick, BW4 8QJ
Mobile: 07700 900482
Email: ellis.venn@example.com
Interested Party reference: IP-208417

21 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Fenmire Lowland Link DCO

Dear Examining Authority,

I am writing about the proposed permanent acquisition and temporary possession at Crowglass Farm. This is a working mixed farm, not an empty block on a land plan. It is also our family home. The plans show the link road crossing our grazing fields and a construction compound beside the yard entrance. I have tried to make these points in the consultation, but the latest drawings still seem to assume that a gate can be moved and everything else will carry on as before.

My wife, Mrs Nera Venn, lives here with me, as does our son Tavi Venn, aged 14. My father Orlan Venn also lives in the farmhouse. The kitchen and bedrooms face the yard. Lorries turning into a compound there would be heard from the house and would meet our own machinery at the narrowest point of the farm. I am worried and sleeping badly over this, but I want the examination to look at the practical access problem, not just the disturbance. We cannot shift the yard to another side of the holding.

The red line takes part of field CG-04, where the sheep are gathered before loading. The proposed haul road cuts between that field and the handling pens. When a flock is moving, the gates have to stay open long enough for the animals to go through without a vehicle coming the other way. A promise that contractors will give way to farm traffic sounds fine on paper. In practice somebody would need to manage it, including early mornings and weekends. Please ask Fenmire Infrastructure Ltd to say who would have authority to stop deliveries, and how I would contact that person when a load of sheep is already at the gate.

The construction traffic assessment counts vehicles on Mere Lane but does not show our movements between the yard, the rented meadow and the lower fields. During lambing, a trailer may make several short trips that would not look important in an annual traffic total. The lane has soft verges and there is nowhere sensible to pass beside our entrance. I have farmed here for over 40 years and know where a wagon's rear wheels go when its driver tries to leave room for a tractor. I would welcome a site visit before any further access drawing is treated as settled.

Drainage is another worry. The ditch along CG-04 takes water from the yard and from land above us. The applicant's drawing appears to put a temporary crossing just upstream of the point where we clear silt each winter. If that section is fenced off, who will be permitted to get in and clear it? Please do not answer simply that drainage will be covered by a later management plan. I need to know the access width, where spoil can be put and whether I am expected to ask a contractor for permission each time. None of that is explained in the current outline arrangements.

There are consequences inside the house as well. Tavi Venn has diagnosed epilepsy, and sudden changes to the routine at home are difficult for us to manage. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide a medical question. I am asking for a definite construction timetable and advance notice if night work or piling is proposed near the farmhouse, so that we can make arrangements rather than hear about it when machinery arrives. My father's rheumatoid arthritis makes a long walk from a remote parking place difficult. The suggestion at the drop-in that we could leave our cars at the far barn while the yard entrance is shut was not a workable solution for him.

I have a £84,000 loan in my name for the replacement milking equipment. Losing the lower grazing for two seasons would affect the way I meet those payments, quite apart from any eventual compensation. The published estimate of £6.2 million for the project compound may be reasonable for the applicant's budget; it does not tell me whether I can keep the farm running while it is built. Please provide a month-by-month land-take plan, including reinstatement of fences and water pipes, rather than treating temporary land as though it has no continuing use.

I also want to correct something recorded at the last community session. Mr Halen Sorr, who lives nearby but has not made a representation, was listed as agreeing that farm access could be shared with the compound. He was talking about the existing field gate, not our yard gate. Cllr Veda Noll asked the same question about turning space at the session. It would help if the meeting note distinguished the two entrances. I have not asked either of them to speak for me.

The ecology material needs care too. Badgers have been seen around Crowglass Wood, and that broad description is sufficient for a public plan. In the survey sheet handed to me, the active badger sett is under the split ash at the south-east corner of field CG-07, 11 metres west of the culvert. The bat maternity roost is behind the loose ridge tile on the east pitch of the old dairy, directly over bay 2. Those exact descriptions should not be repeated in an open-access drawing. Jessa Murle of Siltmere Ecology visited the yard in September and explained why a general note and a confidential plan could be kept separately. I am content for the Examining Authority to receive the detail, but not for it to be put in the public minutes.

I am not opposed to people travelling more easily. I do object to drawings which make the farm look as if it can pause for two years. Please require a revised access arrangement, a usable drainage maintenance route and clear notice of works next to our home before the examination closes. If a site visit can be arranged, the project team can write to me at the address above or use consultation@fenmirelink.example; for a change on the day, my mobile number is above.

Yours faithfully,

Ellis Venn

21 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Fenmire Lowland Link DCO

From: Ellis Venn
Address for correspondence: 7 Wicket Fen Lane, Brindlewick, BW8 4QN
Mobile: 07700 914 638

Further to my letter about the proposed access and drainage arrangements, I am sending this note because the latest construction drawing still treats Crowglass Farm as though it is only a field with a gate. It is a working farm, but it is also where we live. The yard is between the farmhouse and the buildings we use every day. A line drawn across it affects ordinary things such as getting a feed delivery in, bringing machinery back under cover, and getting from the house to the road without meeting a reversing lorry.

I have tried to follow the revisions in the applicant's drawings. On the plan marked FL-LINK-C-204, the temporary access appears to move further from the cattle shed, which is an improvement. But the turning area is shown over the hardstanding where our bulk feed is unloaded. The driver cannot simply use the other side: there is a drain cover there that will not take a loaded vehicle. If Fenmire Infrastructure Ltd intends to strengthen it, I need to see that in the construction method, not just be told at a meeting that it will be sorted out later. At present the contractor's route and ours would cross at the narrowest part of the yard.

My wife, Mrs Nera Venn, lives in the farmhouse with me. Our son, Tavi Venn, aged 14, and my father, Orlan Venn, also live there. That is why I keep asking for the works beside the house to be treated differently from works at the far edge of a field. We can put up with a certain amount of inconvenience. We cannot plan school mornings or livestock movements around an access that might be closed with an hour's warning. A letter delivered to the farmhouse after a closure has started is no notice at all. Please ask for a named site contact, a way of reaching that contact outside office hours, and a minimum period of advance notice except in a genuine emergency.

There is a particular concern about dust when the yard surface is broken up. Tavi Venn has asthma, and dust coming through the kitchen windows is not the same thing as dust on an unoccupied field. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide a medical matter. I am asking for a practical plan: keep the surface damp when necessary, cover loose loads, and say who we contact if those measures are not being used. I would also like the applicant to show where vehicles will wait while the gate is being opened. Waiting on the lane would obstruct the farm entrance, but waiting inside the yard would put them next to the house.

Drainage is the other point that has still not been answered. The ditch along the lower field needs clearing periodically, particularly after a wet winter. The proposed fence leaves room for a person to walk along it, but not for the small machine we use to lift material out. Moving the fence a little on a plan will not help if the ground on the other side is too soft to carry the machine. I have asked for a cross-section showing the usable width, levels and surface, together with a written commitment about who maintains any new culvert. Without that, the maintenance route exists on paper only.

At the community session, Cllr Veda Noll asked whether farm access would be maintained throughout construction. The answer given in the room was yes, but I have not found a drawing that shows how that works on days when the trench crosses our entrance. A temporary plate may allow a car through and still be unsuitable for a loaded trailer. We need the applicant to set out the sequence of works and the period, if any, when the entrance cannot take farm traffic. It would be better to acknowledge a short closure and agree an alternative than to promise continuous access that cannot be delivered.

Mr Halen Sorr, who lives nearby and has not made a representation, asked me whether the lane would be closed to other traffic as well. I cannot answer that from the material currently available. I mention the question because it shows the difference between telling people there may be traffic management and explaining what they should actually expect on a particular day. Please do not publish a neighbour's details in order to deal with my point; the applicant can answer it by making the traffic arrangements clearer for everyone.

I also want to return briefly to ecology. Jessa Murle of Siltmere Ecology said during the visit that the general survey findings could be discussed without putting a precise protected-species location in public material. I agree. There are badgers in the wider area and bats have been recorded around the farm buildings, but those broad facts are not a reason to disclose a confidential plan. Equally, the existence of a confidential plan must not mean that the arrangements for fencing, lighting and access are left unexplained to the people who have to work around them. A plain-language summary would help.

I have worked this holding for over 40 years and know that construction cannot be made invisible. I am asking instead for drawings that reflect the farm as it operates and the farmhouse as an occupied home. If a revised plan is issued, please send a paper copy to the address above as well as placing it on the examination page. The project mailbox, consultation@fenmirelink.example, is useful for general questions, but a last-minute change to a site visit or a delivery needs a telephone call. My mobile number is given above for that purpose.

Yours faithfully,

Ellis Venn

Further technical comments on the Fenmire Lowland Link DCO

These comments concern the traffic, drainage and landscape information accompanying the current construction programme. They are intended to be read with the General Arrangement Plan, the Outline Construction Traffic Management Plan and drawing FLL-TR-APP-017. The issue is not whether construction can take place without any disruption; it is whether the assessed effects match the sequence and working methods that the development consent order would actually permit.

Traffic modelling

The transport assessment uses an average daily construction flow for each phase. That is helpful for assessing the wider network, but it does not show the short periods when deliveries, spoil movements and ordinary local traffic may meet at the same junction. The turning assessment for the temporary access on Link Road L2 should therefore include the busiest hour of the busiest construction week, not only a representative day. It should state the assumed number of vehicles waiting to enter, the length of the longest vehicle, and whether a vehicle can turn without its trailer crossing the opposing lane. A swept-path drawing should show the temporary barriers and signs in their proposed positions rather than on an otherwise empty carriageway.

The assessment should also distinguish through traffic from traffic serving individual work areas. A delivery that enters at the northern compound and leaves through the southern gate has a different effect from one making two trips on the same section of road. The tables in the Outline Construction Traffic Management Plan do not presently make that distinction clear. If a one-way route is intended, it needs to be secured in the requirements and shown on the phasing drawings. If it is only an aspiration, the transport assessment must test two-way construction movements. The same applies to the proposed restriction on deliveries during the morning peak: the restriction should specify times, vehicle classes and how exceptions will be recorded.

Drainage and ground levels

The drainage drawings show the permanent outfall arrangement at West Drain, but the temporary stage needs more detail. During earthworks the surface-water system will not operate as the final drawings show it. The application should identify where clean runoff will be diverted, where silty water will be held, and what happens when a settlement feature reaches capacity during a prolonged wet period. A note saying that the contractor will agree a method later does not establish whether there is enough land within the order limits for that method.

The proposed culvert beneath the embankment should be checked against water levels on both sides of the works during each construction phase. It is not enough to demonstrate the finished arrangement if a temporary haul road or stockpile narrows the flow route for several months. The calculations should include the assumed blockage allowance, the level at which water would first leave the channel and a plan showing the route it would take. Merefold District Council's drainage comments refer to maintaining existing flow paths. A drawing comparing existing, temporary and permanent ground levels would make it possible to see whether that commitment has been met.

Landscape and visual matters

The landscape chapter relies heavily on planting to reduce the effect of the raised section near Alder Sill. The photomontages should make clear which planting is existing, which is proposed and which is expected to be effective only after establishment. A view labelled as a future-year view should not be used to describe the construction phase. It would assist to provide one winter view from the same viewpoint, with the vegetation shown without leaves and the proposed fence, lighting columns and maintenance track visible. The current views are useful, but they do not make those elements easy to distinguish.

The planting schedule also needs to be consistent with the land-take drawings. In places, the landscape plan appears to show a continuous belt where the general arrangement shows a drainage swale and access strip. If the belt must be interrupted, its screening effect should be assessed on that basis. The Environmental Masterplan should identify the minimum planting width that can actually be delivered, rather than a width that depends on a later contractor layout. Replacement planting for failures is sensible, but the maintenance period and the test for deciding that a plant has failed should be stated in the approved plan.

Construction phasing and controls

The programme presents the bridge works, drainage diversion and main earthworks in separate bars. It is not clear whether those activities can overlap. That matters because the combined effect may be greater than the effect of any one activity assessed on its own. A single drawing for each phase should show the active working area, haul routes, stockpiles, temporary lighting and drainage measures. The drawings need not prescribe every item of equipment, but they should set the limits within which the contractor may work. In particular, a change from the indicated northern compound to a southern compound should not be treated as a minor site decision if it changes traffic routes or the location of night-time lighting.

The Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan promises monitoring and corrective action, but several triggers remain undefined. For example, it says that wheel washing will be increased if mud is carried onto the highway. The approved version should say who checks the road, how frequently checks are made during wet weather, what action follows a failed check and where the record is kept. Similar measurable steps are needed for silt control and lighting direction. This is not a request for every site instruction to be written into the development consent order. It is a request for enforceable limits and a clear route for dealing with a departure from the assessed scheme.

Finally, the documents should use the same phase names and drawing revisions throughout. The transport appendix refers to Phase 2B while the drainage note calls the equivalent work Stage C. The application may intend those to mean the same thing, but that should not be left to inference. A short revision table, cross-referencing the assessment, plans and draft requirements, would help the Examining Authority and the local authority test whether the proposed controls cover the works assessed.

The same cross-check is needed for the transport material. The traffic forecast in Appendix T4 assumes that all bulk fill reaches the works from the east, using the B742 Mirebank Road and the proposed Sedgefen Junction. The construction traffic management plan, however, leaves open use of Lowbank Lane during an undefined “short-term contingency”. Lowbank Lane has not been modelled as a construction access in the worst-case daily flow. If it is to remain a possible route, the assessment should say how many movements it could carry, for how long, and what would trigger its use. If it is not part of the assessed scheme, the management plan should rule it out rather than leave the question for a later contractor decision.

The turning counts also need explaining. Table 6-3 uses a peak of 96 heavy goods vehicle movements per day, while Figure T4.11 shows 62 at Sedgefen Junction in the same construction quarter. These figures may represent different directions or different definitions of a movement, but the captions do not say so. A single schedule giving arrivals, departures and total two-way movements for each access and work phase would make the junction assessment reproducible. It should include deliveries for the drainage outfalls and temporary haul-road stone, not just the main earthworks. Those smaller activities may overlap with the busiest period rather than occurring neatly afterwards.

Fenmire Infrastructure Ltd proposes to check final delivery routes before works begin. That is useful for managing a road closure, but it is not a substitute for assessing the normal route now. The draft requirement should tie the approved construction traffic management plan to the maximum flows tested in Appendix T4 and require a documented review if those flows are expected to be exceeded. A weekly log of gate counts would give Merefold District Council a practical means of checking compliance. The log should distinguish loaded and empty heavy vehicles and should be available on request, rather than appearing only in an end-of-project report.

There is a similar issue with the landscape drawings for the Fenmire Lowland Link DCO. The photomontages show the finished embankment with planting established, whereas the programme suggests the southern verge may remain exposed through two growing seasons. The bare-earth view matters here because the raised profile will be seen against an otherwise low horizon. Drawing FLL-LV-204 Rev C gives the intended planting mix but not the maximum time that a completed earthwork can remain unplanted. The applicant could resolve this with a phase-by-phase schedule for topsoiling, sowing and replacement planting, together with a winter view from the same viewpoints used in the visual assessment.

The proposed screening should also be assessed as mitigation, not assumed to work as soon as it is installed. A hedge at the foot of an embankment will not screen the upper slope in its first year. If the landscape conclusion depends on mature growth, the assessment should state the interim effect and the year in which the planting is expected to provide that screening. This is particularly relevant where the alignment crosses the open approach to Merepool Cut. I am not arguing for an artificially tall instant hedge; a realistic account of the early years would be more helpful than a finished-state image alone.

The drainage information has improved, but the drawings and the hydraulic note still use different assumptions for the western attenuation basin. Plan FLL-DR-118 Rev D shows a maintenance strip inside the basin fence, reducing the available storage footprint. Calculation sheet FLL-HY-09 appears to use the earlier outline footprint. The difference may be small, but the claimed freeboard is also small during the design event. Please provide a calculation for the geometry actually shown on the plan, including the access strip, sediment allowance and the outfall control setting. The design should not rely on a future detailed-design exercise to demonstrate that the basin fits within the land shown for it.

The assessment says that temporary drainage will be installed before the main strip of topsoil is removed. That order should be carried into the construction sequence for Phase 2B, especially at the crossing of the Old Mere Drain. The method statement currently allows temporary ditching “as required”, without showing which areas can be stripped before a silt-control measure is operational. A simple sequencing plan could identify the first discharge point, the settlement capacity available at each stage, and the point at which the permanent system takes over. It would also clarify who checks the controls after heavy rain and where an exceedance is recorded. There is no need to prescribe every length of temporary pipe in the DCO; there does need to be an enforceable order of operations.

Merefold District Council has asked for confirmation of the receiving watercourse capacity. The response refers to the modelled design flow but does not address the period when the new outfall is connected and the upstream ditch remains partly diverted. That temporary arrangement deserves its own check. The contractor may reasonably seek flexibility in choosing pumps or temporary pipes, provided the approved method demonstrates that the receiving channel will not be overloaded and that a blocked outlet has a safe overflow route within the works area.

Taken together, these are matters of consistency rather than a request to redesign the Fenmire Lowland Link DCO. One consolidated phase table, with drawing revisions and the traffic, landscape and drainage assumptions beside each phase, would show what has actually been assessed. The final requirements could then point to that table. Without it, the detailed documents can each appear acceptable in isolation while describing slightly different works. I would welcome a response that identifies the controlling revision for each topic and explains how later changes will be checked against the assessed limits.

Further technical comments on the Fenmire Lowland Link DCO

For the avoidance of doubt, the request for a controlling phase table is not an objection to using detailed design. Some flexibility will be needed as ground conditions become clearer. The point is that the limits of that flexibility should be readable in one place. The present documents use different descriptions for the eastern compound, the temporary crossing and the order in which the drainage connections are made. A contractor could follow one drawing correctly and still produce a sequence that is not the one used for the traffic or flood calculations.

On construction traffic, the assessment should state whether the daily HGV figures are totals for the whole route or maxima that might occur at each work front on the same day. Table CT-4 gives a peak of 84 two-way HGV movements, while the phasing note says the eastern earthworks and bridge works may overlap. If 84 is a route-wide ceiling, that should be secured. If it is not, the junction assessment for the B6174 Moor Drove and Larkfen Lane needs to show the overlapping case. The proposed trigger for reviewing the Construction Traffic Management Plan is presently expressed as a 'material change in activity'. That phrase does not tell anyone when a revised traffic run is needed. A numerical threshold, together with a requirement to record movements by phase, would be more useful.

The swept-path drawing for the Larkfen Lane access also appears to assume that the passing place is available before deliveries begin. The programme places its construction in the same phase as the first deliveries. Please confirm which comes first. This is not a request for an additional access: a short hold point in the programme would resolve it. The same point applies to the temporary wheel wash, which ought to be operational before bulk material is taken away, not merely by the end of the site-establishment period. Routing signs should refer to the approved access drawings rather than a later contractor sketch that may use different road names.

Landscape treatment needs a similar distinction between early works and the finished scheme. Drawing FL-ENV-206 Rev C shows a planted bund north of the link, but the construction layout uses that strip for soil storage until the final season. The photomontages appear to show the bund at opening year. If it cannot be formed until after the storage area is cleared, the opening-year view should show the intervening condition. Alternatively, the soil-storage location can be changed and the bund brought forward. Either solution may be reasonable; the assessment should not rely on both at once.

The proposed planting schedule describes a ten-year establishment period but does not explain what happens where replacement planting is repeatedly lost to wet ground. Merefold District Council asked in its drainage comments whether the bund interrupts the shallow overland flow towards Fenmire Cut. That question should be answered on the grading plan, not left to the landscape maintenance plan. A low point or controlled gap may be needed, but it must not become an unassessed discharge route. The finished levels, planting specification and drainage detail should therefore use the same cross-sections.

In relation to surface water, the calculation for the western basin includes a 40% climate-change allowance, whereas the temporary works note uses rainfall figures without saying whether the same allowance applies. I recognise that a temporary settlement feature may be designed to a different standard from a permanent basin. The standard and the intended duration should nevertheless be stated. The calculation also needs to distinguish clean runoff diverted around an excavation from water that has passed through disturbed ground. Combining those flows on a diagram makes it difficult to tell which discharge is subject to settlement before reaching Fenmire Cut.

The drawings show a shut-off valve at Outfall F2, but there is no clearly marked inspection position or explanation of how the valve can be reached during a flood. This is an operational issue rather than an argument about the outfall's location. It would help if the requirement for the detailed drainage scheme covered access, inspection and maintenance as well as pipe size. The same scheme should identify what happens if the receiving ditch is already full when pumping is proposed. A statement that pumping will be 'managed appropriately' is not an overflow design.

Badger activity has been noted in Reedveil Wood, and the ecology text discusses general protection measures along the works corridor. Those general measures should be coordinated with the lighting plan: the drawing showing overnight compound lighting extends beyond the compound boundary, while the ecology appendix assumes a darker corridor beside the wood. I am not asking for a new survey location to be published. I am asking for the lighting specification, hours of use and ecological assumptions to describe the same arrangement. A lighting contour at the boundary would make this check possible without putting sensitive survey details on the general arrangement drawing.

Finally, the draft requirement on the Construction Environmental Management Plan should make clear which documents are approved before each phase starts and which can follow later. At present, 'prior to commencement of the relevant part' is used for the traffic plan, drainage details and landscape works, but 'relevant part' is not defined consistently. A single phase schedule could identify the works that may start after each approval and the documents that must already be in place. It could also record any assessed maximum that a later approval must not exceed. That would give Fenmire Infrastructure Ltd, Merefold District Council and those checking compliance a common reference, rather than three slightly different accounts of the same sequence.

The phase schedule also needs to match the assumptions in Chapter 9 of the Environmental Statement. The traffic tables use a peak of 46 HGV movements per day on Marshgate Road, whereas the indicative programme shows drainage and embankment operations running together for six weeks. It is not clear whether those operations were combined in the model or assessed separately. If the latter, the draft requirement should prevent overlap until a revised construction traffic assessment has been approved.

The same point applies to runoff. Drawing FLL-DRA-204 shows a temporary settlement basin west of the proposed haul road, but the outfall shown on the phase diagram appears to serve the permanent ditch only. The drawings should identify where water goes during the changeover, the design storm used for temporary storage, and who approves any diversion before earthworks begin. This is not an objection to the principle of the Fenmire Lowland Link; it is a request for an auditable sequence. Fenmire Infrastructure Ltd and Merefold District Council could resolve it through one numbered table cross-referenced in the final management plan.

The table should also set out the hold points between stripping the eastern fields and opening the permanent drainage channel. At present, Drawing FLL-DRA-204 and the Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan describe different sequences for installing the silt fence. The fence needs to be in place before any topsoil is moved, not at the end of the first construction phase. The temporary basin should remain available until the permanent channel has passed its inspection and the old outfall has been sealed.

For traffic, the forecast should show construction vehicles using Sedgewick Lane during each phase, rather than just a daily total for the whole site. A peak-hour figure would make it possible to check the proposed passing places against the turning movements at the haul-road entrance. Fenmire Infrastructure Ltd should provide the revised phase diagrams to Merefold District Council before the relevant works start. A condition requiring approval after works have begun would not answer the sequencing problem.

EAST CURLEW PARISH COUNCIL
Draft minutes of the ordinary meeting held on 17 September 2026 at the Council Room, 3 Market Court, Fennick, FN2 4LT

Present: Cllr Tamsin Grell (Chair), Cllr Oren Blay, Cllr Nia Fenwick and Cllr Rowan Pike. In attendance: Mara Ellery, Clerk to East Curlew Parish Council. Members of the public: Davin Foyle, Lessa Morwin and Idris Venn.

1. Apologies and interests
Apologies were received from Cllr Selma Dray. No disclosable interests were declared. The Chair reminded everyone that these were parish council minutes, not a transcript of the public questions, and asked that points for the forthcoming examination be sent in writing as well.

2. Previous minutes
The minutes of 20 August 2026 were approved, subject to changing ‘western access’ to ‘eastern access’ in item 7. The Chair signed the amended copy. The Clerk said the correction would also be made to the copy on the noticeboard.

3. Fenwater Link Development Consent Order: examination matters
The Council considered the latest consultation material from Fenwater Link Ltd concerning the proposed construction compound, haul route and drainage outfall. The project website, https://fenwater-link.example/documents, was noted as a useful source of the current plans. Councillors felt that the revised drawing was clearer than the earlier one, but it still did not show how pedestrians would pass the temporary entrance on Bramble Lane when two lorries met.

Davin Foyle asked whether the compound would operate on Saturday mornings. The Chair said the draft construction timetable appeared to permit it, although the Council would ask the applicant to confirm the hours and any exceptions. Lessa Morwin described poor sleep when heavy vehicles used the lane during previous works. The Council noted the concern but could not establish from the plans how much traffic would use that route. Idris Venn said the footpath diversion looked longer on the ground than it did on the drawing; the Clerk will request a measured diversion plan.

The Clerk reported that a letter had been received from Lessa Morwin about school-day traffic. It said that Jori Morwin, aged 14, has diagnosed epilepsy and that unpredictable queues at the crossing make the journey difficult. Councillors agreed to raise the crossing arrangements in their submission without repeating the family's medical detail. The Clerk will check whether a staffed crossing has been assessed, rather than suggesting that the Council can require one.

The Council's earlier examination correspondence carries Interested Party reference IP-092481. The Clerk explained that this number should be used on the response form, but it is not the planning reference for the separate householder item below. Members approved a short response seeking a swept-path drawing, enforceable delivery hours and a plan showing access to the recreation field throughout construction. Cllr Fenwick asked that the response distinguish between what the Council had observed and what residents had reported. Agreed.

4. Ecology information
Councillors discussed the environmental statement's description of badger signs in Gorsebarrow Wood. The location given there was broad, and the Council did not propose to speculate about occupied setts in its public response. A separate confidential survey note supplied to the Clerk identifies the badger sett in the bank 12 metres east of stile 3 on Bramble Lane, immediately behind the north-west corner of Field 17. The Council agreed not to reproduce that note in its submission or on the village noticeboard. The Clerk will instead ask the applicant, through the examination process, whether the proposed fencing and working distances reflect the latest survey.

Cllr Pike also mentioned a newspaper article at https://marshledger.example/local/haul-road, which several residents had forwarded. Members agreed that its traffic figures should not be quoted until the underlying count is available. The Chair pointed members to the examination documents at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects for the formal record. The Clerk will circulate the relevant drawing numbers, not screenshots, before the deadline.

5. Unrelated householder application
The Council considered application 26/00418/HOU for a rear dormer and single-storey extension at 8 Wicket Close, Fennick, FN2 6RE, submitted by Mrs Elspeth Vane. The Chair made clear that this application is not part of the Fenwater Link examination. No member of the public spoke on the item. Councillors had no objection in principle, but asked the local planning authority to check the proposed roof material against the conservation-area guidance. The Clerk will send this as the Council's consultation response and will not attach any of the DCO correspondence.

6. Correspondence and administration
The Clerk confirmed that the Council's shared mailbox, clerk@eastcurlewpc.org.uk, remains the preferred route for public comments. A message sent directly to mara.ellery@eastcurlewpc.org.uk had not reached the shared folder until after the agenda was issued. For urgent access issues the Clerk had also been given a resident's mobile number, 07963 420 811; it will not appear on the public contact list. The Clerk asked that councillors avoid forwarding personal correspondence to the whole mailing list merely to show that it had been received.

The Clerk's correspondence address for this meeting was recorded as 14 Plover Fold, Dunmere, DV4 8QP. The Council agreed that future published agendas should give the Council Room address or the shared mailbox instead, as the correspondence address is a home address and visitors should not call there. Printing for the examination response can be met from the existing administration budget.

7. Date of next meeting
The next ordinary meeting will be on 15 October 2026 at the Council Room. The meeting closed at 8.46 pm.

Minutes prepared by Mara Ellery
Clerk, East Curlew Parish Council

East Curlew Parish Council
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held in the Council Room, East Curlew, on 15 October 2026 at 7.00 pm

These minutes are supplied as an attachment to the Council's response in the examination of the Fenwater Link Development Consent Order. They include other business dealt with at the same meeting. They are not a record of an examination hearing.

Present: Cllr Tamsin Grell (Chair), Cllr Oren Blay, Cllr Nia Fenwick, Cllr Rowan Pike and Cllr Selma Dray. Mara Ellery, Clerk, East Curlew Parish Council, took the minutes. Members of the public present for all or part of the meeting: Davin Foyle, Lessa Morwin and Idris Venn. No apologies were received.

1. Previous minutes and matters arising
The minutes of the previous ordinary meeting were approved. The Chair noted that the shared mailbox, clerk@eastcurlew-pc.org.uk, is now being used for examination correspondence. The private correspondence address printed in the earlier minutes should not be copied into the response cover sheet. The Council Room remains the address for notices and for anyone wishing to inspect the paper copy of the documents by appointment.

2. Public participation
Davin Foyle asked whether the temporary construction compound was still shown on the land parcel behind Wren Lane. The Clerk said that the latest plan carried the same parcel number, FL-17, but the drawing had a new revision letter. Councillors agreed that the response must cite the revision actually in the examination library rather than the version brought to the September meeting.

Lessa Morwin said that construction traffic before school would make the walk along Mill Causeway difficult. Lessa Morwin also referred to Jori Morwin, aged 11, who has diagnosed epilepsy, and asked that the Council not include the family's circumstances in the published response. The Chair agreed: the Council's point is about the crossing and the absence of a continuous footway, not an individual child. Several people said the proposed hours had caused anxiety and poor sleep; no individual health details were needed to make the highways point.

Idris Venn asked for an explanation of the noise figures. The Chair said the Council could ask the applicant to explain the difference between an average figure and the short, louder events residents might hear. Members of the public were thanked and the meeting returned to council business at 7.32 pm.

3. Fenwater Link Development Consent Order
The Chair introduced the draft comments on Fenwater Link Ltd's construction traffic management proposals. This was the Council's response as a parish council, not a collection of the personal representations read out at the meeting. Cllr Oren Blay proposed adding a request for a staffed crossing at Mill Causeway during school arrival and departure times. Cllr Nia Fenwick supported the addition but said that the wording should not imply that the Council had measured traffic itself. Resolved unanimously to submit the amended request.

Cllr Rowan Pike reported that the drainage drawing still showed an outfall close to the ditch at the eastern end of Wren Lane. The Council had not seen evidence explaining who would clear that ditch during construction. The Clerk will ask for a maintenance responsibility table, including the period after the temporary works are removed. The Council did not object to the principle of a drainage outfall without that information; it could not assess the proposed arrangement properly.

On ecology, Cllr Selma Dray noted the reference to badger activity in Curlew Wood. That is a broad location and the Council will not put survey coordinates in its public response. A separate confidential survey note identifies a badger sett at the north end of the second drainage ditch, 18 metres east of gate FL-G4. The Clerk was asked to check with the case team how any necessary protected-site information should be supplied, rather than attaching that note to these minutes or circulating it with the ordinary agenda papers. Members also wanted the general requirement for an ecologist on site during vegetation clearance retained in the draft comments.

The Council discussed the applicant's proposed working hours. Cllr Tamsin Grell said the draft should distinguish routine deliveries from an emergency delivery needed to make a work area safe. It was agreed to request a named point of contact for out-of-hours complaints, but not to print a worker's direct number in the submission. The applicant's project mailbox, fenwaterlink@projects.example, may be quoted if it remains the advertised shared contact. The Clerk will check the examination website at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/national-infrastructure-planning before the response is sent. The Council made no allegation about the conduct of Fenwater Link Ltd; the request concerns how complaints would be logged and answered.

4. Planning application not connected with the DCO
Application EC/26/0417/HOU, Mrs Elspeth Vane, 6 Reedbank Terrace, East Curlew, EC3 4PL: single-storey rear extension. This was a district planning consultation and was not part of the Fenwater Link examination. Cllr Selma Dray declared a non-pecuniary interest as a near neighbour and took no part in the vote. The Council resolved, four votes in favour, to make no objection subject to the planning authority considering surface-water run-off to adjoining gardens. The Clerk was asked to send that response through the district council's planning portal, separately from the DCO material.

5. Administration and close
The draft DCO response, with the changes agreed above, is to be circulated to councillors by the shared mailbox for a final check of document references. Circulation is for checking transcription and references; it does not authorise new policy points after this meeting. The Chair will confirm the final text on behalf of the Council. The next ordinary meeting is scheduled for 12 November 2026. The meeting closed at 8.38 pm.

Clerk, East Curlew Parish Council

Appendix 1 — Technical points agreed for the Council’s Fenwater Link DCO response

This appendix records the technical points agreed at the meeting for incorporation into the response. It is not a separate objection to the principle of the Fenwater Link. References below are to the consultation version of the Environmental Statement (ES) and should be checked against the final examination library numbering before submission. Where the Council asks for further work, it is asking for information capable of being examined, rather than an assurance that a matter will be dealt with later.

1. Traffic modelling and access

East Curlew Parish Council considers that the construction traffic assessment should show the morning and afternoon peak-hour flows separately for Marshgate Road, the B4176 Fen Causeway and the junction serving the proposed eastern compound. The tables in ES Chapter 8 combine light vehicles and heavy goods vehicles in a way that makes the change at the smaller junctions hard to follow. A simple table of existing flows, forecast background flows and construction flows, with the same units and assessment year throughout, would help. The Council does not seek a different strategic model merely because it disagrees with a forecast. It asks for the inputs and assumptions relevant to the parish roads to be made clear.

The proposed restriction on construction vehicles using Mill Drove is welcomed, but the outline Construction Traffic Management Plan says only that the restriction will be ‘communicated’. It should specify the permitted approach routes, the location of signs, how delivery instructions will be issued, and how a wrongly routed vehicle will be recorded and dealt with. The tracking drawings should also cover the temporary access during the drainage works, when the eastern compound entrance is shown as unavailable. No conclusion about swept-path adequacy should depend on vehicles reversing from a public road unless that arrangement is expressly assessed and secured.

The ES refers to a ‘typical’ daily delivery profile. That is useful as an illustration, not as an enforceable maximum. The response should request a reasonable worst-case daily profile for the overlap between earthworks and cable installation, including school-term traffic in the background model. This point is about the capacity and safety of the highway network; it does not suggest that a particular collision will occur.

2. Landscape, lighting and visual material

The landscape drawings show new hedgerow planting along the northern edge of the link road. The Council supports that approach in principle but asks that the planting schedule identify the length, initial height, maintenance period and replacement obligation. The year 1 and year 15 visualisations should use the same viewpoint and field of view, with a clear note of the assumed growth rate. Viewpoint LV-06 on Common Bank appears to be taken from behind an existing hedge. A second winter view from the public verge would make the road’s visibility easier to assess. This is a request for representative visual material, not for the removal of the existing hedge.

The draft lighting strategy distinguishes permanent junction lighting from temporary compound lighting, but its plan does not mark the limits of spill at the eastern compound. The final strategy should include the hours of use, column heights, orientation and a contour plan for the construction period. The Council’s preference is for task lighting only where safe working permits, with fittings directed away from the open fen. A statement that lighting will be ‘minimised’ is too general to check after consent.

3. Drainage and flood risk

The drainage strategy proposes attenuation beside Lower Sedge Field and a controlled discharge to the Fenwater Drain. The calculations should be provided for the full impermeable area, including temporary hardstanding retained for more than one construction season. ES Appendix 12.3 appears to use a different paved-area figure from the engineering layout in Drawing FW-DR-204. The response should identify this discrepancy without assuming which figure is correct. The applicant should confirm whether the stated storage volume accommodates the agreed climate-change allowance and whether any exceedance route crosses the proposed maintenance track.

The outline maintenance plan should say who will inspect the attenuation basin, how often sediment will be removed and how access will be maintained after construction. These are operational matters that ought to be secured in the DCO requirements or an approved drainage document. The Council also requests a plan showing temporary drainage arrangements for each construction phase. Permanent attenuation cannot be relied on for a phase in which it has not yet been built or connected. The information should distinguish clean runoff from water requiring treatment before discharge.

4. Construction phasing and controls

The indicative programme shows bridge works, utility diversions and formation of the link road as overlapping activities. A phase plan would assist in understanding which haul route and compound access operate at each stage. It should show when the temporary crossing at Reed Dyke is installed and removed, and when the public footpath diversion begins and ends. The Council is not seeking a fixed start date: it seeks an intelligible sequence and controls that remain effective if the programme changes.

The outline Construction Environmental Management Plan should include measurable triggers for dust suppression, wheel cleaning and inspection of highway deposits. It should state where monitoring records will be kept and how an identified breach will be corrected. The Council accepts that detailed method statements can follow consent, provided the DCO secures the minimum standards and approval process. A reference to compliance with ‘good practice’ alone does not provide a clear test.

5. Policy and drafting

The final response should refer to the fictional East Curlew Local Plan Policy EC-7 and the Fen Basin Transport Strategy 2025 only where they bear directly on the assessed effects. The Council’s position is that mitigation must be traceable from the ES to the relevant DCO requirement, obligation or certified plan. If a commitment is relied upon to reduce a significant effect, the response should ask where that commitment is secured. The Council should avoid presenting preferences about the appearance of drawings as policy conflicts. Document references are to be checked before the appendix is sent with the agreed response.

6. Technical matters for the agreed response

The Council reviewed the transport, landscape and drainage points to be carried into the appendix. The traffic tables supplied by Fenwater Link Ltd give an opening-year weekday peak but do not show whether the same turning assumptions were used for the construction peak at the Bramble Fen Road/Alder Mere Lane junction. The agreed response should request the input flows and a short reconciliation table, rather than another general assurance that the junction has capacity. Construction vehicle routing must be shown on the certified plan and tied to a requirement covering diversions and temporary closures.

The landscape figures distinguish winter and summer views from Marshbell Wood, but the proposed earthwork is drawn at different heights in the sections and photomontages. This is a drawing consistency point, not a new objection to the alignment. The appendix should identify the relevant sheet numbers and ask which height has been assessed. References to East Curlew Local Plan Policy EC-7 should be confined to the resulting visual effect, if the corrected drawings change it.

On drainage, the attenuation basin is described as operational before the main hardstanding is laid, whereas the outline programme suggests the basin may be completed later. The response should ask for the construction-stage runoff arrangement, including where discharge rates are controlled and how exceedance flows are directed. The Merefen Drainage Board's proposed maintenance access should remain unobstructed on the final works plan.

The Council agreed that the Fen Basin Transport Strategy 2025 is relevant to cumulative traffic assumptions, not to the colour or presentation of the plans. No additional policy list is required. These points will be checked against the environmental statement and draft requirements before submission.

Present: Cllr Tamsin Grell (Chair), Cllr Oren Blay, Cllr Nia Fenwick, Cllr Rowan Pike and Cllr Selma Dray. Clerk: Mara Ellery. Public: Davin Foyle, Lessa Morwin and Idris Venn.
