BRINDLE LINK WATER TRANSFER SCHEME
Environmental Statement, Appendix 8.6: Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey
Document reference BLWTS-ES-8.6 | Revision 2 | 14 May 2026

1. Purpose and status

This appendix reports the 2025–26 walkover and vantage-point surveys undertaken for the Brindle Link Water Transfer Scheme. It should be read with Chapter 8, Biodiversity, and the Outline Ecological Management Plan (OEMP). The scheme comprises a buried transfer main, a small pumping station and temporary construction compounds between Wisp Fen and Merebank Reservoir. Brindle Water Partnership is the applicant. Survey drawings use the project’s ME local grid, rather than Ordnance Survey coordinates; the two systems must not be treated as interchangeable. Fine-scale records in section 4 are supplied for examination and construction planning. The public OEMP deliberately uses broader areas because the precise records should not be reproduced on site noticeboards or in general correspondence.

2. Methods and limitations

Fenreach Ecology completed otter checks on 18 November 2025, 9 February 2026 and 23 April 2026. Surveyors walked accessible banks of Brindle Cut and the two connecting drains, looking for spraints, prints, feeding remains, slides and potential resting places. The northern bank was not entered during February because it was flooded. Bird work comprised five early-morning visits, two evening visits and observations from the reservoir embankment; the visits were spread across the breeding season rather than treated as one continuous watch. Ms Leni Ward, MCIEEM, of Fenreach Ecology checked the restricted field sheets before this appendix was issued. The project team can be contacted through ecology@brindlewater.invalid; individual surveyor details are not required for construction queries.

The ME grid is useful for comparing records within the red-line boundary but gives a false impression of certainty if copied without its precision. Thus ME 48 73 describes a broad part of Wisp Fen, whereas ME 480 729 identifies a shorter reach where otter prints were recorded on exposed silt. Neither entry identifies a resting place. A footpath user might still find signs elsewhere after rain, and absence of signs on one visit is not evidence that a bank is unused. The working drawings distinguish confirmed features from places which merely looked suitable from the opposite bank.

3. Survey results: general records

Otter spraints were found at three bridge abutments and one culvert apron. Prints and a slide were also recorded along the lower Brindle Cut. The pattern is consistent with animals using the watercourse for movement and feeding; the survey does not establish the number of animals or a breeding territory. Reports of otters around Wisp Fen are useful background, but are too vague to locate a holt. A field note from a nearby landholder, Mrs Tamsin Rowe of 7 Sedge End Cottages, Mireford, MF4 8QP, described an animal crossing the towpath after dusk. That account has not been used to classify any particular bank feature. Cllr Ewan Thorne also raised concern about night working beside the cut at the community briefing; the proposed lighting controls address that concern irrespective of where the animal was seen.

Bird observations included hunting marsh harrier over the reed fringe, a passing peregrine, and breeding behaviour by a hobby pair in the eastern tree line. The record 'marsh harrier over Wisp Fen, ME 48 74' is a broad flight observation, not a nest position. Common reedbed birds were mapped separately on Drawing 8.6B. An old kestrel box on the reservoir maintenance shed, ME 4814 7309, was empty on both checks; its position is retained on the drawing so contractors do not mistake it for a new mitigation box. No inference about Schedule 1 nesting should be drawn from the flight records alone.

4. Restricted feature records

One occupied resting feature was confirmed from repeated sprainting, fresh prints and a camera check undertaken without entry into the bank. The occupied otter holt is beneath the east-bank rootplate at local grid ME 48327 73164, 11 m upstream of the red sluice. The rootplate was not lifted, and there was no attempt to establish whether young were present. A separate hollow beneath the footbridge was inspected from the path and remains a potential, not confirmed, resting place. The two features have different treatment in the method statement and should not be merged merely because both appear within the same broad grid square on the public plan.

The bird watch confirmed an active nest: the active hobby nest is in the third poplar north of the disused pump, local grid ME 47986 73612. Adults exchanged prey nearby on two visits, but observers did not approach the tree or seek a view into the nest. The location is included here to allow the ecologist to set the works exclusion area before clearance. It is not a suggested viewing point. Survey effort will be repeated before any works in the eastern tree line, since occupation in 2026 cannot be assumed for a later season. The applicant’s public project page, https://www.brindlelink.invalid/ecology, carries the general habitat plan but not these feature records.

5. Avoidance, mitigation and monitoring

No piling, bank excavation or tracked-plant access is proposed within the initial holt exclusion area. Its boundary will be pegged by the ecological clerk of works using the restricted drawing, with fencing placed from the landward side. If the construction method changes, work will stop pending a revised assessment and any licence or consent that is required. The contractor must not interpret an unfenced length of bank as available for storage. Night lighting will be directed away from Brindle Cut, with temporary screens where the haul route passes the reeds; the OEMP specifies inspection of the screens after high winds.

Tree works within the hobby consultation area will be programmed outside the nesting period where practicable. Before clearance, a suitably experienced ecologist will check the area and agree a hold point with the site manager. If nesting activity is observed, the relevant works will remain on hold until the ecologist advises that disturbance risk has passed. This is a precaution, not a promise that the pair will use the same tree again. The OEMP also requires a toolbox talk covering what operatives should do if they encounter fresh otter signs, and where to record sightings without circulating exact locations by group message.

Post-construction checks will take place in the first and third suitable survey seasons. Results will be compared with the baseline signs and habitat condition, not presented as a census of individual animals. The working record will be held by Fenreach Ecology, while a summary without pinpoint locations will be provided to the applicant and the local planning authority. A link circulated during consultation to https://fenwatch-records.invalid/notebook is an independent field notebook and is not part of the submitted evidence base.

Environmental Statement Appendix 8.6: Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey
Brindle Link Water Transfer Scheme

8.6.1 Purpose and handling of records

This appendix sets out the field evidence used in the assessment of effects on otter and Schedule 1 birds. It should be read with Chapter 8, Biodiversity, and the Outline Ecological Management Plan (OEMP). Brindle Water Partnership commissioned Fenreach Ecology to check the watercourse crossings, the temporary working areas and the adjacent trees. Survey sheets contain more precise information than the public figures. Those sheets are retained in the restricted ecological record and should not be added to a contractor's general drawing pack.

The survey corridor includes the Alder Mere Drain, two unnamed ditches and the southern edge of Gorsefold Wood. Figure 8.6a shows the corridor at a scale suitable for understanding the assessment; it does not show holts or nest trees. References such as SP 76 31 identify a broad survey square only. They are not instructions for finding a resting place. In the earlier consultation response, Cllr Ewan Thorne asked whether the absence of symbols on the public figure meant that no protected species had been found. It does not: locations have been generalised deliberately.

8.6.2 Method and limitations

Walkovers were undertaken on 14 February, 29 April and 18 June 2025, with banks viewed from both sides where access was agreed. Surveyors looked for footprints, spraint, feeding remains, slides and suitable cover. Bird checks used vantage points outside the working corridor, followed by a tree check before leaf-out. The June visit was carried out after heavy rain; the low ditch margins were under water and absence of tracks on that date has not been treated as absence of otter.

Access was not available to one garden beside the drain. Mrs Tamsin Rowe, whose home adjoins that reach and who is not taking part in the examination, reported seeing an otter cross the towpath at dusk. This is a useful supporting record, not verification of a holt. The precise resting-site conclusions below rely on field signs checked by Ms Leni Ward of Fenreach Ecology against the restricted field sheets. Her check found that an early draft photograph caption put one feature on the wrong bank; the caption has been corrected, not the original observation.

8.6.3 Otter evidence

Spraint was recorded at four bridge or culvert structures, including the Mill Lane culvert, and footprints occurred on exposed silt farther upstream. These signs indicate use of the watercourse for movement and feeding. They do not establish the number of animals or continuous occupation of any one reach. A possible couch beneath fallen willow branches was recorded within Gorsefold Wood; its position is deliberately described at woodland scale because the evidence did not justify calling it a holt.

One confirmed holt is recorded at SP 76249 31586, beneath the north-bank root plate immediately downstream of the old brick sill. Freshly worked material and repeated tracks were present on two visits. This location is supplied in this controlled appendix so that the crossing design and exclusion fencing can be checked; it must not appear on public-facing ecological plans. The construction working-width drawing shows the relevant reach as an exclusion zone rather than marking the entrance. No excavation, storage of spoil or lighting is proposed within that zone.

At the open-cut crossing farther east, the bankside route will be maintained until a temporary dry passage is in place. Trenches will be covered or provided with a means of escape at the end of each shift. Lighting will be directed away from the water and switched off when not required. If fresh signs appear during construction, work in the affected reach will pause for review under the OEMP. This is a precaution, not a claim that every print identifies a new resting site.

8.6.4 Schedule 1 birds

A hobby was seen hunting above Alder Mere on two visits. This broad observation is shown on Figure 8.6a and should not be read as a nest record. Subsequent watches established a breeding site at SP 76412 31904, in the upper fork of the dead pine beside the disused east-bank pump plinth. The tree will be retained. Works that could cause disturbance within the agreed stand-off area will be timed outside the breeding period, subject to a pre-start check by the ecological clerk of works. If the tree is unused in a later season, the stand-off will still require review rather than automatic removal.

Barn owl pellets were found in the western ditch barn, and a bird was observed entering it once. The evidence is consistent with use of the building, but the survey did not establish an active nest there. By contrast, an active barn owl nest was recorded in the loft space above the south door of the old sluice store, 18 metres north of survey peg BW-17. That location is withheld from the general site induction map. The store is outside the permanent land take, although vehicle movements on the nearby haul route could cause disturbance. The route will therefore be screened before works begin and checked during the breeding period.

8.6.5 Assessment and follow-up

With the exclusion measures, timing controls and supervised pre-start checks in place, the assessment predicts no significant residual effect on the local otter corridor or the recorded breeding sites. That conclusion depends on implementation, rather than on a fixed assumption that animals will stay in the same places. Records of new signs will be entered in the restricted ecological log; reports for the applicant and local planning authority will use broad reach descriptions. The OEMP provides the stop-work procedure if a previously unrecorded resting or nesting site is found.

Post-construction monitoring will repeat suitable walkovers in the first and third survey seasons. It will compare access through the crossings, bankside cover and evidence of use with the baseline. A lower count of footprints after rain, by itself, will not be reported as a population decline. The public summary may refer to Gorsefold Wood and SP 76 31, but it will not reproduce the pinpoint locations in this appendix.

Brindle Link Water Transfer Scheme
Environmental Statement, Appendix 8.6: Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey (restricted locations)
Revision 2, October 2026

8.6.1 Purpose and status

This appendix supports the ecological assessment for Brindle Water Partnership. Fenreach Ecology completed the walkovers and checked the restricted field sheets. It is supplied to the Examining Authority and relevant statutory consultees for examination purposes; the location details in Tables 8.6A and 8.6B are not intended for the public-facing summary. References to a record being ‘confirmed’ describe the evidence observed on the survey date, not a guarantee of continued occupation. The OEMP stop-work procedure described in the preceding section still applies if signs are found elsewhere.

8.6.2 Survey coverage and limitations

Surveyors walked accessible banks of the proposed transfer corridor and the adjoining drainage connections in April, June and September 2025. They searched for otter footprints, spraint, slides, feeding remains and resting places, and recorded birds by sight and call without approaching active nests. The September visit followed rain, which made prints easier to see but removed some older signs. High water prevented inspection of approximately 90 m of the south bank below Crossing C2. No absence conclusion is drawn for that length. Grid references were read from the field GPS and then checked against the annotated habitat plan; their apparent precision should not be taken as a measure of survey accuracy.

The broad location SP 76 31 is suitable for the public summary. The six-figure references retained in the working habitat plan describe survey compartments rather than resting or breeding places and are not reproduced here. By contrast, the ten-figure references and bank or tree descriptions below identify sensitive features and must stay with the restricted copy. Gorsefold Wood, shown on Figure 8.6-1, is a landscape reference, not a disclosed nest position.

8.6.3 Otter evidence — Table 8.6A

O1. A probable occupied holt was recorded at SP 76482 31593, beneath the east-bank alder root plate 14 m upstream of Crossing C2. Fresh spraint was present on two visits, with flattened vegetation at the entrance. An individual was not seen entering, so ‘probable’ is retained. The two metre exclusion shown on an early working sketch is wrong and must not be used for setting out; the OEMP requires the ecologist to determine an appropriate stand-off before any nearby activity.

O2. Prints and a slide were recorded beside the northern ditch within the same survey reach. This is a field-sign record, not evidence that a second holt exists. A possible resting cavity was seen from the opposite bank, but high water prevented confirmation; its mapped point is therefore omitted from this appendix pending re-survey. Badger paths were also present in Gorsefold Wood. Neither those paths nor the woodland name locates a sett.

O3. Mrs Tamsin Rowe, a nearby landholder who has not made a representation in the examination, reported seeing an otter crossing the access track after dusk. The account was entered as an unverified observation rather than used to move the mapped survey boundary. The original field note includes the witness’s home address, 17 Pikeglass Lane, New Brindle, NB4 8TU, solely so the survey team could clarify the date; it has no bearing on the ecological conclusion and should not appear on the public record.

8.6.4 Birds — Table 8.6B

B1. A confirmed marsh harrier nest was recorded at SP 76714 31702, in the fork of the lone ash 32 m south of the western gate of Plot B17. The location is a restricted breeding-site record, including where Plot B17 appears on the published land plans. Adults carried food on the June visit. No approach to the tree was made. The absence of a bird on the September walkover is consistent with the survey season and is not evidence of abandonment.

B2. A hobby was seen hunting above Gorsefold Wood on one occasion. The observation is given at woodland scale because no nest was found. A barn owl pellet was collected from an unused field shelter; this indicates use of the area but not a Schedule 1 breeding site. These records are included to explain why retained trees and dark corridors matter, not to imply that every tree supports a nest.

8.6.5 Avoidance and conservation plan

The alignment keeps the permanent works away from the confirmed resting and nesting features. At Crossing C2, the contractor must retain a continuous dry ledge, avoid lighting the watercourse and fence the agreed working area before vegetation clearance. Temporary pumps, fuel storage and overnight plant parking must remain outside the ecologist-approved stand-off. The precise fence line will be marked on a controlled construction drawing, not on the general arrangement plan. If water levels require a change in access, work must pause for review rather than simply shifting the fence closer to the bank.

For birds, vegetation clearance should take place outside the relevant breeding season wherever practicable. A pre-start check is still required: a calendar restriction does not establish that a tree is empty. If a protected nest is found, the ecologist will define the exclusion and advise on licensing requirements before work resumes. Replacement planting will connect the retained bankside cover, and the lighting design must avoid spill towards the ditch. These are commitments in the OEMP, not suggestions for a later contractor to decide whether to adopt.

8.6.6 Record handling and follow-up

Ms Leni Ward of Fenreach Ecology checked the restricted points against the field sheets on 12 October 2026. Queries should go through the shared project mailbox, ecology@brindlewater.example, rather than circulating the annotated sheets. Cllr Ewan Thorne asked at the community briefing whether monitoring would be published. The applicant will publish reach-level findings after the first and third post-construction survey seasons, including whether crossings remain passable and bankside cover has established. It will not publish a live map of holts or protected nests. That distinction also applies if the findings are appended to a response to an Examining Authority question.

8.6.7 Restricted species records

Fenreach Ecology’s October 2026 walkover recorded otter spraint and a slide in the Brindle Beck survey area (coarse grid square SK 48 63). These field signs indicate use of the watercourse, but do not by themselves establish a resting place. A probable holt was recorded at SK 48217 63406, under the east bank root plate of the twin alder immediately downstream of culvert C4. The restricted field sheet also plots an active peregrine nest at SK 48692 63741, on the north-facing ledge of the disused quarry wall. Neither point should appear on public drawings.

Mrs Tamsin Rowe reported seeing otters near the old footbridge; this observation has not been treated as a holt record. Cllr Ewan Thorne’s request for published monitoring can be met through reach-level reporting. The OEMP must require pre-works checks, a no-entry buffer around confirmed breeding sites, and review of crossing cover after construction. Exact points will remain in the controlled survey file.

text:
6. ECOLOGY AND NATURE CONSERVATION

6.1 Introduction

This chapter assesses the likely significant ecological effects of the proposed Brindlefen Solar and Storage Project (the Project). Brindlefen Energy Ltd proposes solar arrays, a battery compound, access tracks and associated drainage across approximately 112 hectares of predominantly arable land near Merefold. The assessment covers construction, operation and decommissioning. It should be read with the habitat plans and the confidential protected-species annex; the latter is not reproduced in the public Environmental Statement.

Prepared by: Dr Elin Voss, Senior Ecologist, Reedglass Ecology Ltd
Document reference: BF-ES-06, revision 2, 14 September 2026
Enquiries: ecology@reedglassecology.example

6.2 Baseline and survey approach

The survey area includes the application boundary and an appropriate buffer, extended where ecological connections warranted it. Desk records were obtained in January 2025. Walkovers took place between March and September 2025, with follow-up checks in May 2026 after the western access alignment changed. Surveyors recorded hedgerows, ditches, woodland edges, buildings and field margins. Access was unavailable to one off-site paddock; its boundary was viewed from the public footpath. This limitation does not prevent an assessment of likely significant effects, although a pre-construction check remains necessary.

The land is principally improved grassland beneath rotational crops, with species-poor hedges and occasional mature ash and oak. Merefold Drain connects the northern fields to Willowglass Wood. The drain, hedgerows and woodland edge provide a route for commuting wildlife. Records of badgers within the wider Merefold area and bats in Willowglass Wood are background context only: those descriptions do not identify an individual resting place. No statutory designated site lies within the Order limits.

6.3 Badger

Field signs comprised paths, hairs and spoil. Badger activity was recorded along the northern field boundaries, and setts have previously been reported in Willowglass Wood. These are broad descriptions, not a basis for directing works. During the May 2026 check, an active main sett was recorded in the low bank immediately behind the third oak east of the locked blue maintenance gate on the north side of Field F7. Two entrances were fresh, with bedding visible at one entrance. A subsidiary sett was found under the western end of the stone culvert carrying Track T4 across Merefold Drain. The positions are shown only on confidential drawing BF-ECO-17C; the public constraints plan shows a wider precautionary area instead.

Neither sett is within the array footprint. Track surfacing and cable installation could nevertheless cause disturbance if undertaken without controls. The construction environmental management plan (CEMP) will establish fenced exclusion areas, prohibit storage and night lighting nearby, and require a further survey before groundworks. Any activity for which a licence is necessary will not begin until the required licence has been obtained. The exact fence line will be set by the ecologist following that check rather than inferred from this chapter.

6.4 Bats

Climbed-tree inspections and emergence surveys identified occasional use of cavities and buildings by common pipistrelle and brown long-eared bat. Bats were recorded foraging along Merefold Drain and the western hedge. Activity was generally lower in the open central fields. A small, non-breeding day roost was confirmed in the loose fascia board on the east side of the old pump shed beside Access A2. The shed is retained and is outside the working width.

A soprano pipistrelle maternity roost was confirmed within the split lintel above the middle, south-facing loading door of the brick cart house at the eastern end of Track T4. Counts and behaviour indicate breeding use, so this feature has been treated as a high-sensitivity constraint. A large barbastelle roost, assessed as likely to support a breeding group, was also recorded inside the lightning-split oak 11 metres north of the point where the western hedge meets Merefold Drain. Detailed locations and survey photographs are restricted to the confidential annex and will be supplied to those carrying out authorised works on a need-to-know basis.

The cart house and oak will be retained. A no-dig working method is proposed where the cable route approaches the cart house, and the route has been moved away from the oak. Temporary construction lighting will face inward, use hoods and be switched off when not needed. Operational lighting is limited to movement-activated units at the battery compound. The retained hedges will remain dark so that the commuting corridor continues to function. Replacement bat boxes are supplementary mitigation, not a justification for removing either breeding feature.

6.5 Birds and other fauna

Breeding bird surveys recorded skylark in arable fields, linnet in hedges and a barn owl hunting over the rough margins. The barn owl nest was located on the upper shelf immediately inside the northern ventilation opening of the disused grain tower beside the eastern turning head of Track T4. The tower is outside the Order limits, but deliveries could pass close to it. The access schedule therefore avoids intensive movements in the adjacent section during the sensitive breeding period, subject to a check by the ecological clerk of works. Other nests may occur in hedgerows and will be dealt with through standard pre-clearance checks. Otter footprints on a muddy reach of Merefold Drain were not evidence of a holt; no holt was identified within the survey area.

6.6 Effects and monitoring

Without mitigation, construction could disturb resting and breeding sites and sever commuting routes. With the route changes, retained features and CEMP controls described above, residual effects are assessed as not significant at the local scale. This conclusion assumes that fencing, lighting controls and seasonal checks are implemented in full. The ecological clerk of works will record compliance weekly during clearance and at each relevant cable crossing. Habitat establishment will be checked in years 1, 3 and 5, with failed hedge planting replaced in the next suitable season. The precise protected-site records will remain in the controlled annex rather than be copied into routine progress reports.

6.7 Cumulative and in-combination effects

The cumulative review considers the Brindlefen Solar and Storage Project alongside other reasonably foreseeable development in the wider area, including the permitted Rillbank Lane Substation Extension and the proposed East Mere Agricultural Reservoir. The review uses the current construction programmes supplied for those schemes. Their programmes may change, so this assessment focuses on whether overlapping activity could affect the same habitats or movement corridors, rather than assuming particular start dates.

The three schemes would together increase temporary construction traffic on Rillbank Lane. This has limited direct ecological significance because vehicles would use the existing carriageway and designated site accesses. A more relevant pathway is the possibility of simultaneous clearance of boundary vegetation. The substation extension would affect a short length of managed grass verge; the reservoir proposal would retain its principal hedgerows. Neither scheme is expected to remove vegetation forming a continuous link with the hedgerows retained by the Project. Cumulative fragmentation is therefore not predicted. This conclusion depends on each scheme implementing its stated boundary protection measures.

Lighting has also been considered cumulatively. The reservoir proposal does not include permanent external lighting, while the substation extension would use task lighting only when maintenance is required. The Project's operational lighting would normally remain off and would be directed away from retained vegetation when activated. On that basis, there would be no continuous illuminated corridor across the three sites. If construction periods overlap, the contractors should coordinate temporary lighting so that adjacent work fronts do not illuminate the same boundary at once.

6.8 Habitat delivery and management

The landscape proposals provide native hedgerow reinforcement, species-rich grassland beneath and between panels, and a shallow wetland margin adjoining Broomwick Drain. These measures are intended to replace lower-value arable habitat with a more varied structure; they are not relied upon as immediate substitutes for any protected resting or breeding place. The design retains the existing watercourse banks and provides a maintenance strip so that routine access does not require repeated cutting of new planting.

Grassland establishment will use a locally appropriate seed mix suited to the site's soil conditions. The first two growing seasons will require more frequent cuts to control competitive plants, with arisings removed where practicable. Thereafter, most areas will be managed by a late-season cut or light grazing, subject to ground conditions and electrical safety requirements. Small patches of taller vegetation will be retained on rotation to maintain cover through winter. Management beneath panels may differ where shade and restricted machinery access limit growth; these areas will be monitored rather than assigned an unrealistic uniform target.

Hedgerow gaps will be planted with mixed native stock and protected from grazing until established. Replacement planting will be required where failures compromise continuity, not merely where a numerical survival threshold is missed. The wetland margin will be allowed to develop without routine dredging. Removal of accumulated sediment would take place only where needed to maintain drainage function and would follow an ecological check. No new channel connection is proposed.

6.9 Biodiversity metric and policy context

The biodiversity calculation is reported separately in the Habitat Management Schedule, using the habitat areas and condition assumptions shown on the submitted plans. Its forecast is a modelled outcome, not a finding that new habitats already exist. In particular, the projected condition of species-rich grassland depends on suitable establishment, control of nutrient enrichment and continued management throughout operation. The schedule therefore identifies measurable indicators, including sward composition, the extent of bare ground and the continuity of planted hedges.

The proposals have been reviewed against Mirewick Local Plan Policy NE4, which seeks to avoid unnecessary habitat loss and secure long-term management of retained and created features. The layout has been adjusted to keep development out of the principal hedgerow corridors and away from the banks of Broomwick Drain. Where temporary working space is required, reinstatement is specified in the construction drawings. The assessment does not treat a future gain recorded in the metric as permission to damage a retained feature during construction.

6.10 Uncertainty and adaptive response

Reedglass Ecology Ltd prepared the habitat interpretation from field records, aerial mapping and the engineering layout available at the time of assessment. Conditions can change between survey and construction, particularly in arable margins and unmanaged vegetation. Pre-commencement checks will confirm whether the assumptions used for clearance remain valid. If a protected species or a previously unrecorded feature is found, work in the affected area will stop while the ecological clerk of works agrees an appropriate response. This is a contingency measure, not a substitute for the route and timing controls already included in the design.

The monitoring programme will compare delivered habitats with the management objectives, rather than relying only on whether planting survives. A review after each scheduled monitoring visit will identify corrective actions and the person responsible for instructing them. Possible responses include changes to cutting frequency, replacement of unsuccessful planting and localised control of invasive vegetation. Any material change to the approved habitat areas or management objectives will be recorded with a revised plan so that the basis of the biodiversity calculation remains clear.

6.11 Summary of residual effects

Subject to implementation of the measures in this chapter and the Construction Environmental Management Plan, no significant adverse residual ecological effect is predicted at the local scale. Retention of established linear features provides the main avoidance measure. Proposed grassland, hedgerow and wetland habitats offer a potential longer-term improvement, but that outcome remains dependent on establishment and management. Brindlefen Energy Ltd will retain responsibility for securing the monitoring and remedial works described above throughout the relevant management period.

6.12 Delivery, verification and adaptive management

6.12.1 This section should be read with the Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP), the Landscape and Ecology Management Plan (LEMP) and the Biodiversity Net Gain Assessment. It explains how the ecological measures described above will be checked during construction and carried into operation. The assessment assumes that retained habitats remain outside the permanent works footprint, except at the crossing points shown on the application plans. A change to a crossing, compound boundary or drainage outfall would require an ecological review before that change is made on site. The review is not a substitute for any approval required under the development consent order.

6.12.2 Brindlefen Energy Ltd will require its principal contractor to mark the construction limits before vegetation clearance starts. Protective fencing will be installed around retained hedgerows, ditches and woodland edges where plant movements could otherwise cause damage. The fencing must be visible to delivery drivers and must not be moved to create temporary storage space. Materials, fuel and excavated soil will be kept within designated working areas. The contractor will inspect the fencing at the start of each main work stage and following any incident that could have displaced it. Records of defects and corrective action will be retained with the site environmental records.

6.12.3 The construction programme will seek to avoid removal of suitable nesting vegetation during the main bird breeding period. Where that cannot reasonably be achieved, the relevant area will be checked before works proceed and an appropriate exclusion area will be maintained if an active nest is found. The exact location of any such nest should be recorded in the contractor's restricted ecological records rather than circulated with general progress reports. This is a precautionary procedure: the surveys for the environmental statement do not establish that every hedge or field margin will hold a nest during construction.

6.12.4 Temporary lighting is expected to be limited to welfare and security needs. Lamps will face into the working area, use shields where practicable and be switched off when not required for safe working. The purpose is to preserve relatively dark routes along retained boundary vegetation. General bat activity was recorded along hedgerows in the survey area, but the assessment does not depend on a claim that a particular hedge contains a maternity roost. If the detailed security design introduces lighting beyond that assessed, the lighting layout and predicted spill will be reviewed against the ecological assumptions before installation.

6.12.5 Soil handling is relevant to the establishment of proposed grassland beneath and between the solar arrays. Topsoil should not be mixed with subsoil or spread while waterlogged. The LEMP will specify seed mixtures suited to the recorded soil conditions and will allow for local adjustment where ground conditions differ from those assumed at design stage. Establishment will be assessed by vegetation structure, cover and the presence of undesirable species, rather than by whether every sown species appears in the first growing season. Failed areas will be re-prepared and sown or planted as necessary. Cutting material will be removed where needed to prevent the gradual enrichment of the intended species-rich areas.

6.12.6 The proposed wetland margins beside the new drainage features are dependent on appropriate water levels and on the avoidance of prolonged construction runoff. Temporary drainage controls will therefore be in place before bulk earthworks in the relevant catchment. Sediment trapped by those controls will be removed without depositing it on retained vegetation. During operation, routine inspection will identify erosion, excessive silt accumulation and blocked connections. Remedial work will use methods proportionate to the issue and, where practicable, will avoid the period when vegetation is establishing or wildlife is most likely to be using the margin.

6.12.7 Monitoring under the LEMP will comprise an initial establishment check and subsequent condition checks during the management period. These visits will compare the delivered habitats with the approved habitat plan and the assumptions in the Biodiversity Net Gain Assessment. They will also identify practical issues, such as grazing pressure, failed hedgerow plants, invasive species or damage at access gates. A monitoring report should distinguish between a temporary shortfall that can be corrected through routine management and a change likely to prevent the stated habitat objective being met. The latter will require a documented remedial proposal and a further check of its outcome.

6.12.8 The cumulative assessment considered the permitted Rillbank Lane Substation Extension and the proposed East Mere Agricultural Reservoir. Each could generate short periods of construction activity in the wider area, although their programmes and final working methods are not fixed for the purposes of this chapter. The potential combined effects are therefore assessed conservatively by considering overlapping vegetation disturbance, traffic on local routes and lighting. They do not alter the conclusion for the Brindlefen Solar and Storage Project, provided the avoidance and management measures remain in place. This conclusion should be revisited if a materially different adjoining scheme is approved before construction begins.

6.12.9 Reedglass Ecology Ltd has based this chapter on the survey information, design drawings and scheme commitments available at the assessment date. Survey findings are a description of conditions observed, not a guarantee that mobile species will be absent later. Pre-construction checks, the change-control procedure and the LEMP provide the means of dealing with that uncertainty without assuming that all works must stop whenever wildlife is encountered. Where a check identifies a constraint not addressed by the agreed method, work in the affected area will pause while an appropriate method is established. Unaffected work may continue, subject to the site controls already described.

6.12.10 With these controls secured, the predicted residual effects remain as stated in section 6.11. The proposed habitat gains should be reported as delivered only when the relevant habitats have been established and are being managed to the approved objectives; proposed planting on a drawing is not, by itself, an ecological outcome.

6.13 Monitoring and adaptive management

6.13.1 The Landscape and Ecology Management Plan (LEMP) will set out the sequence for creating, establishing and maintaining the retained and new habitats. Its purpose is to turn the measures assessed in this chapter into tasks that can be inspected. Brindlefen Energy Ltd will retain responsibility for delivery throughout construction and operation, whether the work is carried out by its own contractor or a land-management contractor. Reedglass Ecology Ltd will review the ecological monitoring results against the objectives in the LEMP and advise where a change to management is required.

6.13.2 Before construction begins, the contractor will mark the retained hedgerows, ditch margins and habitat buffers on the ground. Temporary fencing will be checked after material deliveries and following any alteration to the working area. A drawing showing a buffer is not a substitute for keeping plant, spoil and fuel storage out of that buffer. The construction environmental management plan will therefore identify the permitted access points and the person responsible for authorising any temporary access needed for maintenance or an emergency repair.

6.13.3 Habitat creation will be recorded by parcel rather than reported as a single site-wide area. The record will include the date of seeding or planting, the seed mix or planting stock used, ground preparation, and any departure from the approved specification. Photographs from fixed points will help distinguish a failed establishment area from an area that has simply developed more slowly. The first review will take place after the initial growing season, with further reviews at the intervals in the LEMP. Where weather prevents a meaningful assessment, the reason and the revised survey date will be recorded.

6.13.4 The success criteria will relate to habitat condition as well as extent. For grassland, these include the establishment of the specified mix, control of injurious weeds and a management regime that allows flowering and seed set. For hedgerows, gaps, survival and the development of a varied structure will be checked. Replacement planting alone will not be treated as evidence that the intended condition has been reached. If a parcel is not progressing towards its target, the response may include revised cutting, reduced grazing pressure, reseeding or replacement planting, according to the cause identified.

6.13.5 Monitoring will also check that operational activities do not erode the retained habitat. In particular, vegetation clearance around security equipment must not widen into the hedgerow buffers by default. Any change to lighting will be assessed for spill onto boundary habitats before installation. Routine panel washing is not expected to require discharge to the ditches; if the maintenance method changes, the drainage and pollution controls will be reviewed through the change-control procedure described in section 6.12.

6.14 Cumulative effects

6.14.1 The cumulative assessment considers the Brindlefen Solar and Storage Project together with other developments for which sufficient information is available. The Rillbank Lane Substation Extension is permitted and could overlap with the early construction period. The East Mere Agricultural Reservoir remains a proposal; its construction programme and detailed habitat measures are not fixed. These differences in certainty have been reflected in the assessment rather than assigning the same programme to all three schemes.

6.14.2 The most likely shared pathway is temporary disturbance to species using the connected field-boundary network. Survey work recorded bat activity along boundary hedges, but does not indicate that the whole agricultural area functions as a single, uniformly used flight corridor. The construction assumptions for each scheme have therefore been considered alongside the position of retained hedges, proposed working hours and any breaks in connectivity. The assessment does not rely on an assumption that mobile species will be absent later in the programme.

6.14.3 Construction of the substation extension could coincide with deliveries and cable works for the project. If that occurs, the principal combined pressure would be activity near the Rillbank Lane boundary, rather than a permanent loss of the same habitat. The retained boundary vegetation and controlled working areas reduce that pressure. The two construction managers will exchange relevant programme information before works begin so that avoidable simultaneous clearance of adjacent sections does not occur. This is a coordination measure, not a claim that one scheme can control the consented programme of the other.

6.14.4 The reservoir proposal may alter land management beyond the project boundary. Its available plans show retained field boundaries, but they do not provide a final establishment schedule. A precautionary assumption has therefore been made that its proposed habitat gains are unavailable when assessing combined construction effects. On that basis, the temporary effects identified for the project remain localised and do not combine to produce a significant effect at the wider landscape scale. This conclusion will be revisited if a material change to either scheme introduces a new shared impact pathway.

6.14.5 The assessment of water-related effects also considers whether construction runoff from separate sites could reach the same ditch system. The project drainage design separates clean runoff from areas used for fuel and concrete, provides temporary silt controls during earthworks, and requires inspection after heavy rain. It is not appropriate to count those controls as habitat enhancement. They are measures to prevent deterioration while the works take place. No cumulative improvement in water quality has been assumed.

6.15 Conclusions

6.15.1 The assessment distinguishes between effects during construction, when disturbance and accidental damage are the main risks, and effects during operation, when habitat management determines whether the proposed gains are achieved. General records of badger activity in the wider survey area and bat activity along boundary hedges inform the precautionary working methods; they do not, on their own, establish a significant residual effect. Pre-construction checks will address the possibility that conditions change between survey and works.

6.15.2 Subject to the embedded design measures, construction controls and LEMP being implemented, no significant adverse residual ecological effects are predicted. That finding does not remove the need to document departures from the approved methods or to correct failed habitat establishment. The monitoring records will provide the evidence for those decisions and for reporting progress against the approved objectives.

6.16 Monitoring and adaptive management

6.16.1 The Landscape and Ecological Management Plan (LEMP) will translate the commitments in this chapter into a schedule of works, measurable establishment criteria and inspection requirements. Brindlefen Energy Ltd will retain responsibility for delivery throughout construction and operation. Reedglass Ecology Ltd will review monitoring results and advise whether remedial action is needed. The LEMP will distinguish between routine maintenance, such as replacing failed hedge plants, and changes to the approved management approach, which will require agreement through the relevant approval mechanism.

6.16.2 A baseline condition record will be completed before vegetation clearance or soil stripping begins. It will include photographs from fixed points, habitat condition sheets and a record of existing hedge gaps. Subsequent inspections will be carried out after the first growing season and at intervals specified in the LEMP. A dry summer, for example, would not by itself demonstrate that a proposed grassland mix has failed; the inspection will consider cover, species composition and whether bare ground is persisting beyond the establishment period. Where a target is not being met, the record will identify the likely cause, the corrective work and the date for checking its effectiveness.

6.16.3 Monitoring is intended to test the performance of the measures rather than repeat the full baseline survey every year. The principal indicators will be hedge establishment, the condition of retained boundary vegetation, the development of species-rich grassland and the suitability of drainage features for the intended habitat mosaic. Records of common bat activity along field boundaries may help interpret changes in habitat use, but should not be treated as a substitute for habitat-condition evidence. General reports of badgers in the wider landscape will be considered during pre-construction checks and, where necessary, in the review of working methods.

6.17 Construction-stage controls

6.17.1 The Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP) will set out the sequence of ecological protection measures before works commence in each area. Protective fencing will define retained vegetation and watercourse buffers, with access points shown on the construction drawings. The fencing will remain in place until the relevant heavy works have finished. Materials storage, vehicle turning and temporary lighting will be excluded from those buffers unless a specific method has been approved. These requirements apply equally to short-duration activities, including cable installation and reinstatement.

6.17.2 Vegetation removal will be programmed to avoid the main nesting-bird season where practicable. If removal is needed during that period, a check immediately beforehand will establish whether works can proceed without disturbing active nests. The check does not replace the requirement to avoid harm if an active nest is found. Night working is not proposed as the normal construction arrangement. Any temporary lighting required for safety will be directed away from hedges and drainage corridors, limited to the task area and switched off when not in use.

6.17.3 Drainage controls will be installed ahead of earthworks that could generate sediment-laden runoff. The design includes settlement measures at construction outfalls and staged reinstatement of disturbed ground. Inspections following heavy rainfall will identify blocked grips, erosion or sediment movement. The presence of an inspection record alone is not evidence that the control is effective: defects must be corrected before the affected activity continues where there is a credible pathway to receiving habitat.

6.18 Cumulative effects

6.18.1 The cumulative review considers the Rillbank Lane Substation Extension and the East Mere Agricultural Reservoir alongside the Brindlefen Solar and Storage Project. These schemes have different delivery programmes and their construction footprints do not overlap. There remains a potential for concurrent vehicle movements, noise and temporary disturbance within the broader agricultural landscape. The assessment has therefore considered whether shared habitat corridors could be affected at the same time, rather than assuming that separation of the development boundaries rules out a combined effect.

6.18.2 The Rillbank Lane Substation Extension involves a compact operational site and associated works near an existing electrical corridor. The East Mere Agricultural Reservoir includes land-forming and an operational water feature. On the information available for this assessment, neither would remove the retained boundary network relied upon by this project. There is uncertainty about their precise construction periods; the conclusion consequently assumes a reasonable worst-case overlap of earthworks. With the proposed buffers, lighting controls and sediment measures in place, a significant adverse cumulative effect on habitats or ecological connectivity is not predicted.

6.18.3 That conclusion should be revisited if an approved scheme changes materially, particularly where a revised layout affects the same boundary vegetation or drainage connection. A change in programme alone would not necessarily alter the conclusion. What matters is whether the combined works introduce a new pathway, extend the duration of disturbance to a meaningful degree, or prevent the agreed mitigation from functioning.

6.19 Conclusions and commitments

6.19.1 The assessment has applied the mitigation hierarchy. The layout retains the principal hedges and drainage corridors; construction methods address short-term risks; and the LEMP provides for habitat creation, establishment and longer-term management. Residual effects have been assessed on the basis that these measures are secured and implemented, not merely shown on an illustrative landscape drawing.

6.19.2 Table 6-24 of this chapter draws together the measures requiring delivery, their timing and the document in which each is specified. It should be read with the CEMP, the LEMP and the final drainage details. If those documents use different terminology for the same habitat area, the approved drawings and measurable LEMP criteria will govern implementation. The final plans will also show temporary working areas, so that reinstatement obligations are not overlooked after construction.

6.19.3 No significant adverse residual ecological effect is predicted for the Brindlefen Solar and Storage Project, either alone or cumulatively with the schemes assessed above. The predicted habitat improvements depend on successful establishment and subsequent management. Monitoring and corrective action are therefore integral to the conclusion, rather than optional enhancements to be decided after consent.

6.20 Protected species

6.20.1 Reedglass Ecology Ltd completed walked transects and dusk surveys between April and September 2025. Badger signs occurred across the western fields. One active sett was recorded in the bank 12 m east of gate G4 at the northern end of Field 7. Badger setts were also noted more generally in Alderwash Wood; no further sett position is given here.

6.20.2 Common pipistrelles used the western wall of Old Mere Barn. A bat maternity roost was confirmed in the roof void of Millhook Farm’s east byre, directly above the blue loading door. A barn owl nest was recorded inside the north-west ventilation opening of Pump House P3. These locations are supplied to inform the protective working zones, not as an invitation to visit them.

6.20.3 Brindlefen Energy Ltd will mark exclusion areas before works, retain dark corridors and install replacement roost features. Reedglass Ecology Ltd will review the monitoring results under the LEMP and recommend corrective measures where required.
