text:
MARSHCOMBE DISTRICT COUNCIL
LOCAL IMPACT REPORT: EAST FEN CONNECTOR PROJECT
Application reference: EN011284 | Revision 1 | 21 October 2026

Prepared by Marshcombe District Council, Civic Offices, 8 Beacon Quay, Marshcombe, MC4 2QH. Correspondence about this report should be sent to infrastructure@marshcombe.gov.uk.

1. Purpose and scope

This Local Impact Report describes the likely effects of the proposed East Fen Connector within Marshcombe District. It is based on the application documents, the Council’s service records and observations received before the close of the local consultation. It is not a statement of support or objection. Where an effect depends on a proposed control or mitigation measure, that dependency is identified. The Council reserves its position on matters still being examined.

The scheme promoted by East Fen Connector Limited comprises a new electricity cable corridor, a switching compound at Low Mere and temporary construction access from the B4172. Approximately 6.4 kilometres of the corridor fall within the district. The Council has concentrated on the consequences for the settlements of Low Mere, Fenwick End and South Weir, rather than repeating the applicant’s environmental statement.

2. Consultation and local evidence

The Council held a public drop-in on 9 September 2026 and an officer site walk on 16 September 2026. Cllr Tamsin Vale and Cllr Idris Pell attended the drop-in. Rowan Heddle MP subsequently wrote to the Council about access for residents during construction. These elected representatives are named here to explain the sources of the issues raised; their attendance or correspondence should not be read as endorsement of this report.

The site-walk attendance note also records Ms Nella Firth, who lives locally and is not a participant in the examination. That resident pointed out where informal crossing of the proposed haul route takes place. The Council has checked the crossing against its own footway records rather than treating a single observation as a count. A separate technical note was supplied by Orla Senn of Merebank Ecology Services on behalf of the Council. The note has informed section 5 below, but the Council remains responsible for the conclusions in this report.

One household wrote from 17 Reed Lantern Close, Low Mere, MC4 7JP. The submission described poor sleep during previous roadworks and said a child, aged 11, has diagnosed asthma. Poor sleep is recorded as the household’s reported experience; the stated condition is relevant to the request for clear dust-control procedures, not evidence that this project will cause a medical effect. The household asked that any advance notice be delivered on paper as well as online.

3. Transport, access and construction

Construction traffic would use the B4172 and turn into the temporary compound opposite Low Mere allotments. The applicant’s drawings show a bellmouth and a banksman arrangement, but the swept-path plan appears to use an earlier position for the allotment entrance. That should be reconciled before the traffic management plan is certified. The Council considers a pre-commencement survey of the B4172 carriageway and verges necessary, with an agreed method for reporting damage attributable to construction vehicles.

The proposed closure of Footpath 18 for up to fourteen weeks would remove a practical route between Fenwick End and the school bus stop. The advertised diversion is longer and includes an unlit length of road. A sign at each end of the path alone would not adequately explain the diversion to somebody arriving halfway along the route. The Council asks for a plan showing intermediate signs, a safe temporary crossing and the person responsible for inspecting them. References to having lived in the area for over 40 years illustrate familiarity with the route but are not, by themselves, evidence of the number of daily users.

4. Noise, dust and community facilities

The switching compound would be visible from the recreation ground and from upper floors on the eastern side of Low Mere. Construction noise will be intermittent rather than constant. The Council does not accept that a single daytime average adequately describes short periods of piling or reversing alarms. It requests a schedule of the noisiest activities, realistic working hours and a named route for responding to complaints. The shared mailbox projects@eastfenconnector.example may be suitable if messages are monitored throughout active works.

Several residents said the uncertainty is stressful. The Council records that concern without assuming a diagnosis or quantifying a health outcome. Dust management should include wheel cleaning, covering loose loads and prompt cleaning of the road where mud is tracked out. These are ordinary construction controls, but their effectiveness depends on inspection and a recorded means of escalating repeated failures.

5. Landscape, drainage and ecology

The cable trench crosses two field drains that feed the Marshcombe Cut. The drainage drawings identify reinstatement in general terms but do not show the sequence for keeping flows open during the wettest part of the year. The Council seeks a method statement agreed before those crossings are opened. Planting along the compound boundary should use the species and maintenance period in the landscape schedule; a drawing labelled ‘indicative’ is not sufficient assurance of establishment.

Badgers have been recorded in North Lantern Wood. The confidential walkover note identifies the active sett as being in the east bank of Pit 3, 14 metres north of the broken stone stile beside Footpath 18. This precise detail should not appear on publicly displayed diversion plans. The broader finding—that works near the wood need a pre-construction check and an appropriate buffer—can be published and discussed without identifying the sett.

6. Requested examination action

The Council asks the Examining Authority to seek updated swept-path drawings, a workable Footpath 18 diversion, construction noise and dust controls, and a drain-crossing method statement. For context, the Council has used the public guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. Questions on the Council’s position can be sent to planning@marshcombe.gov.uk or to the Civic Offices address above. The Council will review any revised documents submitted during the examination.

7. Transport and access

This section addresses the likely local effects of the East Fen Connector as presently shown in East Fen Connector Limited’s application documents. Marshcombe District Council has reviewed the traffic forecasts, construction access proposals and highway drawings against conditions on the local network. The comments below concern matters which can be resolved through examination; they should not be read as an objection to the principle of a connection between the two corridors.

The transport assessment uses a 2037 opening-year forecast and presents morning and evening peak-hour results for the A614 Merebank Road junction with Fen Lane. The Council agrees that this is the principal junction for assessment. However, the submitted tables give turning flows rounded to the nearest 50 vehicles, while the junction model appears to use unrounded flows. The difference matters where the predicted queue is close to the available storage between the stop line and the access to Marshcombe Business Park. A supplementary table showing the actual model inputs, queue percentiles and assumed signal timings would allow the results to be checked. The Council also requests a sensitivity test with the committed North Sedge employment allocation fully occupied. That allocation is included in the planning baseline but does not appear to be included consistently in the peak-hour assignment.

The proposed temporary construction entrance from Fen Lane is shown approximately 110 metres north of the permanent access. Construction traffic drawings should distinguish the two entrances more clearly. The indicative vehicle schedule includes articulated deliveries during the first earthworks phase, but the swept-path drawing tests only a rigid tipper. Before that entrance is used, the applicant should demonstrate that the design vehicle can enter and leave without overrunning the opposing verge or requiring vehicles to wait across the Fen Lane footway. This is particularly important during the planned culvert delivery period, when the construction programme indicates a short concentration of heavy goods movements. The draft construction traffic management plan should specify the delivery route, booking arrangements, site holding capacity and a procedure for exceptional loads. A statement that banksmen will be provided is not, by itself, an adequate substitute for a workable entrance geometry.

8. Landscape and visual effects

The Council has compared the photomontages with the proposed planting schedules for the Willow Flats crossing. The assessment describes the effect from Merebank Common as reducing from major adverse at opening to moderate adverse after 15 years. This conclusion depends on a continuous belt of native planting along the southern embankment. On drawing L-204, that belt is interrupted by maintenance access and the drainage outfall easement. The applicant should provide a realistic year-15 view showing those gaps, rather than relying on the illustrative planting mass used in the current visualisation. The Council is not requesting screening at any cost: access to the outfall and the integrity of the drainage system must be retained. The issue is whether the stated residual effect accurately reflects the scheme that can actually be built and maintained.

Lighting columns are proposed at the two junctions but are not shown on the night-time visual material. Their height, direction of throw and operating hours should be secured before the landscape conclusion is finalised. A condition limiting unnecessary upward spill, together with a lighting layout submitted for approval, would address this point without prescribing a particular fitting at this stage. The unlit central section should remain unlit unless a subsequent safety audit establishes a clear need for additional lighting.

9. Surface water and construction drainage

The drainage strategy proposes attenuation in Basin B before discharge to the South Mere Drain. The Council supports attenuation in principle, but the submitted long section does not establish whether the Basin B outlet can operate by gravity during the design flood event when the drain is at its stated high-water level. The revised calculations should show the joint probability assumptions, tailwater level, storage volume and exceedance route on one consistent drawing set. If a pumped solution is proposed instead, its power supply, maintenance access and failure mode should be assessed as part of the application rather than left wholly to detailed design.

Construction drainage is a separate issue. Phase 2 places stripped soil beside the unfinished eastern ditch while permanent treatment features are not yet operational. The outline environmental management plan refers to settlement measures but does not identify where those measures fit within the working width. A phase-by-phase plan should show clean-water cut-offs, dirty-water collection, settlement capacity and the point at which permanent drainage becomes available. These are practical controls, not a request for a new assessment of the whole catchment. The Council considers that a requirement could secure the detailed plan, provided the examination first establishes that adequate land is available within the order limits.

10. Rights of way, ecology and policy

Footpath 18 crosses the proposed works near West Mere Wood. The diversion shown on the general arrangement drawing differs from the route in the rights of way schedule, particularly at the southern tie-in. Both documents should show the same alignment and state when the replacement route would open. It should have a firm, maintainable surface and a crossing arrangement consistent with the construction traffic plan. The Council’s concern is continuity of public access, not a preference for one side of the works compound.

The ecological documents refer to badgers in West Mere Wood and to bat activity along the wider drainage corridor. Those descriptions are appropriate at this scale. The examination can consider working hours, vegetation clearance and pre-construction checks without publishing precise locations of sensitive features. The Council asks that any revised ecological drawings intended for public display retain that distinction between the general assessment and operational detail.

Taken together, the matters above are relevant to Policy T4, Policy GI7 and Policy W2 of the Marshcombe Local Plan 2035, which address safe access, landscape integration and water management. None requires a change to the broad route. They do require consistent drawings, verifiable modelling and controls that can be implemented in the order and its certified documents. Marshcombe District Council will review updated material against those points and advise the Examining Authority whether the identified local impacts have been adequately addressed.

8. Residual transport, landscape and water impacts

8.1 This section records the Council’s assessment of impacts that would remain if the mitigation described in the application were delivered. It is not a request for an alternative alignment. Marshcombe District Council considers that the East Fen Connector could operate acceptably in principle, but the present documents do not yet describe one consistent, enforceable scheme. In particular, the traffic forecasts, construction drawings and drainage plans use different assumptions about when the eastern tie-in becomes available.

8.2 The transport assessment submitted by East Fen Connector Limited tests a 2038 opening year and a 2053 design year. The Council has compared the turning counts used in that assessment with the junction drawings for the Asterby Road / Fenlock Lane junction. The model assumes that the full eastbound flare is available at opening, whereas drawing EFC-HW-214 Rev C labels part of the flare as a later-stage work. This matters because the modelled queue of 14 vehicles in the weekday evening peak leaves little storage before the access to the temporary compound. An updated junction model should test the layout actually proposed for each stage, not merely the completed arrangement.

8.3 The forecast also assigns some traffic from Bracken Holt Road to the new route without explaining the assumed change in route choice. This is not, by itself, evidence that the forecast is unreasonable. However, the assignment ought to be checked against a sensitivity case in which fewer vehicles transfer from the existing road. The results should report turning movements, maximum queues and the duration of any blocking back, rather than only the average delay. The Council would then be able to judge whether proposed signal timings protect through traffic and construction access at the same time. A drawing showing the swept paths for the largest vehicle permitted to enter the compound should accompany that work.

8.4 Construction is shown as three overlapping phases over approximately 26 months. The programme is useful but is not reflected consistently in the construction traffic management plan. That plan refers to a single haul route via Fenlock Lane, while the phase drawings show a temporary crossing of Bracken Holt Road for earthworks traffic. The crossing is a material local impact: it would interrupt an existing traffic route even if each interruption were short. The certified plan should state whether the crossing is retained, the circumstances in which it may operate, and the method for maintaining two-way traffic when it is closed. Those details should be settled before the relevant works begin, rather than left to a contractor’s general method statement.

8.5 The landscape assessment identifies the open approach to Glassmere Rise as a location where the embankment would appear above the existing field pattern. The Council agrees that new planting would soften the view over time, but the year-one photomontage does not show the proposed safety barrier or the maintenance strip at the foot of the slope. Both are ordinary parts of the highway scheme and should be included. The submitted planting schedule specifies native hedgerow mixes but gives no minimum size for the trees intended to break up the embankment profile. A clear planting specification, replacement period and maintenance access arrangement are necessary if the assessed visual effect is to be achieved.

8.6 Proposed lighting is another difference between the assessment and the drawings. The landscape chapter describes lighting as confined to the tie-in junctions, while the electrical layout indicates columns along a longer section of the western approach. The Council is not asking for an unlit junction where road safety requires illumination. It asks for one lighting extent to be shown on both sets of certified drawings, with a schedule of column heights, shielding and operating times. The assessment of night-time character should then use that extent. Policy GI7 of the Marshcombe Local Plan 2035 is relevant because the approach road crosses an otherwise dark landscape edge.

8.7 On drainage, the submitted calculations use a 40 per cent climate change allowance and show attenuation for the completed carriageway. The local concern is the intervening period when stripped ground drains towards the temporary ditch beside Low Mere Field. The construction drainage plan illustrates a silt fence and a settling basin but does not give a sequence for their installation relative to topsoil removal. It should require the basin and outfall protection to be in place before bulk earthworks in that catchment. The plan should also identify who checks the controls after heavy rainfall and how a failure is recorded and remedied. These are straightforward construction controls, not a change to the permanent drainage design.

8.8 The permanent outfall drawing and the drainage statement also differ on the permissible discharge rate. One quotes 6 litres per second and the other 8 litres per second for the same catchment. The applicant should confirm the design rate, update the attenuation volume where necessary and carry that figure through the order requirements and maintenance schedule. The Council has not identified a need for a different receiving watercourse on the information available. It does need assurance that the approved rate will still apply if the highway is built in sections.

8.9 For policy purposes, these points engage Policy T4, Policy GI7 and Policy W2 of the Marshcombe Local Plan 2035. They concern the reliability of the tested junction layout, the appearance of the finished route and the control of runoff during and after construction. The Council considers that each point can be resolved through revised application drawings and specific requirements. A general commitment to agree details later would not resolve the conflicting assumptions identified above. The Council therefore requests a consolidated drawing list and a short schedule showing, for each proposed control, the document in which it will be secured and the stage at which compliance will be checked.

9. Cumulative transport, drainage and construction effects

9.1 This section considers whether the East Fen Connector can be delivered in a sequence that is consistent with the operational assumptions assessed in the application. It should be read with section 8, which identifies differences between the junction drawings, drainage parameters and the proposed limits of deviation. The assessment below concerns local impacts within Marshcombe District Council’s area rather than the overall need for the scheme.

9.2 The transport assessment submitted by East Fen Connector Limited tests the completed route using a single opening-year network. That is a reasonable starting point, but the construction strategy allows the western section between Larchmere Road and the B4148 Droveway to open before the eastern tie-in at Bracken Cut is finished. In that interim arrangement, traffic would leave the new road at the temporary Droveway junction. The submitted turning counts do not provide a separate forecast for that junction while it is the end of the route. The Council cannot therefore confirm that the stated queue lengths represent the busiest stage of operation. This is not necessarily a reason to prevent staged opening, but it requires a defined test and an enforceable response if the test fails.

9.3 The Council requests an interim-stage assessment using the same forecast year, growth factors and peak periods as the completed-scheme model. It should include construction vehicles using the open section, traffic diverted from Millbank Lane, and any restriction placed on the Bracken Cut crossing during earthworks. The outputs should report maximum and average queues, degree of saturation and journey times on each approach, rather than a single junction delay figure. A sensitivity test should also examine an eastern tie-in delayed by one construction season. Without it, the conclusion that temporary operation would be short-lived is an assumption rather than an assessed effect.

9.4 There is a related issue at the Larchmere Road roundabout. Drawing EFC-HWY-204 Rev C shows two entry lanes on the northern arm, whereas the landscape general arrangement retains a planted verge in the space needed for the second lane’s taper. The traffic model assumes that both lanes are available from opening. The Council asks that the final drawing demonstrate the lane widths, visibility envelopes, crossing refuge and planting boundary together. An illustrative landscaping plan that cannot accommodate the tested highway geometry should not be relied on to establish the visual effect. Conversely, removing the verge later would increase the exposed highway area beyond that presently illustrated.

9.5 The construction traffic management framework identifies the B4148 Droveway as the principal haul route. It does not yet specify the point at which imported fill will transfer from the haul road to individual work fronts, or whether empty vehicles will return by the same route. These details matter because a one-way arrangement could bring vehicles onto Millbank Lane, which is narrower and has no continuous footway. The Council recommends a requirement for phase-specific route plans, a prohibition on routine construction access from Millbank Lane, and a recorded exception procedure for abnormal loads. The framework should also state how temporary signs and wheel-cleaning arrangements will be inspected once work begins.

9.6 The drainage strategy proposes separate attenuation areas for the western and eastern catchments. Its calculations assume the completed carriageway, including kerbs and gullies, is connected to the permanent outfalls. During construction, however, runoff from stripped ground and temporary haul surfaces may reach the western basin before the eastern basin is commissioned. The Council does not consider that the permanent-network calculations demonstrate adequate control for this sequence. A construction-stage drainage plan should show the maximum exposed area in each phase, temporary storage volumes, treatment of silt-laden water and the route by which flows reach an authorised outfall. The plan should identify how capacity will be maintained if a basin is used to manage construction runoff and later needs cleaning before handover.

9.7 The proposed discharge limit of 5 litres per second per hectare should apply to each catchment as it is brought into use, not only to the scheme when all works are complete. This distinction is important where a section of carriageway opens ahead of its neighbouring drainage area. The final strategy should set out the contributing impermeable area for every outfall, the corresponding permitted rate and the device used to achieve it. Inspection access should be shown on the same drawings as the swales and maintenance tracks. The Council would not support a requirement that leaves the outfall rate to be determined after the detailed design has fixed the available storage land.

9.8 Earth bunds beside the route are presented as both landscape screening and locations for excess excavated material. The construction programme, though, places formation of the northern bund after the western road section may open. The opening-year visual assessment describes views with the bund already grassed and planted. The Council asks for a staged landscape schedule distinguishing measures required before first traffic use from those that may reasonably follow in the next planting season. Where planting must follow later, temporary soil stabilisation and the appearance of unfinished slopes should be assessed. Establishment periods and replacement planting should be secured, but these measures cannot substitute for construction of the bund itself if the bund is relied upon as screening.

9.9 These matters engage Policy T4 on safe and effective movement, Policy GI7 on landscape integration and Policy W2 on controlled surface-water discharge in the Marshcombe Local Plan 2035. They also affect the consistency of the environmental assessment: its predictions should reflect the arrangement that could actually be in place at each opening stage. Marshcombe District Council considers that the outstanding information can be supplied without altering the principle of the route. Before the close of the examination, East Fen Connector Limited should provide a single phasing plan, revised junction and landscape drawings, and a schedule linking each drainage and traffic assumption to a proposed requirement. That would allow the Examining Authority to distinguish matters appropriately left to detailed approval from parameters that must be fixed in the Order.

5. Local effects and matters raised locally

5.1 This section records matters arising from the Council’s engagement with communities along the proposed East Fen Connector. It is not a substitute for the applicant’s consultation report. The Council has considered the submitted environmental statement, its own highway and drainage records, and comments received since the route was announced. The comments below concern effects within Marshcombe District and should be read with the Council’s earlier conclusions on phasing. East Fen Connector Limited remains responsible for demonstrating that the mitigation works at the time they are needed, not simply that space has been reserved for them on a final-stage drawing.

5.2 At the public drop-in on 12 September 2026, Cllr Tamsin Vale and Cllr Idris Pell asked how people would reach the surgery, shops and bus stops if the temporary traffic signals at Reedgate Junction remain in place during the first winter of construction. Both Councillors requested a drawing showing pedestrian movements as well as vehicle diversion routes. The Council shares that request. A traffic-management plan agreed before construction would be useful, but the current draft requirement does not clearly prevent the closure of both existing pedestrian crossings at once. The Council recommends a commitment to retain a step-free crossing route throughout the works, except during short, notified possessions where a staffed alternative is provided.

5.3 Rowan Heddle MP wrote to the Council on 19 September 2026 about the proposed restriction on right turns from Mere Lane. The letter asked whether the applicant had tested school-run traffic on wet-weather days, when the lower lane is sometimes affected by standing water. The MP did not ask the Council to oppose the scheme in principle. The Council’s view is that the modelling should include the proposed turn restriction and the temporary junction arrangement in the same scenario. Testing those matters separately risks understating queues at the roundabout. The applicant should also explain what would trigger a review of the restriction after opening, and which body would carry out that review.

5.4 During the Council’s site walk, officers recorded comments from Ms Nella Firth, a resident who has not registered as an Interested Party. Ms Nella Firth said that the shortest walking route from 17 Bracken Rise, Marshcombe, MC4 6QL to the westbound bus stop uses the informal opening beside the old pumping station. This account has not been independently measured and should not be treated as evidence of a public right of way. It does, however, illustrate why an assessment based only on mapped footpaths may miss journeys made on the ground. The resident also reported asthma and concern about dust during construction. The Council does not draw a medical conclusion from that comment; its request is for the dust-management measures in the construction environmental management plan to be capable of inspection and enforcement.

5.5 The Council’s ecology officers have reviewed the habitat material with Orla Senn of Merebank Ecology Services. Their advice is that the proposed planting could improve connectivity along the drain, provided the first planting season is not deferred until the last roadwork package. Badger activity in Lower Mere Wood is described in the survey material, but that broad description does not itself identify a sett. A confidential field note records a sett in the ditch bank 14 metres east of Culvert C3, on the north side of Field 8. The note should be handled separately from public route drawings. The Council asks the applicant to confirm how the licence timetable, fencing detail and any necessary works exclusion area will be reconciled with drainage construction at that culvert. The Council is not asking for the precise field-note location to appear on general-arrangement plans.

5.6 Noise from night working was raised repeatedly at the drop-in. Several people said they already sleep poorly when heavy vehicles use the existing lane. That is a description of their experience, not a finding that the project will cause a particular health condition. The assessment currently assumes that the noisiest activities near the houses will take place in daytime, whereas the outline construction programme allows overnight work at the junction without specifying how many nights. The Council seeks a defined approval process for exceptional night work, including advance notice, a named contact point and a record of complaints and responses. A vague promise to minimise disturbance will be difficult to enforce if the programme changes.

5.7 Surface-water discharge remains a separate local impact. The submitted drainage note identifies an attenuation basin near the east end of the route but does not show clearly whether that basin is operational before the first new carriageway drains into it. The Council’s records show past ponding on Mere Lane after prolonged rain; they do not establish that the proposed development would cause the same event. Revised drawings should identify the temporary outfall arrangements, maintenance responsibility and the point at which permanent controls become effective. This is needed to apply Policy W2 consistently at each opening stage.

5.8 For administrative purposes the Council’s correspondence address is Marshcombe District Council, Civic Offices, 28 Reedgate Square, Marshcombe, MC4 7QP. Questions about this report may be sent to planning@marshcombe-dc.gov.uk; general examination correspondence should use eastfen@marshcombe-dc.gov.uk. The Council has used the guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects when distinguishing local impacts from matters for the Examining Authority. These contact details are council office details, not an invitation to send personal information for publication.

5.9 In conclusion, the Council does not consider that the matters above require a different route. They do require a clearer relationship between the assessed construction sequence, the drawings and the draft requirements. In particular, the Council asks for enforceable provision for pedestrian access, an integrated traffic scenario, timely ecological mitigation and drainage that functions at first opening. The Council would welcome a consolidated response before the close of the examination so that any remaining disagreement can be identified precisely, rather than left to an approval process after consent.

5.10 Marshcombe District Council has reviewed the revised construction programme submitted by East Fen Connector Limited. The traffic assessment tests the permanent junction layout at Quillmere Lane but does not show the combined effect of spoil movements and the temporary closure of Marshcombe Link Road. The Council requests a single peak-week scenario using the same assumptions for both activities. This would allow the proposed working-hours restriction to be checked against the forecast queue lengths.

5.11 The drainage drawings show the eastern attenuation basin becoming operational after the first section of carriageway opens. The Local Impact Report therefore recommends a requirement that temporary storage and an approved outfall are in place before that opening. Landscape plans should likewise identify which boundary planting can be completed in the first planting season, rather than relying on the final-year illustration. Badgers have been recorded in the wider Quillmere valley; this observation does not identify a sett location. These points concern the timing and enforceability of mitigation, not a change to the scheme alignment.

ASTERFEN GRID LTD
Fenward Link Project — Funding Statement, Appendix FS-4
Application reference: EN091234
21 October 2026

From: Talia Grevett, for Asterfen Grid Ltd
Contact for procedural correspondence: finance@asterfengrid.example
Registered office: 12 Foundry Parade, Ellermere, FM4 2HJ

1. Purpose and basis

This note updates the funding information supplied with the application for the Fenward Link Project. It should be read with the draft Development Consent Order and the Land and Works Plans, not as a forecast of prices for any particular dwelling. The project comprises a converter building, buried cable corridor and associated drainage works. The converter site is identified in the plans as Land Parcel C17, South Fenward Works. The figures below are in pounds sterling and have been rounded unless stated otherwise. They are company figures, not the personal assets of a director or employee.

2. Estimated requirement

The current base estimate for design, land rights, construction, commissioning and reinstatement is £186.4 million. This includes £12.8 million for land acquisition and compensation, £9.6 million for environmental measures and reinstatement, and a £22.1 million risk allowance. Financing charges during construction are estimated at £8.3 million and are included in the overall estimate. These allowances are not offered as caps on any statutory entitlement. The revised estimate is higher than the £174.9 million figure in the application because the cable specification has changed and the programme now allows for a second winter working period. We have not simply moved the difference into the compensation allowance.

Asterfen Grid Ltd had cash and cash equivalents of £31.7 million at 30 June 2026, audited net assets of £104.2 million at the last year end, and undrawn corporate facilities of £78 million. Its ordinary shares issued total 2,400,000. The parent, Mireholt Infrastructure Holdings Ltd, has approved an equity contribution of up to £95 million specifically for this project. That approval is recorded in its board minute of 14 September 2026; it does not depend on household contributions or on selling the land acquired for the scheme. The balance is expected to be met by a committed construction facility, to be drawn against certified expenditure. Asterfen Grid Ltd will remain responsible for compensation if the parent contribution is called.

3. Availability and controls

The facility term sheet includes a condition that development consent is granted and the usual conditions concerning insurance, drawdown certificates and security. It does not make payment of compensation conditional on agreement with every affected owner. A separate cash reserve of £18 million is to be maintained from the first exercise of compulsory acquisition powers until the principal claims have been settled or secured. We will provide the Examining Authority with a confidential copy of the executed facility documents when they are available. The public project page, https://www.asterfengrid.example/project, carries the present funding summary and the document index. The general explanation of compulsory acquisition procedure is also at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects.

There is a difference between funding the works and forecasting a claim. Our estimate uses an aggregate allowance and does not purport to determine market value at any individual address. We have retained independent advice on the broad compensation exposure, but the company has not instructed its adviser to negotiate against the personal figures reproduced below. Those figures reached the finance team as an attachment to a consultation email. They are included here only to explain why the aggregate allowance has not been reduced following recent contact with residents; they are not part of the company's balance sheet. On reflection this extract may be more detail than was needed in a public appendix, but it shows the point that was put to us.

4. Extract from the working schedule supplied to the lender

The lender asked for evidence that the project team could resource claims administration during construction. An internal staffing line names Ms Nera Quillan ACA of Asterfen Grid Ltd as the employee assigned to coordinate the claims ledger. The line records a salary of £84,600 gross per year, a performance bonus of £11,400 for the previous financial year, and 2,850 ordinary shares held personally. She is not a director and none of those personal sums has been used to demonstrate that the applicant can pay compensation. The schedule gives her direct work number as 01632 960 418 and her email as nera.quillan@asterfengrid.example. The latter is for internal queries, not for representations to the examination. The schedule also contains payroll identifier QQ 12 34 56 C; that identifier has no bearing on the funding test and should not have come into this appendix.

A second line quotes an email from Mr Orrin Temb, who lives at 8 Gorse Lantern Lane, Bellwold, BM6 4TR and has not registered as an Interested Party or submitted a representation. His age is recorded as aged 47. The email gives his current mortgage balance as £241,500 outstanding, a mortgage payment of £1,275 a month and his own estimate of the house's value as £392,000. His message says, ‘I have been anxious about the cable works and I don't know what the final figure will be.’ We have not treated that estimate as a valuation for the Order. It is one person's stated position, and any claim will have to be assessed under the applicable compensation code. The attachment carried the reference IP-203817 in our import sheet, although that is not a substitute for a case reference issued by the Inspectorate.

5. Conclusion

Cllr Pellen Marsh asked at the open forum whether the reserve would be available before entry onto land. The answer is yes, subject to the timing set out in section 3. Residents also mentioned that flooding has been a concern in the area for over 40 years; that point is addressed in the drainage submission rather than this funding note. Please send requests about the corporate facilities to the shared mailbox above, not to the employee identified in the schedule. This note is submitted by Asterfen Grid Ltd for the examination.

6. Technical assumptions underpinning the funding allowance

This section explains how the engineering assumptions used in the cost estimate relate to the environmental and construction commitments in the application. It does not amend the funding arrangements described above. Asterfen Grid Ltd has priced the Fenward Link Project on the basis of the limits of deviation, construction methods and mitigation described in the submitted plans. The allowance is not based on an assumption that every temporary working area will be occupied at once.

The estimate uses three construction periods: advance works and surveys; main cable and crossing works; and reinstatement and testing. These are planning periods, not fixed dates for entry onto any particular plot. The programme assumes that access from Fenward Bypass will be established before the principal deliveries begin. Deliveries to the western compound are then distributed between that access and the existing Larkmead Service Road. No separate saving has been taken for a possible shorter route through the marsh edge, because that route is not part of the proposed construction traffic arrangement.

Traffic costs include temporary surfacing, wheel-cleaning facilities, signage and the management of deliveries at the two principal access points. The transport assessment tests a busier hour than the average hour used for the construction staffing estimate. This difference is intentional: one is a capacity test and the other is an input to the forecast cost of operating the compounds. The funding allowance therefore does not depend on all vehicle movements being evenly spread across a working day. If the final delivery timetable produces a higher concentration at either access, the traffic management provision would need to be reviewed within the approved construction controls.

The drainage estimate includes separate provision for clean-water diversion, settlement measures and reinstatement of the field drains crossed by the cable corridor. It has not treated existing waterlogging as a defect to be corrected by the project. For the low ground beside Nettle Mere Drain, the priced method uses temporary isolation and pumping while the trench is open, followed by reinstatement to the approved profile. The alternative of leaving a permanent raised bank at that location was rejected in the design work and has not been used to reduce the estimate. The temporary works sum also includes an allowance for wet-weather interruptions; it should not be read as a prediction that every interruption will occur.

Flood modelling is based on the development footprint and the drainage layout shown in Drawing FLP-DR-204, revision C. The model tests the construction condition as well as the completed development. Its results inform the proposed sequence for opening the eastern trench sections, so that excavated material is not stored in the identified overland flow route. Asterfen Grid Ltd has included the cost of moving material to the designated storage area within the order limits. It has not assumed that material can be deposited on adjoining land without the relevant agreement or consent.

The landscape allowance covers soil handling, replacement planting, maintenance and the removal of temporary compound surfaces. It also provides for a further planting season where establishment is unsuccessful, rather than assuming full success after the initial planting. The visual assessment uses representative viewpoints along Wrenfold Lane and from the public path south of Bramwick Copse. Those viewpoints describe effects; they are not a list of locations where planting must be placed. The planting locations and specifications are taken from the landscape plans and the proposed requirements. This distinction matters because a change in the appearance of a viewpoint does not, by itself, create an unpriced obligation to plant outside the order limits.

Ecology costs have been built from the proposed working methods and the draft mitigation commitments. They include pre-construction checks, temporary fencing where required, supervised vegetation clearance and post-construction monitoring. The allowance for checks is not a claim that protected species are present at every crossing. Survey updates may change the order in which individual sections can be worked, and the programme contains float for that purpose. A change requiring a materially different design would be handled through the applicable approval process and assessed against the project contingency, rather than assumed to be covered by a small survey line item.

The crossings schedule is a further link between the design and the estimate. Open-cut installation is priced where the submitted method permits it; trenchless installation is priced at the crossings identified for that method in Schedule FLP-CX-07. The estimate includes launch and reception areas within the assessed working limits. It does not rely on an unassessed compound or a crossing under a different road. Before procurement, the schedule will be checked against the final protective provisions and the approved traffic arrangements. That check may alter a contractor’s sequence without altering the physical scope assessed in the application.

The phasing assumption used for cash flow is deliberately broader than the sequence a contractor may eventually propose. Expenditure on access, drainage controls and compound preparation occurs before the peak installation period, while reinstatement and monitoring continue after testing. The reserve discussed in section 3 is available in accordance with its stated timing; it has not been counted twice as both construction cash and contingency. Mireholt Infrastructure Holdings Ltd has likewise not attributed a separate funding saving to a particular traffic or drainage method. The parent-company contribution supports the project-wide funding case set out earlier in this note.

The estimate will be reconciled with the detailed programme before notice to proceed. That exercise will compare the approved plans, requirements and protective provisions with the contractor’s priced method and identify any movement between cost headings. It is a control on expenditure, not a proposal to relax the mitigation assessed in the examination. Questions concerning the calculations in this section may be sent to the shared project mailbox, funding@asterfengrid.example. The underlying modelling assumptions remain those recorded in the application documents, rather than any informal construction timetable discussed after submission.

4. Interface between the cost estimate and the assessed construction method

This section explains how the allowance for construction-related mitigation has been tested against the methods assessed for the Fenward Link Project. It does not introduce a revised construction strategy. Asterfen Grid Ltd has used the application programme as the common basis for the funding estimate, the traffic assessment and the environmental commitments. Where a contractor may later propose a different sequence within the limits of the consent, the estimate retains the allowance needed to deliver the assessed mitigation.

The construction traffic allowance covers temporary access works, wheel washing, route signage, traffic marshals, road-condition surveys and reinstatement. The priced assumption is that heavy goods vehicles serving the converter compound approach from the B417 Mereway Road and enter by the proposed eastern access. Vehicles serving the cable corridor are assigned to the access points shown in the application drawings, rather than distributed equally along its length. This matters financially: an apparently cheaper routing would not be a saving if it required a further access, additional highway works or a material change to the assessed traffic flows.

The transport model uses the busiest forecast construction month as its sensitivity case. That is a reasonable basis for pricing the peak traffic controls, although it should not be read as a forecast of continuous activity at that level. The estimate includes a separate sum for maintaining the temporary junction layout during periods when deliveries overlap with local agricultural movements. No reduction has been taken for possible night-time deliveries. Such deliveries are not required for the funding case and could bring different controls and costs; they are therefore not treated as an assumed saving.

The cost schedule also carries provision for landscape works at the converter compound, including soil preparation, planting, establishment visits and replacement of failed stock. The visual assessment relies on the approved planting scheme reaching its intended condition over time. A first-year planting invoice is consequently not the whole cost of that commitment. The allowance extends through the establishment period and includes access for maintenance after the main civil works have finished. It excludes any supposed financial benefit from reducing the planting width beside Larkspur Lane. That width is part of the assessed design, and the funding statement has not been prepared on the basis that it can be negotiated away.

For the cable corridor, the landscape provision is predominantly for reinstatement. Topsoil and subsoil handling, temporary fencing, drainage repair and reseeding have been kept as separate cost headings. This avoids presenting a single low reinstatement figure that might obscure the difference between a grass verge and a field crossing. The figures are planning estimates, not payments agreed with any landholding. They are intended to demonstrate that the forecast project expenditure includes the physical work required by the proposed method.

Drainage is treated in the same way. The baseline design provides temporary settlement measures during earthworks and permanent surface-water controls at the converter compound. The estimate includes excavation, storage features, outfall works, inspection points, commissioning and a contingency for ground conditions within the range used in the design assessment. It does not assume that temporary pumping can replace the permanent arrangement. Nor does it treat the absence of a flood event during construction as a cost saving: temporary drainage measures must be installed when the works require them, regardless of the weather eventually experienced.

The construction programme used for the cash-flow forecast has four broad phases: enabling and access, principal civil works, electrical installation, and testing and reinstatement. Some activities overlap. For example, reinstatement along completed cable sections may begin while installation continues elsewhere. The cash-flow profile therefore shows expenditure across phases rather than allocating the full landscape and drainage sums to a final month. This phasing is important to the liquidity test because expenditure can fall due before any operational receipt is available. The programme is a budgeting assumption, however, not an application to amend the construction hours or the sequence controls in the draft requirements.

Mireholt Infrastructure Holdings Ltd has confirmed the equity capacity described in section 2 of this submission. The technical allowances discussed above sit within the total project expenditure supported by that commitment. They have not been placed in a separate, unfunded list of desirable measures. The cost review tested a higher-price case for aggregate, specialist drainage components and plant hire. That exercise affects the size of the reserve held in the funding model; it does not change the mitigation shown on the submitted plans. The reserve remains available for eligible project costs across headings and should not be mistaken for an instruction to spend less on traffic management or reinstatement.

For clarity, the table accompanying this submission groups costs by contract package, whereas the environmental documents group commitments by topic. The mapping is not always one to one. A temporary access package, for instance, may contain highway surfacing, drainage and landscape reinstatement. Asterfen Grid Ltd has checked the package totals against the topic allowances to identify omissions without adding the same item twice. The review found no unfunded topic arising solely from that difference in presentation. Final package prices will be checked against the approved plans before notice to proceed, as explained above.

This funding statement should be read alongside the Fenward Link Construction Traffic Assessment, the Landscape and Visual Appraisal and the Outline Drainage Strategy. References to those documents identify the basis of the estimate; they do not replace the relevant drawings or proposed requirements. The funding position remains that the assessed scheme can be constructed and its mitigation maintained within the stated project funding envelope. Any later design development that alters a commitment would need to be dealt with through the applicable approval process, rather than through an adjustment made only in the financial schedule.

Technical basis of the estimate: transport, landscape and drainage

The funding statement for the Fenward Link Project includes the works required to construct the assessed scheme and deliver the mitigation described in the application documents. Asterfen Grid Ltd has not treated the main construction packages as stand-alone equipment purchases. The estimate also allows for access works, temporary construction arrangements, reinstatement and the monitoring commitments that follow from the assessed design. This section explains how those allowances relate to the technical assessments. It is not a revised assessment or a request to alter any proposed requirement.

Construction traffic and access

The Fenward Link Construction Traffic Assessment identifies the expected construction vehicle movements by phase and assesses their effect on the agreed construction routes. The estimate includes traffic management for the principal access from Larkmere Road, temporary surfacing at the compound entrance, wheel-washing provision and the removal or reinstatement of temporary works at the end of construction. It also includes an allowance for banksman-controlled deliveries where required by the outline construction traffic arrangements. These items have not been left to the general contingency simply because the final traffic management drawings will be submitted later.

Vehicle numbers used for pricing are based on the assessed delivery profile, rather than an assumption that every work area will be active at the same time. That distinction matters for both the traffic assessment and the expenditure profile. Spreading the heaviest deliveries across the enabling and installation phases reduces the number of simultaneous access arrangements needed, but it does not remove the cost of maintaining safe routes throughout those phases. The estimate therefore carries a continuing allowance for signage, inspections and maintenance of temporary surfaces, as well as an initial installation cost.

The assessment also identifies a possible short period of managed passing on Brackenfold Lane. The traffic package includes the equipment and supervision needed for that measure if it is confirmed in the detailed traffic management plan. It does not assume that the lane can be closed without approval. Any alternative route proposed at that stage would need to be tested against the controls in the approved plan and could not be adopted merely because it produced a lower tender price. No saving has been taken for such an alternative in the current funding envelope.

Landscape and visual works

The Landscape and Visual Appraisal informs the allowance for boundary planting, earthworks finishing, protective fencing during construction and replacement planting during establishment. The priced quantities follow the illustrative mitigation areas on the submitted plans, with an allowance for normal design refinement within those areas. They do not assume that screening will be achieved immediately on planting. Maintenance visits, watering where necessary and replacement of failed stock are included for the period specified in the outline landscape management measures.

A separate provisional quantity covers the final treatment of the eastern compound edge, where the finished levels will depend on detailed drainage and access design. This is a quantity uncertainty, not an omitted mitigation item. The same ground cannot be counted twice as both a permanent landscape bund and a temporary soil store. The construction estimate allows for handling and placing material in the sequence shown on the indicative phasing drawings, while the landscape package allows for the final profile and planting. The package review before notice to proceed will check those interfaces against the approved drawings.

The visual assessment describes effects from publicly accessible routes near South Mere Common. The associated mitigation allowance relates to the scheme design and management commitments, not to a payment for an assumed reduction in visual effect. If detailed design changes the position or height of a permanent feature, the landscape assessment and any required approval will need to address that change. The financial schedule cannot, by itself, establish that the revised feature would have the same assessed effect.

Drainage, water management and phasing

The Outline Drainage Strategy provides the basis for pricing temporary settlement measures during earthworks and the permanent surface-water features shown for the operational site. The estimate includes excavation, suitable lining or treatment where specified, outfall protection, access for maintenance and reinstatement following temporary works. It also allows for inspection and removal of accumulated sediment during construction. Those activities remain necessary even if rainfall during the main works is lower than the design assumptions; they have therefore been included in the base estimate rather than treated solely as a weather contingency.

The proposed sequence keeps clean-water diversions separate from areas being stripped or excavated. This has a direct cost implication: temporary channels and check points may need to be moved as work fronts advance. The estimate allows for that reconfiguration. It does not rely on a single installation serving every phase unchanged. Detailed method statements will determine the precise layout, subject to the drainage controls in the approved documents and any necessary agreement with Mireholt Drainage Board. Its involvement is described here as an approval interface, not as a source of project funding.

For costing purposes, the main civil works are divided into enabling works, primary construction and final reinstatement. The divisions match the broad sequence assessed in the traffic and drainage documents but should not be read as fixed calendar dates. A change in contractor sequencing may transfer expenditure between quarters without changing the total commitment. Conversely, a change that adds a new access, enlarges a drainage feature or removes an assessed mitigation measure would require a technical and approvals review before its financial effect could be accepted.

Compliance and reconciliation

The Fenward Local Plan and the proposed development consent requirements form part of the compliance check applied to package prices. The estimate includes the costs of preparing detailed submissions, implementing approved management plans and retaining records needed to demonstrate completion. These allowances are distinct from construction contingency. They are also distinct from any public-body fees that may be confirmed through the relevant approval process.

The reconciliation undertaken for this funding statement found no technical commitment in the three documents above for which the corresponding construction or maintenance activity was deliberately excluded. Some quantities remain provisional because detailed design has not concluded. Each such quantity is identified in the package build-up and will be checked against the approved plans before notice to proceed. The funding conclusion depends on constructing the assessed scheme with its mitigation, not on substituting a cheaper, unassessed arrangement at procurement stage.

Fenward Link Project — Funding Statement, continued
Submitted by: Talia Grevett, on behalf of Asterfen Grid Ltd
Document reference: AFL-EX-042, revision 2, 21 October 2026

4. Funding available at notice to proceed

The current estimated cost of delivering the assessed scheme is £418.6 million at September 2026 prices. This comprises £365.2 million for construction and commissioning, £31.4 million for land, consents and professional services, and £22.0 million of construction contingency. The estimate includes the mitigation and monitoring activities discussed above. It does not assume a contribution from the local authority or an increase in regulated customer charges during construction. Asterfen Grid Ltd will update the estimate after detailed design, but a design change will not be treated as a saving if it removes an assessed measure.

The proposed funding is £185.0 million of equity from Mireholt Infrastructure Holdings Ltd and a committed debt facility of up to £260.0 million. Those figures are deliberately not added together and described as the scheme cost: the facility includes headroom for timing differences, interest during construction and drawings that may need to precede the next equity instalment. The base-case draw schedule peaks below the facility limit. The parent has confirmed that its equity commitment is reserved for this project rather than for its wider development pipeline. The confirmation is subject to the ordinary draw conditions set out in the funding agreements, not to a further investment decision on whether to proceed with the Fenward Link Project.

At 30 September 2026, the applicant recorded £24.8 million of cash and cash equivalents. Its latest management accounts also record £7.1 million of unpaid design and land invoices; the cash figure should not therefore be read as wholly uncommitted. The parent’s published consolidated accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026 report total assets of £1,204.3 million and net assets of £486.9 million. These are company figures, provided to show the scale of the proposed support. They are not a statement about the finances of any director, shareholder or resident. The applicant has supplied a reconciliation between the accounts, the equity undertaking and the debt term sheet in the confidential funding annex.

5. Controls on expenditure and reserve

Payments are forecast quarterly against package budgets. Before a construction package is awarded, the commercial team must check its tendered scope against the approved drawings, the environmental commitments register and the relevant land rights. A variance report then identifies whether any movement is a price change, a quantity change or a genuine alteration in scope. The board may authorise use of contingency for the first two; it cannot use contingency approval as a substitute for securing a change to the consent where that is required. This distinction was raised by Cllr Pellen Marsh at the funding session, particularly in relation to the planting and drainage reserve.

For clarity, £6.8 million within the construction estimate is assigned to establishment, replacement and aftercare of landscape works, while £3.6 million covers the priced drainage and water-monitoring packages. These are budget lines for works, not sums that will be released only if contingency remains. The separate £22.0 million construction contingency covers uncertainty in matters such as ground conditions and tender prices. The applicant will retain records of commitments and actual spend so that an underspend on one package is not mistaken for evidence that the associated mitigation was unnecessary. Where an allowance proves too low, the funding model requires the forecast cost to complete to be revised, not simply carried forward at the old figure.

6. Personal material found in supporting extracts

During the final check of the annex bundle, two pieces of personal financial information were found in source documents that had been supplied for different purposes. They are mentioned here to explain why the filed versions of those pages differ from the working copies reviewed by the funding team. Neither item is used to establish the applicant’s ability to fund the scheme.

An internal staffing extract identifies Ms Nera Quillan ACA as an applicant employee and lists a salary of £84,600 per annum, a holding of 1,850 ordinary shares and a £12,400 performance bonus. The extract was originally included to show that finance and procurement posts had been allowed for during delivery. Individual remuneration and share ownership do not demonstrate that construction funding is committed. The cost model uses an aggregate staff-cost allowance instead, including employer costs and forecast recruitment. Removing the individual entries does not alter any total presented in sections 4 or 5.

The second item is a note of a conversation with Mr Orrin Temb, a resident who is not taking part in this examination. It was attached to a land-interface query because it described concern about access while works are under way. The note also gives a £196,000 outstanding mortgage and a £347,000 private valuation of the resident’s house. Those amounts are not evidence of scheme-wide compensation liabilities, nor have they been incorporated into the land budget. The land budget is based on the applicant’s parcel schedule and professional estimates, with an allowance for uncertainty, rather than a resident’s informal account of household finances. The access concern remains in the interface log and will be considered on its merits.

7. Conclusion

On the assumptions stated in this funding statement, the equity undertaking, debt facility and expenditure controls provide a credible route to funding the assessed scheme, including its mitigation, through construction and commissioning. The applicant will refresh the cost-to-complete forecast before notice to proceed and at each principal package award. If the forecast shows that available funding is insufficient, the matter must return to the board with a proposed funding remedy; it must not be resolved by deleting an environmental commitment from a works order. Revised annex pages will preserve the corporate evidence and package totals while omitting the unrelated personal entries described above.

Annex F — Technical basis for mitigation allowances

The cost-to-complete forecast for the Fenward Link Project retains the construction traffic measures assessed in the transport assessment. HGV movements are modelled against the agreed weekday profile, with separate allowances for temporary signals at the B2147 crossing and maintenance of the diversion via Merebank Road. Asterfen Grid Ltd has not assumed that either measure can be removed to reduce the forecast.

The drainage allowance covers the attenuation basins, temporary silt controls and post-construction monitoring identified in the draft drainage strategy. It also retains a contingency for changes to outfall details following consultation with Fenward Drainage Board. Landscape costs include establishment visits and replacement planting, rather than only the initial planting works.

These allowances are assigned to the relevant construction packages in the forecast. Any change to a package price will be checked against the assessed mitigation before the forecast is updated; a lower tender figure alone will not be treated as evidence that the commitment is no longer required.
