BRINDLEWICK PARISH COUNCIL
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held on 14 October 2026 at the Parish Room, Market Square, Brindlewick, FN8 2JP

Present: Cllr Nessa Harrow (Chair), Cllr Tobin Kest, Cllr Elva Marden, Cllr Perran Vale and Cllr Iona Sedge. Also present: Mara Ellwick (Clerk) and three members of the public, Beren Thist, Lottie Fenner and Oren Quill. The members of the public were attending as local residents and are not parties to the Woldmere Link examination.

1. Apologies and declarations
Apologies were received from Cllr Ruan Pell. Cllr Kest declared an interest in item 7 as a member of the village hall committee. No other interests were declared. The Chair reminded everyone that the meeting was being minuted, not recorded, and asked speakers to keep comments on the Woldmere Link DCO to the published plans where possible.

2. Previous minutes
The minutes of 9 September 2026 were approved as an accurate record and signed by the Chair. The Clerk said the missing attachment to the highways letter had now been obtained. It will be put with the council papers rather than copied into these minutes.

3. Woldmere Link DCO: consultation and examination timetable
The Clerk reported that Woldmere Link Infrastructure Ltd had circulated revised construction traffic drawings and a note about the temporary compound east of Brindlewick. The deadline for the council's written representation is 30 October 2026. Members agreed that the response should focus on the proposed route past the school crossing, access to the playing field and the absence of a clear arrangement for restoring the verge after construction. These are matters the parish council has raised before but the latest note does not, in the council's view, settle them.

Cllr Marden said the swept-path drawing appears to show a lorry using the pavement at the bend by Lantern Row. The drawing is labelled WL-TR-204 Rev C; members asked that this reference be quoted accurately in the response. Cllr Sedge asked whether the applicant's traffic count included the Friday market. The Clerk will seek clarification through the examination mailbox, examinations@woldmerelink.example, rather than contacting individual staff.

In the public participation part of this item, Beren Thist said traffic already leaves them feeling stressed when walking across Market Square. Lottie Fenner said she had lived in the parish for over 40 years and did not think the proposed banksman position could be seen from the school gate. Oren Quill asked whether construction deliveries would be allowed before 8 am. The Chair explained that the council could pass these points to the Examining Authority, but could not answer on behalf of the applicant. Nobody present objected to the points being summarised in the council's response; the Clerk will not attach the attendance sheet.

Members discussed the ecological appendix. The survey refers generally to badgers in Thistledown Wood, which the council considered useful context for its comments on lighting. A separate field note circulated to members identifies a sett at the base of the split ash, 12 metres north of the eastern stile on Footpath 6. The Chair asked that this detail not be repeated in the public representation and that the council instead request a confidential check by the relevant ecologist. No photographs of the location are to be uploaded with the submission.

Resolved: the Clerk will prepare a draft representation, for approval by email from councillors by 23 October, addressing construction traffic, pedestrian safety, compound reinstatement and the lighting assessment. The council's position remains that a workable construction plan is needed; the council has not voted to support or oppose the DCO as a whole. The Clerk will submit the agreed text with the council's reference BPC/26/114.

4. Footpaths and drainage
Cllr Vale reported standing water near the northern end of Footpath 3 after recent rain. The highways team has been asked to inspect the blocked grip. Members agreed that this ordinary maintenance issue should not be presented as evidence of an effect from the Woldmere Link scheme. The Clerk will check the works list next month. Cllr Harrow also noted that a gate latch on the playing-field path was loose; Cllr Pell had offered to look at it when available.

5. Planning applications (not part of the DCO)
The council considered application FW/26/0871, alterations to the rear roof of Dorian Brack's home at 6 Kettlewick Fold, Brindlewick, FN8 3RL. Dorian Brack was not at the meeting and has not made a representation to the Woldmere Link examination. Members had no objection to the roof alteration, subject to the planning authority considering overlooking from the new window. The Clerk will send that short response through the normal planning portal. The Chair stressed that this was a separate household application and should not be included in the DCO submission or its supporting papers.

6. Finance
The payments schedule, including the Parish Room heating invoice and the quarterly grounds-maintenance charge, was approved. Cllr Kest asked for the two printing invoices to be shown separately next month so that DCO-related copying can be identified in the council's published accounts. No decision was made to commission outside advice. The balance reported to members was £18,420.16; this is the council's account balance, not a resident's financial information.

7. Village hall noticeboard
Because of the declared interest, Cllr Kest did not take part in the decision. Members agreed to replace the water-damaged backing board. The noticeboard may carry the examination deadline and the project mailbox but must not display residents' contact details from correspondence received by the council.

8. Clerk's correspondence and next meeting
The Clerk advised that general council correspondence may be sent to clerk@brindlewickparish.example. Her working contact for documents requiring a named recipient is mara.ellwick@brindlewickparish.example; members asked that this not be printed on the village noticeboard. The Clerk's correspondence address held for postal delivery is 14 Mothbell Lane, Fennick, FN8 4QJ, which is her home address, not a parish office. The next ordinary meeting will be held on 11 November 2026 at 7.00 pm. The meeting closed at 8.48 pm.

Mara Ellwick
Clerk, Brindlewick Parish Council

Brindlewick Parish Council
Minutes of the ordinary meeting held at Brindlewick Village Hall on 11 November 2026, commencing at 7.00 pm

Present: Cllr Nessa Harrow (Chair), Cllr Tobin Kest, Cllr Elva Marden, Cllr Perran Vale and Cllr Iona Sedge.
In attendance: Mara Ellwick (Clerk). Members of the public: Beren Thist, Lottie Fenner and Oren Quill.
Apologies: Cllr Ruan Pell.

1. Declarations and previous minutes
No interests were declared in the Woldmere Link item. Cllr Tobin Kest declared an interest in the village hall repairs discussion because of his membership of its committee. The minutes of the meeting of 14 October 2026 were approved as a correct record, subject to correcting the spelling of Mothbell Lane in item 8. The Chair signed the paper copy.

2. Public participation
Beren Thist asked whether the council had received a proper answer about construction traffic using the bend by the old weighbridge. The Chair said the applicant's latest traffic note had arrived, but the council had not yet compared its figures with the school drop-off period. Lottie Fenner said that the prospect of night working was causing her stress and poor sleep. She asked for any night-work notice to be put on the noticeboard as well as online. Oren Quill said that lorries already mount the verge after heavy rain and asked whether a photograph would help. Members agreed that photographs of the road could be sent to the council's shared mailbox, provided no house numbers or registration plates were shown. The public session closed at 7.19 pm.

3. Woldmere Link DCO examination
The council considered the supplementary construction traffic note submitted by Woldmere Link Infrastructure Ltd. Cllr Elva Marden observed that the diagram marks a passing place on Wicker Fold as existing, whereas the surface there is currently grass. Cllr Perran Vale said the council should distinguish between an objection to the route and a request for an enforceable traffic plan; he favoured making the latter point clearly. Members agreed that the response should ask who will inspect the passing places before work starts, how mud on the highway will be dealt with and where residents can report an out-of-hours delivery.

The Clerk confirmed that the examination timetable and published documents can be found at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects-the-examination-process and that the applicant's project page is https://woldmerelink.example/examination. Councillors requested a short paper version of the deadlines for the noticeboard. The Chair reminded members that comments made to the parish council are not automatically representations to the Examining Authority. Resolved: the Clerk will circulate a draft response to councillors for comment by 18 November. The final text is to be approved by email, with the decision recorded at the next meeting. The council's submission should give the council's shared address, clerk@brindlewickparish.example, rather than a resident's contact details.

4. Unrelated household planning application
Members considered application FN/26/0418/HOU, described on the agenda as a single-storey rear extension at 6 Thimble Row, Brindlewick, BW3 7LP, for Dorian Brack. The Chair noted that this is an ordinary household application for the district council and is not part of the Woldmere Link examination. Cllr Iona Sedge asked that the minutes make that distinction, as the two notices had been pinned close together on the board. No neighbour objections had been sent to the parish council. Following discussion of the roof height shown on drawing B-04, the council resolved to make no objection, but to ask the district council to check the proposed rainwater outlet. The Clerk will submit that comment under the planning reference, without attaching correspondence received on the DCO.

5. Drainage at Bell Sward
Cllr Perran Vale reported standing water beside the footpath after last week's rain. It was agreed to ask the highways team whether the roadside grip is on its maintenance list. Members did not agree to commission ditch work on land outside council ownership. Cllr Nessa Harrow asked for the matter to return to the December agenda if no reply is received. A photograph of the location may be attached to the request; the council will not publish photographs showing people at nearby homes.

6. Village hall and noticeboard
Cllr Tobin Kest left the discussion of the hall's request for a contribution towards gutter repairs and took no part in the vote. The council agreed in principle to a contribution of up to £450 from the buildings budget, subject to sight of an itemised quotation. The remaining councillors also agreed to replace the cracked cover on the parish noticeboard. The examination deadline sheet can be displayed there, but letters from members of the public must not be pinned up. The old backing board has been taken away; there is still a problem with rain getting in at the bottom edge.

7. Correspondence and next meeting
The Clerk reported that the postal address held for council correspondence remains 14 Mothbell Lane, Fennick, FN8 4QJ. This is the Clerk's home address, not an office open to callers. For routine enquiries the shared mailbox remains clerk@brindlewickparish.example. The next ordinary meeting is scheduled for 9 December 2026 at 7.00 pm. The meeting closed at 8.36 pm.

Mara Ellwick
Clerk, Brindlewick Parish Council

Pell & Plane Joinery
14 Kiln Spur, Brindlewick, BW9 4QX
Tel: 07700 900463
Email: ewan.pell@pellplane.example

21 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Marrin Link Road Development Consent Order (EN010984)

Dear Inspectors,

Objection to the proposed construction traffic route through Brindlewick

I am Ewan Pell, a self-employed joiner trading as Pell & Plane Joinery. I work from the workshop behind my house at the address above. This is my own representation, not a submission for the other businesses on the lane. My Interested Party reference is IP-40627. I object to the Construction Traffic Management Plan as presently drawn because it sends heavy vehicles along Kiln Spur, which is a narrow residential lane and also my only practical route to customers. I support improving the main road, but the building of it should not make this lane unusable for months at a time.

The plan shows lorries leaving the temporary compound at Plot 17 and turning past the entrance to Kiln Spur. The swept-path drawing appears to assume that the verge opposite the junction is available for vehicles to overrun. It is not a hard verge. After rain it breaks up, and the road surface carries the mud straight towards the drain by my workshop gate. I have already reported blocked gullies here twice in the last year. Please do not treat the turning movement as a line on a drawing without somebody checking what happens when a delivery van or a bin lorry is coming the other way.

Most mornings I load doors and fitted units into my van, PV26 KRL, before setting off. Timber deliveries arrive at my workshop during the day, sometimes on a rigid lorry. If the contractor's vehicles queue across my entrance I cannot simply move the delivery to another site: this is where the machinery is. I am 47 and have worked in joinery for over 20 years, but I have never had a job where the proposed answer to access problems was just 'agree arrangements with residents'. Who would I ring at six in the morning, and what authority would that person have to stop a convoy?

I asked Lysa Norr of Hushward Traffic Ltd about this at the drop-in event. I was told a banksman could be used at busy times, but that assurance is not in the document submitted for examination. The answer also did not cover Saturdays. Please put the banksman locations, working hours and a clear procedure for keeping private accesses open into a requirement, rather than leaving it to a later conversation with the contractor. I would welcome a site visit by the Examining Authority at the start of a working day; the layout is quite different when vans are parked outside the small units.

There are people living along this route, not just workshops. My neighbour Mrs Tilda Fenn lives beside the bend nearest the compound. I mention this because construction dust and idling exhaust would reach that house first, and Mrs Tilda Fenn has been diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide anyone's medical needs; I am asking it to require a proper assessment of the route that has actually been proposed. My own poor sleep over the traffic plans is not the basis of this objection. The drawings and the lack of enforceable limits are.

My 11-year-old daughter, Orla Pell, walks with me to the school crossing on some mornings before I open the workshop. The crossing is outside the stated haul-road boundary, but lorries taking the advertised route would still pass it. The traffic tables count vehicles by day, not by the twenty minutes when families are at the crossing. Cllr Faye Tress raised the same timing issue at the parish meeting on 7 October 2026. I ask for a condition preventing construction HGV movements through the village at school arrival and leaving times, with those times set after discussion with the school.

I am also concerned about the ditch beside the compound. Badger signs have been noted in Marrin Wood, which is a broad area and does not by itself show where any animals are living. During my walk along the public footpath I saw an active badger sett in the eastern bank of the drainage ditch, 18 metres south of the gate to Plot 17. The ecology drawings supplied to residents do not appear to mark it. That precise location should be checked by a qualified ecologist before fencing or ditch works begin, and should not be put on a public noticeboard. My concern here is that a last-minute discovery will lead to another unplanned diversion of construction vehicles onto Kiln Spur.

The applicant, Marrin Link Infrastructure Ltd, has put the latest plans at https://www.marrinlink.example/plans and says comments may be sent to planning@marrinlink.example. I have read Revision C of the traffic plan rather than relying on the leaflet. An account of another scheme at https://roadwatch.example/reports/haul-routes is not evidence about Brindlewick, so I have not based this objection on it. For comparison, the district highways team can be contacted at its office, Unit 4, Larch Exchange, Dunfell, DF2 8LN. The drawings should be tested against the width of the actual road and the deliveries that already use it.

Finally, please do not assume that a short closure is harmless to a sole trader. I still have my outstanding business loan of £18,400 to pay, regardless of whether a customer can get to the workshop to inspect a job. I am not seeking compensation through this letter. I want the examination to secure an alternative compound access if possible, and otherwise a binding traffic schedule, a staffed junction, a dust and mud-cleaning regime, and a named contact who can resolve an obstruction immediately. I would be grateful if this letter could be placed with the traffic representations.

Yours faithfully,

E. Pell — Pell & Plane Joinery, proprietor

Further note to my letter: construction access and the working day

Dear Examining Authority,

I am Ewan Pell, a self-employed joiner trading as Pell & Plane Joinery. I am sending this further note because the access drawing discussed at the drop-in does not show what happens when a delivery vehicle meets a customer van outside a working home. My workshop is at 18 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP. That is also my family’s home, not an industrial yard with another entrance at the back. I have lived in this part of Dunfell for over 40 years, but the proposed construction arrangement would be quite unlike the ordinary traffic we have managed during that time.

The plan identifies a route past Bracken Fold to the southern compound. Drawing ML-TR-042 shows a passing place, but it appears to be measured from the edge of the tarmac rather than the usable width between the hedge and the drainage lip. Please ask Marrin Link Infrastructure Ltd to demonstrate how a laden tipper and an incoming timber delivery would pass there without either mounting the verge or stopping across a driveway. The compound itself is a development site, so I do not object to its address being published. What matters is the trip from that site to the wider road.

My timber merchant generally gives me a morning rather than a precise arrival time. Once the driver has unloaded, I need room to turn sheet material into the workshop; leaving it on the roadside in wet weather can spoil a whole order. I also have customers bringing doors for repair. These are not large numbers of trips, but they cannot all be rearranged around an unpublished convoy. If a bank of lorries is released at 8.30, a promise to keep the carriageway ‘open’ is not much use when nobody can pull in. A closure notice put up the evening before would be particularly difficult for a person working alone.

My daughter Orla Pell, aged 11, walks towards the school bus stop at roughly the time the draft schedule shows vehicles entering the lane. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide where any particular child should walk. I am asking for a supervised crossing arrangement at the junction, with an actual person present at the times specified in the construction traffic management plan. Orla has epilepsy, so an unexpected wait beside reversing vehicles is an additional concern for our household. Noise and worry affect my sleep too, although that is not the basis of my objection.

The neighbour whose gate is nearest the proposed holding point, Mrs Tilda Fenn, at 20 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP, is not making a representation as far as I know. I have not supplied a statement on her behalf. She told me that a driver already has to pause opposite her gate when the refuse lorry comes through. I mention the conversation only to explain why a swept-path exercise should include the gates and bins on the ground, rather than an empty-road photograph. Please do not treat her name or address as permission to contact her.

At the project drop-in, Ms Lysa Norr of Hushward Traffic Ltd showed me the preliminary routing sheet. I appreciated her taking the time, but the sheet had a one-way arrow where drivers currently meet traffic coming the other way. I emailed the project mailbox, traffic@marrinlink.example, afterwards and received the standard acknowledgement. The copy sent from my own business address was ewan.pell@pellandplane.example, and my mobile is 07700 914 286 if the case team needs to clarify what I drew on the sheet. I would rather any published version of this note did not expose those personal contact details.

Cllr Faye Tress raised the timing of compound movements at the parish meeting on 14 October 2026. The answer given there was that the contractor could ‘manage peaks locally’. That needs turning into limits which a resident can check. I suggest a maximum number of heavy-vehicle movements per hour, no queuing on Bracken Fold, and a prohibition on arriving before the staffed junction is operating. There should also be a telephone number for a shared traffic desk, not merely an instruction to ask whichever banksman happens to be nearest. If the route is blocked, the desk must have authority to hold the next vehicles at the compound.

Mud is not a cosmetic issue for me. Sawdust and grit tracked into a customer’s finished cabinet mean sanding it again. The proposed wheel wash is shown inside the compound boundary, but the road from its exit to our lane needs inspecting after rain, with cleaning recorded. I photographed a vehicle parked across my loading space last month; its registration was GX26 VPM. It was not identified to me as a project vehicle, and I am not alleging that it was one. It simply illustrates how little spare width exists when even one driver stops in the wrong place.

I have read the general advice at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects and understand that this examination is considering the proposed controls, not settling an individual delivery dispute. I also found a local discussion page at https://dunfell-lanes.example/compound-traffic, but its photographs are not survey evidence. Please rely instead on measured widths and on a trial with representative vehicles, witnessed at the hours the compound would actually operate.

One ecological point should not get lost in the traffic discussion. Badger activity has been noted in Bracken Wood, which is a broad area and tells drivers nothing useful about an individual sett. The survey appendix, however, marks a badger sett at the foot of the second ash immediately east of field gate G7 on Bracken Fold. That precise description should not appear in a publicly available traffic plan. Protecting the verge from overrunning would help both wildlife and road users without publishing a location that could put the sett at risk.

For completeness, my personal finances make a lost week of workshop access difficult: the next repayment on my business loan is £412. I give that figure to explain the practical urgency, not to ask the Examining Authority to assess my accounts. Please secure an alternative access if it is feasible. If it is not, I ask for enforceable hours, no roadside holding, a staffed junction, prompt road cleaning and a traffic contact able to act while an obstruction is happening. Those are modest protections for a route that still has to serve the people already using it.

Yours faithfully,

E. Pell
Pell & Plane Joinery, proprietor

SUPPLEMENTARY NOTE TO MY LETTER ON CONSTRUCTION TRAFFIC
Marrin Link Road examination
21 October 2026

From: Ewan Pell
Pell & Plane Joinery
18 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP

I am sending this as a short addendum to my objection because the revised construction traffic note has come out since I wrote the main letter. I am a self-employed joiner and Pell & Plane Joinery operates from my home, not from a separate industrial unit. Vans bringing boards and collecting finished work have to get to my gate. The new drawing still shows construction vehicles using Bracken Fold but does not show what happens when a delivery vehicle meets one coming the other way.

My van, registration QZ26 KLM, is usually loaded in the morning. I cannot simply park it round the corner while lorries pass: carrying kitchen units along the pavement would put them at risk of damage and block the pavement for everybody else. The route plan calls the stretch outside my property a ‘passing opportunity’. It is also where I need to open my gates. Please do not count a private entrance as spare road width unless its owner has agreed to its use, and I have not.

The drawing appears to measure the carriageway but not the space needed for people getting out of vehicles. On 14 October I watched two ordinary delivery vans pass there. One had to stop, and the driver of the other mounted the verge. That was without a construction convoy or a person walking to the bus stop. It is a small observation, not a traffic survey, but it is exactly the situation the construction plan needs to deal with.

Mrs Tilda Fenn at 20 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP is not making a representation as far as I know. I mention the house only because it faces the bend shown on drawing CT-07. Please do not treat this as permission to contact my neighbour. The revised swept-path line runs across the strip where the household puts its bins on collection day. If bins are moved, the contractor ought to tell residents beforehand where they are meant to go, rather than leaving the collection crew to sort it out.

At the project drop-in, Ms Lysa Norr of Hushward Traffic Ltd told me that a banksman could be arranged ‘if there was a problem’. I do not think an arrangement that starts after somebody rings up about a blocked road is enough. I would like the banksman, or another trained traffic marshal, to be there for each planned movement of the longest loads. I understand that the applicant cannot promise a clear road every minute, but it can publish an arrival window and prevent vehicles waiting on Bracken Fold while the compound gate is shut.

Cllr Faye Tress raised the school-run timing at the parish meeting. That was a useful point, although the issue is wider than the school run. My daughter, Orla Pell, is 11 and walks with me to the bus stop on some mornings. She has diagnosed asthma. I am not claiming that the scheme will cause a medical problem; I am asking for the dust controls and road cleaning in the draft plan to be made specific enough to check. ‘As required’ does not say who decides, or how quickly a muddy road will be cleaned after a complaint.

I have also been diagnosed with tinnitus. A marshal shouting instructions or lorries sounding reversing alarms outside the workshop for long periods would make concentration difficult, although I accept that warning devices are needed for safety. My objection is principally about safe access, not a request to remove alarms. I have felt stressed by the uncertainty, but that feeling is not the basis on which I ask the Examining Authority to decide the application.

There is another practical cost which may not be obvious from the drawings. My personal overdraft currently stands at £1,180, so a missed installation slot is not something I can absorb easily. I am not asking for my private accounts to be discussed in the examination. I give the figure to explain why a contractor telling me at 8 am that the road will be shut ‘for a bit’ would be a serious problem. If a closure is needed, I need written notice, a realistic end time and a named person with authority to let booked trade deliveries through when it is safe.

The revised ecology sheet refers to badgers in Bracken Wood and bats along the Bracken Fold hedgerow. Those broad descriptions are sufficient for this public letter. My concern remains the repeated overrunning of the verge, not the publication of any protected animal’s location. The applicant could put temporary edge protection in place and have the ecological clerk of works inspect it after heavy vehicle movements. That would be more useful than another general statement that drivers will take care.

I have seen a copy of a local traffic count at www.dunfellledger.invalid/road-counts, but I cannot tell whether its figures include trade deliveries. The examination documents at www.gov.uk/government/collections/marrin-link-road-examination should be the basis for the decision. If Marrin Link Infrastructure Ltd relies on a count to dismiss residents’ observations, please ask it to state the count dates, hours and vehicle classes plainly. Questions could be sent to the project mailbox, planning@marrinlink.invalid; my own work address is ewan.pell@pellandplane.invalid and my direct number is 01632 960 482, but I would prefer substantive answers to appear on the examination website so everyone can see them.

I still object to the proposed use of Bracken Fold without an enforceable access and traffic arrangement. I would welcome a revised plan showing where large vehicles wait, who controls the bend, how household collections continue and what residents do when the agreed arrangements fail in practice. These are not reasons to stop every construction vehicle. They are reasons to settle the details before the first one arrives.

Yours faithfully,

E. Pell
Pell & Plane Joinery, proprietor

Further letter concerning construction traffic
Marrin Link Road Examination — reference ML/2026/041
21 October 2026

Dear Examining Authority,

I wrote earlier about the proposed use of Bracken Fold by construction vehicles. I am sending this further note because the latest traffic drawing appears to show a holding area but does not say how a driver arriving before the gate opens would reach it. I am Ewan Pell, the proprietor of Pell & Plane Joinery. My workshop is at my home, 18 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP, and the delivery doors face the road shown as a possible route to the compound. This is a home as well as a place of work; I cannot simply move the workshop for the construction period.

I make fitted cupboards and repair staircases. Sheet timber comes in on a small flatbed, usually once or twice a week, and I sometimes load a finished job into my van before the school run. A lorry waiting opposite the doors would leave no room to turn a board safely. It is not enough to say that construction deliveries will be booked: the driver who is early, lost, or refused entry is the one who will be outside my gate. Please put a dimensioned swept-path drawing in the examination library showing both my flatbed and an HGV at the bend, rather than treating the width on the plan as usable width all the way along.

The photographs I submitted with my first letter show the bend by Bracken Fold Orchard in ordinary daylight. They do not show the bins set out on collection morning, or the cars briefly stopped when children are collected. My daughter, Orla Pell, aged 11, walks along that stretch to meet her friend. I am not asking for her journey to be treated as more important than anyone else's. I am asking how a marshal stationed at the compound entrance, out of sight of the bend, could deal with a child already on the footway when a vehicle starts to reverse. The note saying 'no reversing on the public highway' needs an exception procedure, a contact number and a record of each occasion it happens.

There is also an ordinary access issue at the lower end of the fold. Mrs Tilda Fenn of 20 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP is not making a representation, as far as I know. A refuse vehicle has to stop near that house because it cannot turn at the closed gate. I mention this to explain the physical pinch point, not to speak for my neighbour. If the applicant intends to move the collection point, it should show where it goes and who tells households, including those not using the examination website.

At the project drop-in, Ms Lysa Norr of Hushward Traffic Ltd showed me a sketch with a blue arrow indicating that vehicles would approach from the bypass. The drawing now in the library has arrows at both ends of Bracken Fold. I may have misunderstood the sketch, so I ask Marrin Link Infrastructure Ltd to say whether the permitted approach has changed, and to identify the drawing that a haulier will actually receive. A general promise to brief drivers does not answer that. Nor does a sign at the bypass help a driver who has already passed it.

Cllr Faye Tress raised the start time for deliveries at the parish meeting. I support the request for a stated first arrival time, not just hours during which work may take place. A queue forming at 06:45 would affect households even if the gate did not open until 07:30. I have lived here for over 20 years and am used to farm vehicles using the lane; it is the prospect of repeated arrivals without somewhere to wait that concerns me. I have had poor sleep worrying about access to the workshop, but that is not a claim that every journey on this road causes harm.

For completeness, I have asthma, and dusty idling vehicles immediately outside the workshop doors would make it difficult for me to work there. I understand that a traffic plan cannot promise no dust at all. It can require engines to be switched off, specify where a rejected vehicle goes, and give the site manager authority to stop deliveries if the holding area is full. P.S. — supplementary note on construction traffic
Marrin Link Road examination
21 October 2026

I am adding this after signing because the access photograph mentioned in my letter does not show what happens when two vehicles meet at the bend. I am Ewan Pell, the proprietor of Pell & Plane Joinery, and I work from home at 18 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP. My workshop is behind the house. Timber deliveries, customers collecting finished doors and my own trips out to fitting jobs all use the same narrow entrance. The concern is not that I should have priority over everybody else. It is that a traffic plan based only on whether an HGV can turn the corner will miss the ordinary movements that already take place there.

On a typical working morning a supplier may arrive without an exact appointment, because the van has several drops to make. If a construction lorry is waiting opposite my gate, the supplier cannot pull in safely and cannot simply go round the block. The route drawing ought to mark waiting places as well as the route itself, and it should state that drivers must not use a residential entrance as an informal passing bay. Please do not put this down as a request for compensation. I am asking for a rule the banksman and driver can understand before the first delivery is made.

The photographs were taken from my entrance and from the public pavement. I have not photographed anybody through a window. The entrance at 20 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP belongs to Mrs Tilda Fenn, who is not making a representation as far as I know. It is shown only because the two entrances sit close together and a lorry waiting across one will usually obstruct the other. I do not think it would be fair to ask that household to negotiate separately with every contractor. A single published access procedure would be better for both houses.

I attended the project drop-in and spoke to Ms Lysa Norr of Hushward Traffic Ltd about deliveries arriving before the advertised working hours. I was told the contractor could deal with that through instructions to drivers, but I have not found the instruction in the submitted traffic papers. I may have missed it. If it exists, please give its document number and the paragraph rather than another general assurance. Cllr Faye Tress also raised the timing of construction vehicles at the parish meeting. That was a sensible question, not a proposal to shut the road to all other users.

There is a school-bound pedestrian movement past my gate. My daughter Orla Pell, aged 11, sometimes walks that way. I mention this to explain why a marshal should check the pavement before waving a lorry across it, not to suggest that my family requires a special arrangement. A marshal stationed only at the compound gate will not be able to see around the bend. A temporary sign saying 'pedestrians have priority' is not the same as a person being able to stop a reversing vehicle. If the applicant proposes banksmen, the plan should say where they will stand and how they will communicate with drivers when the pavement is occupied.

Noise is another practical issue, though I accept there will be some disturbance while a road is built. I have had poor sleep when vehicles idle outside, and I worry about what months of it will do to our wellbeing. Those are reasons to prevent avoidable idling, rather than reasons to prohibit construction. My daughter has asthma, so I would particularly welcome a clear commitment that engines will be switched off during a hold-up, except where running them is necessary for safety or equipment. A simple record of complaints and the action taken would let residents see whether that commitment is working.

Please keep the access arrangement separate from any discussion of my accounts. My outstanding personal loan of £7,450 is not a measure of the road's effects on the business, and I have not asked the Examining Authority to assess it. The relevant evidence is the width of the entrance, the frequency of deliveries and whether customers can reach the workshop without being directed into a queue of site traffic. Marrin Link Infrastructure Ltd can check those matters on site. If it wants a visit, I can make time provided the appointment is agreed first, as I cannot leave tools and an unfinished job unattended whenever a contractor calls.

For correspondence, my personal email is ewan.pell@example.org and my mobile is 07700 900654; please do not put either on a public traffic drawing. The project mailbox planning@marrinlink.example is a better place for general updates. At the drop-in I was also given lysa.norr@hushwardtraffic.example as an individual contact, but a route query should not depend on one employee being available. A shared mailbox, a telephone contact during deliveries and an escalation step for a blocked entrance would be more reliable. I looked at the examination timetable at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate and at a resident's unofficial map at https://routewatch.example.org/marrin-bend; the latter is useful for orientation but should not replace the applicant's controlled drawing.

Lastly, the note about badger signs around Birchwhistle Wood in my earlier letter was not an invitation to publish a more detailed wildlife location alongside the haul-road plan. An ecologist can deal with that separately. For this traffic note I ask for three things: a scaled drawing showing where vehicles may wait; enforceable arrival and idling instructions; and a procedure that a resident or delivery driver can use when an entrance is blocked. If those are provided before works start, there is a reasonable prospect of keeping Bracken Fold usable for everyone.

Ewan Pell

Supplementary technical note: construction access and controls

This note follows my request for a scaled drawing of vehicle waiting areas and a workable procedure for blocked entrances. The points below concern the construction arrangements for the Marrin Link Road, rather than the principle of the road. They should be capable of being checked against the final Construction Traffic Management Plan (CTMP) before the first haul movements take place.

The current access drawing shows a route between the temporary compound and the B417 Marrin Road, with Bracken Fold marked as a local access road. It does not clearly distinguish a permitted delivery route from an emergency diversion route. That distinction matters. A driver following a sat-nav instruction could otherwise treat the shorter route through Dunfell as available whenever the compound gate is busy. The CTMP should contain one numbered route plan, at a readable scale, with arrows for each direction of travel and an explicit list of roads not to be used by construction HGVs. The same revision number should appear on the plan supplied to hauliers and on the version available for inspection.

A swept-path assessment is also needed at the compound entrance and at the B417 Marrin Road junction. A line showing that one articulated vehicle can turn is not enough if another vehicle is approaching. The assessment ought to show the design vehicle, vehicle dimensions, assumed kerb clearance, opposing traffic movements and any area that has to remain clear. Where the turning envelope crosses the opposing lane, the CTMP should explain who stops traffic, how that person communicates with the gate and what happens if a vehicle arrives outside its allocated slot. No vehicle should be sent to circle the local roads while a slot becomes free.

The traffic forecast in the Environmental Statement reports daily two-way HGV totals. Daily averages are useful for network modelling but are a poor test of a narrow road during an active delivery hour. The applicant, Marrin Link Infrastructure Ltd, should publish an hourly arrival profile for each main construction phase, including the peak earthworks period and any overlap with utility diversions. It should distinguish bulk-material trips from abnormal loads and waste movements. If loads are rescheduled following rain or a plant breakdown, the forecast peak may move rather than disappear. A short sensitivity test for that bunching would make the conclusions more reliable.

Waiting space should be demonstrated on the compound layout, not assumed to exist because the gate is set back. The drawing needs to identify the usable length behind the gate, pedestrian crossing points, barriers, turning space and the position of any wheel-wash queue. The capacity calculation should allow for a vehicle stopped at the wash while the next vehicle waits clear of the public highway. If there is no room for both, arrivals must be metered from a designated off-road holding area. A lay-by on B417 Marrin Road should not be described as a holding area unless its dimensions, legal status and effect on other traffic have been assessed.

The application material says that temporary signals may be used during tie-in works. The location and duration of each signal phase should be specified in the programme, including the maximum expected queue length in both directions. Those predictions should be tested alongside the construction arrival profile rather than against background traffic alone. The CTMP should say when the signals will be removed, how access will be maintained during a failure and which activity must stop if queues reach the compound junction. A statement that operatives will monitor conditions is not a measurable control without a threshold and a recorded response.

Drainage is relevant to this access arrangement. Runoff from the hardstanding must not be directed towards Bracken Fold or allowed to carry sediment into the roadside grips. The compound plan should show levels, the line of the temporary drainage system, the position of the wheel wash and the point at which collected water is treated or removed. The drainage detail should be coordinated with the traffic drawing: a bund, sump or maintenance vehicle must not occupy the space counted as HGV waiting capacity. The temporary works should also have an inspection schedule after heavy rainfall, with a means of recording defects and the date of repair.

For landscape purposes, the compound edge facing Birchwhistle Wood is likely to look different during winter works from the screening shown in the summer visualisations. Temporary lighting is the more immediate issue. The final lighting schedule should give column positions, mounting heights, aiming angles and hours of operation, with an isolux plan showing spill beyond the working area. Badger signs have been recorded around Birchwhistle Wood; that is a general ecological constraint, not a reason to place a precise wildlife location on a public haul-road drawing. Ecological controls can be documented separately without weakening the requirement for a usable traffic plan.

There also needs to be a single method for checking compliance. Gate logs could record booked and actual arrival times, vehicle type, route instruction issued and any refusal of entry. Monthly summaries should report out-of-slot arrivals, occasions when the highway was obstructed, complaints about idling and the corrective action taken. The summary need not contain driver details. It should be available through the project document library so that the traffic commitments can be compared with what happens during construction.

These requests do not require a fresh route assessment from the beginning. They require the assumptions already used in the Environmental Statement to be carried through into drawings, thresholds and site instructions. If the CTMP, compound layout and temporary drainage plan contradict one another, the approved controls will be difficult to operate. I ask the Examining Authority to require a coordinated set of final plans, with a clear revision history, before the relevant construction phase starts.

Further technical comments on the construction controls

I have looked again at the proposed construction sequence for the Marrin Link Road, in particular the relationship between the temporary compound, the haul-road tie-in and the drainage works. The documents give useful individual descriptions of these activities, but it is still not clear which layout will apply when two activities overlap. That matters because a swept-path drawing prepared for an empty compound does not show whether a vehicle can make the same turn while drainage materials are being stored beside the access. The final construction traffic management plan (CTMP) should include a drawing for each phase, not just a single drawing labelled ‘typical arrangement’.

For the northern access, the assessment assumes that construction vehicles will approach from Dunfell Relief Road and turn into the compound without waiting on the carriageway. The junction drawing should be checked against the largest vehicle actually expected during each phase, including any vehicle delivering precast culvert sections. It should show the available stacking length inside the gate, the gate’s operating position and the space kept clear for vehicles leaving the site. A swept path that uses the whole width of the access may be acceptable on paper but is of little value if a temporary fence or wheel-wash unit occupies part of that width. Any change to the compound entrance should trigger a fresh check before it is used.

The traffic tables also need to distinguish daily totals from the busiest hour. An average of several deliveries across a day cannot demonstrate that there will be no queue if most deliveries arrive together at the start of a shift. I suggest that Marrin Link Infrastructure Ltd set a maximum number of arrivals in a rolling one-hour period for each access, with a booking system for larger loads. The limit should appear in the CTMP and in the instructions given to suppliers. There should also be a procedure for turning away an unbooked vehicle without directing it to wait on Bracken Fold or another local street.

The effect of construction traffic on the Dunfell Relief Road roundabout has been assessed using the forecast network at an assumed opening year. The updated assessment should state whether the same background growth, signal settings and committed developments have been used consistently for the road scheme and the construction phase. If a junction is predicted to operate close to capacity, a small change in the assumed arrival pattern could make a noticeable difference. A sensitivity run with the busiest construction hour coinciding with the network peak would be more informative than a further annual-average figure. The inputs and outputs should be supplied in a form that allows the highway authority to repeat that check.

There is a similar sequencing point in the surface-water material. The temporary drainage plan shows interception ditches along the haul route, whereas the compound drawing shows stockpiles in approximately the same corridor. The drawings should identify where the ditch will go during that phase, where it will discharge, and how runoff will be managed before the permanent attenuation basin is available. Referring to the completed drainage system does not answer what happens during the first weeks of earthworks. A rainfall response procedure should identify the inspection frequency for silt controls and the point at which work in an exposed area must pause.

I would also welcome a clearer distinction between clean water and water from working areas. The present wording says that runoff will be ‘managed appropriately’, but does not identify which temporary features are treatment measures and which are only conveyance routes. The final plan should mark the relevant catchments, temporary storage capacity, overflow routes and discharge points on one drawing. It should show how those features change as the cuttings are excavated. This would make it possible to check whether the proposed controls still work if one section is built out of the order illustrated in the Environmental Statement.

The landscape drawings for the eastern embankment appear to show the finished planting after establishment. For a useful construction-phase comparison, the Examining Authority should also receive a view of the bare earthworks and temporary lighting from the public footpath by Alder Mere. The lighting assessment should specify mounting heights, directions and hours of use for the compound, rather than relying on a general commitment to prevent spill. These details could be secured through the same phase drawings as the traffic and drainage controls, so that a change in compound position is assessed across all three topics.

The ecological material refers to bat activity around Alder Mere Wood and general badger signs in the wider survey area. Those are useful descriptions of survey coverage, not a reason to leave the construction boundary uncertain. The plans can show exclusion fencing, dark corridors and the limits of vegetation clearance without publishing precise protected-species locations. Where a boundary or lighting arrangement changes, the ecological clerk’s check should take place before the revised layout is used. That is a practical hold point, rather than a request for an open-ended further survey.

Finally, the requirements in the draft development consent order should say what is to be approved, by whom, and at what stage. ‘Substantially in accordance with’ a drawing is difficult to apply when several drawings use different compound edges. I suggest a schedule identifying the controlling revision of each plan, followed by a requirement for coordinated phase drawings before works start in that phase. This would be consistent with the construction-management approach described in the Dunfell Local Transport Framework, but would make the controls testable on site. The purpose is not to stop reasonable changes during construction. It is to ensure that a change to one discipline is checked against the others before it becomes the working arrangement.

Supplementary note to my written representation
Marrin Link Road — construction traffic at Bracken Fold
21 October 2026

From: Ewan Pell, Pell & Plane Joinery
Home and workshop: 18 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP
Interested Party reference: MLR-IP-0427
Application reference: MLR/2026/04

I am sending this note because, after finishing my comments on the draft requirements, I realised I had not explained properly what a working day at this address looks like. I am a self-employed joiner. The workshop is at the back of my home, not on an industrial estate, and deliveries and collections have to use the same short frontage as everyone else in the fold. I object to the proposed construction traffic arrangement for the Marrin Link Road unless it is changed and made enforceable. I am not objecting to the road just because a lorry might pass my house.

The drawings appear to send vehicles for the South Tern Compound along Old Kiln Lane and then past the entrance to Bracken Fold. One plan shows the compound gate set back from the lane; another seems to put the waiting area by the gate itself. If a tipper arrives early, the driver cannot magic up space that is not there. The likely result is a queue on the lane, with vans trying to get round it. The transport assessment counts movements across an hour, but an average does not tell you what happens when three loads arrive within ten minutes and a timber delivery is trying to leave the fold. Please show the maximum arrivals in any fifteen-minute period, not only the daily total.

I normally load boards into my van between 7.15 and 8.00. Some boards are long and I have to pull forward before I can turn safely. On two or three mornings a week a supplier brings sheet material; that vehicle is bigger than my van and cannot reverse all the way up the fold. The current traffic-management wording says deliveries will be ‘timed to avoid peak periods’, but it does not define the period or say what happens if a subcontractor turns up regardless. A booking system should include a holding location away from homes, instructions to drivers, and a record the highway authority can inspect. It should expressly prohibit waiting or reversing at the Bracken Fold junction.

My daughter, Orla Pell, aged 11, walks to the school bus stop on Old Kiln Lane. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide where one child may walk. I mention this because the crossing point used by families is just beyond the bend and is absent from the contractor's route sketch. Orla Pell has diagnosed asthma, so dust control is a particular concern for our household as well as a normal construction obligation. I have felt anxious about the proposed traffic, but that feeling is not a substitute for evidence about the route. The applicant should count pedestrians at the bus stop in term time and assess the bend with a laden vehicle, rather than relying on a desktop swept-path drawing alone.

At the drop-in, Ms Lysa Norr of Hushward Traffic Ltd said the marshals would be there ‘when needed’. That was a conversation, not a published undertaking, and I cannot find a commitment to a marshal at the compound gate during the morning delivery window. Cllr Faye Tress raised the timing of compound traffic at the parish meeting too. The answer then was that details would come later. Later is fine for choosing a contractor; it is not fine for deciding whether the route can work at all. A marshal cannot resolve a queue unless the plan also says where excess vehicles go.

The effect is not only inconvenience. In September I lost £1,840 of my own earnings when access to the workshop was blocked during unrelated utility works and I had to rearrange fitted-kitchen jobs. I give that figure to explain why ‘occasional short delays’ can matter to a sole trader; I am not claiming it as a forecast of compensation from this project. Mrs Tilda Fenn at 20 Bracken Fold, Dunfell, DF3 6QP has asked me whether emergency access would be kept clear. Mrs Tilda Fenn is not making a representation and I do not speak for that household. The question is a sensible one and the traffic plan should answer it without expecting residents to phone a site manager each time.

There is also a small ecology point. Badger setts have been recorded in Alder Copse, which is too broad a description to guide a driver. My concern is that temporary parking will spread off the authorised compound. The ecological clerk's confidential working plan should account for the sett entrance in the bank 14 metres north of the third field gate on Old Kiln Lane, opposite the disused lime shed. That detail does not need to go on public driver notices; those notices simply need to say where parking is permitted. The publicly discussed £2.4 million landscape budget would be better protected by keeping construction vehicles within the agreed boundary from day one.

I ask for a revised construction traffic management plan to be submitted before compound works begin, with the peak-arrival figures, bus-stop assessment, booking and holding arrangements, and a clear drawing of the gate and no-waiting area. It should state who approves changes and how residents are told before a route or working hour changes. A monthly complaints total is not enough: if access is blocked on Tuesday morning, the remedy must be available on Tuesday morning.

For contact about this representation, please use 07700 900462 or ewan.pell@pellplane.example. The project mailbox traffic@marrinlink.example is useful for general notices but should not replace a named duty contact during deliveries. I have read the general guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects and the applicant's submitted plans. I can attend a site walk if the Examining Authority considers one helpful, though I would need the time agreed around booked work.

Yours faithfully,
Ewan Pell

Further comments on the transport and drainage documents

I have looked again at the transport model submitted by Marrin Link Infrastructure Ltd. The comparison in Table 6.4 is between an average weekday in the 2028 opening year and the same forecast year without the scheme. That is useful, but it does not show what happens during the temporary traffic-management stages. In particular, Stage 2 diverts eastbound traffic from the Marrin Road junction onto Lowmere Lane while the new bridge deck is lifted. The construction traffic management plan should include a separate assignment for that stage, with queue lengths at the Lowmere Lane / Station Road junction reported in vehicles as well as minutes. A percentage change in journey time is difficult to check against what the junction can physically hold.

The drawing titled General Arrangement Sheet 14 shows the haul access immediately before the existing bend on Lowmere Lane. The swept-path plot appears to assume that no vehicle is waiting to turn right into the access. Please test one articulated delivery vehicle entering while another is leaving, with the proposed temporary signals operating and with the pedestrian refuge retained. If this cannot be done inside the highway boundary, the delivery schedule should prohibit opposing movements rather than rely on drivers sorting it out at the gate. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should specify the trigger for suspending deliveries if queues reach the Station Road junction.

There is also a drainage point which deserves an answer before the final design is fixed. The Flood Risk Assessment puts the attenuation basin on the south side of the link, but the outfall route on Drainage Plan DP-07 crosses the area shown as the temporary topsoil store. The construction sequence needs to say whether the outfall will be installed before that store is formed. Otherwise the temporary works may leave runoff from the stripped ground discharging towards the Lowmere Lane ditch without the proposed treatment train in place. A simple phasing drawing showing temporary cut-off drains, the basin commissioning date and responsibility for maintaining silt controls would be more informative than a general commitment to good practice.

For landscape matters, the cross-sections use planting at its anticipated mature height in some of the viewpoint illustrations. The Examining Authority should also have equivalent year-one views from the Station Road footway and the public path beside North Wold Field. Screening that takes ten or more years to establish is not mitigation for the opening year. I am not asking for a different alignment on the basis of these points. I am asking for the traffic tests, drainage sequence and early-year visual material to be secured in the relevant requirements, with the updated drawings available for examination before those requirements are settled.

The draft Construction Traffic Management Plan still treats the Station Road junction as if all delivery vehicles arrive at a steady hourly rate. That does not test the short queues likely when the morning shift starts and aggregate lorries overlap. Marrin Link Infrastructure Ltd should provide a sensitivity run showing the busiest 15-minute period, with turning counts separated from through traffic. The results should identify whether temporary signals are needed and who would be responsible for checking queue lengths during construction.

There is a similar gap in the drainage sequence. Drawing DCO-DR-07 shows the permanent basin serving the eastern cutting, but the programme does not say what intercepts runoff while that basin is being built. A temporary settlement arrangement should be shown on a phasing plan, with a clear trigger for bringing the permanent system into use. These are practical details, not objections to the principle of the Marrin Link Road, and they should be resolved before the construction requirements are approved.

text:
MEREFOLD LAND & LEGAL LLP
Suite 4, Foundry Exchange, 18 Quay Lane, Ellindale, EL4 7QJ
Main office: 01632 960 400 | planning@merefoldlegal.example

Elena Voss | Land and compensation team
Direct dial: 01632 960 412
Email: elena.voss@merefoldlegal.example

21 October 2026

By email to the Planning Inspectorate case team

Dear Examining Authority,

Fenmere Link Railway Order (EN012345)
Deadline 4 submission on behalf of Tamsin Orr: compulsory acquisition of land at Hawthorn End Farm
Interested Party reference: IP-348271

We act for Tamsin Orr, the owner and occupier of Hawthorn End Farm. This letter responds to the Applicant's revised Book of Reference and the note on access arrangements filed at Deadline 3. It is intended as a written representation in the examination, not as an objection to a railway in principle. The concern is whether the powers sought over this particular holding are no wider than reasonably needed, and whether the working farm can continue to operate during construction.

For correspondence concerning the land interest, our client's residential address is 4 Wold Bank Lane, Kelwick, KW3 8ND. Please use this office for examination correspondence rather than writing to the house. The application site itself is identified on the plans as plot 14/2, the eastern part of Hawthorn End Farm beside Wold Bank Lane. Those plan references should be retained in any published version of this submission so that the point can be understood.

Plot 14/2 is shown for permanent acquisition, although the Applicant's construction drawing appears to use most of it only as a temporary turning area. The strip beside the drainage ditch is needed for access between the yard and the north fields. Moving a vehicle across the proposed railway access would be particularly difficult during the autumn lift, when trailers need to turn without reversing onto the public road. The present wording would allow the whole plot to be fenced indefinitely. We ask for a marked-up plan distinguishing the land required for the permanent works from temporary working land, and for the permanent acquisition limit to be pulled back accordingly. A promise to discuss the detail after consent is not an adequate substitute for a limit on the Order powers.

The revised Book of Reference also describes the rights sought over plot 14/4 as a right of passage. In the draft Order that right appears broad enough to permit storage of plant and spoil. These are not the same thing in practical terms. If storage is intended, it should be stated, assessed and time-limited; if it is not, the drafting should expressly exclude it. Our client has been farming here for over 40 years and knows the turning constraints, but the issue does not depend on accepting any particular account of past use. A swept-path drawing for the largest construction vehicle would help everybody test the proposal.

At the open-floor hearing, Cllr Ada Bell asked whether an emergency farm crossing could remain available whenever the eastern gate is closed. That is a sensible question which the Deadline 3 note does not answer. The note refers instead to a temporary route through North Spinney, without saying who will maintain its surface or how livestock movements will be separated from construction traffic. Please could the Applicant identify the proposed gate positions, hours of closure, and the person with authority to authorise an urgent crossing. We do not seek a general veto over construction activity; we seek an arrangement that can actually be used on a wet weekday when the site manager is elsewhere.

A neighbouring occupier, Milo Crewe, mentioned at a private farm access discussion that the ditch backs up after sustained rain. Milo Crewe is not a participant in this examination, and we mention the observation only to explain why an untested temporary route across the ditch is a poor fallback. The Applicant should provide the culvert dimensions and the maintenance responsibility in the final drainage schedule. The Land Drainage Statement refers to badger activity in North Spinney; that is a broad habitat reference, not a reason to publish a precise wildlife location. Our client's ecological adviser separately recorded a sett in the small bank immediately behind gate G3 on plot 14/2, 9 metres north of the culvert. That location should be treated confidentially when the crossing design is reviewed.

There is a personal dimension to the proposed disruption, although the compulsory acquisition case must stand on its planning merits. Our client is 71 and has rheumatoid arthritis. The repeated changes to the access drawings have caused poor sleep and considerable worry. We provide that context to explain the need for a clear, written access protocol, not to suggest that normal examination scrutiny should be dispensed with. Our client has also supplied us, in confidence, with an outstanding personal mortgage balance of £186,400; it should not be copied into any public land valuation table. By contrast, the Applicant's published estimate of £2.1 million for the acquisition and reinstatement package is a project cost and can properly be discussed in the examination.

We have asked the Applicant for a drawing showing the permanent fence line, a schedule of temporary occupation dates, and an undertaking about reinstating field drains before land is handed back. The response so far directs us to the general construction code. That code is useful, but it does not identify this farm's two access points or say what happens if both are obstructed on the same day. We would welcome a short issue-specific meeting and will circulate agreed notes through the examination mailbox, rather than asking the ExA to resolve an engineering detail without the necessary drawing.

For completeness, the project documents are available on the Applicant's website at https://fenmere-link.example/documents and the examination timetable is on https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects-the-examination. An unrelated field-drainage article previously forwarded to us, https://www.ruralfieldnotes.example/culverts, is not relied upon as evidence. The request above rests on the submitted plans and on conditions that can be checked on the holding.

We ask the Examining Authority to require a response to these points before the close of the examination, with any revised plan numbered and dated. Our client remains willing to agree proportionate rights, provided that the agreement reflects the land actually required and safeguards a workable route to the north fields.

Yours faithfully,

Elena Voss
Land and compensation team | Merefold Land & Legal LLP
Pronouns: she/her
For and on behalf of Tamsin Orr

Annex 1 — Technical observations on access, drainage and construction sequencing

This annex develops the request in the covering submission for a numbered, dated revision of the access plan. It concerns the works shown at the northern edge of the holding and the proposed connection to Mere Lane. It does not propose an alternative railway alignment. The issue is whether the rights sought under the Fenmere Link Railway Order correspond to the access and drainage arrangements that will be available once the Fenmere Link Railway is built.

1. Access geometry and traffic assumptions

The submitted construction traffic note treats the Mere Lane access as a minor agricultural entrance. Its swept-path drawing, however, shows a vehicle entering from the east and leaving to the west; it does not show the reverse movements or a vehicle meeting an oncoming vehicle at the gate. Those omissions matter because the temporary bellmouth is also shown as serving deliveries to the northern works compound. The same drawing appears in two places with different gate positions. The Applicant should confirm which position has been modelled and provide one controlled drawing for the examination record.

A revised drawing should show the carriageway edge, verge, ditch, gate, visibility splays and the full turning envelope, rather than a vehicle outline alone. It should distinguish construction use from the permanent agricultural access. The construction route is described as temporary, but the proposed permanent right of way appears to follow part of it. If the temporary surface is to be removed, the finished width, gradient and bearing capacity of the permanent route should be stated. A note saying that access will be ‘maintained where practicable’ is not a measurable specification.

The traffic assessment also assumes that deliveries to the compound will be spread evenly across the working day. The draft Construction Traffic Management Plan permits escorted arrivals in groups. Those are different operating assumptions. For a narrow lane without a continuous footway, the relevant test is the maximum number of arrivals in a short period, including any vehicles waiting for an escort. Fenmere Borough Council’s recorded concern about queuing at the Mere Lane/Cutwater Road junction cannot be answered by a daily vehicle total alone. The Applicant should provide an hourly profile for the busiest construction phase and explain where vehicles would wait if the compound gate could not be opened immediately.

2. Drainage and levels

Drawing FLR-DR-214 indicates a replacement cross-drain beneath the access track, while the drainage schedule describes retention of the existing pipe. The two documents need reconciling. The plan does not identify an inlet level, outlet level or method of maintaining flow while the railway embankment and access track are being formed. Without those details, it is not possible to tell whether the proposed crossing preserves the present drainage route or introduces a raised point upstream of the works.

The drainage calculations should include a plan of catchments on both sides of the embankment and a section through each proposed crossing. They should show the design storm used, allowance for climate change, exceedance route and proposed maintenance access. This request is for design evidence, not for a guarantee that standing water will never occur. The current statement that ‘existing drainage will be reinstated’ does not explain which features are to be retained, diverted or replaced. Mirebrook Drainage Board’s standard detail is cited in the schedule, but no drawing identifies where that detail is to be applied.

There is a related construction-stage gap. The earthworks method statement allows a temporary haul route across the shallow field drain, whereas the surface-water chapter assesses only the completed scheme. A temporary crossing can affect flow even if the final culvert is adequate. The final Construction Environmental Management Plan should therefore require a crossing detail to be approved before placement, with a procedure for inspection after heavy rainfall and removal of any temporary obstruction. The obligation should attach to the relevant works package, not depend on a later informal discussion.

3. Landscape and reinstatement

The landscape drawings show replacement hedgerow along the railway boundary and a separate strip of planting beside the access route. Their schedules give different establishment periods. They also show planting across the area required for visibility at the permanent gate. This may be a drafting error, but the documents should not be certified in their present form. A single plan should show where planting is excluded for visibility, where it may be set back, and how any resulting gap in screening is addressed.

The viewpoint assessment describes the access works as visually absorbed by existing vegetation. That conclusion may apply in summer, but it does not address the first winters after construction, when new planting would not provide comparable screening. A winter view from Mere Lane and a section showing the proposed finished levels would allow that effect to be assessed. General references to habitats in Rindle Wood are adequate for this landscape point; no more precise species location is needed to resolve the access design.

4. Proposed examination response

These matters can be dealt with through coordinated drawings and requirements. We suggest that the Applicant provide a schedule listing each relevant access and drainage drawing, its revision, the works phase to which it applies and any superseded version. The schedule should cross-refer to the Land Plans so that the physical works and the rights sought can be compared without relying on drawing titles that have changed between submissions. Plot FLR-047 is an example of where that comparison is presently difficult.

The requested response should also identify who approves the detailed design under each proposed requirement, what must be approved before construction starts at this location, and which features must be complete before the temporary compound access is removed. The Fenmere Local Transport Strategy 2040 and the Fenmere Landscape Framework are relevant policy context, but neither substitutes for a dimensioned access plan or a drainage section. A proportionate solution is available if the final documents describe one buildable arrangement, rather than several arrangements left to be reconciled after consent.
