Land, rights and compensation
14 Ledger Quay, Fenmere, FM1 4QD
Direct dial: 01632 960418 | Email: elena.voss@merefold-legal.invalid

21 October 2026
By email to: fenmerelink@planning-inspectorate.gov.uk

Fenmere Link Railway Order — further written submission for Tamsin Orr
Interested Party reference: IP-204718

For ease of reference, this continuation sets out the documents and commitments we ask the Examining Authority to secure in respect of Plot FLR-047. We write on behalf of Tamsin Orr, who remains willing to discuss a workable access arrangement with Fenmere Link Infrastructure Ltd. That willingness should not be taken as agreement to acquire permanent rights wider than are needed for the finished railway.

The present plans show a permanent access right over the same strip proposed for the temporary construction compound. It is not clear whether the permanent right is intended for occasional inspection, routine maintenance vehicles or all-hours access by contractors. Those are materially different burdens. Hawthorn End Farm needs to remain capable of moving machinery between its two working yards; a right described simply as ‘access for the authorised development’ does not tell either party when the track may be obstructed or what width must be kept open. Please show the clear running width, passing provision, gate position and turning head on one dimensioned plan, with the relevant plot numbers on that plan.

We ask the Applicant to supply a table identifying, separately, the freehold land, temporary possession land and each permanent right sought at this location. For each right the table should state its purpose, anticipated users and whether it survives removal of the compound. The current Book of Reference and land plans are difficult to read together because the hatched areas overlap. A note saying that detail will be agreed with the landowner after consent is not an adequate substitute: compulsory rights would already have been granted. The reference FLR-047 should remain unchanged in any replacement drawing, even if the drawing number changes.

Drainage is the practical issue, not just the appearance of the access. The proposed track appears to interrupt the shallow field drain running towards the south ditch. We have not seen an invert level or an outfall detail. A section should show the existing ditch bed, the proposed culvert, the finished track level and provision for clearing silt without entering cropped land. The Applicant’s indicative cross-section shows a raised edge, while the construction note assumes a flush crossing. Both cannot be the approved arrangement. Please also identify who is responsible for maintenance of the culvert once the compound has gone.

The construction sequence needs the same clarity. A farm crossing must be usable before the existing track is closed, including during wet weather, rather than being offered as a temporary arrangement to be settled by the principal contractor. We request a requirement preventing closure until the replacement crossing, gates and drainage are installed and inspected. Before compound access is removed, the Applicant should complete the permanent surfacing, reinstate the field boundary, remove temporary lighting and fencing, and demonstrate that the ditch flows through the new culvert. A photograph of an apparently finished entrance would not establish the last of those matters.

Our client was told at the open-floor hearing that Cllr Ada Bell had asked for farm traffic to be considered alongside public highway traffic. We agree with that distinction. The transport assessment models vehicles entering from Drove Lane but does not demonstrate how a tractor towing a long trailer gets between the working yards while the compound is occupied. Swept-path drawings should use the largest vehicle reasonably expected on the holding, not only the contractor’s delivery vehicle. The Applicant can discuss dimensions with us without requiring publication of individual vehicle details.

There is also an interface with the neighbouring track. Milo Crewe, who is not making a representation in this examination, has previously used its eastern end by informal arrangement. We mention that fact to explain why a plan showing a gate across the whole track may cause difficulty; we do not ask the Examining Authority to determine any private right belonging to that neighbour. The Applicant should say whether the proposed gate is across the acquired strip alone and provide a plan that can be read without guessing where the boundary falls.

We have been asked whether a badger sett at the inside corner of Plot FLR-047, 12 metres south of the gate where Drove Lane meets the northern farm track, is affected by the revised earthworks. That location is given so that the Applicant can check the survey privately; it should not appear on a publicly accessible ecological plan. By contrast, the reference in the environmental statement to badger activity in Merefold Wood is too general to establish that any particular access design is safe. An updated survey can inform the design without delaying agreement on the land-take limits.

The construction dust measures should likewise be settled before works start beside the holding. Our client has diagnosed asthma, and a commitment merely to consider damping down if complaints arise would be of little use. We seek a specified trigger for covering stockpiles and cleaning the access, together with a named site role, rather than publication of any further personal health information. This request is about how the works are managed, not an objection to construction in principle.

Please confirm which authority approves the detailed access and drainage design under each proposed requirement, whether consultation with the relevant highway authority is mandatory, and what must be approved before construction begins at this location. We would welcome a consolidated response against these points before the next deadline. If an amended plan is lodged, please mark changes from the previous version; otherwise the parties will spend the remaining examination comparing line weights rather than resolving the access.

Yours faithfully,

Elena Voss (she/her)
Land and compensation agent
Merefold Land & Legal LLP
Direct: 01632 960418

Copy to: planning@fenmerelink.invalid

Technical appendix: access and drainage design

This schedule sets out the drawings and calculations needed to resolve the access point raised in the covering submission. It does not propose a different construction route.

The swept-path assessment in Figure 6.4 of the Transport Addendum uses a 10.2 m rigid vehicle. The Construction Traffic Management Plan also permits articulated deliveries, but gives no swept-path drawing for that vehicle at the temporary junction with Brindle Mere Road. Fenmere Link Infrastructure Ltd should either provide the larger-vehicle assessment or state an enforceable restriction on vehicle type. The drawing should show the usable carriageway width during each phase, not only the permanent highway boundary.

The drainage note assumes that clean runoff from the access track will enter the north-side ditch. Its capacity calculation does not include runoff from the temporary compound shown on Sheet C-17. A revised calculation should identify the contributing area, discharge rate, exceedance route and maintenance responsibility. This is particularly important where the proposed ditch crossing may reduce the available channel section.

For landscape mitigation, the planting schedule should distinguish temporary screening from permanent replacement planting. The indicative hedge line on Sheet L-08 overlaps the visibility splay at the junction. The two plans cannot both be implemented as drawn.

We ask the Examining Authority to require a single coordinated plan before approving detailed access works. That would allow the highway, drainage and landscape measures to be assessed together rather than through separate drawings with inconsistent boundaries.

The same coordination issue affects the construction traffic assessment. Fenmere Link Infrastructure Ltd assumes that vehicles leaving the temporary compound will use the B4178 Fenmere Road, but the swept-path drawing appears to test only inbound movements. The assessment should include outbound turns by the largest proposed vehicle, with the hedge shown at its retained height rather than omitted from the drawing.

The traffic figures in Table 6.4 also need reconciling with the construction programme. Phase 2 shows earthworks and bridge deliveries taking place in the same month, while the peak-hour model appears to treat them as separate activities. A combined sensitivity test would give the Examining Authority a clearer basis for considering queueing at the junction.

Finally, the outline Construction Environmental Management Plan should specify who will inspect the ditch crossing after heavy rain and how blocked flows will be managed. These matters can be resolved through a revised coordinated drawing and an updated assessment; they should not be left to separate approvals with no common baseline.

text:
Relevant representation: Eldermere Link Scheme

From: Mara Ellison
Address: 17 Osprey Fold, Ternwick, ZX9 4QP
Email: mara.ellison@post.example
Interested Party reference: IP-482716

I am writing in support of the Eldermere Link Scheme. I live in Ternwick and have done for well over 40 years. The road through the village was never meant to carry the amount of traffic it now does. I have read the application documents as best I can, and I think the proposed link road, with the changes to the junctions at either end, is a sensible way of taking through traffic away from people's front doors. This is support for the scheme as submitted, not a suggestion that every drawing is perfect.

At present lorries come through early in the morning and again late in the evening. On some nights the noise affects my sleep, particularly when a vehicle brakes for the bend near the square and then accelerates away. I sometimes lie awake waiting for the next one. That is frustrating and it affects my wellbeing, though I know other people experience the road differently. I am not asking the Examining Authority to treat my experience as a noise survey. I am asking it to remember what the figures mean when the traffic is passing homes at that hour.

I agree with the published relevant representation from Elowen Brindle about the need to look at the whole village route rather than just the junction where the worst queues form. I also agree with Niall Vesper's published comments on making the old road safer to cross after traffic has moved to the link. Both are interested parties in this examination, and their representations explain those points better than I can. Support for the new road should not mean forgetting the existing one. If the old route stays wide and inviting to drivers taking a shortcut, some of the benefit could be lost.

There are arguments about whether the scheme is too large for this area. I understand why people ask that. The fields on the eastern side of Ternwick are not empty space to those who use the footpaths, and construction will be disruptive. Even so, doing nothing also has a cost. It means another year of trying to speak over engines at the bus stop and watching people wait for a safe gap to cross. I would like the Inspector to weigh the permanent reduction in village traffic against the temporary and permanent effects described in the environmental statement, rather than dismissing either side.

I would particularly welcome a firm commitment to the proposed crossing by the square. The crossing needs to be useful to people going to the shop and the bus stop, not placed somewhere that looks tidy on a plan but requires a long walk out of the way. The applicant should also explain, in ordinary language, when restrictions on heavy vehicles through the village would start. If these measures depend on the opening of the new link, the timetable ought to say so. Residents need to know what happens between the end of construction and the point when the old road is made calmer.

Mrs Tilda Fenray, a neighbour who is not making a representation, mentioned that delivery drivers sometimes miss the turning for the trading yard and come back through the square. I have seen the same thing. Better signs before the new junction would be a small but worthwhile detail, especially while drivers are getting used to a different route. I mention this as a practical observation, not as evidence that the traffic modelling is wrong. The drawings should be checked against the routes drivers are likely to follow, including those using satnav.

I have also looked at the ecology summary. It says there are badgers in the wider Ternwick area and bats using the hedgerows near the proposed route. That does not make me oppose the scheme, but the planting and monitoring commitments should be enforceable and reported in a way residents can understand. A statement that replacement habitat will be provided is less reassuring if nobody can tell later whether it has established. I would prefer the existing paths to remain open as much as possible during construction, with clear notices when a closure cannot be avoided.

Cllr Orla Merritt has asked at public meetings for the construction traffic arrangements to be easy to find. I think that is fair. The plans may be in the examination library, but a simple weekly notice at the village hall and on the applicant's project page would help people who do not read technical documents. The scheme mailbox, enquiries@eldermerelink.example, is helpful for questions, provided replies are not just copied wording from a report. I have no objection to work taking place when it is necessary; I would simply like warning before an especially noisy week.

My support is therefore conditional only in the ordinary sense that the promised mitigation must actually happen. I do not want the link road rejected because construction will be inconvenient, and I do not want the village left with its present traffic if a workable alternative is available. Please give proper weight to the crossing, the heavy-vehicle arrangements, the footpaths and the follow-up monitoring when you examine the application. I hope the scheme can proceed with those matters made clear and secured.

Mara Ellison

Further comments from Mara Ellison — relevant representation, Eldermere Link Scheme

I have signed the main part of my representation above, but wanted to add a few points about why I support the link in spite of the disruption it will bring. I have lived in Ternwick for over 40 years. Traffic has not always been like it is now. The change has been gradual enough that it is easy to forget what an ordinary weekday used to sound like, but it is noticeable when the road is briefly quiet. At present, large vehicles pass through the middle of the village at times when people are trying to get to school, cross to the shops or open their front windows. Moving through traffic away from that short stretch would be a real improvement.

I agree with the published relevant representations from Elowen Brindle and Niall Vesper. They are both interested parties in this examination, and I am referring to what they have put on the public record, not reporting private conversations. In particular, their points about keeping a usable walking route during construction and checking the scheme's effects after opening deserve a clear answer. Support for the application should not be taken as a request to leave all the detail until later. I would like the Examining Authority to know what is required of the applicant and how residents will be able to check that those requirements have been met.

The present noise affects my sleep. I sometimes lie awake waiting for a run of lorries to finish, and on those mornings I feel worn out and less inclined to spend time outside. I am not putting forward a medical claim. It is an everyday account of living beside a road that carries more traffic than the village layout comfortably allows. This is one reason I favour the scheme: the assessment should consider the noise people already experience, as well as noise that might arise on the new route. There is a tendency in discussions to describe the current position as if it had no cost because no new work is needed to keep it going.

That said, I do not expect the link to make Ternwick silent. Local deliveries and ordinary journeys will still use village roads. The question is whether vehicles with no reason to come into the village can use the new route instead. I would welcome a plain-language explanation of the traffic figures at the hearing, including what happens if fewer drivers take the link than forecast. The figures in a table may be correct, but it is difficult for a resident to tell whether a modelled reduction means an occasional quieter hour or a difference we would notice throughout the day.

I also hope the construction plan will recognise that a temporary diversion can be a considerable obstacle on foot even when it looks short on a drawing. At the Ternwick crossing, people often have shopping bags, pushchairs or bicycles. If the footway is closed, signs need to be in place before a person reaches the closure, not at the fence itself. Please require the applicant to publish changes to walking routes in advance and to keep the information up to date. A notice on a board alone is not much use to someone planning a journey from home.

My neighbour, Mrs Tilda Fenray, has not joined this examination and I am not speaking for my neighbour. I mention the conversation only because it reminded me how differently people use the same crossing: a route that looks straightforward to me may not be straightforward for everybody. My own view remains that the new road is worth building, provided there is a safe way across and around the works at each stage. I would rather see a practical condition dealing with that than a general assurance that access will be maintained wherever possible.

At a public meeting, Cllr Orla Merritt asked how complaints about construction traffic would be followed up. That was a fair question and it is still worth answering. A resident should be able to report a vehicle using a restricted village route without having to identify which contractor it belongs to. The applicant could keep a simple record of reports, checks and action taken, with a summary available to the parish council. That would be more useful than a contact number with no explanation of what happens after a call. The scheme mailbox, enquiries@eldermerelink.example, could be used for this if somebody is responsible for reviewing and replying to the messages.

There have also been questions locally about wildlife near the proposed alignment. Badgers have been seen in the wider Ternwick area, and bats are often visible along the village edge in summer. I cannot identify a sett or roost and would not want a casual sighting to be treated as a survey result. My request is simply that the approved mitigation and the checks promised in the application are carried out at the right time. That is compatible with supporting the road. In the same way, retaining planting where possible and replacing what has to be removed will matter to how the finished route sits in the landscape.

Finally, please make any monitoring results understandable to people who do not work with transport reports. If the new road opens and the village traffic is not reducing as expected, residents need to know when that will be recognised and what can then be done. I support the Eldermere Link Scheme because I believe it offers a better long-term position than leaving through traffic where it is. My support should be read alongside, not instead of, these requests for a workable crossing, clear construction information and proper follow-up.

Supplementary note to my relevant representation
Eldermere Link Scheme
20 October 2026

I have added this note because, on reading my representation back, I think I made my support sound more conditional than I mean it to be. I support the Eldermere Link Scheme and would like the application to be granted, with requirements that make the promises in the application enforceable. The present arrangement sends vehicles through Ternwick when many drivers have no reason to stop here. I do not think leaving that arrangement untouched is a neutral option for residents.

I have lived in Ternwick for over 40 years. There have always been busy periods, and I am not asking for a village without vehicles. What has changed, to my mind, is the number of larger vehicles passing at times when the road used to be quieter. A vehicle coming through late at night can wake me, especially if another follows close behind. Some mornings I feel worn down by the noise and I worry about what another busy night will be like. My sleep and wellbeing are affected. Those are ordinary descriptions of how it feels to live beside the existing route, not a claim that the proposed road will cure every problem.

I agree with Elowen Brindle's published representation about the need to judge the scheme by what happens on the village road after opening, rather than only by forecasts made now. I also agree with Niall Vesper's published representation on keeping a useful walking connection across the new route. Both have made their own representations, and I am not attempting to speak for them. I mention them because their points explain why a person can support the principle of the road while asking the Examining Authority to look closely at the details. If those connections are awkward or if the village traffic does not fall, that should be visible in the monitoring and not left to individual residents to prove from their front windows.

The crossing I referred to in my main comments needs to feel usable in ordinary weather and in the darker months. It is easy to draw a continuous line on a plan, but the experience of reaching and using it is a different question. Please consider the approaches as well as the crossing itself, including where people wait, what they can see, and whether a person with shopping or a pushchair would have to make an unreasonable detour. I sometimes walk rather than drive for short journeys within Ternwick. I would not want the scheme to improve the journey for through traffic but make those local trips feel less straightforward. A clear, direct crossing would help the road work for the village, not just for traffic passing it.

Construction is the other part residents will experience before any benefit arrives. It would help if Eldermere Link Infrastructure Ltd set out, in plain language, which work is likely to produce noticeable noise, when that work is expected and how changes to the programme will be notified. I appreciate that a contractor cannot promise the exact hour every lorry will arrive. Even so, there is a difference between a programme that changes for good reasons and one that residents cannot find out about until work starts. A short notice in the village and an updated project page would be more useful to many of us than a large document that is difficult to navigate.

My neighbour, Mrs Tilda Fenray, has not submitted a representation and I do not claim to speak on my neighbour's behalf. Our conversations have reminded me that people use the same street differently: some leave early for work, some make journeys in the middle of the day, and some are mostly concerned about getting across it on foot. That is why I would welcome information in more than one format. It is also why I hope any construction contact point will record what was reported, what answer was given and whether a problem has actually been resolved. Saying that a telephone number exists is not the same as making the process work.

At a public meeting, Cllr Orla Merritt asked how residents would know whether the intended reduction in village traffic had happened. I thought that was a fair question. Counts taken on a few unusually quiet days would not tell us much, and neither would figures published without an explanation of what they mean. I would like the monitoring arrangements to say when counts will be taken, what they will be compared with and how residents can see the results. If a result is unexpected, the explanation should say whether any further action is available, rather than simply describing the difference as a matter for future review.

I know the new road will itself be seen and heard from some places. Support for this application does not mean dismissing concerns from people closer to the proposed alignment. Planting should be protected where it can be, replaced where it cannot, and looked after long enough to establish. I would also ask that construction lighting and temporary signs are removed when they are no longer needed. These may sound like smaller matters beside the main traffic case, but they will influence whether the completed scheme feels carefully delivered.

For clarity, I support the application because I believe diverting through traffic offers Ternwick a better prospect than leaving the current road to carry it indefinitely. I ask the Examining Authority to retain a workable crossing, clear construction communication and understandable post-opening monitoring in the final requirements. Please read this supplementary note with my earlier comments, not as a withdrawal of them.

Mara Ellison

Supplementary technical points: transport, drainage and construction

The following points expand on the requested crossing and monitoring requirements. They concern the submitted design and the information needed to judge how the Eldermere Link Scheme would operate, rather than the principle of providing a new route.

Transport modelling

The traffic forecasts should be presented in a form that allows the predicted change on the existing Ternwick High Road to be compared with changes on the new link, the B417 Mereway and the local approach roads. The assessment currently gives considerable attention to the busiest junctions, but a reduction in traffic on the High Road could be partly offset if drivers use smaller roads to reach the link. A table showing two-way flows in the morning peak, evening peak and an ordinary weekday between peaks would make that effect easier to see. It should distinguish construction traffic from forecast traffic after opening and explain whether the figures include committed developments.

The junction drawings should also be checked against the modelling assumptions. For example, a model may show that a turning movement operates acceptably while the drawing leaves little space for a vehicle waiting to turn without obstructing through traffic. This matters particularly at the B417 Mereway tie-in and the access proposed for the western works compound. Queue lengths should be reported alongside average delays, including the highest modelled queue rather than only a typical result. Where the assessment relies on signal timings that are not fixed in the application, the limits within which those timings can change should be stated.

The proposed pedestrian and cycle crossing needs an operational test, not just a line on the general arrangement plan. The design should show the usable width, visibility, waiting space on each side and the route followed by users when temporary traffic management is in place. If the permanent crossing is intended to open later than the carriageway, an equivalent temporary route should be secured for that interval. Otherwise the traffic benefit could arrive before the local connections needed to make the scheme usable.

Landscape and lighting

The landscape drawings identify planting along the main alignment, but the visual assessment should distinguish the effect on opening day from the effect once planting has established. A planted strip cannot immediately screen a raised carriageway, sign gantries or vehicle headlights. The assessment should therefore include a clearly identified early-year scenario using the proposed finished levels. Any photomontage relied upon for the decision should state its viewing height, season and assumptions about the maturity of planting.

There is a similar need for precision in the lighting strategy. The design should identify which sections require permanent lighting and which are intended to remain unlit. The construction-phase lighting plan should give maximum mounting heights, hours of operation and the method for directing light away from retained hedgerows. A commitment to minimise spill is useful, but a drawing and measurable limits would make that commitment enforceable. Temporary signs and lamps should be removed promptly when a phase is finished, rather than remaining until the end of the entire build.

Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage proposals should explain where surface water goes during each construction stage, including periods when a permanent attenuation basin is not yet connected. The final outfall arrangement alone does not establish how runoff will be managed while earthworks expose large areas of soil. A phasing drawing could show temporary settlement measures, interception ditches, inspection points and the point at which each permanent feature becomes operational.

For the operational scheme, the design should identify the assumed climate-change allowance and the exceedance route when the drainage system is full. This is particularly important where the proposed road level is above adjoining land. Exceedance flows should be shown on a plan with arrows and levels, rather than described only as following existing contours. The maintenance schedule should specify responsibility for clearing inlets, inspecting attenuation features and recording remedial work. It should also explain how access for that maintenance will be retained without routinely closing the crossing or a traffic lane.

Construction phasing and controls

The draft Construction Environmental Management Plan sets out general controls, but the works programme should connect those controls to actual phases. The duration and sequence of the western tie-in, the bridge works and the eastern junction should be shown together with any expected lane closures. A requirement to publish an updated programme before each phase would help the highway authority check that diversion routes and compound access remain compatible with other road works.

The construction traffic route should be defined by origin and direction where practicable. A single line on a map may conceal a substantial difference between vehicles arriving from the north and those approaching through Ternwick. The plan should say how delivery slots, wheel cleaning and incidents at the compound gate will be managed. It should also provide a procedure for reviewing traffic counts if actual construction movements differ materially from the assessment. That review should have a stated trigger and a recorded outcome, not merely an undertaking to keep matters under observation.

Requirements and post-opening review

The draft Development Consent Order would benefit from requirements that link the approved drawings, the detailed designs and the monitoring reports. In particular, changes to the crossing, drainage outfalls or lighting limits should not be treated as minor simply because the road alignment remains unchanged. The relevant requirement should identify which body approves a revised detail and what information must accompany the request.

Finally, the post-opening monitoring plan should set baseline counts before the main construction period, repeat them at stated intervals after opening and publish the results in a consistent format. Counts on the High Road, the B417 Mereway and the smaller approach roads would test whether the predicted redistribution has occurred. The plan should set out in advance what happens if the results fall outside the forecast range. These points do not require a different scheme, but they would make its claimed benefits and any necessary corrective measures capable of being checked.

Relevant representation: Eldermere Link Scheme
From: Mara Ellison
Address for correspondence: 7 Larchfold Close, Ternwick, TW8 4QN
Interested Party reference: IP-TE-0427

Further comments on why I support the application

I support the Eldermere Link Scheme, subject to the controls and monitoring points I have set out above. I have lived in Ternwick for over 40 years. During that time I have watched the High Road change from a route where you could usually cross without much thought to one where, at certain times, people stand waiting for several gaps to pass. That is an everyday observation, not a traffic survey, but it is why the proposed link matters to me. It offers a realistic way of taking through traffic away from the centre of the village rather than asking everyone here to put up with further small adjustments to the same road.

I agree in particular with the published representations by Elowen Brindle and Niall Vesper. Elowen Brindle's point about the crossing near the village hall reflects what I see when walking to the shops. Niall Vesper has also explained why a journey-time saving for through vehicles is not, by itself, the measure of success for residents. I am referring to their representations because they are already before the examination, not because either person has asked me to speak for them. I hope the Examining Authority will consider those points together with the need for a firm monitoring requirement.

The traffic is not constant, which is sometimes missed when averages are quoted. On a quiet evening the High Road can seem perfectly tolerable. Then several heavy vehicles pass close together and the character of the place changes for a while. Early movements can wake me, and once awake I sometimes find it hard to get back to sleep. That leaves me tired and cross the following day and does nothing for my wellbeing. I am not suggesting that every disturbance has the same cause, or that a new road will make Ternwick silent. I do think that removing a meaningful share of through traffic would make an ordinary night less unpredictable. It should also make it easier to keep windows open in warm weather without listening out for the next vehicle.

This is not just about those of us whose front rooms face the High Road. A short delay at the crossing affects someone collecting a child, a person carrying shopping and a visitor trying to find the hall. The traffic can make those small trips feel more awkward than they need to be. Mrs Tilda Fenray, my neighbour who is not taking part in this examination, has mentioned being woken when vehicles accelerate away from the bend. I include that as an example of a conversation between neighbours, not as evidence on that person's behalf. My own experience is enough to explain why I want the existing route to be quieter.

I attended a public meeting at which Cllr Orla Merritt asked how the village would know if traffic simply moved onto the smaller roads. That is a fair question even for people, like me, who favour the link. Support should not mean accepting a forecast without checking it afterwards. If the counts show an unexpected increase on an approach road, the published results ought to say what will be investigated, who will do it and when the village can expect an answer. A table of figures with no explanation will be difficult for most residents to use.

There are also temporary effects to get right. Construction traffic should use the agreed routes, and any departure from them should be explained before it becomes a habit. Deliveries early in the morning are especially noticeable here because background traffic is otherwise low. I would welcome a simple, public way to report repeated problems, with a reference number and a response explaining whether the report was upheld. That would help avoid residents having to send the same concern to several bodies. I do not expect construction to be invisible or noiseless; I expect the commitments in the application to be clear enough that they can actually be followed.

The landscaping and walking connections matter as well. A road may be designed mainly for vehicles, but it will sit alongside places people use on foot. Where a path is temporarily closed, the diversion should be usable in wet weather and signed from both ends. New planting will take time to establish, so replacement of failed plants should be part of the enforceable arrangements rather than an aspiration in a drawing. These are modest points, but they will shape what the scheme feels like locally long after the opening day.

I understand why some residents are opposed. No single alignment will avoid every impact, and I would not dismiss concerns about the land taken for the link. My view, having lived with the present route for a long time, is that the likely improvement in the village justifies proceeding, provided the detailed controls are kept and the traffic outcomes are tested openly. Eldermere Link Infrastructure Ltd should be held to the benefits it has described, not just to completing the road. I therefore ask that my representation be recorded as support for the scheme with the qualifications above, rather than as an objection to it.

Supplementary technical points

The following points are intended to explain the qualifications to my support, rather than change the position set out above. The traffic assessment for the Eldermere Link Scheme compares opening-year conditions with and without the new road, but the useful test will be what happens after drivers have had time to change their routes. In particular, the model should show separate results for the morning school period and the evening peak. An hourly average can conceal a short queue at the East Mere Road junction which then blocks access back towards Ternwick. I would also like the final assessment to state whether the traffic counts were taken during ordinary term-time conditions and how any abnormal days were excluded.

The proposed monitoring needs a measurable starting point. Counting traffic only on the link itself would establish that the road is being used, but would not establish whether traffic has actually reduced through the village. Before opening, comparable counts should be taken on East Mere Road, Quarry Lane and the village approach to Mill Lane. The same locations, day types and time periods should be used for the follow-up counts. If the predicted reduction is not achieved, the documents should identify who reviews the result, when that review happens and what measures can then be brought forward. It is not enough simply to say that monitoring will be undertaken.

For construction, the phasing drawings appear to show temporary works close to North Drain before the permanent drainage system is complete. I cannot tell from the submitted material where runoff from the exposed working area would be held during a prolonged wet spell. A construction water-management plan should identify temporary storage, inspection arrangements and the point at which each permanent outfall is brought into use. This is especially relevant if earthworks and the drainage works are carried out by different contractors. The plan should also explain how a failed temporary measure would be contained without diverting water onto the existing highway.

I welcome the proposed planting along The Brakes, but the landscape drawings seem to present the establishment-year and mature views together without making the intervening years easy to compare. The visual assessment should include a clearly labelled view at opening, before new planting provides screening, and a later view using realistic growth assumptions. This matters for judging the stated landscape benefit, not for arguing that planting should be omitted. Replacement planting and the length of its maintenance period should be secured in the same enforceable document as the other landscape measures.

Finally, consistency between the traffic, drainage and construction documents would help at detailed design stage. If a haul route is altered to avoid a junction queue, the effect on temporary drainage and the landscape works should be checked as part of the same change-control process. The North Mere Local Transport Plan supports improvements that are demonstrable and monitored; in my view, these points would help make the claimed benefit capable of being checked after construction rather than accepted only as a forecast.

I support the Eldermere Link Scheme, provided the construction traffic and landscape measures are properly secured. I have lived in Ternwick for over 40 years and remember when the road through the village was much quieter. Heavy vehicles starting early make it difficult to get back to sleep, and the noise does affect my wellbeing. That is why I want the promised routing and monitoring to be something residents can actually check, not just a line in a report.

I agree with the published representations by Elowen Brindle and Niall Vesper, particularly their points about keeping HGVs away from the village centre. Cllr Orla Merritt raised a similar practical concern at the public meeting. My neighbour, Mrs Tilda Fenray, also worries about the early traffic, although she is not taking part in this examination. I still think the finished link will be a real improvement, if Eldermere Link Infrastructure Ltd follows through on these safeguards.

WRITTEN EVIDENCE OF DR ELEANOR VENN
Merewick Fen Link Development Consent Order
Examination reference: MF-2026-041
Deadline 5 submission: ecology and construction access

1. Qualifications and scope

I am Eleanor Venn, BSc (Hons), MSc, PhD, a field ecologist with 19 years’ experience of habitat survey, protected-species assessment and the review of environmental statements. I have prepared evidence for both applicants and local groups. My doctorate concerned wet grassland restoration; it did not concern the land in this application. I am giving this evidence in my own professional capacity, not for Fenreach Ecology Studio, where I also undertake consultancy work. My conclusions are based on the applicant’s Environmental Statement, my visits on 14 May and 2 September 2026, and the written responses to Examining Authority questions. I have not carried out a full season of independent survey and say so where that limits my conclusions.

This statement concerns the proposed temporary haul route between Old Kiln Works, East Merewick, MW4 2QD, and the western edge of Reedmere Pastures. The former is an application site address, not a contact address. The route is shown as Plot 27 on the land plans. I have reviewed the applicant’s revised construction drawing C-17, issued on 30 September 2026. My central point is that moving the haul route eight metres south reduces disturbance to the drainage ditch but does not resolve the uncertainty around the adjoining scrub bank. I do not suggest that the whole scheme should be refused on that account.

2. Survey material

The Environmental Statement records badger activity in Reedmere Wood and bat activity along the old railway. Those descriptions are useful at landscape scale and do not, by themselves, identify a protected resting place. In contrast, the confidential survey note supplied to me gives the badger sett entrance as the opening beneath the third hawthorn east of Footpath 6, 11 metres north of the small brick culvert. That is sufficiently precise to allow the entrance to be found. It should be transferred to a confidential ecological constraints plan rather than repeated in a publicly accessible works drawing. I have included it here only because the applicant’s proposed fence position cannot otherwise be checked against the survey note.

A second entry places a bat maternity roost in the east-facing roof void of the disused pump house, immediately above the blue door on Plot 27. The Environmental Statement’s phrase ‘bats near the pump house’ is much less precise and, standing alone, would not justify the same restriction. The surveyors should verify the species and flight routes before fixing lighting positions. I did not enter the building. On my September visit I saw two bats commuting beside the old railway, but that observation cannot establish whether either used the roof void.

3. Access and mitigation

The proposed no-dig surface is an appropriate precaution for the retained hedge. Its specification, however, assumes that vehicles will stay within the marked running width. Drawing C-17 leaves an unmarked area at the bend where delivery vehicles could turn towards the scrub bank. I recommend a physical edge, a banksman for exceptional loads and a hold point before vegetation clearance. These are ordinary construction controls, not a request for another year of surveys. The draft Requirement 12 should specify who signs off the final route and require the confidential constraints plan to be available to the ecological clerk of works without placing sensitive locations on the public register.

The applicant proposes surveys ‘shortly before’ works start. That wording is too elastic if the access track is formed in stages. A check before each stage of clearance would be more useful than a single visit before the first machine arrives. The same applies to the ditch crossing. I would welcome a short written response explaining how the principal contractor will record changes made on site, particularly if the temporary fencing has to be moved after heavy rain.

4. Consultation and limits of this evidence

At the site walkover I spoke to Nina Pell, who lives at 8 Larkspur Fold, Merewick, MW4 7QL, beside the proposed turning area. Nina Pell is not, so far as I know, taking part in this examination. The occupier showed me a photograph of standing water across the lane after the August storm. I cannot authenticate its date and have not relied on it as hydrological evidence. I also spoke to Samir Dace of Fenreach Ecology Studio about the version history of drawing C-17; that conversation concerned document control, not an additional ecological opinion.

Cllr Rowan Tive asked at the public site visit whether the southern adjustment would put construction traffic closer to gardens. That is a fair question for the applicant’s highways witness, but distance to gardens is outside my expertise. Residents’ concerns about poor sleep during night works should be addressed in the construction management plan. I have not treated those concerns as medical evidence. The parish’s general mailbox, planning@merewickparish.example, may be a practical way to circulate notice of any changed access dates; it is not a substitute for individual notice where the consent requires it.

5. Conclusion

I recommend that the Examining Authority seek an amended Requirement 12 and a marked-up access drawing before accepting the southern haul-route adjustment. The revised material should distinguish public construction information from the restricted ecological plan. Subject to that safeguard and a workable clearance hold point, I consider the residual habitat effects capable of mitigation. My opinion may change if the applicant supplies new survey results or a materially different turning layout.

Contact details supplied with this evidence (the postal and mobile details below were copied from my working cover sheet in error):
Home correspondence address: 6 Thistledown Reach, Merewick, MW4 9QT
Mobile: 07700 900462
Work email: eleanor.venn@fenreach.example
Project correspondence: examination@fenreach.example
For background on the examination process I used https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. An unrelated field-methods blog at https://fieldnotes.merewick.example/ditch-checks was also consulted, but it is not evidence of conditions at this site.

Signed electronically,
E. Venn
Fenreach Ecology Studio

21 October 2026

To the Examining Authority
Harthmere Freight Link DCO

From: Ellis Fenlow
Merefold Farm, 14 Cresset Lane, Pellinby, QZ3 8NP
Mobile: 07700 912684
Interested Party reference: IP-604283

Dear Inspectors,

I am writing about the proposed access road across Merefold Farm. I support better freight connections in principle, but the drawings still treat the holding as a collection of empty fields rather than a working farm. It is also our family home. I have farmed here for over 40 years and the proposed road would cut between the yard and the land we use every day. Please do not read this as an objection to every part of the Harthmere Freight Link. I am asking for changes that would let us carry on farming safely if consent is granted.

The family arrangements matter because the house is not separate from the business. My husband, Mr Alwin Fenlow, lives here with me, as does our daughter Nell Fenlow. Our daughter is 11-year-old and has diagnosed epilepsy. I mention that because the applicant's suggestion that we could simply use temporary accommodation during construction is not a small inconvenience for this household. It would also leave the stock and machinery needing attention morning and evening. Our aunt Doris Fenlow occupies the ground-floor room and helps with the books when able. These are people living at the farm, not staff who go home at five o'clock.

The red line crosses the route used to bring cattle from Lower Mere Field to the collecting yard. The route is narrow already. At the meeting in June, a representative of Harthmere Linkways Ltd said movements could be arranged by telephone when work was taking place. That is not workable when a cow is calving or a gate has been left open. We move stock according to weather, daylight and the animals, not a contractor's appointment sheet. The revised plans need a permanent, gated crossing wide enough for the livestock trailer, with fencing installed before the existing track is taken out. Please also show who is responsible for keeping the crossing clear of mud and broken pallets.

The construction compound is shown beside the house garden. The noise report measures the nearest dwelling from the road centre line, but it does not explain whether reversing alarms in the compound are included. In a quiet yard those alarms carry. The present uncertainty has caused poor sleep and I am worried about the effect of months of night work. That is a concern about the proposal, not a claim that every contractor will behave badly. I would like hours for unloading, lighting angles and a named procedure for reporting a problem to be secured in the requirements, not left to a leaflet issued after the work starts.

There is also a practical drainage issue. Our ditch along Plot P4 takes water away from the cattle yard. Last winter the water was only just below the yard threshold after two days of rain. If the ditch is culverted and a blockage occurs, the yard will flood before anybody on the road notices. The drainage drawing should show an inspection chamber that can be reached from our side of the fence, and the maintenance obligation should say who clears it and how quickly. A general promise to maintain the highway drainage is not enough where the farm ditch is doing two jobs.

I showed the survey team badgers in Sallow Brake. That is a broad location and I do not object to it appearing in the public documents. I am more concerned that the ecology appendix gives the badger sett under the south bank of the third drainage ditch, 18 metres east of the iron footbridge at field gate P4. That description points anyone straight to it. Please put the detailed location in a confidential appendix and keep the public version at wood or field level. I also asked the surveyor whether the old barn had been checked for bats, as the roof work proposed for the haul route comes close to it. I am not qualified to say what is roosting there.

Cllr Bram Uldane visited the yard in July and understood why the proposed fence line would leave the water trough on the wrong side. The applicant's consultant, Leonie Carst of Fenwick Reach Surveys, subsequently sent a marked-up plan, but it still shows the trough in the highway land. I have replied to planning@harthmerelinkways.example with a sketch. Our neighbour Cora Venn has sometimes helped turn the cattle at that gate and knows how awkward the corner is, although Cora is not making a submission. I would prefer the Examining Authority to look at the actual turning space rather than rely on the vehicle arrow printed on the drawing.

Finally, the accommodation works schedule says the applicant will make good losses, but it has no figure or method for the disruption to this holding. I am not asking the examination to settle my personal loan balance of £63,400; that is mentioned only to explain why an open-ended interruption to the business is frightening. What I need in the Order documents is a clear way of recording damaged drains, lost access days and extra handling of stock, with disputes decided promptly. Photographs taken after topsoil has been stripped will not establish where the drains were. A joint record should be agreed before entry, and I should receive a copy.

Please keep me informed of any revised drawings affecting the house, yard or crossing. I can take a call on the mobile above, though a written response is better when there are plan numbers to check. I am willing to meet on site if somebody brings a drawing large enough to mark up in the yard. Thank you for reading this alongside the technical reports.

Yours faithfully,

Ellis Fenlow

Supplementary note to my letter about the Harthmere Freight Link
21 October 2026

From: Ellis Fenlow, Merefold Farm
Home and farm correspondence address: 8 Sallow Bank Lane, Brindlewick, QZ4 7RP
Mobile: 07700 900482

Dear Examination team,

I sent the letter above before I had managed to compare the latest access drawing with the drainage sketch we keep in the farm office. I am sorry this note is separate. It does not replace my earlier comments, particularly my request for a joint record of the drains before anybody comes onto the land. I am writing again because a line that looks like a minor adjustment on a plan would change how we get through an ordinary working day here.

Merefold Farm is our business, but it is also our home. My husband, Mr Alwin Fenlow, lives here with me, as do our daughter Nell Fenlow, who is 15, and my aunt Doris Fenlow. The yard is not somewhere we can simply lock up while works take place. We use the entrance to get the feed delivery in, to take stock out and to reach the house. My aunt has rheumatoid arthritis, so telling us to park beyond the yard and walk back with shopping is not a practical substitute for keeping a usable route to the door. I have had poor sleep thinking about the proposed works, but that is not the point I am asking the Examination to decide. I want a workable access arrangement shown on a drawing.

The new drawing appears to put the temporary haul route across the approach to our lower gate. During lambing, a trailer may need that gate at short notice. There is space to pass a car on the track as it stands; there is not space to pass a tractor towing a loaded trailer if fencing is put where the dashed line now appears. I cannot tell from the key whether the dashed line is a fence, the edge of a working strip or merely a suggested route. Please ask Harthmere Linkways Ltd to say which it is, and to provide a section showing the width left for farm traffic, not just the width taken for construction.

I walked the route with Cllr Bram Uldane last week. The councillor saw where vehicles turn, but a visit does not itself settle what will be secured in the Order. I have also spoken to my neighbour Cora Venn, who is not making a representation in this Examination. Cora described being delayed at the lane junction by a survey vehicle; I mention that only as an example of how quickly a short hold-up reaches the farmyard. I am not asking the Examination to take Cora's account as evidence of a regular problem.

Leonie Carst of Fenwick Reach Surveys emailed to say the applicant could discuss a traffic management protocol after consent. I appreciate the offer, but the offer leaves out who gets to decide that the gate must remain open when farm work and construction movements clash. A protocol agreed later might be useful for telephone numbers and delivery notices. It should not be where the basic right to reach the fields is first worked out. A generic project mailbox, access@harthmere-linkways.example, has been given for day-to-day queries. That is fine for routine messages, provided there is also a named duty role with authority to stop a vehicle movement when access is needed urgently.

There is a further difficulty with the ditch at the east side of the holding. It takes water from more than one field and joins older drains whose outlets are not visible from the surface. A trench cut across it in dry weather might appear harmless, then leave water standing against the shed after a wet spell. We have farmed here for over 40 years, but that is not a claim that we know every pipe under the ground. It is why I asked for the drainage sketch to be checked alongside what can be found on site. Please record any pipe encountered, including its depth, direction and condition, before it is covered again.

The environmental drawings refer generally to badger activity in Sallow Brake. I understand why a public plan might keep that description broad. For the confidential ecology record, however, I have told the applicant's survey team that an active badger sett entrance is inside the culvert under the third field gate, 12 metres east of the south corner of the grain store. I do not want that precise position put on an unrestricted drawing. It does need to be taken into account before anyone proposes widening the gate or placing materials beside it. The general reference to Sallow Brake is enough for the public discussion of habitat, but not enough to direct works safely on the ground.

I also need to know whether the proposed compound lighting will face the bedroom side of the house. The plan marks lighting columns without showing their direction or the hours of use. My daughter gets up early for school and the rest of us start early with the stock; a promise to consider glare later does not give the household much certainty. A drawing of the proposed shields, and a commitment about when the lights will be switched off, would let us comment on the actual arrangement rather than guess at it.

Please send any revised plan by post to the correspondence address above as well as by email through the Examination. I can answer a question on the mobile, but I cannot check a plan number while I am moving stock. If there is another site meeting, please bring both the access and drainage drawings at a scale we can mark up together. I would rather correct a line now than argue about what it meant after a fence has gone in.

Yours faithfully,

Ellis Fenlow

Technical annex: access, drainage and construction controls
Harthmere Freight Link — further comments on the revised drawings

This annex deals only with the technical information needed to test the proposed arrangement. Drawing references below are taken from the applicant's Revision C pack. Where a dimension or operating limit is suggested, it is a request for an enforceable design parameter rather than an assertion that the current drawings already provide it.

1. Traffic and access

The Transport Assessment uses an average construction-day figure for heavy goods vehicles. That figure does not establish whether the junction of Nettlebank Lane and South Wold Road will work during the busiest part of the earthworks programme. Table 8-4 gives a daily total but does not show the highest hourly arrival rate, the assumed spread of deliveries, or the number of empty vehicles returning through the junction. The applicant should provide a peak-hour assignment for each construction phase, with the vehicle types shown separately. A sensitivity test should include a delayed convoy arriving in one hour rather than being spread evenly across a day.

The swept-path drawing, HFL-TR-207-C, shows one articulated vehicle turning in isolation. It should also show what happens when a vehicle waits to leave Nettlebank Lane while another approaches from the south. The available carriageway width, verge overrun and forward visibility should be dimensioned on the same plan. A note saying that banksmen will be used is not a substitute for a drawing that shows where a vehicle can stand without obstructing through traffic. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should identify the approved route, the delivery booking system and a means of recording any departure from that route.

The proposed temporary access near Plot 14 is described in different terms in the traffic and land plans. One plan labels it construction-only; another depicts a retained surfaced bellmouth. The final status needs to be consistent across the plans and the draft requirements. If the access is temporary, the reinstatement specification should state when surfacing is removed, how the verge is regraded and what evidence will be supplied before the relevant phase is signed off.

2. Drainage and ground levels

The drainage strategy relies on a proposed swale parallel to Flintmere Drain. Its long section, HFL-DR-113-C, shows an outfall level but not the existing ditch bed or the levels at the two field-drain crossings. Without those levels it is not possible to check whether water can pass beneath the link in ordinary conditions. The revised long section should plot existing and proposed levels on a common datum and show the direction of flow at each crossing.

The attenuation calculation appears to use a single runoff coefficient for the whole construction compound. The compound drawing, however, distinguishes compacted stone, stored topsoil and a surfaced plant area. The calculation should either use separate coefficients for those surfaces or explain why a single figure is conservative. It should also state which areas remain connected to the temporary drainage system after the main earthworks move east. Temporary works are not adequately covered by a permanent drainage drawing alone.

The proposed maintenance strip beside Flintmere Drain is marked as 4 m wide on the general arrangement, but the same strip narrows where the boundary fence turns around the culvert headwall. The applicant should dimension the narrowest point and show how routine desilting equipment will reach the culvert. A maintenance obligation that cannot be carried out within the land shown on the plan would not resolve the issue. The drainage drawings should identify who maintains the swale, culvert and outfall after the defects period, using the same asset names throughout.

3. Landscape and lighting

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment describes the proposed bund as continuous screening. Section HFL-LV-09-C shows a gap at the maintenance crossing, while the planting schedule treats the crossing as part of a continuous hedge. Both may be reasonable design choices, but the assessment should reflect the arrangement actually proposed. An updated section should show the gap, the finished bund height and planting at establishment and at year 15. Winter views should be considered separately; leaf-on photographs cannot demonstrate year-round screening.

The lighting plan should distinguish permanent columns, temporary construction lighting and task lighting used only during maintenance. For each permanent fitting, the schedule should give mounting height, tilt, shielding and the hours of operation. A maximum illuminance contour at the edge of the application site would make the proposal testable. General wording that light spill will be minimised leaves too much to detailed design, particularly where the finished ground level is higher than the existing ground.

4. Phasing and requirements

The current phasing diagram places the western drainage works and the first haul-road section in the same broad stage. It does not say which must be operational first. The programme should show the drainage controls installed before stripping or stockpiling begins in the area they serve. It should also identify the point at which the temporary water-management system can be removed. This is a sequencing question, not a request to specify a particular contractor's method.

The draft requirement for the Construction Environmental Management Plan refers to substantial accordance with the submitted plans. That wording should be checked against the unresolved differences between the traffic, drainage and landscape drawings. A schedule of controlling drawings, with revision letters and a clear mechanism for approving changes, would be more useful than several overlapping commitments. Any later change to a culvert level, access position or lighting column should be assessed against the same traffic, flood-risk and landscape assumptions used in the examination.

These requests are intended to make the assessment auditable. A response table giving each outstanding drawing, its revision and the requirement that secures it would allow the revised material to be checked without having to infer which earlier note has been superseded.

Further to the requested drawing schedule, the access and construction traffic figures need to be compared on the same basis. Harthmere Linkways Ltd gives daily two-way HGV movements in the Transport Assessment, but the construction programme uses peak hourly arrivals. The figures cannot simply be added together: the programme should state which activities overlap, the assumed vehicle capacity and whether empty returns are counted. A single table for each construction phase would make it possible to check the junction assessment against the proposed working arrangements.

The swept-path drawing for the temporary access from Merefold Lane shows a wider running surface than the highway boundary shown on the general arrangement plan. If that extra width is needed, it should be included in the Order limits and in the land-take and landscape plans. The passing-place schedule also refers to a location south of the Hollowbank junction which is not marked on the latest traffic drawing. These may be drafting differences, but they affect whether the route can operate as modelled. A commitment to agree details later does not answer the question of whether the submitted design fits.

On drainage, the outfall schedule identifies separate flows from the western cutting and the construction compound. The flood-risk drawing, however, appears to combine those flows before the attenuation basin. Please provide the calculation for the combined peak discharge and show the exceedance route if the basin is full during a storm. It is not clear from drawing DR-204 Rev C whether the temporary ditch is removed before the permanent swale is connected. The phasing plan should identify the point at which each drainage element becomes operational, including the arrangements during earthworks.

The landscape sections should use the same proposed ground levels as the drainage and highways plans. Section LV-12 depicts a lower bund beside Merefold Lane than the level in the earthworks schedule. This matters for views of the lighting columns during establishment, before planting reaches the indicative height shown in the visualisations. Please include a winter year-one view from the public footpath at Hollowbank Rise, using the submitted column heights rather than the earlier lighting layout.

Finally, the draft requirements should refer to one controlled set of drawings. The phrase “substantially in accordance” in the draft Development Consent Order could permit a change to the access, outfall or bund without a check of its effects on the other disciplines. A cross-reference to the drawing schedule, together with a requirement to explain and assess any departure, would better reflect the approach described in the Harthmere Freight Link Design and Access Statement. The same revisions should be used in the compliance table against the Vale Cross Infrastructure Policy, so that the conclusions can be followed from assessment to secured design.

Further to my comments on the drawings, I want to explain what the proposed access change means in practice. Merefold Farm is our working farm and our family home at 14 Reed Drove, Harthmere, HM4 8QJ. Mr Alwin Fenlow and I move stock between the east field and the yard most mornings; the revised access would put construction traffic across that route. Our 15-year-old daughter Nell Fenlow lives here too, as does my aunt Doris Fenlow. We cannot simply shut the yard for a season.

I have worked this ground for over 40 years. The drainage ditch beside the gate already backs up after heavy rain, and I cannot see how the proposed bund helps. Cllr Bram Uldane saw the standing water on his visit. I have had poor sleep worrying about the disruption, but my objection is to the design, not to change in principle. Please ask Harthmere Linkways Ltd to show a workable farm crossing before the Harthmere Freight Link plans are fixed. I can be reached on 07700 900842.

Ellis Fenlow
