text:
Health representation concerning the Letchmere Battery and Grid Connection Project
Application reference: EN090314
From: Mara Pell
Address for correspondence: 14 Copper Mews, Letchmere, LM4 8QP
Email: mara.pell@postgrove.example
Interested Party reference: IP-24817
Date: 21 October 2026

I am writing as a resident about the proposed battery compound at East Bank Fields and the associated cable works. I am not objecting to batteries in principle. My concern is that the health chapter treats air quality as a question of whether a numerical limit is likely to be exceeded, without really explaining what living alongside the works would be like. The route to the site passes homes, the school crossing and the small shops. People do not experience emissions as an annual average on a spreadsheet. We experience lorries going past the front door, dust on a dry day and engines waiting at temporary lights.

I have been diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and migraine with aura. I use a beclometasone preventer inhaler, carry a salbutamol reliever inhaler and take sumatriptan tablets when needed. I am giving this information reluctantly, because it is difficult to explain why the proposed controls matter to my household without saying it. I do not expect the Examining Authority to decide my individual health needs. I do ask that the assessment takes seriously the difference between a modelled average and a short period of very poor conditions outside someone's home. I would also like the medical details in this paragraph removed before publication if possible.

My daughter, Elsi Pell, is aged 11 and has autism spectrum disorder and a moderate learning disability. Changes to the journey to school can be difficult for our household to manage, particularly if the crossing is moved with little notice or if construction vehicles arrive in groups at the same time as pupils. I mention this because the traffic management plan talks about vehicle numbers but says very little about how notices will reach families who need time to plan. A clear, accessible notice before any change would help. This is not a request to stop all works near the school; it is a request to make the arrangements predictable and to keep the walking route open wherever it is safe to do so.

I have lived in this part of Letchmere for over 20 years. On still mornings, dust from ordinary road traffic is already visible on window ledges. The environmental statement says the construction dust risk will be controlled by good practice, but it does not say who checks whether that practice is actually happening at the gate. What happens when a load arrives uncovered, or when a road sweeper misses a side street? A complaints number after the event is useful, but it cannot replace someone with authority to pause an activity while a problem is put right. Please require a named role on site, a log of inspections and a simple way for residents to see what action followed a complaint.

The applicant, Alder Silt Energy Ltd, says deliveries can be scheduled outside the busiest hours. I would welcome that, but the draft wording seems to leave too much to later agreement. In particular, it should say whether drivers will be told not to wait with engines running on Copper Lane, and where a vehicle goes if the site gate is not ready. The existing lay-by is beside the footway and is not a suitable informal waiting area. The documents also use the phrase 'where practicable' several times without saying who decides what is practicable. That needs tightening up before consent is given.

My health is affected by uncertainty about the works, and poor sleep has made the prospect feel worse. I am not presenting those feelings as a separate diagnosis or claiming that every noisy day is a medical emergency. Other residents have said much the same about wellbeing, including people who support the scheme overall. Good information would help: a weekly look-ahead for especially dusty activities, a plain-English explanation of any change to the haul route, and a contact point that is actually monitored while work is taking place. The project mailbox, enquiries@letchmere-grid.example, could be used for this if replies are prompt and residents are not simply sent back to a long technical appendix.

At the drop-in, Mrs Tamsin Rell, a neighbour who is not making a representation, asked whether the temporary lights would remain over weekends. The answer given in the room was that this was still being worked out. That exchange is why I am concerned about details being left until after examination. Cllr Olan Firth also asked for a timetable that people could put on a noticeboard. I agree with that practical suggestion. It would be especially helpful to have one version of the timetable covering the cable works and the compound, rather than two contractors issuing different dates for the same stretch of road.

Please could the Examining Authority ask for a firmer construction traffic plan, enforceable dust checks and notices that give households enough time to adapt? Please also ask for air quality monitoring locations to include the homes nearest the access route, not just the site boundary. I know that monitoring does not prevent an incident by itself; its value is that it shows when a control has failed and prompts a response. The results should be published in a form ordinary residents can read, with an explanation of any missed measurements.

I hope these points are treated as a request for workable safeguards rather than opposition to the energy transition. I want the project to be assessed on what will happen in our streets, not only on what appears possible under ideal site management. Thank you for considering this representation.

Supplementary technical points: construction effects and the health assessment

This note adds technical points to the request for workable safeguards above. The Letchmere Battery and Grid Connection Project should be assessed against a realistic construction programme, including overlapping activities, rather than against a sequence in which each disruptive task happens separately. Alder Silt Energy Ltd's draft programme shows earthworks, cable installation and delivery of battery equipment as distinct phases, but it does not make clear whether vehicle movements from one phase have been carried into the assessment of the next. A combined peak-week schedule would make the traffic, dust and noise conclusions easier to test.

The transport assessment uses a weekday average for construction vehicle movements. An average is useful for network modelling, but it does not describe the days when several large components arrive or when excavated material leaves the site. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should state a maximum number of two-way HGV movements in any day and any hour, identify which vehicles count towards that limit, and explain how bookings will be checked. It should also identify what happens if a delivery is late. A booking system is not a control if a delayed vehicle is simply added to the following hour's movements.

The proposed route from the A4176 Fenway Road via Sedgefold Lane should be checked at the narrow bend beside Letchmere Common. The swept-path drawing in Transport Appendix TR-04 appears to show one vehicle passing through that bend, not the situation in which an HGV meets an oncoming bus or agricultural vehicle. The assessment should include that encounter, temporary waiting arrangements and the effect of any waiting on the road behind. It should explain whether marshals would be needed for particular loads. Any restriction on access should be tied to a drawing and a condition, not left to a later discussion with the contractor.

Air quality predictions should distinguish exhaust emissions from tracked-out mud and dust raised again by ordinary traffic. For construction dust, the assessment should set out the assumed length of open haul road, the area of exposed soil and the frequency of water-cart use during dry weather. The statement that damping-down will occur 'as required' does not say who decides when it is required. A daily inspection record, a trigger for additional suppression and a stop-work procedure during persistent visible dust would be more testable. Monitoring results should be reported alongside the activity taking place that day, so a low reading during an inactive period is not presented as proof that controls worked during earthworks.

The same need for clear assumptions applies to noise. The indicative plant list should be reconciled with the construction programme, particularly where piling, compaction and cable trenching could take place at the same time. The assessment gives representative daytime levels, but no short-duration maximum for unloading metal equipment or reversing at the compound. A prediction should not assume every item operates continuously; equally, it should not exclude a credible combination merely because the tasks appear under different headings. Proposed working hours, the process for exceptional work and advance notice arrangements should be included in the draft controls examined now.

Operational noise requires a separate check. The proposed battery units, transformers and cooling equipment may have different operating patterns depending on demand and temperature. A single typical-load scenario is therefore insufficient. The acoustic assessment should show the assumed operating state for each source, the combined level at the nearest assessment positions, and the uncertainty applied to manufacturer data. If the design relies on acoustic enclosures or barriers, those features should be specified sufficiently for a requirement to secure them before operation. Post-installation verification should use a stated method and a clear route for correcting an exceedance.

Drainage is also relevant to the reliability of the proposed controls. The surface-water strategy refers to swales along the eastern compound edge and attenuation within Plot B7. It should show how sediment-laden construction runoff will be kept separate from the permanent drainage system before the ground is stabilised. The design should test a blocked inlet and an extreme rainfall event, including where exceedance flows would travel. A maintenance schedule should state who inspects the swales, how often silt is removed and what temporary measures apply while a drainage feature is being repaired. These details matter because standing water and repeated muddy road conditions can undermine otherwise sensible site-management measures.

The landscape drawings should be consistent with the proposed earthworks levels. Viewpoint LV-06 is presented as a summer view with established planting; the examination also needs a winter-year-one view, before screening has matured. The height of battery containers, fencing, lighting columns and any acoustic barrier should be shown against the finished ground level, not just the existing level. For lighting, the submitted plan should give the direction, mounting height and operating controls for each fitting. A broad commitment to minimise spill is hard to assess without those parameters.

Ecology controls should be joined up with the construction method, while avoiding unnecessary disclosure of sensitive locations. The ecological summary notes badger activity in Brindle Wood and bat activity along the eastern hedgerow. These are broad habitat descriptions, not reasons to omit practical measures. The construction plan should show the retained hedgerow buffer, the limits of night-time lighting and the procedure if protected-species evidence is found during works. Any genuinely sensitive location can be provided in a restricted annex rather than on a public route drawing.

Finally, the draft requirements should be checked against the Letchmere Local Health and Environment Framework and the Fenway Construction Code. References to a future plan should specify its minimum contents, approval point and enforcement mechanism. For each significant effect, the examination material should say what is predicted, what control is proposed, how compliance will be measured and what action follows a failure. That would make the health assessment useful throughout construction and operation, rather than only at the decision stage.

Technical comments on the assessment and proposed controls

The following points concern the way the Letchmere Battery and Grid Connection Project has assessed effects on the surrounding area. They are not an objection to battery storage in principle. The difficulty is that several conclusions in the Environmental Statement depend on controls that are described only as matters for a later management plan. The examination should be able to test those controls now, particularly where construction traffic, noise and drainage could act together.

Construction traffic

The transport chapter gives daily totals but does not show how movements would be distributed across the busiest hours. A daily average is of limited help when deliveries are likely to coincide with the start of other construction work in the Fenway employment area. The applicant, Alder Silt Energy Ltd, should provide an hourly profile for each construction phase, separating heavy goods vehicles, staff vehicles and abnormal loads. The profile should cover the cable works as well as the battery compound; treating those activities as separate projects risks understating the busiest period if their programmes overlap.

The proposed route from the A6178 along Letchmere Road passes the Mill Dyke junction. The assessment uses a single turning-count survey at that junction without explaining whether the count represents a typical weekday or a quieter period. A sensitivity test using higher background flows would help. So would a drawing showing the swept path for the largest routine delivery vehicle, with any temporary changes to signs, kerbs or verge protection marked clearly. The Transport Statement refers to a construction traffic management plan, but it should state the maximum number of heavy vehicle arrivals per hour, permitted delivery windows and how breaches would be recorded. Otherwise the plan cannot be compared with the figures used in the assessment.

Noise and air quality

The noise chapter compares predicted levels at representative receptors, yet its construction scenario appears to assume that earthworks, cable trenching and compound assembly will not operate at the same time. That assumption needs to be secured in the phasing programme or replaced with a combined assessment. The tables should also distinguish between a short, exceptional activity and a level expected on many working days. Where temporary screening is relied upon, the requirement should identify its minimum height, the work areas it must screen and the point by which it must be installed.

For the operational assessment, the equipment schedule should identify the tested sound-power data used for the inverters, cooling plant and transformers. A commitment to select equipment with ‘similar performance’ is too open-ended unless the relevant maximum sound-power levels and tonal characteristics are included in a requirement. Commissioning measurements should be taken under conditions when cooling equipment is working at an appropriately high load, not only during a convenient quiet test. If the measured levels exceed the assessed envelope, the requirement should provide for corrective work and a repeat survey before unrestricted operation.

The air-quality assessment relies on dust suppression and wheel cleaning but leaves the inspection frequency to a future contractor. The Fenway Construction Code gives a useful starting point. For this site, the dust plan should additionally identify the haul-road surfacing sequence, the location of wheel-cleaning facilities and the circumstances in which dry cutting or bulk earth handling must stop. Complaints data alone would not be a reliable measure of whether the controls are working. Daily inspection records and a defined response to visible track-out would be more useful.

Landscape, lighting and ecology

The visual assessment includes winter views, which is welcome, but some photomontages show planting at a maturity that would not exist during the early years of operation. The conclusion should separate the initial effect from the effect after planting is established. Planting specifications should include replacement duties, irrigation during establishment and a test for gaps in the retained hedge. A statement that screening will be ‘maintained’ does not say what happens if part of it fails.

The lighting strategy should distinguish security lighting needed for an incident from lighting used for routine access. Routine lighting ought to be limited to the task area and switched off when it is not needed. The final design should state mounting heights, beam direction and the boundary limits used in its calculation. Badgers have been recorded in Brackenfold Wood, but that is a broad habitat reference rather than a reason to publish precise survey findings on an unrestricted drawing. The public requirement can specify survey timing, a stop-work procedure and the ecological sign-off needed before vegetation clearance without disclosing sensitive locations.

Drainage and emergency arrangements

The drainage chapter addresses ordinary rainfall but is less clear about flows when an access track is partly blocked by construction materials. The submitted calculations should test the temporary construction layout as well as the finished scheme. They should identify where exceedance water travels, whether it could enter Mill Dyke and who checks that silt controls remain in place after heavy rain. The proposed attenuation basin must also remain accessible for inspection throughout cable installation.

The Battery Safety Management Outline refers to containment of firefighting water but gives no volume or isolation arrangement. These matters affect the drainage design and should not be left entirely to a post-consent document. The examination needs a plan showing the containment area, the valves or other isolation measures, inspection responsibilities and the route for removing contaminated water. This is a design-interface issue, not simply an operational procedure.

Requested clarification

A consolidated commitments schedule would make these matters easier to examine. It should put each modelling assumption beside the corresponding requirement, drawing or management-plan provision. Where an assumption cannot be secured, the assessment should be rerun on a reasonable worst-case basis. Letchmere Borough Council and the Fenway Drainage Board should then be able to comment on the same set of limits that the decision-maker is asked to approve, rather than on promises whose detail is deferred.

Health representation: Letchmere Battery and Grid Connection Project

I am writing separately about health because the drainage points in my earlier section do not explain what construction and emergency access could mean for this household. I support a reliable electricity supply. I am asking the Examining Authority to test the health assumptions against the actual working arrangements before deciding whether those arrangements can be secured.

My name is Mara Pell. I live at 17 Reedglass Walk, Letchmere, LM4 8QJ, near the proposed cable route. I have lived in Letchmere for over 20 years. My interested party reference is IP-047219. Please use that reference if this section is separated from my earlier comments about containment and drainage.

I have diagnosed asthma and chronic migraine. I use a daily budesonide inhaler and keep a salbutamol inhaler for flare-ups. I also take sumatriptan tablets when a migraine starts. These details are not offered as a claim that the project will cause an attack. They explain why a general statement that effects will be temporary does not answer my concern about dust, exhaust and changes to access on the days when works are closest to homes. I can manage ordinary day to day conditions, but the assessment should not assume that residents can simply go elsewhere during an unexpectedly dusty shift.

My daughter, Elsi Pell, is 11 years old and has autism spectrum disorder. Elsi has occupational therapy appointments, and an unpredictable change to the usual journey can be difficult to manage. I am not saying that disability means the cable route cannot be built. I am saying the traffic and construction plans need to describe what residents will actually be told when the programme changes. A notice saying works will occur at some point during a six-week period is not much use for planning an appointment or explaining to a child why a familiar crossing is closed that morning.

The Environmental Statement discusses dust suppression, vehicle movements and monitoring, but I cannot tell from it whether the highest predicted movements coincide with excavation beside Reedglass Walk. In particular, I would like a table showing the assumed daily HGV numbers for that stretch, the hours for loading and spoil removal, and the control to be applied if a road is visibly dusty despite the proposed measures. A promise to inspect the road is different from a commitment to stop a particular activity until the problem has been dealt with. Please say who makes that decision and how residents can report an issue while the work is happening, not just afterwards.

There is also the question of air quality during an incident at the battery site. I understand that the application considers fire response separately from routine construction. I am not asking the Examining Authority to predict an individual medical outcome. My concern is that the documents describe where vehicles can enter and where water can be contained, but say less clearly how nearby households would receive a prompt, consistent instruction if smoke affected the route used to leave the area. The response plan ought to identify who issues an alert, the means of doing so if mobile coverage is poor, and how that instruction is coordinated with any road closure. It should not leave residents trying to interpret several different updates.

At the drop-in, Mrs Tamsin Rell, a neighbour who is not making a representation, asked whether the applicant would provide advance notice of the noisiest cable works. The answer we heard was that the contractor would engage with the community. That may be well meant, but I could not find a minimum notice period in the draft commitments. Cllr Olan Firth also asked about a single point of contact. I would support that, provided the contact details are kept current and someone can act on reports rather than merely log them. A shared address such as planning@alder-silt-energy.example would be easier for residents to find than a different number on each contractor's leaflet.

I have had poor sleep when trying to work out whether the lane will be open the next morning. That is a description of how uncertainty feels, not an assertion that all construction disturbance is a medical emergency. The distinction matters. The application should assess likely noise and air quality effects using realistic working hours, and it should also give people information early enough to organise ordinary family life. Both points can be addressed without publishing anyone's health records or relying on residents to explain a diagnosis to a site operative at the gate.

Could Alder Silt Energy Ltd provide a combined programme for the cable works near homes, including the activities most likely to generate dust and the thresholds that trigger additional suppression or a pause? Could it explain whether its monitoring locations reflect homes beside the haul route, rather than only the battery compound boundary? I would also welcome a plain-language version of the incident communication procedure for comment during the examination. Letchmere Borough Council may be able to advise on local air quality information, while the Fenway Drainage Board's comments on incident water should be read alongside, not instead of, the arrangements for warning residents.

I ask that any approved construction plan fixes responsibility, minimum notice and a way of checking that promised measures have happened. If the applicant cannot yet identify the haulage pattern or warning method, that uncertainty should be stated and assessed. I do not expect there to be no disruption. I do expect the decision to be based on a workable set of limits, with a route for correcting problems quickly when the work on the ground differs from the drawings.

Technical points on construction controls and the environmental assessment

The assessment for the Letchmere Battery and Grid Connection Project should use one consistent construction programme across its traffic, air quality, noise and drainage chapters. At present the busiest traffic month is described as an average in one place and as a maximum daily movement in another. Those are not interchangeable. The examination needs a table showing, for each phase, the number of heavy goods vehicle arrivals and departures, the working days assumed, the shift times and the activities taking place simultaneously. The table should include the cable connection works, not only the main compound. Without that common set of assumptions, it is difficult to tell whether the proposed controls have been tested against the busiest credible period.

The Draft Construction Traffic Management Plan identifies Beryl Lane as the principal approach but does not show how vehicles would be held when two loads arrive close together. Its swept-path drawings appear to assume that the opposing lane is empty at the bend by the Aster Cut bridge. That may be possible under managed traffic, but management should be described as a requirement rather than an aspiration. The plan ought to specify where a vehicle waits, who authorises its onward movement, and what happens when the holding area is full. A daily cap alone will not prevent a short queue at the bridge if deliveries are bunched into the same half hour.

The junction assessment for the Wrenfold Link also needs a sensitivity test for the overlap between earthworks and electrical deliveries. The present model gives a single set of peak-hour results, while the programme allows for those activities to overlap if earlier work is delayed. A reasonable worst-case test would apply the higher of the two delivery profiles during that overlap and report queue lengths as well as average delay. The model should state whether it includes abnormal loads, escort arrangements and temporary restrictions on turning movements. These are practical matters for the traffic order and for the construction plan; they should not be deferred to an unspecified discussion after consent.

Dust controls should follow the same phase assumptions. The earthworks area, temporary stockpiles and any unsealed section of haul route need to be shown on a single plan with the construction drainage features. Watering a route can reduce dust, but it may increase the volume of silty runoff requiring treatment. The environmental assessment should therefore explain how the measures work together during dry weather followed by heavy rain. A condition that simply requires dust suppression and drainage protection, without an agreed layout or inspection trigger, would leave an avoidable gap between two sets of otherwise sensible commitments.

The position of the temporary settlement features relative to Aster Cut is important. The drainage drawings show the proposed outfall but do not clearly distinguish clean water from water draining active work areas. Fenway Drainage Board has asked for clarity on discharge rates, and that request should be answered with the calculations and a plan of the flow paths for each construction phase. The plan should identify where water is isolated if a settlement feature is overtopped or a pump fails. This does not require every pipe fitting to be fixed in the development consent order, but the maximum discharge, the treatment standard and the means of checking compliance should be secured before works start.

For noise, the predicted levels should be presented against the hours during which each noisy activity might actually occur. The cable trenching description refers to work progressing along the route, whereas the noise chapter relies on a representative plant group at fixed assessment locations. A moving source can be assessed, but the assessment should say how long it is expected to remain in each section and what plant would operate at the same time. If weekend work is retained as an option, it should be assessed as such, with defined circumstances for its use. Otherwise the proposed normal hours are not a reliable limit.

There is also a landscape issue with the proposed screening beside Fenmere Copse. The visualisations show established planting, while the programme indicates that the compound could be in use before new planting has taken hold. The examination should have a first-year view and a later-year view from the same agreed viewpoints. Temporary fencing, lighting columns and the height of stored materials should be included in the first-year version. This would give a clearer basis for deciding whether temporary screening is necessary and whether any height limit on materials should be written into the construction requirements.

Lighting is treated separately in several documents, although it is part of the same construction scene. The lighting strategy should give a maximum mounting height, an orientation plan and a method for checking that light is not spilling beyond the working area. It should also explain the arrangements when works stop for the night: whether security lighting remains on continuously, is motion-operated, or is switched off except during an incident. A statement that fittings will be directional is helpful but not measurable on its own. The same agreed lighting plan should be used for the landscape appraisal and the ecological assessment so that they assess the same proposal.

Finally, Alder Silt Energy Ltd should be required to keep one controlled register of the construction commitments made across these documents. Letchmere Borough Council needs to be able to identify which plan is current, what parameter has changed and whether the change remains within the assessed envelope. The register should cross-refer to the relevant development consent requirement and state how non-compliance will be recorded and corrected. This is not a request to prevent ordinary adjustments in construction methods. It is a request for the limits relied on in the assessment to be visible, enforceable and consistent from one technical chapter to the next.

Health representation – construction air quality and wellbeing

Further to my comments about keeping the technical documents consistent, I want to explain why the construction air quality assessment matters to my household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide whether the Letchmere Battery and Grid Connection Project will cause a particular illness. I am asking it to check whether the applicant has assessed the activities people will actually experience, including the access route, temporary compounds, deliveries and any changes to the working hours.

I am Mara Pell, and I have lived in the Letchmere area for several years. I have diagnosed asthma and chronic migraine. I use a salbutamol inhaler and take prescribed propranolol. I give this information reluctantly because it helps explain why an assessment expressed only as an annual average does not answer my concern. My point is not that every dusty day will cause a medical emergency. It is that short periods of dust, exhaust and noise may make ordinary days harder to manage, particularly if residents do not know when the most disruptive work is planned. My health is affected by uncertainty as well as by what happens outside the house, though I realise that feeling alone is not a measurement of air quality.

My 11-year-old daughter, Elsi Pell, has autism spectrum disorder. A sudden change to a familiar journey or a prolonged queue of construction traffic can make getting to school difficult. I am not suggesting that the project must stop because one family finds change difficult. I am saying that advance notice, a reliable timetable and a contact who can deal with a problem on the day would make a practical difference. The assessment should also consider the route children take to school rather than assuming that the nearest residential façade represents all exposure. A child waiting by a crossing is not necessarily in the same situation as somebody indoors behind a closed window.

The air quality chapter appears to treat construction dust mainly by reference to the boundary of each work area. That may be a reasonable starting point, but it does not tell us enough about HGV movements along Merebank Lane or vehicles waiting to turn into the northern compound. The lane is narrow in places. A statement that engines will be switched off when parked is welcome, but who will check it, and will a driver waiting in a moving queue count as parked? I would like the applicant to show the assumptions used for daily vehicle numbers, the busiest hour and the length of time the northern access will be used. Those assumptions should match the traffic assessment and the construction management plan.

Dust from an open field is not the same as dust tracked onto the road and lifted again by passing traffic. I would like a commitment to inspect the lane during dry weather, clean it when needed and record complaints and the action taken. Please do not leave the wording at ‘where practicable’ without saying who decides what is practicable. If the applicant proposes to move a compound or change a haul route, the same check should be done again before work starts at the new location. This is especially important if deliveries are concentrated into fewer hours than the figures in the environmental statement suggest.

There is also the question of notification. The documents refer to a community liaison arrangement, but I cannot see a clear period of notice for earthworks, road closures or deliveries of unusually large equipment. An email sent after the work has begun is not useful. A short notice showing the expected dates, times and route, with an update if these change, would allow households to plan. It should be available on paper as well as online. Not everybody checks a project website every morning, and a generic project mailbox such as letchmereproject@alder-silt.example is only helpful if somebody reads it and replies in time.

At the drop-in, Mrs Tamsin Rell asked whether the applicant would publish the results of any dust monitoring. I understood the answer to be that monitoring would be considered if complaints were received. That seems backwards. A complaint cannot establish what the air was like beforehand, and residents should not have to guess whether a visible cloud is within an agreed limit. I am not asking for expensive equipment at every gate. I am asking for a clear trigger for additional monitoring, a record of inspections and a way for Letchmere Borough Council to see those records. Cllr Olan Firth also raised the need for information to reach households away from the immediate site boundary, because the route extends beyond that boundary.

I appreciate that Alder Silt Energy Ltd cannot control every source of dust or traffic in the area. There are farm vehicles and normal roadworks, and it would be unfair to attribute everything to this project. Equally, that is a reason to keep an accurate record, not a reason to leave the mitigation vague. The proposed works near drainage channels should be coordinated with Fenway Drainage Board, particularly where a wet road or mud from the site might lead to more cleaning and more vehicle movements. I want the construction plans to explain how those activities fit together, rather than placing each matter in a separate document with a different set of working assumptions.

This representation is about practical safeguards, not a claim that a particular health outcome has already been proved. I feel anxious about the possibility of poor sleep and about being unable to tell whether an unexpected dusty spell is normal or the result of something going wrong. Those feelings are real, but I have kept them separate from the medical information above. The Examining Authority can help by requiring measurable controls, advance notice and a simple route for residents to report a problem and find out what was done. If the final construction documents use the same access routes, hours and vehicle figures throughout, the resulting assessment will be much easier to understand and trust.

Mara Pell

Technical matters for the examination

The following points concern the assessment and control of the Letchmere Battery and Grid Connection Project, rather than any prediction about an individual household. They are intended to make the proposed limits capable of being tested during construction and operation.

The traffic assessment should distinguish an average construction day from the busiest delivery day. Table 7.4 of the Transport Assessment gives daily two-way heavy goods vehicle totals, but the draft Construction Traffic Management Plan does not show how many vehicles could arrive in a single hour. That distinction matters on Reedbank Lane, where opposing large vehicles cannot pass throughout its length. A daily cap alone would allow most deliveries to be concentrated around the start of the working day. The final plan should specify an hourly delivery limit, the permitted route from the East Letchmere Link and a holding arrangement within the application site so that vehicles do not wait on the public highway.

The swept-path drawings also need to reflect the temporary condition, not just the completed junction. Drawing TR-06 shows the finished access with its proposed visibility splays. It does not show how vehicles will turn while the verge is being excavated or when temporary traffic signals are in place. Before that work starts, an updated drawing should be agreed with Letchmere Borough Council. It should include the location of the signals, pedestrian provision and the position of any temporary barriers. The reference in the draft plan to a traffic marshal is useful, but it is not a substitute for a drawing that demonstrates a workable layout.

Construction noise is considered in Chapter 11 of the Environmental Statement using representative plant lists. The lists do not make clear whether trench excavation for the cable route and foundation work at the battery compound may occur at the same time. If simultaneous working was assumed in the prediction, the assessment should say so plainly. If it was not, the Construction Environmental Management Plan should prevent that overlap where it would raise the assessed noise level at a receptor. Monitoring should be tied to the predicted worst-case activities, with results recorded in a form that can be compared with the assessment. A statement that monitoring will take place ‘as necessary’ is not a measurable commitment.

The same point applies to dust. The proposed measures—covering loads, damping down and keeping the haul route clean—are sensible, but the draft wording leaves their use to the contractor’s discretion. A trigger for inspecting the site boundary and the access road would be more useful than a general promise to manage dust. The inspection record should note the weather, the activity under way, any visible track-out and the action taken. These are practical checks of site management, not a request to assume that every visible plume indicates a breach.

For operational noise, the assessment should identify which equipment can run concurrently at night. The layout includes inverter units, ventilation equipment and transformers, while the submitted acoustic summary presents a combined rating level. The calculation sheets should be available to the Examining Authority so that the assumed duty cycles and any tonal corrections can be checked. Any required acoustic enclosures should be secured as part of the approved design, not left to a later choice between different products. A post-commissioning test should be carried out under a defined operating condition and should state what happens if the approved limit is exceeded.

Surface water is another issue requiring a clear sequence of controls. The Flood Risk Assessment proposes attenuation before discharge to the Sallow Drain, but the outline construction plan gives little detail about runoff while the permanent system is incomplete. Exposed ground, temporary stockpiles and vehicle movements could change the route taken by water across the site. Fenway Drainage Board should be asked to review the temporary drainage layout as well as the finished design. The relevant requirement should prevent commencement of major earthworks until temporary settlement and interception measures are in place. Inspection after heavy rain should be recorded, including whether any silt has reached the drain.

The landscape drawings show proposed planting along the northern boundary of the compound. Screening is presented in several visualisations as though it will already be established, although the planting schedule indicates a period of growth before that effect is achieved. The examination should therefore consider the early operational view as well as the later view. The planting plan should specify replacement of failed plants, the period of maintenance and how access for inspecting the fence and drainage features will be maintained without repeatedly cutting back the screening. This is especially relevant from the Brindle Footpath, which is shown on the public rights of way plan.

The ecology information should also remain consistent across the final documents. Badger setts have been recorded in Brindle Copse, and the outline measures refer to further checks before works begin. That is an appropriate precaution, but it should not be treated as a reason to leave the construction boundary undefined. Any necessary changes to fencing or working methods should be documented and passed into the site briefing. The same applies to proposed controls on lighting near habitat edges: the lighting plan, ecology measures and construction programme should describe one agreed arrangement rather than three separate intentions.

Finally, the requirements should identify which plans require approval, who keeps the monitoring records and when those records must be produced. The draft Statement of Common Ground with Letchmere Borough Council lists construction management and drainage as matters still under discussion. It would assist the examination to see whether the final agreed wording resolves the points above. Without that detail, a commitment may sound reassuring but remain difficult to enforce when two construction activities coincide or a temporary arrangement differs from the assessed one.

Further technical comments on the construction assessment

The transport and environmental assessments need to use the same construction scenario. At present the traffic chapter appears to model a peak month for the battery compound, while the construction programme allows trenching for the grid connection and delivery of drainage materials during that same period. It is not clear whether the modelled peak includes those movements. Alder Silt Energy Ltd should provide a single weekly profile, by vehicle class and access point, for the Letchmere Battery and Grid Connection Project. This would let the Examining Authority check the assumed busiest week against the limits proposed in the draft Development Consent Order.

The difference matters at the junction of Merebank Road and Silt Lane. The drawings show a widened bellmouth, but the swept-path plots use an articulated vehicle entering without an opposing vehicle waiting to turn. A plot showing two-way operation at the forecast peak would be more useful, particularly where temporary fencing reduces visibility. The assessment should also say whether abnormal loads, aggregate deliveries and workforce vehicles use the same gate. If separate gates are proposed, their opening dates and routes should appear in the construction traffic management plan rather than being left to the contractor to determine later.

The submitted flow tables report daily totals, whereas disturbance from construction traffic depends partly on when movements occur. An hourly profile for the first and final hour of permitted working would test whether deliveries are likely to bunch around shift changes. The tables should distinguish vehicles entering from vehicles leaving; combining them into a two-way figure can conceal a short queue at the gate. A plan for holding vehicles within the site, rather than on Merebank Road, would provide a clearer basis for assessing the proposed controls. These are requests about the assumptions and management of traffic, not a request for a particular traffic forecast to be preferred.

Dust controls should be tied to the programme used for traffic. The proposed water bowsers may be adequate while internal haul roads are open, but the assessment does not explain how clean running surfaces would be maintained when the drainage crossing is excavated and access is narrowed. The soil-management plan should identify the maximum exposed area in each phase, the triggers for suspending handling in dry and windy conditions, and the location of wheel-washing equipment before export of excavated material begins. A requirement simply to have regard to weather would be difficult to audit. Records of inspections, complaints received and corrective action should be retained in the same format throughout the works.

The drainage drawings also need reconciling with the construction programme. The permanent attenuation basin is shown near the eastern boundary, yet the outline sequence suggests that this area may first be used for temporary storage. The application should explain what provides equivalent runoff storage until the basin is operational. Fenway Drainage Board may wish to confirm whether the temporary discharge rate and the permanent rate have been assessed on comparable catchment areas. The calculations should cover the compound, haul routes and grid-connection works, including any short period when stripped ground drains towards the temporary crossing. A plan should identify who checks silt controls after heavy rainfall and where the results are recorded.

On landscape effects, the year-one visualisations should show the as-built security fencing and lighting columns without relying on planting that has not yet established. The later visualisations can then show the expected screening at a specified height, provided the maintenance commitment states how failed planting will be replaced. Viewpoints from the public sections of Silt Lane and the Merebank footpath are useful, but the wirelines should state the assumed ground levels and finished platform level. This is particularly important if material from excavation is to form a bund: its height, width and construction date should be fixed in the parameter plans and assessed consistently in the landscape and drainage chapters.

The lighting assessment describes low-spill fittings but does not include a dimensioned drawing of the temporary construction lighting arrangement. It should distinguish task lighting during trenching from the permanent security scheme and identify the maximum mounting height, direction of fittings and hours of use. The ecology and landscape documents could then refer to the same drawing. General references to badgers in Willow Fen Wood and bats along the field boundaries do not establish that a particular protected site lies within the works, but they do support checking that temporary lighting is included in the assessed scheme.

Finally, the proposed controls should distinguish between documents approved before any works and documents approved before a particular phase. For example, a drainage strategy approved after site clearance would not resolve how runoff is managed during clearance. Letchmere Borough Council and Fenway Drainage Board should be given the same revision of the relevant plans when consulted, with a clear schedule showing which requirement secures each measure. That would make it possible to compare the final plans with the assessed construction envelope, rather than trying to assemble the scheme from separate chapters and later contractor submissions.

Health representation — Letchmere Battery and Grid Connection Project
From: Mara Pell

I am concerned that the construction controls described above do not say what happens when dust or vehicle emissions reach homes near the access route. I have diagnosed asthma and chronic migraine, and I use a salbutamol inhaler. On days when the air is poor I already find it difficult to keep windows open. This proposal makes me anxious about our wellbeing, particularly during site clearance and cable trenching.

Elsi Pell, my 11-year-old daughter, has autism. A clear timetable for noisy and dusty works would help our household plan, but it would not replace proper monitoring and a way to report problems promptly. At the drop-in, Mrs Tamsin Rell raised a similar concern about construction traffic; Cllr Olan Firth also asked how complaints would be recorded.

I ask Alder Silt Energy Ltd to provide Letchmere Borough Council with the monitoring locations and trigger levels before clearance begins, not after the first complaints arrive.
