text:
Relevant Representation: Merefen Link Energy Scheme
Application reference: MF-2026-014
From: Jory Fenwick
Interested Party reference: IP-628417

I object to the proposed Merefen Link Energy Scheme. I understand the need to improve the electricity network, but the route chosen by Merefen Link Transmission Ltd puts the construction compound and access track much too close to homes on Hallow Mere Lane. I ask the Examining Authority to look again at the alternative route along the old quarry edge, rather than treating it as dismissed because it would cost more. The documents say the compound is temporary. Four years of lorries, lights and reversing alarms does not feel temporary to those of us beside it.

I live at 14 Hallow Mere Lane, Merefen, MF4 8QT. The entrance marked CA-3 on the plan is opposite our front windows, not tucked behind the hedge as the visualisation suggests. The hedge is thin in winter. I have lived in Merefen for 40+ years and know that water sits across this part of the lane after heavy rain. The traffic assessment counts the vehicles but does not, as far as I can see, explain how two large vehicles will pass when the school minibus is stopped. I am anxious about that arrangement. Anxiety about a road layout is not the same thing as accepting that the layout is safe.

My daughter Mara Fenwick is 11-year-old and waits for the minibus at the lane end. I do not want a child's details used as an argument instead of proper traffic evidence, but it matters that the proposed morning delivery period overlaps the time children are there. My son Ruan Fenwick has asthma. Dust from stripping the fields and from vehicles on a dry track is therefore more than an inconvenience in our household. The construction management plan says water will be sprayed when necessary, without saying who decides when it is necessary or how residents can get a prompt response. I also have a diagnosis of chronic migraine. Flashing lights and repeated alarms can make it difficult for me to function, particularly when I am trying to work from home. I am not asking the Inspector to assume everyone has the same health concerns; I am asking for enforceable limits instead of a promise to be considerate.

My mother Edda Fenwick, who visits to help with the school run, has rheumatoid arthritis and cannot simply walk the longer diversion shown for pedestrians. The applicant's drawing labels the diversion as a short alternative, but it includes an uneven farm crossing. Please check the route on the ground before accepting that description. I have lost sleep over this proposal, although I realise poor sleep by itself will not tell you whether a mitigation measure works.

Our neighbours have raised separate practical points. Mrs Tessa Venn, at 8 Hallow Mere Lane, Merefen, MF4 8QT, told me that the drainage ditch behind the proposed compound overtopped in the last storm. She is not submitting a representation and I have not asked her to. I mention the conversation because the flood report calls the ditch dry for much of the year; the photograph I sent with this form shows standing water there in September. Another neighbour, Darian Venn, keeps bees and is worried about losing the flowering verge. Those are their concerns as described to me, not a substitute for the applicant carrying out a proper survey. Cllr Elwin Morrell also raised the need for a safe crossing at the village meeting. I agree with that point, regardless of which access option is selected.

I attach my marked-up copy of the ecology plan. It is right to say that badgers have been seen in Brindle Copse; that is only a broad description. The plan's survey appendix, however, places an active sett at the base of the split ash 18 metres east of field gate FG-7, immediately beside the proposed track. That location should not be repeated on public versions of the plan. The same appendix identifies a bat maternity roost in the roof void of the disused pump house at grid reference MF 38142 72605. I am concerned that the proposed lighting could affect it. I am not claiming to be an ecologist, and I would welcome a clear explanation of how the lighting design deals with the survey findings. The general proposal for replacement bat boxes in Brindle Copse does not answer that question.

There is also a problem with how people can comment on changes. The revised construction timetable was put on the Merefen Link Transmission Ltd project site, https://www.merefen-link.example/documents, but the leaflet delivered here still showed the earlier timetable. A neighbour without reliable internet would not know that weekend works are now proposed. I emailed the project mailbox, enquiries@merefen-link.example, on 12 October 2026 and received an automatic acknowledgement, but no answer to the question about Saturday deliveries. This is criticism of the consultation process, not of the person who operates that inbox.

The noise figures deserve another look. A consultant, Nella Brice of Merefen Acoustic Advice, spoke at the drop-in and said the highest figures represented a short worst-case period. The table in the submitted report does not show how many days that period might last or whether piling and vehicle movements could happen together. Please require that information before deciding whether the proposed working hours are reasonable. The applicant's published construction budget may explain its preferred route, but it does not show what residents will experience at their windows.

I would prefer the application to be refused unless the compound is moved. If it is approved, I ask for a binding route for HGVs, no deliveries during school pick-up and drop-off, a measured dust trigger with a named team responsible for acting on it, and a clear limit on night lighting. Residents also need advance notice of closures by post, not just an update on a website. These are ordinary protections for a lane that will remain home to people during construction. Please record this as an objection and contact me about any hearing on traffic or construction effects.

Jory Fenwick
jory.fenwick@postmere.example
07123 648 205

Supplementary points to my relevant representation
Merefen Link Energy Scheme — case reference ML/2026/014

I am adding this note because the form did not leave enough room to explain why the proposed construction compound beside Sedgeglass Lane is not a minor inconvenience. I live at 14 Sedgeglass Lane, Greymere, GM4 6QH. The application plans call the entrance Plot C17 and show the compound operating for eighteen months. That may look temporary on a programme, but the lane is where children walk, people wait for the bus and residents open their windows. I have lived here for over 40 years and have never seen traffic of the size shown in the transport assessment using it regularly.

The drawings seem to assume that a vehicle can turn into Plot C17 without affecting the opposite verge. On my walk along the lane last Friday, two ordinary delivery vans could not pass there without one stopping. A banksman would not solve the queue behind an HGV, particularly at school times. My daughter Mara Fenwick, who is 11, walks that way with other children. My son Ruan Fenwick, aged 16, cycles to the bus stop. I am not suggesting they should be given special treatment; the point is that the assessment describes traffic movements but barely describes the people already using that space. Please require an observed, school-day survey before accepting the proposed access.

The same issue affects the two houses nearest the bend. My neighbour Ms Tessa Venn told me she cannot see around parked vehicles when she leaves her drive. Darian Venn, who lives with her, showed me where a lorry mirror came over the hedge during a survey visit. Neither of them is making a representation, as far as I know, and I am mentioning them because the swept-path line on the plan does not show what a driver can actually see. I would not want their account treated as consent to the route. Cllr Elwin Morrell also attended the public drop-in and asked whether the applicant had checked the bend on a weekday morning. That was a fair question, not an endorsement of the design.

Noise is another matter where the averages disguise the effect. At present I can hear the morning bus from my kitchen, but not continuously. The assessment appears to combine the unloading, reversing alarms and ordinary plant noise into a daytime figure. A short alarm close to a house is still intrusive even if the average complies with a limit. My mother Edda Fenwick stays at my home several days a week. She has rheumatoid arthritis and sometimes rests in the front room in the afternoon. I have asthma, so dust from the proposed hardstanding is more than a question of whether the window ledge looks dirty. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide medical evidence from this letter. I am asking for monitoring at homes, with an enforceable response when a trigger is exceeded, rather than monitoring only at the compound fence.

At the consultation event I spoke to Nella Brice of Merefen Acoustic Advice. Her explanation was helpful, but I understood her to say that the night-time calculation assumes the lighting and security equipment will not need a generator. The plan leaves that possibility unclear. A later email from nella.brice@merefenacoustic.example pointed me to the applicant's noise chapter; it did not answer where a generator would go if one were brought in. The general project mailbox, planning@merefenlink.example, acknowledged my follow-up. I would like the applicant to put a drawing and a firm restriction before the examination closes, rather than leave the detail to a construction contractor.

I also want to correct a possible impression from my earlier comments. I am not opposed to the cable connection itself. I object to putting its busiest construction activities beside homes when the application has not shown why the alternative compound at Old Kiln Yard was rejected. Old Kiln Yard is identified as a site on the applicant's options plan, not somebody's home. The published budget for Merefen Link Transmission Ltd may favour Plot C17, but cost alone does not make the effects on this lane acceptable. I feel anxious about the works and have slept poorly since the route was announced; those feelings are not a substitute for examining the drawings and conditions properly.

There is an ecology point too. Badger setts have been reported in Bracken Fold Wood, although that description is much too broad to tell anyone where a sett is. During a walk with the survey group I was shown an entrance at the southern lip of the disused marl pit, 18 metres east of marker post ML-17, behind the split ash. I give that detail for the confidential ecology record, not for a public map. I am concerned that the proposed temporary drainage ditch reaches the pit. I have not identified an otter holt or a bat maternity roost, and I do not want a general sighting of bats along Sedgeglass Lane mistaken for either of those things.

For completeness, the £1,460 still owing on my personal loan is not part of my objection; I mention it only because the consultation form asked whether I could pay for independent advice. I used the publicly available plans instead, including the examination index at www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects and the applicant's project page. A local news page at https://greymere-ledger.example/traffic/compound-bend contains a photograph of the bend, but the Inspector should rely on a site visit rather than its caption. Please send any procedural reply through the case team rather than publishing my home address. My Interested Party reference is IP-438217.

I therefore maintain my objection. If the compound is not moved, the consent should at least specify the access hours, prohibit school-time HGV arrivals, locate any generator away from homes, and require a dust and noise response that residents can use without having to prove harm after it has occurred. The applicant can still build a useful connection without treating Sedgeglass Lane as spare construction space.

Jory Fenwick

Further technical grounds of objection — Merefen Link Energy Scheme

The remaining points concern the construction assumptions and the controls that would appear in the development consent order. They do not depend on a particular occupier of Sedgeglass Lane. The applicant, Merefen Link Transmission Ltd, should be required to show that the scheme can be built within a defined working area and to a defined programme, rather than leaving the important details to be settled after consent.

Construction traffic and access

The Transport Assessment models the morning and evening peaks, but its construction case appears to use average daily HGV numbers. That is not a satisfactory test of the access from Sedgeglass Lane into Fenmere Road. Deliveries for a cable pull, concrete pour or compound set-up will not necessarily arrive evenly through the day. A revised assessment should test the busiest reasonably foreseeable hour for each construction phase, including two-way HGV movements, staff vehicles and any abnormal load escort. It should state the assumed vehicle lengths and swept-path tolerances. An articulated vehicle staying within the swept path on paper is not the same thing as a vehicle making the turn without blocking the opposite carriageway.

The proposed traffic management plan refers to temporary signs and banksmen, yet it does not fix a holding area. If vehicles arrive early or together, the plan must say where they wait without using the bend, the verge or the junction mouth. Plot 14C is shown as construction land in one drawing, but the access drawing does not demonstrate that it can function as a queueing area while plant and materials are stored there. This discrepancy should be resolved before any order is made. The routing commitment should also be enforceable: a driver instruction in a later contractor handbook would not provide the same certainty as an approved route plan and a condition requiring its use. The examination should ask for the number of deliveries assumed in each of the three construction phases, not merely a project-wide total.

Landscape and visual effects

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment treats the compound lighting as a temporary effect, although the phasing diagram allows it to remain for 26 months. Its viewpoint photography was taken in leaf, and there is no comparable winter view from the public path across Greymere Common. The omission matters because the proposed screen planting would not be established when the compound is first used. The applicant should submit a winter photomontage showing the fencing, lighting columns, storage stacks and the tallest item of routinely parked plant. A bare outline of the permanent electrical equipment does not describe the construction view.

The Outline Landscape Plan offers replacement planting after the works. It should also identify which existing hedgerow lengths would be removed temporarily, the maximum gap at any one time and the season in which reinstatement would occur. If screening is relied on in the significance assessment, its assumed height and establishment period need to be stated. Otherwise the assessment should describe the unmitigated construction view and explain why that view is acceptable. Greymere Borough Council’s Landscape Character Note for the Fenmere Fringe is a useful local baseline, but its description of narrow lanes and enclosed fields should be applied to the temporary works as well as to the completed scheme.

Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage drawings show clean-water interception around the compound but do not explain how runoff from disturbed ground would be managed during stripping and trench excavation. The proposed settlement measures should be sized against a stated design storm, with an allowance for the volume of water already held on site before that storm. A plan that simply says silt fencing will be used does not show where water goes when the fence overtops. This is particularly relevant on the falling ground towards the Merefen Cut, where the construction boundary and the indicated flow arrows are very close together.

The Flood Risk and Drainage Statement also assumes that temporary stockpiles can be kept away from the low point. It would be helpful to show the stockpile exclusions on the same drawing as the haul route, welfare area and turning space. If those uses compete for Plot 14C, the drainage strategy may not fit the available land. The detailed construction plan should specify inspection after heavy rain, a procedure for removing accumulated sediment and a stop-work trigger when containment fails. These are practical matters, not a request to redesign the permanent drainage system.

Ecology and phasing

The ecology chapter records bat activity around Brackenmoss Wood and signs of badgers in the wider survey area. Those are broad findings, not a reason to publish precise locations in the traffic or compound drawings. The useful question for this examination is whether night working and lighting are necessary for the activities proposed beside the wood. The construction programme should distinguish unavoidable cable-pull operations from routine storage and vehicle movements. Lighting should be task-specific, directed into the working area and removed when the relevant phase ends. A general promise to follow good practice is less useful than a drawing showing the maximum lit area and a schedule of permitted lighting hours.

Policy and controls sought

Policy INF4 of the Greymere Borough Local Plan 2037 calls for construction impacts to be managed through the design and delivery of infrastructure. The Construction Environmental Management Plan is presently described as an outline document, while matters central to the assessment are deferred to the contractor. Before consent, there should be a single revised set of drawings and tables identifying the compound footprint, peak traffic case, queueing provision, drainage layout and worst-case lighting arrangement. The final plan can refine methods, but it should not be allowed to enlarge the assessed envelope by treating every omission as a detail. If the applicant’s website at https://merefen-link.example/documents is updated with revised plans, the examination should identify the document versions relied upon so that the enforceable limits are clear.

The effect of these omissions is not abstract for my household. I live at 17 Reedwharf Close, Fenmere, FM4 8QP, which is close to the proposed access route. I have lived in this part of Fenmere for over 40 years, but I have never seen a proposal that would put so much construction traffic through the lane at once. I am not objecting to electricity infrastructure in principle. I am objecting to consent being granted before the practical limits of this particular scheme are settled.

My daughter, Mara Fenwick, is 11 and walks to the school bus stop beside the old pump house. My son, Ruan Fenwick, is 16 and cycles the same lane to college. The transport assessment counts vehicle movements but says very little about children using the lane before 8 am. On the drawing, the temporary bellmouth appears to take up the verge where people stand back when a lorry comes through. Please require a swept-path drawing that shows where a pedestrian can actually wait, with the temporary fencing and signs in place, not just an unobstructed road on paper. A banksman at the compound gate will not help someone further along the lane.

My mother, Edda Fenwick, stays with us at the address above. Edda has rheumatoid arthritis and cannot quickly step off an uneven path to avoid a vehicle. I have asthma and already use an inhaler on dusty days. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide our medical treatment. These points explain why a generic promise to keep dust down does not answer the question of what happens when uncovered loads pass the houses. My health is affected by the thought of years of works, although I appreciate that worry on its own is not a prediction of air quality. The applicant should give an enforceable routeing plan, a method for covering loads and a clear trigger for stopping work if dust controls fail.

I have also spoken with the neighbours immediately across the lane, Tessa Venn and Darian Venn. They are not making representations and did not ask me to speak for them. They described the difficulty of getting a car out when delivery vehicles meet at the bend. That is why I raised queueing provision in the previous paragraph: saying drivers will book slots does not show where an early driver would safely wait. Please do not take my account of that conversation as their consent to use their driveway or land. Their home is 19 Reedwharf Close, Fenmere, FM4 8QP, and the current access sketch seems to show a waiting area uncomfortably near it. I would welcome a plan that makes the boundary unmistakable.

At the drop-in event on 9 September 2026, Cllr Elwin Morrell asked whether the lane could remain open during utility diversions. I understood the answer to be that details would follow. That answer may be honest, but it is not a basis for assessing the worst case now. The acoustic note prepared by Nella Brice of Merefen Acoustic Advice uses a daytime average. It does not show the effect of a short period of reversing alarms outside a bedroom window, or explain which of the several possible compound layouts was modelled. I am not alleging that the modelling is dishonest; I am asking for the model inputs and a drawing that matches them. I have had poor sleep since the route was announced, but that does not replace proper noise evidence.

There is also an ecological issue that needs handling without putting sensitive wildlife locations on a public map. Badgers have been recorded in Glassmere Wood, a broad area that local people know. During the summer I saw signs beside the lane. I reported to the project ecology team that a badger sett entrance is in the bank 14 metres east of the western stile on Footpath 7, beneath the twin ash trees. I mention that detail here only so that the examination team can check whether the confidential survey covers the same place. The public-facing plans should show the necessary protection measures without publishing a pinpointed location. My concern is that the proposed drainage ditch could alter that bank if the contractor is left to adjust its line later.

I wrote to the project mailbox at merefenlink@planning-inspectorate.gov.uk about the missing cross-section. I later received a reply from the applicant's consultant address nella.brice@merefenacoustic.example, but the attachment was the earlier drawing again. For completeness, my own email is jory.fenwick@reedpost.example and the mobile number I gave when registering was 07700 846 219. My Interested Party reference is MFEN-2047. I include these details to help match this representation to my earlier query, not because I want them printed in a public report. The postcode FM4 8QP appears on the wider consultation map as a general area label; it should not be treated as a substitute for a property-by-property access assessment.

I ask the Examining Authority to require the revised drawings and tables described above before the close of examination, followed by enough time for residents to comment on them. If the final construction arrangements remain within a clearly assessed envelope, I could at least understand what is being decided, even if I still object. A requirement that merely says matters will be agreed later with the highway authority would leave the main effects on this lane unresolved. Please record this as an objection to the Merefen Link Energy Scheme, and please consider a site visit at the morning bus-stop time rather than only in the middle of a working day.

Jory Fenwick

Supplementary points to my relevant representation
Merefen Link Energy Scheme
From: Jory Fenwick

I have already asked for the construction access drawings to be made available before the examination closes. I also want to explain why the present description of the works does not give us a reliable picture of day-to-day effects. My objection is not to an electricity connection in principle. It is to asking residents to accept years of disruption on the basis of drawings that leave the timing, position and management of the works uncertain.

At 18 Sedge Turn, Marlinby, MF4 8RL, the front rooms face the lane. The traffic assessment counts vehicles on the main road, but the lane is where people wait, cross and reverse out of short drives. A convoy of three lorries is quite different from three lorries spread through a whole morning. The documents do not say whether drivers will be instructed to wait at the compound at Plot 14, Estuary Rise, Marlinby, if a delivery slot is missed. I have seen how quickly a queue forms when a van stops at the bend. Please do not leave a traffic management plan to settle this after consent.

My daughter Mara Fenwick, aged 11, uses the bus stop on school mornings. My son Ruan Fenwick, aged 16, sometimes walks the same route later in the day. I am not asking for the children to be treated as a reason to refuse all works. I am asking for a drawing showing the temporary footway, the crossing point and what happens when the footway has to be closed. Saying that a marshal will be present is not enough if the marshal's location and hours are unknown. We have lived in this area for over 40 years as a family, but familiarity with the lane will not make an unmarked diversion safe.

The consultation summary says that residents generally supported short working days. That was not the impression at the drop-in. Mrs Tessa Venn from the next house asked what would happen to access when the trench passed the adjoining drives. Darian Venn was also there and asked whether emergency vehicles could still get through. Neither neighbour has made a representation, as far as I know, and neither should have to rely on my account of that conversation. A written, property-by-property answer from Merefen Link Transmission Ltd would be more useful than another general assurance about maintaining access.

I also want the noise evidence tested against actual use of the houses. I have diagnosed asthma, and dust during dry spells is a particular worry for me. My mother Edda Fenwick stays at my home and has rheumatoid arthritis; getting out to appointments is difficult enough without discovering at the gate that a pedestrian route has moved. The noise itself has caused poor sleep while preliminary survey vehicles have been around, although I am not claiming that poor sleep is a medical diagnosis. These are practical reasons for wanting notice of each closure, a clean walking route and a named point of contact for resolving problems on the day.

At the public meeting, Nella Brice of Merefen Acoustic Advice said the proposed monitoring positions would represent the nearest homes. I could not see a monitor location on the plan that corresponded to the houses at the bend. I have asked for the underlying measurements rather than just a colour-coded contour. The follow-up email from nella.brice@merefenacoustic.example gave a direct number, 01632 960 417, but pointed me back to the same figure. I am not criticising the individual; the issue is whether the applicant's assessment captures the stop-start engine noise and reversing alarms we will hear at the front of the houses.

There is an ecological matter as well. Badgers have been reported in Flintmere Wood, and I appreciate that a wood-wide reference is not a precise record. Separately, I gave the survey team a note identifying a sett in the bank immediately behind the third field gate on the east side of Wisp Lane, opposite marker post 7. Please keep that precise location out of any public version of my note. The ecology chapter should still explain, without publishing the location, how works nearby will be checked and how a stop-work decision would be made.

Cllr Elwin Morrell said at the open meeting that the council wanted the applicant to show a workable walking route before construction began. I agree, but ‘before construction’ could mean after consent, when residents have little opportunity to question a changed layout. The examination page at www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects explains how representations are considered; it does not replace a clear plan for this lane. I would prefer the applicant to put its revised drawings into the examination now, with a short period for comments. Material on the unrelated site https://marlinby-lane-watch.example/traffic is not part of my evidence, and I mention it only because a leaflet directed residents there instead of to the examination documents.

Please acknowledge this supplementary note under IP reference MF-28417. If a site visit is arranged, the morning bus-stop period is still the most informative time. The applicant can use the project mailbox, merefenlink@projects.example, for general notices, but individual closure notices need to reach the affected homes in good time. My own contact details for correspondence are jory.fenwick@residentmail.example and 07700 900 418. I supplied those details so the case team can contact me, not for inclusion in a public copy. My car registration, MF26 JOR, appears on the photograph I sent of the bend; the vehicle is incidental to the point shown in that photograph.

I remain opposed to the scheme as currently described. Properly assessed access, noise and pedestrian arrangements might reduce some of the harm, but they need to be examined while there is still a chance to change them.

Jory Fenwick

Technical addendum: access and drainage

The transport assessment for the Merefen Link Energy Scheme uses an average weekday flow on Fenbarrow Road, but the construction programme shows deliveries concentrated in the first six weeks of cable laying. The junction capacity table should therefore test the busiest construction hour, including the temporary signals at the Fenbarrow Road/Low Mere Lane junction, rather than spreading vehicle movements evenly across the day. The swept-path drawing also appears to assume that the verge beside Plot C14 is available for turning; the order limits do not clearly include that strip.

On drainage, Merefen Link Transmission Ltd proposes a temporary compound on the lower part of Reedwash Field. The flood-risk appendix gives the permanent substation runoff rate but not a separate rate for the compacted compound during construction. A phase-by-phase drainage drawing would help Merefen District Council assess compliance with Policy W7 of the Draft Merefen Local Plan. These are matters for the examination, not objections to renewable infrastructure in principle.

text:
FENMERE BOROUGH COUNCIL
LOCAL IMPACT REPORT: BRINDLE MERE LINK ROAD
Planning Inspectorate reference: EN010248
Submitted at Deadline 3, 21 October 2026

1. Purpose and status

This Local Impact Report (LIR) is submitted by Fenmere Borough Council as the host authority for part of the proposed Brindle Mere Link Road. It describes likely impacts on the borough, rather than setting out a final position on whether development consent should be granted. The applicant is Brindle Mere Infrastructure Ltd. Officers have used the submitted Environmental Statement, the Council's highway records and responses received during the Council's ordinary engagement work. Where a matter remains uncertain, the report says so. The Council's examination correspondence address is Civic House, 18 Foundry Square, Bellwick, BW4 7QJ; the shared mailbox is planning@fenmere.gov.uk. The Council has also referred residents to www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects for an explanation of the examination process.

2. Borough context

The proposed road runs from the existing Bellwick distributor road, across the low fields at Marn Dyke, to a new junction near Little Sedge. The application boundary includes parcel P17 and sections of Footpath 6 and Bridleway 2. These identifiers are used in the plans and do not identify a household. The route passes working farmland, a drainage channel and two small areas of woodland. Willowhush Wood is used for informal walking; badger signs have been reported there, but that description does not identify a sett. The Council has not treated general references to bats in the Marn Dyke corridor as evidence of a particular maternity roost.

The scheme could shorten some journeys to the industrial estate. The benefit will depend on the final junction controls and on whether traffic diverts back through Little Sedge at peak times. The traffic tables supplied at application stage use a 2024 base year; they need to be read alongside later counts, particularly at the school crossing. The Council requests an updated walking and cycling drawing, with widths shown at the pinch point by the drainage bridge. A statement that the path will be 'improved' is not enough for residents to understand what they will get.

3. Engagement and community effects

At the Council's open drop-in on 9 September 2026, Cllr Asha Fenwick asked whether the temporary haul route would remain open during the autumn term. Cllr Bram Ellery raised the loss of the informal verge used by people walking from Little Sedge. Nella Carden MP subsequently wrote to the Council seeking a clearer account of construction hours. These are requests for information, not evidence that the elected members have endorsed or opposed the application.

The attendance note also records Tari Moss, who attended as a local resident and is not an Interested Party in the examination. Several attendees said they felt anxious about night-time vehicle movements and worried that poor sleep would follow. Those comments describe anticipated effects, not medical diagnoses. One resident, Ms Livia Dorn of 7 Nettle Fold, Larkfen, BW4 7QB, provided photographs of the narrow frontage beside the proposed diversion. In correspondence she said her daughter, Mara Dorn, aged 11, has epilepsy and that unexpected flashing lights can cause difficulties for her. The Council has not tested that account, but asks the applicant to explain how advance notice of overnight works will reach affected households. The resident's contact details, livia.dorn@example.org and 07700 900416, were supplied for follow-up, not for public enquiries. Her Interested Party reference was IP-20487.

A separate email from survey contractor Ellis Vane of Asterfold Ecology Ltd gave ellis.vane@asterfoldecology.example as a direct address. The Council has used the contractor's survey findings where they are relevant, but this LIR does not adopt the contractor's conclusions without qualification. The generic project mailbox, enquiries@brindlemere-link.example, remains the appropriate address for questions to the applicant. Residents also pointed officers to https://fenmere-daily.example/road-works-archive; that article has not been used as a traffic-count source.

4. Construction, land and ecology

Construction would temporarily alter access to the allotments and require closures of Footpath 6. The current outline diversion appears to add a substantial distance for users with pushchairs. The Council seeks a phasing plan that identifies which crossing will be available each month, rather than a single indicative line on a plan. Dust controls should address the dry section by Marn Dyke as well as the compounds. The vehicle plate BW26 FEN was recorded in one resident's photograph of a survey visit; the Council does not rely on the plate to establish who carried out the visit.

For completeness, a restricted ecology field note was accidentally reproduced in an early engagement pack. It described a badger sett entrance at the eastern culvert mouth, 3 metres south of gate G4 in parcel P17. That detail is not needed to understand the Council's conclusion that pre-construction checks and an enforceable species method statement are required. General mitigation, including replacement planting and checks before clearance, can be discussed in the public examination without publishing precise protected-site locations.

The applicant's draft requirement on drainage should specify who maintains the balancing basin after handover. The Council's estimate of £1.8 million for related highway works is a public project cost, not a valuation of any resident's property. It should not be confused with the personal figure supplied by Ms Livia Dorn: her outstanding mortgage is £143,600. That figure is not material to the Council's assessment of drainage or traffic effects and should be omitted from any public summary.

5. Requested examination actions

The Council asks the Examining Authority to request an updated junction assessment, a legible construction-access programme, and a revised public-rights-of-way plan before the close of the examination. It also asks the applicant to confirm how the shared complaints line will operate outside office hours. These requests are made without prejudice to the Council's continuing discussions on the draft Development Consent Order. Further correspondence can be sent to planning@fenmere.gov.uk, quoting EN010248.

Prepared and submitted on behalf of Fenmere Borough Council.

Annex A – Supplementary technical assessment
Brindle Mere Link Road Local Impact Report
Fenmere Borough Council

A1. Purpose and scope

This annex records the Council’s technical assessment of the traffic, landscape, drainage and construction information submitted by Brindle Mere Infrastructure Ltd. It supplements the examination actions requested in section 5. The Council has assessed the scheme as shown on General Arrangement Plan LR-204, revision C, together with the Environmental Statement and the draft Construction Environmental Management Plan. References to effects below are to local effects within Fenmere borough. The annex does not replace the assessment required of the applicant under the Environmental Impact Assessment process.

A2. Traffic and access

The proposed road would connect East Fenmere Road to the Beldwick Bypass by way of two new roundabouts. The applicant’s 2038 forecast indicates a reduction in through traffic on Merebank Lane, but the forecast depends on a substantial transfer of vehicles from the existing town-centre route. The Council accepts that reassignment is likely in principle. It cannot yet confirm its scale because the submitted junction files do not contain a consistent set of turning movements for the morning peak. In particular, the flows shown for East Fenmere Road in Table 8.14 do not reconcile with those in the roundabout capacity assessment.

The afternoon-peak model shows queues extending beyond the proposed western splitter island in the high-growth case. This is not, by itself, evidence that the junction is unacceptable: the reported queue occurs for a short part of the modelled hour. Nevertheless, the model should be rerun with the revised bus stopping arrangement shown on Drawing LR-318, revision B. That arrangement reduces the distance available for vehicles leaving the bus stop to merge before the roundabout. The Council also requests a sensitivity test retaining the present speed limit on Merebank Lane, rather than assuming a lower limit before the relevant traffic order has been made.

Construction access is proposed from the Beldwick Bypass for the main compound and from East Fenmere Road for the drainage works. The two access points appear suitable in broad terms, subject to visibility splays being maintained and deliveries being scheduled outside the school travel peaks. The draft programme does not say whether both accesses would operate at the same time during earthworks. This matters because the traffic assessment distributes construction vehicles between them, while the draft traffic management plan describes a single signed haul route. A month-by-month access schedule, consistent across both documents, is needed before the Council can assess the temporary network effects.

A3. Landscape, public rights of way and ecology

The road crosses open farmland at the edge of the Merebank Vale landscape area. Its most noticeable element would be the raised approach to the eastern roundabout, particularly in views from the Beldwick Ridge path. Proposed hedgerow planting would soften those views over time but would not screen the earthworks in the first years after opening. The Council therefore considers the operational effect to be moderate adverse initially, reducing as the planting establishes. This differs from the applicant’s assessment of a minor effect throughout operation; the difference should be recorded rather than treated as an error in the photomontages.

Footpath FM/12 would be diverted around the southern side of the western roundabout. The diversion shown on Rights of Way Plan ROW-07, revision D, has a different alignment from that shown on the general arrangement plan. Both drawings should show the same route, crossing point and proposed connection to the retained field path. Where temporary closures are necessary, the diversion signage should be installed before the existing route is obstructed. The Council seeks a requirement for a final rights-of-way management plan, including arrangements for maintaining access during construction.

The Environmental Statement records bats along the Merebank Vale hedgerows and badger activity in the wider survey area. These are appropriate matters for the ecological management plan, but the available information does not alter the Council’s landscape conclusion. The proposed replacement hedgerows should use locally appropriate species and connect with retained boundaries wherever practicable. Lighting at the eastern roundabout should be limited to the area required for highway safety; the final lighting design should demonstrate how spill onto adjoining habitat has been minimised.

A4. Drainage and flood risk

The route crosses two shallow drainage channels that discharge towards Brindle Mere. The proposed attenuation basins are intended to restrict discharge to the existing greenfield rate for the design storm, with an allowance for climate change. The Council’s review finds the principle acceptable. However, the current drainage schedule assigns the same contributing area to Basin 2 and to the separate roadside filter drain. The applicant should correct the schedule and provide updated calculations before the detailed drainage design is approved.

The proposed outfall from Basin 2 is shown on Drainage Plan DR-11, revision E. The plan gives its invert level but not the level of the receiving channel at the point of connection. Without both levels, the Council cannot confirm that the outfall will drain freely during ordinary high-water conditions. The detailed design should also identify who will maintain the basins, how sediment will be removed, and what access will be available for inspection. These points can be secured through the drainage requirement, provided that the requirement applies before the relevant drainage works begin.

A5. Policy and overall conclusion

The Fenmere Local Plan 2040 supports transport schemes that improve network resilience while avoiding unacceptable harm to landscape character, water quality and public access. On the information presently available, the Council considers that the link road could meet those objectives, subject to resolution of the modelling discrepancies, a consistent construction-access programme and enforceable mitigation. This is a qualified conclusion, not confirmation that every effect has been fully assessed. The Council asks the Examining Authority to retain these matters on the examination agenda until the revised documents have been reviewed.

A6. Community evidence received since the draft report

Fenmere Borough Council has reviewed the notes from its September 2026 drop-in at the Civic Offices, 14 Quay Square, Fenmere, FM1 3QA. The notes are not a substitute for the applicant’s consultation report: some attendees came only to ask where the drawings could be seen, and the Council did not ask them to make formal representations. They do, however, help identify matters requiring a response from Brindle Mere Infrastructure Ltd. This section records local effects rather than determining whether individual accounts are correct.

Tari Moss, who is not registered as an Interested Party, described difficulty crossing Mere Lane at the existing farm access when agricultural vehicles turn in. The Council has not independently counted these movements. The submitted construction traffic assessment assumes that most heavy goods vehicles will approach from the west, but the draft traffic management plan leaves an eastern approach available for abnormal deliveries. Cllr Asha Fenwick asked at the October member briefing whether that exception might become the normal route when the western junction is congested. The Council requests a vehicle-by-vehicle definition of the exception, a booking procedure and a record that can be inspected during construction. A promise to encourage drivers to use the preferred route would not address this concern.

The Council also received photographs from Livia Dorn of 8 Flax Mill Cottages, Fenmere, FM2 5QT. Her photographs show standing water beside the footway after rain, but do not establish its source or how often it occurs. She supplied the registration FM26 QXZ for a delivery vehicle which she says mounted the kerb; the Council has not sought to identify its driver. Correspondence about her photographs should be sent through the Council’s transport@fenmere.example.org mailbox rather than to the personal address or number she provided, livia.dorn@merepost.example and 07700 900 438. The contact details are included here only because they were copied into the working version of the report in error and should not appear in the published version.

Livia Dorn said her daughter, Mara Dorn, aged 11, uses that footway to reach the school bus. Mara Dorn has diagnosed epilepsy, and the family asked whether the proposed temporary crossing would have a staffed marshal when the footway is diverted. The Council cannot assess an individual’s needs in this report, but considers the question about the crossing relevant to the scheme generally. The applicant should show the diversion width, the location of barriers and how pedestrians will be assisted when construction vehicles enter the compound. Worry about using an unfamiliar diversion was also expressed by other attendees; that is a description of an effect, not evidence of a medical condition.

A7. Landscape, verges and ecology

Cllr Bram Ellery raised the loss of the broad verge at the southern end of Mere Lane. The verge provides space between people walking and passing vehicles, especially where the footway narrows by the old culvert. The Council asks for a cross-section at this point at both opening year and the end of the proposed planting-establishment period. Planting shown on a general arrangement drawing should not be relied upon to provide usable pedestrian space. Replacement planting may soften views of the embankment but will not replace the verge’s present function if it is fenced off.

The Council’s ecology officer has reviewed the survey note prepared by Ellis Vane of Asterfold Ecology Ltd. It describes badger activity in Brindle Wood, which is a broad location and does not, by itself, establish a conflict with the proposed works. A separate working annotation states that an active sett entrance is 6 metres east of field gate G4, beneath the third hawthorn south of the Mere Lane culvert. That annotation should be held in the restricted ecological schedule, not reproduced on a public drawing. The same applies to the reported bat maternity roost in the north gable of the disused pump house at grid reference FM 41862 70514. These records have not yet been reconciled with the applicant’s latest earthworks boundary. The Council is not asking that survey evidence be withheld from the Examining Authority; it is asking for an appropriately controlled version for examination and a generalised version for publication.

A8. Construction hours and public access

Nella Carden MP sought clarification of the proposed Saturday hours after constituents noticed that the outline construction programme and the draft code of construction practice use different wording. The Council’s reading is that routine works would finish at 13:00, while concrete pours could continue later with prior notice. That reading must be confirmed in one document. Notice to residents is helpful, but it is not a substitute for an enforceable limit or a clear procedure for exceptional work. The Council requests that the applicant identify who authorises an exception, the grounds for doing so and where the decision will be logged.

The Council has served the area for over 40 years in different administrative forms; this is not evidence about the age of any particular resident. Its rights-of-way team considers that the proposed temporary closure of Footpath 6 is longer than necessary if the drainage crossing is installed before the embankment is formed. An alternative sequence should be tested before the closure period is fixed. Any signed diversion must be available before the existing route is obstructed, including at weekends. The public examination library is accessible via https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate; enquiries intended for the Council’s rights-of-way team may be sent to paths@fenmere.example.org.

A9. Matters requested for the examination

In summary, Fenmere Borough Council requests a corrected construction route plan, a reconciled set of working-hours provisions, a dimensioned pedestrian-diversion drawing and an ecology schedule that distinguishes restricted records from public plans. The Council will review revised material against the local impacts described above. It does not at present seek to change its qualified overall conclusion in A5. If the applicant proposes a different access arrangement or drainage sequence, the Council may need to update this report so that the Examining Authority has a clear account of the resulting local effects.

Appendix 1 – record of local points raised after A9

This note accompanies the Local Impact Report and does not alter the conclusion in A5. Fenmere Borough Council’s planning office is at Civic House, 14 Meregate Square, Fenmere FM4 7QL. Requests for the public drawings may be sent to planning@fenmere.example.org. The examination timetable is available through https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate.

At the member briefing on 16 October 2026, Cllr Asha Fenwick asked whether the amended haul route for the Brindle Mere Link Road would keep construction vehicles off School Lane at collection time. Cllr Bram Ellery said the verge shown beside Plot 18 appears narrower on the diversion drawing than it is on the ground. Nella Carden MP had separately requested a single table setting out the proposed construction hours. These are requests for clarification, not objections to the principle of the scheme.

The Council’s drop-in record also notes that Tari Moss described poor sleep during the trial traffic counts. Ms Livia Dorn supplied photographs of the same verge and explained that her daughter, Mara Dorn, aged 10, has asthma; the photographs should not be treated as evidence of a measured air-quality exceedance. The Council has not published either resident’s contact details in this report.

Ellis Vane of Asterfold Ecology Ltd advised the Council that the public ecology schedule could identify survey areas without reproducing restricted species records. Brindle Mere Infrastructure Ltd should confirm which version of that schedule will accompany its next submission. Please keep any replacement drawing numbers consistent across the access and pedestrian-diversion plans.

CHAPTER 8: ECOLOGY
Merefen Grid Link Environmental Statement | October 2026

8.1 Scope and method

This chapter assesses the construction and operation of the proposed Merefen Grid Link, comprising a buried cable, temporary haul route and switching compound between Brindle Marsh and East Rill. The study area includes the Order limits and adjoining land where disturbance or habitat fragmentation could occur. Habitat walkovers were completed in April and September 2025. Species surveys followed the methods described in Appendix 8.1; access was not available to every building, and conclusions for those buildings remain provisional. Survey results are presented here at the level needed to explain the assessment. The locations of sensitive features should not be used as public access directions.

8.2 Baseline habitats

The route crosses mainly improved pasture and arable fields, with hedgerows, two drainage ditches, scattered mature trees and a short section of wet woodland at Ashlorn Copse. The switching compound would occupy the edge of Field M9, which has low botanical diversity. The ditch beside Old Mill Lane carries water in most months and provides a continuous habitat connection towards the marsh. No irreplaceable habitat was recorded within the permanent land take. Hedgerow H12 has gaps but remains an important commuting feature for bats. The Applicant has treated these features as separate receptors rather than assuming that all land within the Order limits has equal ecological value.

8.3 Badgers

Evidence of badger activity included paths, snuffle holes and three entrances considered to be in current use. Badger signs occur in Ashlorn Copse and across the fields north of Brindle Marsh; these broad descriptions do not identify an individual sett. The principal sett entrance was recorded at chainage 2+340, 11 m west of the haul-route centreline, beneath the exposed roots of the three-stemmed ash at the south end of Field M4. A second, apparently occasional-use entrance was found in the earth bank immediately behind gate G7, 6 m north of the eastern hinge post. Neither entrance would be excavated, but both are close enough to works for vibration, lighting and accidental obstruction to be relevant. Sett status may change between the survey and construction. A pre-start check will therefore be completed before groundworks in each affected field, with any necessary licensing agreed before works proceed.

8.4 Bats

Activity detectors recorded common and soprano pipistrelles along most hedges, with lower numbers of other calls around the ditch corridor. Foraging bats were also recorded near Ashlorn Copse; that is a general area observation, not evidence that the entire copse is a roost. The building survey identified a common pipistrelle day roost beneath the loose slate above the east porch of Halwick Lodge. This is a small, non-breeding roost and no works are proposed to that roof. By contrast, emergence and re-entry surveys confirmed a soprano pipistrelle maternity roost inside the west gable void of Caldor Barn, directly above the upper hay door. The haul-route alignment passes the barn, although the building itself is outside the construction boundary. The count varied between visits, as expected during the maternity period.

A large barbastelle roost was also confirmed in the hollow pollard tagged T84, 3 m south of the ditch crossing at chainage 4+125. Its use by a rare species and the number emerging mean that the location is treated as highly sensitive. No tree works are currently proposed there. The baseline remains subject to change if wind damage or land management alters the tree before construction. Lighting design will retain a dark corridor along Hedgerow H12 and the ditch, with inward-facing, shielded temporary luminaires where night work cannot be avoided. The detailed lighting plan must demonstrate that spill onto the barn and the retained pollard is avoided; a drawing showing lamp positions alone will not be sufficient.

8.5 Birds and other fauna

Breeding-bird surveys found a typical farmland assemblage, including skylark in open fields and nesting opportunities in the mature hedges. Barn owls were seen hunting over the pasture on two evening visits. An occupied barn owl nest was confirmed on the joist above the second stall from the west in the lower loft of Fenlow Byre. The byre is outside the permanent works but could be affected by temporary lighting and vehicle movements. References elsewhere in the survey notes to barn owls around East Rill describe foraging activity only and should not be read as additional nest records. No otter holt was found during the accessible ditch survey. Footprints near the western culvert show that otters may pass through the corridor, but do not establish a breeding site.

8.6 Effects and mitigation

Without mitigation, haul-route use could disturb badgers and breeding birds, while lighting could interrupt bat movement and affect roost emergence. Trenches left open overnight would also present a risk to small mammals. The construction environmental management plan will require covered excavations or escape ramps, a speed limit on the haul route, and checks of vegetation immediately before clearance. Hedgerow removal will be restricted to the minimum construction width and reinstated with locally appropriate native planting. Where works cannot avoid the bird breeding season, an ecologist will check the affected vegetation before it is cut. That check is not permission to disturb an active nest.

A marked exclusion area will be established around each retained sett and sensitive roost before plant arrives. Its position will be supplied to the site team on controlled drawings, not inferred from the indicative habitat plan. Works supervisors will be briefed on stop-work procedures if a new entrance, roost or nest is found. Monitoring will include a post-construction check of reinstated hedges and the effectiveness of the dark corridor. Subject to these measures, the residual effect on the surveyed populations is assessed as not significant. This conclusion depends on the lighting and exclusion commitments being carried into the final construction documents.

7.13 Verification of ecological records

The conclusion in Section 7.12 relies on the distinction between survey records used to set working limits and the indicative habitat information shown on the public figures. This section records the basis for that distinction. Merefen Grid Link Ltd has retained a restricted ecological register for use by the ecological clerk of works and the principal contractor. The register was checked against the final walkover notes by Dr Elva Norr MCIEEM of Fenlark Ecology Ltd on 18 September 2026. The locations below are given so that the proposed avoidance measures can be understood; they are not instructions for the site team to locate a feature without the controlled drawings.

Badger activity was recorded at several points along the cable corridor. Feeding signs and well-used paths occurred across West Merefen Wood, but those observations do not by themselves identify a sett. The principal sett was recorded on the northern bank of the disused drainage ditch, 8 m south-east of the junction of farm track T2 and the field gate on Plot 16. Fresh spoil, bedding material and entrances of differing ages were present. A smaller outlier sett was found in the earth bank immediately behind the second gatepost on the east side of Brindle Lane, opposite access A4. Its use was intermittent during the survey period. No entrance is proposed to be closed under the current design. The contractor's exclusion fencing will be set from the entrances confirmed at the pre-start check, rather than from the centre of the habitat polygon on Figure 7.6.

Bat activity surveys identified commuting along the retained hedge north of Fenwick Drain and foraging over the wider pasture. Static detectors recorded common pipistrelle, soprano pipistrelle and smaller numbers of barbastelle passes. These records describe use of a broad corridor; they do not establish that every tree in it contains a roost. Emergence surveys confirmed a small common pipistrelle day roost behind a loose fascia board on the south elevation of Old Kiln Store. This is not a maternity roost, and the building is outside the construction footprint. A soprano pipistrelle maternity roost was confirmed behind the third weatherboard from the left beneath the north gable of Reedfold Barn, directly above the rainwater hopper. Repeated emergence counts, rather than detector passes alone, were used to classify it.

A separate survey found a large barbastelle roost in the split trunk of the marked ash immediately west of culvert C7, 6 m north of the cable centreline on Plot 23. The tree is retained. The count is treated as a minimum because some animals returned before the survey ended; the assessment has not assumed that the same number occupies it throughout the season. Barbastelles were also recorded in West Merefen Wood, a deliberately broad location which should not be read as another identified roost. No lighting column is proposed beside the retained ash or the hedge linking it to the wood. The temporary lighting schedule requires inward-facing fittings and shields, with a check of spill at the hedge before night working begins.

Barn owl was observed hunting over rough grassland on two visits. An occupied nest was subsequently recorded on the rear ledge inside the upper eastern hay opening of Northfold Byre, above the fixed ladder. The building will not be altered by the scheme. Barn owls were also seen in fields around Merefen, which is a general observation and not a second nest location. The haul route passes the byre on an existing track. Deliveries close to it will be scheduled outside the breeding period where practicable, and the ecological clerk of works will confirm the position before any exceptional movement is authorised. This measure does not replace the need to avoid disturbance if the nest remains active later than expected.

7.14 Construction controls and residual effects

For all retained features, exclusion fencing must be in place before vegetation clearance or ground disturbance in the relevant work area. The ecological clerk of works will sign off its position against the restricted register and record any change in a site instruction. The public construction drawing shows the general working corridor only. It should not be used to measure a buffer from a symbol, because the symbol may have been displaced for legibility. Plot 23 is a land reference, not a roost coordinate. Equally, records of badgers in West Merefen Wood are too coarse to direct an operative to an entrance.

If an entrance, occupied roost or active nest is found where none was recorded, work in the immediate area will stop. The ecologist will assess the finding and advise whether the working method, programme or licence position needs to change. No operative should move a fence, lift a board or inspect a tree cavity merely to resolve a discrepancy between a drawing and what is visible on site. Toolbox talks will cover that point, together with storage of materials away from retained hedges and the reporting route for unexpected finds.

The landscape scheme retains the principal east-west hedge and replaces the short section lost at access A4 with locally appropriate planting. Reinstatement will be checked in the first and third growing seasons. Monitoring will record survival and gaps, not only whether planting was completed. Where failures interrupt the intended dark corridor, replacement planting or a change to temporary lighting will be agreed through the construction environmental management process. The applicant has made the general construction documents available through planning@merefengridlink.example; the restricted register is issued only to those who need it to carry out the controls.

Provided the avoidance, lighting and pre-start checks described above are secured, significant residual effects on the recorded badger, bat and barn owl populations are not predicted. That judgement is based on retention of the identified structures and habitat links. It would need to be reviewed if the final design introduced demolition, tree removal or permanent lighting in an area currently shown as retained.

6.8 Residual effects and monitoring

6.8.1 This section draws together the ecological controls for the Merefen Grid Link and explains how their delivery will be checked. It should be read with the Habitat Management Plan (MGL-APP-6.8) and the Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan (MGL-APP-7.2). The assessment covers the cable corridor, the proposed Merefen Converter Compound and the temporary working areas shown on the application plans. It does not assume that a species is absent simply because it was not recorded during a particular visit.

6.8.2 The principal design measure is to keep the permanent footprint within intensively managed fields and existing access corridors wherever practicable. The working width narrows at watercourse crossings and beside retained hedgerows. Open-cut construction will be avoided at the principal drains identified on the constraints plans; the detailed crossing method remains subject to ground investigation and approval under the final construction method statement. These measures reduce habitat loss at the outset rather than relying on planting after construction.

6.8.3 Temporary land take will be restored using the soil-handling sequence in the Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan. Topsoil and subsoil will be stored separately, with storage areas kept clear of retained ditch margins. Reinstatement will follow the existing field pattern unless the Habitat Management Plan specifies a wider buffer. It is important that reinstatement is judged by vegetation establishment, not only by completion of earthworks. Areas that fail to establish will be reseeded or replanted in the next suitable season.

6.8.4 Fenlark Ecology Ltd reviewed the 2026 survey results against the current limits of deviation. Most of the grassland within the temporary working areas is species-poor, but the drain margins and connecting hedgerows provide movement routes through an otherwise open landscape. Those links will remain continuous during operation. During construction, gaps needed for vehicle movements will be kept to the minimum width required for safe access and closed when that access is no longer needed. Where a closure cannot be completed in the same planting season, a temporary boundary treatment will be used.

6.8.5 Badger activity was recorded in the wider study area. No conclusion in this chapter depends on publishing the position of a sett. The relevant controls are a pre-start check, a clearly marked exclusion area where required, and a stop-work procedure if new field signs are found. Those requirements apply to temporary compounds as well as the permanent works. The pre-start check is necessary because use of the surrounding farmland may change between the survey and the start of construction.

6.8.6 Bat activity was concentrated along retained linear habitats, particularly hedgerows and drains. The lighting strategy therefore treats these features as dark corridors. Task lighting will be directed into the working area, used only while the task is taking place, and removed when the activity ends. The contractor will record any departure from the approved lighting layout, including its reason and duration. General references to bats in Merefen Marsh do not identify a roost location and are not a substitute for the restricted survey information used by the ecological clerk of works.

6.8.7 The open fields also support foraging birds, including barn owl. The assessment does not identify a significant operational effect from the buried cable. During construction, exposed excavations will be checked and covered or provided with an escape route where practicable. Vegetation clearance will be programmed outside the main nesting season where possible; where that is not possible, a check immediately before clearance will determine whether works can proceed. This is a precautionary measure and does not imply that a nest is present at every clearance location.

6.8.8 Watercourse protection will be implemented alongside the measures for terrestrial habitats. Clean runoff will be kept separate from water that has passed through active work areas. Fuel storage and refuelling will take place on contained surfaces away from drains, with spill materials available at each work front. The crossing method statement will set out how flow is maintained and how disturbed banks are reinstated. Marrow Fen Drainage Board will be consulted on the final drainage arrangements before the relevant works begin.

6.8.9 Construction phasing matters to the ecological assessment. Not all sections of the cable corridor will be open at once, and temporary access will move as work progresses. The programme submitted before commencement will identify when hedgerow gaps are created, when they are closed, and when reinstatement can take place. If a change in sequence would leave a habitat link interrupted for longer than assessed, Merefen Grid Link Ltd will review the effect and propose an amended measure before implementing that change. The same review will apply if a temporary compound is moved into an area shown as retained on the application plans.

6.8.10 Monitoring will be proportionate to the predicted effects. The ecological clerk of works will keep a record of pre-start checks, instructions given at work fronts and any stop-work events. Establishment checks will be undertaken after the first and third growing seasons following reinstatement. They will consider hedgerow continuity, the condition of ditch-margin planting and whether invasive species have become established on disturbed ground. The checks are intended to trigger corrective action, rather than simply to confirm that planting was carried out.

6.8.11 The Outline Construction Environmental Management Plan will be developed into a final plan before the relevant stage of works. Its ecological provisions will be cross-referenced to the lighting plan, soil-management procedure and watercourse crossing method statements so that conflicting instructions are not issued to contractors. The public version may describe survey findings at landscape scale; records requiring controlled circulation will remain in the restricted register. General document queries may be sent to planning@merefengridlink.example.

6.8.12 On the basis of the present design, the measures above are capable of avoiding significant residual ecological effects. This finding is conditional on retaining the identified habitat connections, implementing the construction controls and completing remedial works where monitoring shows that reinstatement has not succeeded. It is not an approval of an unrestricted construction method. Any material change to the footprint, lighting or crossing design will require an ecological review against the same criteria before it is adopted.

6.9 Protected species: restricted ecological record

6.9.1 This section records the locations used to design the exclusion zones. It is for controlled circulation and is not to be copied into the public works drawings. Dr Elva Norr MCIEEM of Fenlark Ecology Ltd completed the follow-up checks for Merefen Grid Link Ltd in May 2026. Survey coverage included hedgerows, drainage ditches and buildings within the proposed working corridor; access was not available to every adjoining field.

6.9.2 Badger activity was recorded across Brackenmere Wood. The active main sett is on the north bank of Ditch 14, 7 m east of culvert MF-03, beneath the third hawthorn from the field gate. A second entrance was recorded elsewhere within the wood, but its status could not be confirmed. Tracks and spoil alone have not been treated as evidence of an additional main sett.

6.9.3 Bats were observed commuting along the Fenlark Drain. A common pipistrelle day roost was found in the west gable of Lintwick Stores. The maternity roost is in the eastern roof void of Hallowmere Pump Barn, directly above the second south-facing louvre. No works to that roof or lighting directed towards its openings are proposed during the breeding season.

6.9.4 Barn owl foraging was recorded over the rough grassland. The occupied nest is inside the west-end beam box of Hallowmere Pump Barn, immediately above doorway B2. Its location, and the roost and sett locations above, must be checked against the final access drawings by the ecological clerk of works; operatives should receive exclusion-zone plans rather than this record.

6.9.5 The Marrow Fen Drainage Board has been consulted on ditch crossings. Temporary fencing, a pre-start inspection and reinstatement of hedgerow gaps remain required. If access or the crossing design changes, the relevant surveys must be reviewed before clearance starts.
