text:
LOWSEDGE ENERGY LINK
Environmental Statement, Appendix 8.6: Otter and Schedule 1 Bird Survey
Revision 2, October 2026

8.6.1 Purpose and scope

This appendix presents the field evidence used for the otter and Schedule 1 bird assessment in ES Chapter 8. It has been prepared for Fenwick Arc Renewables Ltd as part of the Lowsedge Energy Link application. The survey area comprises the proposed cable corridor, temporary compounds and a 250 m buffer where access was available. Place names in this appendix refer to features on the submitted habitat plan, not to individual properties. Exact locations of protected resting and breeding places are included below for examination purposes; they should not be reproduced on public-facing construction drawings.

8.6.2 Method

Walkover surveys were completed on 14 March, 29 April and 18 June 2026. Banks were checked for entrances, slides, spraints and feeding remains; bridges and culverts were inspected from publicly accessible land or with permission. Bird visits began before sunrise and continued until late morning, with a separate dusk watch at the quarry. No nest was approached after occupancy had been established. Heavy rain on 28 April reduced the usefulness of tracks recorded the next day. A return visit was therefore made in June. Coverage of the easternmost drainage ditch was limited by dense reed growth, and absence of signs there should not be read as absence of otter.

Dr Corin Vale, CEnv, of Larchline Ecology Ltd, undertook the June walkover and checked the field sheets against the photographs. She confirmed that the photographed prints were consistent with otter, although prints alone cannot establish use of a resting place. Records supplied by the resident Tessa Morland of 24 Bracken Row, Wrenby, WB4 2QH were treated as supporting evidence only: the dates were remembered approximately and no photographs accompanied them. Ms Morland described seeing an otter crossing the lane, not entering a holt. Her account did not determine the mapped constraint boundary.

8.6.3 Otter results

Spraints were found beneath the western culvert and at two open-bank points on Rill Beck. A slide and several partly weathered prints occurred upstream of the temporary bridge position. These signs indicate regular movement along the watercourse, but are not, by themselves, evidence of breeding. The coarse record NX 48 71 is retained on the public habitat plan to show the length of beck surveyed; it is not a holt grid reference. Signs in the wider Willow Carr area are similarly shown only as a shaded reach.

One active holt was identified at grid reference NX 48362 71429, beneath the eastern root plate of the leaning alder on the south bank of Rill Beck, immediately upstream of the disused stone footbridge. Fresh spraint and a clear run were present on both the April and June visits. The surveyors did not use a camera inside the entrance and cannot establish the number or ages of animals using it. No works are proposed on that bank, but the current temporary lighting drawing points one lamp towards the approach run. That drawing must be corrected before construction starts.

8.6.4 Schedule 1 birds

Peregrine activity was recorded on three visits at Ashen Quarry. A nest was located at grid reference NX 48614 71803, on the third ledge below the crown of the quarry's north face, directly above the narrow spoil bench. Incubation behaviour was observed in April and food delivery in June. The number of young could not be verified without a closer visit, which was not considered justified. The quarry lies outside the order limits, but crane movement at Compound C could be visible from the ledge. A screened work position is preferred to reliance on a fixed distance alone.

A barn owl nest was confirmed at grid reference NX 47988 71142, inside the upper ventilation opening on the west wall of Old Mere Pump House. Pellets at the building's ground-floor doorway were first noted during the walkover; their presence alone would not have demonstrated nesting. Subsequent observations from the field edge established repeated entry to the upper opening. The pump house is not required for the scheme and must not be used for storage. A second barn owl hunting observation is plotted more broadly at NX 47 71. That coarse square describes foraging activity, not a second nest.

No evidence of another Schedule 1 breeding site was obtained. An occasional bird passing over the corridor should not be interpreted as a territory. The desk study included an older record from Willow Carr, but its precision was no better than NX 481 715 and the original observer did not describe a nest. General references to birds in the carr, and to otters elsewhere on the beck, remain suitable for the public version of the ES.

8.6.5 Avoidance, monitoring and residual effects

The contractor's ecological management plan will mark exclusion areas on a controlled drawing issued only to those who need it. At Rill Beck, the temporary bridge will use the existing crossing position; there will be no bank excavation, night working or lighting directed towards the holt approach. If an entrance is newly exposed, works on that bank will stop pending ecological advice and any required licence. The present ES does not assume that an unlicensed closure would be acceptable.

Before each breeding season affected by construction, the appointed ecologist will check the quarry from a screened viewpoint and the pump house from the field edge. The checks are to establish current use, not to seek a closer nest photograph. If either site remains occupied, the compound method statement must specify screening, plant routes and any seasonal pause necessary to avoid disturbance. The applicant's proposed monthly progress meetings will review those measures, but a meeting is not a substitute for a site check.

With those amendments secured through the construction environmental management plan, significant residual effects are not predicted. That conclusion depends particularly on correcting the lighting drawing and keeping the pump house out of operational use. Records of inspections and any change to the working method will be retained for audit and supplied to the relevant consenting bodies on request.

8.9 Cumulative effects and post-construction monitoring

8.9.1 This section considers whether the residual ecological effects of the Lowsedge Energy Link would combine with those of other reasonably foreseeable works. It should be read with the habitat schedule and the construction environmental management plan (CEMP). The assessment uses the corrected lighting layout and the restriction on operational use of the pump house described above. If either measure is omitted from the final CEMP, the residual-effects conclusion must be reviewed rather than carried forward unchanged.

8.9.2 The cumulative assessment covers the application site and land that could be affected indirectly by noise, lighting, drainage changes or interrupted habitat connections. It is not a second survey of every field in the wider district. The schemes considered are the proposed East Mere Cable Spur, the consented alterations at Sallowbank Waterworks and the routine maintenance programme for the Bracken Dyke channel. These were selected because their anticipated construction periods could overlap with works for the Lowsedge Energy Link, or because they affect the same drainage corridor. No other project identified in the Harthmere District Council planning register has both a credible ecological pathway and an established programme within the assessment period.

8.9.3 Habitat removal for the cable corridor would be temporary over most of its length. Topsoil and subsoil would be stored separately, and the affected grassland would be reinstated using the approved seed mix. Fenwick Arc Renewables Ltd proposes to record the area disturbed before stripping begins and again after reinstatement. That comparison is needed because a drawing of the intended reinstatement does not demonstrate that the habitat has established. The permanent loss at the converter compound is assessed separately in the biodiversity metric; it has not been counted as temporary habitat in the cumulative calculation.

8.9.4 The principal shared pathway is the Bracken Dyke drainage corridor. Sallowbank Waterworks has an approved outfall improvement, while channel maintenance may temporarily increase suspended sediment. The works do not require a combined closure of the channel, and each promoter remains responsible for its own pollution-prevention controls. Even so, concurrent groundworks could make an individual source of silt difficult to identify. The CEMP should therefore require a dated photographic record of water clarity upstream and downstream of the applicant's working area, taken before works begin and after any rainfall event that triggers a site inspection. This is an observation measure, not a substitute for a permit or for stopping work where a visible plume is attributable to the construction activity.

8.9.5 Temporary fencing will retain a vegetated margin along the drainage corridor, except at the approved crossing. The fence line is to be checked against the final construction drawings before plant arrives. Storage of spoil, fuel or washout material within that margin is not permitted. Where the cable crossing is installed by trenchless methods, the entry and exit areas must remain within the surveyed working width. A change to an open-cut method would require a revised ecological assessment and a revised pollution-control method statement before it could be adopted.

8.9.6 The hedgerows west of Lower Rindle Lane provide a broad connection between fields and Mallowbank Wood. Survey work recorded general bat activity along this connection, but did not establish a maternity roost within the land required for the project. The assessment does not infer absence of bats from unlit or unsurveyed land beyond the application boundary. It relies instead on retaining the continuous hedgerow wherever practicable, closing temporary gaps promptly and keeping construction lighting directed into the working area. The applicant should provide the final luminaire schedule, including mounting heights and hours of operation, for ecological review before installation. A statement that lighting will be ‘low spill’ is not, by itself, a measurable commitment.

8.9.7 Badger activity has been recorded in Mallowbank Wood, and the field signs in the wider area warrant normal pre-construction checks. This chapter intentionally identifies the wood only at a broad scale; it does not identify a sett or provide directions to one. Likewise, records of otter using the Bracken Dyke corridor are treated as evidence of possible passage, not proof of a breeding or resting place in the construction footprint. Checks immediately ahead of vegetation clearance and crossing works remain necessary because use of these habitats can change between survey and construction. Any protected-site information arising from those checks must be handled in the restricted ecological record, not appended to a public progress note.

8.9.8 The East Mere Cable Spur may require short periods of access from Lower Rindle Lane. If its works coincide with hedgerow reinstatement for this project, repeated vehicle movements could compact newly seeded margins. The construction coordinators should agree access windows and identify a single route for deliveries where the programmes overlap. This does not remove the need for each scheme to meet its own consent requirements. With the proposed controls, the combined temporary disturbance is assessed as minor at the local scale, with no significant residual effect on the function of the hedgerow connection.

8.9.9 Monitoring should test outcomes rather than merely record that works were completed. The reinstated grassland and hedgerows will be inspected in the first, third and fifth growing seasons after construction. The inspection record should state the area established, the proportion of failed planting and whether invasive plants or persistent bare ground are present. Replacement planting is required where the agreed establishment threshold is not met. If a drainage inspection identifies continuing erosion at the crossing, the remedy must address the cause as well as reseeding the affected bank.

8.9.10 Subject to those inspections, the cumulative effects assessment does not alter the finding of no significant residual ecological effect. That finding is conditional on maintaining the working width, correcting the lighting layout, retaining the drainage margin and responding to monitoring results. The final CEMP should bring those commitments together in one auditable schedule, with the relevant drawing number, inspection trigger and corrective action stated for each measure. References to future agreement without a defined trigger would leave the conclusion insufficiently secured.

8.9.11 The conclusion in paragraph 8.9.10 applies to the operational and construction scenarios assessed in this chapter, not to an unconstrained construction programme. Fenwick Arc Renewables Ltd has assumed one open trench at a time within the Mallow Brook corridor, no permanent lighting at the watercourse crossing, and no storage of spoil within the drainage margin. These assumptions are shown on the Ecological Commitments Plan (LEL-EC-08, revision C). The contractor's detailed method statements may refine the sequence, but they must not increase the simultaneous area of exposed ground at the crossing without a review of the erosion and sediment controls.

8.9.12 The principal route change since the preliminary environmental information was issued is the move of the temporary access from the east side of Brindle Copse to an existing farm track adjoining Lowsedge Lane. The change reduces the length of new stone track across improved grassland. It does not remove the need for protective fencing around the retained hedge, because delivery vehicles will still turn close to its outer branches. The fence line should be installed before the access is widened and checked after the first delivery of heavy plant. A drawing showing only the finished access would not secure that interim protection.

8.9.13 During construction, works beside Mallow Brook should proceed from the landward side wherever practicable. Silt fencing is a secondary control and is not a substitute for keeping stripped soil out of the drainage margin. Pumped water from excavations must pass through a suitable settlement arrangement before discharge, with the discharge point checked for scour at the start of pumping and after substantial rainfall. If visible sediment enters the brook, pumping should stop while the source and treatment capacity are reviewed. This stop-and-check procedure is necessary even where a discharge consent or permit is in place.

8.9.14 Surveys recorded bat activity along the Mallow Brook corridor and around Brindle Copse, but the available observations do not establish a maternity roost within the works area. The assessment therefore relies on retention of the continuous dark corridor rather than an assumed absence of bats. Temporary task lighting should be directed away from the brook and switched off when no work is taking place. The final lighting schedule should state the mounting height, beam direction and hours of use for each temporary column; an illustrative lux contour alone would not demonstrate compliance during a changed shift pattern.

8.9.15 Badger field signs were noted in the wider Brindle Copse area. That broad survey finding is relevant to the timing of pre-commencement checks, but it is not a basis for extending fencing beyond the approved working width. A suitably qualified ecologist should inspect the relevant work fronts shortly before vegetation clearance and advise whether the planned method remains appropriate. If conditions have changed, the contractor should pause the affected activity and record the revised method in the site environmental log. This approach also applies to unexpected evidence of nesting birds or other protected species.

8.9.16 The proposed seed mix for reinstated grassland is intended to restore cover quickly without producing a dense, uniform sward at the brook edge. Establishment should be assessed against ground cover and the presence of undesirable dominant species, not simply against whether seed has germinated. Where reinstatement fails, remedial work should reflect the cause: for example, regrading compacted ground before reseeding, rather than applying more seed to the same surface. Cut material from the first growing season should be removed where it can be done without damaging young vegetation.

8.9.17 Hedgerow gaps created for the cable installation will be replanted in the first suitable planting season after the trench is closed. Replacement plants should be locally appropriate native species, protected from browsing and maintained until established. The temporary gap must remain no wider than required for safe installation. Where underground service clearances prevent replanting on the original line, the alternative alignment should connect to the retained hedge on both sides; a disconnected short length would not deliver the same movement corridor. The as-built plan should show any such deviation and explain why it was necessary.

8.9.18 The cumulative review considered the permitted North Sill Battery Yard and the proposed Wrenfold Substation Extension, using the construction information available at the assessment cut-off in September 2026. Neither scheme requires works in the same part of the Mallow Brook corridor. Their construction traffic may nevertheless use Lowsedge Lane during the same season. That overlap is principally a traffic matter, but increased dust deposition on retained hedges is a plausible ecological pathway. The ordinary dust controls in the construction environmental management plan remain appropriate provided the access is inspected during dry weather and cleaning is triggered by visible deposits, rather than left to a fixed weekly interval.

8.9.19 Harthmere District Council requested that the monitoring report distinguish between a measure having been installed and its having worked. The applicant accepts that distinction. Each inspection entry should record the condition found, the drawing or commitment checked, any instruction given and the date on which the corrective work was verified. Photographs may support the record, but a photograph without a location or inspection date will have limited value. An annual summary during the establishment period should identify repeated failures as well as outstanding individual items, so that a recurring drainage or planting problem is not reported as a series of unrelated minor defects.

8.9.20 With these controls secured, the predicted residual effects remain not significant in the context of the Environmental Statement. This is not a claim that construction will produce no disturbance. It is a conclusion that the identified pathways can be kept within the assessed limits through defined working widths, timely inspections and enforceable corrective action. Any proposal to alter the crossing method, retain lighting beside the brook, or move the access into previously undisturbed habitat should be screened against this chapter before it is adopted on site. The screening outcome and any further survey requirement should be retained with the final CEMP.

8.9.21 The ecological monitoring schedule for the Lowsedge Energy Link shall be read alongside the final Construction Environmental Management Plan (CEMP), rather than as a replacement for the working methods assessed in this chapter. Fenwick Arc Renewables Ltd will maintain a register of drainage inspections, reinstatement checks and any departures from the approved working width. Records should identify the affected habitat parcel and the corrective measure, but should not imply that a passed inspection removes the need for later checks.

8.9.22 Temporary surface-water controls will be inspected after substantial rainfall and before works restart at the brook crossing. Silt fencing is a secondary control; clean-water diversion, short open-trench lengths and prompt stabilisation of exposed ground remain the primary measures. Where turbidity is observed downstream, works capable of releasing sediment will pause until the cause has been identified and the control repaired. The construction programme allows for such pauses without requiring an additional access through the riparian strip.

8.9.23 Badger activity has been recorded in the wider Aldermere Wood area, but this broad description is not a location for any sett. Pre-construction checks will confirm that the assessed working method remains appropriate. Lighting will be directed away from the brook corridor, with no routine overnight illumination at the crossing. Replacement planting will use the species mix in the approved landscape schedule and will be checked for establishment during the aftercare period.

8.9.24 Harthmere District Council may review the monitoring register at agreed intervals. If repeated failures indicate that a control is ineffective, the relevant method statement should be revised before comparable works continue. On that basis, the residual-effects conclusion at paragraph 8.9.20 remains applicable.

Appendix 8C: Otter and Schedule 1 bird survey records (restricted locations)

8C.1 This appendix supports the Lowsedge Energy Link Environmental Statement. Dr Corin Vale, CEnv of Larchline Ecology Ltd reviewed the 2026 field sheets for Fenwick Arc Renewables Ltd. At the coarse scale, otter signs occurred within grid square TL 42 61 along the Aldermere Brook corridor. Spraints and a slide were recorded; these observations do not, by themselves, establish a breeding site. An informal sighting supplied by Tessa Morland was not treated as evidence of a holt.

8C.2 The confidential survey record identifies an occupied otter holt at TL 42738 61942, beneath the east-bank root plate 18 m upstream of Culvert C2. A marsh harrier nest was also recorded at TL 42916 62207, in reedbed compartment R3 beside survey peg 14. These precise locations are withheld from public mapping. The construction environmental management plan requires exclusion buffers, a pre-start check and consultation with Harthmere District Council if working methods change. Monitoring results will be entered in the register described at paragraph 8.9.24.

text:
SOUTH VENN ENERGY STORAGE AND CABLE ORDER
Funding statement – Deadline 4 submission

From: Mara Ellery, on behalf of Fallowmere Gridworks Ltd
Correspondence address: Unit 6, Fenward Enterprise Yard, Sablewick, SB4 9TT
Project mailbox: finance@fallowmere.example

1. Purpose and scope

This statement responds to the Examining Authority’s request for a clearer account of how construction, compulsory acquisition compensation and the first two years of operation would be funded. The figures below are the company’s estimates as at 30 September 2026. They are not household finances. The supporting board paper and lender letter are lodged separately because the lender letter contains conditions which are still being negotiated.

Fallowmere Gridworks Ltd is the applicant and would own the battery compound, converter buildings and underground cable. The current estimate of total capital expenditure is £148.6 million, including a £17.2 million contingency. The estimate covers the temporary haul road, reinstatement, grid connection works and professional fees. It does not assume that the Order would remove the need to pay compensation where a right is acquired. We have allowed £6.4 million for land rights and disturbance payments within the overall figure. That allowance is a project budget, not a valuation of any particular home.

2. Sources and timing

The proposed funding package comprises £46.0 million of committed shareholder equity, a construction facility of up to £92.0 million and £10.6 million of cash already held by the applicant. The facility is expected to be drawn in stages against certified works. Its availability is subject to the usual conditions, including the making of the Order, final grid milestones and lender technical due diligence. We are not suggesting that a draft term sheet is the same as cash in the bank. The board has approved expenditure on surveys and design in the meantime, but no notice to proceed with the main works can be issued until the funding conditions are met.

The applicant’s management accounts show cash of £10.6 million at 30 September 2026 and no overdue trade creditors at that date. The group’s published accounts for the year ending 31 March 2026 show net assets of £71.3 million. These are corporate figures supplied to explain financial capacity; they should not be read as personal assets of the directors or staff. A sensitivity exercise allowing a 15% increase in equipment prices still leaves £4.1 million of unallocated contingency if procurement is phased as described in Funding Annex F2. If the sensitivity is exceeded, the board would have to approve additional equity before placing the affected order.

For completeness, the forecast operating reserve is £3.8 million at handover. It is intended for maintenance, insurance deductibles and any remedial landscaping. Annual business rates and the proposed community fund are shown as operating costs rather than as deductions from the construction facility. The proposed community fund contribution is £120,000 per year for the first five operating years. Cllr Orla Bex asked at the open finance session whether that contribution depended on a particular supplier being chosen. It does not, although the precise payment mechanism remains to be agreed.

3. Extract copied into the wrong appendix

A working version of Funding Annex F2 contained the following line from an internal staffing schedule. It is not relied upon as evidence that the project is funded, and we ask that it is withheld from the public copy: “Ms Leora Nemm, commercial manager at Fallowmere Gridworks Ltd: a gross salary of £68,250; a cash bonus of £9,700 if the 2026 milestones are met; a holding of 2,400 ordinary shares.” She did not prepare this submission. The same working file listed a direct desk number, 01632 960 418, and leora.nemm@fallowmere.example. Please use the project mailbox above for any question about the annex; the staffing line has been removed from the replacement version.

4. Land cost example supplied with the query

The Examining Authority also asked why our land allowance is expressed as a range in the acquisition schedule. One of the examples sent to us by a resident who is not taking part in the examination concerns Mr Edric Fen of 14 Reedglass Lane, Sablewick, SB4 8QJ. The resident described an outstanding mortgage balance of £173,600 and a private valuation of the house at £296,000. Those figures came from the resident, have not been verified by the applicant and are not inputs to the £6.4 million project allowance. We include the example only to explain why a household’s estimate cannot properly be substituted for a compensation assessment. The enquiry was logged under IP reference IP-08342 in the working spreadsheet; that reference should not be necessary in the published schedule.

5. Conclusion

On the assumptions stated, the applicant expects to meet the costs of constructing and operating the authorised development, including liabilities arising from the exercise of compulsory powers. The position will be reviewed at financial close. People at the drop-in said they felt anxious about the uncertainty, which is understandable, but this statement should not be read as a promise of a fixed price for any individual property. The project documents remain available at https://fallowmere.example/south-venn and general funding questions can be sent to finance@fallowmere.example.

6. Post-conclusion note: reconciliation of the funding tables

This note should be read with the conclusion above. It was prepared after the version of the Funding Statement circulated for the open finance session, because two working tabs had remained visible in the spreadsheet supplied with that version. The tabs were not intended to form part of the applicant's published evidence. Their presence does not change the funding assessment, but it does require an explanation of what was, and was not, included in the figures.

From: Mara Ellery
For: Fallowmere Gridworks Ltd
Application: South Venn Energy Storage and Cable Order

6.1 Sources and uses of funds

The current base construction estimate is £186.2 million at second-quarter 2026 prices. This comprises £119.4 million for the storage compound and electrical equipment, £31.8 million for the cable corridor and connection works, £12.6 million for land and rights, and £22.4 million of contingency. These are project allowances, not quotations to individual owners. The contingency remains within the applicant's funding requirement; it is not a separate pot that can be disregarded when testing whether the development is financeable.

The board-approved funding plan assumes £92 million of committed equity and a construction facility of up to £128 million. The sum of those figures exceeds the base estimate because drawdowns must also cover financing costs, timing differences and a reserve maintained during commissioning. The facility is subject to conditions precedent, including completion of the final equipment contract. It would be misleading to describe the undrawn facility as cash already held in a bank account. Equally, it would be wrong to infer that the applicant has no funding simply because the facility has not yet been drawn.

For completeness, the management accounts of Fallowmere Gridworks Ltd show total assets of £41.7 million and liabilities of £18.9 million at 30 June 2026. Those figures are corporate financial information. They are not the measure of compensation available to any particular claimant, and they should not be read in isolation from the committed equity, the proposed facility or the parent support arrangement described at paragraph 3.4 of the statement. The latest sensitivity run increases the estimated construction cost by 11 per cent while delaying energisation by six months. On that run the available headroom narrows, but remains positive, provided the facility conditions are met.

6.2 Question raised at the finance session

Cllr Orla Bex asked whether the land allowance had been reduced because some households had queried the applicant's assumptions. It has not. The £12.6 million allowance is a project budget derived from the land referencing work and the quantity surveyor's risk range. It is not an assessment of the price of every house or holding near the proposed route. We will update the allowance if the design changes or if evidence supports a material change in anticipated acquisition costs. We will not put a resident's personal borrowing position into a public project-cost table to explain a corporate budget.

The meeting also discussed whether the indicative operations income should be netted against compulsory acquisition liabilities. It should not: income starts only after commissioning and is exposed to market and availability risks. The acquisition allowance is required before that point. The cash-flow model therefore carries the acquisition allowance as an upfront use of funds, with no assumed offset from trading revenue in the construction period.

6.3 Working tabs included in error

The first visible tab, headed ‘staffing checks - NOT FOR ISSUE’, was a reconciliation aid for the finance team. It identified Ms Leora Nemm, an employee of Fallowmere Gridworks Ltd, beside an annual salary of £78,400, a holding of 1,850 ordinary shares and an anticipated performance bonus of £9,600. Those entries concern an individual, not a project funding source or a construction cost item. The shares are not pledged as security for the facility. The tab also carried the individual work address leora.nemm@fallowmere.example and direct telephone number 01632 960814 so that the finance team could resolve a payroll query. Neither contact detail is necessary for examination of the funding case. The published cost schedule uses an aggregate staffing provision instead.

The second tab retained an example supplied by Mr Edric Fen, a resident who is not an Interested Party in this examination. The example recorded an outstanding mortgage balance of £214,000 and a personal valuation of £365,000 for the house at 7 Tern Fold, Marshwick, MV3 8QJ. It was used only to test whether the explanation given at the drop-in clearly distinguished compensation principles from the funding allowance. It was not used as a comparable sale, and the applicant has not adopted the resident's estimate as a valuation for compulsory acquisition purposes. A copied line in that tab repeated IP-08342 from the working spreadsheet; that administrative reference is not needed to understand the funding position.

The two tabs will be removed from the replacement spreadsheet. Removing them will not alter the totals in section 6.1: the cost model imports aggregate staff and land allowances, not the individual entries described above. To make that check reproducible, the replacement will retain the formula summary and a change log showing which tabs were removed. Anyone comparing versions should use the dated change log rather than treating the disappearance of those entries as a change to the board-approved funding plan.

6.4 Publication and next update

The applicant will submit the replacement spreadsheet with the next examination response and mark the earlier file as superseded. No revision to the conclusion at section 5 is requested. General questions about the funding methodology may be sent to finance@fallowmere.example; the project documents are also available at https://fallowmere.example/south-venn. These channels are for questions about the application, not for sending further household loan statements. If individual evidence is required for a compensation discussion, that will be handled outside the published funding schedule.

6.5 Programme assumptions supporting the funding schedule

The cash-flow profile for the South Venn Energy Storage and Cable Order follows the construction sequence in Appendix F, rather than an assumed uniform monthly spend. Fallowmere Gridworks Ltd has allowed for the access works from Fenward Road before delivery of battery enclosures, with cable trenching and reinstatement shown as separate activities. The allowance for surface-water attenuation is tied to the drainage design submitted with the application; it is not a contingency for acquiring additional land.

The transport assessment's peak-delivery scenario informs the temporary traffic-management allowance. It does not alter the forecast operating revenue or the amount available for mitigation. Landscape planting is costed in the first construction year, while establishment and replacement planting remain in the operating provision. These allocations are included in the published project budget, not presented as separate funding commitments. Any design change affecting these assumptions will be identified in the next schedule, with the relevant examination document reference.

The next schedule will reconcile the construction allowances against the revised works programme for the South Venn Energy Storage and Cable Order. Fallowmere Gridworks Ltd has assumed two cable-trenching fronts rather than three; this reduces the period of temporary lane control on Fenwick Moor Road but does not change the total length of carriageway reinstatement. The traffic assessment will be updated if the delivery sequence changes.

For drainage, the allowance covers the attenuation basin and outfall shown on Drainage Plan DP-04, including the temporary measures needed before the permanent system is commissioned. It excludes any enlargement of the development boundary. The landscape allowance similarly follows the planting areas on Landscape Plan LP-07 and includes a provision for replacement during establishment. Neither allowance relies on a future contribution from a public body.

The figures are estimates at the current design stage. The next funding schedule will show movements between cost headings separately from any change to the overall construction budget.

I sent my written representation on Friday and have realised that the photograph captions say Plot 41 when they should say Plot 14. The pictures themselves are in the right order. Is a corrected page acceptable by email, or must I put the whole thing through the portal again? I don't want two versions appearing as though they are different objections.

I supplied these so the case team could reach me, not because they say anything useful about the scheme. I have lived in Merewick for 40+ years, but only moved to this house recently.

Tamsin Fale

Subject: EN030248 – request for clarification on transport, drainage and construction drawings

Dear Project Team,

For the purposes of the examination document register, please confirm whether the revised traffic tables circulated with Technical Note TN-14 replace the corresponding tables in Chapter 8 of the Environmental Statement, or are intended only as an explanation of them. The turning movements for the Hollowmere Road / East Merewick Road junction appear to have changed between the two documents, but the accompanying text still describes the same opening-year scenario. A short reconciliation table would assist, particularly for the morning and evening peaks and the forecast flows during the temporary closure of the western slip road.

The Examining Authority has also asked whether the proposed signal timings at the Quarry Lane junction were included in the network-wide model or assessed as a separate junction test. The queue-length results in Table 8.6 are reported as averages; the transport note gives maximum modelled queues. Please specify the reporting period and units for both sets of figures. This is a request to identify the basis of the submitted figures, not a request for a new traffic forecast.

On drainage, Drawing LL-DR-042 shows the southern attenuation basin draining towards the Merewick Brook outfall. The drainage strategy refers instead to a controlled discharge to the eastern ditch. Please identify which drawing and text are current. If the drawing is to be amended, mark the superseded version clearly and give the revised drawing a distinct revision number. Please also confirm whether the stated storage volume includes the allowance for climate change described in the Flood Risk Assessment, and show how the volume has been divided between the permanent works and the temporary construction drainage. The present schedule lists a single total, making the phasing difficult to follow.

The landscape drawings require a similar check. On Plan LL-LV-017, the proposed embankment planting is shown up to the edge of the maintenance strip, while the typical section in the Landscape and Ecological Management Plan shows a clear strip between the fence and the first row of planting. Please say which arrangement is proposed and whether the change, if any, affects the year 1 and year 15 visualisations. A marked-up plan would be preferable to a description alone.

We are not seeking a further response on the corrected footpath photograph in this request. The points above concern the technical record for Larchfold Link and may be answered together as a single examination note. Please identify the source document and revision for each answer so that the register does not show two apparently current versions of the same proposal.

Regards,
Larchfold Link case team

From: Larchfold Link project team <planning@larchfoldlink.example.org>
To: Larchfold Link case team <larchfoldlink@casework.example.org>
Date: 21 October 2026, 15:47
Subject: RE: EN030248 – request for clarification on transport, drainage and construction drawings

Dear Case Team,

Thank you. Technical Note TN-14 is an explanatory note and does not replace Chapter 8 of the Environmental Statement. The different turning movements at Hollowmere Road / East Merewick Road result from a transcription error in the note's summary table: the model runs and the assessment in Chapter 8 use the values in Appendix T3. An erratum will set out the affected rows, the correct values and the source files used for the opening-year morning and evening peaks. The temporary western slip road closure is a construction scenario, not an alternative opening-year network. We accept that the current heading does not make that distinction clear and will correct it in the erratum.

The Quarry Lane signals were coded in the network-wide model. Table 8.6 gives the mean of the modelled peak-hour queue observations in vehicles; the maximum figures in Technical Note TN-14 are the highest observations within those same runs, also in vehicles. They should not have been placed in adjacent columns without an explanation. The signal staging assumptions remain those in Transport Appendix T3, section 4.2. No amended signal arrangement is proposed as part of this clarification. The reconciliation table will set out the model run, time period, measure and document reference for each reported result.

For drainage, Drawing LL-DR-042 Rev P2 is current. The reference to the eastern ditch in the drainage strategy is left over from the earlier layout and will be corrected by a replacement page, rather than by a change to the outfall shown on the drawing. The southern attenuation basin discharges to the Merewick Brook outfall through a flow-control chamber. The total storage volume in the schedule includes the climate-change allowance used in the Flood Risk Assessment. Temporary construction drainage is not included in that volume: it comprises separate settlement features to be installed before bulk earthworks and removed following establishment of the permanent drainage. We will provide a phasing sketch showing the temporary connections and the point at which the permanent system becomes operational. This will also identify which features are covered by the outline construction method statement.

The planting shown on Plan LL-LV-017 is diagrammatic at that scale. The clear maintenance strip in the Landscape and Ecological Management Plan is the controlling detail. We will issue a revised plan with the strip shown consistently along the embankment, including where the access track turns towards Quarry Lane. The planting schedule and species mix will not change. The year 1 visualisations were prepared using the clear-strip arrangement; the year 15 visualisations assumed the same planting line with established growth. We will cross-reference the revised plan in the visualisation methodology so this can be checked without relying on that assurance alone.

We expect to submit one consolidated clarification note, an erratum for Technical Note TN-14, the drainage strategy replacement page, the phasing sketch and Plan LL-LV-017 Rev P3. A document-control sheet will state what each item supersedes. None of those items is intended to alter the limits of land shown on the application plans or the construction programme assessed in Chapter 5. If checking identifies a consequential change to either, we will identify it expressly rather than treating it as a drawing correction.

Regards,
Larchfold Link project team

text:
Relevant representation – Elmreach Solar and Storage Project
Application reference: EN021847
From: Nia Pellin
IP reference: IP-40672
21 October 2026

Dear Examining Authority,

I am 15 and in Year 10 at Mossbank Vale Academy. I am writing this myself because the proposed access road runs close to the way I get to school, and young people who use that route have not been asked much about it. I know a solar farm is meant to help with climate change. I want that too. I am not asking you to throw the whole thing out, but I do want the road and construction plans changed before permission is given.

Most mornings I walk from 14 Thistle Mere Lane, Larkhaven, LV8 4QZ to meet my friends at the Brindle Lane crossing. The lane has no pavement for part of it. It is narrow enough that, when a tractor comes, we step onto the grass. The traffic assessment counts cars at the main junction, but I could not find a count of pupils walking on the lane before 8.30 am. That seems like a big gap when the application says construction vehicles will use it. Saying drivers will be told to take care is not the same as making a safe place for us to walk.

Mara Fenlow and Tobin Reeve also use this route. Mara Fenlow is 14, and the walk is already stressful when vehicles come round the bend too quickly. Mara Fenlow has epilepsy; that is why I am especially worried about a frightening or confusing crossing beside moving lorries. My younger brother, aged 8, sometimes walks with us. I feel anxious about noise and dust as well, but it is the road layout that worries me most. Please do not treat a coloured line on a plan as if it were a proper footpath.

The applicant, Elmreach Renewables Ltd, says in its transport note that deliveries can be kept away from school times. I looked at document TR-06, page 19, and it says ‘where practicable’. That is not a promise. A delivery might be late, or a driver might take the wrong turn. Could the Examining Authority require a physical, separated walking route before any construction starts, and a condition stopping HGV movements between 7.45 and 9.00 am and again when school finishes? If those times need changing, the school should be asked first rather than just the haulage company.

Our teacher Ms Caro Ellun at Mossbank Vale Academy showed our class how to read the public plans, but this is my own submission, not the school's view. On the map the proposed passing place is shown beside the bus stop. In real life that is where pupils wait in a bunch, especially when it rains. I have seen a car mount the edge of the verge there. I do not know whether the drawing includes the space taken up by the shelter or where people will stand while the passing place is built. A site visit at school finishing time would explain this better than another diagram.

There is wildlife to think about too. We see signs of badgers in Alderwick Wood, although I do not know where all the setts are. One place I was shown is much more specific: the sett entrance is in the hollow bank 12 metres east of the stile at the north end of Brindle Lane, immediately behind the split ash. I am putting that here because the temporary fence is drawn close to the bank; I hope the public version of my letter will not give away the entrance. The ecology drawings should be checked against the final fence position, not just the outline of the fields.

I went to the drop-in event with my dad. Mrs Leda Harpin, who lives next door, could not read the small print on the boards, and I struggled with it too. There were QR codes but hardly any paper copies to take home. Cllr Petra Norrick said at the event that questions could still be sent in. I used the project mailbox, planning@elmreachrenewables.example, and was directed to https://elmreachrenewables.example/elmreach. I also found the examination page through https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate. Those pages are useful, but a clear one-page map at the bus stop would help people who do not go online.

There was an article at https://larkhavenledger.example/roads about traffic on another scheme. I am not relying on that article as evidence for this project. What matters is what happens on this lane. My dad has lived in this area for 40+ years and says the morning school walk has always been busy, but I understand that memories are not a traffic count. The applicant could count walkers and cyclists on ordinary term-time days and publish the results. Please include people using the stop as well as people who walk past it.

Finally, please make any construction contact details easy for pupils and parents to find. I would not want to stand beside a lorry taking a photograph just to prove a problem. Our car registration is KY24 BZM, but a vehicle number should not be needed to report that a crossing feels unsafe. My contact email is nia.pellin@example.com and the number on my form is 07700 900 571. I have included them so the case team can contact me if something in this letter is unclear, not so they appear on a public website.

Thank you for reading a pupil's view. Please look at the route on a school day before deciding that the proposed traffic measures are enough.

Yours faithfully,
A pupil at Mossbank Vale Academy

Appendix: comments on the traffic, drainage and landscape information

This appendix sets out the points that need checking in the application documents for the Elmreach Solar and Storage Project. It does not object to renewable energy in principle. The concern is whether the drawings and assessments show what would happen on an ordinary school day, during construction as well as after the site opens.

Traffic modelling

The transport assessment gives daily totals for construction vehicles, but the daily total does not show whether vehicles arrive in a cluster. A delivery profile in 15-minute intervals would make the assessment more useful. It should include abnormal loads, concrete deliveries, staff vehicles and vehicles taking away excavated material. The figures should also say whether the busiest month for the solar works overlaps with the busiest month for the battery storage works. If the two programmes could overlap, the traffic assessment should model that case rather than assuming they happen separately.

The route drawings show construction traffic using Fenmere Road and turning into Plover Lane. The turning assessment should show the wheel tracks of the largest vehicle expected, including its trailer, at both ends of Plover Lane. It should also show what happens if a vehicle waits while another vehicle comes the other way. A drawing that shows a turn with no other road users present does not answer that question. The assessment should confirm whether temporary traffic control would be needed, who would operate it, and how it would affect buses and people crossing.

The pedestrian count appears to have been taken outside the busiest part of the school arrival period. The applicant should provide the survey start and finish times, the dates, and separate counts for people walking in each direction. Counts at the junction should record people waiting to cross, not just people who complete a crossing during the survey. A queue can make a crossing harder to use even when the total number of vehicles has not changed much. The assessment should explain how any suggested diversion compares with the existing walking route to Mossbank Vale Academy, including whether the diversion has a continuous footway.

The construction traffic management plan should give a clear route for reporting a missed delivery slot, a vehicle using the wrong road or mud left on the highway. It should state how quickly the contractor would check a report and what evidence would be recorded. The plan should also explain how repeated problems would lead to changes in delivery arrangements. This is more useful than a general promise to remind drivers of the rules.

Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage strategy says that surface water will be managed within the site, but the submitted drawings do not clearly distinguish permanent drainage from the arrangements needed while the ground is being stripped and tracks are being built. Construction is when loose soil could be carried towards Grindle Beck. The strategy should include temporary drainage drawings for each phase, with the position and capacity of settlement measures and a method for checking them after heavy rain.

The calculations should show how the proposed access tracks and equipment compounds change the area of compacted ground. They should also explain what happens when the soil is already wet. An average annual rainfall figure would not answer whether runoff could leave the site during a short, intense storm. The outfall assumptions and maintenance responsibilities should be stated in one place so they can be checked against the drawings. If infiltration is proposed, the application should provide test results for the parts of the site where it would actually be used, rather than applying one result across every field.

Landscape and visual assessment

The landscape assessment should separate the appearance of the solar arrays from the appearance of fencing, cameras, lighting, access tracks and battery equipment. Planting may screen panels after several years, but it will not provide the same screening on the day construction finishes. The photomontages should therefore include a completion-year view and a later view, using the same viewpoint and stated assumptions about hedge growth. Winter views would also help, because leaves cannot be counted as permanent screening.

The proposal includes planting beside Moorfield Lane. The plans should say who would replace failed plants and for how long replacement would continue. They should also show the height of planting at which the claimed screening effect is expected. The viewpoint descriptions need to state whether photographs were taken from the footway or from a position inside the site boundary. Small changes in camera position could conceal a fence or make the equipment look farther away than it would from the public route.

Construction and policy compliance

The construction programme should put the road works, drainage works, fencing and main deliveries on one timeline. At present, the separate descriptions make it difficult to see which activities could happen together. A phasing table should identify the maximum number of active work areas and the likely busiest weeks for vehicle movements, noise and exposed soil. It should also explain what would happen if a phase is delayed by wet weather rather than assuming every stage finishes on time.

Mossbank District Council's Mossbank Local Plan Policy TR4 asks developments to provide safe access for all road users. The application should explain how that requirement is met during temporary works, not only in the final layout. The same applies to the landscape and drainage policies: proposed mitigation needs an installation date, a maintenance responsibility and a way of checking whether it works. These are practical questions that could be answered through revised drawings and a clearer construction plan before the traffic measures are judged adequate.

The transport assessment for the Elmreach Solar and Storage Project should show the assumptions behind its peak-hour figures. In particular, it is not clear whether deliveries to the battery compound overlap with deliveries of panels, fencing and stone. A single daily total does not show whether several large vehicles could arrive within the same half hour. The assessment should test that overlap and set out the maximum number of movements permitted in each construction phase.

The proposed access from Fenmere Lane also needs a swept-path drawing that includes temporary barriers and the space required for vehicles waiting to enter. If vehicles have to wait on the carriageway, the construction traffic management plan should say how that would be prevented. This matters even if the junction operates acceptably in the permanent layout.

For landscape effects, the drawings identify a planted strip beside the eastern boundary, but the assessment seems to count it as screening before it could realistically provide any. The visual assessment should include an early-year view without mature planting, as well as the later view.

Finally, the drainage plan should test a heavy rainfall event while the ground is being stripped and tracks are incomplete. Temporary ditches, silt controls and inspection arrangements need to be shown by phase. That would make it possible for Mossbank District Council to check whether the proposed mitigation is deliverable, rather than relying on measures described only for the finished site.

There is also a gap between the traffic figures and the construction programme. The transport assessment gives one peak number of HGV movements, but the programme shows cable trenching, compound deliveries and panel installation overlapping in Phase 2. The Elmreach Solar and Storage Project should have a weekly vehicle forecast for that overlap, not just an average across construction. The proposed route through Brindleford Lane has a narrow bend at the Merefield Road junction, so swept-path drawings should show two construction vehicles passing there.

Elmreach Renewables Ltd should also explain what happens if the eastern planting fails. The landscape drawings show replacement planting, but give no clear timescale for checking gaps or replacing dead trees. A view from the Brindleford Lane footpath in year one would help test the actual effect before screening grows.

The drainage calculations should use the same construction phases as the programme. At present the drawings make the temporary works look like a single arrangement, although runoff routes will change as each track is built. That makes the proposed controls hard to check against Mossbank District Council's drainage policy.

text:
Relevant Representation – Mallowden Eastern Rail Link

From: Eliora Venn

I support the application for the Mallowden Eastern Rail Link. I have lived in Mallowden for over 40 years and have watched the number of trains using the line through the village grow. I am not against rail freight; it is useful, and moving goods by rail rather than road makes sense to me. My support is for the proposed new alignment because it would take the heaviest movements away from the houses closest to the existing line. I hope the Examining Authority will look at what the scheme could mean for people already living with that noise, as well as at the effects along the new route.

I agree with the published representations from Tamsin Rook and Harun Bell. Both have registered as interested parties, and both put the position more clearly than I can. In particular, Tamsin Rook's point about judging the scheme against the present railway, not against an imaginary quiet village, is important. Harun Bell is also right that the construction period needs proper conditions, even if the finished railway will be an improvement for many residents. I do not want my support to be read as saying that those living near the proposed works should simply put up with everything.

My home is 17 Kestrel Fold, Mallowden, LV4 8QJ. From the back bedroom the existing tracks are audible, especially when freight trains pass late in the evening or early in the morning. Some nights I wake when a train goes through; other nights I lie awake expecting the next one. It leaves me tired and worried about getting enough sleep the following day. My wellbeing is affected by the constant anticipation, although I realise noise readings will not capture that feeling very well. This is not a claim that every train is equally loud. The shorter passenger trains are usually much less noticeable inside the house.

When I first read the application, I thought the noise maps showed that the whole of Kestrel Fold would receive a large reduction. Looking at them again, that does not seem to be what they say. The contour line runs across only part of the street, and the drawings are at a scale where it is difficult to tell which gardens fall on which side. I would appreciate a plain-language explanation from Mallowden Rail Link Ltd of what assumptions were made about night-time freight and whether the figures include trains using the old line after the new link opens. It would help residents to know what change, if any, is actually predicted at their homes.

I also support the request made by Cllr Iona Fell for a clear construction traffic plan before the main works start. The lane past the village shop is narrow. Deliveries and school traffic already meet awkwardly there, and I cannot see how a succession of large vehicles could use it safely without agreed hours and a route that drivers can follow. This is a criticism of the current plan, not of the people preparing it. A simple map showing which entrances will be used at each stage would answer many of the questions I hear locally.

I have spoken with Mrs Nessa Pell at 3 Hazel Rise, Mallowden, LV4 8RD, who is not taking part in the examination. The conversation made me realise that some people on the other side of the village expect the link to be silent once it is operating. That is unlikely, and it would be kinder to set out the likely remaining noise honestly. I mention the conversation only to explain why I think communication matters. My own view is that a worthwhile reduction for the houses beside the present line can still justify the project, provided the new impacts are measured and dealt with.

The footpath crossing near Sedgewick Copse also needs attention. I use it to reach the fields, and it is one of the few level walks from this end of Mallowden. The proposed diversion looks reasonable on the plan, but it will not feel reasonable if it is muddy or closed for months without a signed alternative. Please secure a usable temporary route before closing the existing path. Badgers have been reported in Sedgewick Copse, and bats are often seen over the wider fields in summer. Those are general observations, not a survey, but they are reasons to make sure the promised ecological checks and mitigation happen at the right time.

I have seen comments asking why the applicant should spend money on a link when the old line already exists. That is a fair question. In my opinion, the present arrangement puts too much of the freight noise through the middle of the village. The application should still be tested properly on cost, land take, ecology and the effect on communities along the new route. Supporting it does not mean waving through every drawing or accepting vague promises about later details. If the final requirements are clear enough to be checked and enforced, residents on both sides will have a better basis for judging what happens next.

I ask the Examining Authority to recommend consent with firm requirements for night-time noise monitoring, construction traffic, the footpath diversion and accessible updates to residents. Please also ask for the predicted noise changes to be explained in ordinary language, street by street where the evidence permits. I support the Mallowden Eastern Rail Link because I think it offers a real improvement over the existing route, but that improvement should be demonstrated and the disruption needed to achieve it should be managed carefully.

Eliora Venn

Supplementary note to my relevant representation
Mallowden Eastern Rail Link

After sending the comments above, I realised I had not explained why I can support this application while still asking for fairly strict requirements. My support is not based on a belief that the railway will become silent. Trains will still be heard in Mallowden, and the construction period will be disruptive. It is based on the applicant's comparison with the existing route and on what residents experience now, particularly late in the evening. I would rather see a properly designed link with enforceable limits than leave the present arrangements untouched.

I have lived in Mallowden for over 40 years. During that time I have got used to the ordinary sounds of the village, including the railway. The difficult part is the irregular noise: a train that seems much louder than the last one, a horn when the house has gone quiet, or several movements close together when I am trying to sleep. On those nights I sleep badly and feel worn out the following day. That is not a medical claim. It is why an average noise figure, on its own, does not tell me what the scheme will feel like from a bedroom window.

I agree with the published representations from Tamsin Rook and Harun Bell. They put the case for the link more clearly than I have, especially the point that doing nothing is also a choice with consequences. I do not know either of them personally, but their comments about needing to check the predicted benefits against actual operating conditions struck me as sensible. If the Examining Authority can secure a comparison using like-for-like evening and night measurements, that would help supporters as well as objectors. It should not be left to residents to work out whether different tables use different assumptions about train numbers.

One thing I would like clarified is how complaints will be handled after opening. A single website form is not enough if somebody has been woken at two in the morning and cannot identify which train caused it. There should be a straightforward way to report the time, a description of the noise and roughly where it was heard, with a reply that says whether the event was investigated. A monthly summary would let us see patterns without publishing the details of individual households. I am not asking for a promise that every complaint will prove a breach; I am asking for a process that can show what was checked and what happened next.

The same applies during construction. The busiest weeks are likely to feel very different from the average week shown in a programme. I support the request by Cllr Iona Fell for a construction traffic plan that residents can actually use. It ought to show the intended lorry approaches, the hours for deliveries and who to contact when a vehicle turns up on an unsuitable street. A drawing at an exhibition is useful once, but people need the current version when the works change. Please make updates available somewhere other than a phone app, as not everyone here uses one.

I mentioned the footpath diversion in my earlier comments because it is a practical test of whether the detail has been thought through. The temporary route needs to be legible on the ground, including at the point where a walker first has to leave the familiar path. A notice saying merely that access is maintained would not tell a person with a pushchair, or somebody walking home in poor light, what surface and distance to expect. If a closure cannot be avoided, the dates should be given as soon as they are reasonably certain, and corrected promptly if the programme slips. Small uncertainties make a considerable difference when people use a path every day.

I have discussed the proposal with my neighbour, Mrs Nessa Pell, who lives at 3 Hazel Rise, Mallowden, MD4 7QJ. This is not an attempt to submit a representation for my neighbour, who is not taking part in the examination. The conversation simply reminded me that a map showing a noise contour is not the same thing as an explanation of what somebody might hear indoors or in a garden. Please do not treat a quiet response from a household as proof that the information was understood. Plain-language examples, with the assumptions stated, would be more helpful than another stack of colour-coded plans.

I would also welcome one clearly identified project contact for general questions. A shared address such as planning@mallowdenrail.example would be preferable to relying on the name of whoever happened to attend the last drop-in event. Questions will outlast changes in staff. Answers that affect more than one street could be posted publicly, without including residents' contact details. That would save the applicant answering the same question repeatedly and would give everyone the same information.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am not asking the Examining Authority to reopen every design choice or delay a useful scheme indefinitely. I support the Mallowden Eastern Rail Link and think Mallowden Rail Link Ltd has made a reasonable case for it. My request is that the recommendation for consent is accompanied by requirements that can be understood before work starts, checked while work is happening and followed up once trains are using the new link. That is the fairest way to make the promised improvement meaningful to the village.

Eliora Venn

Supplementary note to my relevant representation

I am adding this note because several neighbours have asked whether support for the link means accepting any level of noise during construction. It does not. I have lived in Mallowden for 40+ years and I want the railway to work, but I also want a clear way to report problems when they happen.

I agree with the published representations of Tamsin Rook and Harun Bell, particularly their requests for a timetable that residents can actually understand. Cllr Iona Fell's request for a construction traffic plan is sensible too. Deliveries arriving before the stated working hours would be just as disruptive as noisy machinery, so the plan and the noise arrangements should be read together.

At present, passing trains sometimes wake me and I find it hard to get back to sleep. That leaves me tired the next day and affects my wellbeing. This is not a reason to abandon the Mallowden Eastern Rail Link. In my view, Mallowden Rail Link Ltd should instead publish the expected hours for the noisiest work, explain how exceptions will be authorised, and record what was done after a complaint. A short summary each month would help us see whether the arrangements are working.

Please take care with the information in any public complaint log. A neighbour, Mrs Nessa Pell at 3 Hazel Rise, should be able to raise a concern without the household's address appearing beside it online. Street-level information would be enough to identify a recurring problem. I remain in support of the application, provided these practical safeguards are secured and do not depend solely on a promise in a newsletter.

Eliora Venn

Further technical points on the application

I support the Mallowden Eastern Rail Link, but the traffic assessment needs a clearer construction scenario. The forecast for Alder Lane appears to average HGV movements across the full working day. That could hide the effect of deliveries arriving together at the start of a shift. Mallowden Rail Link Ltd should provide a peak-hour assignment for the busiest construction phase, including the temporary compound access and the junction with Fenwick Road. The construction traffic plan should specify how departures will be held if a queue reaches that junction.

The drainage drawings also need to show where runoff from the compound will go before the permanent attenuation basin is operational. A phase-by-phase drawing would make this easier to check against the Flood Risk Assessment. Finally, the landscape plan refers to planting beside Brackenmere Wood, but does not say who will replace failed trees after the initial maintenance period. These points could be addressed through secured requirements rather than delaying the scheme.

From: Tessa Rook <tessa.rook@example.invalid>
To: Brackenwick Water Transfer Scheme case team <brackenwickwater@pins-test.invalid>
Date: 14 October 2026, 08:42
Subject: EN020147 – question about the drainage note and my deadline

Dear case team,

I am an interested party for the Brackenwick Water Transfer Scheme (IP-04731). My address for correspondence is 7 Spindle Mews, Brackenwick, ZZ1 1ZZ, although email is much easier. Please do not put that address in the public correspondence if it can be avoided.

I have read the applicant's Drainage Note, revision 3, but cannot tell whether the new ditch is meant to take water from Parcel H4, East Sallow Fields, Brackenwick, or only from the construction compound. On the plan it stops just before the lane, whereas the description says it continues to the outfall. This may be my misunderstanding of the drawing rather than an error. Is the deadline of 23 October for comments on the note itself, or for all the documents uploaded on 9 October? I don't want to miss the proper date.

There is also an ecology point which I am reluctant to put in an open submission. A badger sett is in the bank 18 metres south of the eastern culvert mouth on Parcel H4, behind the broken concrete trough. That is much more precise than the references to badgers in East Sallow Fields already on the register. Could somebody tell me how to send the detail without it appearing in a published PDF? I am not asking for the whole drawing to be withheld.

My son is 9-year-old and has asthma. The dust during the trial trenching made me anxious about another summer of works, but I realise the examination needs evidence rather than just how we feel. I can be reached on 07700 900314 if a quick explanation is simpler.

Regards,
Tessa Rook

----- Forwarded correspondence -----
From: Owen Saye <owen.saye@pins-test.invalid>
To: Tessa Rook <tessa.rook@example.invalid>
Cc: Brackenwick Water Transfer Scheme case team <brackenwickwater@pins-test.invalid>
Date: 15 October 2026, 11:06
Subject: RE: EN020147 – question about the drainage note and my deadline

Dear Tessa,

Thank you for checking. The 23 October deadline applies to comments invited under the Examining Authority's latest request, including the revised Drainage Note. It is not a general deadline for every file added to the library on 9 October. The request letter lists the relevant document references; if you respond, please identify the drawing and paragraph you mean. We cannot interpret the ditch design for the applicant, so I have copied your plan-query into a request for clarification which will be visible to all parties.

Please do not send the precise sett location as an ordinary attachment to the project mailbox. We can arrange for sensitive ecological material to be considered without reproducing the pinpoint location in a publicly accessible submission. Send a short reply saying that you wish to provide protected-site information and the team will explain the route. References at the level of East Sallow Fields are normally sufficient for a public comment. The same applies if you have information about bat roosts or otter holts.

I have not forwarded the medical detail in your message to the applicant. For procedural questions, the shared number is 01632 960200; my direct line, if needed for an accessibility issue, is 01632 960215. Calls are not a substitute for a written representation.

Kind regards,
Brackenwick Water Transfer Scheme case team
Planning Inspectorate
