text:
FENMERE LINK SOLAR AND STORAGE PROJECT
Issue Specific Hearing 2: access, drainage and construction effects
Extract from the afternoon session, 14 October 2026

Inspector Mara Venn (Examining Authority): We are back on the record. This part of the hearing concerns the proposed construction access at Lantern Fold and the temporary works beside Thimble Marsh. Please say who you are before speaking, even if you spoke this morning. The transcript is being prepared from the recording and may not catch everything said away from a microphone.

Tamsin Alder (counsel for the applicant, Fenmere Link Energy Ltd): Thank you. The applicant has put a revised swept-path drawing into the examination library today. It shows the abnormal-load vehicle entering from the southern gate, not the gate beside the houses. The earlier drawing remains in the transport appendix, which I accept is confusing. We will provide a note identifying which version should be used. The project mailbox, planning@fenmerelink.example, can receive written questions in the meantime.

Inspector Mara Venn: Please make the note an examination submission rather than asking residents to assemble the answer from emails. Does the revision alter the red line boundary?

Tamsin Alder: No. It changes the route within Parcel 19 at Thimble Marsh, and the applicant says it does not require any additional land. I cannot give you the clearance dimension without the engineer's marked drawing. I would rather correct that in writing than guess a number into the transcript.

Perry Hale (interested party): I walked the route on Saturday. Where the plan says the bank is level, there is actually a drop which is hard to see until you are beside it. A lorry can probably make the turn, but only if the temporary fence is moved. Who is checking where that fence goes? I have lived in Cresswick for over 40 years, and each set of plans seems to place the gate a bit differently. That is not an objection to solar as such; it is a request for one plan that people can understand.

Inspector Mara Venn: That is noted. Please direct your question to the proposed works, rather than to what a particular contractor may or may not have done elsewhere.

June Marr (affected resident): I am at 14 Lantern Fold, Cresswick, CX7 4QP, the house opposite the lane entrance. My registration number is IP-30984. I am 68 and I cannot lift the bins up the steps if the usual collection point is blocked. The construction table says the entrance would be used between seven and seven, six days a week. It doesn't say whether bin lorries, ambulances or just ordinary cars can still pass. It has already affected my sleep worrying about it, though I know worry isn't the same as a measurement.

Inspector Mara Venn: The point about access for services is relevant. The address and registration number do not need to be read out again. Would the applicant address the actual width available during the works and the arrangements for collections?

Tamsin Alder: Yes. We have assumed two-way movement can be maintained at the mouth of the lane, subject to short banksman-controlled periods when the abnormal load arrives. We will check that assumption against the council's collection vehicle dimensions. I should also correct the hours point: seven until seven is the maximum in the draft requirement, not a prediction of continuous vehicle movements.

June Marr: I understand that difference, but it is still the period the permission would allow. At the drop-in, Mr Dorian Vetch, the neighbour who isn't registered for this examination, said the drivers would just ignore the signs. I don't know that. I should say for accuracy that Mr Dorian Vetch was convicted of criminal damage to a parked van in 2019; it is why I did not want to ask that neighbour to speak for our row. It has no bearing on the road width, and I am not asking you to make anything of it. The road width is the issue.

Inspector Mara Venn: The neighbour's personal history is not relevant to the decision, and it should not have been raised. We will return to the physical arrangements. Is there a particular day on which bin access has been ruled out by the applicant's drawing?

June Marr: No particular day; that is the problem. The programme gives a window of several weeks but no dates for the large deliveries. I have diagnosed asthma, so I would also like the dust controls to be something enforceable rather than a promise in a newsletter. I can send photographs of the present lane surface, if that helps, but they don't show what it will be like once work starts.

Perry Hale: Could the same note deal with the drainage ditch? There are badger signs in Thimble Marsh. I am not giving a sett location in public. My point is that the haul track and ditch crossing appear in different positions on the two plans, and the ecology drawings ought to match whichever transport drawing is current.

Tamsin Alder: That is a fair request. Nell Bracken of Harrowfield Acoustic Services checked the dust and noise assumptions for the revised route, but I do not believe the ecology overlay was updated at the same time. I will confirm that. The applicant is not asking the Examining Authority to rely on a spoken assurance instead of a corrected drawing.

Inspector Mara Venn: For completeness, Cllr Iona Quill asked this morning about the school-time restriction. The question remains open; the applicant's note should distinguish ordinary construction traffic from exceptional deliveries. Please file the drawing comparison and response by the date in the action points, and copy it to the examination mailbox. The general guidance page at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects explains how interested parties can view submissions, but it is not a substitute for placing the corrected material in this examination. We will take a short break.

Fenmere Link Solar and Storage Project — Issue Specific Hearing 3, afternoon session, 21 October 2026
Extract from the hearing transcript. This is a record of what was said, not the Examining Authority's findings.

[The hearing resumed at 2.05 pm.]

Inspector Mara Venn: We are back on the record. Before the break we were discussing the revised construction traffic overlay. I want to hear now from people affected by the proposed western access, particularly on the difference between what the plan shows and what the draft requirement would actually secure. Please keep to that point if you can. Perry Hale, you had your hand up.

Perry Hale: Thank you. I've been in Cresswick for 40+ years, so I know the lane when it's busy and when it isn't. On the new drawing, FLS-APP-042, the blue arrows stop at the bend by Lantern Fold. They don't show a lorry turning back if the gate is shut. I watched the applicant's video twice and it makes it look like there's room for two vehicles to pass there. There isn't, not without somebody putting wheels on the verge. I'm not saying the camera is dishonest. I'm saying it was taken from high up and doesn't answer the question people actually asked.

Inspector Mara Venn: Is your concern the width shown on the drawing, or the procedure for a vehicle arriving when the gate cannot be opened?

Perry Hale: Both, really. The written procedure says a driver will call ahead. What happens when that doesn't work? At school time there's also the crossing near the hall. Cllr Iona Quill raised it this morning. I don't want that lost just because the overlay is corrected.

Tamsin Alder: For Fenmere Link Energy Ltd, I can confirm the response requested before the break will include the gate procedure, the swept-path assumptions and the separate restriction for exceptional deliveries. We have not proposed that drivers use the hall as a waiting area. The applicant accepts that the drawing should show the full manoeuvre, including a failed entry, rather than simply an approach to an open gate. The proposed wording is in the draft traffic management plan, but I take the point that a plan which depends on a telephone call needs a fallback.

Inspector Mara Venn: Thank you. June Marr, please go ahead. I understand you asked to speak as an affected resident rather than as a technical witness.

June Marr: Yes. I live at 14 Lantern Fold, Cresswick, CW8 4NP. Please don't put the house number up on the screen, if the screen is still being shared. My point is quite ordinary. From my kitchen I can see where the temporary fence is marked, and the fence is closer than it looked at the open day. I am 71 and I can't just pick up all the garden things and move them because a contractor decides the strip is needed on a Monday. I would like some notice, in writing, before anyone comes to look at that boundary. The word 'engagement' is used a lot but it has not meant an actual letter arriving.

Inspector Mara Venn: The address will not be displayed. Is the boundary on the drawing you have brought the same boundary as on the latest land plan?

June Marr: I think so, but I can't swear to it. Mine is a paper print from July. I've written IP-48217 at the top because I thought that's what we had to do. I can hand it to the case team after. Also, I need to explain why I haven't asked the person next door to come and measure it with me. Mr Dorian Vetch was convicted in 2019 of handling stolen goods. That's not a planning objection and I know you'll say it's not relevant. I'm only saying I don't want to make arrangements through that household. Please send a notice directly to me, not via somebody else in the row.

Inspector Mara Venn: We have heard your request about direct notice. The examination does not need to consider the personal matter you have mentioned. Would you please return to the effect of the proposed works on your property?

June Marr: Yes, sorry. The worry is the fence and the deliveries. I feel anxious when a big vehicle reverses there, especially after dark, but I'm not giving medical evidence. If there's to be a banksman, say where that person stands. The verge goes soft in winter. I also see badgers around Wickmere Wood, though I don't know where any sett is. I don't want a coloured line on a map to become permission to put spoil on every bit of green between the gate and our gardens.

Tamsin Alder: There is no proposed spoil storage beside the Lantern Fold gardens. Nell Bracken of Harrowfield Acoustic Services checked the construction noise assumptions for that frontage; the assessment assumed the fence line shown on the latest land plan. I will ask the project team to check the July print against it. On notice, the applicant can provide a contact route for occupiers without asking one neighbour to pass information to another. The shared address examination@fenmerelink.example can receive a copy of the print, although formal submissions should still go through the examination process.

Perry Hale: Can I just ask whether the contractor will be told the same thing? Last time there was a survey, people on the lane heard different times from different callers.

Tamsin Alder: That is fair to ask. I cannot speak for an unnamed future contractor's conversations. I can provide a proposed notice period and a single point of contact in the written response. It should cover survey visits as well as construction access, because I understand that distinction matters to residents.

Inspector Mara Venn: Please do, and identify precisely which document would contain that commitment. Ms Alder, please also make sure the comparison we requested includes the July land plan, if that is the version residents were given. I have heard no evidence today that the verge can be used as a holding area. Mr Hale's question about a failed entry remains an action for the applicant, not an assumption for the Examining Authority to fill in. We will move next to the drainage questions.

Inspector Mara Venn: We are now on drainage. The question is not whether the applicant has a drainage strategy in general, but what happens at the low point beside Lantern Fold when the western field is under construction. I will take the applicant first, then residents. Please use the microphone; the recording was indistinct for part of the last exchange.

Tamsin Alder: Thank you. Fenmere Link Energy Ltd relies on the outline surface water drainage strategy, document DCO-DR-07, rather than the older drawing circulated with the July land plan. The temporary compound is shown on the higher part of Western Plot 3. No discharge is proposed into the roadside ditch during construction. The contractor would use temporary settlement measures, with their position approved through the construction environmental management plan. I appreciate that saying “the contractor would” is not the same as showing where everything goes, and we will produce a marked-up plan for the next deadline.

Perry Hale: Sorry, I think that is exactly the difficulty. On the ground the ditch looks as if it ends at the lane, but it goes under it. When we had that very wet week last winter, the water came back across the track rather than flowing away. I have lived in Cresswick for over 40 years and I have not seen anyone lift the cover to check it. I am not offering myself as a drainage engineer. I am asking whether the calculation includes a blocked culvert, because it does block.

Inspector Mara Venn: That is a clear question. Can the applicant point us to a blockage allowance in DCO-DR-07?

Tamsin Alder: Not to a line number at this moment. I can take that away. The hydraulic model includes an exceedance route, but I do not want to suggest that it answers the particular blocked-culvert scenario until the drainage team checks. The drawing should distinguish the existing culvert from the proposed swale. They are quite close on the small-scale plan.

June Marr: May I come in there? My home is 11 Lantern Fold, Cresswick, CW4 8LN, immediately below the lane. I am 69 and I cannot be expected to shift heavy boards across the door every time somebody predicts rain. That isn't a request for the applicant to buy boards. I want to know who watches the temporary drainage on a Sunday, when the compound is shut. The last flood left mud in the kitchen. It has made me anxious whenever I hear rain overnight, although I know that isn't a measurement for your assessment.

Inspector Mara Venn: We can record that experience. Please do not feel you have to establish the engineering mechanism yourself. Is your question about inspection frequency, or about the person residents can contact if an obstruction is seen?

June Marr: Both, really. The number on the leaflet just rings out. I also need to correct something I said in my written note. Dorian Vetch, who lives next door, was convicted of criminal damage after breaking a culvert gate in 2019. I mentioned it because people keep saying that gate was never touched. But that isn't why the water came into my house, and I don't know whether the proposed works alter it. Please don't take it as a drainage survey.

Inspector Mara Venn: Understood. We do not need to explore a neighbour's history to answer the drainage question. We will concentrate on the physical condition of the culvert and the proposed monitoring. For the record, I have not made any finding about the cause of the earlier flooding.

Tamsin Alder: I agree with that approach. The applicant can confirm whether a pre-commencement CCTV inspection of the culvert is feasible and, if so, how defects would be dealt with before soil is stripped. The proposed community contact will be a staffed number during active works, with an out-of-hours route for flooding reports. I would rather put the actual protocol before the examination than improvise one aloud today.

Perry Hale: Could the plan show the outlet as well? On the version I was sent, the arrow points towards Orchard Brake and then stops. Badger setts have been reported in Orchard Brake, but I am not asking for anybody to publish their exact positions. I am asking whether a blocked outlet sends water along the footpath or towards the houses. Those are not the same thing.

Inspector Mara Venn: Yes. Show the receiving point and the exceedance direction, without disclosing protected-species locations. I have a note that Cllr Iona Quill asked earlier whether the parish had been sent the revised drawing. The applicant should answer that in the same written response, with the date and version actually supplied, not just a statement that consultation took place.

Tamsin Alder: We can do that. The ecology and drainage drawings can be overlaid at an appropriate scale for the examination, with sensitive ecological detail withheld from the public copy. On monitoring, the site supervisor's checklist is proposed to include the ditch before and after forecast heavy rain. We need to specify who signs the checklist and where the record is kept.

Nell Bracken of Harrowfield Acoustic Services: I appreciate this is the drainage item, but can I clarify that the proposed pump shown beside the settlement tank is temporary? The noise table assumed operation in daylight only. If the drainage answer now assumes pumping overnight, the noise table will need revisiting. I have not modelled an overnight pump at Lantern Fold.

Inspector Mara Venn: That is useful, thank you. It is precisely why the written answer must set out a workable sequence rather than separate assurances from different disciplines. We will record three actions: the blocked-culvert test, the marked-up drainage and exceedance plan, and the inspection and contact protocol, including any implications for overnight pumping. June Marr, does that capture what you need answered?

June Marr: Yes. A drawing I can read and a number that works would be a start. I don't expect anyone to promise there will never be another flood.

Inspector Mara Venn: Thank you. We will leave the residential drainage point there for now and turn to the wider construction sequence. Tamsin Alder, could Fenmere Link Energy Ltd explain how the haul route shown on the revised construction plan relates to the traffic assessment? The plan appears to put the eastern compound into use before the temporary access from Merebank Road is complete.

Tamsin Alder: Yes. The intention is that the first deliveries are limited to fencing, welfare units and materials for the access itself. Those vehicles would use the existing field entrance from Merebank Road. Bulk deliveries, including stone for the internal tracks, would not start until the temporary access and its visibility splays had been installed. I accept that the note on Sheet C-12 says “compound operational” rather than “compound establishment”. That wording is too broad and we will correct it.

Inspector Mara Venn: Does the traffic model distinguish those two stages, or has everything been assigned to one peak construction month?

Tamsin Alder: The assessment tests a peak week for the main build and a separate, lower establishment period. Its junction counts include the stone deliveries in the peak week, not in the establishment period. The revised programme should make that distinction visible without requiring somebody to work backwards from the transport appendix.

Inspector Mara Venn: I would like the written answer to include a table with the maximum daily two-way movements for each phase, the assumed working days and the access used. Please distinguish heavy goods vehicles from light vehicles. The authority needs to be able to compare the limits in the construction traffic management plan with the numbers assessed at the Merebank Road junction.

Tamsin Alder: Understood. We will also align the terminology in the transport assessment and the outline management plan. At present one document calls the activity “site preparation” and the other calls it “early works”, which is not helpful.

Inspector Mara Venn: It is not. On routing, the swept-path drawing shows vehicles approaching from the west, but the draft plan merely says drivers should avoid Cresswick centre where practicable. Is the western approach proposed as a binding route or just an assumption in the model?

Tamsin Alder: A binding route for heavy goods vehicles. The words “where practicable” were intended to deal with road closures, not to offer a routine alternative. We can specify the approved diversion process, with a record of the closure and prior agreement before the alternative is used. Light vehicles are not assigned to that route in the same way.

Inspector Mara Venn: Please make that clear, and do not use a management-plan provision to change an assessed route without explaining the environmental consequences. Turning to landscape, Sheet L-08 shows a planted bund along the northern edge. In the cross-section it is three metres high, whereas the landscape schedule specifies two metres. Which is the design the assessment relies on?

Tamsin Alder: The cross-section is correct for the central section beside the inverter area. The two-metre figure applies to the lower sections near the drainage swales. We will add chainages and levels to the drawing so the change in height is identifiable. The visual assessment used the three-metre profile centrally and the lower profile at either end; it did not assume a continuous three-metre embankment.

Inspector Mara Venn: And the planting on that bund is described as providing screening at year five. What happens in the earlier years? I am asking about the physical assessment, not whether the scheme is acceptable overall.

Tamsin Alder: In years one to four the bund provides the principal screening of the low equipment. The planting adds seasonal filtering but is not treated as opaque. The photomontage set contains both the opening-year and year-five views, though the viewing-point key on the submitted plan is out of date. We will provide a corrected key and confirm the camera positions used for the revised images.

Inspector Mara Venn: That correction should be separately identified, please. I do not want a replacement drawing uploaded without an explanation of what has changed. On drainage, is the bund included in the surface-water model? It seems capable of redirecting runoff towards the western swale.

Tamsin Alder: It is included in the proposed-ground model. Runoff from the bund drains through the planted shoulder into the adjacent swale; there is no pipe taking that water directly to the outfall. The calculation uses the completed ground levels. During construction, before the shoulder is established, temporary check dams and a silt fence are proposed. We need to add those controls to the phasing diagram discussed earlier.

Inspector Mara Venn: Yes. The permanent model and the temporary works must not be presented as though they cover the same condition. Does the swale retain its design storage if the maintenance track crosses it at chainage 420?

Tamsin Alder: The crossing is a short culverted section. The storage calculation excludes its footprint and includes the upstream and downstream swale reaches. The drawing presently marks the culvert size but not the invert levels; those will be added to the marked-up drainage plan. We will also confirm that the crossing does not create a low point outside the designated exceedance route.

Inspector Mara Venn: Finally, on policy compliance, the draft planning statement says the design minimises permanent hardstanding. Please check that claim against the latest compound layout. The permanent turning area appears larger on Sheet C-12 than in the area schedule.

Tamsin Alder: That is a fair point. The area schedule predates the turning revision. We will update the figure, identify the permeable and impermeable parts separately, and show whether the change affects the runoff calculation or the land-use assessment. I would rather give one reconciled figure than ask the Examining Authority to choose between drawings.

Inspector Mara Venn: Thank you. The action is a reconciled phase table, routing provision, landscape levels and visual key, temporary drainage controls, and an updated hardstanding schedule. The written response should cross-refer to the blocked-culvert test already requested. We will take a short pause before considering the draft requirements.

[Hearing resumed at 11.42 am]

Inspector Mara Venn: We are back on the record. The next item is the draft requirements. I want to keep this fairly practical. The action list before the pause dealt with information still to be supplied; it did not mean that every matter can simply be left to a later approval. Could the applicant explain which construction details would be secured before works start in each phase?

Tamsin Alder: For Fenmere Link Energy Ltd, the intention is that Requirement 7 would require a construction environmental management plan for the relevant phase. That plan would include the drainage measures, wheel-cleaning arrangements, dust controls and the haul-route drawing. We accept that the current draft says “substantially in accordance with” the outline plan without identifying which drawings are controlling. A revised draft can list them, while allowing detailed dimensions to be agreed within the limits of deviation.

Inspector Mara Venn: How would that work for the western access? The transport assessment models vehicles entering from Merewick Road, but drawing FL-TR-024 shows the temporary gate set back from the carriageway. Is the queue storage measured from the gate or from the highway boundary?

Tamsin Alder: From the gate in the model. The drawing shows approximately 38 metres between the highway boundary and the gate, though the swept-path sheet uses an older gate position. We need to reconcile those sheets. The maximum arrival rate in the peak construction hour is 22 heavy goods vehicles, not 22 in each direction. We will put that plainly in the response because the table heading is misleading.

Inspector Mara Venn: And the assessment of the junction with Lantern Lane assumes the eastern compound is active at the same time?

Tamsin Alder: Yes, for the busiest six-week construction scenario. That is a conservative combination, although the programme shows the eastern cable works finishing earlier. We do not ask the Examining Authority to rely on that programme to reduce the assessed traffic. The revised phase table will show the overlap assumed in the model and the overlap proposed for construction management.

Inspector Mara Venn: Turning to landscape, Requirement 10 refers to the landscape and ecological management plan. I cannot presently tell whether replacement planting lost during cable repair would fall within the five-year establishment period or start a fresh period. What is intended?

Tamsin Alder: A fresh five-year period for any replacement planting. We can say so in the requirement. We will also check that the maintenance drawing uses the same hedge lengths as the landscape masterplan. There is a difference of about 140 metres near Ashen Mere, apparently because one sheet includes an existing hedgerow. The project is not proposing to remove that length.

Inspector Mara Venn: Thank you. The viewpoint schedule also needs to distinguish an existing view from a photomontage. At viewpoint LV-09, the proposed bund is visible in the wireline but appears to disappear behind vegetation in the year-one illustration. Please give us the assumed bund crest level and the planting height used for that illustration.

Tamsin Alder: We will. The crest is designed to follow the existing field edge rather than form a level platform, so a single height may not describe it adequately. We can provide chainages and spot levels, together with a section through the highest part. The year-one planting depiction should not imply mature screening.

Inspector Mara Venn: On drainage, the outline strategy proposes an infiltration trench beside the battery compound, but the ground investigation describes variable permeability. Is the trench a necessary part of the design, or one option subject to testing?

Tamsin Alder: One option. The impermeable area has been included in the runoff calculations irrespective of whether infiltration proves feasible. If the detailed testing rules it out, the design would route that flow to the lined attenuation basin. We propose a requirement that prohibits discharge from the compound until the detailed scheme, including the outfall and exceedance route, has been approved. We will provide calculations for both cases rather than leaving the fallback as a sentence in the strategy.

Inspector Mara Venn: Please include the blocked-culvert test in both cases. The concern is not only the water level within the application boundary. The drawings should show where water would go if the crossing beneath Merewick Road could not pass the design flow, and whether the temporary construction drainage changes that route.

Tamsin Alder: Agreed. The temporary arrangement will be drawn separately. The existing ditch will remain open until the diversion is functioning; that sequence can be secured in the phase plan. We will identify the inspection point on the drawing as well, without relying on an undefined commitment to “regular monitoring”.

Inspector Mara Venn: Finally, policy compliance. The planning statement cites the Fenmere Development Framework 2042 as support for low-carbon infrastructure, but its landscape policy also requires effects on the Ashen Mere corridor to be minimised. The updated statement should address both limbs. It is not enough to cite the favourable paragraph and refer us elsewhere for the qualification.

Tamsin Alder: Understood. We will provide a short policy matrix linking each relevant provision to the assessment chapter and the proposed mitigation. Where the conclusion depends on the revised levels or drainage figures, the matrix will say that expressly. We expect to submit the consolidated response by the deadline in the examination timetable.

Inspector Mara Venn: Thank you. Those are actions, not findings. We will now move to the next item.

text:
21 October 2026

From: Rowan Fenwick
Fenwick Bench & Joinery
17 Cinderbank Lane, Larchmere, LM4 8QT
Tel: 07700 814632
Email: rowan.fenwick@fenwickbench.example
Interested Party reference: IP-403971

To the Examining Authority
Merevale Bypass and Freight Link

Dear Inspectors,

I am a self-employed joiner working from home. Please take this as my objection to the construction traffic arrangements proposed by Merevale Corridor Ltd, particularly the use of Cinderbank Lane for deliveries to the eastern compound. I support getting heavy traffic out of Larchmere in the long run. My objection is to the way the works would put heavy vehicles onto a lane that is barely wide enough for two cars now.

My workshop is behind our house. Customers collect finished doors and cabinets from the front, and I take materials in with my van, registration QV26 JLX. I cannot simply tell people to use another entrance: there is only one. The traffic management plan shows the lane as a suitable route because it is marked as a through road. That is correct on a map, but it misses the pinch point beside the old pump wall and the bend at Bracken Ford. A lorry coming round that bend occupies most of the road. Drivers already mount the verge when they meet my van.

The applicant says deliveries will normally take place between 07:00 and 19:00. Those are the hours when I work and when most customers call. Even a short closure can leave a collection stranded on my drive or prevent me getting to a fitting job. I have worked in this area for more than 20 years and am used to ordinary farm traffic; this is not an objection to every vehicle bigger than a car. The difference is the proposed number of movements, day after day, and the lack of anywhere safe to wait.

There is also a practical issue with the swept-path drawing, which I raised at the September consultation event. It appears to assume that the verge opposite my entrance can be driven over. That verge is soft after rain and has a ditch immediately behind it. I would like the applicant to provide a drawing based on a site visit, not just another line drawn over an aerial photograph. If cones are put along the edge, please show where a delivery van is meant to pass a construction lorry. Saying that drivers will be courteous is not a traffic plan.

My daughter, Pippa Fenwick, aged 14, waits near the lane for the school minibus. She has diagnosed asthma, and I am concerned about dust from vehicles stopping and starting outside the house. I am not suggesting the scheme caused that condition. I am asking for a proper dust-control commitment and a safe, signed waiting place during the works. The noise and uncertainty are already causing stress and poor sleep in our household. Those feelings are real, although they are not the main basis of my objection.

Mrs Elin Voss, who lives further along the lane and is not making a representation, told me about two occasions when a delivery driver reversed towards the bend because there was no room to pass. I did not witness those incidents and cannot verify the dates. I include the account because the applicant should check how its route would work in practice, rather than treating the lane as an empty strip on a plan. Cllr Tamsin Prew also asked about passing places at the public meeting; I have not seen an answer in the updated documents.

I have read Brynna Grey’s submitted representation about access to Bracken Ford. I agree with its suggestion that the compound should be served from the new temporary haul road as early as possible. Until that road is available, large deliveries should come by the western gate, with a published exception procedure rather than an open-ended promise to avoid Cinderbank Lane ‘where practicable’. The site identified as Eastern Compound Parcel EC-4 has space for vehicles to turn within the works boundary. They should not be turning across residents’ entrances.

The environmental appendix mentions badgers in Willowbreak Wood. That is a broad location and does not, by itself, tell the Examining Authority where anything is. For the confidential ecology record, however, I have seen a badger sett under the hawthorn bank 12 metres east of Gate 3 on Cinderbank Lane. I ask that this precise detail is kept out of the public version of my letter and passed to the ecological clerk of works. I am mentioning it because widening at that gate, if proposed later, needs to be checked before anyone starts cutting back the bank.

The effect on a small business has not been assessed in any useful way. I still owe £18,400 on my workshop loan, so losing reliable access is not just an inconvenience to me. I am not asking the Examining Authority to compensate me through this letter. I want a workable arrangement before consent is granted. By contrast, the £6.2 million shown for traffic measures in the applicant’s budget is a project figure, not evidence that my entrance will remain usable.

Please require a binding construction traffic plan with a maximum vehicle size for Cinderbank Lane, an enforceable delivery timetable, a named contact available while deliveries are taking place, and advance notice of any closure. A generic inbox such as planning@merevalecorridor.example may be suitable for written comments, but somebody must also be able to deal with a lorry actually blocking the entrance. The temporary haul road should be built before regular compound deliveries begin, not described as something to be reviewed later.

Finally, please do not record my workshop address as the applicant’s suggested lay-by or as a public meeting point. It is our home as well as my place of work. I am willing to meet the traffic team on site if that helps them understand the bend. I just need a plan that works on the ground before the first convoy arrives.

Yours faithfully,

Fenwick Bench & Joinery

Technical note: transport, drainage and construction sequencing
Merevale Bypass and Freight Link

The following points concern the assumptions used in the application documents rather than the principle of providing a freight route. Fenwick Bench & Joinery asks that they be resolved through revised plans and enforceable requirements, not left to a contractor's later judgement. The main issue is that the Transport Assessment treats Cinderbank Lane as a continuous two-way route during construction. Its usable width changes markedly between the railway bridge and the proposed compound entrance. A model based on link capacity alone cannot show what happens when two large vehicles meet at the bend, or when a turning vehicle waits for a gap in traffic.

1. Traffic assessment

The junction assessment should be rerun with separate construction phases, including the period before the temporary haul road opens. The current assignment appears to place most heavy goods vehicles on Harrowmere Road, while the construction routing drawing also permits access from Cinderbank Lane. Those two assumptions need to agree. Please provide the hourly arrival and departure profiles, the proportion of articulated vehicles, the assumed delivery windows and the vehicle lengths used for swept-path analysis. Daily totals are not enough to test whether a short queue blocks the lane at a particular time. The assessment should also distinguish a regular delivery day from the busiest day of earthworks movements.

The drawings for the Cinderbank Lane access show a vehicle entering the compound, but not one leaving while another is waiting to turn in. Swept paths should cover both directions at the gate and the railway bridge, with the vehicle body and mirrors shown rather than just wheel tracks. Any passing place should be dimensioned and built before the traffic it is intended to accommodate is allowed onto the route. It should not rely on informal use of the verge. The drawing should show sightlines in both directions and make clear whether gates will be set back far enough for an arriving vehicle to wait wholly off the carriageway.

The proposed construction traffic management plan says that banksmen may be used where required. That wording does not establish where they would stand, how drivers would receive instructions, or whether opposing movements would be held while a vehicle negotiates the bend. A revised plan should mark controlled sections and specify how communication works if radio contact fails. It should also identify a place for a delivery to turn around if its booked slot is missed. Sending an unbooked lorry down the lane and hoping it can wait safely at the gate is not a workable fallback.

2. Surface water and water quality

The drainage strategy should explain how runoff from the haul road will be handled during the interval between initial earthworks and the permanent drainage installation. The permanent attenuation basin shown east of the link does not answer that question if its outlet and treatment train are not yet operating. Temporary ditches, settlement capacity, check dams and the location of any discharge point should be shown on a phase drawing. This matters particularly where the haul road crosses the shallow fall towards Merevale Brook. A method statement should give inspection triggers after heavy rain and a means of removing accumulated silt without driving plant into the watercourse margin.

The submitted calculations use a single impermeable area for the completed scheme. They should be supplemented by a sequence of calculations showing the exposed working area at each stage, including stockpiles and the compound. The applicant should confirm whether the basin remains accessible for maintenance after the landscape bund is formed. If maintenance vehicles must cross a public path, the crossing and temporary closure arrangements should be identified now. The requirements should also prevent drainage features being removed merely because a later phase is expected to provide replacement capacity; the replacement must be operating first.

3. Landscape and lighting

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment gives useful completed-scheme views from the Wickfold Roundabout approach, but the construction views do not appear to show the maximum height of stored material. A phase plan should identify the permitted stockpile zones and their maximum heights, including any temporary screening. The visual assessment should then test those limits, rather than a representative arrangement that a contractor is free to change. Planting along Harrowmere Road will take time to establish. The drawings should therefore separate the screening available on opening day from the effect predicted at year fifteen.

The proposed compound lighting is described only as task lighting. The application should provide mounting heights, aiming angles, operating hours and a drawing of spill beyond the working area. If movable columns are proposed, the management plan needs a limit that applies to them as well as to fixed fittings. An assessment using only the permanent road lighting layout would not address compound operations. The same drawing should show the relationship between lighting, retained hedgerows and the proposed ecological corridor. This is a request for a measurable lighting design, not a blanket objection to lighting needed for safe work.

4. Securing the sequence

A workable order would be: install temporary drainage and erosion controls; complete the haul road and its passing places; inspect the access and turning areas; then permit regular compound deliveries. The relevant requirement should define who approves each stage and what evidence is submitted before the next one begins. The Construction Environmental Management Plan can supply operating detail, but it should not be able to alter the approved access route or postpone essential infrastructure without further approval. Merevale Corridor Ltd should also reconcile the route drawing, traffic tables and phasing programme so that all three describe the same scheme. These are matters capable of being checked on drawings and through conditions; they need not wait for a problem to occur on Cinderbank Lane.

That sequencing is not an optional tidy-up. It is the difference between a construction plan that can be checked in advance and one that leaves residents and small businesses to report problems after lorries have started using the lane.

Further written representation on construction traffic
Merevale Bypass and Freight Link
21 October 2026

From: Rowan Fenwick, trading as Fenwick Bench & Joinery
Workshop and home address: 14 Cinderbank Lane, Larkwash, LV4 8QJ
Telephone: 07700 914682
Email: rowan.fenwick@fenwickbench.example
Interested Party reference: IP-482716

I make fitted cupboards and repair timber windows from the workshop behind my house. This is not a large yard with a separate delivery entrance. My timber comes on a medium flatbed, usually once or twice a week, and finished work goes out in my own van, registration KY26 FVW. If the proposed compound traffic uses Cinderbank Lane before the haul road is working, the drawings do not show how my supplier and an HGV are meant to pass at the bend beside the old pump house. The traffic table gives a daily total, but I need to know what can happen in the same ten minutes.

I am not asking for an exemption for my business. Other people use the lane to get to work and school, and agricultural vehicles already take time to turn through the narrow bit. I am asking the Examining Authority to require a practical plan for the construction period, not just an assurance that drivers will be told to take care. I have worked here for over 20 years and have seen what happens when a delivery driver follows a satnav rather than the route on a contractor's sheet. I am worried about the effect on my work and about poor sleep while this remains uncertain; I am not putting that forward as a medical claim.

The applicant's response says deliveries will be booked. It does not say whether a missed booking can wait safely without blocking a driveway, who tells suppliers about a route change, or where a vehicle goes if the compound gate is shut. Could the final Construction Traffic Management Plan give the gate opening hours, a holding location off the public highway and a number for reporting a vehicle in the wrong place? The number should be a staffed project line, not an individual resident's number. A daily log of HGV arrivals, departures and complaints would also make the proposed limits capable of being checked.

There is a particular problem at the workshop entrance. A vehicle turning in needs the width of the entrance clear for a short time. Last month a delivery had to reverse back towards the pump house because another vehicle came round the bend. It was awkward, not an accident. I have attached a sketch marked Workshop Access, showing the sight line and the part of the verge that is already worn. It is a sketch, not a measured highway drawing, and I would welcome a site visit before any final swept-path drawing is relied upon. The applicant should show two vehicles meeting there at the times it expects to run deliveries, rather than using an average flow across the whole day.

My daughter, Pippa Fenwick, aged 13, walks along this stretch to the school bus. Pippa Fenwick has asthma. Dust controls and a safe walking route therefore matter to our household, although the highway issue stands without that personal point. The current plan marks a pedestrian diversion but stops it at the compound entrance. It needs to say how somebody on foot gets past a queue at the gate and where the crossing point will be while the temporary drainage works are being dug. Please do not treat a banksman at the gate as a substitute for a continuous route.

I spoke with my neighbour Elin Voss about the bend. Elin Voss is not making a representation, so I am only mentioning the conversation to explain why I checked the plan again. Brynna Grey has already submitted a representation about the same missing passing-place detail; the concern is not confined to the entrance to my workshop. At the public meeting Cllr Tamsin Prew asked whether the haul road would be available before bulk excavation. The answer I heard was that the programme was still being reviewed. The requirement ought to settle that order of work, rather than leaving the answer in a later programme that the public may never see before deliveries begin.

The ecological drawings also need care when used to decide where vehicles can wait. There are badger signs in Brackenfold Wood, which is a broad observation and not a reason to stop every vehicle. I have, however, given the case team a separate note locating a sett in the bank 11 metres east of the north gate to Plot 7, immediately below the second ash tree on the southern verge of Cinderbank Lane. That position should not appear in a public traffic map. A surveyor can check it when deciding whether a proposed waiting or turning area is suitable. I have also seen bats around Brackenfold Wood at dusk, but I cannot identify a roost and am not claiming one.

For clarity, I support conditions requiring the haul road and passing places to be inspected before routine compound deliveries start; no waiting on Cinderbank Lane; a signed route for drivers; and a procedure for stopping deliveries when that route is unusable. The applicant's project mailbox, planning@merevalecorridor.example, would be a sensible place to publish the traffic plan and updates. The examination documents at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects are also accessible to people who do not use social media. I do not think a link to https://larkwash-roadwatch.example/traffic-diary, which has been passed around locally, should be treated as the approved source of instructions to drivers.

Please record this as an objection to the construction traffic arrangements as presently drafted, rather than an objection to every part of the bypass. If the route, sequence and monitoring are made enforceable before work begins, I can plan timber deliveries around them. At present I cannot tell my supplier which days or hours will be workable.

Yours faithfully,
Fenwick Bench & Joinery

Further technical points: access, drainage and construction sequencing

The request for a revised access drawing is not just a request for clearer arrows. The current construction traffic assessment for the Merevale Bypass and Freight Link assigns movements to the eastern and western compounds, but the highway capacity tables appear to combine vehicles using different entrances. That makes it difficult to test the effect of a change in route during a particular phase. Merevale Corridor Ltd should provide a table, by week and by entrance, showing forecast light vehicles, rigid vehicles and articulated vehicles separately. The table should identify peak hours as well as daily totals. An annual average conceals the short periods when excavated material and imported stone are moving at the same time.

The assessment should also distinguish vehicles serving the project from existing freight on Cinderbank Lane. Where a model assumes that construction lorries arrive outside the network peak, the associated delivery booking rule should appear in the Construction Traffic Management Plan as an enforceable measure, not merely in an explanatory note. A forecast based on staggered arrivals is of limited value if two subcontractors can book the same arrival slot. The booking system should record the authorised entrance, the load type and any rejected or diverted arrival. Weekly anonymised totals would allow the forecast and actual operation to be compared without publishing driver information.

The swept-path drawings need a further check at the temporary junction with Bent Sluice Road. The linework seems to show a long vehicle entering while a vehicle is waiting to leave, but does not show where a following vehicle would stand without blocking the running lane. This may be a drawing convention rather than a design defect. Either way, a separate plan should show the waiting position, visibility envelope and extent of any temporary verge strengthening. If the junction operates by banksman control during the earthworks phase, the assessment should model that controlled operation rather than an unrestricted priority junction. The maximum queue length matters particularly when the western compound is receiving stone for the embankment.

The traffic appendices also use different descriptions of the route past Glassmere Roundabout. One describes it as the normal delivery route; another calls it a contingency route during resurfacing. Those are materially different assumptions. The final route schedule should say which stretches are permitted for routine deliveries, which can be used only after a recorded closure, and who authorises that change. The schedule should be cross-referenced to the signs and the driver briefing. Signs alone will not resolve an inconsistency between a booking instruction and a published route plan.

On drainage, the Draft Drainage Strategy relies on temporary settlement features before the permanent swales are connected. The order of works is therefore important. It should show how runoff will be intercepted when the existing ditch is cut but the new outfall is not yet commissioned. A statement that temporary measures will be installed ‘as required’ does not specify a design standard or identify the point at which additional storage becomes necessary. The applicant should provide a phase-by-phase drainage drawing with temporary catchment boundaries, discharge points, inspection access and the proposed response if a settlement feature reaches its operating limit. These details can be submitted without tying the construction team to a single proprietary product.

The same issue arises where haul-road construction and drainage excavation overlap. Imported stone may alter the flow path before the permanent cross-drains are available. A short construction-stage water balance, including the assumptions about exposed ground and pumping, would be more useful than another description of the completed scheme. The monitoring commitment should identify what is measured and how often, rather than saying only that conditions will be checked. It should be possible to tell whether an exceedance triggers maintenance, a pause in work or a change to the temporary layout.

For landscape purposes, the planting shown beside Sallow Copse should not be treated as effective screening from the day it goes in. The Landscape and Visual Schedule appears to compare construction views with a completed landscape, but several viewpoints would face the haul road before the proposed bund is formed. A phase-specific drawing should show the sequence: clearance, temporary fencing, haul-road use, bund formation and planting. The winter view should be included, because the screening assumption is least reliable then. This is a request for a realistic construction baseline, not for a different alignment through the copse. References to bats across Sallow Copse remain appropriately general in the public version of the drawings.

The application documents should use one consistent set of phase names. At present ‘enabling works’ seems to include drainage installation in one document and exclude it in another. That difference affects both the traffic totals and the period during which temporary screening is needed. A simple phase register, with start and finish criteria rather than fixed calendar promises, could resolve it. Each assessment table could then state the phase or combination of phases it represents. Where phases may overlap, the combined worst case should be assessed instead of assuming they happen one after another.

Finally, the proposed requirements should link the approved construction documents to what happens on site. A requirement to submit a plan is not by itself a commitment to follow its vehicle limits, route restrictions or drainage triggers. The approved plan should state how a material change is recorded and what must be checked before the change takes effect. That would give the examining authority a clear basis for comparing the assessment with the scheme as built, while leaving reasonable flexibility for ordinary changes in construction method.
