text:
Relevant representation: Bexmere Fen Connector Road
Application reference: BX020014
Submitted by Avery Fenwick, 14 Thistlebank Close, Pelcross, PC4 8QT
Interested Party reference: IP-45871
Email: avery.fenwick@fenmail.example

I object to the Bexmere Fen Connector Road as currently proposed. I am not against improving the route to the industrial estate. The lorries already use the village road, and something needs doing about that. My objection is to putting the new junction, earthworks and construction compound so close to the houses at the south end of Pelcross when the assessment does not seem to reflect what it is like to live here. I ask to be registered as an interested party and to speak at any hearing about traffic or noise.

The plans call the land beside Thistlebank Close an agricultural buffer. On the ground it is the only open space between our homes and the estate. We can hear reversing alarms on still evenings even with the present arrangement. The road would move that activity nearer, not farther away. The applicant's noise figures seem to assume that an average over a whole day tells the story. It doesn't tell you about a lorry tailgate banging at half past five in the morning, or several vehicles braking at once by the proposed roundabout. The figures also appear to be taken at a point farther from the bedrooms than the nearest houses actually are. Could the Examining Authority please ask for a measurement at the end of Thistlebank Close, with the assumed night-time traffic clearly stated?

Mrs Tamsin Kelrow at 6 Wrenfold Rise, Pelcross, PC4 8QU is not making a representation, as far as I know, but asked me to explain what happened during the trial ground investigations. A drilling vehicle was parked across the pavement on two mornings, leaving people to walk in the carriageway. That is not proof that construction will always be badly managed. It does show why a promise to 'maintain pedestrian access' needs a drawing showing how it will work. My other neighbour, Eldric Venn, said the contractors gave no notice of the second visit. I mention both conversations because the access arrangements in the draft construction plan look fine on paper and rather different at the kerb.

I have been diagnosed with chronic migraine. I am not suggesting that the scheme caused it. I am worried about frequent flashing beacons and the prospect of night work close to the house, because those things can make an ordinary day much harder for me. I am stressed and sleeping badly already, which I know is not in itself evidence of a medical condition caused by the road. My daughter Liora Fenwick, aged 11, has asthma and uses a prescribed inhaler. Dust controls therefore matter to our household in a practical way, not just as a line in a management plan. Please require a named point of contact for residents and a clear procedure for stopping particularly dusty work until the problem is put right.

My mother, Edria Fenwick, lives at 2 Thistlebank Close, Pelcross, PC4 8QS. Edria Fenwick has limited mobility following a stroke and relies on the level route along the pavement to reach the bus stop. The proposed temporary diversion goes round the back of the compound, but I cannot find its gradient or surface specified anywhere. A route being technically open is no help if it is rutted, unlit or flooded. These are everyday journeys, including school trips and trips to the pharmacy, rather than occasional recreational walks.

I have lived in this area for over 40 years, and the small lanes flood more often than the drawings suggest. At the last public event, Cllr Oren Halwick asked whether the attenuation basin would still have capacity after successive wet days. I have not seen a straightforward answer. The council's offices at 1 Market Court, Pelcross, PC4 2AA are an appropriate place for a public copy of any revised drainage drawings; I do not think residents should have to search several document libraries to compare versions. The project's general enquiries address, planning@mirefordlinkways.example, is useful, but an acknowledgement is not an answer to a specific question.

There are also ecological details that deserve care. Badger setts have been identified in Bexmere Wood, and bats are regularly seen over the fields west of the village. I am not asking for every field margin to be left untouched. However, a badger sett is in the bank 8 metres east of Gate 3 on the southern edge of Lot 12, immediately behind the yellow pump housing. That location should not be circulated in an unrestricted public plan. The applicant should explain, in a suitably restricted ecology document, how the working area and vehicle movements will be kept clear of it. The draft fencing drawing does not make this obvious to a lay reader.

Our outstanding mortgage balance is £147,600, so simply moving away while construction happens is not a realistic answer for us. I mention this only because relocation has been suggested in conversation as though every household can choose it. I am not asking the Examination to assess my house value. I am asking it to assess the effects on people who will remain beside the works. The published link at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/national-infrastructure-planning-examinations explains how to make this representation, but it cannot substitute for readable local plans. I also found a report at https://pelcross-observer.example/roads/compound-questions; it raised useful questions, although I would prefer the applicant's own evidence to answer them.

Please consider moving the compound farther from homes, limiting the hours for high-noise operations, providing a properly surfaced pedestrian diversion before any closure, and monitoring dust where residents actually live. If the road is consented, those measures should be enforceable requirements, not intentions to be discussed later. I would welcome a response in plain language, particularly on the night-time assumptions and the location of the nearest monitoring point.

Avery Fenwick

Further points to my relevant representation — Bexmere Fen Connector Road

I am adding this note because, after sending my representation, I looked again at the applicant’s construction drawings. I remain opposed to the Bexmere Fen Connector Road as currently proposed. My earlier request for a plain-language response was not meant to suggest that a leaflet alone would resolve the problems. The location of the compound, the loss of a safe walking route and the uncertainty about night working need changes to the scheme, not better wording around it.

The drawings appear to put the temporary compound on the land between the proposed road and Wrenfold Rise. On a plan it looks like spare space. From the houses it is the open gap that currently separates people from activity on that land. The plan shows a fence but gives no useful picture of the lighting, generators, vehicle movements or where materials will be stacked. I do not think residents should have to wait for a later contractor’s plan to find out whether lights will face bedroom windows. If that location is retained, there should be a binding layout showing where the noisy equipment will go and a limit on use outside normal daytime hours.

Mrs Tamsin Kelrow, who lives on Wrenfold Rise, asked me whether the compound gate would be used before 7 am. Mrs Kelrow is not making a representation, as far as I know, and I am mentioning the question because I could not answer it from the material provided. The drawings show an access, but the wording about deliveries seems to allow exceptions without saying how often. Eldric Venn also pointed out that the proposed wheel-wash exit is close to the bend where walkers cross to the bus stop. Neither neighbour should have to rely on informal assurances about a gate that could operate for months.

The pedestrian diversion needs the same level of detail as the road itself. My daughter, Liora Fenwick, is 11 and uses the path towards Pelcross most school mornings. The alternative indicated by arrows on the map appears to send walkers beside an unlit drainage ditch and then across the compound access. I have walked it after rain; part of it was mud rather than a usable path. I am not asking for the current route to stay open during unsafe construction work. I am asking for a surfaced, lit alternative, with the crossing in place and inspected before the existing path is closed. A statement that the contractor will ‘seek to maintain access’ is not enough.

There is also a health reason why advance notice matters in our household. I have diagnosed asthma, and dust from prolonged dry-weather works can make it difficult for me to be outside. That does not mean construction must stop whenever it is windy. It means the applicant should specify what equipment will measure dust, what level triggers action and who residents can contact when a visible cloud reaches the houses. A monitor at the far side of the site would not show what is happening at the nearest gardens. The general statement that the works may affect wellbeing is not a substitute for a response to this practical point.

My mother, Edria Fenwick, lives at 18 Thistlebank Close, Pelcross, PC4 7QN. Edria has rheumatoid arthritis and cannot easily take a long diversion to reach the bus. I give that address only to show why the proposed replacement stop and crossing matter to an actual journey; please do not treat it as consent to publish a household contact address. The transport plans should show the walking distance during each construction stage, not merely the final position of the stops. They should also explain what happens if the permanent footway is finished later than the carriageway.

I agree with Cllr Oren Halwick’s question about where water from the new hard surface will go in a heavy storm. The reply circulated after the meeting discussed the design standard, but I could not find a drawing showing what happens if the ditch beside the diversion is already full. This is not an allegation about anyone’s conduct. It is a request for a drawing that ordinary residents can check against the ground. I have lived in Pelcross for 40+ years and remember water sitting across the lower path, although I cannot give the exact dates.

I am concerned about wildlife as well, but want to distinguish what I know from what I have heard. Badgers have been seen in Harker Wood, and people have mentioned bats along the tree line. Those are broad locations and do not establish where any breeding or resting site is. On a walk last week I noticed fresh spoil beside the northern drainage grip, precisely 12 metres east of the second timber stile on Footpath 6; the entrance under the hawthorn there appears to be an active badger sett. I ask the Examining Authority to pass that observation to the ecology team without placing its exact position on a public map. Proper survey work, rather than guesses from residents, should inform any protective measures.

I have seen the applicant’s project updates at https://bexmerefenconnector.example/updates, but the latest page does not answer the question about night-time assumptions. The Planning Inspectorate guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects-examination-of-applications explains the examination process, not the proposed working hours on our street. Please ask Mireford Linkways Ltd for one consolidated schedule stating which activities may happen at night, the maximum number of nights, the noise limit at the nearest homes and the procedure for notifying residents. A generic mailbox such as enquiries@bexmerefenconnector.example would be useful for reporting problems, provided somebody is required to respond.

I still feel anxious about what the works may mean for daily life, especially if the compound and path closure overlap. That feeling is not evidence of an impact by itself. The drawings, proposed access and missing construction details are why I object. I ask that the scheme be changed before consent, or that enforceable requirements settle these matters before any relevant works begin.

Avery Fenwick

Addendum to my relevant representation — Bexmere Fen Connector Road

I am sending this addendum because I realised after submitting my earlier comments that the access drawings do not show what happens to people who use the footpath in the evening. Please read it with my representation, not as support for any part of the current scheme. I live at 18 Brackenfold Terrace, Pelcross, PX4 7QJ, and the route past Parcel BF-14, Fenedge Lane is the way I normally walk to the shops. The application reference on the notices is BFCR/2026/04. I have lived in Pelcross for over 30 years, but I cannot tell from the plans whether a pedestrian would be sent along the carriageway or turned back at the compound gate.

The diversion line on the plan looks straightforward when seen from above. On the ground there is a narrow bend where two people cannot comfortably pass, and there is no street lighting after the last house. It is no answer to say residents can use another route without saying which one will be kept open, how it will be signed and who will check the signs after dark. If a temporary path is proposed, its width, surface and drainage should be fixed before the existing route is closed. Please also show where a person with a pushchair or mobility aid would wait while construction vehicles turn. I do not think that can safely be left to the contractor's discretion.

Mrs Tamsin Kelrow, at 7 Wrenfold Rise, Pelcross, PX4 1NT, told me she had not understood that the compound entrance could operate before the permanent junction was finished. She is not making a representation and I have not asked her to. I mention the conversation only because the same confusion is likely for others reading the summary leaflet. Eldric Venn, another neighbour who is not taking part, pointed out that the leaflet marks the path closure but gives no start or finish date. I cannot verify a date either. Please require a notice at both ends of the path before each closure, with a telephone contact for someone who can actually deal with a blocked route, rather than another general assurance that access will be maintained.

This affects our family in quite ordinary ways, as well as through the noise issue I raised before. My 11-year-old daughter, Liora Fenwick, walks with me on that path on some school afternoons. I am not asking the Examining Authority to design a school route for one child; I am asking it to check that the proposed alternative is usable by families throughout the works. My mother, Edria Fenwick, lives at 12 Thistlebank Close, Pelcross, PX4 2LM. She has rheumatoid arthritis and sometimes joins us for the shorter part of the walk. A longer route with an uneven verge would not be an equivalent replacement for her. A drawing showing the temporary surfacing and crossing points would allow residents to comment on something definite.

I also want to be clear about my own health because my previous comments may have sounded like a general complaint about feeling worried. I have been diagnosed with chronic migraine, and interrupted sleep can make an episode more likely for me. That is why the proposed possibility of night-time movements matters personally, although the planning question remains whether the limits and monitoring are adequate for all nearby homes. I have had poor sleep since reading the construction information; that is how I feel, not a separate medical diagnosis. My objection does not depend on the ExA accepting my account of an individual illness. It depends on the applicant giving measurable limits and explaining what happens when they are exceeded.

At the parish drop-in, Cllr Oren Halwick asked where water from the temporary haul road would go during heavy rain. I thought it was a fair question. The reply referred to the permanent road drainage, which is a different matter. The ditch beside the path already holds water after a downpour, and tracking mud across the entrance could make the bend slippery even if no property floods. Mireford Linkways Ltd should provide a construction drainage drawing and say who will inspect the ditch. I do not say the applicant has ignored drainage deliberately; I say the documents do not let a resident see how this particular stage of work will be managed.

There is an ecology point which I hesitate to put in a public letter, but the location needs to be checked against the surveys. I have seen signs of badgers in Wisp Alder Wood, which is only a broad area and may tell the surveyors nothing new. More specifically, the badger sett entrance is 12 metres east of the southern stile on Footpath 9, in the bank immediately behind the third willow. I ask that this detail be handled carefully rather than reproduced on a public diversion map. I am not an ecologist and cannot say whether the entrance is active. A short note from the applicant's ecologist explaining whether the compound fence or temporary lighting has been checked against the survey would be more helpful than another general statement about protected species.

Finally, the map linked from the residents' notice at https://pelcross-pathnotes.example/map is not an examination document as far as I can see. It may be out of date, which is one more reason for the applicant to publish a single, dated plan through the examination library. A generic contact such as enquiries@bexmerefenconnector.example is useful for day-to-day questions, but it should not replace clear drawings or an enforceable requirement. Please send any acknowledgement to avery.fenwick@example.net, or telephone me on 07700 900 482 if clarification is needed. My Interested Party reference is IP-482617. I remain opposed to consent on the information presently available, while being willing to comment on a properly specified diversion, drainage plan and night-working schedule.

Supplementary technical points — Bexmere Fen Connector Road

The following points concern the adequacy of the submitted design and assessments. They do not depend on individual circumstances. Mireford Linkways Ltd should provide a consistent set of drawings and model outputs before the effects of the scheme can be judged reliably. Several documents describe the same junction or drainage feature at different levels of detail, and it is not always clear which drawing controls where the text and plans differ.

Traffic and junction operation

The transport assessment reports average peak-hour delay at the proposed D1 junction with Marshgate Road, but gives less attention to the longest queues predicted within each model run. An average can conceal a short period during which a queue reaches the preceding access. The applicant should provide maximum and 95th-percentile queues for each arm, separately for the opening year and design year, with the modelled storage lengths shown on the junction drawing. The results should distinguish construction traffic from ordinary traffic rather than assuming that both occur in the same proportions throughout the works. A sensitivity test with a higher proportion of heavy vehicles is needed because the construction programme itself anticipates concentrated deliveries of aggregate.

The assignment of traffic to Fenbank Lane is also uncertain. The assessment treats the lane mainly as a local access route, while the proposed connector could make it an attractive alternative when Marshgate Road is delayed. The submitted select-link diagram should be supplemented by turning movements at the Fenbank Lane junction and an explanation of how the route-choice assumptions were calibrated. If the model predicts little reassignment, the reason should be stated, not simply left in the software output. A clear account of the assumed speed limits, junction priorities and any banned turns is necessary for that comparison.

Construction phasing

Drawing C-214 shows a temporary haul connection east of the D1 junction, whereas the construction narrative refers to a western access during the first earthworks phase. The two arrangements have different implications for vehicle turning and for the length of temporary carriageway required. A single phase plan should show which access is open in each month, the direction of haul movements, and the point at which the permanent junction becomes available. It should also identify any periods when the existing Marshgate Road footway is closed. A commitment to sign a diversion is not enough without a drawing demonstrating that the diversion is continuous and can be used while deliveries are taking place.

The construction traffic figures are presented as daily totals. For highway management, the likely busiest hour matters more. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should therefore set a maximum hourly number of heavy-vehicle movements at each access and explain how compliance will be recorded. It should say where vehicles wait if they arrive before their booked slot; waiting on the public highway should not be treated as an unplanned overflow arrangement. These limits need to be requirements or secured plan commitments, rather than examples of what the contractor might choose to do.

Landscape and lighting

The visual assessment illustrates the finished road after planting has matured, but the first winter after opening is likely to be materially different. The assessment should include an opening-year winter view from the public path across Bexmere Fen, using the same viewpoint and field of view as the submitted summer visualisation. The proposed earth bund appears higher on the section drawing than on the illustrative landscape plan. Its crest level, slopes and planting depth should be stated in one schedule so that visibility and land-take can be checked against the same design.

Lighting is described as limited to junction safety, yet the lighting plan does not show a calculated spill contour beyond the highway boundary. A contour plan and the assumed mounting heights would make it possible to assess the effect of the D1 junction lighting separately from temporary lighting during construction. The final choice of fittings may be left to detailed design, but maximum height, operating hours and a measurable limit on spill should be fixed now. Without those parameters, the assessment of the unlit fen edge is only an aspiration.

Drainage and flood risk

The drainage strategy relies on attenuation beside the road embankment. Its drawings should show the usable storage volume, not just the excavated basin volume, because freeboard and permanent water reduce the space available during a storm. The calculation should identify the assumed outfall level and test the case in which the receiving ditch is already high. There is also a discrepancy between the drainage schedule and drawing D-108 over the position of the maintenance access. This should be resolved before land requirements are finalised.

The stated exceedance route follows the road verge towards Fenbank Lane. It is not apparent where water goes once it reaches the lane or whether the temporary construction layout obstructs that route. An annotated level plan, with arrows and spot levels at the low points, would be more useful than a general statement that flows remain within the highway corridor. Maintenance responsibility for the ditch, flow-control chamber and attenuation basin should be assigned in the draft requirements, with access available without closing a traffic lane wherever practicable.

Ecology and document control

The ecological documents refer generally to bats and badgers around Bexmere Fen. These broad references do not identify a protected site and need not appear on public plans at a more precise scale. The technical issue is whether the proposed dark corridor, planting and drainage margins will remain effective after construction. The monitoring plan should specify measurable outcomes and a response if they are not achieved, rather than promising a review with no action threshold.

Finally, the commitments scattered between the transport assessment, drainage strategy and outline management plans should be brought into one numbered schedule. Each item should identify the drawing or plan to be approved, the stage at which approval is required, and the body responsible for checking it. That would make the scheme described in the assessments match the scheme that could actually be built. Until those points are resolved, the present technical material does not demonstrate that the connector's construction and operational effects have been adequately controlled.

Relevant representation: Bexmere Fen Connector Road

I am writing as a resident of Pelcross to object to the application by Mireford Linkways Ltd in its present form. I understand why a safer route for through traffic is wanted. My objection is that the route now put forward moves too much of the risk and disturbance onto the houses and paths at the edge of the village. The technical commitments also need to be made enforceable, as explained above. I ask to be registered as an Interested Party so that I can comment on any revised plans.

The traffic figures do not describe what it is like at the Wrenfold Rise junction at school time. Cars already wait across the pedestrian crossing when drivers cannot see a gap. The proposed change to the junction mouth looks small on a drawing, but it will bring turning vehicles closer to the footway used by children going to the bus stop. My daughter, Liora Fenwick, aged 11, uses that route. The crossing assessment ought to cover an ordinary wet weekday, not only the modelled average hour. I am not saying that every journey will become impossible; I am saying that a child should not have to judge whether a lorry is about to turn across the pavement.

I have spoken to Mrs Tamsin Kelrow, who lives at 6 Wrenfold Rise, Pelcross, PX4 7RH and is not taking part in this examination. That house faces the proposed construction access. Mrs Kelrow's concern is that the access drawing shows a clear sightline by assuming the verge is kept cut back, while the construction programme says little about who will maintain it. Eldric Venn, another neighbour who is not submitting comments, has pointed out that delivery vans sometimes stop opposite the junction. Those conversations are not survey evidence, but they explain why the applicant should test the junction as it is actually used. Neither neighbour has asked me to speak for them.

Noise needs the same attention. The assessment gives annual and daytime averages, but the loudest events for us are individual vehicles accelerating out of the bend. A barrier that reduces the average may still leave bedrooms exposed when vehicles are highest above the road level. Please require a plan showing the final road height, barrier ends and the likely sound level at the nearest upper-floor windows. There should be a way to correct the barrier if monitoring finds it does not perform as predicted, not just a report placed on a website. I feel anxious about the prospect of night works and have had broken sleep while trying to understand the changing drawings. Those feelings are real, although they are not a substitute for proper noise measurements.

There is a more particular reason I need the construction arrangements to be clear. I have been diagnosed with chronic migraine, and bright temporary lighting directed towards our windows can bring on attacks. I do not ask the Examining Authority to decide my care. I ask it to require downward-facing lights, a stated switch-off time where safety permits, and advance notice of any exception. My mother, Edria Fenwick, lives at 14 Thistlebank Close, Pelcross, PX4 8LT and has rheumatoid arthritis. On days when walking is difficult, the current short route to the bus stop matters. A diversion that is described only as ‘temporary’ could make that journey substantially longer. Please put the proposed pedestrian diversions and their maximum durations into the construction plan before consent, rather than leaving them to a contractor.

The ecological material also needs to be handled carefully. I have seen badger signs in Alderhook Wood, but I cannot tell from signs alone which routes the animals use. During a site walk I was shown a sett in the bank 12 metres east of the northern stile on Footpath 9, immediately below the split ash. That precise location should not be published in an unrestricted version of my comments. My broader point is that the fencing and culvert design should be settled before vegetation is removed. It would not help to promise a wildlife passage and then discover that its approaches are blocked by the drainage works. I have also heard bats in the wider wood; that is not a claim that I have located a maternity roost.

Cllr Oren Halwick asked at the village meeting who would check the drainage outfall after the first winter. I thought it was a fair question. In the application documents I can find several bodies named as consultees, but no simple statement of who receives a complaint, who investigates and how quickly a blocked outfall must be cleared. The same applies to mud on the road during construction. The applicant should provide one public contact route, such as connector@mirefordlinkways.example, and keep a dated record of reports and actions. A project mailbox is more useful than asking residents to find an individual contractor who may have left the site.

I have lived in this area for over 40 years, and I know that local recollection does not replace measured evidence. It should, however, help the Examining Authority identify where the measurements and enforceable requirements are missing. The proposal could be improved by a safer crossing design, fixed limits on the pedestrian diversion, lighting and noise controls, and a numbered schedule stating who checks each drainage and ecological measure. I would welcome revisions that deal with those points. At present I cannot support the order as drafted. Please acknowledge this representation and send examination correspondence to avery.fenwick@example.test; I do not consent to that address appearing in the published copy.

Avery Fenwick

Further to my representation, I object to the Bexmere Fen Connector Road in its present form. Mrs Tamsin Kelrow, who lives on Wrenfold Rise, has described standing water after heavy rain. Eldric Venn has raised the same concern with me. Neither is making a submission, so I ask the Examining Authority to consider the drainage evidence rather than treating our accounts as survey results.

My daughter Liora Fenwick, aged 11, uses the crossing by the proposed works to reach the school bus. The suggested diversion is not clear on the plans. My mother, Edria Fenwick, lives at 7 Thistlebank Close, Pelcross, PX4 8NL and has rheumatoid arthritis; a longer walk to the bus stop would be difficult. I have asthma and am concerned about construction dust. I am also worried and sleeping badly, though I recognise that is not itself evidence of an air-quality breach.

Cllr Oren Halwick asked about drainage. Mireford Linkways Ltd should answer that point and clarify how it will assess badger activity across Bexmere Fen.

Avery Fenwick
