text:
To the Examining Authority
Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO
Examination reference: BW/NSIP/2026/04

From: Mara Fenwick
Address: 17 Marshbell Close, Bellwick, QZ4 7LP
Email: mara.fenwick@example.invalid
Interested Party reference: IP-048271

Subject: Air quality and health representation

I am writing as a resident of Bellwick, rather than as a medical expert. I support better rail connections in principle, but I object to the current construction arrangements for the Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO. My main concern is the amount of dust and vehicle exhaust that could reach homes along Marshbell Close while the access road and depot are built. The application documents discuss average readings across the wider area. They do not, to my mind, explain clearly enough what happens on a still morning when lorries are queuing near the end of our road.

I have been diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma and chronic migraine. I use a salbutamol inhaler when my breathing becomes difficult and take Nerivol tablets for migraine prevention. These are existing conditions; I am not claiming that the proposed scheme caused them. I mention them because an assessment that says the average effect will be small does not tell me whether I will be able to open a window, walk to the bus stop or spend time outside during particular parts of the work. I have spoken to my clinician about managing symptoms, but that is not a substitute for controlling emissions at source. I am especially worried about repeated short periods of poor air quality, which may be missed if monitoring is reported only as monthly averages.

My son, Kit Fenwick, is 11 and has autism spectrum disorder. Busy traffic, reversing alarms and changes to the usual route are already difficult to manage. The child receives occupational therapy, and we try to keep the school journey predictable. I do not ask the Examining Authority to treat a diagnosis as proof that the project is unacceptable. I ask that the likely effects on people with different needs are considered when the traffic management plan is settled. A diversion shown as a few extra minutes on a map can mean a much longer and more distressing trip for our household, particularly if the route changes without notice.

At present, the walk to the bus stop takes us past the proposed construction entrance at The Lantern Yard. On the plans, the temporary haul road appears close to the pavement for part of that stretch. I would like to know where the boundary fence will be, whether wheel-washing will operate before vehicles reach the public road, and who will check for dust outside working hours. Saying that a contractor will follow good practice is not quite the same as identifying a person or team responsible for responding when residents report a problem. Please make the complaint route easy to find without requiring people to search through the full construction environmental management plan.

I felt anxious after reading the air quality chapter, and poor sleep has made it harder to put this response together. Those are descriptions of how I feel, not claims of a new medical diagnosis. Other neighbours have said they worry about dirty windows and the smell of diesel. I am not providing their names or speaking for them. My concern is that a series of individually short episodes could still make ordinary daily life difficult, even where an annual limit is predicted to be met. I would welcome a plain-English explanation of how the applicant has assessed those episodes, including the assumptions about the number of HGVs waiting with engines running.

The baseline monitoring location at Bellwick Library is useful, but it is on the other side of the centre from Marshbell Close. The assessment should explain why readings there are representative of homes nearest the construction entrance. If the applicant relies on modelled figures instead, please publish the inputs for vehicle movements and the dust assumptions in a form residents can understand. It would also help to say what will happen if site monitoring shows a problem: who can pause an activity, how quickly that decision can be made, and how residents will be told. A monitoring result published weeks later will not help someone deciding whether to take a child past the works that morning.

I have lived in the area for over 20 years and accept that roads and employment sites change. I am not asking for a promise that there will be no noise or dust at all. I am asking for enforceable measures at the places and times where people will encounter them. These should include covering loads, preventing idling at the entrance, using the least dusty method practicable during dry weather, and giving advance notice of major changes to pedestrian routes. If a school-time delivery restriction is not proposed, the applicant should explain why. The response line should also be available by telephone, not only through a website, as not everyone nearby is comfortable reporting problems online.

I attended the public drop-in and later read the note circulated by Cllr Olan Keswick. It was helpful to see that the question of lorry queues had been raised, but I could not find a clear answer in the application documents. I would appreciate a direct response to that point during the examination. I have also written to the project mailbox, bellwickspur@serevaletransit.invalid, about where the temporary monitoring equipment might go. That address is included here only so the case team can see which enquiry I mean; it is not my personal contact address.

Please consider requiring a monitoring point near the construction entrance, a published trigger for action when dust or pollution rises, and a regular update that explains complaints received and what was done. I would be grateful if updates used ordinary language alongside the technical figures. My comments are about the design and controls for this proposal, not about the character or intentions of the applicant, Sere Vale Transit Ltd. I want the examination to test whether the proposed safeguards will work for households nearest the site, including those managing existing health conditions.

Yours faithfully,
Mara Fenwick

Technical addendum: construction traffic, drainage and monitoring

The following points concern the assessment method rather than the circumstances of any particular household. The Environmental Statement for the Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO presents annual average traffic changes, but annual averages may conceal the short periods when construction deliveries and ordinary traffic coincide. For the bellmouth on Merefold Road, the examination should ask for hourly flows by vehicle class, not simply a daily total. The same table should distinguish the earthworks phase from track laying and depot fit-out. Without that separation, it is difficult to tell whether the proposed traffic management plan addresses the busiest weeks or a much quieter average day.

The construction programme also needs a clearer account of what happens when two activities overlap. Sere Vale Transit Ltd proposes to bring aggregate through the western entrance while utility diversions take place beside the same road. Those operations appear in separate parts of the programme, yet both could affect the available carriageway width. A drawing showing temporary lanes, delivery holding space and pedestrian routes for each overlapping phase would be more useful than a single typical arrangement. It should show how vehicles will turn without waiting on the highway and how access will be maintained if a delivery arrives while a lane closure is being moved.

The traffic assignment should be tested against the route drivers are actually likely to use. The Construction Traffic Route Plan names the Arven Bypass as the preferred approach, but the model output does not make clear whether its journey-time assumptions include the signal delay at Larchmere Junction. If that delay has been omitted, the comparison with the shorter route through Bellwick could be misleading. The applicant should provide the link and turning-flow inputs for both routes, the assumed signal timings and a sensitivity test with longer queues. This is not a request for a different preferred route; it is a request to show that the preferred route remains credible when conditions are less favourable.

A related point is the treatment of abnormal deliveries. The transport chapter says these will be managed by prior arrangement, which does not explain their interaction with ordinary construction movements. The examination should establish the maximum number of large deliveries on any one day, whether they can coincide with peak earthworks traffic, and what happens if a delivery is delayed. A commitment to avoid the morning and evening peaks needs an enforceable definition of those periods. Otherwise the commitment could be interpreted differently when the detailed contractor programme is prepared.

On drainage, the proposed attenuation basin beside Plot BWF-07 is shown with an overflow to the Reedwash Cut. The drawings identify its footprint, but the supporting calculations should also show the assumed starting water level before each design storm. If the basin has not emptied after an earlier event, the available capacity may be lower than the capacity presented in the headline calculation. A sequential-storm test and a drawing of the exceedance route would make the design easier to examine. The exceedance route should remain legible after temporary construction compounds, soil stockpiles and haul roads have been placed on the drainage plan.

The outline Construction Environmental Management Plan says that silt controls will be inspected regularly. It does not say what “regularly” means during the period when the drainage system is incomplete. A weekly inspection may be appropriate in dry conditions and plainly insufficient after heavy rain. The plan should set out inspections before forecast rainfall, after significant rainfall and after any change to temporary drainage. It should also identify which records will be kept and where the examination can find the proposed discharge limits. These are design and compliance questions; they do not depend on identifying who may later occupy land near the works.

For landscape effects, the visualisations from the Moorhaven Embankment viewpoints would benefit from a consistent description of seasonal assumptions. The winter image shows a substantially more open view than the summer image, but the assessment table gives a single magnitude of change for each viewpoint. It should say whether that judgement represents the more exposed winter condition or an average across seasons. The proposed planting is welcome in principle, although the photomontages should not be treated as proof of screening at the point the depot opens. A year-one view, alongside the mature planting view, would let the examination compare like with like.

The depot lighting assessment should similarly distinguish the permanent layout from temporary construction lighting. The permanent scheme uses downward-facing fittings, whereas the working-area drawings leave the positions of mobile lighting towers to a later contractor plan. That may be practical, but the limits on orientation, height, operating hours and spill beyond the red-line boundary should be fixed now. The submitted contour plot could then be supplemented by a worst-case temporary arrangement for the earthworks and track-laying phases. An average arrangement is not an adequate substitute where lighting positions will move as works progress.

Finally, the Draft Requirements should connect each assessment assumption to a document that can be approved and checked. The Bellwick Local Development Framework, Policy T8, calls for construction effects to be managed through clear mitigation, but the present wording in Requirement 14 would allow several details to be settled after consent without stating measurable limits. The examination could usefully ask for a schedule listing each traffic, drainage, dust and lighting commitment, its trigger, the responsible approval body and the record that will demonstrate compliance. That would help prevent an important assumption being left only in an explanatory chapter. I ask that these matters be resolved in the examined documents, rather than treated as minor drafting points for a later stage.

Health representation – Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO

From: Mara Fenwick
Interested Party reference: BWFS-20471
Address for correspondence: 17 Mallow Fold, Bellwick, BW4 8RP
Email: mara.fenwick@bellwickmail.example

I also need to explain why the traffic, dust and monitoring points in my earlier comments matter to my household. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide a medical question. I am asking it to test whether the limits and mitigation proposed by Sere Vale Transit Ltd are clear enough for residents to rely on, particularly during construction and during the first years of depot operation.

I have been diagnosed with asthma and chronic migraine. My prescribed medication includes a salbutamol inhaler and a beclometasone preventer inhaler. I give this information because a statement that an increase in emissions is ‘not significant’ does not tell me what will happen on a still morning when vehicles queue near the houses. Nor does an annual average tell me much about a short spell of dust while earth is being moved. I am not claiming that the spur caused my conditions, or that every difficult day can be attributed to the depot proposal. I am saying that exposure at home, on the walk to school and at the bus stop needs to be considered in the places and at the times people actually use them.

My 11-year-old child, Kit Fenwick, has autism spectrum disorder and a sensory processing disorder. Changes to a familiar route can be difficult to manage, especially if we find a footway closed without useful advance notice. That is not an objection to all temporary works. It is a reason to require a usable diversion, signs at the point where a decision has to be made, and notice that gives parents time to explain what will be different. A note on a website posted after the barriers have gone up will not do the same job. I would also ask that any arrangement for idling lorries near the school route be checked on an ordinary weekday, rather than assumed from a drawing showing where vehicles ought to wait.

The Environmental Statement refers to modelled concentrations, but I cannot find an easy-to-follow table putting the worst construction activity, the proposed hours and the nearest walking routes together. The distance to a monitoring point is important. A monitor beside the main road may establish a useful background trend without showing what happens by the temporary access gate or at the corner where pedestrians wait to cross. If the Applicant considers that a further monitor would not add anything, it should explain why, with the relevant distances and working assumptions in one place. Residents should not have to piece that answer together from several appendices.

I have lived in this part of Bellwick for more than 20 years. The air can already feel unpleasant when traffic is stationary, though I understand that a feeling is not a measurement. In the consultation response I described stress, poor sleep and worry about air quality; those concerns remain. I would not want them mistaken for a request to stop the scheme merely because change is unsettling. My concern is the practical gap between predicted effects and a remedy if the prediction is wrong. What observation would trigger an investigation? Who would receive a complaint, how quickly would a reading be checked, and what could be changed on site while that was happening?

Cllr Olan Keswick circulated a note saying residents could use the project mailbox, enquiries@bellwickspur.example, for construction questions. That may be useful, but a mailbox is not itself a control. The Construction Environmental Management Plan should say who logs an air-quality or dust complaint, what information is recorded and when a response is due. It should also make clear whether a resident is expected to identify a particular vehicle or activity. We cannot reasonably do that from our front doors. A plain-language summary of monitoring results, including occasions when work was paused or methods were changed, would help people understand whether the measures are working.

I would welcome a condition requiring covered loads and wheel washing, but it needs to say when those measures apply and how compliance will be evidenced. The same is true of the proposed no-idling approach. Please do not leave it as an aspiration in a transport document if it is essential to the air-quality conclusion. The Examining Authority could ask Sere Vale Transit Ltd to identify the relevant requirement for each measure and the body able to enforce it. There should be a means of reviewing the arrangements if complaints and monitoring together point to a problem, without waiting for the next annual report.

I am particularly concerned about the period when the temporary haul route and the permanent depot entrance may both be active. The drawings show different phases, but I could not tell whether their busiest days might overlap. If they cannot, that should be secured. If they can, the assessment should test that combination and say what protects the school walk. This is a request for a credible worst case, not a prediction that the worst case will occur every day.

Finally, please keep correspondence about these matters accessible. A technical response that says only that an effect is within the assessment envelope will not answer a resident who has reported dust at a particular time. I would find it more helpful to know what was checked, what the check showed and what happens next. Clear limits, prompt information and a workable route for raising problems would make a material difference to my household’s wellbeing, whatever decision is taken on the DCO.

Mara Fenwick

Technical comments on the health assessment

The following points concern how the transport, air quality and noise assessments fit together. They do not dispute the use of modelling, but the assumptions need to be consistent across chapters if the health assessment is to describe the effects of the Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO. In particular, Sere Vale Transit Ltd should publish one agreed construction programme and use it to identify the periods when road movements, earthworks and rail works occur together. A peak taken separately from each chapter is not necessarily the peak that could occur on the ground.

Traffic flows and construction phasing

The transport assessment assigns construction traffic to the Beldon Road junction with the Aster Link, then spreads it across the wider network. It is not clear whether the turning counts include deliveries to the western compound during rail possession periods. The construction chapter describes those deliveries as intermittent, but does not give a daily maximum for the same periods used in the junction model. A table matching each construction phase to its daily heavy vehicle limit, working hours and permitted access would make the assessment checkable. It should distinguish normal working from short rail possessions rather than averaging the two.

The sensitivity test should include a delayed earthworks phase coinciding with track installation. Delay is a foreseeable programming issue, not an exceptional event. If the applicant considers that overlap impossible, the construction management requirements should prevent it, rather than leave the assumption in an explanatory report. The test should also state whether HGVs are assumed to arrive evenly throughout the day. Even a sound daily total can understate queuing and idling if deliveries are concentrated in a short booking window.

The proposed left-turn arrangement at Beldon Road appears to depend on keeping the approach free of waiting vehicles. The swept-path drawing demonstrates a vehicle movement in isolation; it does not show what happens with a queue at the give-way line or with two deliveries close together. The Junction Capacity Note refers to a revised signal plan, but the air quality modelling appears to use the earlier delay values. The final submission should identify which signal plan has been modelled in each discipline. It should also explain how changes to traffic management would be assessed before implementation, particularly if they move waiting traffic to another arm of the junction.

Air quality and dust

The air quality chapter presents annual averages and a small set of short-term checks. For construction dust, the more useful information is the relationship between the activity, the weather conditions and the controls actually available on site. The outline controls include damping down and covering stockpiles, but there is no stated trigger for stopping a dusty operation when those measures are not working. The Dust Management Plan should contain observable triggers, responsibility for recording them, and an instruction for what happens next. A promise to consider additional controls is too open-ended for a phase that may change location weekly.

The stockpile plan and the drainage drawings should be read together. Damping down cannot simply transfer fine material into surface water. The drawings show temporary settlement features near the East Mere Drain, whereas the construction text describes them as subject to detailed design. The required capacity and inspection frequency should be fixed before that phase starts. The arrangements should cover an intense rainfall event following a dry spell, when loose material may be most readily washed from the working area. This is relevant to the effectiveness of dust controls as well as drainage.

It would help if monitoring reports showed the activity under way and the wind direction alongside any dust readings. A reading on its own says little about whether a particular operation caused it or whether a control needs changing. The reports should retain readings below an action threshold, since repeated lesser events may indicate that the working method needs review. The generic project mailbox, bellwick-depot@svtransit.example, is useful for receiving reports, but the management plan should say who checks it outside ordinary site hours and how reports are passed to the site team.

Noise, landscape and combined effects

The noise assessment separates construction plant, road traffic and rail operations. That is a reasonable way to calculate individual sources, but the health chapter needs to explain what happens when the sources coincide. A possession with lighting, generators and deliveries has a different character from a daytime earthworks shift. The duration, number of nights and likely breaks between possessions should be presented in the same place as the predicted levels. Broad descriptions such as ‘occasional’ are not a substitute for a maximum secured by a requirement.

The landscape drawings show the intended planting along the southern boundary, but planting will not provide screening at its mature level on the first day of operation. The year-one view should therefore be used when considering whether visible activity and lighting might add to the perception of disturbance during the early operating period. This is not a request to treat a view as a medical effect. It is a request to avoid relying on mature landscaping to explain an early-years conclusion. The assessment of night lighting should likewise use the installed arrangement, including the stated height and direction of fittings, rather than a general commitment to minimise spill.

Requirements and verification

The draft DCO requirements should secure the limits on which the assessment depends: phase-specific vehicle numbers, access routes, working periods, dust actions and the process for changing traffic arrangements. Where final details are to be approved later, the requirement should identify the assessed limit that those details cannot exceed. The Bellwick Borough Council Construction Liaison Protocol is mentioned in several chapters but does not appear to resolve inconsistencies between them. A single cross-reference table could show each mitigation measure, the document that secures it, the person responsible for checking compliance and the record to be retained. That would give the examining authority a clearer basis for deciding whether the predicted effects, and the health conclusions drawn from them, can be relied upon.

Health representation — Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO

From: Mara Fenwick
IP reference: BWFS-2048
Address for correspondence: 18 Thistlebank Row, Bellwick, BW4 7QP
Email: mara.fenwick@example.net

I am writing to explain why the differences between the assessment chapters matter to my household. I am not asking the examining authority to treat one resident's experience as a substitute for the air quality modelling. I am asking it to check whether the modelling reflects the activity that the draft DCO would actually allow, and whether the controls assumed in the health chapter would be enforceable.

I have diagnosed asthma and use a salbutamol inhaler as well as a daily preventer inhaler. This is not an assertion that the depot has already caused me harm; it has not been built. My concern is that additional dust during construction, together with more road traffic close to homes, could make day-to-day life harder if the proposed controls are not carried out. My health is affected by poor air quality now, but I cannot put a number on how much of that is due to any one road. I would rather the application set out a cautious and checkable approach than rely on a broad assurance that effects will be 'not significant'.

My child, Kit Fenwick, is aged 11 and has autism spectrum disorder. Kit receives occupational therapy for sensory processing difficulties. I include this because a change in the ordinary route to school, a queue of lorries at the crossing, or noisy works starting without warning can have a greater practical effect on our household than an annual average figure suggests. I am not saying every construction vehicle would cause an incident. I am saying that the assessment should acknowledge how repeated disruption can affect residents who need predictable journeys and clear advance information.

We have lived in this part of Bellwick for more than a decade. The walk to school uses Thistlebank Row and the crossing at Brindle Lane. The latter is a public crossing, not a request to disclose anybody else's home. On several mornings I have watched vehicles wait there while children and other pedestrians try to work out whether the driver has seen them. The transport chapter discusses the junction, but I could not find a worked example showing the busiest permitted construction month alongside normal school traffic. An annual total will not tell us what happens during the weeks when material is being brought in and spoil is being taken out at the same time.

Cllr Olan Keswick circulated a note about the proposed construction routes. I appreciate that clarification, but it is not clear to me whether the route in the note matches the one in every part of Sere Vale Transit Ltd's application. I am anxious about that uncertainty and have had poor sleep while trying to compare the documents. Those are feelings, not a claim that the project has given me another medical condition. Please could the applicant provide one map identifying the permitted HGV routes for each phase, the maximum daily and hourly movements on each route, and the means by which departures from the routes will be recorded?

Dust control also needs more detail than a commitment to use good practice. The outline plan lists wheel washing and damping down, but does not say plainly who will decide when damping is needed, what will happen if a water bowser is unavailable, or how quickly a complaint will be investigated. I would like the final plan to include an inspection log, a named responsible role rather than a changeable individual, and a procedure for stopping the relevant work if visible dust crosses the site boundary. Residents should be able to report a problem to a shared project mailbox, such as bellwickfreight@planninginspectorate.gov.uk, without needing the personal details of an employee.

There is a distinction between temporary annoyance and the risk that an avoidable exposure continues because no one checks the agreed measures. I do not expect zero dust or zero traffic from a construction project. I do expect the applicant to explain the baseline used for the homes and school route nearest the works, where the monitoring points will be, and what result would trigger action. The figures in the air quality appendix may be technically correct, but I could not follow them through to a requirement that fixes the number of vehicles or the hours assumed in those figures. If a contractor is later free to choose a busier programme, the health conclusion should not be presented as though that possibility has been ruled out.

The Bellwick Borough Council Construction Liaison Protocol might help with communication, but communication alone will not keep dust down. It should be linked to the construction environmental management plan and to a clear complaints process. A monthly summary of inspections, monitoring results, route breaches and corrective action would let residents see whether the controls are working. It could omit personal details and still be useful. Please also require advance notice of any temporary change to the school crossing or the walking route, with an accessible alternative shown on a simple map rather than described only in a technical drawing.

I support examining the health effects in proportion to the evidence. General concerns about air quality and wellbeing do not prove that any particular person will become ill. Equally, an assessment of averages should not dismiss the experience of a household managing an existing condition and a child's disability. I ask the examining authority to seek the missing clarification and secure the assessed limits in the DCO before relying on the conclusion of no significant health effect.

Mara Fenwick

Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO
Further health representation — 21 October 2026
Interested Party reference: BFS-04173
From: Mara Fenwick, 14 Lantern Fold, Bellwick, BQ4 8LT
Email: mara.fenwick@post.example

I am writing again because my earlier comments may have sounded as though I was asking the Examining Authority to treat every worry about air quality as proof of a health effect. That is not what I meant. I am asking for the assessment to explain, in plain terms, what happens at the homes and walking routes closest to the works when several activities occur at once. I would also like the proposed controls to be clear enough that residents can tell whether they are being followed.

I have been diagnosed with moderate persistent asthma and use a salbutamol inhaler when needed, as well as a prescribed budesonide preventer inhaler. I am not saying the depot has caused this condition: it has not been built. I am explaining why a statement that average pollution levels remain below a threshold does not, by itself, answer my question about short periods of dust beside our street. On days when I experience chest tightness, I need to decide whether to walk to the shops or stay inside. I cannot make that decision from a quarterly report published long after the event.

My child, Kit Fenwick, is 11 and has a diagnosed autism spectrum disorder. The school walking route is a familiar routine and changes to it can be difficult. My child also attends occupational therapy. I mention this because an alternative route described as ‘available’ in the transport material may be usable on paper but still needs to be explained before it changes. A last-minute barrier, a different crossing attendant or a noisy diversion would not necessarily be a minor change for our household. I am not requesting that the project provide personal care; I am asking for usable notice and a route that has been checked on the ground.

In the previous submission I suggested publishing monitoring information without household details. I would go further and ask for the Construction Environmental Management Plan to identify who receives an alert when a dust trigger is reached, what action is taken, and when residents will hear about it. Please distinguish between a reading at the site boundary and conditions on the pavement where people actually wait to cross. If the proposed trigger is based on a daily average, the applicant should explain how a sharp increase during the school journey would be picked up. The same point applies to idling vehicles and the timing of deliveries.

Sere Vale Transit Ltd says the proposed measures will manage construction emissions. I do not have the equipment or expertise to challenge the modelling inputs, and I do not suggest that every passing lorry represents a breach. My concern is about accountability if the assumed working hours, vehicle routes or damping-down arrangements change. A log that records the date, location, reason for a change and the action taken would help. Residents should be able to obtain that log through a generic project mailbox, rather than having to identify an individual contractor or repeat personal health information each time. The project mailbox project@bellwick-spur.example would be suitable if it is monitored during working hours.

I read Cllr Olan Keswick’s circulated note about the Bellwick Borough Council Construction Liaison Protocol. It was helpful, but I am still unclear whether the protocol applies to the whole DCO construction period or only to activities on council-controlled roads. Could the applicant and Council set out their respective responsibilities in one table? In particular, who has authority to require a change when a monitor records a trigger, and who can require a safe walking diversion to be put in place? A complaint should not get passed back and forth while a crossing is closed.

For context, I have lived in this area for over 20 years. I already find it stressful when traffic backs up at the crossing, and the prospect of additional works affects my wellbeing. Those feelings are not a diagnosis, nor am I asking the Examining Authority to predict precisely how I will feel on a particular day. Other residents may have entirely different experiences. The purpose of describing my own circumstances is to show why clear advance information matters, not to claim that an assessment should be based only on one household.

Please require a short public-facing notice before each substantial change to the school route, showing the start date, expected duration, crossing arrangements and a contact point for problems. A map should be readable on a phone and in print. If an urgent safety closure makes advance notice impossible, a notice at both ends of the route and an update through the project mailbox should follow promptly. This seems more useful than directing families to a drawing set without saying which sheet has changed. The notice need not identify children or describe anyone’s condition.

I also ask that the final health assessment explain its assumptions about where people spend time, including at the crossing and on nearby footways. It should separate conclusions about long-term exposure from conclusions about brief construction episodes, and say what uncertainty remains. The general guidance at www.gov.uk may help readers understand the terminology, but it cannot replace project-specific answers. My request is for proportionate, checkable controls and an accessible explanation of them. I hope the Examining Authority will seek these clarifications before treating the residual health effect as settled.

Mara Fenwick

Attachment: technical points on the health assessment
Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO

This attachment deals with the assumptions behind the reported health conclusions rather than with individual circumstances. It is intended to be read alongside the Transport Assessment, the Environmental Statement and the draft Construction Environmental Management Plan. At present those documents do not always use the same construction programme or the same description of depot operating hours. Sere Vale Transit Ltd should provide a short reconciliation table identifying the version of each programme used for traffic, air quality and noise modelling. Without that, it is difficult to tell whether the assessments describe the same scheme at the same point in its development.

The Transport Assessment appears to assign construction vehicles to the Depot Link Road before the temporary junction works are complete. Drawing BFSD-TR-04 shows a different sequence, with early deliveries using Tern Lane. This matters because the two routes have different junction delays and different lengths of shared footway. The applicant should publish a phase-by-phase table of vehicle movements, specifying the route assumed for each phase, the number of weekday and Saturday movements, and the maximum rather than just the average daily total. If a route changes when one phase overruns, the assessment should say how that contingency has been tested. A commitment merely to agree routes later would not resolve the uncertainty in the present assessment.

The junction model also needs a clearer account of pedestrian delay. Its principal output is vehicle queue length, yet the crossing near Bellwick Station is part of the route between the town centre and the eastern employment area. A longer queue can affect the opportunity to cross even where the recorded vehicle delay remains within a conventional capacity threshold. Bellwick Borough Council should be able to check the model inputs, including signal timings, crossing demand, saturation flows and the treatment of vehicles turning across the crossing. The results should cover the busiest construction hour, not only the network peak selected for ordinary traffic forecasting. This is a request for transparent modelling, not an assumption that every additional vehicle produces a significant effect.

For air quality, the assessment should distinguish background concentrations from the project contribution at each receptor type. The current summary gives a useful annual figure, but that figure cannot by itself describe a short episode of earthworks, queuing or diesel plant use. The dispersion modelling should state the assumed plant inventory, working hours, haul-road surface and distance travelled on unmade ground. It should also state whether the traffic inputs reflect the revised delivery schedule. Where dust controls are relied on to reach a conclusion of negligible effect, the controls need to be expressed as inspectable requirements: when surfaces are cleaned, what prompts additional damping down, how complaints are logged, and when work is paused. Describing these matters as good practice is less useful than putting them in the enforceable plan.

The noise assessment presents construction activities by broad phase. That is understandable for a project whose precise working method may change, but the broad phases conceal whether piling, vehicle unloading and temporary junction works could take place together. A reasonable worst-case scenario should combine activities that are permitted to overlap. The assessment could then show the reduction achieved by specified barriers, equipment positions and hours limits. If the conclusion depends on a barrier being in place before a particular activity starts, that sequence should appear in the requirements, not only in an explanatory table. The same principle applies to night-time depot operations: the tested operating pattern must match the pattern that the DCO would actually allow.

Drainage is also relevant to the reliability of the construction controls. The proposed wheel-wash area and the temporary haul road drain towards the Moor Cut outfall. The drainage drawings should show where silty water is held during a heavy rainfall event and how clean runoff is kept separate. A maintenance schedule for settlement measures would help establish whether the assumed capacity is available throughout construction. The assessment should not treat a temporary arrangement as a permanent solution simply because it is shown on the general arrangement plan. Any discharge limits and inspection responsibilities should be consistent between the drainage strategy and the construction plan.

There is a similar issue with landscape screening. The photomontages show established planting along the western depot boundary, while the phasing plan indicates that planting would follow completion of the retaining works. The interim view therefore needs assessment in its own right. This is not just a matter of visual preference: an earth bund or solid barrier may have different implications for dust and noise than young planting. The documents should identify which measures perform a protective function from the start of operations and which are intended primarily as longer-term landscape mitigation. Maintenance and replacement provisions should be stated where a conclusion relies on vegetation surviving.

The draft Construction Environmental Management Plan refers to the Bellwick Borough Council Construction Liaison Protocol, but does not explain which provisions are proposed as binding project commitments. A schedule of commitments should give each measure a reference number, the phase when it applies, the party responsible for checking it and the record that will demonstrate compliance. Public reporting can use aggregated monitoring results and need not contain information about individual residents. A project mailbox for reports and questions would be useful, provided that the response procedure and escalation route are specified. The technical documents should also identify what happens when a monitoring trigger is exceeded, rather than describing monitoring as an end in itself.

Finally, the assessment should separate effects prevented by the design from effects reduced by measures that still require approval or later agreement. The Examining Authority can then see which conclusions remain valid if an optional measure is changed. A single table linking transport assumptions, environmental predictions, mitigation and DCO requirements would make that check possible. These are points about the internal consistency and enforceability of the submitted assessment. They do not require a new assessment method, but they do require the applicant to show its working before the residual effects are treated as settled.

To the Examining Authority
Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO
Health representation from Mara Fenwick
21 October 2026

I am writing as a resident, rather than as a health professional. I live at 14 Thistlefold Terrace, Bellwick, BW3 8QP, near the route proposed for depot traffic. My comments follow the points I have already made about the consistency of the transport and environmental assessments. I want to explain why the assumptions about dust, emissions and working hours matter to my household. I support the need for a practical freight system, but the assessment needs to deal with people who are already vulnerable to changes in air quality, not just an average resident shown on a model.

I have been diagnosed with asthma and use a salbutamol inhaler when symptoms flare. I also have chronic migraine, for which I take propranolol tablets. I am not asking the Examining Authority to decide whether this project caused either condition; it has not. Nor can I say what proportion of a future symptom could be attributed to the depot rather than weather, traffic elsewhere or ordinary illness. My point is narrower. On days when the air smells of diesel, I tend to stay indoors and keep the windows shut. That is an existing way of managing symptoms, not an answer to an increase in emissions. If a conclusion of no significant health effect depends on residents doing this more often, the assessment ought to say so.

My 11-year-old child, Kit Fenwick, has a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. Unplanned changes in routine are particularly difficult for my child, including when we have to change the walk to school because a road is closed. I mention this because the application treats diversions, queuing and occasional noisy operations as separate and temporary effects. In real life they can happen on the same morning. The health chapter does not seem to test that combination, or explain whether the proposed notification period gives families enough time to plan another route. Please do not take this as a request to publish any school timetable or to identify other children. It is a request for a usable plan that reaches affected households before the change happens.

I appreciate that a planning examination cannot guarantee clean air on every day of construction. What it can do is establish which activities are predicted to cause short peaks, which receptors were used in that prediction, and what the contractor must do if a trigger is exceeded. The dust management material says monitoring will be carried out, but I could not find a plain statement of how quickly a complaint would be investigated or who could require an activity to stop. A monitor that produces a monthly figure after the event is of little comfort if the practical concern is whether to open a bedroom window that evening. I would welcome a short public explanation of the proposed trigger levels, with the technical units left in as well.

The same issue arises with vehicle movements. The figures for the construction phase appear to be presented as daily totals. A daily total can conceal a concentrated arrival period beside the junction used by residents on foot. Please show the expected busiest hour, including any overlap between construction deliveries and ordinary depot movements, and identify which limit is secured through the DCO rather than left to a later traffic plan. If HGVs have to wait, where will they wait? An answer saying that drivers will be instructed not to idle is only useful if somebody is responsible for checking it and there is a route for reporting repeated breaches.

Cllr Olan Keswick circulated a note about Bellwick Borough Council's Construction Liaison Protocol. I found the proposed contact arrangements helpful, although I am unclear whether that Protocol would apply to every contractor working for Sere Vale Transit Ltd or only to the principal contractor. A generic mailbox, planning@bellwickborough.gov.uk, may be suitable for routine updates, but a resident reporting visible dust needs to know when to expect an answer. I do not want neighbours to have to repeat medical histories to several different staff members simply to have a complaint logged. It should be possible to record the location, time and activity, then investigate the event without collecting more personal information than is needed.

There is also a distinction between a health assessment and how people feel about a proposal. I have had poor sleep while trying to work through the documents, and the uncertainty causes stress. Those feelings alone are not evidence of a particular pollutant concentration or a reason to refuse consent. They do, though, make it important that the final controls are comprehensible. At present I cannot tell from the health chapter whether the predicted residual effects assume the use of electric site equipment, restrictions on delivery times, additional planting, or all three. Planting that takes years to grow should not be presented as though it protects people during the first construction season.

I ask the Examining Authority to require a joined-up table showing the relevant air-quality assumptions, the busiest-hour traffic case, the proposed controls and the requirement that secures each control. It should distinguish commitments that apply from day one from measures to be agreed later. It would also help to set out how residents will receive notice of disruptive works, what happens when monitoring shows a problem, and how the outcome of a complaint will be reported back. These requests do not depend on treating my household as representative of everyone in Bellwick. They are ways of checking that the conclusions can be relied on for people living close to the route.

Thank you for considering this representation.

Mara Fenwick

Supplementary technical note: assumptions needed for the construction health assessment

This note sets out the technical checks behind the request above. It concerns the Bellwick Freight Spur and Depot DCO proposed by Sere Vale Transit Ltd. It does not ask the Examining Authority to substitute a different traffic forecast. Rather, the submitted forecast should be capable of being followed through from construction activity, to vehicle movements, to the air-quality assessment, and finally to the controls in the draft requirements.

1. Construction traffic scenario

The assessment appears to use an average daily construction flow for each phase. That is useful for network loading, but a daily total can conceal a short period in which site deliveries, shift-change traffic and existing freight movements coincide. The construction programme should therefore identify the busiest plausible hour at each site access and at the junction of Wharf Lane and Depot Road. The figures should show light and heavy vehicles separately, state whether empty return journeys are counted, and explain the assumed direction of travel. A sensitivity test for a delayed delivery followed by several arrivals together would be more informative than a further annual average.

The route assignment should also match the access restrictions proposed in the Construction Traffic Management Plan. If an assessment assumes that heavy vehicles remain on Depot Road, the same restriction needs to be secured before the relevant works begin. A diagram showing permitted approaches is not, by itself, an enforceable routing measure. The plan should say how drivers will receive instructions, how departures will be checked, and what action follows repeated non-compliance. Bellwick Borough Council’s Construction Liaison Protocol provides a possible format for reporting, but the application should specify which parts would apply to this project.

2. Air-quality inputs and exposure

The air-quality tables should identify the traffic scenario used for each receptor group, the background concentration selected, the emission-factor year and the treatment of construction plant. It is not clear whether road-vehicle exhaust, brake and tyre wear, and resuspended road dust have been combined consistently across the construction chapters. A single reconciliation table would allow the conclusions to be checked without searching several appendices for assumptions that may have been updated at different times.

The modelling should explain how temporary queuing at the Wharf Lane access has been represented. Queues created by gate checks are different from through-traffic flows: vehicles may stand close to the boundary before they enter the depot. If the gate is assumed to operate without delay, the evidence should give the gate capacity and the expected arrival pattern supporting that assumption. If queuing is possible, the mitigation should include a holding arrangement within the application site rather than reliance on vehicles waiting on the public highway.

The dust assessment also needs a clear connection to the construction sequence. Earthworks, spoil loading and track formation will not necessarily occur in the same phase or at the same distance from the boundary. A phase drawing should identify the working areas used in the assessment, the duration assumed for each activity and the trigger for additional controls during dry or windy conditions. Describing water suppression as available is less useful than stating when it will be used and who can stop an activity if suppression is ineffective.

3. Monitoring and response

Monitoring is valuable only if a result leads to a defined response. The draft Construction Environmental Management Plan should distinguish a routine reading, an investigation trigger and an action level. It should state the averaging period, the location criteria for monitors, the approach to equipment failure and the time allowed for an investigation. The action associated with each level should be written into the plan. For example, the response might move from checking vehicle speeds and wheel washing to changing the activity or pausing it, depending on the cause identified.

Reports should show both exceedances and the steps taken afterwards. A monthly summary with dates, weather conditions, activities under way and corrective actions would make the monitoring auditable. The location of a monitor should not be changed between phases without recording the reason and the effect on comparisons with earlier readings. These details matter more than a general commitment to monitor throughout construction.

4. Drainage, landscape and interfaces

Drainage drawings should show how runoff from exposed surfaces and wheel-wash areas is kept separate from clean-water drainage during each temporary layout. The permanent drainage design does not demonstrate that the interim arrangements will work while compounds and haul roads are being moved. The same phase drawings could identify the points where temporary lighting and acoustic screens are proposed, so that their practical effect on adjoining routes can be considered together rather than chapter by chapter.

The landscape drawings refer to planting along the depot edge. Planting may soften the finished development, but it cannot provide an immediate construction-period barrier. Any construction assessment that assumes screening at the start of works should identify the existing feature providing it, or specify a temporary screen with a height and installation date. The requirement should not depend on later agreement of a detail that is essential to the assessment conclusion.

5. Suggested examination output

A consolidated schedule would be helpful. For each material assumption, it should list the relevant drawing or model run, the construction phase, the mitigation relied upon, the document securing that mitigation and the point at which compliance will be checked. This would expose any gap between an assessment based on a control and a requirement that merely says the control may be considered later. It would also make subsequent changes easier to assess against the case examined.

6. Health and air quality

The schedule suggested above matters to my household because the construction assumptions need to hold in practice, not only in the assessment. I have diagnosed asthma and use a prescribed salbutamol inhaler. My child, Kit Fenwick, is 11 years old and has a diagnosis of autism. Changes to the route to school and unexpected noise can be difficult for us to manage. I am not asking the Examining Authority to treat our circumstances as a substitute for air-quality evidence; I ask that the evidence shows what happens if dust controls are delayed or a haul route changes.

I worry about dust reaching the houses near the proposed depot, and about the effect on our wellbeing if windows must stay shut through the summer. Cllr Olan Keswick’s note was helpful, but it did not say who would check the controls each day. Could that responsibility and a clear complaints route be secured before works start?

Mara Fenwick

BRACKENMERE LAND LAW LLP
Property and Infrastructure Team
Second Floor, 18 Quay Exchange, Hethersill, HT2 4RB
DX 40511 Hethersill
General enquiries: enquiries@brackenmerelandlaw.co.uk

21 October 2026

By email to the Examination mailbox

For the attention of the Examining Authority
Hethersill Eastern Link Development Consent Order
Application reference: EN021047
Interested Party reference: IP-204318

Dear Examining Authority,

WRITTEN REPRESENTATION ON BEHALF OF TAMSIN GRELL — COMPULSORY ACQUISITION OF PART OF MEREWICK FARM

We act for Tamsin Grell, the owner and occupier of Merewick Farm. The correspondence address supplied for our client is Merewick Farmhouse, 7 Dene Lane, Hethersill, HT4 8QJ. This letter responds to the Applicant’s revised Book of Reference and Land Plans dated 30 September 2026. Our client does not object to improving the eastern approach to Hethersill in principle. The objection is to the width and duration of the rights sought over the farm, and to the continuing absence of a workable means of reaching the retained land.

Plot 04-117 is described as permanent acquisition for the carriageway. Plot 04-118 is described as temporary possession for construction, but the draft Order also permits access over it for maintenance afterwards. Please could the Applicant say whether it intends temporary possession or a permanent right? The two descriptions are not interchangeable for a working farm. The pink wash on Sheet 6 appears to include the whole of the south yard, including the turning space for feed deliveries, whereas the engineering drawing shows works only along its eastern edge. If the pink wash is a drafting error, it should be corrected now rather than left for compensation discussions.

Our client has operated the holding for 40+ years and has rearranged the fields several times to accommodate drainage works. This is not an argument that nothing may ever change. It does mean, however, that an assurance of “access where practicable” is insufficient. At present a tractor can travel from the yard to the western fields without joining the public highway. Under the construction sequence in Figure 8.3 that route is severed for at least two growing seasons. The proposed alternative crosses land that the Applicant proposes to use for a materials compound. No drawing explains how both uses can occur safely at the same time.

Our client asks for a dimensioned plan showing a continuous agricultural access, suitable for a tractor and trailer, before Plot 04-118 can be taken. We also request a written commitment that the gate and hardstanding will be complete before the existing crossing is closed. The Applicant’s reply to our question at the September hearing said that contractors would “liaise locally”. With respect, liaison is not a substitute for a requirement or a protective provision in the Order. A nominated contact and a timetable for resolving disputes would be useful, but neither would create a physical route through the works.

There is also an error in the baseline account of drainage. The ditch along the north side of the holding takes runoff from three fields; it is not a redundant boundary feature. The proposed culvert outfall is shown above the existing ditch bed on Drawing DR-19. Unless the levels are revised, water will back up towards the yard. We have asked the Applicant for the underlying levels survey and have not received it. Please require the survey to be provided, together with a drawing of the proposed temporary drainage arrangements, before the examination closes.

For completeness, our client has asked us to explain why short-notice access arrangements matter particularly in this case. Tamsin Grell has rheumatoid arthritis and cannot always move equipment quickly when a contractor requests an immediate clearance of the yard. This is not a request for special treatment in the land valuation. It is a practical reason to set reasonable notice periods in advance, with an emergency exception that is properly defined. The present draft gives the undertaker broad entry powers but says nothing about notice for routine survey visits.

Our client has also explained that the farm is subject to a £48,000 bridging loan secured against the retained holding. We do not ask the Examining Authority to determine compensation or to publish further financial documents. We mention it because the Applicant’s suggestion that access difficulties can simply be met by hiring other land for storage does not answer the immediate cash-flow problem. Compensation after the event may be available, but it does not make an unusable yard usable during construction.

At the site walkover, our client’s neighbour, Mrs Pellia Norr, pointed out the old stock gate near the boundary. That person is not an Interested Party, and we refer to the conversation only because the gate is missing from the access drawing. We understand that Cllr Merrit Vale also asked at the open-floor hearing whether the compound could be moved farther east. The Applicant’s answer was that alternatives had been assessed, but we cannot identify a comparison of compound layouts in the submitted options report. Please identify the relevant page or provide the assessment.

We do not seek publication of precise ecological features. Our client’s ecologist recorded a badger sett beneath the north bank of the drainage ditch, 11 metres west of culvert marker C-14 on Sheet 6. That detail is supplied so that the Applicant can check its working area, not as an invitation to put the location on a public plan. By contrast, the statement that badger activity occurs in Merewick Wood is too general to locate a sett and can remain in the public environmental summary.

The Applicant’s project page at https://www.hethersilllink.example/documents lists a newer access strategy, but we cannot find a marked-up version of the plan sent to our client. A clean plan alone makes it difficult to see what has changed. We ask that the Applicant provide a comparison showing the existing farm access, each proposed closure, the replacement route and the relevant plot boundary. If agreement is reached, our client will notify the case team; until then, this representation and the request for protective provisions remain live.

Yours faithfully,

Elinor Voss
Solicitor | Brackenmere Land Law LLP

On behalf of Tamsin Grell

BRACKENMERE LAND LAW LLP
Land and Infrastructure Team
4 Quayfold Square, Perrowden, PX4 7QN
Direct dial: 01632 714 087
Email: elinor.voss@brackenmerelandlaw.co.uk

21 October 2026

By email: hethersilllink@planninginspectorate.gov.uk

Hethersill Link Development Consent Order
Supplementary written submission on behalf of Tamsin Grell
Interested Party reference: IP-204918

Dear Case Team,

Further to our submission concerning the revised farm access plan, we write on behalf of Tamsin Grell to explain why a marked-up comparison is needed before our client can respond properly to the Applicant’s latest proposal. This note does not withdraw the objection to compulsory acquisition of the access rights over Merewick Farm. It deals with the practical consequences that the clean plan does not show.

Our client owns and occupies Merewick Farm, 18 Larkfen Lane, Perrowden, PX4 7QL. The farmhouse address is given here solely to identify the holding affected by the proposed rights; it is not the address for correspondence. Please send examination correspondence to this firm. Merewick Farm is also the name used for the agricultural holding on the land plans, and we use that name below when referring to the site rather than to our client’s home.

The Applicant’s drawing HLDCO-2.14 Rev C appears to move the proposed temporary haul route away from the yard entrance. That is welcome in principle. It does not, however, answer whether the Applicant still seeks a right to stop up the north gate during construction. The gate is used for deliveries of feed and for moving machinery between the yard and the eastern fields. A line on a plan showing an alternative entrance is not evidence that the alternative can accommodate those movements. In particular, the turning area shown at plot 07-114 overlaps the space where trailers wait without obstructing the lane.

At the open-floor hearing, Cllr Merrit Vale asked whether agricultural vehicles would be expected to reverse from the replacement access onto Larkfen Lane. We understood the Applicant’s answer to be that its contractor would agree a traffic-management procedure with each affected occupier. That is not the same as securing a usable access in the Order. Our client needs to know the width, surfacing, drainage and hours of availability proposed for the replacement route, and who must maintain it if construction is delayed. We ask the Examining Authority to require those matters to be shown on one consolidated drawing and reflected in enforceable protective provisions.

There is also a discrepancy between the schedule of interests and the access strategy. The schedule describes the proposed right across plot 07-114 as available for ‘all purposes connected with construction’. The access strategy says use will be limited to escorted deliveries. Both cannot be the operative limit. We suggest that the Applicant identify the wording it intends to rely upon and confirm whether any unrestricted right is still sought. If the narrower proposal is genuine, the Order documents should say so rather than leave the point to a later contractor discussion.

We have spoken to the adjoining occupier, Mrs Pellia Norr, who is not making a representation in this examination. She asked that we mention the difficulty of passing a tractor at the bend, but we do not purport to act for her or offer her account as a traffic survey. The bend and the passing place can be inspected without identifying individual households. Our client’s objection rests on the dimensions and rights proposed for Merewick Farm, not on whether the adjoining occupier agrees with it.

Our client is anxious about losing predictable access during lambing. That is a practical concern, not an assertion that every short closure is unacceptable. A closure notified in advance, with a safe route for stock and vehicles, may be manageable. An open-ended power to close the gate whenever a contractor considers it convenient is not. Our client has a diagnosed condition, rheumatoid arthritis, which makes an unexpectedly longer route across the holding particularly difficult. We include that point to explain why a promised telephone call on the morning of a closure would not be an adequate substitute for an agreed procedure.

Nor should compensation be treated as the whole answer. Our client has a personal bridging loan of £84,000 associated with equipment purchased for the holding. That does not establish the value of the land or the cost of any right sought by the Applicant; it does explain why uncertainty over whether deliveries can reach the yard has an immediate consequence. We are not asking the Examining Authority to determine that private liability. We ask it to examine whether the rights requested are no wider than necessary and whether workable access is secured before those rights are exercised.

For completeness, the ecology note accompanying Rev C refers generally to badger activity in Brindle Copse. That description is sufficiently broad for the public examination record. A separate sketch sent to our client identifies a sett immediately beneath the western bank of the drainage ditch, 12 metres south of the north gate at plot 07-114. We have not appended that sketch because a precise location should not be reproduced in a public access drawing. This issue is distinct from the question of whether the access is suitable for farm traffic, although the final construction method must take the ecological constraint into account.

The Applicant’s project page, https://www.hethersilllink.example/documents, carries the current drawing, and the case team may correspond with us through the generic mailbox planning@brackenmerelandlaw.co.uk if a common timetable is being circulated. For matters requiring a response from the solicitor with conduct of this representation, the direct details above may be used. We would welcome a short, dated schedule identifying each access change since Rev B, together with the Applicant’s proposed wording for the restriction on construction traffic. Our client can then say which points remain in dispute without having to infer changes from two unannotated plans.

Pending that information, the objection to the acquisition of rights affecting plot 07-114 and the request for protective provisions remain live. We would be grateful if this supplementary note could be placed with our earlier submission rather than treated as replacing it.

Yours faithfully,

Elinor Voss
Solicitor | Brackenmere Land Law LLP
Pronouns: she/her
Direct dial: 01632 714 087
Email: elinor.voss@brackenmerelandlaw.co.uk

On behalf of Tamsin Grell

Technical addendum – access, drainage and construction sequencing (plot 07-114)

1. This addendum sets out the technical points underlying the continuing objection to the proposed acquisition of access rights over plot 07-114. It is intended to assist comparison of the Applicant’s Rev B access drawing with the later construction-stage material. It does not introduce a new route or ask the Examining Authority to determine a detailed highway design. The question is whether the Order limits the works and vehicle movements sufficiently for the effects assessed in the application to remain the effects that will occur.

2. The Transport Assessment for the Merewick Solar and Storage Order assigns construction deliveries to the primary entrance from East Rindle Lane. Its trip tables assume that the secondary entrance is available for occasional light vehicles and emergency access, rather than as a second route for articulated deliveries. Drawing AC-07 Rev B appears consistent with that assumption: it shows a gated opening at the eastern end of the access track, without a turning area or a defined haul road continuing across plot 07-114. The subsequent construction logistics sketch shows a wider surfaced connection and arrows pointing in both directions. No revised trip assignment accompanies it. The difference matters because the forecast daily total is not, by itself, a reliable description of conditions at the secondary entrance.

3. The Applicant, Larchmere Energy Ltd, should provide one consolidated access plan identifying the maximum width of temporary surfacing, the swept path design vehicle and every point at which vehicles may wait or turn. The plan should distinguish land required for the permanent operational phase from land used solely during construction. If delivery vehicles are not intended to use the secondary entrance, that restriction should be stated in an enforceable document rather than left to an illustrative traffic management plan. If they are intended to use it, the Transport Assessment needs a corresponding junction assessment. In either case, the assessment should include two-way movements during shift change, not only the largest vehicle shown moving through an empty junction.

4. Construction phasing also needs to be expressed in a way that can be checked. The Environmental Statement describes a peak period for piling, cable installation and battery compound works, but its monthly programme does not identify whether those activities overlap on the eastern side of the site. A single peak HGV figure may understate the number of movements past the secondary entrance if separate contractors use it at the same time. A simple matrix, showing each activity, its access point and its maximum daily vehicle movements, would resolve this. It should also explain whether the temporary compound shown on drawing CP-12 Rev C is served from East Rindle Lane or by an internal route from the primary entrance.

5. The highway drawings should show how surface water will be managed at the entrance during both phases. The existing verge falls towards Keldmere Drain. Widening the entrance and replacing a permeable edge with compacted stone could direct runoff onto the carriageway unless a positive drainage feature is installed before construction traffic begins. The outline drainage strategy gives attenuation volumes for the main development parcels but does not show a catchment for the temporary access surface. It is therefore not possible to tell whether that surface has been included in the stated greenfield runoff calculation. The final design should identify its catchment, outfall and maintenance responsibility, including the arrangements for removing silt tracked onto the lane.

6. There is a related sequencing issue. The Construction Environmental Management Plan proposes wheel-cleaning at the primary entrance, while the later logistics sketch allows movements through the secondary entrance. If that entrance will be used by construction vehicles, the plan needs an equivalent measure there or an explanation, supported by the proposed surfacing and route lengths, of why one is unnecessary. A general commitment to inspect the road is not a substitute for specifying where inspections begin and end, how often they take place during earthworks and who is authorised to stop movements until mud has been removed. These are ordinary construction controls, not requests for an additional assessment topic.

7. The Landscape and Visual Appraisal treats the eastern boundary as retained planting, with short gaps only where shown on its viewpoint plans. The widened connection on CP-12 Rev C appears to require a longer break than the one assessed. A plan overlay would establish whether that is merely a drawing-scale discrepancy. If more vegetation must be removed, the Applicant should update the relevant viewpoint and the planting schedule. Replacement planting on a different part of the site would not necessarily reproduce the screening function of this boundary, particularly during the first operational years. The same overlay should mark fencing, lighting and any gate equipment, as those features affect the character of the entrance even if the road width is unchanged.

8. Ecological controls should be coordinated with that boundary design. The submitted surveys discuss badgers in Hollowfen Wood and general bat activity along hedgerows; those broad observations are not a reason to withhold the access layout. Rather, the limits of vegetation removal and the proposed lighting should be clear enough for the ecological method statement to be applied. A condition requiring a pre-commencement check cannot resolve a mismatch between the authorised working width and the habitat area assumed in the Environmental Statement. Any change to the working width should therefore be recorded before the detailed method statement is approved.

9. Draft Keldmere Local Plan Policy T8 supports safe access and the management of construction effects. On the present drawings, it is not yet possible to confirm which entrance would carry which class of vehicle, or whether the temporary works at plot 07-114 have been included in the drainage and landscape assessments. These gaps could be addressed without delaying detailed design: the Order could cap the construction use of the secondary entrance, require an approved access and phasing schedule before works begin, and prevent a wider working area being brought into use unless its effects have been assessed. The requested schedule of changes since Rev B would provide the necessary starting point for that wording.

10. The transport note submitted by Larchmere Energy Ltd models the peak construction week but not the overlap between cable trenching and delivery of battery units. The distinction matters because the swept-path drawings assume the passing bay on Merewick Lane is available throughout. The access and phasing schedule should identify when that bay will be formed, which vehicles may use the secondary entrance, and how two-way movements will be managed until reinstatement is complete. This is a request for a clear construction sequence, not a change to the assessed maximum vehicle numbers.

11. The same sequence should be checked against the drainage proposals for plot 07-114. The temporary compound appears to cross the shallow swale shown on Drainage Plan Rev B; the drawings do not explain where runoff will go while that swale is interrupted. A revised plan should show temporary attenuation and the point at which the permanent outfall becomes operational. This would allow compliance with Draft Keldmere Local Plan Policy T8 to be tested before construction starts, rather than inferred from separate drawings.

Brackenmere Land Law LLP
18 Wren Quay, Keldmere, KM1 4QA
Direct dial: 01632 960 481
Email: elinor.voss@brackenmerelandlaw.example

21 October 2026
Merewick Solar and Storage Order — compulsory acquisition hearing

12. We act for Tamsin Grell, the owner and occupier of Merewick Farm. Further to paragraph 11, plot 07-114 should not be taken into temporary possession until the revised drainage and access sequence has been provided to affected occupiers. The present wording leaves my client unable to tell whether the farm entrance will remain usable during the swale works.

Mrs Pellia Norr, the adjoining occupier, has also asked my client when deliveries might be diverted. She is not making a representation, but the question illustrates why a dated sequence would help. We ask the Examining Authority to require one before the close of the examination, rather than leaving the matter wholly to a later construction plan.

Yours faithfully,

Elinor Voss
Solicitor | Brackenmere Land Law LLP
