text:
To the Examining Authority
Merewick Solar Park — written representation
21 October 2026
From: Ellen Wray
Interested Party reference: IP-204918
Address for correspondence: 14 Sedgeglass Lane, Brindlewick, BW4 8QP

I object to the proposed solar farm. I am not against renewable energy. I have lived in Brindlewick for over 40 years and know the fields between Tern Drove and Merewick Copse well. They are working land, but they are also the open approach to the village. The application documents keep describing the site as screened. That may be true in a photograph taken from one particular point in summer. It is not what you see walking the footpath in February, when the hedges are bare and the ground rises towards the substation field.

I ask the Examining Authority to look at the proposal from the public right of way along Tern Drove, not just from the roadside viewpoints selected by the applicant. The panels, fencing, cameras and access tracks would be seen together, across several fields. Calling the panels temporary does not make a development lasting decades feel temporary to those of us who use that path every week. The submitted landscape drawings also show planting at its expected mature height. They do not show the years in which it would be little more than guards and thin saplings.

My second concern is the sourcing of the panels. I allege that Larchmere Solar Holdings Limited has knowingly profited from forced labour in the supply chain for the Merewick Solar Park project. I appreciate this is a serious allegation. The applicant should therefore be required to publish a proper account of where the polysilicon and finished modules would come from, and how its checks work beyond a statement from the next supplier in the chain. General discussion of Xinjiang is not, by itself, proof about a particular shipment. Equally, a promise that procurement will be sorted out later is not enough for a project presented as being in the public interest now. I have seen background reporting at https://www.solarwatch-ledger.example/articles/2025/chain, although I do not suggest that article establishes the origin of these proposed panels.

Some neighbours say that, with the war in Ukraine, any domestic electricity generation must be accepted wherever it is placed. I understand the urgency, but that is not a reason to stop asking what is being bought or how this particular site will be built. The war has affected people and energy prices; it does not turn a weak supply-chain answer into a strong one. Solar generation is worthwhile, but the applicant still has to demonstrate that its claimed benefits are delivered responsibly. Please do not read this as an objection to people from any country. It is a request for evidence about products and contracts.

The construction traffic assessment seems especially detached from daily conditions. Tern Drove has passing places rather than a continuous width suitable for two large vehicles. At the school run there are pedestrians at the bend by the old pump house, and a driver meeting a delivery lorry there has nowhere sensible to go. The swept-path plan uses an unobstructed junction. It does not account for the bin collection vehicle, parked cars or somebody leading a horse. I would like to see a construction traffic plan with delivery hours, a booking system and a named contact for problems. A generic undertaking to manage traffic is not sufficient.

My daughter, Iris Wray, aged 11, walks part of this route with me. She has diagnosed asthma, so the proposed dust controls matter to us in a practical way. I am not claiming that the solar farm would cause her condition. I am saying that the current commitment to damp down the tracks ‘as necessary’ leaves residents guessing who decides when it is necessary and how complaints will be checked. My sleep is poor when heavy vehicles start early; that is an effect I can describe, not a medical diagnosis. Please require a clear start time and a way of recording breaches that residents can actually use.

Drainage needs more explanation too. Water already gathers beside the lower gate after prolonged rain. The flood note considers the panels and the main access track, but says little about compacted ground under the temporary compounds. The applicant should show how those areas will be restored, who will inspect them and whether runoff will be monitored beyond the first winter. I cannot judge the hydraulic calculations, but I can see that the ditch on Plot 07 is shallow and is sometimes full before a storm has finished. Those ordinary observations ought to be tested rather than dismissed.

There is also wildlife information that should not simply be placed on a public plan. Badgers have been reported in Merewick Copse, which is a broad location and not the issue. In the survey material I was shown, the active sett is 3 metres north of the stile at the east end of Tern Drove, beneath the third hawthorn from the gate. Please keep that precise description out of any public version of my representation and ensure that the ecologist, rather than a contractor following an unmarked drawing, checks the working area. The application should explain the buffer and how it would be maintained during fence installation.

Mrs Pella Thorne, who lives nearby but is not making a representation, asked me whether the night-time security lights would stay on continuously. I could not find a definite answer. Cllr Alden Fenn raised a similar question at the Brindlewick Parish Council meeting in September, but the note of that meeting only says lighting would be minimised. That wording could cover a great deal. Please ask for a plan showing each fitting, its direction, the trigger for switching it on and the hours when maintenance crews may attend.

For these reasons I ask that consent is refused unless the outstanding evidence can be examined properly and enforceable limits are put in place. A long list of matters left for later approval would not give residents a meaningful opportunity to understand what will happen on the ground. I would welcome a site visit in winter, when the views and drainage concerns are easiest to understand.

Yours faithfully,
Ellen Wray

Annex: technical points on the Merewick Solar Park application

This annex sets out the technical matters that need to be resolved before the effects of the proposal can be assessed. The points concern the submitted plans and assessments, rather than matters that could safely be settled through a later management plan.

1. Construction traffic and access

The Transport Assessment models deliveries to the compound as an average across the construction period. An average is of limited use where the busiest days will involve panels, mounting frames, inverter equipment and aggregate arriving at the same time. Larchmere Solar Holdings Limited should provide a daily maximum, with separate figures for heavy goods vehicles, light commercial vehicles and staff vehicles. The assessment should also identify which deliveries could be rescheduled if a programme slips. Without that information, the proposed limit on vehicle movements cannot be checked against the programme it is supposed to control.

The swept-path drawings show the proposed access from Fenfold Lane, but do not show two construction vehicles meeting on the approach from the Willow Rigg Road junction. Several of the passing places shown on the route plan are existing gateways, not formed lay-bys. They should not be counted as available passing space without a drawing confirming their width, surfacing and visibility. The applicant should also state whether vehicles will be required to turn around inside the compound. A routeing requirement is only useful if the site can accommodate the vehicles that arrive by the approved route.

The Construction Traffic Management Plan should be approved before any works begin, including hedgerow removal and access construction. It should contain a booking system, a procedure for missed delivery slots and a method for recording actual movements. A commitment to brief drivers, on its own, would not establish whether the assessed route was used. The submitted material does not explain how the movement records would be made available for checking during construction.

2. Landscape and visual assessment

The landscape drawings rely heavily on new boundary planting to screen the arrays. The visualisations distinguish between construction and a later established-planting scenario, but the intervening years are the period when the development would be most open. A year-one and year-five view should be supplied from the Fenfold Lane bend and the higher section of Willow Rigg Road. Both should use the same camera position and field of view as the submitted baseline photography so that the predicted change can be compared.

The proposed planting is shown as a continuous belt in places where the access, drainage outfall and cable route interrupt it. Those gaps matter because the inverter units and security fencing would otherwise be visible through them. Planting schedules should identify the maintained height and width of each belt, not simply the size of stock at planting. Replacement requirements should also specify when a failed plant is to be replaced and how long the replacement obligation lasts. The assessment should not treat screening as complete merely because planting has been installed.

3. Drainage and ground conditions

The Flood Risk and Drainage Statement says that the panels will not materially increase runoff because the ground below them remains permeable. That may be a reasonable starting assumption, but it does not address concentrated drip lines, repeated vehicle tracking or compaction beneath temporary storage areas. The drawings should distinguish permanent tracks from temporary construction surfaces and show how each area is to be reinstated. Infiltration test results should be presented alongside the locations and depths of the tests, rather than as a site-wide rate without context.

The proposed swales discharge towards the eastern field boundary. The drawings do not make clear whether the swales have sufficient storage when an outfall is restricted, or where exceedance flows would go during an event beyond their design capacity. A plan showing overland flow paths, proposed finished levels and the position of any bunds is required. This should cover the compound and access as well as the panel fields. A condition requiring a final drainage scheme later would not resolve whether the current layout leaves enough land for the necessary features.

4. Construction programme and restoration

The programme divides the works into broad phases but does not indicate how long exposed ground, open trenches or temporary stockpiles would remain in each area. The environmental measures are therefore difficult to match to the likely disturbance. A revised programme should identify the order of access works, cable installation, panel assembly and reinstatement, together with the maximum area that may be disturbed at one time. It should say what happens when wet weather prevents reinstatement on the planned date.

The restoration drawing shows removal of equipment at the end of operation, but it is unclear whether buried cable and foundations would also be removed. The decision should not leave that choice entirely to a future scheme. The applicant should set out which items would remain, the depth at which they would remain and the basis for concluding that the land could be returned to its former use. Any proposed exceptions should be marked on a plan.

5. Policy and enforceability

The Merewick District Renewable Energy Policy supports renewable generation subject to acceptable effects on landscape, highways and water management. It does not remove the need to assess those effects against a defined layout and construction envelope. At present, several important limits appear only as intentions in supporting documents, while the draft requirements refer to plans to be agreed later. The examining authority should request a consolidated schedule identifying the maximum panel height, maximum number and dimensions of ancillary buildings, construction vehicle limit, working hours and lighting parameters.

Each limit should point to a numbered drawing or a measurable value. Where flexibility is sought, the range should be assessed now rather than treated as an administrative detail. Brindlewick Parish Council's request for clearer access information is consistent with that approach: the issue is not whether a management plan can eventually be written, but whether the likely worst-case effects of the proposal can be understood before consent is decided.

Traffic and construction access

The transport assessment for Merewick Solar Park appears to model an average construction day rather than the busiest plausible day. That distinction matters because deliveries of panels, mounting frames, inverter units and aggregate may overlap with earthworks and cable installation. Larchmere Solar Holdings Limited should provide a week-by-week forecast showing the highest number of two-way heavy goods vehicle movements, not just a total for the construction period. The forecast should explain whether vehicles serving the grid connection works have been included. If those works are outside the present assessment, the conclusion on highway effects is incomplete.

The proposed access from Fenbarrow Road is shown at an indicative location, but the submitted swept-path drawing does not demonstrate two large vehicles passing at the access mouth. Nor does it show how a vehicle arriving early would wait without obstructing the carriageway. The examination would benefit from a drawing based on the largest delivery vehicle proposed, with forward-entry and forward-exit movements demonstrated. Visibility splays should be plotted against the achievable speeds on Fenbarrow Road rather than an assumed low approach speed. Any hedge removal needed to obtain those splays belongs in the landscape assessment as well as the highway drawings.

A construction traffic management plan cannot resolve these points simply by stating that deliveries will be booked. It should specify enforceable routing, the location of a holding area and how drivers would be directed if the access is temporarily blocked. The assessment should also account for the overlap between construction traffic and agricultural machinery using the same narrow road. There is no need to assume constant congestion to recognise that a short period of queuing at a bend or junction could have a material effect. A sensitivity test for the peak delivery week would provide a more useful basis for examination than the currently presented daily average.

Landscape and visual assessment

The landscape material relies heavily on planting along the eastern and southern boundaries. The photomontages should distinguish the appearance at first operation from the appearance after planting has become established; the latter cannot stand in for the former. Drawings should also identify the finished ground level beneath the panels, because even modest changes in level affect how much of the arrays is visible above existing hedges. For each representative viewpoint, the assessment should state which parts of the view would contain panels, fencing, cameras, inverter housings or the proposed substation. Treating these as a single undifferentiated solar-farm element makes it difficult to test the claimed magnitude of change.

The assessment describes the edge of Gorsefen Meadow as having a contained character. That description does not adequately address views across the shallow valley from the public right of way on the ridge. Screening at the site boundary would not necessarily screen the upper portions of panels or lighting columns from an elevated viewpoint. A winter view is particularly important: the submitted summer photographs show dense foliage, while the claimed screening depends partly on deciduous planting. The examining authority should seek a verified winter photomontage and a section through the valley, using the maximum panel and structure heights proposed for consent.

The landscape management proposal also needs measurable commitments. A requirement to maintain hedgerows in good condition would be difficult to apply without a minimum retained height, a timetable for replacement planting and an inspection period. Planting should not be assumed to remove adverse effects immediately. If the applicant's assessment depends on screening after a specified number of growing seasons, the documents should identify the effects during the intervening period and explain how those effects have been weighed.

Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage strategy states that operational runoff will remain broadly comparable to the existing situation because land beneath the arrays will remain permeable. This needs testing against the layout. Rainfall shed from a panel falls along its lower edge, and repeated concentrated runoff can create channels on sloping ground before it infiltrates. The strategy should show panel orientation, row spacing and the slopes where concentrated discharge is most likely. It should then explain whether grass cover alone is sufficient or whether additional measures are required at particular rows. A general promise to manage runoff by detailed design does not establish that the proposed layout can accommodate those measures.

The submitted flood mapping places most equipment outside the mapped flood extent, but the treatment of temporary compounds and cable trenches is less clear. Construction may alter drainage pathways even where permanent structures do not. The applicant should provide a construction-phase surface-water plan identifying temporary hardstanding, stockpiles, trench crossings and the sequence for reinstating disturbed soil. It should also specify how runoff carrying sediment would be intercepted before reaching the field drains that discharge towards Merewick Beck. The plan should be secured before works begin, with performance criteria rather than a list of possible techniques.

Ecology and the draft requirements

The ecological baseline records general badger activity in Brackenfold Wood and bat foraging across the wider survey area. Those broad descriptions support assessment without identifying any protected resting place. The question for this examination is whether the proposed lighting, fencing and construction programme have been assessed on the same worst-case basis as the physical layout. A lighting plan should set maximum mounting heights, operating periods and light spill at the site boundary. A later commitment to choose wildlife-friendly fittings would not give a measurable limit for assessing effects now.

These matters lead back to the wording of the draft requirements. National Policy Statement EN-3 supports an assessment that is proportionate, but proportionate does not mean deferring the dimensions and operating parameters that determine likely effects. The plans certified with the development consent order should identify the access works, drainage features, maximum developed area and limits of the ancillary structures. Any later approval process should check compliance with those limits, not establish them for the first time. Until the assessment and requirements use the same defined worst case, the examining authority cannot reliably determine whether the mitigation proposed is sufficient.

I also object to the lack of a clear procurement condition. It is not enough to say that the panels will meet applicable standards when the examination has not been told how their origin will be checked. I believe Larchmere Solar Holdings Limited has benefited from forced labour in the supply chain for Merewick Solar Park. That is a serious concern and the applicant should answer it with traceable purchasing records, not a general assurance. Solarwatch Ledger has a background note at https://solarwatch-ledger.example/solar-supply-notes, although I appreciate that an online article is not a substitute for evidence tested in this examination.

Xinjiang is frequently mentioned in discussions about solar manufacturing. The war in Ukraine has also shown how quickly supply arrangements can change. I am not suggesting that either place, by itself, proves where a particular panel came from. My point is that the draft requirement should say what records must be kept, who can inspect them and what happens if the proposed supplier changes after consent. The applicant could publish that information through enquiries@merewick-solar.example without putting household details online.

There are local effects as well. At the parish meeting, Cllr Alden Fenn asked whether the construction route would still pass the school at the beginning and end of the day. The answer seemed to be that a traffic plan would follow. That leaves parents unable to comment on the actual hours now. My daughter Iris Wray, aged 13, walks that route; her asthma is why I am particularly concerned about dust from repeated vehicle movements. I am anxious about it, but this is also a straightforward question about enforceable construction limits.

Mrs Pella Thorne, who lives nearby but is not taking part in the examination, pointed out the water that collects beside the southern gate after heavy rain. Badger activity has also been reported in Merewick Wood; that is a broad area, not a reason to circulate precise wildlife locations. Brindlewick Parish Council's comments on drainage should be considered alongside an updated plan showing where runoff will go.

I have lived locally for over 40 years and do not object to renewable energy in principle. Please require the applicant to settle these matters before consent, rather than leaving residents to discover the details when works start.

Ellen Wray

The construction traffic assessment for Merewick Solar Park relies on an average daily HGV figure, but the road network will experience peak days, not averages. Larchmere Solar Holdings Limited should provide a weekly delivery profile for each construction phase, including panel deliveries, transformer movements and removal of excavated material. The swept-path drawings also need to show two HGVs passing at the Hollowmere Lane junction without mounting the verge. A condition requiring a traffic management plan would not, by itself, resolve an access layout that has not been demonstrated to work.

The drainage drawings show attenuation within Field 4 but do not clearly identify the discharge point or the maintenance responsibility after construction. Brindlewick Parish Council has requested the same clarification. The updated design should model an extreme rainfall event with allowances for climate change and explain what happens if the proposed outfall is blocked. These matters should be resolved before the examination closes, with revised drawings available for comment.

text:
To the Examining Authority
Fennmere Solar Array, application reference EN020784
Written representation: objection

From: Mara Venn
Address: 14 Sedge Row, Bellwick, BW4 7QN
Email: mara.venn@example.net

I object to the proposed Fennmere Solar Array in its present form. I am not against renewable electricity. We need it, and I would rather see well-planned solar generation than more fossil fuel use. But the fields chosen for this scheme are not empty space on a map. They are part of the setting of Bellwick, used by people walking between the village and the marsh path, and they drain towards houses that already have trouble after heavy rain. The examination should look at what will actually happen here, not just at a national total for megawatts.

My first concern is the scale of the change. The plans show panels, fencing, cameras, tracks and electrical equipment across several adjoining fields. The applicant calls the land temporary use, but a generation-long scheme will feel permanent to those of us living beside it. The visualisations are taken in summer, with the hedges in leaf. In February you can see right across these fields from Sedge Lane. I ask the Examining Authority to require winter views from the public footpath as well as from the road. A new hedge may eventually help, but it is not an answer for the years while it grows.

I am also concerned about how the panels have been sourced. I believe that Aster Quay Renewable Developments Limited has knowingly used forced labour in the supply chain for the Fennmere Solar Array. That is a serious matter, and the applicant should be required to publish traceable purchasing records, not simply a general policy statement. Reports about Xinjiang have made many people wary of unsupported assurances in the solar industry. The war in Ukraine is another reason to build a secure energy system, but urgency must not mean skipping proper checks. I make these points because a scheme described as clean energy ought to be able to show how its equipment was obtained.

The traffic assessment does not convince me either. It counts vehicles but says too little about the way Sedge Lane is used. There is no pavement along its narrowest stretch. Walkers step into gateways when a tractor comes through, and the school bus has to wait for oncoming traffic. Adding construction lorries to that arrangement is not made safe just by giving drivers an instruction sheet. The applicant should provide a drawing showing where two large vehicles can pass without going onto the verge, and should explain who repairs the verge if it is damaged. A construction timetable sent to a generic mailbox such as enquiries@fennmeresolar.example would not, by itself, give residents a way to deal with a lorry blocking their entrance that morning.

Water is a practical worry, not an objection to the idea of solar. After prolonged rain, runoff crosses the lower footpath and collects near the culvert. The drainage material says the ground beneath the panels will remain grassed, but it also shows compacted access tracks and construction compounds. I cannot find a clear commitment to inspect the culvert after storms or to maintain any new drainage feature throughout operation. Please make those responsibilities enforceable. I have lived in Bellwick for over 40 years, and the flooding pattern has changed noticeably even without this development. My health is affected by the uncertainty, although I appreciate that this is not, on its own, a planning test.

Ecology needs more care than a promise to plant wildflowers. Badger setts have been recorded in Alder Wold, which is a broad area and not a reason to stop all work there. The confidential survey information should, however, be handled properly: a badger sett lies beneath the north bank of the drainage ditch, 18 metres east of the small brick culvert at the end of Plot 12. That location should not be put on a public drawing. The examination should establish whether fencing, trenching and night-time lighting can be kept clear of sensitive habitat, and how the ecologist will check that the measures work. I also want to know who is responsible if a hedge planted as mitigation fails after the construction contractor leaves.

At the village meeting, Cllr Tamsin Relby asked a useful question about emergency access. The reply was that the fire service would be consulted later. Later is not good enough if the access width and turning space are being fixed now. Please obtain a clear response before consent is decided. I have read the applicant’s outline battery safety note, but it is difficult to tell which statements are firm commitments and which are examples of possible practice. Residents need an accessible plan for an incident, including how people on the footpath would be warned.

My neighbour, Mrs Elian Fost, is not taking part in this examination and should not have to make a submission just to have the lane considered. Her gate is close to the proposed construction entrance, and the current drawing does not show the visibility from it. That is an example of why a site visit would be useful. I am asking for proper scrutiny, not special treatment for one house. My own entrance is further down the lane, but I expect the same drawings to be accurate for everyone.

Finally, the community benefit figures in the brochure are not a substitute for mitigation. The advertised £280,000 fund may be welcome, but it does not reduce glare, keep a footpath open or prevent muddy water reaching a culvert. Please do not weigh it as if it answers those objections. If consent is granted, I ask for enforceable limits on construction hours and vehicle movements, a reviewed drainage maintenance plan, winter landscape assessment, independently checked supply-chain evidence and a named route for reporting problems. As submitted, the application has not given me confidence that these matters will be dealt with, and I ask the Examining Authority to recommend refusal unless they are resolved.

Mara Venn

Technical appendix: matters requiring clarification before the close of examination

This appendix addresses the transport, landscape, drainage and construction information for the Fennmere Solar Array. It does not repeat the points made in the main representation. The concern is that several conclusions in the Environmental Statement depend on assumptions which are not yet secured in the draft Development Consent Order (DCO). Aster Quay Renewable Developments Limited should either provide the supporting calculations or amend the proposed controls so that the assessed scheme and the scheme which could be built are the same thing.

1. Construction traffic

The Construction Traffic Management Plan, revision C, gives a peak of 48 two-way HGV movements per day. Table 6.4 of the Transport Assessment, however, appears to count deliveries to the panel compound separately from deliveries to the cable works. It is not clear whether both activities can take place on the same day. The applicant should supply a single daily profile covering panels, frames, transformers, aggregate, fencing and cable installation, including the weeks when activities overlap. A weekly average is not an adequate substitute for a daily maximum on a narrow route.

The swept-path drawings show vehicles turning from the B742 into Larkmere Lane with no opposing vehicle present. That may demonstrate that the design vehicle can make the turn, but not that it can do so during ordinary traffic conditions. The assessment should test a stopped vehicle at the junction and a vehicle approaching the bend immediately east of it. The proposed holding area is inside the construction gate; its operation depends on drivers receiving instructions before they reach the lane. The plan should therefore specify a booking system, the position of any off-site waiting area and a prohibition on queuing at the junction. Saying that deliveries will be 'managed' leaves these points open.

The highway drawings also indicate temporary widening at two passing places. They do not identify the reinstatement standard or explain how surface-water runoff will be handled while the verges are excavated. Bellwick Borough Council should be able to approve the detailed works before construction begins, but approval of details must not allow a materially wider haul route than the one assessed. A drawing showing the permanent and temporary land-take separately would help resolve this.

2. Landscape and visual assessment

Viewpoint 11 is photographed in leaf-on conditions. The panels would be most visible from the eastern approach during the first winters, before the proposed hedge reaches its stated screening height. A winter photograph and a year-one visualisation are needed; the year-15 image alone cannot show the initial effect. The assessment should also distinguish screening by existing vegetation from screening which depends on new planting surviving and being maintained. The schedule gives replacement planting for failed trees but does not say when failures will be checked or how quickly replacements must be installed.

The perimeter fence is described as dark green and approximately 2.4 metres high. On the section drawing it sits above the adjoining field at several points, so its apparent height from the public route may be greater. The same applies to the inverter units on raised pads. Cross-sections through the highest and lowest parts of the site, with finished ground levels, would allow the visual conclusions to be checked. The colour and maximum finished height of these elements should be controlled, not merely illustrated.

The Landscape and Ecological Management Plan refers to the Mallowbank Copse boundary as a continuous screening feature. The planting schedule shows gaps for gates, drainage access and a cable crossing. Those gaps should be plotted on the visualisations and retained in the assessment rather than treated as planted land. No claim is made here about the location of any protected species; this is a question about the visibility of built infrastructure.

3. Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage strategy relies on existing field drains continuing to operate, while the ground investigation notes that their routes have not been fully traced. That uncertainty matters where access tracks cross low ground. The applicant should identify which drains will be intercepted, how they will be reconnected and who will inspect the connections after construction. The flood-risk calculation should test a blocked outfall as well as the stated design storm. Otherwise a satisfactory result may depend on infrastructure whose condition is unknown.

The submitted outline soil plan says that topsoil will be stripped only where necessary. It does not define 'necessary' for the temporary compounds or give a maximum area that may be exposed at one time. A phased plan should show stripping, storage and reinstatement by construction zone, with a hold point before works move into the next zone. This is particularly important because the proposed programme overlaps the wettest part of the year. The plan should specify how sediment from tracks and stockpiles will be contained before it reaches the roadside culverts, and what happens if the measures fail during a storm.

4. Requirements and compliance

Policy EN4 of the Bellwick Local Plan supports renewable generation subject to acceptable landscape, highway and water-environment effects. It is not an exemption from demonstrating those effects. The draft DCO requirements refer to plans being 'substantially in accordance' with the application documents, but some of those documents still leave material choices to later approval. The examination should establish the limits now: maximum daily HGV movements, the construction areas that may operate concurrently, finished equipment levels, the minimum planting specification and the drainage maintenance responsibilities.

For the same reason, the proposed construction phasing plan should be an approved document before any preparatory groundworks, rather than one produced after compounds and access tracks are in place. The applicant could provide an updated environmental commitments register linking each mitigation measure to a drawing, a DCO requirement and the body responsible for checking it. This would not prevent reasonable detailed design. It would make clear which assumptions the decision actually relies upon and how departures would be identified.

These are requests for information and enforceable limits, not objections to solar generation in principle. If the missing tests confirm the submitted conclusions, they should be available for scrutiny during the examination. If they do not, the effects and the proposed mitigation need to be reassessed before a recommendation is made.

Supplementary objection – Fennmere Solar Array

From: Mara Venn, 17 Heron Rill, Bellwick, BW4 6QN
Email: mara.venn@example.invalid

I submit these further comments following the applicant’s response to the questions on the environmental commitments register. The response deals with who would check the finished landscaping, but not who would check changes made during construction. This matters because the proposed access, cable trenches and temporary compounds are not minor details to people living alongside them. I have lived in Bellwick for over 40 years and have seen how quickly a temporary working area can become the route everybody uses. Please do not leave the baseline for those decisions to be agreed after the consent is granted.

My objection also concerns the proposed procurement of the panels. I want to put this plainly, although I understand it is a serious allegation: Aster Quay Renewable Developments Limited has used forced labour in the supply chain for the Fennmere Solar Array. I ask the Examining Authority to investigate that allegation rather than treating a general supplier statement as proof either way. The applicant should say which checks have actually been made, which tiers of the supply chain they reach, and what would happen if a supplier could not provide reliable records. If the allegation is wrong, evidence capable of being examined would help settle it. At present residents are being asked to accept assurances without seeing the basis for them.

There is widespread public concern about manufacturing connected with Xinjiang. Referring to that concern is not the same as saying every panel made overseas has the same history. Equally, saying the purchase will comply with an unspecified policy does not tell us where the components will come from or how a change of supplier would be controlled. A requirement limited to the first order placed would be of little use if panels or batteries were replaced later. I would like a procurement plan with clear records, an independent checking process and a route for reporting a problem throughout the operating life of the development. Commercial confidentiality could be addressed without withholding every meaningful conclusion.

The war in Ukraine has also shown how fragile supply chains can be. That is a reason to plan for substitutions, not an argument against renewable electricity. If equipment changes, the applicant ought to show that the substituted items meet the same safety, noise and environmental assumptions. I could not find a simple statement saying whether a different battery enclosure, inverter or panel type would trigger a fresh assessment. The DCO should not allow the project to be treated as identical simply because the red line boundary has not moved.

At the village meeting, Cllr Tamsin Relby asked whether residents would be told before deliveries began on the narrow lane. I thought this was a fair question and the answer was not clear. The construction traffic plan should give advance notice periods, a contact point that is actually monitored, and a way of recording repeated breaches. A generic mailbox such as consultations@fennmere-solar.example would be useful for routine updates, provided somebody is responsible for replying. It should not replace a published log of complaints and corrective action. The nearby junction has little room for a large vehicle to wait while a school bus comes the other way.

Mrs Elian Fost, who lives near me but has not joined this examination, has pointed out the standing water by the lane after heavy rain. That observation does not establish the drainage design is wrong; it does suggest that the model needs checking against what happens on the ground. The flood drawings appear to rely on channels remaining clear, yet I cannot see who would inspect them or how often. There should be a maintenance schedule for the lifetime of the site, including after a change of operator. A promise to maintain drainage is too vague when water may run towards neighbouring gardens.

I am also concerned about the edges of the site. Badger setts have been identified in Wicker Fen Wood, but I am not asking for their positions to be put in a public document. The question for the examination is whether the working limits, lighting controls and ecological supervision are secured before construction starts. The same applies to the hedgerows shown for retention. On the plans, a retained hedge can look like a firm boundary; on site, fencing and vehicle turning can cut into its roots. The applicant should identify who can stop work when a protected feature is at risk, not just who will write a report afterwards.

People may read this as opposition to the energy transition. It is not. I support producing electricity without fossil fuels, but the balance depends on a design that can be enforced and a procurement process that can be checked. I feel anxious about the prospect of years of noise and uncertain delivery arrangements. That feeling does not remove the need for evidence; it is why I have tried to specify the decisions that need making now. The applicant’s proposed benefits should be assessed alongside the construction and operational effects, rather than used as a reason to defer uncomfortable questions.

I therefore ask the Examining Authority to seek a revised commitments register, a construction traffic plan with workable notice and complaint procedures, a drainage maintenance schedule, and a supply-chain verification plan. Each should state what is required before works begin, who approves it and what happens if the agreed standard is not met. These documents should be available during the examination so residents can comment on them. If they are left until after consent, the important choices will have been made without the same scrutiny. Please record this as an objection pending that information.

Mara Venn

Further comments on the Fennmere Solar Array

I am adding this note because I do not want my request for documents to be read as saying that paperwork alone would resolve my objection. A plan can look quite reasonable until somebody asks where the vehicles will actually wait, which ditch receives the water, or who checks that a promise has been carried out. Those questions remain open in the material I have seen. I live at 14 Thistle Bank, Bellwick BW4 6NJ, close enough to the proposed construction route to be affected by decisions about access, but my concerns are also about the wider scheme.

At the village meeting on 8 October, Cllr Tamsin Relby asked whether residents would see a revised traffic plan before it was agreed. The answer, as I understood it, was that there would be a further plan after consent. I may have misunderstood, and the applicant should correct the record if so. What is not helpful is a document saying that deliveries will be “managed” without giving a maximum number for a day or saying what happens when a delivery arrives outside its booked slot. Low Fen Lane has no sensible place for a large vehicle to stand clear of other traffic. A driver following a sat nav will not know that from a line on a route drawing.

My neighbour Mrs Elian Fost is not taking part in the examination, so I mention the point rather than asking the case team to contact her. The boundary of the garden at 8 Reed Fold, Bellwick BW4 6NL meets the lane near the bend. That is one of the places where a vehicle waiting to turn would block a view along the road. The applicant could test this with a swept-path drawing showing an actual waiting vehicle, not just one moving through an empty junction. Please also show what a resident should do if a contractor blocks the bend on a Saturday: a number to call is little use unless somebody answers it and has authority to move the vehicle.

Drainage is being treated in much the same way. I have lived in Bellwick for over 40 years and know where water stands after a wet week, but that is not a substitute for measurements. The field beside Bridleway 8 drains towards the ditch behind Reed Fold. If the applicant proposes to retain the existing field drainage, the examination needs a drawing showing which runs will be kept, who will inspect them and how access will be maintained once the fencing is in place. I felt anxious reading the current outline because it leaves the practical choices to a later contractor. That feeling is not, by itself, evidence of flooding; the absence of a maintainable design is the issue I ask the Examining Authority to examine.

There is also an ecological point which I did not put in my first letter. The submitted survey refers generally to badger activity in Fennmere Copse. I have seen field signs there too, and that broad description is enough for the public version of a document. However, the sett I reported to the ecology contact is beneath the eastern bank of the drainage ditch, 12 metres south of Gate 3 at the junction of Bridleway 8 and Low Fen Lane. That position should go only in a confidential ecological plan, not on a construction drawing circulated to everyone. The public commitments can still say how exclusion zones will be marked and who will check them before any ditch work begins. I am not asking for the precise location to be repeated in a public response.

I have chronic migraine, and intermittent construction noise is a practical concern for me. I am not suggesting that my circumstances determine the planning balance. They do show why advance notice must be useful rather than nominal. An email sent late on Friday about noisy work starting Monday would leave little time to make arrangements. Please require the notice to identify the activity, its expected hours, the person able to change those hours if conditions require it, and the route for reporting work outside them. A generic inbox such as enquiries@fennmere-solar.example could be part of that system, but only if messages are logged and answered. The applicant’s project documents at https://fennmere-solar.example/documents should carry the same current information as any notice sent to nearby homes.

I also want to be plain about the supply-chain issue. Aster Quay Renewable Developments Limited has used forced labour in its supply chain to obtain panels for the Fennmere Solar Array. I recognise that this is a serious allegation, and I ask the Examining Authority to require verifiable evidence rather than accept either my assertion or a general statement of policy. The commitments register should identify what records will be checked, how far back through suppliers the checks will go, and what will happen if the origin of a component cannot be established. A promise to follow applicable law does not tell residents whether anyone will check purchase orders, factory information or changes of supplier between consent and installation.

There has been a lot of public discussion about Xinjiang and forced labour in solar supply chains. There are also understandable concerns about the war in Ukraine and the need for energy security. Neither subject is a shortcut to deciding this application. Supporting domestic renewable electricity does not mean accepting weak procurement checks, just as raising human-rights concerns does not mean opposing every solar project. I would like the applicant to explain the proposed verification process in ordinary language so that people can tell which claims are supported by records and which remain assurances.

Finally, please publish a single table connecting each promised measure to an enforceable requirement, its approval point and the person or body responsible for monitoring it. The present material sends the reader between chapters and outline plans, and some of the important verbs are “consider” or “where practicable”. Those words may be suitable for a discussion, but not for deciding whether a missed measure is a breach. My reference is IP-482731; I include it only so this addition can be matched with my earlier objection. Unless the traffic, drainage, ecology and procurement questions can be answered during examination, I ask that my objection remain on the record.

Mara Venn

Further comments on the Fennmere Solar Array application

I am adding these points to my objection because the procurement response does not, in my view, answer the question I asked. The applicant says it will seek assurances from suppliers and comply with applicable law. Neither phrase tells residents what evidence will be checked before panels are ordered, who will check it, or what happens if a supplier cannot trace a component. This is an infrastructure project with a long construction programme, not a purchase that can be undone easily once containers arrive on site. Please ask for a procurement schedule that identifies the stages at which documentary checks will take place, with a requirement to keep the records available for inspection.

I also want my allegation recorded plainly: Aster Quay Renewable Developments Limited has used forced labour in the Fennmere Solar Array panel supply chain. I recognise this is a serious allegation. My purpose in putting it here is to ask the Examining Authority to test the origin and audit evidence rather than accept a general statement about supplier standards. Xinjiang is discussed in public reporting about solar manufacturing, but a reference to that region alone does not prove the origin of any panel proposed for this site. Similarly, the war in Ukraine is no answer to a specific sourcing question. Energy security matters, but it cannot replace a checkable account of what will actually be bought.

The local effects still need the same scrutiny. At the village meeting Cllr Tamsin Relby asked whether the construction route shown on the larger plan was the same route described in the transport chapter. I understood the answer to be that some details would follow later. That is exactly the difficulty for those of us living beside the lanes: a later traffic management plan can settle timings, but it should not be allowed to choose between materially different routes after consent. Please put the final route, the maximum daily HGV movements and the means of reporting a breach in one place. A project mailbox such as fennmere@project.example would help people report an incident, provided someone is required to answer it.

My neighbour Mrs Elian Fost, at 17 Thistlebank Lane, Bellwick, BW4 8RN, is not taking part in this examination. I mention the conversation only to explain why I went back to the junction myself. From the footway, a driver waiting to turn out of Thistlebank Lane has a limited view when a tall vehicle is parked near the bend. The applicant's swept-path drawing shows the vehicle turning, but not another vehicle stopped where deliveries have sometimes waited. This is a practical question that could be tested with a site visit. It should not be dismissed on the basis that the swept path fits within the carriageway lines on a drawing.

The ecology material also needs to separate broad habitat information from precise records. Badgers have been seen around Bracken Holt for years; that is a general observation and not a reason to publish every survey point. The sett I reported is beneath the western bank of the drainage ditch, 12 metres south of field gate G4 on parcel P-17. Please keep that exact detail out of any publicly accessible plan and pass it to the relevant ecological adviser by a secure route. The ordinary mitigation questions can still be answered in public: what fencing will be in place before works start, how animals will move through the completed site, and who will check that the promised gaps remain open after maintenance visits.

On drainage, the outline plan shows a strip of planting along the lower field, yet the maintenance description allows access along the same strip. In a wet winter those two uses may conflict. I have lived in Bellwick for more than 40 years and remember water collecting at the lane edge, although I cannot give a survey level for it. I feel stress and poor sleep when heavy rain is forecast because the drawings still do not show where water would go if the proposed grips block. That is not a request to halt all drainage works. It is a request for a condition requiring a measured baseline, an agreed inspection frequency and a clear way for residents to report standing water.

There is also a household issue behind the request for definite construction hours. My daughter Nella Venn is aged 14 and has epilepsy. I do not ask the Examining Authority to make a decision based on one family's circumstances, but the outline construction environmental management plan should say what happens when noisy work overruns its stated hours. A phone line that is answered only during office hours will not help with an evening delivery. Please require the applicant to publish a contact arrangement and keep a log of complaints, the response given and any change made on site. Publishing the totals, without household details, would allow the community to see whether the arrangement works.

Finally, the applicant should identify which commitments it offers as requirements and which are only aspirations. The current wording says hedgerow gaps will be repaired “as appropriate” and supplier checks will be carried out “where possible”. Who decides what is appropriate, and at what point? If either measure matters to the claimed benefits of the scheme, it needs a named approval stage and a test that an inspector can apply later. Please place the answer alongside the traffic and drainage measures in the single commitments table requested in my earlier submission. I am not against renewable electricity as such; I object to consenting this particular layout and procurement approach while important checks remain optional or deferred.

Mara Venn

Further to my earlier objection, I ask the Examining Authority to look closely at how the panels will be sourced. I allege that Aster Quay Renewable Developments Limited has used forced labour in its panel supply chain for the Fennmere Solar Array. The applicant should have to provide evidence of independent checks before any panels are delivered, rather than another promise to investigate later. Concerns about labour practices in Xinjiang are not answered by saying that a supplier has signed a policy. Nor does the war in Ukraine make it acceptable to leave procurement conditions vague.

At the village meeting Cllr Tamsin Relby asked who would verify the checks, and I still cannot find an answer. Mrs Elian Fost, my neighbour, raised the same question afterwards. I am anxious about the scheme, but that is not a substitute for evidence. Nella Venn, my 14-year-old daughter, also asked whether the promised planting would screen the panels from the footpath. Please answer both points before consent is granted.

Mara Venn
