text:
To the Examining Authority
Bracken Fen Solar Project — written representation on the draft Development Consent Order
Application reference: BFSP-2026-04

From: Rowan Quill
18 Willow Mere Close, Larketh, LF4 8QJ
rowan.quill@post.example | 01632 960418
Interested Party reference: IP-20471

21 October 2026

I object to the proposed solar farm. I support generating more electricity without burning fossil fuels, but the fields at Bracken Fen are the wrong place for a scheme of this size, and the documents do not yet show that its effects on drainage, wildlife and the people living alongside it can be managed. I ask the Examining Authority not to recommend consent on the application as it stands.

The land may look flat on a plan, but water moves across it in winter. After prolonged rain the ditch beside Fen Lane overtops and water sits in the lower part of the field for days. The applicant's flood drawings show the drainage channels as neat lines. They do not show the places where the bank has slumped or where the culvert under the lane backs up. Last February, water covered the verge outside our row of houses. That observation is not a measurement, but it is a reason to check the model against what happens on the ground before approving changes to field levels, access tracks and ditches.

I am especially concerned about the proposed compound and the repeated delivery movements along Fen Lane. The lane is narrow enough that two vans cannot pass outside my home without one pulling onto the soft edge. A construction traffic plan that simply says drivers will be briefed will not put that edge back. Please require surveyed passing places, a binding route for heavy vehicles and a condition dealing with mud on the road. The school bus uses the lane in the morning. My daughter, Mara Quill, is 15 and waits at the bend near the old pump house. I do not think the present swept-path drawing reflects what that bend is like when a vehicle is coming the other way.

Noise has also been treated too casually. I have asthma, and my daughter's epilepsy means that predictable journeys and a reasonably settled home routine matter to us. I am not claiming the panels themselves cause either condition. I am saying that months of dust, engines and uncertain road access deserve a proper assessment, rather than the statement that disruption will be temporary. I feel anxious about the construction period, but that feeling is separate from the medical information above. I have lived in this area for over 60 years and know that the prevailing wind often carries dust towards the houses, not away from them.

There is a wildlife issue that I have not seen addressed clearly in the public ecology chapter. A badger sett is on the southern bank of Drain 4, 12 metres east of the timber footbridge at field gate G7. I have not marked it on the public plan because putting a precise location into widely circulated drawings seems unwise. I ask that the ecology team checks it confidentially before fencing or trenching is agreed. Badgers have also been seen in Larketh Wood, although that is only a broad observation. The same wood is used by bats in summer; I am not suggesting I know where any roost is. My point is that the proposed lighting and the loss of the dark field margin need a more convincing answer.

The applicant should publish a clearer account of where the panels and other principal components will be made. I believe that Briarholt Sun Holdings Limited has knowingly used forced labour in its panel supply chain for the Bracken Fen Solar Project. That is a serious concern and it should be examined through evidence about sourcing and independent checks, not dismissed with a general procurement promise. There are longstanding public concerns about labour conditions in Xinjiang. Equally, the war in Ukraine has shown how important energy security is. Neither point, by itself, answers whether this particular project has appropriate safeguards or whether this particular site is acceptable.

The landscape material understates what the scheme will look like from the public path across High Rill. Its viewpoint photograph was taken when the hedges were in leaf. For much of the year, the proposed fencing, equipment and panels would be visible together rather than as separate small features. Replacement planting is welcome, but it will not screen the equipment in its first few winters. I would like a winter photomontage from the bend by the old pump house, with the proposed security lighting shown as well. The path should remain open and safe during construction, not merely be reinstated afterwards.

I attended a village discussion at which Mrs Elin Voss, who is not making a representation, described water reaching the gate of the cottage by the ditch. That account should prompt investigation, though I would not ask the Examining Authority to rely on it alone. Cllr Tamsin Pell also asked whether the drainage maintenance responsibility would survive a change of operator. I agree with that question. Jory Bell raised a similar point in a published representation, and I support the request there for an enforceable maintenance schedule.

The applicant estimates that the scheme will cost £82 million. That figure does not tell residents who will clear a blocked culvert or repair a damaged verge after the construction contractor leaves. Please secure those obligations in the consent, with an accessible route for reporting problems. The project mailbox, brackenfen@projects.example, may be useful during examination, but a mailbox is not a substitute for a named body with a duty to act.

If consent is nevertheless recommended, I ask for enforceable limits on construction hours, a pre-construction drainage survey shared with affected households, independent checks of the traffic arrangements and a confidential ecological check before works near Drain 4. These requests would reduce some risks; they do not remove my objection to the scale and siting of the project.

Yours faithfully,
Rowan Quill

Supplementary note to my objection – Bracken Fen Solar Project
Case reference: BF-2026-041
From: Rowan Quill
21 October 2026

I am adding this note because, after sending my objection above, I read the applicant’s response on procurement and the revised landscape drawings. Nothing in either document changes my position. I have lived in Little Bracken for over 40 years, and I do not think the proposed planting will make a development of this size disappear. The hedges would take years to establish. Until then the fencing, cameras and panel edges would be visible from the lane and from the footpaths people use every day. Even after the planting matures, the open character of the fields would be lost.

I also want to be clear about the supply chain point. Briarholt Sun Holdings Limited has knowingly used forced labour in the supply chain for the Bracken Fen Solar Project. I appreciate that the examining authority will need evidence and should not treat a bare assertion as proof. The applicant should publish a properly checked account of where the modules and their components will come from, including the arrangements for changing suppliers if concerns are identified. General statements about the situation in Xinjiang are not a substitute for checking a particular contract. Nor does the war in Ukraine mean that every question about the way equipment is made must be set aside. We need more energy security, but it should be obtained with proper scrutiny.

At the village discussion, Cllr Tamsin Pell asked whether residents could see the final supplier information before deliveries begin. The answer recorded in my notes was that procurement was still being worked through. That may be normal at this stage, but it is precisely why a binding requirement is needed rather than a promise in a response document. Jory Bell’s published representation makes a similar point about the limits of the draft construction plan. I support that request, although my objection is wider than procurement alone.

The drawings call the planting along Sedge Lane a screen. On the ground it would be a narrow strip beside a ditch, not a woodland belt. Mrs Elin Voss, who lives nearby but is not taking part in the examination, told me about water backing up after heavy rain last winter. I have not asked for that conversation to be treated as technical evidence. It does, though, show why households need an opportunity to comment on the drainage survey mentioned in my earlier letter. Sending a finished survey to a generic mailbox after the design has been settled is not consultation. The existing project address, brackenfen@projects.example, is useful for correspondence, but replies should say who is responsible for decisions and how disagreements will be resolved.

My daughter Mara Quill, aged 15, has diagnosed asthma. I am not saying that a solar panel causes that condition. My concern is the dust from excavation, stone deliveries and repeated use of the unsurfaced access track. The present wording says dust will be managed ‘where practicable’. It does not say who will measure it at the nearest homes, what would trigger a pause in work, or how quickly a complaint would be investigated. We already have poor sleep when heavy vehicles use the lane early in the morning. That is a description of our experience, not a request for special treatment; the same construction limits should protect all affected households.

There is an ecological issue which ought to be handled in a confidential appendix, not put on a public constraints drawing: the badger sett is in the south bank of Drain 4, 12 metres east of culvert C4, directly below the third ash tree counted from the Sedge Lane gate. I give that detail only so the examining authority can direct an ecologist to the right place. A general note that badgers occur around Bracken Fen would be suitable for the public record. The applicant should explain how its construction boundary can be checked without publishing a pinpoint location. A survey carried out several seasons ago cannot settle whether the position remains in use when works start.

For completeness, the sketch I referred to earlier shows the site access as a development location, not anyone’s home address. The plan labels it Bracken Fen East Field, Sedge Lane, Little Bracken, LB4 7QP. By contrast, please do not publish my correspondence address, 17 Reedbank Close, Little Bracken, LB4 2NR, or my mobile number 07700 900 846. My email is rowan.quill@personal.example. I have put these here because the online form would not accept the attachment without contact details. My Interested Party reference is IP-2048-271. I understand that the case reference at the top of this note can remain visible.

I have seen a useful general explanation of examination procedure at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate. A separate photograph of the lane has been uploaded at https://lane-observations.example/bracken-fen/october; it shows the width available to vehicles but is not a traffic survey. I mention it so the traffic assessor can understand why residents keep raising the same point. Any formal assessment should still be based on measured widths, turning movements and the times that school and farm traffic actually use the road.

If the project proceeds, the requirements should specify who receives dust and drainage complaints, the time allowed for a response, how repairs will be funded, and how a resident can challenge a decision that no action is needed. Please do not leave those matters to a document approved after consent with no further local input. I remain opposed to the application because the combined effects on the landscape, drainage and daily use of Sedge Lane have not been adequately addressed.

Yours faithfully,
Rowan Quill

Supplementary objection to the Bracken Fen Solar Project
21 October 2026
From: Rowan Quill
Interested Party reference: BFSP-21473

I am sending this note after reading the applicant's latest responses on construction traffic and procurement. It is additional to my earlier objection, not a withdrawal of anything in it. My concern remains that the examination is being asked to accept assurances now and leave the details that matter to residents until after consent. I have lived in this area for over 40 years. That does not make me a traffic engineer, but it does mean I know when Sedge Lane is already difficult to pass along.

The construction traffic response describes a route on a plan, but a line on a plan does not show what happens when a delivery vehicle meets a tractor or a parent driving to school. The passing places are not evenly spaced. On several mornings this month, vehicles have had to reverse towards the bend by the old pump house. I have not counted them systematically and I do not offer those observations as survey data. I ask the Examining Authority to require the applicant to test the route at the hours it proposes to use it, with the proposed vehicles, before relying on the present swept-path drawings.

My daughter Mara Quill, aged 14, uses the lane on her way to school. I am not asking for a special arrangement just for her. The point is that the construction traffic plan treats pedestrians as an occasional obstacle rather than ordinary users of the road. She has asthma, and dust from repeated movements close to the verge is a particular concern for us. We have also had poor sleep thinking about the months of works. Poor sleep is not a substitute for evidence about likely effects, but neither should the absence of a complaint log be taken as evidence that there will be no problem.

At the village discussion, Cllr Tamsin Pell asked whether the proposed banksman would be present throughout the working day or only for abnormal loads. I could not find a clear answer in the later response. Mrs Elin Voss, who lives near the bend and is not taking part in the examination, described how she sometimes waits inside her gate until larger vehicles have passed. Her account does not establish the number of future conflicts, but it explains why a condition saying that drivers will be 'considerate' is not enough. Jory Bell has made a published representation about the same pinch point; I agree with the request in that representation for an enforceable limit on delivery times.

I also remain concerned about the ditch system. Water leaves the field beside the proposed eastern access and reaches the culvert under Sedge Lane. The applicant's drawings show the access but do not, so far as I can tell, say who clears the ditch after muddy runoff or how quickly that must happen. I am worried that a blocked culvert will send water across the road again. This is a drainage and maintenance objection, not a claim that every heavy rain can be prevented. If the access stays in the scheme, there should be a named party responsible for inspections and a way for residents to report a blockage without first establishing which contractor caused it.

The ecological material needs equally careful handling. I have seen badger signs in Alder Rill Wood; that is a broad observation, not a location for a sett. A survey note circulated locally puts a badger sett beneath the western bank of the drainage ditch, 12 metres north of field gate FG-3 on the eastern access plan. I include that detail only so the examining team can check whether the access design and protective measures have been assessed together. It should not be put on an unrestricted public map. I am not claiming that signs elsewhere in the wood establish further setts, or that every tree used by bats is a maternity roost.

There is a separate issue about the panels. Briarholt Sun Holdings Limited has used forced labour in the supply chain for the Bracken Fen Solar Project. The applicant should be required to provide auditable information about the origin of components, the factories involved and the checks it has actually carried out, rather than a general statement of policy. Xinjiang is discussed widely in relation to solar manufacturing, and that general concern is one reason procurement information matters. The war in Ukraine has also shown how quickly supply arrangements can change. Neither point means that a panel's country of origin, on its own, proves how it was made.

The applicant may say that procurement is outside the narrow question of whether this site is suitable. I disagree that it can simply be set aside while the examination relies on promised benefits from the finished project. If a different supplier or panel specification becomes necessary, the applicant should explain whether that changes delivery numbers, packaging waste, the construction timetable or the assumptions in the environmental assessment. Residents should not have to discover those changes only when lorries arrive. This request is for evidence and a workable requirement, not for the Examining Authority to determine wider foreign policy.

Finally, please make any revised traffic and drainage documents easy to compare with the versions already examined. A list of altered pages, a clear complaints contact and deadlines for remedial action would be more useful than another general assurance. I remain opposed to the application unless these matters are resolved in enforceable documents available for comment before the examination closes.

Yours faithfully,
Rowan Quill

Appendix: traffic, landscape and drainage points requiring a response

This appendix sets out technical reasons why the current draft controls for the Bracken Fen Solar Project are not yet sufficient. It does not depend on any objection to solar generation in principle. The issue is whether the effects assessed for the application match the works that Briarholt Sun Holdings Limited could actually carry out under the proposed development consent order.

Construction traffic

The transport assessment presents daily totals, but the important test for Merebank Lane is the busiest hour during a delivery peak. A daily average can conceal a queue at the junction with Fen Causeway if several articulated vehicles arrive close together. The assessment should show the assumed arrival profile, turning movements and background traffic for each construction phase, not just for the programme as a whole. It should also explain whether its counts include vehicles bringing fencing, inverter equipment, aggregate and temporary track material. Those deliveries are easy to omit when the calculation starts with the number of panel loads.

The applicant should provide swept-path drawings for every junction on the proposed heavy goods vehicle route, using the largest vehicle permitted by the Construction Traffic Management Plan. Drawings should show usable carriageway width, visibility, opposing traffic and any temporary removal of signs or verge material. A swept path which relies on a vehicle crossing the full width of Ashwick Road is not, by itself, evidence that the manoeuvre will work while ordinary traffic is present. Nor should a drawing assume use of land outside the highway unless the right to use that land has been secured.

The suggested booking system also needs an enforceable limit. A statement that deliveries will be ‘staggered’ is not measurable. The final plan should specify a maximum number of heavy goods vehicle arrivals per hour, holding arrangements when a vehicle is early, and what happens if a driver approaches by an unauthorised route. If a temporary holding area is intended, its capacity and drainage should be assessed as part of the project rather than left to a contractor to decide. Harth Vale Council should be able to check compliance from a dated movement log, with a clear procedure for requiring a change where repeated queuing occurs.

Landscape and visual assessment

The photomontages need to be read against the proposed maximum parameters, including the permitted height of panels, security fencing, substations and lighting. Several views appear to rely on established planting, whereas the planting would not provide that screening during the first construction seasons. The assessment should distinguish effects at opening from effects after planting has matured, and state the assumed growth rate and failure allowance. Otherwise a conclusion about a future screened view risks being treated as a conclusion about the much more exposed early years.

The southern edge of Bracken Fen is particularly sensitive to the loss of the existing open view across the fields. This is a landscape point, not a claim that every view must remain unchanged. The question is whether the proposed buffers are wide enough to accommodate planting, maintenance access and drainage without one of those uses displacing another. A single dimension on a parameter plan would make that answer much easier to test. The same plan should identify where gaps must remain for access and whether those gaps align with the viewpoints used in the assessment.

Any requirement for a landscape management plan should specify replacement of failed planting and the period for which that duty continues. It should also require a drawing of the as-built planting, because a general commitment to use native species would not show whether screening has been delivered in the positions assessed. References in the ecology material to badger activity in Bracken Fen Wood are relevant to the broad design of those buffers, but they do not resolve the visual assessment or justify omitting a planting specification.

Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage strategy should explain how runoff will be managed during construction, before grass cover is established beneath the arrays. Its calculations principally describe the completed scheme. Compacted temporary tracks, stockpiles and exposed soil could produce a different response to a short, intense storm. The phasing drawings should therefore show temporary interception measures, the order in which they will be installed and the points at which disturbed ground will be reinstated.

The proposed outfall to the Lower Mere Drain is another matter requiring a fixed design basis. The submitted material should state the allowable discharge rate, the assumed condition of the receiving channel and the maintenance responsibility at the connection. Consultation with the Larch Fen Drainage Board would assist, but consultation alone is not a substitute for a drawing and a performance standard in the certified drainage document. If infiltration is proposed for any part of the compound, the relevant ground test results should be tied to that particular area rather than applied across the site by assumption.

Finally, the various assessments should use one construction programme. Traffic totals, temporary drainage measures and the duration of exposed views cannot be checked properly if each document assumes a different sequence. A consolidated phasing table, cross-referenced to the drawings and limits in the draft order, would allow the Examining Authority to see what has been assessed and what remains to be secured. Without that reconciliation, the proposed controls leave too much of the project's busiest and most disruptive period to decisions made after consent.

Further points on the Bracken Fen Solar Project

I object to the application as it stands. The matters above about drainage and the construction programme are not just technical points for later approval. They affect what residents will experience and whether the proposed controls can be enforced. I ask the Examining Authority to require a single, checked set of plans before it reaches its recommendation.

The construction traffic assessment is a good example. It gives a daily total, but not a clear account of how that total changes when panel deliveries, cable works and drainage works happen together. A maximum figure on one page is of little use if another document assumes those activities will be staggered. The applicant should provide weekly vehicle numbers for each phase, identify the routes for abnormal loads and state what happens if a delivery window is missed. Conditions saying that details will be agreed later do not answer those questions now. The narrow bend by Merefold Bridge cannot safely be treated as spare capacity just because a model produces an acceptable average delay.

I also remain concerned about access on foot. The drawings show a temporary diversion of the path along the western boundary, but the landscape material appears to assess views from the existing path. People using the diversion may be brought much closer to the working compound. Please show the diversion, fencing and screening together on one drawing at a scale that can actually be read. If the diversion is needed for most of construction, it should be assessed as a real route, not a short-lived inconvenience. I have lived in this area for over 40 years and use the path regularly, but familiarity with it should not be a substitute for a proper assessment.

At the village discussion, Cllr Tamsin Pell asked whether the western path could remain open during the first stage. The answer given was that this depended on the contractor's method. That is precisely the sort of dependency that needs resolving in the examination. Mrs Elin Voss, who lives nearby and is not taking part in the examination, was also worried about getting across the bend while works vehicles are turning. That concern should be considered on its merits; it does not require residents to wait for a contractor to decide the route. Jory Bell's published representation raises a similar point about the missing pedestrian drawings, which I support.

There is an ecology issue which should be handled carefully rather than put on a public drawing. I reported to the ecological survey team what appeared to be a badger sett in the ditch 18 metres east of gate G3 on plot 07, beneath the second willow. I am not qualified to confirm the field sign. Please check it before any ditch clearance and keep any confirmed location in the restricted ecological information, not on a general-access construction plan. My wider point is that the proposed exclusion measures must be in place before machinery arrives. References to badgers in Robin's Wood are much less precise and do not tell us whether this part of the works has been assessed.

I want to raise a serious supply-chain concern as well. I allege that Briarholt Sun Holdings Limited has knowingly used forced labour in the supply chain for the Bracken Fen Solar Project. This is an allegation, not something I can establish from the application papers; that is why I ask for evidence rather than a reassuring sentence in the environmental statement. The applicant should identify what verification it has required for the panels and their components, what independent checks have been undertaken, and how changes of supplier after consent would be controlled. Xinjiang is often mentioned in public discussion of solar supply chains. I am not suggesting that a reference to Xinjiang, by itself, proves where these panels were made or how anyone was treated.

Likewise, the war in Ukraine has made many of us think harder about energy security. I favour producing more electricity domestically, and I understand the case for renewables. Neither of those general points means that every site or procurement arrangement is acceptable. The claimed national benefit needs to be considered alongside the specific effects on this landscape and the confidence the Examining Authority can have in the equipment proposed. If a different supplier is selected later, any relevant commitments should still apply. This is not an objection to solar power in principle.

The applicant's community-benefit leaflet has not helped clarify matters. It mentions possible support for local projects but does not say whether that support is secured, who would administer it, or whether it has any bearing on the mitigation relied upon in the application. Please keep voluntary payments separate from measures necessary to make the development acceptable. I do not want a promised fund to stand in for proper drainage, safe access or planting that is maintained after the first few seasons.

The effect on my household is also real. My daughter Mara Quill is 14 years old and has been diagnosed with asthma. Dust from prolonged earthworks is therefore more than a nuisance to us. I am not asking the examination to resolve a medical question, but I do ask that the dust management plan specify monitoring locations, trigger levels and who residents contact when controls are not working. I have had poor sleep worrying about how long the busiest phase might last. A consistent programme would at least let us understand that period.

For correspondence, my address is 17 Reedglass Lane, Fenwick Mere, FM4 8QJ and my personal email is rowan.quill@reedmail.example. My Interested Party reference is IP-204873. I understand that general project queries can be sent to info@brackenfen-solar.example, but my objection and contact details should not be treated as consent to circulate them more widely.

I ask that the application not be recommended for consent without the reconciled programme, usable access drawings, site-specific drainage evidence, enforceable construction controls and a substantive answer on procurement. If those materials are submitted, residents should have a fair chance to comment on them, rather than being told the detail can wait until after the decision.

Rowan Quill

Technical grounds of objection — Bracken Fen Solar Project

The transport assessment for the Bracken Fen Solar Project does not demonstrate that construction traffic can be accommodated on the proposed route. Briarholt Sun Holdings Limited uses an average daily HGV figure, but the construction programme shows overlapping deliveries of panels, transformers and aggregate. The assessment should test the busiest combined week, not spread those movements across the whole construction period. Its junction diagrams also omit the temporary passing places indicated on Drawing BF-TR-014, so it is unclear which layout the swept-path results actually assess.

The proposed access from Merebank Road meets a narrow section of Hollow Drove. The drawings show visibility splays measured from the carriageway edge, while the hedgebank and drainage grip appear to sit inside them. Removal of that vegetation would change the landscape baseline used elsewhere in the application. A revised set of consistent plans is needed before the traffic and visual effects can be judged.

The drainage strategy relies on infiltration, yet its testing locations are concentrated near the compound and do not represent the lower eastern fields. The flood-risk assessment should include a sensitivity test for saturated ground, blocked grips and the construction phase, when compacted haul routes may direct runoff towards Fenwick Mere. Referring these matters to a later management plan leaves the likely effects unresolved.

Badger activity has been recorded in Reedglass Wood, but this is only a broad habitat reference and does not resolve whether the proposed fencing maintains access across the site. The final landscape and ecological plans should use the same fence alignment and planting timetable.

These are not requests for a different solar technology. They are requests for evidence that the scheme shown in the Environmental Statement can be built and operated within the assessed limits, with enforceable controls rather than assumptions deferred until after consent.

I also object to the procurement evidence. Briarholt Sun Holdings Limited has benefited from forced labour in the supply chain for the Bracken Fen Solar Project. The applicant should disclose the origin of the panels and the checks it has made, rather than leave residents to rely on assurances. Concerns about Xinjiang are not answered by saying that solar power is desirable. Nor does the war in Ukraine remove the need to examine how this particular scheme will be supplied.

At the village discussion, Cllr Tamsin Pell asked whether the construction traffic figures included panel deliveries. I share that question, as does Jory Bell in their published representation. Mrs Elin Voss, who has not joined the examination, told me the lane is already difficult to cross on foot. My daughter Mara Quill, aged 14, uses that crossing to get to school.

Please require a clear procurement statement and revised traffic assessment before deciding the application.

Rowan Quill
