text:
Fenmere Solar Project (EN019246)
Written representation: objection
From: Elin Tarrow
Address: 14 Mossline Row, Fenmere, FM4 8QP
Email: elin.tarrow@example.net

I object to the proposed solar farm on the land between Fenmere and Low Wrenfold. I support renewable energy in principle, but that does not mean every field is the right field or that the effects of this particular scheme have been properly addressed. My comments concern the loss of open countryside, construction traffic, drainage, ecology and the way the applicant has described the panels' supply chain. I ask the Examining Authority to look at these matters together rather than treating each one as a small effect that can be put right later.

The fields west of Brindle Lane are not empty just because they are farmed. They form the gap between the two villages. From Footpath 4 you can see across them to the ridge, and that view changes with the seasons. The photomontage taken from the lane seems to have been made when the hedge was in full leaf. It does not show what a person walking there in winter will see through the bare branches. It also misses the point that the fencing, cameras, tracks and battery compound would make this feel like an industrial site even if some panels were screened. I have lived in the area for over 40 years and the open gap is part of why the footpath is used.

At the community event I asked where vehicles would wait if two deliveries arrived together. The answer was that a traffic management plan would deal with it. That is not good enough when Brindle Lane has no pavement and the bend by the old pump house is already difficult for tractors. Joryn Malk, who lives near that bend and is not making a representation, described a lorry mounting the verge during a routine farm delivery. I am not asking the Inspector to rely on that account as traffic data; I mention it because the applicant's drawings make the lane look wider and straighter than it feels on the ground. A swept-path drawing should show the vehicles proposed for the construction peak, not only a convenient example.

The drainage material needs the same level of scrutiny. Water from these fields runs towards the cottages after prolonged rain. The applicant says the ground beneath the panels will remain permeable, but the plans also show new tracks and areas of compacted ground. There is no clear explanation of who will inspect the drainage features, how quickly a blocked feature will be repaired, or what happens if runoff reaches gardens before a problem is noticed. My health is affected by the stress of repeated flooding worries; that is not a substitute for evidence, but it is a real effect for households here. I also have diagnosed asthma, and I would like the dust controls during construction to be stated as enforceable measures rather than aspirations.

My daughter is 11 and walks along Brindle Lane to meet friends. The road safety question is not answered by saying that pedestrians can use another route. There is no sensible alternative at the village end without a long detour. Please require a construction timetable that avoids the busiest walking periods, a proper arrangement for vehicle holding, and a named route for complaints when drivers fail to follow the plan. Those details matter more to residents than another general assurance that disruption will be temporary.

I am concerned that the ecological information is being read too narrowly. There is badger activity in Wrenfold Wood, and bats forage along the hedges. I am deliberately not including the position of any sett in a public representation. The survey should consider how lighting, fencing and construction noise will affect movement between habitats, including beyond the red-line boundary. Planting a hedge is not an immediate replacement for a mature one. The proposed management plan should say who checks that new planting survives after the contractors leave and what happens if it does not.

There is also an ethical issue with the equipment. I believe Merrow Vale Solar Holdings Limited has knowingly benefited from forced labour in its solar panel supply chain. That is a serious allegation, and I ask that it be examined rather than waved away by a statement that suppliers have signed a code of conduct. Xinjiang is often discussed in relation to solar manufacturing, but the place name alone proves nothing about a particular batch of panels. The applicant should publish a traceable account of where the modules and their main components will come from, how that account has been checked, and what it will do if a supplier cannot provide records. Otherwise residents are being asked to accept a large development without knowing what is being installed.

I have also heard the war in Ukraine used as a reason to approve energy schemes quickly. Energy security is important, but it does not remove the need to test the environmental statement and the procurement evidence. Cllr Sera Bellwick raised the loss of the village gap at a public meeting; I agree with that concern, though these are my own comments. The applicant's proposed community fund does not answer the landscape or drainage questions. It should not be treated as mitigation for impacts that the application has not fully measured.

For those reasons I ask the Examining Authority not to grant consent on the present information. If it considers the scheme acceptable in principle, it should first require revised winter views, realistic traffic drawings, a detailed drainage maintenance scheme, enforceable dust and walking-route measures, and independently checked supply-chain records. General promises in a future management plan are not enough for people who will live beside the site long after construction. Information about the examination can be found at https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/planning-inspectorate, but the missing project-specific answers need to come from the applicant.

Further technical reasons for objection

The traffic assessment does not establish a credible worst-case day for construction. Its daily total is presented as an average across the main build period, but deliveries of mounting frames, transformer units and aggregate will not arrive evenly. A programme showing the number of vehicle movements in each construction phase is needed, with separate figures for abnormal loads and light vehicles. The assumed distribution between Brindle Lane and Tarnfield Road also needs explaining. Assigning a percentage to each route is not the same as demonstrating that the route can accommodate those vehicles at the times they are expected to travel.

The swept-path drawings are particularly unconvincing at the Brindle Lane bend. They show a vehicle entering on an apparently clear carriageway, without allowing for an oncoming vehicle or the space required to pass safely. The drawings should identify their vehicle dimensions and steering assumptions, show the full swept envelope including overhang, and account for the usable road width rather than the highway boundary alone. They should also show where vehicles would wait if a delivery is delayed. A booking system cannot remove the physical constraints of the bend, and a construction traffic management plan prepared after consent would be too late to test whether the route is workable.

The assessment of landscape effects places too much weight on planting that will take years to establish. The proposed southern hedge would be small at installation and would not screen panels, fencing or inverter buildings in winter. Photomontages should distinguish existing vegetation from proposed planting, and should show the view at opening, not only at a notional mature stage. The viewpoints in the Draft Merefold Landscape Character Study (2024) provide a useful starting framework, but the application should also assess views along the public footpath at the edge of Hollowmere Wood. A single photograph from its entrance does not represent the changing view along the route. The conclusion of a ‘minor’ effect therefore appears premature.

Panel height is described differently in the design and landscape material. One drawing gives the top edge as 3.1 metres above ground level, while the visual assessment appears to rely on a lower profile. This matters where the ground rises across plot 12: a level or typical section will understate the apparent height from the footpath. The applicant should provide cross-sections on the actual surveyed levels, including fencing, CCTV poles, inverters and the access track. The same maximum dimensions should then be secured in the consent documents. Without that consistency, the photomontages cannot reliably describe the scheme that might be built.

The drainage strategy relies on the assertion that grass beneath the panels will maintain infiltration. It does not adequately test what happens during installation, when repeated vehicle movements may compact the soil before the permanent vegetation is established. Nor does it show how concentrated runoff at the lower panel edges has been addressed on the steeper parts of plot 12. Calculations should include the construction phase, an allowance for climate change, and an explicit sensitivity test for reduced infiltration. The proposed swales need dimensioned sections and a clearly identified exceedance route so that water does not simply leave the application site at its lowest boundary.

There is also an unresolved maintenance issue. The drainage drawings identify several shallow channels but give no practical account of how sediment will be removed, where access will be maintained, or who will inspect the channels during operation. The existing outfall toward Larkmere Brook should be surveyed before works begin and monitored after heavy rain, with a clear trigger for remedial work. It is not sufficient to say that these matters will be agreed in a later plan if the capacity and land required for maintenance have not yet been demonstrated. Merefold District Council and Dunrick Drainage Board should be able to review the same final set of drawings, rather than separate assumptions in separate documents.

Construction phasing is relevant to both drainage and visual impact. The indicative programme allows access tracks and compounds to be formed before the boundary planting, while the environmental measures assume planting will provide an early buffer. Those statements cannot both be relied upon without a more precise sequence. The programme should identify when topsoil will be stripped, how exposed ground will be stabilised, when drainage features will become operational, and how long each compound will remain in place. Temporary lighting, fencing and stockpiles should be shown on a plan for each phase, not left to a contractor to position later.

The ecological assessment records badger activity in Hollowmere Wood and bats in the wider landscape. Those general findings are useful, but they do not resolve whether the proposed night-time working restrictions can be enforced. The limits on lighting hours, direction and spill should be stated as measurable requirements and carried through to the construction documents. The assessment should also explain how the habitat management proposals will work alongside routine access for panel cleaning, vegetation cutting and drainage maintenance. A measure that looks suitable on an illustrative habitat plan may be lost if the same strip is needed as a vehicle route.

Finally, the proposed controls are scattered across the environmental statement, design drawings and outline management plans. A single commitments schedule should identify each measure, its drawing reference, the stage at which it must be in place, and the body responsible for checking it. Where an assessment depends on a particular delivery route, maximum structure height or drainage specification, that assumption must become an enforceable limit. My objection is not to the use of technical plans in principle; it is to leaving the evidence for fundamental design choices until after consent. The Examining Authority should require the revised information during this examination so its conclusions can be tested publicly.

I also object to the way the supply-chain question has been dealt with. In my view, Fenmere Helio Developments Limited has knowingly profited from forced labour in the supply chain for the Brindle Heath Solar Farm. This is a serious allegation, but the examination documents provide no panel procurement information that would allow residents to check where the modules will come from. The applicant should publish its proposed suppliers, the relevant audit arrangements and what happens if a supplier changes after consent. A general promise to comply with the law is not an answer to a question about what will actually be installed here.

There is wider public concern about manufacturing in Xinjiang. I am not saying that every panel made in China has the same history, and I do not have access to the applicant's purchasing contracts. That is precisely why the answer ought to be evidenced rather than left to a construction contractor at a later date. Likewise, the war in Ukraine has shown how quickly energy supply arguments can change. Supporting domestic renewable power does not mean every scheme, of any size and in any place, should be waved through. The applicant uses energy security as though it answers the separate questions of land use, design and sourcing. It does not.

The fields beside Brindle Lane are not an empty space on a drawing. They are worked fields with hedges, wet corners and a public path that people use to reach the village without walking on the carriageway. I have lived in this area for over 40 years and have seen water stand there after ordinary winter rain, not just after the exceptional storms referred to in the flood chapter. The proposed swales may help, but the drawings do not show how soil compacted by construction traffic will recover, or who checks the drainage when the site is operational. An annual inspection noted in an outline plan is too vague if the first problem is water running across the lane.

Joryn Malk, who lives at 7 Brindle Lane, Fenwick Mere FM4 7QL and is not making a representation, showed me photographs of muddy water at the bend last February. I mention this because the transport route puts heavy vehicles through that same bend. The photographs are not a technical flood study, and I am not asking the Examining Authority to treat them as one. They do, however, illustrate why a site-specific baseline matters. The applicant should be required to record pre-construction ditch levels and provide a named route for reporting blocked drains, with a timescale for clearing them. Otherwise residents will be passed between the highway authority, the landowner and a site manager.

At the public meeting Cllr Sera Bellwick asked whether the proposed passing places would remain available after the build. That was a fair question and, as I understood the answer, it was not settled. The construction traffic assessment counts vehicle movements but does not properly address what happens when a tractor meets a delivery lorry at the narrow section by the old gate. Asking drivers to be courteous is not a traffic management measure. The plan should identify which gates will be used, prohibit waiting on Brindle Lane and show where a vehicle can turn if an entrance is temporarily closed. Any route change should come back for public scrutiny rather than being agreed informally once consent has been given.

I am also concerned about the experience of using the footpath alongside the southern fields. The applicant's photomontages are taken from selected viewpoints, but a walker will be beside fencing for a much longer stretch than any single picture suggests. Planting is offered as the answer, although it will not screen the installation in its first winters. There is no clear drawing showing the height of the security fence, the finished ground levels and the proposed hedge together at the closest point to the path. Please ask for that drawing at a scale people can read. I feel anxious about losing the open view, but I recognise that a feeling is not itself evidence of a landscape effect.

Construction dust is a more practical concern for me. I have diagnosed asthma, and dry-weather movements along the access track could make it harder for me to use the path. The outline dust measures say that water may be used where needed; they do not say who decides when it is needed, or whether the path would be kept open during spraying and deliveries. I am 67, but I still walk that route most days. A short, enforceable method statement, including a way for residents to report a problem without putting personal details on a public noticeboard, would be much more useful than several pages saying impacts are expected to be minor.

The ecology material refers to badger activity in Merebank Wood and bats along the northern hedgerow. I am not asking for protected sites to be marked out in a public answer. My point is that the proposed lighting controls should cover temporary construction lighting as well as the permanent installation. The compound plan shows where the cabins are likely to stand, but not the direction of any security lights or how late they may remain on. If night work is genuinely exceptional, it should be defined as exceptional in the requirement, not simply described that way in the narrative. The same applies to hedge removal: the drawings and the programme must agree about what is retained.

For these reasons I ask the Examining Authority to request the outstanding drawings, a firmer traffic plan, drainage monitoring proposals and verifiable procurement information before closing the examination. If those matters are left to discharge after consent, the people who use Brindle Lane will not have a proper chance to test the answers. I am not objecting to solar generation as such. I am objecting to this application being treated as complete when too many of its important choices are still expressed as intentions. Please record my objection to the Brindle Heath Solar Farm as submitted.

Elin Tarrow
18 Merebank Close, Fenwick Mere FM4 7QP

Appendix A — Technical matters requiring clarification
Brindle Heath Solar Farm | Application reference TR010899

1. Construction traffic

The transport assessment gives a daily average for HGV movements, but an average does not show the busiest hour on Brindle Lane. Deliveries of frames, modules and aggregate are likely to bunch around the start of each working day. The assessment should provide an hourly profile for the busiest realistic construction week, showing arrivals and departures separately. That profile should then be tested against the existing peak-hour flows, not just against an all-day total. The figures in the traffic chapter and the outline construction programme also need reconciling: one assumes several work fronts can be active at once, while the other appears to spread deliveries across successive phases. Both cannot be the basis for the same peak forecast without an explanation.

The swept-path drawings show the design vehicle negotiating the junction of Brindle Lane and the B742, but they do not show what happens when a vehicle approaches from the opposite direction at the same time. A forward-visibility drawing, with the hedge in its proposed construction condition, would be more useful than a centreline measurement alone. The submitted tracking also appears to rely on an overrun of the verge at the inside of the bend. If that is intended to be temporary hardstanding, its dimensions, drainage treatment and removal date should be on a plan. If it is not intended, the tracking needs correcting. This is a drawing issue rather than something that can sensibly be settled by wording in a later traffic management plan.

The proposed booking system is welcome in principle. Its effectiveness depends on where an early vehicle can wait without blocking the carriageway, who checks compliance and what happens if two vehicles arrive despite their slots. A plan showing the holding area and the route back to the site would make that commitment testable. The project traffic mailbox, transport@brindleheathsolar.example, may be useful for reporting incidents, but an email address is not a substitute for a published procedure with response times and a record of corrective action. The Fenwick Mere Roads Authority should be consulted on the procedure before it is described as agreed.

2. Landscape and visual effects

The landscape chapter treats the new hedge as effective screening relatively early in the operating period. The photomontages, however, show it at a height that may take longer to establish, particularly where the proposed planting crosses exposed ground. Year-one and year-five views should be provided using stated hedge heights and an indicated failure rate. The assessment should also distinguish screening in leaf from winter views. Calling a view ‘filtered’ does not say how much of the panel surface or fencing remains visible through a newly planted hedge.

There is a further mismatch between the layout and the landscape schedule at the northern edge of Brindle Heath. The schedule describes retention of the existing field boundary, while the access drawing indicates a temporary gap for plant. The final set of plans should identify every retained, removed and reinstated length in the same way, including the width of any construction gap. Replacement planting is not equivalent to an established hedge during the construction period. That temporary effect belongs in the assessment, even if the hedge is eventually restored.

The viewpoint selection covers the longer public views reasonably well but says little about the approach along Brindle Lane, where the project would first appear between existing field boundaries. A short sequence of views along the road would explain this better than one photograph at a bend. It would also help to show the security fencing, inverters and access tracks consistently; the panels alone are not the entire development.

3. Surface water and ground conditions

The drainage strategy assumes that grass cover beneath and between the arrays will maintain infiltration. It does not set out how that assumption will be checked once construction traffic has crossed the fields. Compaction is most likely at access points, turning areas and repeated plant routes, precisely where runoff can become concentrated. The drainage plan should mark those routes, show where temporary ground protection is proposed and specify what testing will trigger remediation before the drainage works are signed off.

The outline strategy refers to swales and shallow basins, but the drawings do not consistently identify their outfalls. Each basin should have a labelled catchment, proposed exceedance route and maintenance access. The assessment should also test an event occurring while part of the site is stripped and the permanent vegetation is not yet established. Reliance on the completed scheme's grass cover does not address the construction phase. Any discharge to the Alder Rill should be presented together with the assumptions for sediment control; the receiving watercourse cannot simply be named as the end point of an arrow.

Monitoring should be practical rather than open-ended. A pre-construction baseline, inspections after substantial rainfall during earthworks, and a defined handover test for reinstated soil would allow the Fenwick Mere Drainage Board to assess whether the proposed measures are working. The results and any remedial work should be recorded in a format that can be checked against the approved plan. This request concerns the performance of the drainage design, not a request for another general commitment to good practice.

4. Ecology, phasing and policy

Badgers and bats are mentioned in the ecology chapter in broad terms. Those general references do not require precise wildlife locations to be put on public drawings. What is needed publicly is a clear timetable for survey updates, ecological supervision where clearance is proposed, and the point at which the construction team must stop and seek revised advice. The same timetable should be cross-checked against hedge removal and reinstatement on the landscape plans.

Finally, the planning statement relies on Policy EN4 of the Fenwick Mere Development Framework for its account of landscape change. Its conclusion should be revisited after the traffic, planting and drainage plans have been made consistent. The question is not whether renewable generation has benefits; it is whether the assessed design and the design that could actually be built are the same scheme. Conditions can secure detailed implementation, but they should not have to choose between conflicting drawings after the examination has ended.

Further representation on Brindle Heath Solar Farm

I am writing to object to the proposal as it stands. I support renewable electricity, and I understand why landowners and the applicant want a decision, but the remaining inconsistencies are not small matters to be sorted out once the machinery arrives. They affect what people will see from the lanes, how water will leave the site and whether construction traffic can use the roads safely. I ask the Examining Authority to require one coordinated set of plans before the examination closes, rather than leaving the local community to work out later which drawing was meant to apply.

The access note still describes the Brindle Lane bend as having adequate forward visibility. That does not match what happens when two agricultural vehicles meet there, let alone a delivery lorry and a car. My neighbour Joryn Malk, who lives near the bend and is not taking part in this examination, has had to reverse around it on several occasions. I mention this as a practical example, not as a traffic count. The applicant should provide swept-path drawings for the vehicles it actually intends to use, with the hedge in its proposed retained position. A drawing that assumes the hedge has been cut back while the landscape plan shows it staying is not an answer.

At the public meeting Cllr Sera Bellwick asked whether a temporary banksman would be present during the busiest delivery period. The reply seemed to be that this could be considered in the construction traffic plan. In my view that is too late if the safe operation of the access depends on it. Please put the proposed hours, maximum daily movements, passing arrangements and any banksman requirement in the examination record now. Residents also need to know whether deliveries will be routed past the school at the start of the day. I feel stressed about that prospect and have had poor sleep, but I am not asking the Examining Authority to treat my feelings as a substitute for proper highway evidence.

I have lived in this area for over 40 years and have watched water sit on the low part of Claypit Field after heavy rain. The drainage note refers to infiltration, while the latest layout shows a track running across the same shallow hollow. If that track is raised, water may be diverted towards gardens rather than held where it falls. The Fenwick Mere Drainage Board should be asked to comment on the revised levels, not just the earlier outline drawing. The Fenwick Mere Roads Authority should likewise be given the final access layout. My concern is with the proposal, not with either authority's staff.

There is also an ecology point which I do not want simply copied into an unrestricted drawing. During a walk I noted the sett opening in the bank 11 metres east of the southern gate to Claypit Field, beside marker post CF-7. That position ought to be passed to the examination team in a restricted annex for the ecologist to check. Elsewhere, I have seen badger activity in Alder Hollow Wood, but that is a broad description and should not be treated as a mapped sett. The applicant's surveys should explain how the final cable route and any temporary compounds avoid disturbance. Saying an ecologist will attend clearance is not the same as showing where work can safely happen.

I also want to raise the provenance of the panels. I allege that Fenmere Helio Developments Limited has used forced labour to supply panels for Brindle Heath Solar Farm. That is a serious concern and the applicant should be invited to publish the evidence it relies on for its procurement claims, including how it checks subcontractors. I am aware that there is public discussion about Xinjiang and forced labour in global manufacturing. That wider discussion does not establish the history of any particular shipment; the examination needs a clear and checkable account rather than a reassuring sentence in a policy document. The war in Ukraine has also made the value of domestic energy security much more obvious. Supporting that objective should not mean accepting an unexplained supply chain or overlooking the local impacts of this layout.

The construction programme is another example of details being presented separately when they need to be read together. If the western hedge is removed first, the temporary view from the houses will be quite different from the photomontage showing mature screening. If planting has to wait until the following season, say so, and show what temporary fencing will look like in the meantime. I have been diagnosed with chronic migraine, so repeated early vehicle movements close to my home would be particularly difficult for me. That personal point is additional to, not a replacement for, a sensible assessment of construction noise for everyone affected.

For completeness, the address I gave for correspondence is 14 Wrenfold Close, Fenwick Mere, FM4 6QP, and my reference is IP-083471. If a hearing date changes, I can be reached at elin.tarrow@homepost.example or 07700 954 218. Please do not publish those details in a version put online. I used the general planning@fenwickmere-roads.example mailbox for the highway query and have also read the examination guidance at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. An unrelated article at https://civic-lantern.example/solar-check was circulated locally, but I have not relied on it for the claims above.

I ask for the traffic, drainage, ecology, procurement and landscape documents to be reconciled before consent is considered. Conditions will be useful for carrying out an agreed scheme, but they should not be used to decide afterwards which version of the scheme was approved.

Elin Tarrow

Traffic, drainage and landscape matters

The construction traffic assessment for Brindle Heath Solar Farm needs to describe the same scheme as the construction programme and the draft traffic management plan. At present, the assessment appears to use an average daily delivery figure, while the programme shows several activities taking place at once: piling, cable trenching, inverter installation and the delivery of panel frames. An average may be useful for estimating total vehicle movements, but it does not establish what happens on the busiest day. The applicant should provide a week-by-week forecast of two-way HGV movements, with assumptions for loads per vehicle and any deliveries that cannot be rescheduled.

The proposed route uses Brindle Lane before reaching the site access. The swept-path drawing shows an articulated vehicle entering the access, but it does not clearly show the vehicle meeting an oncoming farm vehicle at the narrow bend or passing a vehicle waiting to turn. The drawing also appears to assume that the full carriageway is available. The verge is not a suitable substitute for carriageway width unless it is expressly designed, drained and maintained for that purpose. Fenwick Mere Roads Authority should be asked to confirm the vehicle type used in its review, not just whether the access geometry complies on a drawing.

The traffic management plan mentions banksmen and timed deliveries, but it does not say where a vehicle would wait if it arrived early or if the gate were closed. Waiting on Brindle Lane would obstruct through traffic. A holding area inside the site, available before the main construction deliveries begin, should be shown on a plan with capacity for the forecast peak. The plan should also set out a procedure for missed slots and for exceptional loads. These are practical matters that ought to be resolved before consent, rather than left as a general promise to agree details later.

There is also an inconsistency between the drainage figures and the construction phasing drawings. The drainage strategy describes grass cover beneath the panels as part of the long-term surface-water response. During trenching and track construction, however, bare ground and compacted temporary working areas will be present. The calculations should test that temporary condition separately. They should include the proposed compounds, haul routes and any stockpiles that could interrupt overland flow towards Wickfen Drain. A permanent scheme that performs adequately after planting does not, by itself, demonstrate that the construction period is acceptable.

The outfall arrangement requires particular care. The drawing marks a connection towards Wickfen Drain but gives no clear sequence for installing the outfall, protecting the channel and bringing attenuation into operation. It should not be assumed that temporary pumps or silt controls will remain effective without an inspection and maintenance regime. Fenwick Mere Drainage Board should be given a drawing showing the outfall levels, the proposed discharge control and access for maintenance after the solar farm becomes operational. That drawing should match the limits of land shown in the application plans.

The flood-risk material refers to a design storm and an allowance for climate change, but the exceedance route is difficult to follow across the different plans. If water exceeds the capacity of the swales, the application should show where it travels and whether any fencing, inverter bases or raised tracks divert it. This is especially important where tracks run across the natural fall of the land. The solution may be straightforward, such as additional cross-drainage, but it should be identified and assessed as part of the proposed development.

On landscape effects, the photomontages are helpful but they should be read alongside the seasonal planting assumptions. The visual assessment relies on hedgerow reinforcement along Larchmere Lane. Its conclusion for the early operational years appears to depend on growth that has not yet occurred. The applicant should provide a schedule stating planting heights at installation, the expected time before effective screening and the treatment of gaps if plants fail. Winter views should be addressed in the same way as summer views; a line on a landscape plan is not the same as an established hedge.

The proposed security fencing and battery compound also need to appear consistently in the visual material. Some viewpoint descriptions discuss the panels and planting but say little about the compound's taller equipment, lighting columns or service vehicles. If lighting is limited to occasional maintenance or security events, that limit should be secured in the requirements. Otherwise the assessment should examine the lighting that could actually be installed and used. The revised visualisations should use the same compound layout as the general arrangement plan.

The earthworks drawings indicate local regrading near the access and drainage features. The amount of soil moved, where it will be stored and whether it will be reused on site should be quantified. Bunds should not be described as temporary in one document and treated as permanent screening in another. Similarly, a construction track cannot be excluded from the landscape assessment if it remains for maintenance throughout operation. A single annotated plan distinguishing temporary and permanent works would make these effects much easier to understand.

Finally, the proposed requirements should refer to definite plans and measurable outcomes. A requirement to submit a later traffic plan cannot resolve an unresolved peak traffic figure; a later drainage design cannot choose a different discharge route without its effects being assessed; and later planting details cannot supply screening assumed in the visual conclusions from the first year. I ask that the applicant publish a coordinated set of revised drawings, calculations and phasing tables before the examination closes. That would allow the highways, drainage and landscape conclusions to be tested against one identifiable version of Brindle Heath Solar Farm.

I also object to the way the sourcing of the panels has been treated as a matter outside the examination. The land would be occupied for decades, and the public is entitled to understand the environmental and ethical consequences of the equipment chosen for it. I allege that Fenmere Helio Developments Limited uses forced labour in its solar-panel supply chain for Brindle Heath Solar Farm. I appreciate that this is a serious allegation, and I am not asking the Examining Authority to accept it simply because I have written it here. I ask instead for the applicant to identify the panel manufacturer, the origin of the polysilicon and the checks made on each stage of the supply chain, so that the claim can be properly tested. A statement that suppliers must comply with a policy is not evidence that they have done so.

There has been widespread public concern about labour conditions in Xinjiang. Equally, the war in Ukraine has shown how abruptly energy markets and supply routes can change. Neither point, on its own, proves anything about the particular panels proposed here. But they are reasons to require a transparent procurement plan before consent, not a promise to produce one after the contractor has been appointed. If the applicant intends to change suppliers during construction, the same checks should apply to the replacement equipment. The examination should not be left comparing a landscape scheme for one set of panels with a sourcing statement for another.

Turning to the local effects, the revised drawings still do not give a convincing picture of the view from Brindle Lane. The photomontage looks along the straight section, whereas drivers approaching the bend see the fencing and the northern edge of the array almost head on. Joryn Malk, who lives near that bend and is not taking part in the examination, asked me whether the new hedge would be outside the security fence or squeezed into the strip beside it. I could not answer from the plans. That is not a minor presentational point: a hedge planted too close to the fence will either fail to grow properly or require repeated cutting, leaving the panels visible for much longer than the assessment implies.

At the public meeting Cllr Sera Bellwick asked why the applicant's cross-section showed mature planting but the construction timetable allowed the access track to open before any planting was required. I thought that was a fair question. Please require a cross-section at the bend showing the existing ground level, fence, track, panel height and proposed planting at installation and at year five. The drawing should use the same levels as the drainage drawings. At present, one document appears to rely on a shallow roadside swale while another suggests a raised bund in roughly the same place. Both cannot occupy the full width shown.

I remain concerned about construction traffic. The average daily figure is not the figure residents will experience on the morning when deliveries coincide with school traffic and farm vehicles. The junction table in Transport Note TN-07 gives totals for a month but does not state the busiest expected hour or how many abnormal loads might arrive on the same day. A banksman at the site gate will not help if two lorries meet at the narrow culvert further down the lane. The applicant should provide the swept-path drawing for that culvert and a booking system with an enforceable maximum number of deliveries per hour. Complaints should be logged through a published contact route, not just passed to whichever subcontractor happens to be on site.

The ecological information needs similar care. Badgers have been recorded in Ashfold Wood, which is a broad area and not itself a reason to withhold the whole survey. However, the survey appendix places a badger sett in the eastern bank of the drainage ditch, 12 metres north of the Brindle Lane culvert beside field gate G4. That precise detail should not appear in a public version of the appendix. The Examining Authority can still consider a confidential plan when checking whether the proposed trenching and fence posts keep a suitable distance from the sett. Publishing a less detailed version would protect the animals without removing the evidence needed to assess the scheme.

Surface water is another point where a later management plan is being asked to do too much. The applicant says runoff will be controlled at the greenfield rate, but the calculation uses one discharge point while the layout shows two possible outfalls. Fenwick Mere Drainage Board should be given a single design to comment on, including the route by which water reaches its maintained drain and the arrangements for clearing silt after construction. I do not want the Board's ordinary maintenance access blocked by a fence or an area of replacement planting. If access is meant to be retained, it should be marked on the works plan and secured for the whole operating period.

I have lived in this area for over 40 years, and I know that does not make my recollection a substitute for measurements. It does explain why I am asking for the measurements now. The application has enough detail to show a substantial change to Brindle Heath, but not yet enough consistent detail to establish how its traffic, drainage and screening measures fit together. I ask the Examining Authority to require the applicant's answers and corrected plans during the examination, when residents and the relevant authorities can examine them, rather than leaving the difficult choices to be made after consent.

Yours faithfully,
Elin Tarrow
47 Thistledrift Close, Merefold, FM4 8QJ

Appendix A – Technical matters referred to in the objection
Brindle Heath Solar Farm

This note sets out the plan-based questions raised in the objection. It concerns the adequacy of the submitted assessment, not the principle of renewable generation. The matters are connected: the construction traffic estimate determines the access design, the access design affects roadside planting, and changes to planting and ground levels affect both views and surface-water routes. A requirement to submit separate details later would not, by itself, demonstrate that the scheme assessed now can be built without those conflicts.

1. Construction traffic and access

The Transport Assessment uses an average daily delivery figure, while the outline programme shows several activities occurring in the same phase: fencing, internal tracks, piling and electrical works. An average across the construction period is not the useful figure for Brindle Lane. The assessment should identify the busiest expected week and day, including the number of two-way heavy goods vehicle movements, staff vehicles and any abnormal loads. It should also state whether delivery figures include vehicles removing excavated material or bringing in aggregate for the tracks. If the intention is to balance material on site, a cut-and-fill schedule should be provided rather than treating that assumption as settled.

Drawing CT-04 shows the proposed access from Brindle Lane, but the swept-path drawing appears to use a different kerb line. The discrepancy is small on paper and potentially important for a vehicle meeting traffic at the bend. Fenwick Mere Roads Authority should be asked to confirm which drawing it has reviewed. The plans should show the full width of any temporary widening, where the widening ends, and how the verge would be reinstated. The applicant should also explain what happens if a delivery arrives when the holding area is occupied; a statement that drivers will be instructed not to wait on the highway does not provide a workable alternative.

The draft Construction Traffic Management Plan refers to an agreed delivery route through Merefold but does not fix the route or show how it would be enforced. A route plan, temporary sign schedule and arrangements for reporting a route breach should be examined before consent. These measures need to account for the overlap between peak delivery days and the proposed installation of the grid connection. It is not clear from the current documents whether the grid connection movements are included in the headline construction totals.

2. Landscape and views

The landscape drawings rely heavily on new hedges along the western and southern field boundaries. The visual assessment should distinguish between a hedge immediately after planting and one at its assumed design height. Several photomontages are labelled as summer views, when the existing vegetation provides its greatest screening. Corresponding winter views would make the extent of change easier to assess, particularly where fencing and inverter compounds would sit above the hedge line. This is a request for consistent visual evidence, not an assumption that planting can never provide screening.

There is also a practical question about the maintenance strip shown between the panels and boundary planting. In places the strip seems narrower than the width required for access to the drainage features. If plant has to cross newly planted areas to clear a ditch, the screening shown at maturity may not be achievable. The applicant should provide a single dimensioned plan showing panels, security fencing, hedges, ditches and maintenance access together. Separate plans at different scales make it difficult to see whether all five elements fit.

The Landscape and Ecological Management Plan mentions replacement planting after failures but gives no clear test for when a gap becomes a failed section of hedge. It should specify the inspection frequency, replacement season and minimum stocking level, with an enforceable period extending beyond initial establishment. References to badgers in Brindle Heath Wood and to bats along the wider hedgerow network are useful context; they do not resolve the layout question at the development boundary. The proposed lighting controls should cover temporary construction compounds as well as permanent equipment.

3. Drainage and ground conditions

The drainage strategy proposes shallow swales and infiltration in part of the site, but the infiltration results are presented without a plan tying every test pit to the particular feature it is intended to support. Fenwick Mere Drainage Board should be given a schedule matching each feature to its contributing area, test result, design event and proposed exceedance route. A general statement that runoff will remain within the red line is insufficient if the low points on the grading plan do not coincide with the indicated storage areas.

The cross-sections should also show what happens at the track crossings. A swale cannot function as drawn if a compacted access track interrupts its fall and the culvert location is left to the contractor. The construction-phase drainage drawing is especially important: soil stripping and temporary stockpiles may change the direction of runoff before the permanent swales are available. The outline measures refer to silt fencing, but they do not show the sequence for installing temporary storage relative to the first earthworks. That sequence should form part of the assessed construction method.

4. Phasing and controls

The works plan divides the site into broad construction areas, while the programme groups activities by task. A combined phasing drawing would clarify which access, drainage and screening measures must be in place before work begins in each area. The draft requirements should then refer to that drawing and set objective approval points. Phrases such as ‘where practicable’ and ‘as necessary’ are difficult to apply where a feature is relied upon in the environmental assessment.

The National Policy Statement for Renewable Energy Infrastructure supports renewable energy development, but it also calls for impacts to be assessed and mitigated on a sound evidential basis. The request here is for revised drawings, peak-period figures and linked management measures during the examination. If those documents show the layout works, they would narrow the disagreement. If they show that one measure displaces another, the resulting change ought to be assessed openly before the final decision.

The remaining concern is that the traffic, drainage and landscape documents do not appear to use the same construction sequence. For Brindle Heath Solar Farm, this matters because the temporary access works, cable trenching and installation of the perimeter bund are shown in overlapping periods. A measure cannot be counted as mitigation during a month in which it has not yet been built.

The Construction Traffic Management Plan assumes a daily average of 46 two-way HGV movements in its busiest phase. The Transport Assessment, however, tests the Brindle Lane/Mereford Road junction using 32 movements. It is not clear whether the higher figure includes deliveries for the battery compound or whether those deliveries have been placed in a separate phase. An average is also insufficient for the narrow section of Brindle Lane: deliveries may arrive together when a crew or crane is booked for a particular day. A day-by-day programme for the busiest six weeks, with the vehicle assumptions reconciled across both documents, would be more useful than another statement that arrivals will be managed.

The swept-path drawing shows a vehicle entering from Mereford Road while another vehicle waits clear of the junction. It does not show where that second vehicle would wait when the temporary haul road is occupied by vehicles leaving the site. Nor does it test a breakdown on the single-track length. The proposed banksman arrangement may help at the gate, but it cannot create passing space farther along Brindle Lane. Fenwick Mere Roads Authority should be asked to confirm whether the junction model and swept-path test use the same vehicle dimensions and the same peak-hour assumptions. That is a technical check, not a request for a general endorsement of the scheme.

Drainage needs the same cross-check. Drawing DR-14 places an infiltration strip beside the eastern panel rows. The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment shows that strip as part of a planted buffer, while the Construction Environmental Management Plan identifies it as a possible area for temporary storage. Storage would compact the ground before the strip is expected to function. The applicant should provide one marked-up construction drawing which prohibits storage on the infiltration area and identifies the point at which it becomes operational. Fenwick Mere Drainage Board should also be given the revised runoff calculations, including the assumptions for compacted construction surfaces and the period before vegetation establishes.

The flood-risk figures compare pre-development and operational runoff, but the construction period is neither of those conditions. Exposed soil, temporary tracks and stockpiles may all alter the route by which water reaches the western ditch. The proposed silt fencing is described only in general terms. A drawing showing the drainage catchments for each phase, together with inspection and maintenance triggers after heavy rain, would make the commitment capable of being checked. No additional discharge to the ditch should be assumed acceptable merely because the final scheme is described as permeable.

There is a similar timing issue with visual screening. Viewpoint 7, taken from the public path near Alderwash Wood, is assessed on the basis of a planted boundary that will take time to establish. The photomontage illustrates a later year, not the first winter when the panel frames and compound fencing are likely to be most apparent. A first-year winter image from the same viewpoint should be supplied, with the proposed bund height and planting height stated separately. Existing vegetation should not be counted twice as both retained screening and new mitigation.

The ecology material mentions badger activity in Alderwash Wood and general bat use along field boundaries. Those are reasons to keep the proposed dark corridor and boundary planting continuous; they do not, by themselves, demonstrate that the corridor shown on the layout will remain unobstructed by security fencing or drainage works. A single constraints plan could show the required widths without publishing any precise protected-species locations.

Fenwick Mere Local Plan Policy EN7 and the National Policy Statement for Renewable Energy Infrastructure do not require every effect to be eliminated. They do require the decision-maker to understand the effect being accepted. The present documents leave avoidable uncertainty about the busiest construction days, the temporary drainage condition and the unscreened first-year view. Revised, mutually consistent plans should be examined before those effects are treated as adequately mitigated.

There is also a procurement question which the revised plans cannot answer. I believe Fenmere Helio Developments Limited has knowingly used forced labour in its panel supply chain for Brindle Heath Solar Farm. The applicant should publish an auditable account of where the panels and their components will come from before consent is granted. Xinjiang is often raised in discussions about solar supply chains, but a place name alone does not establish the origin of these particular panels. The war in Ukraine has also shown why energy security matters; that does not excuse leaving procurement questions unanswered.

At the public meeting Cllr Sera Bellwick asked whether any supplier checks would be independently verified. I could not find an answer in the examination documents. Joryn Malk, who lives near the Brindle Lane bend and is not taking part in this examination, also worries about the construction traffic. I feel anxious about the proposal, but my objection is to the gaps in the evidence, not to renewable energy in principle.

Elin Tarrow

text:
To the Examining Authority
Brackenmere Fields Solar Project
Written representation — objection
Application reference: BFSP-2026-04
IP reference: IP-482731

From: Rowan Venn
17 Cinder Lane, Low Sedge, FM4 8QP
Email: rowan.venn@homepost.example

I object to the proposed Brackenmere Fields Solar Project. I live beside the eastern approach to the site, and my objection is not to renewable energy in principle. It is to the scale of this particular scheme, its effect on the lanes and fields around Low Sedge, and the gaps in the information the applicant has provided. Several of the mitigation measures sound reasonable until you try to work out who will carry them out and when. I ask the Examining Authority to consider the combined effect on residents rather than treating each impact as a separate, minor matter.

The construction traffic assessment relies heavily on vehicles using the Asterby Link Road before turning into Mill Drove. That does not reflect how the junction works at school times. A lorry waiting to turn occupies most of the available width, and vehicles coming the other way mount the verge. The proposed banksman is shown only at the site entrance, not at the bend by the cottages. The applicant should be required to submit a revised route assessment based on observed conditions during the morning and afternoon peaks, with a clear procedure for stopping deliveries when the route is blocked. Saying drivers will be reminded to take care is not a traffic management plan.

My son Felix Venn, aged 11, has diagnosed asthma. Dust from the haul route is therefore a particular concern for our household, especially if the temporary surface breaks up in dry weather. I am not claiming every passing vehicle will cause a medical emergency. I am asking for enforceable limits on vehicle speeds, wheel washing that is actually monitored, and a named point of contact who can arrange an immediate inspection when dust reaches homes. The outline plan says complaints will be reviewed in due course; that is too vague for something happening outside a kitchen window on the day.

There is also a question about the panels themselves. I allege that Brackenmere Solar Developments Limited knowingly relies on forced labour in the panel supply chain for the Brackenmere Fields Solar Project. This is a serious concern and the applicant should provide independently checkable information on the source of the panels and their main components, rather than a general assurance about procurement policy. Xinjiang is often discussed in connection with supply-chain risks, but mentioning a place is not evidence about any particular shipment. Equally, the war in Ukraine has shown how quickly international purchasing arrangements can change. A condition which checks only the supplier named at consent would be of little use if the order is later moved.

The landscape drawings also understate what will be visible from Mill Drove. They show planting at a mature height, although for the first years it will be low enough to see straight over. From my upstairs window the view would be of fencing, tracks and rows of panels across what is now an open field. I have lived in Low Sedge for over 40 years and know that the hedges grow unevenly on this exposed ground. I feel anxious about the change, but I recognise that feeling anxious is not, by itself, a planning test. A realistic year-one visualisation and a funded replacement-planting obligation would make the evidence more useful.

The ecological material needs the same practical approach. Badgers have been seen near Tallow Copse; that is a broad observation, not a mapped sett. During a walk with the landowner's permission, however, I recorded a badger sett in the ditch 12 metres east of gate G4 on the southern edge of Field 7. I have not put a sketch of that spot on the public noticeboard because it could draw attention to it. The detailed fencing design should be checked by the project ecologist before groundworks, including whether animals will still be able to move between the remaining hedgerows. I do not object to the proposed habitat improvements, only to counting them as benefits before their delivery is secured.

I spoke with Mrs Elva Sorn at 6 Sedge Bank, Low Sedge, FM4 8QR about the drainage ditch after the September rain; she is not making a representation and I do not speak for her. The water had overtopped near the culvert, while the submitted plan marks the ditch as having spare capacity. That difference should be investigated on site. Cllr Maren Pell raised the same drainage question at the Low Sedge community meeting on 8 October 2026, but no revised drawing has been circulated as far as I can see. The meeting note can be requested from planning@lowsedgecouncil.example.

I also ask that the promised community fund is kept out of the assessment of harm unless its purpose and administration are specified. It cannot compensate for an unsafe junction or a drainage design that does not work. The applicant's published construction budget may be relevant to whether the proposed measures are deliverable, but residents should not have to guess which measures are funded. The examination should seek a table setting out each commitment, its trigger, the responsible party and the means of enforcement. For reference, the government's general NSIP guidance is at https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/nationally-significant-infrastructure-projects. A separate discussion of panel purchasing appeared at https://fenmere-ledger.example/report/panels; I include that link only to explain why I asked the supply-chain question, not as proof of my allegation.

I would welcome renewable generation on a properly assessed site. As submitted, this proposal leaves too much to later agreement, when those affected will have less opportunity to question it. Please require the further traffic, drainage, landscape, ecology and procurement evidence before reaching a conclusion. If consent is nevertheless recommended, the controls need to be precise enough for residents and the local authority to tell whether the applicant is complying. I would appreciate confirmation that this representation has been received.

Rowan Venn

Supplementary technical points — Low Sedge Solar Park
Application reference: FM-NSIP-2046-017

The points below concern the adequacy of the submitted assessment and the wording of any requirements. They do not depend on the choice of panel manufacturer. I refer to the current layout as Layout 4B, although the Environmental Statement sometimes calls the same drawing the ‘maximum parameters layout’. That difference needs clearing up: a change in label should not allow a later design to occupy land that was not assessed.

Traffic and access

The construction traffic assessment gives daily two-way HGV totals but not the peak hourly movements for each phase. That matters at the Fenmere Lane/Bramble Cut junction, where a delivery vehicle waiting to turn can prevent other traffic passing. The model uses an average construction day. It should also test the weeks when mounting frames, transformers and aggregate arrive together, with the workforce vehicles included. The swept-path drawing shows a single articulated lorry entering the site in isolation; it does not show a vehicle meeting another at the narrow bridge or the recovery movement if an access gate is shut.

The proposed Construction Traffic Management Plan is largely a list of matters to be settled later. Before determination, the applicant should identify the haul route from the strategic road network, the number and capacity of any passing places, and whether loads would be prohibited during the school arrival and departure periods. A requirement that merely calls for a plan to be approved would leave the basic feasibility of the route unresolved. The assessment should also state whether the temporary access at Field 12 is included in the order limits and who would maintain its drainage during construction. The project mailbox, solarcase@fenmerevale.example, can receive revised drawings, but putting a drawing online is not a substitute for assessing its effects.

Landscape and visual effects

The photomontages appear to assume that the northern hedge has reached the proposed mature height. Existing gaps are visible on the ground and on the submitted baseline photographs. An additional winter view should show the arrays, perimeter fencing and inverter cabins before replacement planting has established. The assessment describes these items separately, although they would be seen together from the Bracken Hollow footpath. It should assess their combined horizontal extent, not just whether each individual structure is below the skyline.

The suggested hedge mix is welcome, but the stated five-year establishment period does not explain what happens if a section fails in year four. A measurable replacement obligation, followed by a further establishment period for replacement plants, would be more useful than a general promise to maintain screening. There should also be a maximum height and finish for the battery compound fencing. The mitigation drawing currently shows a dark colour without specifying a finish or stating whether security lighting is included in the night-time visual assessment.

Drainage and flood risk

The flood-risk report treats the area beneath panels as grassland with unchanged runoff characteristics. That may be reasonable after establishment, but the first winter of construction is different: stripped haul routes, compacted assembly areas and stockpiles can direct water across a field even if the completed scheme does not add much impermeable surface. The applicant should provide temporary drainage drawings for each phase, including the locations and capacities of settlement measures, rather than leaving these to the principal contractor. The drawings should demonstrate where exceedance flows go when a temporary feature is blocked.

The proposed outfall to the East Rill is described as ‘subject to agreement’ with the South Mere Drainage Board. That phrase is not evidence that the outfall level, receiving capacity or maintenance access are workable. The board’s published channel-maintenance strip should be shown on the general arrangement plan, with panels, fencing and planting kept outside it. There is also an inconsistency between the drainage schedule’s 1-in-100-year plus climate allowance and the lower allowance shown on the attenuation sketch. One set of calculations and an identified design standard are needed before any conclusion about residual risk can be reached.

Ecology and land management

Badger setts have been recorded in Bracken Hollow Wood, and bats use the wider East Rill corridor. These are broad descriptions, not locations from which any particular feature could be found. The ecological assessment should explain how survey results have informed the order limits and the construction programme, without placing sensitive feature coordinates in a publicly accessible management plan. It should specify who checks fencing and lighting before works begin, the action required if a protected species is encountered, and how a change to the working area would be assessed. ‘Toolbox talks as necessary’ is too imprecise to be an enforceable measure.

The biodiversity net gain calculation relies on creating species-rich grassland beneath the arrays. Shading, the spacing of panel rows and the proposed cutting regime need to be reflected in the habitat condition assumptions. The outline landscape and ecological management plan promises monitoring, but does not identify a threshold that would trigger remedial action or say how long the replacement habitat would then be monitored. Those details affect whether the claimed gain is deliverable, rather than being minor matters of presentation.

Controls requested

The examination should require a reconciled drawing register and phase-specific traffic and drainage information. If the scheme proceeds, the certified plans should set enforceable limits for construction movements, lighting, fencing and land-take. Any later approval process should be confined to details within those assessed limits. Fenmere Vale Council should be given the drawings and monitoring reports in a form it can check against the consent, with a clear procedure for correcting a breach. Those are practical controls on the proposal, not an objection to solar generation in principle.
