Further technical grounds of objection

The objection also rests on the way the construction effects have been assessed. The traffic, landscape and drainage documents appear to use different assumptions about when the various parts of the Low Sedge Solar Project would be built. That matters because a shorter programme with more activities happening at once can have quite different effects from a longer programme in which each field is completed in turn. The applicant should provide one construction programme that is used consistently across those assessments, not three separate illustrative timetables.

Construction traffic

The transport assessment relies on an average number of daily vehicle movements. An average conceals the likely peaks during panel deliveries, formation of the access tracks and removal of excavated material. Drawing AS-TR-014 Rev C shows a construction entrance from Cinder Bank Lane, but the swept-path drawing appears to test a single articulated vehicle in an otherwise empty carriageway. It does not test a delivery vehicle meeting a farm vehicle, nor does it show where either could wait without blocking the road. Marsh Drove is described as an alternative route in the construction narrative, although no equivalent junction assessment is supplied for it.

The applicant should provide hourly arrival profiles for the busiest construction weeks, with separate figures for heavy goods vehicles, light vans and staff vehicles. The assessment should identify whether deliveries would be booked into fixed slots and what would happen if a slot were missed. A promise that vehicles would not queue on the highway is not, by itself, a method of preventing queues. The Construction Traffic Management Plan should specify a holding location, a means of communicating with drivers before they reach the rural road network, and a procedure for turning away an early vehicle. It should also make clear whether the proposed restriction at Brettle Junction applies to all construction traffic or only to vehicles above a stated weight.

Landscape and visual effects

The landscape assessment gives substantial weight to new boundary planting. Its photomontages show the proposed hedge after establishment, while the conclusions about construction effects rely partly on that same screening. New planting cannot screen deliveries or earthworks before it has grown. The applicant should show the construction view, the first operational year and the established-planting view separately, using the same camera position and field of view. A table explaining which hedges are retained, gapped up or entirely new would make the assessment easier to check.

The proposed fencing is also treated inconsistently. On one drawing it follows existing field boundaries; on another it cuts across an open field to accommodate a maintenance route. That change may be small in plan view but important when seen against the skyline from Old Sedge Lane. The landscape assessment should test the final fence alignment, the maximum panel height and the proposed inverter enclosures together. It should not assume that a line of planting outside the order limits will be available for mitigation unless its delivery and maintenance can be secured.

Drainage and construction phasing

Drawing AS-DR-022 Rev B identifies permanent swales but provides little detail about temporary runoff control before those swales are connected. The drainage strategy says existing runoff routes will be maintained. It does not demonstrate how this would be achieved while tracks are compacted, cable trenches are open and stockpiles occupy the lower parts of the fields. North Fen Drain receives flows from more than one part of the site, so a field-by-field calculation alone may miss the combined effect of simultaneous works.

A construction-stage drainage plan is needed for each phase. It should identify temporary settlement measures, inspection frequency, responsibility for clearing them and the point at which permanent features become operational. The applicant should model a storm occurring when exposed ground is at its greatest extent, rather than assuming every field is already grassed. Fenmere Drainage Board should be given the opportunity to comment on the discharge assumptions and on access for future maintenance. That is a technical request, not a suggestion that the Board has approved or opposed the scheme.

The soil handling plan needs the same phasing information. Its limits on working in wet conditions are sensible in principle, but the programme does not allow any time for weather-related stoppages. If a paused operation leaves a trench or stripped area open, the drainage controls must still work. The plan should state when temporary tracks would be removed, how compacted ground would be reinstated, and what measurable condition would trigger further remediation. Saying that land will be restored to its previous condition is not a test that can be applied on site.

Ecology and policy

The ecological material refers generally to bats using Mereglass Wood and to badger activity in the wider survey area. Those broad descriptions are sufficient for a public account of the issues; an exact protected-species location is not needed to understand this objection. The technical question is whether lighting, fencing and the construction timetable have been assessed together. In particular, temporary lighting for winter work should be included in the same assessment as permanent security lighting. A condition requiring a later lighting plan would not resolve a design conflict that is already apparent.

Fenmere Vale Local Plan Policy LV7 requires landscape effects to be addressed through the layout as well as through mitigation planting. The current documents do not show clearly which changes to the layout were made in response to the identified views. The applicant should provide a short design-evolution schedule that links each material layout change to the effect it is intended to reduce. That would let the examination distinguish an avoided impact from one merely described as capable of being screened later.

For these reasons, the traffic, drainage and landscape conclusions should not be treated as settled. The missing information could change the assessed peak effects and, potentially, the layout or construction method. It should be submitted in a coordinated revision, with a clear list of superseded drawings and enough time for technical review.

Further comments on the technical evidence

The coordinated revision requested above should start with a single construction programme. At present, the Construction Traffic Management Plan appears to assume that the eastern compound will be available before the internal haul road is complete, while the drainage drawings show temporary attenuation occupying part of the same area. Both assumptions may be reasonable in isolation, but they cannot operate at the same time without a different access arrangement. A month-by-month programme, tied to drawing revisions, would make that conflict testable. It should identify when each compound, crossing and temporary drainage feature is installed and removed, rather than relying on a general statement that works will be phased.

Traffic and access

The Transport Assessment treats deliveries to the panel fields as relatively even across the construction period. That does not follow from the proposed sequence of earthworks, fencing and electrical installation. If the northern fields are prepared together, HGV arrivals could be concentrated at the Moor Drove access for several weeks. The assessment should give the maximum daily movements for each access, including abnormal loads, concrete deliveries, workforce vehicles and vehicles removing spoil. A daily average over the whole construction period is not a substitute for a peak-day test.

The junction capacity exercise also needs to use a consistent baseline. The turning counts in Table 6.4 were taken on an ordinary weekday, whereas the route description refers to seasonal movements serving other land uses along Moor Drove. The applicant should explain whether those movements were captured, excluded or represented in a sensitivity test. This is not a request to assume the worst possible traffic on every day. It is a request to show what happens when a plausible seasonal background coincides with the busiest construction phase. The same scenario should be used in the highway safety and noise assessments, so that their conclusions can be compared.

Swept-path drawings for the temporary access show vehicles entering and leaving in forward gear, but the usable carriageway width on Fenmere Lane is not labelled between the proposed passing places. The drawings should show the actual swept envelope, verge overrun and visibility available when opposing vehicles meet. Passing places need their own construction detail and a reinstatement requirement. A commitment to agree their precise position later would leave the examination unable to assess whether the route is workable without additional land or vegetation removal.

Drainage and ground conditions

The Flood Risk Assessment relies on maintaining existing runoff rates, but the proposed land management will alter how water moves across the surface. Panel drip lines, compacted maintenance tracks and the cable trenches all warrant consideration in the infiltration assumptions. The drainage strategy should distinguish the temporary construction condition from the completed scheme: exposed soil and stored materials create different risks from established grass cover. It should also state the rainfall event, climate-change allowance and blockage assumption used for each outfall calculation.

The drawings show attenuation beside the West Mere Cut, with discharge indicated through an existing field connection. The connection's condition and capacity are not established in the submitted material. Before that discharge is relied upon, the applicant should provide a survey of the connection and confirmation of the permissible rate, together with an alternative if the connection cannot be used. Fenmere Drainage Board should have the opportunity to review the revised calculations. The board's involvement would not, by itself, resolve an unexplained difference between the levels on the drainage plan and the levels used in the hydraulic model.

There is a related construction issue at the proposed cable crossing. The method statement refers to a trenchless installation, while the environmental plans retain space for an open-cut working area. Those are materially different operations near a watercourse. The application should either assess both or commit to one method, specifying the working width, dewatering arrangements and reinstatement standard. A later method statement can add detail, but it should not be used to choose between effects that have not been examined.

Landscape and design

The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment assesses planting at establishment and at a later mature stage. However, several photomontages use a proposed hedgerow height without explaining when that height is expected to be reached. The baseline photograph, the unmitigated view and each mitigated year should be clearly labelled. Where planting is the principal reason for reducing an assessed effect, the planting specification, maintenance period and replacement obligations should be secured in terms capable of enforcement.

The western edge of the array remains particularly difficult to understand because the parameter plan allows equipment to move within a broad zone. The maximum height of panels, inverters and security infrastructure should be assessed together in the most exposed permitted position. Otherwise the illustrated layout may appear less intrusive than the layout that the development consent would actually authorise. A defined setback from the West Mere Cut could also serve drainage maintenance and landscape purposes; if it is proposed as mitigation, its width should be fixed on the controlling plan.

Policy and examination documents

The Planning Statement cites NPS EN-1 and NPS EN-3 in support of the need for renewable generation. That need does not remove the requirement to assess local effects using a consistent scheme description. The National Planning Policy Framework discussion is similarly brief on whether avoidable impacts have first been addressed through design. A revised policy schedule should identify the evidence relied upon for each relevant provision and distinguish matters resolved by the design from matters left to later approval.

Finally, the application documents need one consolidated drawing register. References to Layout Plan Rev C remain in some reports, while other documents assess Layout Plan Rev D. The applicant should mark each superseded figure, explain any change to the maximum design parameters and provide a short comparison of resulting effects. Without that reconciliation, the Examining Authority and technical consultees are being asked to reach conclusions on different versions of the scheme. My objection on these technical grounds remains until a coordinated set of evidence can be tested.

Further to the drawing-register point above, I ask that the technical assessments be checked against one defined version of the project before any conclusion is reached on its effects. This is not simply an administrative matter. A change in the position of an access, inverter station or drainage basin can alter the assumptions used in several reports at once. The applicant should identify which drawings constitute the assessed scheme and provide a table showing where each change between Layout Plan Rev C and Layout Plan Rev D has been taken into account.

The transport assessment is a particular concern. Its junction calculations use an hourly construction-vehicle profile, but the Construction Traffic Management Plan discusses deliveries by day rather than by hour. It is therefore unclear whether the model includes simultaneous deliveries of panels, aggregate and transformer equipment during the busiest phase. The swept-path figures for the Briarfen Lane access show the largest delivery vehicle entering on an apparently clear carriageway; they do not show how a vehicle would pass a waiting outbound lorry or how traffic would be managed if a delivery arrives outside its booked slot. A revised assessment should test the peak hour arising from the actual programme, state the assumed vehicle types and set out the arrangements for turning vehicles away without reversing onto the highway.

The proposed routing also depends on the condition of the narrow section between Low Sedge and the western site entrance. The application says that banksmen and temporary signs can address the constraint, yet neither measure increases the available road width. Before those measures are accepted, the applicant should provide a dimensioned passing-place plan, the anticipated number of escorted movements and a method for recording damage to verges and drainage grips. Fenmere Vale Council should be able to comment on that information as highway authority. This is a request for evidence about the route, not an assertion that every construction vehicle will cause damage.

For landscape and visual effects, the photomontages are useful but do not resolve the mismatch between the planting shown on the illustrative views and the planting specified in the landscape schedule. Several views appear to assume a continuous hedge at an established height. The schedule instead allows gaps at gateways and says that replacement planting will be agreed after construction. The assessment should distinguish the appearance at first installation from the appearance once planting is established, using the same fence, panel and vegetation heights as the parameter plans. It should also explain how screening is to be maintained where easements restrict tree planting. An assessment based solely on a mature landscape would understate the effects during the early operational years.

The drainage strategy requires similar reconciliation. It describes infiltration as the preferred approach while the outline drainage plan shows attenuation with a controlled discharge. The choice matters because the two approaches have different consequences for exceedance flows, maintenance and the location of infrastructure. The applicant should publish the ground-test results relied upon, identify the design storm and climate-change allowance used for each basin, and show overland flow routes if an outlet becomes blocked. Fenmere Drainage Board should be asked to review the proposed discharge points and maintenance access. A condition requiring a later detailed design is not a substitute for establishing now whether the space and levels needed for that design are available within the order limits.

Construction phasing also needs to be expressed consistently. The environmental statement assumes that soil stripping, access construction and cable installation will occur in separate areas, but the indicative programme shows overlap without identifying the maximum area of exposed ground. A phase plan should specify the extent of temporary compounds, stockpiles and disturbed soil for each stage. It should link those stages to the erosion controls and to the traffic figures, so that the assessed worst case is recognisable across disciplines. General references to adaptive management do not demonstrate what will happen if heavy rainfall interrupts the planned sequence.

I ask the Examining Authority to seek a coordinated revision of these documents, rather than separate assurances in responses to individual questions. The outstanding issues are capable of being tested, but only if the applicant supplies consistent parameters, calculations and drawings in time for technical consultees to review them. Until then, the claimed residual effects of the scheme remain insufficiently evidenced.

I object to the proposed solar farm. The coordinated revision requested above must also explain where the panels will come from and how the applicant has checked its supply chain. I allege that Aster Fell Solar Infrastructure Limited has used forced labour in the supply chain for this solar farm. That is a serious concern and I ask the Examining Authority to require evidence, not just a general assurance. There are well-known concerns about labour practices in Xinjiang. The war in Ukraine is another reason to be clear about the origin and security of imported equipment; neither issue is answered by the drainage documents.

Closer to home, Felix Venn, my 11-year-old son, uses the path beside the proposed construction access. Mrs Elva Sorn also walks there but is not taking part in this examination. Cllr Maren Pell's drainage question still needs a proper answer. I feel anxious about the traffic and runoff, particularly after heavy rain. Please do not approve the scheme on the basis of documents that do not agree with each other.

Rowan Venn
